10550-a-select-collection-of-old-english:
W. Carew Hazlitt edited this ninth volume of Dodsley's old English plays, in the fourth edition of 1874 to 1876. Dodsley first issued the collection in 1744; Hazlitt arranged it by date, revised it, and added notes from all commentators. The volume serves students of Tudor and Stuart drama.

How a Man May Choose a Good Wife from a Bad, The Return from Parnassus, Wily Beguiled, Lingua, and The Miseries of Enforced Marriage make up the set. The first comedy, acted by the Earl of Worcester's servants and printed in 1602, is praised for broad, merry humor. Readers get rare early plays with full scholarly notes.
10956-indian-speeches-1907-1909:
Viscount Morley, Secretary of State for India, collected his speeches on Indian government from 1907 to 1909 in this volume. The speeches cover the Indian budget, the civil service, proposed reforms, and relations between Hindus and Muslims, delivered in the Commons, the Lords, at Arbroath, and at Oxford. Three older state papers, from 1833, 1858, and 1908, are appended.

Morley argues for gradual reform within British rule, with elected Indian members gaining a larger voice in councils. He rejects the claim that kindness is always read as fear in the East, and he defends his reforms as just, prudent, and necessary. The book is a key source for the Morley-Minto reforms and for how London debated India's future before the First World War.
14467-the-fine-lady-s-airs-1709:
Thomas Baker's comedy of 1709, reprinted by the Augustan Reprint Society in 1950 with an introduction by John Harrington Smith, satirizes fashionable London ladies and their admirers. The play was staged at Drury Lane.

Lady Toss-up and her circle trade gossip, scheme over suitors, and declare against marriage while courting attention, as country squires and town beaux blunder through their plots. Baker's dialogue is brisk and arch, full of period slang. The reprint gives modern readers a lively sample of early eighteenth-century comic theater, annotated for study. Baker wrote several comedies, but this one stayed his best known.
16275-some-account-of-the-life-of-mr-wil:
This 1948 Ann Arbor reprint presents the Rowe-Tonson edition of Shakespeare's plays from 1709 and its importance for Shakespeare studies. Based substantially on the Fourth Folio of 1685, Rowe's edition was the first truly edited edition. He modernized spelling and punctuation and made sensible emendations. He added dramatis personae, divided plays systematically into acts and scenes, and gave scenes distinct locations. It was also the first illustrated edition in a handy format.

Rowe's volume first brought the plays within reach of average readers' understanding and pocketbooks, and first included an extended life and critique of Shakespeare. Scholars from Pope onward have debated Rowe's text ever since. The file offers students a window on how modern Shakespeare editing began.
2109-history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-:
Carlyle follows Frederick through the last stage of his apprenticeship at Ruppin, from 1732 to 1736, after the catastrophe that nearly cost him his head. The new question is whom the crown prince shall marry. Ruppin gave Frederick a regiment to command and a wife chosen for politics, not love.

Princess Elizabeth Christina of Brunswick-Bevern enters the story, and debates in the royal family and the Tobacco-Parliament run long. Carlyle shows Frederick learning obedience in visible things, especially command of the Goltz regiment. His obedience in outward things masked a private mind that was already forming its own views.
22059-balthasar-and-other-works-1909:
Anatole France, the great French man of letters, wrote the tales gathered in Balthasar and Other Works. Mrs. John Lane's English translation appeared in 1909. The title story concerns Balthasar, one of the three wise men of the Christmas story. France presents him as a king in Ethiopia, learned in the stars.

Other pieces include The Curé's Mignonette, The Daughter of Lilith, and The Red Egg. France treats saints, devils, and scholars with the same gentle irony. His prose is smooth, his learning worn lightly, and his sympathy always with the weak. These short works show the humane wit that later won him the Nobel Prize.
23694-homo-1909:
F. Hopkinson Smith published Homo in 1909, a short novel or long story of Parisian society life. It opens after dinner in Mme. Constantin's cozy salon. Guests settle with coffee and cigarettes, pillows adjusted and lounges drawn near the fire, while old Baron Sleyde rattles on about a duel of unusual ferocity that has startled Paris.

Around the table sit Greenough the lanky American, Bayard the African explorer, the young Russian secretary Ivan Petrovski and his bride, and Mme. Constantin herself, nestled among cushions like a kitten. Talk of duels, honor, and love gives way to a story about what people will risk for pride, and Smith's easy, observant prose makes the salon itself the main stage.
23695-the-little-gray-lady-1909:
F. Hopkinson Smith began The Little Gray Lady with fragments of a story surfacing from the lumber-room of his brain. Cuffs of old coats, flounces, and bodice lacings thrust out of bureau drawers. With them come smells: musty trunks of faded letters, chests of mouldy books, and wardrobes of moth-eaten hunting coats.

One relic stands out: a bow-legged high-boy with club feet, deep drawers, and brass handles, scented with lavender and spiced rose leaves. Its owner's laces and long white mitts must be kept fresh. From these small, kept things Smith rebuilds a woman of an earlier day, and the story that follows is a tender act of memory, pieced together from what the past leaves behind.
23696-a-gentleman-s-gentleman-1909:
F. Hopkinson Smith published this 1909 story of artists and friendship along the Thames. Its narrator, a painter, has just heard that his friend Sandy MacWhirter sold two pictures at the Academy and plans to sail. Two months later, Mac himself appears at Sonning-on-Thames, striding down the tow-path with the architect Lonnegan.

Flat on the grass with the river flashing between low-branched trees, the three trade experiences. Mac's fortnight disappearance, his frozen grin, his nights writing letters and days poring over the morning mail all come out. The title's gentleman's gentleman is the loyal friend at the story's heart, and Smith tells their summer reunion with warmth, laughter, and an artist's eye for place.
23697-forty-minutes-late-1909:
F. Hopkinson Smith's Forty Minutes Late begins in snow, half an hour after a train leaves the station. Fine-grained, slanting snow forces its way between vestibule bellows and piles in mounds on platforms and steps. The narrator must lecture fifty miles from Bondville Junction, with only half an hour to spare for his connection.

The conductor will not promise anything, and the porter reports the connecting train sometimes waits ten minutes and sometimes pulls out as they pull in. The narrator forms a plan: porter with one bag, himself with the other, both on the Pullman step, ready to dash. Smith turns a small travel worry into a brisk, funny tale of winter railroading.
23698-fiddles-1909:
F. Hopkinson Smith called this 1909 story Marny's story, not his own, and it begins with Marny hanging a small portrait beneath a great elk's head. Hammer in hand and tack between his teeth, Marny praises Fiddles. He calls him a picturesque liar, a good-for-nothing, breezy, lovable vagabond, and wonders what the young man in the student cap ever did to deserve his place there.

The narrator lets Marny run on, knowing that to interrupt him is to lose the thread of the tale. Bit by bit the story of Fiddles emerges. The elk that only he could have shot, the mayor who would sit up and think, and the young fraud whose charm outlived him all play their part. It is a warm, talkative character sketch in Smith's best manner.
23702-a-list-to-starboard-1909:
F. Hopkinson Smith opened this 1909 sea story in a shipping office on New York's East Side. A short, square chunk of a captain walks in with kindly blue eyes and a mouth that shuts like a rat-trap. He tells the line's manager, flatly, not to send his vessel to sea again.

Her boats have had no paint for a year, her boilers are caked to the top flues, and her pumps cannot handle her bilge water. The slim, well-groomed manager waves an inspection certificate and laughs off the protest. The tale that follows turns on the list to starboard of the title, and on what a captain owes his ship when owners will not listen.
25304-the-shadow-on-the-dial-and-other-e:
Ambrose Bierce's Shadow on the Dial and Other Essays, edited by S. O. Howes in 1909, gathers the satirist's late nonfiction. Bierce notes that the book was meant for his Collected Works, that he did not choose its contents, but that the choice has his approval.

Essays sort out socialists, anarchists, and nihilists, mocking the anarchist who thinks laws create crime as a dog creates a garden thief. A labor essay proposes contracts that force strikes and lockouts to announce themselves thirty days ahead, so the public is not ruined by either side. Bierce's bite remains sharp throughout.
25408-child-life-in-town-and-country-190:
Anatole France's Child Life in Town and Country, published by John Lane in 1919, gathers tender stories of children in France. It shares its volume with the Merrie Tales of Jacques Tournebroche, and its copyright dates to 1909.

Fanchon walks like Little Red Riding-Hood to her grandmother's cottage, but meets no wolf, and finds toothless arms open like an old vine-stock. Germaine, getting well from fever, enjoys convalescence more than full health, watching her doll in a bright room. Other pieces remember fishermen lost at sea and widows at cottage doors.
26337-the-great-events-by-famous-histori:
The Great Events by Famous Historians, volume nine, edited by Rossiter Johnson with Charles F. Horne and John Rudd, appeared in 1905 from the National Alumni. Its plan gives world history as complete narratives in the words of eminent historians, linked by specialist introductions, arranged in order, with indices and reading courses. A Menzel painting of Henry VIII dancing at the Field of the Cloth of Gold fronts the volume.

This volume covers Luther beginning the Reformation in 1517, slavery's introduction by law in America the same year, and Magellan's first circumnavigation in 1519. Cortes capturing Mexico in 1521, Sweden's liberation in 1523, the Peasants' War in 1524, and France losing Italy at Pavia in 1525 follow. The sack of Rome opens the next stretch. Each event speaks through a historian of its own age.
2896-story-of-the-session-of-the-califor:
Franklin Hichborn wrote this day-by-day account of the California legislature's 1909 session as a piece of progressive-era muckraking. The narrative follows bills, lobbyists, and legislators through Sacramento, naming names and quoting telegrams as it goes. One episode tracks the schemes used to drag Assemblyman Marshall Black back to the capital, including a threat that his bills would be held up if he stayed away.

Hichborn's purpose is exposure, showing how corporate pressure and party management shaped lawmaking in the open. The book reads as both history and journalism, since its detail comes from the session floor rather than later memory. It remains a useful record of California politics in the reform years, blunt and specific.
30598-the-works-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Volume nine of the Swanston Edition of Robert Louis Stevenson's works was printed in London in 1911. Its Roman date is MDCCCCXI, and it follows the limited pattern: two thousand sixty copies printed, two thousand for sale. A facsimile of a note found among Stevenson's papers opens the illustrations.

Contents gather Memories and Portraits, opening with The Foreigner at Home, Some College Memories, and Old Mortality, with more portraits to follow. Stevenson recalls travel, school, and friends in essays that blend memory with sharp observation. The volume presents his personal prose in a handsome collected form, for readers who know his novels and want the man behind them.
3085-original-short-stories-volume-09:
Fat Toine of Tournevent rules volume nine, innkeeper of ten Norman cottages by the sea. Known for thirty miles round as Toine-my-extra and Burnt-Brandy, Antoine Macheble made famous a hamlet buried in a valley niche leading to the sea, ten Norman cottages ringed by ditches. The volume adds Madame Husson's Rosier, The Adopted Son, A Coward, Old Mongilet, Moonlight, and The First Snowfall. Later tales move south, with garden walls, orange and lemon trees full of golden fruit, and ladies walking a sandy avenue while children roll hoops.

Sundays of a Bourgeois, Our Letters, The Love of Long Ago, and Friend Joseph complete the set. The volume shows Maupassant shifting between Norman farce and tender recollection.
31632-project-gutenberg-1971-2009:
Marie Lebert's Project Gutenberg, 1971 to 2009, written for NEF at the University of Toronto in 2009 and marked CC0, is a short history of the free-ebook project. Its overview recalls that the first ebook appeared in July 1971, as eText number one of Project Gutenberg. Hart launched it as a visionary project to put literary works in electronic form and spread them worldwide. In the sixteenth century, Gutenberg let anyone have print books for a small cost, Lebert notes. In the twenty-first, Project Gutenberg would let anyone have a digital library at no cost.

The web in 1990 gave it a first boost, and Distributed Proofreaders in 2000 a second. By 2008, production ran at 340 new books a month, with forty mirror sites and tens of thousands of downloads daily.
32956-wilson-s-tales-of-the-borders-and-:
Volume nine of Wilson's Tales of the Borders and of Scotland, revised by Alexander Leighton in 1885, gathers historical, traditional, and imaginative stories from the border country. Its contents include The Cripple, or Ebenezer the Disowned, by John Mackay Wilson, and The Legend of Fair Helen of Kirconnel by Leighton. The rest runs from Tom Duncan's Yarn and the Professor's Tales through The Laird of Lucky's How to Sir Patrick Hume, a tale of the house of Marchmont. A glossary helps readers with Scots words.

The tales move between history and fireside invention, from lairds and packmen to sergeants, recluse figures, and tea-party gossip. Together they preserve the border's way of telling its own past, where a legend, a family quarrel, and a journey to London can all carry the same weight. This volume is a good entry to a long series that kept Scottish local story alive in print.
3347-the-wandering-jew-volume-09:
Cholera stalks Sue's ninth book through a masquerade in the square of Notre Dame, while accounts are rendered and murderers close in. The constant wanderer opens it, with the luncheon and rendering the account. The square of Notre Dame, the cholera masquerade, and the defiance follow, with brandy to the rescue and memories. The poisoner, in the cathedral, and the murderers lead to the patient and the lure.

Good news, the operation, and the torture follow, with vice and virtue and suicide to close. Sue's Paris turns feverish here, with cholera as backdrop and conspiracy as plot. Readers near the serial's end will find its darkest stretch: disguises failing, accounts demanded, and the wanderer's long road running toward its final reckoning.
3559-memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volum:
This ninth volume of Bourrienne's memoirs follows Napoleon in 1807, a year of victories in the east and of new settlements in Europe. Bourrienne, his former private secretary, draws on close knowledge of the emperor's government, even as his own service had ended. Treaties after the eastern victories redrew the map, and Bourrienne follows how paper settlements tried to hold what armies had won.

The narrative moves between camps, courts, and conference tables, where battles won in Poland and Prussia became treaties and new kingdoms. Bourrienne shows how much of Napoleon's power rested on paper: orders, reports, and bargains struck far from the guns. The volume suits readers tracking the emperor at the height of his fortunes.
3576-recollections-of-the-private-life-o:
Constant's ninth volume follows the household as bad news from the fronts reaches Paris and the palace grows quieter. He describes fewer guests, longer silences, and a master who buried himself in work while his empire shrank. Servants still kept the routines of dressing, dining, and travel, but the confidence of earlier years had gone.

The volume shows loyalty under pressure. Constant records the rumors that ran through servants' quarters, the departures of old friends, and Napoleon's own moods as defeat followed defeat. Readers who want the decline of an empire in domestic terms will find here a sober, first hand account from inside the house.
3589-essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volum:
This ninth volume opens Book Two of Montaigne's Essays, with chapters one through six. They treat the inconstancy of our actions, drunkenness, a custom of the Isle of Cea, the saying that tomorrow is a new day, conscience, and the idea that use makes perfect. Montaigne begins by noting how hard it is to reconcile a man's actions into one steady character.

The essays argue that human beings change with mood, company, and age, so judgment must be humble. A man may be brave one day and timid the next, and neither act alone defines him. The volume suits readers who like Montaigne at his most psychological, studying the self as a moving target rather than a fixed nature.
3909-the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rou:
Jean Jacques Rousseau hastens to the Hermitage in his ninth book, too impatient to wait for fine weather, while the Holbach coterie predicts he cannot support solitude for three months. Having lived fifteen years out of his element, he returns to groves, rivulets, and solitary walks that haunted him at Venice, Paris, and amid luxury and spectacles, making him sigh with desire. Retirement and country, he insists, are the only conditions of his happiness.

Quarrels soon disturb the solitude, as Diderot stirs strife and the Natural Son appears in the winter's disputes. Undated letters complicate the record, since Diderot never dated his, and Mesdames d'Epinay and d'Houdetot seldom added more than a weekday. Readers who like Rousseau's retreat will find a book of longing, friendship breaking, and papers in disorder.
5283-tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontain:
The ninth volume of La Fontaine's Tales and Novels gathers Belphegor, The Little Bell. The Glutton completes the trio, the same three tales carried by a companion record in this library. Belphegor, addressed to Miss de Chammelay, places her name with pleasure at the head of what La Fontaine calls the last effusions of his muse.

Belphegor tells of a devil sent to earth to test whether wives damn their husbands, a jest La Fontaine handles with irony and charm. Readers get three tales in which devils, bells, and appetites supply the comedy, in the light verse that made La Fontaine's tales a European success.
5447-uarda-a-romance-of-ancient-egypt-vo:
Georg Ebers pushes his ancient Egyptian romance Uarda toward the frontier in this ninth volume. Pentaur and his companions defend themselves against hostile mountaineers who rush from the woods. About two days from their journey's end, they fight a bloody skirmish with a roving band that seems part of a larger force. The road to Kadesh grows more dangerous as they near it.

Their guide Kaschta grows more familiar with every landmark as the destination approaches, suggesting local knowledge that may matter. The volume mixes travel, fighting, and suspense on the edge of Egyptian power. Readers get the romance in its most adventurous stretch, far from palace and temple.
5458-an-egyptian-princess-volume-09:
Georg Ebers reaches a rescue plot in this ninth volume of An Egyptian Princess. Under Egyptian law, Zopyrus has deserved death, so his friends resolve to travel to Sais and free him by stratagem. Syloson, who has friends there and speaks Egyptian well, offers to help, while Bartja and Darius disguise themselves by dyeing their hair and eyebrows and wearing broad felt hats.

The volume mixes disguise, loyalty, and danger as the rescuers approach a foreign city. Court intrigue gives way to a covert mission, with capture as the price of failure. Readers get an adventurous stretch of the romance, driven by friendship and quick thinking rather than palace ceremony.
5481-cleopatra-volume-09:
After accompanying Dion to the harbor, the architect goes to the Forum in the ninth volume of Georg Ebers's Cleopatra to talk with the men he meets there. All news reaches that meeting place first, and he finds many Macedonian citizens eager to discuss passing events in decisive hours. They fear and hope for the future fate of the city, and the scene grows very animated.

The volume captures Alexandria at a turning point, with citizens debating what Rome will do next. Ebers writes the Forum as the city's ear and voice. Readers get a tense, public stretch of the romance, where ordinary citizens weigh a future they cannot control.
5491-the-emperor-volume-09:
Verus gives an entertainment on the eve of his birthday in the ninth volume of Georg Ebers's The Emperor, and it runs far past the third hour of the morning. Learned Romans who came to Alexandria with the emperor join the most famous Alexandrians, invited by the praetor. The splendid banquet has long ended, but jar after jar keeps coming.

The volume captures a night of Roman Alexandrine high life, with drinking, talk, and display stretching toward dawn. Ebers writes the party as a social stage, where rank and wit compete. Readers get a long, glittering night in Hadrian's Alexandria, seen from inside the feast.
5525-the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-09:
Philippus starts up from the divan where he reclined at breakfast with his old friend in the ninth volume of Georg Ebers's The Bride of the Nile. Before Horapollo lies a half-empty plate, eaten less rapidly than his companion's. The old man looks disapprovingly at the leech, who drinks off his wine and water standing, though he usually sits and enjoys it while talking of matters light or grave.

The volume opens on an old friendship at breakfast, with manners and mood revealing more than words. Ebers uses the meal to show two men at ease and at odds. Readers get a quiet, character-filled stretch of the romance, where breakfast talk carries history.
5538-a-thorny-path-volume-09:
The lady Euryale's silent prayer is interrupted by Alexander's return in the ninth volume of Georg Ebers's A Thorny Path. He brings clothes that Seleukus's wife gave him for Melissa, dressed in his best and crowned like those holding first seats in the Circus. Yet his festal garb accords ill with the pained look on his face, from which joy in life has vanished.

The volume contrasts celebration clothes with private grief, as circus honors meet personal sorrow. Ebers keeps the household's worry close. Readers get a poignant stretch of the romance, where a man dressed for festival cannot hide his pain.
5569-barbara-blomberg-volume-09:
Three years pass. Barbara lives with her husband and the two sons she gave him in a pretty little house. It stands in the modest Saint-Gery quarter of Brussels, in the ninth volume of Georg Ebers's Barbara Blomberg. The capital of wealthy, flourishing Brabant looks very unlike what she expected from Gombert's stories. She has had little share so far in the splendor she expected on the drive to Landshut.

The volume follows Barbara's married life in Brussels, where modest rooms replace court splendor. Ebers writes the gap between expectation and reality. Readers get a domestic stretch of the romance, where a famous singer becomes a wife and mother in a small house.
5911-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1:
The Sierra Morena adventure continues across chapters twenty-four through twenty-seven in this Don Quixote portion. Chapter twenty-four returns to the ragged knight of the Sierra, who thanks Don Quixote for proofs of kindness while beginning his tale. Chapter twenty-five treats the strange things that happened to the stout knight there, chapter twenty-six his refinements of penance, and chapter twenty-seven the curate and barber's scheme.

Readers watch Quixote's madness deepen into deliberate penance, as friends plot a rescue disguised as chivalry. The Sierra chapters favor talk, confession, and comic plotting over battles, letting new characters tell their sorrows. This part suits readers midway through volume one, since its scheme to lure Quixote home drives much of what follows.
7594-the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume:
Part nine of The Caxtons meditates on homecoming as both comfort and reproach. One generation now sits undisturbed, having passed through passion's path, while the young still burn. That contrast is the part's argument, and Lytton states it through a returning youth who finds calm at home strangely sad. Peace, seen from inside trouble, can feel like an accusation.

The part opens that meditation with the father setting his books aside and the narrator speaking to every reader who has been young. Coming back from a hard world, carrying secret troubles, the youth finds quiet walls and elders at peace. A cold wind outside then shifts coach passengers, pulls up cloak collars, and steals warmth. The Caxton house stands as the image of both shelter and judgment.
7648-ernest-maltravers-volume-09:
Sickness and regret darken Book Nine of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Ernest Maltravers. On a fine December afternoon Lumley Ferrers leaves a house where muffled knockers mark illness within, and admits, with rare candor, that a lover's trick has done real harm. His old excuse now rings hollow.

Around a sickbed, love grows gentler as shadows close in, and faith in life beyond death steadies both lover and friend. Maltravers reads and talks beside the patient, finding a calmer hope. The volume closes a long arc of ambition and feeling with grief, pity, and quiet resolve.
7667-what-will-he-do-with-it-volume-09:
A lady in a hired carriage arrives alone at Fawley Manor in Book Nine of Edward Bulwer Lytton's What Will He Do With It? Her step is firm at first, then falters among old groves where childhood summers and a later, sadder visit crowd her mind. She carries a secret Darrell never told his friend.

The volume turns on Caroline's past: a pretty girl thrown in Darrell's way, a marriage made unhappy by rash choice, and designs hid under fine scruples. Memory, regret, and a wish to set matters right drive a quiet, tense journey to an old house.
7680-harold-the-last-of-the-saxon-kings-:
Duke William sits in his Rouen palace in Book Nine of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Harold, subtitled The Bones of the Dead. His table holds a plan for Cherbourg port, Caesar's Commentaries marked in his bold hand, arrows, abbey sketches, and letters from kings who seek his friendship or threaten his rest.

Harold soon comes to Normandy with young kinsmen and learns how short William's temper runs when crossed. A bishop warns him to speak with care, for the duke's arms reach far. The volume sets William's sleepless statecraft against Harold's plain talk, on the road to conquest.
7710-my-novel-volume-09:
Pisistratus shrinks his opening chapters in Book Nine of Edward Bulwer Lytton's My Novel, since his crowd of persons now presses like poor relations at Christmas. The Caxtons themselves are turned out of their rooms to make space, and the heading turns to public life.

The volume asks what public life means for ordinary folk in vestries and town councils, not just for ministers and members. Gossip also brings Count di Peschiera, said to have wagered he would wed his kinsman's daughter and seize the estate. L'Estrange answers with dry scorn.
7723-the-last-of-the-barons-volume-09:
Warwick wakes Hilyard in his prison room in Book Nine of Edward Bulwer Lytton's The Last of the Barons, subtitled The Wanderers and the Exiles. His face has lost its open majesty, and he declares that one night has made him a rebel against Edward of York, though not yet a friend to Henry.

He sends Hilyard riding fast to Sir Robert Welles with a letter, promising Warwick and Clarence will soon join him. Later, on a field, a boy with cloven helm begs for water beside a dying man, while Sibyll offers comfort. Rebellion, exile, and pity for the wounded run through this volume.
7745-the-parisians-volume-09:
Isaura wakes to a brighter world in Book Nine of Lytton's The Parisians, after talk with Alain de Rochebriant. Sunshine seems new, air seems balm, and her heart beats lighter, as if far-off music played. At first she cannot name the cause, then words return: Graham Vane loves her.

A long cold absence has not brought forgetfulness, she decides, and the joy wipes out waiting. The volume lingers on that morning of certainty, when a woman hears love confirmed after doubt. It is a tender pause in a novel otherwise full of politics and plot.
7909-american-historical-and-literary-cu: Part nine of Smith and Watson's American curiosities, as a text file, ends almost as soon as it begins. It gives an editor's note, a title page, and no further prose. The note explains the series is an image work, so readers who want the curiosities themselves should open the linked HTML edition.
8787-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
This ninth part of Dante's Inferno, in Cary's translation, covers cantos twenty-nine through thirty-one. Canto twenty-nine opens with Dante's eyes drunk on the sight of a multitude disfigured by wounds, longing to stay and weep. Until Virgil rouses him: why fasten his sight among the maimed shades, when the valley winds two and twenty miles and the moon already sinks beneath their feet? Time is short, and much remains unseen.

The cantos that follow punish falsifiers: alchemists, counterfeiters, perjurers, and impersonators, diseased and quarrelling in their ditch. Then the giants rise at the pit's edge, vast and chained, guarding the frozen centre of Hell. The part shows Dante moving from pity to judgment, and from human fraud to cosmic scale. It is a strong, self-contained stretch for readers dipping into the Inferno's later cantos.
9107-tales-and-novels-volume-09:
Maria Edgeworth fills this ninth volume of her Tales and Novels with three works: Harrington, Thoughts on Bores, and Ormond. Harrington runs through nineteen chapters, and Ormond through more than thirty. An essay on bores sits between them, sharp and amused. Engravings on steel graced the set, though this edition lacks them.

Edgeworth's wit targets folly, prejudice, and the social climber, while her heroes learn sense through trial. The volume shows her range, from novel to essay. It remains a fine slice of early nineteenth-century Irish-English fiction, lively and moral at once.
9771-alice-or-the-mysteries-book-09:
Book nine of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Alice, or The Mysteries, opens with Lord Vargrave ill at an inn, too sick to move in a severe season. Even in London, relapse slows his recovery, and he bears confinement with impatience. Against his physician's orders, he still transacts official business and consults political friends from his sickroom. Ambition will not rest, even in illness.

The book follows Vargrave's sickroom schemes, as statesmen claim to serve others while serving self. Lytton's prose favors moral irony. A reader gets the ninth book of a Victorian mystery romance, where a villain's body fails but his plots persist.
a-select-collection-of-old-english-plays: Robert Dodsley continues his select collection of old English plays in this ninth volume, with notes by W. Carew Hazlitt. Its opening comedy shows a man choosing a good wife from a bad. The volume adds a return from Parnassus, a wily beguiling, the play Lingua, and the miseries of enforced marriage. The opening comedy, acted by the Earl of Worcester's servants and printed in 1602, may be by Joshua Cooke, named in an old hand on the title page.
a-thorny-path-volume-09:
A Thorny Path darkens in Volume 9 of the novel by Georg Ebers, as Alexander comes back to the house of the lady Euryale. Ebers dresses him for the Circus, crowned like the other guests in the best seats, but his face has lost the open joy that marked it that same morning. He has seen enough to offer his own life for his sister without flinching.

Chapter XXVI weighs what flight would cost the family. Leaving Alexandria means tearing their father from the only home he can bear. It also means Alexander gives up Agatha, the girl he hopes to marry. Her Christian father received him kindly, yet stated plainly that no open pagan will be allowed to court her. Love, faith, and family duty block every road at once in this volume.
alice-or-the-mysteries-book-09: Edward Bulwer Lytton finds Lord Vargrave ill at an inn in the ninth book of Alice, or the Mysteries, too sick to travel in a severe season. Even after reaching London by easy stages, he relapses, and confinement breeds impatience in a man unused to sickness. Illness slows the schemer's plots and lets the novel's other claims press forward.
american-historical-and-literary-curiosi: John Jay Smith's ninth part of American Historical and Literary Curiosities keeps the series' picture-first character, with plates of literary antiquities at its core. The text file is a partial shadow of the book, and its editor's note urges readers toward the HTML file for the full plates. Scholars of Americana will still value it as a guide to the series' holdings.
amphitheatrvm-sapientiae-aeternae-solius:
Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae, the Amphitheatre of Eternal Wisdom, was published in 1609 by Heinrich Khunrath, the German physician and alchemist. Its long subtitle calls the work Christian-Kabbalistic, divine-magical, and physico-chymical at once. Khunrath meant it as a theatre in which true wisdom, found only in God, could be contemplated from every side.

The book is famed for its engraved plates, eleven double plates among them, whose allegories join the alchemist's laboratory with Christ and the cosmos. One famous circular plate shows the laboratory as a chapel of work and prayer. The preface is signed by Erasmus Wolfart, and the plates carry dates from earlier in the decade. It remains the showpiece of Rosicrucian-era alchemy.
an-egyptian-princess-volume-09:
Georg Ebers's An Egyptian Princess, volume nine, in Eleanor Grove's translation, opens on a point of Egyptian law: Zopyrus has deserved death. The Persian noble's fate hangs on the customs of the land his king conquered. In the next chapter a young bride and bridegroom have travelled no farther than Ephesus. Bartja and Sappho's marriage journey has begun.

Late threads gather in this volume: the lovers united, the guilty awaiting judgment, Cambyses' empire settling after madness. Ebers moves his large cast toward their Herodotean ends while granting the invented ones their happiness. Grove's translation sustains the ceremonial tone to the close. The nine-volume set lets a historical romance breathe at epic length. Volume nine is resolution in progress — a bridal road westward, a prisoner's law, and a court learning to live after its king. Egypt's princess has become the story's memory.
angela-foligno-divine-consolation-1909:
Angela of Foligno told her Book of Divine Consolation to her priest. Mary G. Steegmann gave the work English dress in 1909. Angela was a rich wife in Umbria who lost her kin and turned to God. She joined the third order of St. Francis in her grief.

Step by step, she tells how God drew her from a lax life to deep pain and light. Visions of Christ in His pain crowd the mid parts. Her words are raw, bold, and free of all soft gloss. The book is a chief text of women's soul lore of the mid ages.
apuleius-apologia-florida-butler-1909:
Harold E. Butler translated Apuleius's Apologia and Florida into English in 1909. Apuleius, the Roman novelist, had been tried for practicing magic in North Africa. His defense speech survives as the Apologia.

Prosecutors claimed he won his rich wife through spells and enchantments. Apuleius answers with wit, philosophy, and ridicule of his accusers' ignorance. He discusses fish, mirrors, and poetry to show his interests were scholarly. The Florida collects showpieces of his public speaking beside the defense. Together they form the great surviving record of a Roman witchcraft trial. Butler's translation keeps the legal fireworks readable. The speech is long, bold, and full of wit from the first page to the last.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-09:
Volume nine of Burton's Thousand Nights and a Night appeared in 1885, the penultimate book of the main set. Shahrazad's store seems endless even as its appointed end draws near. Kings in her tales keep meeting clever wives, lost sons, and fortunes reversed in a single night.

Burton, nearing his own finish line, still refuses every shortcut in the text. His renderings of verse stay verse, and his notes stay frank about manners and belief. The Gutenberg text of this volume is ebook 55587, set apart from its neighbors in numbering. That quirk aside, the volume matches the rest in dress. One volume more completes Shahrazad's bargain in the main series.
arxiv-2412-00909:
Srikumar Warrier and Gaurav Tomar study flow stability in a swirl combustor in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. They model an annular swirling jet laden with dilute particles, of the kind used in swirl flow burners. Stability analysis shows which flow patterns can grow and disturb the jet.

With uniform particle spread, the spectra show three unstable modes at low particle inertia. As inertia rises toward unity, the centre and shear modes weaken compared with the clean jet. Particle spread varies mostly in the vortex core, not the shear layer. Stronger backflow at the center raises the centre mode's growth. A non-uniform particle profile can stabilize that mode, and the authors trace why through a vorticity budget analysis.
arxiv-2412-02909:
Ankit Tiwari and colleagues found a way in 2024 to strengthen a feeble light-matter interaction that photonic quantum computers need. The cross-Kerr effect, where one light beam shifts another's phase, is normally far too weak for reliable logic gates. Their trick uses squeezing, a quantum technique that quiets noise in one property of light at the expense of another. By alternating squeezing between different quadratures of a single light mode, the interaction is generically amplified.

As an application, they show how the protocol speeds up deterministic controlled-phase gates in photonic architectures. They derive bounds stating how fast and strong the squeezing must be to hold gate errors at a chosen level. Encouragingly, the protocols can tolerate photon losses, the usual deal-breaker. The authors discuss implementations in optical fibers and nanophotonic waveguides, the hardware where such gates would actually run.
arxiv-2412-04509:
Joshua Lee and five co-authors introduced a prompting method in twenty twenty-four that helps language models spot sarcasm. Sarcasm hides its true meaning behind words that say the opposite, so models often take it at face value. Their method, Pragmatic Metacognitive Prompting, asks the model to reason about implied meaning, weigh context, and check its first read against the facts.

The team tested the method on leading models, among them GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet. On GPT-4o it reached the best reported scores on two standard sarcasm data sets. The gains came from prompting alone, with no added training. The authors present the approach as a promising path for sentiment analysis, where tone can flip the meaning of a message.
arxiv-2412-07309:
Anja Alfano and Nick Evans wrote this theoretical physics paper, published in two thousand twenty-four, on a trap in the hunt for new gauge theories. Some strongly coupled theories almost stop running at low energy, a state called the conformal window, and lattice simulations struggle to tell its edge from true symmetry breaking.

Using a simple holographic model, the authors show why. A walking theory can hold several scales apart: where it turns strong, where a key dimension crosses its critical value, and where the condensate forms. On a finite lattice with a weak starting coupling, those gaps can fake an answer. Running the coupling hot instead creates an artefact phase that breaks symmetry right at the cutoff, parked close to the fixed point. They test the lesson on recent ten-flavor lattice data and find its verdict sound.
arxiv-2412-08009:
Hiep Vo Dang, Joseph Choi, and Phong Nguyen introduced FLRONet in twenty twenty-four, for rebuilding full fluid flow fields from a handful of sensors. Engineers often can measure a flow only sparsely, and inverting those few readings into a complete field is ill-posed: many flows fit the same sensors. Learned models exist, but their accuracy often depends on the simulation grid used in training.

Deep operator learning sidesteps that by learning the mapping between function spaces directly. FLRONet's branch-trunk network represents the inverse measurement operator, taking sensor readings to a continuous space-time field. On a standard benchmark it reconstructed flows accurately and robustly, even with noisy or missing sensors. It could also upscale fields in space and time at no extra training — zero-shot super-resolution.
arxiv-2412-09009:
Sumanth Kumar Boya and Deepak Subramani present PINTO, a neural operator that solves partial differential equations, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Such math rules much of the real world, from fluids to heat flow. Most neural tools of this kind must be trained again each time the start or edge terms change.

PINTO is a physics-informed transformer that does not need that fresh training. It learns from the physics loss alone, with no run data at all. Its key new part is a set of units built on cross-attention. They work step by step and fold each new task's terms into the form of the answer. The team tests the design on a range of start and edge value tasks. It copes well with terms it has not seen, and it does so fast.
arxiv-2412-09609:
Gabriel Malavé, Rodrigo Soto-Garrido, Vladimir Juričić, and Bitan Roy built a field theory in twenty twenty-four for a class of materials at the edge of becoming insulators. These generalized Weyl semimetals host points where electron bands touch, with energy spreading at mixed rates along different directions. Interactions can push such a material into an axionic insulating state.

The authors set up a renormalization group method tuned to this transition, controlled by two small parameters. For three-dimensional cases their leading-order analysis finds a gentle, Gaussian transition with mean-field exponents. The same outcome appears for simple Weyl semimetals. A byproduct is a marginal Fermi liquid state, where measured quantities pick up only slow logarithmic changes. The work frames how this exotic critical point should look in experiments.
arxiv-2412-12109:
Zezhi Deng and Ruoxing Yang give an algorithm for adding a new line to an existing transit network, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Real networks have fixed lines and links that cannot be changed to suit a new route. Any new line must thread through what already stands.

Their method builds the line without altering old lines or station links. It also scores how efficient a line and a whole network are, and uses that score while it builds. Tests vary the settings and goals to see where the line lands. In most cases the new line raised overall network efficiency. Poor pairings of search and scoring methods, or high build costs, could instead make things worse.
arxiv-2412-14709:
Byeong-Kweon Oh and Jongheun Yoon solve a problem in number theory in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. They study integral quadratic forms over local rings, and ask when a form can represent all forms of a given rank in a primitive way. Such forms are called primitively n-universal.

Earlier work settled the case of rank one over the p-adic integers, with the minimal rank depending on the prime. Oh and Yoon extend that result to every positive rank and a broad class of local rings. They determine the minimal rank completely for rings where two is a unit or a prime. The result closes a gap in the theory of quadratic forms over local rings.
arxiv-2412-15409:
Li Hua Yu studies how the wave function of a single particle moves from a source slit to a detector, and how measurement fits in. The 2024 paper sets up two thin slits, with free space between. Yu first probes the wave with an extra slit that can be made ever more narrow. The width at which counts drop to half traces the wave's spread.

That trace forms a spindle: pinched at both slits, fat in the middle. This clashes with the plain Schrödinger picture, where the wave grows wider and wider. The probe slit also wipes out phase data. So Yu swaps it for a thin pin that blocks a sliver of the wave. Its small effect on counts is treated by perturbation. The probe function that results is real, yet it holds phase data. It is tied to the wave and to collapse just before detection.
arxiv-2412-15709:
Arati, Devaraj, and Shankhadeep Mondal wrote this mathematics paper, published in 2024. It studies pairs of frames, the redundant coordinate systems used in signal processing, that lose the least information when some of the signal's pieces are erased.

Frames spread a signal across many measurements, so losing a few need not be fatal. But the recovery partner matters: some dual frames rebuild far better than others after erasures. The authors introduce a new score for this, based on the size of the error operator in the Frobenius sense. They characterize the best dual pairs under that score for any number of erasures. They also redo the analysis under two other scores, the spectral radius and the numerical radius. Finally, they give explicit recipes for building certain optimal pairs in finite-dimensional spaces.
arxiv-2412-15909:
Akshit Singh, Karan Bhakuni, and Rajendra Nagar improve, in a 2024 preprint, how neural networks learn the shape of outdoor scenes from laser scans. A neural distance field stores, for any point, its distance to the nearest surface. Such fields help robots map and locate themselves. True distance data for big outdoor scenes does not exist, so training leans on guesses of the expected distance. Those guesses often ignore how surfaces bend. The authors add a signal based on second derivatives of the field, which capture curvature.

With curvature in the training signal, the estimated distances come out truer to the geometry. The method targets large scenes, not just tabletop scans. In head-to-head tests on mapping and localization, it beat the prevalent approaches. The authors say curvature-aware training is a missing piece for neural fields. Robots that read their surroundings through such fields should gain steadier maps.
arxiv-2412-16909:
Oliver Lueghamer and four co-authors boost microscope signals in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Microscopes reveal spatial detail in systems from cells to cold atoms. The challenge is to gain more information per probe particle, since probing can damage the sample. A cavity, a set of mirrors that trap light, can amplify the signal.

Their method uses a self-imaging cavity in a continuous-wave setup. It raised contrast for test samples and for biological samples alike. For thick samples, the cavity yields a new kind of dark-field imaging. Scattered and unscattered light are split by optical path length there. Theory shows the gains hold even when the cavity is not stabilized. Readers get better signal at fixed damage, with simpler hardware.
arxiv-2412-17009:
Byun and co-authors propose Generate to Discriminate, a continual learning method that routes data to expert models. Rules often let institutions share models but not the data behind them. The goal is adapting to new domains without forgetting old ones, the classic catastrophic forgetting trap.

An ensemble of domain experts can fit each site closely, if test samples reach the right expert. G2D trains a domain discriminator on synthetic data to do that routing. Oddly, routing with synthetic data beat training the main classifier on it directly. G2D topped rival domain-incremental methods on both vision and language tasks.
arxiv-2412-18009:
Gopinath Sahoo studies special structures on derived categories in a mathematics paper from two thousand twenty-four. He introduces tensor t-structures on the bounded derived categories of schemes. Past work showed how a perversity function on a scheme gives rise to a t-structure when the scheme has a dualizing complex.

Sahoo shows those t-structures are tensor t-structures, and that every tensor t-structure arises in that way. He first characterizes them through filtrations that generalize earlier results from rings to schemes. He also proves that a smooth projective curve's derived category has no nontrivial tensor weight structures. That extends an earlier result on the projective line to curves of higher genus.
arxiv-2501-00009:
Shengheng Liu, Xingkang Li, Zihuan Mao, Peng Liu, and Yongming Huang sharpen angle-of-arrival estimates for 5G base stations with a model-driven neural network. Their paper, published in twenty twenty-four, recasts the angle task as image rebuilding of a spatial spectrum. Model-based gauges warp in practice thanks to hardware flaws. Pure data tools can lack a firm base.

Their MoD-DNN loops between a convolutional network and a sparse conjugate gradient solver. The loop self-corrects the phase error that shifts with angle. Both simulations and bench tests back the gains. Spectrum calibration and angle reads both improve. The authors pitch the hybrid as a path to truer location services on live networks. It keeps model insight while letting data fix the model's blind spots.
arxiv-2501-02709:
Vivek Myers, Catherine Ji, and Benjamin Eysenbach ask, in a 2025 preprint, whether an agent trained on near goals can reach far ones. Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning teaches policies to head for a stated target. Short trips are easy to learn, long trips are not. The authors name the hoped-for transfer horizon generalization. They link it to a neat symmetry: a good policy should act the same toward a far goal as toward a waypoint on the way there. They call that planning invariance.

Under stated assumptions, their theory proves both traits can hold at once. A policy with the symmetry, trained only on near goals, should then reach goals at any distance. The paper adds fresh experiments and revisits older findings that fit the theory. The authors frame the work as an invitation. Tricks that build invariance elsewhere in machine learning might be adapted to give agents this reach.
arxiv-2501-04309:
Manibrata Sen reviews in 2025 how to test whether neutrinos have hidden traits beyond the standard model of physics. Neutrinos are ghostly particles that barely interact with matter, which makes them a fine probe for new physics. The paper sums up a plenary talk given at a 2024 workshop on neutrino oscillation.

Sen walks through open questions, from where neutrino mass comes from to how the particles might decay. He also covers odd ways they could interact, and a possible link to dark matter. For each topic he weighs what space observations, cosmology, and lab experiments have found so far. The talk shows how these threads tie neutrino science to the biggest questions about the universe.
arxiv-2501-04809:
Shadab Alam and co-authors review, in twenty twenty-five, computer simulations of turbulent convection at middle scales. Convection is the rise and fall of fluid when heated from below. At middle scales, clear patterns can form even when the flow is strongly turbulent. The team studies a flat layer heated below and cooled above, a classic setup. They vary the rules at the top and bottom walls, the shape of the box, and a ratio that compares heat spread to momentum spread.

Low values of that ratio arise in stars, and are hard to reach in lab tests with liquid metals. The review also covers cases that break the simple fluid model, such as compressible flow. Energy loss rate stays a central quantity for mixing there.
arxiv-2501-06209:
Kang, Kim, and Tong build diagram algebras that mirror a class of quantum groups in twenty twenty-four. The quantum groups attach to quivers, graphs that may carry loops. Their mirror objects are Khovanov Lauda Rouquier algebras. The team proves the mirrors are faithful.

Basic building blocks of the algebra match the canonical basis of the group's negative half. A cut down version of the algebra mirrors each top weight module in full. The matching gives hands on tools for computing in the quantum group. Such mirrors, called categorification, lift numbers to structures. The class covered is the Borcherds Cartan type.
arxiv-2501-07209:
Daniel Slamanig surveys the gap between privacy-preserving login theory and practice in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Online sign-in usually runs through central identity providers, which learn much about users. Cryptography offers tools like zero-knowledge proofs and anonymous credentials that hide far more.

These tools are decades old and well understood, yet barely deployed. Slamanig reviews what the math can do, shows real deployment cases, and names the barriers holding adoption back. The EU Digital Identity Wallet serves as the running example, with expert feedback around it aired. A closing note covers the shift to post-quantum methods. The paper asks why strong privacy tech stays on the shelf.
arxiv-2501-08209:
Liuyao Zhang, Jinhui Chen, and Chunjian Zhang use a transport model to study collisions of gold nuclei, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. They track how the average transverse momentum of the particles varies from one collision to the next. These event-by-event swings can reveal how energy is spread when the nuclei first overlap.

The team ran a multiphase transport model across collision energies from three to about twenty billion electron volts. They tracked spread measures up to fourth order and how they change with collision centrality. The pattern breaks the simple scaling seen in plainer models, while scaled versions match measured trends well. A two-subevent check slightly cuts links between nearby particles. Baryons show stronger swings than other particles. The findings sharpen a tool for probing the hot matter made in such collisions.
arxiv-2501-08309:
Luca Galantucci, Giorgio Krstulovic, and Carlo F. Barenghi wrote a physics study from two thousand twenty-five about quantum flow in superfluid helium. It looks at a tangle of thin vortex lines that move, meet, and join again. In the two-fluid view, those lines sit in a normal fluid made of heat-driven motion.

Past work often treated the normal fluid as a plain background that drains energy as heat. Using a model with two-way effects, the authors show each line makes a large wake in the normal fluid. Those wakes can top the mean gap between lines. The result helps explain odd speed patterns seen in heat transfer tests.
arxiv-2501-10509:
Daniel D'Orazio and co-authors explored a violent fate for stars caught near two merging supermassive black holes in 2025. If gas disks drive the binary, nearby stars should be delivered into the disk plane, migrate inward, and become trapped at the edge of the cavity the binary clears. Locked to its slow decay. A trapped star then spirals down with the binary until tidal forces strip it in a runaway process.

For Sun-like stars around binaries in the mass range the space-based sensor LISA will hear. The stripping should produce repeated X-ray flares near the maximum steady brightness, flashing every few hours to days and continuing for decades. Those traits match the recently discovered quasi-periodic eruptions remarkably well. One problem remains: the forecast and seen rates clash, unless mergers of lower-mass binaries are more common than expected.
arxiv-2501-12009:
Chik How Tan, Theo Prabowo, and Wei Guo Foo broke a lattice-based signature scheme in a 2025 cryptanalysis paper. The scheme, proposed at a major conference in 2023, signs messages with convoluted Gaussian sampling and was proved secure in a strong quantum-era model. Such proofs rest on assumptions about what signatures leak, and the authors found a leak the proof missed.

Signatures, averaged the right way, form a ratio whose expected value follows a known heavy-tailed law tied to the secret key. From enough signatures the key can be recovered, and the authors count how many suffice and test the attack in software. They also report flaws in a revised version's parameters, where signing fails or forgery turns easy.
arxiv-2501-13809:
Maryum Sayeed and six co-authors measure how often planets occur round FGK stars as a function of star age, using Kepler data. Planet counts came from confirmed and candidate finds across many Kepler quarters. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Pipeline catch rates correct the counts in each age bin. Ages came from isochrone fits and from spin based clocks. Across a wide span of planet sizes and orbits, no clear trend with age stood out. A faint downward hint appeared only for low mass, metal rich stars. The authors blame weak trends and small samples, and call for sharper ages.
arxiv-2501-15309:
Saikat Roy and four co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on using patches, not whole scans, when a diffusion model cleans up medical images. Diffusion priors can restore scans or boost their detail. Whole image runs cost much time and memory. Patch runs promise a leaner path, but their worth was still an open ask.

The team trains and tests priors on MRI scans in patch form. Small tweaks keep patch seams from showing as flaws. They weigh score, speed, and memory use against whole image runs. They also test if a whole image trained prior can run on patches as is. Tests span many plug-in methods, tasks, and data sets.
arxiv-2501-16909:
Paul Elvinger, Foteini Strati, Natalie Enright Jerger, and Ana Klimovic study how programs sharing one graphics processor get in each other's way, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Even heavy AI jobs leave much of a GPU idle, because their kernels use the chip's parts unevenly over time.

Packing several jobs onto one device would fix the waste, but interference makes performance unpredictable, so operators rarely colocate. The authors dig one level deeper into the contention itself. They map the main shared resources at stake: block schedulers, compute units, the two cache levels, and memory bandwidth. For each kind of interference, they build a method to measure how sensitive a given workload is. That sensitivity map can ground schedulers that promise strict performance. It can also teach developers to write kernels that share gracefully. The work targets data centers that want fuller GPUs without surprise slowdowns.
arxiv-2501-17109:
José Garre-Rubio, Alex Turzillo, and András Molnár name a local property that guarantees a tensor network state's parent Hamiltonian behaves. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Matrix product states compress quantum chains into small tensors, and each state implies a Hamiltonian whose ground space it spans.

The intersection property says that ground space holds nothing beyond the intended states, with degeneracy neatly bounded. Their new property, stability, is checked tensor by tensor and implies the guarantee. It widens the older injectivity condition rather than replacing it. Famous examples like the W state and domain-wall superpositions pass the test, along with their generalizations. The result gives builders a simple local check for global good behavior.
arxiv-2501-17409:
Xiaobei Wang, Shuchang Liu, and colleagues improve how recommender systems learn long-term value from user acts. To recommend is at base a long-term task of picking the best acts. Reinforcement learning can train rules for it. A value function gauges each user's future rewards and guides the rule. The rule may probe new acts to escape local peaks.

The standard method learns the value function from gaps between user states in a row. The team argues this mixes two random factors that are never modeled apart. One is chance from the stochastic policy, and one is chance from the user world. That mix can give weak reward gauges and weak search. They show the two factors can be gauged apart by splitting the temporal-difference loss. The split frame learns faster and stays more robust.
arxiv-2501-17809:
Adrien Currier bounds the count of special critical points on a manifold in two thousand twenty-five. The points are defined through a twisted derivative built from a fixed closed one-form, called beta. A matching homology theory, Morse-Novikov homology, grades spaces by those same twists.

Currier proves that the number of such points of each index is at least the size the homology demands. The result then widens to generating functions that grow in a set way at infinity. A use follows in a branch of symplectic geometry: the bound can detect key chords of a set length in spaces that are locally of that type.
arxiv-2501-17909:
Jan Boruch and three co-authors compute a gravitational index in twenty twenty-five. Their objects are black holes and black strings in five dimensions, within M-theory. A supersymmetric index counts states with signs, giving a robust probe of the objects. That five-dimensional index links to the index of four-dimensional black holes in another theory.

Both theories are compactified on the same Calabi-Yau threefold for the link. The authors find the finite-temperature saddles for the five-dimensional index. They do this by uplifting attractor saddles recently found for the four-dimensional index. For black holes, the uplift makes the two indices match. For black strings, the saddle matches the microscopic index at leading order, even without the usual decoupling limit.
arxiv-2501-18309:
Giorgio Cignarale and co-authors wrote this robotics and logic paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on what teams of robots can be said to know. A robot swarm solves tasks like exploring a space or gathering in one place only if the right knowledge reaches the right robots.

The authors build a framework that joins the physics of moving robots with temporal epistemic logic, the formal study of who knows what, and when. Physical motion and on-board computation are kept in separate layers, so control theory and distributed computing tools each apply cleanly. A method converts a switched hybrid model of the robots into a logic model, step by step through an abstract machine. From that model they derive conditions under which exploring and gathering can be guaranteed. The authors offer the frame as a meeting ground for three fields that rarely talk.
arxiv-2502-01109:
Chang introduces a geometric analogue of Gauss sums over function fields in twenty twenty-five. Gauss sums are classic objects in number theory with rich properties. Function fields in positive characteristic offer a parallel setting. The author builds the new sums and studies their basic behaviour.

He proves a reflection formula, a Stickelberger type theorem, and Hasse-Davenport relations for them. He also determines their absolute values and signs at infinity. The approach differs fully from both the classical theory and earlier arithmetic analogues. The key step is a Gross-Koblitz type formula that ties the sums to special gamma values. The other properties then follow from that formula and gamma function equations.
arxiv-2502-03409: Ellie Pond and Matthew Hale give a way to check that a safety rule can be kept by a machine at run time. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five, in control theory. Such rules can keep a machine out of harm. But a rule is of no use if the machine lacks the power to hold it. The team frames a chain of sum-of-squares tests that find the gain curves tied to a rule. If those tests have answers, the system stays safe as it runs.
arxiv-2502-06809:
Haider and four colleagues argue that neurons in language models speak in ranges, not single switches, in twenty twenty-five. Single neurons were thought to own single concepts, yet most serve many. Across encoder and decoder models, they found a pattern. For a given concept, a neuron's firing sizes form a tight bell shaped range.

Ranges for unlike concepts barely overlap. Their NeuronLens tool reads and steers concepts by those ranges. Steering hit the target concept with far less damage to neighbors than neuron masking. Model performance held up better too. The lens offers a finer grip on model internals.
arxiv-2502-07009:
Sobiya Ashraf and five co-authors watch how chemically active oil droplets organize themselves into patterns. Living microbes swarm and cluster to form colonies and reach food, and droplets serve as simple stand-ins for such behavior. The team varied the droplets' activity level, captured by the Péclet number.

At high activity the droplets pushed forward and linked into shifting chain-like patterns. Lowering activity strengthened the push-apart forces between them, and clustering faded. At low activity, repulsion through the chemical field produced an orderly arrangement instead. The droplets also steered through a soft, structured setting. The results may guide design of tiny swimmers in complex fluids.
arxiv-2502-09709:
Aaron Ouellette and Gilbert Holder compare two ways of squeezing cosmic information from maps of dark matter halos. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Betti curves summarize the topology of the halo pattern. Nearest neighbor distributions summarize its spacing instead. Both promise clues beyond standard two-point statistics. The question is how much each really knows.

Fisher matrices from the Quijote simulations quantify the content. The authors check convergence with care, since simulation counts are limited. Only two parameter directions prove well constrained overall. In that reduced space, the first two Betti curves carry nearly all their method's power. Those curves count components and loops. The comparison guides where future surveys should invest.
arxiv-2502-10209:
Andrea Pizzo and Angel Lozano build a physical framework for holographic MIMO in a twenty twenty-five paper. MIMO systems use many antennas at once. The holographic kind packs antennas close together across a wide aperture, closer than a wavelength apart, which makes them interfere with each other.

That interference, called mutual coupling, is often treated as a nuisance. The framework here builds it in from the physics up, along with signal correlation. The team then works out the information limits of such systems at each signal strength. A neat result: by choosing each antenna's pattern with care, coupling can be made to fight or aid correlation, as the signal level demands.
arxiv-2502-11409:
Xiang Yang and four co-authors study baryogenesis and electron dipole moments in a supersymmetric model in two thousand twenty-five. The model adds triplets and a singlet to the minimal supersymmetric frame. CP violation in it may have seeded the matter excess of the cosmos. The same effects shift electric dipole moments of particles.

A strong first order phase shift at tree level backs the baryon story. Numeric work shows the model can match the seen matter excess. Zones that work for baryogenesis can still fit dipole bounds. That fit needs parts of the electron dipole to cancel each other. Mercury and neutron dipoles are weighed as well.
arxiv-2502-11609:
Yanru Wu and six co-authors help continual learning systems use the kinship between tasks instead of treating each task as a stranger. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Continual learning adds new tasks over time without forgetting old ones. Most methods guard the weights but ignore how tasks relate.

Their task fingerprint, the H-embedding, scores how well skill moves between tasks. It comes from an information measure and is cheap to compute on the fly. A hypernetwork then reads the fingerprint and builds weights fitted to each task. Only the small fingerprint must be stored per task. Training runs end to end without fuss. On image benches the method beat strong rivals at both forward and backward transfer. The code is shared in public.
arxiv-2502-12809:
Veronica Saz Ulibarrena and Simon Portegies Zwart teach a computer to steer its own simulations in this two thousand twenty-five astrophysics paper. Simulating gravitating systems demands adaptive time steps: small steps during rapid change, cheaper large steps in quiet phases. Traditional choices need expert knowledge, fix key parameters for the whole run, and trade accuracy against cost by hand. The authors replace that judgment with reinforcement learning.

Their test problem integrates three equal-mass bodies bound by mutual gravity, a famously chaotic system. The learned controller picks the time-step parameter dynamically as conditions change. Results matched or beat existing methods, including the most commonly used fixed parameter values, without expert setup. The trained controller also transferred to other variable time-step integrators without retraining. The authors present the approach as a route to self-tuning simulations across astrophysics.
arxiv-2502-13809:
Badal Mondal and five co-authors argue that transistors with channels rich in aluminum beat gallium nitride ones for high-power electronics, against what recent theory said. Gallium nitride high electron mobility transistors stall below about six hundred fifty volts. The alloy aluminum gallium nitride, with its wider bandgap, is the natural next material in line.

Past work took it that the sheet of electrons in the channel stayed the same as the aluminum share changed. This study shows the density shifts a lot with the mix and with layer thickness. How well the device does then turns on a tug-of-war between carrier density and electron mobility. With that push and pull in the model, devices rich in aluminum beat gallium nitride at room temperature and above, across mixes. The team say past views could badly misjudge what such devices can do.
arxiv-2502-20109:
Ronald Orozco López works out new q-identities in a two thousand twenty-five math paper. These identities are formulas in a changed calculus, where plain numbers are swapped for q-analogues. Such rules back much of modern combinatorics and the theory of special functions.

The method puts q-differential and deformed q-exponential operators on basic hypergeometric series. Taking the derivative with respect to the parameters of these series brings new formulas out of old ones. Three classic results serve as raw stock: the q-Gauss sum, the q-Chu-Vandermonde sum, and Jackson's transformation formula. Each yields fresh identities under the operators. The paper shows how to make new results in a set way, not by a hunt for each one on its own.
arxiv-2502-21109:
Marina D'Amato, Jeroen van der Laak, and Francesco Ciompi recast tumor detection in pathology slides as a regression problem, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Sound detection in whole-slide images is crucial for cancer diagnosis and treatment planning. Multiple instance learning is the standard weakly supervised approach. It usually needs tumor-free cases as negative examples. Real clinical workflows struggle to supply those.

Instead of sorting slides, their approach works out the tumor percentage in each slide. That target is on hand in clinics across many cancer types. The authors test the approach across organs, specimen types, and clinical scenarios. They test how robust it is when tumor percentages are noisy targets. An amplification technique boosts sensitivity when tumors fill only small regions. Attention and logit maps make what the model predicts clear for pathologists to read.
arxiv-2503-00209:
Vu Minh Hoang Dang and Rakesh Verma gauge vocabulary quality in language data sets with an autoencoder based frame. Word richness shapes model skill, but classic gauges miss context, meaning depth, and build complexity. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Network capacity stands in for richness, diversity, and complexity, giving a live read of how vocabulary size, sentence build, and context depth interact. Tests ran on a fraud text set spanning many domains, and on a classic book set across tongues, genres, and eras. Results back the method's toughness and flex. The authors offer guidance for data curation and model design.
arxiv-2503-00509:
Yuriy Dorn and three co-authors define two new problem classes that unite bandit choice with function optimization. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Classic bandits pick among fixed arms, while optimizers search a curve with only value feedback; the two fields rarely touched.

Here each arm is itself an unknown black-box function to be optimized. One problem asks for learning while earning; the other asks only to name the best function. The setup fits real tasks such as training rival language models. The authors give a reduction that builds bandit algorithms from standard optimizers with known speed. They prove regret bounds inherited from those speeds. Numerical tests show the scheme performs well in practice.
arxiv-2503-01509:
Teemu Säilynoja and three co-authors give practical guidance for checking Bayesian models with pictures. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Analysts plot model predictions against data to judge fit, but common plots can mislead when their hidden assumptions fail.

The authors treat each check itself as a small model that can fail. They offer rules for picking the right plot for continuous data, count data, and mixes of both. Their diagnostics flag when data are likely discrete, when values hit hidden bounds, and when smooth density curves fit poorly. The aim is fewer ad-hoc choices and stronger model criticism. The advice is meant for everyday modeling work, not just theory.
arxiv-2503-02909:
Susan Benecchi and colleagues propose a Roman Space Telescope survey of the deep Kuiper Belt, the solar system's distant fringe of icy bodies. There, object characteristics and the size distribution are inaccessible to any other telescope. The survey's pointing coincides with the search space reachable by NASA's New Horizons spacecraft, so a discovered object might even receive a close flyby.

The survey would discover and determine orbits for as many as nine hundred Kuiper Belt objects. It would characterize the deep belt by finding objects as small as a few kilometers, extending the known size distribution to a new level. That bears on the standard streaming instability model of how these bodies formed, and on the physics of cratering on icy worlds. The survey would also open studies of Kuiper Belt object rotation. Objects found could additionally be observed by New Horizons itself, probing surfaces and satellite systems.
arxiv-2503-03709:
Krishna Akhil and six co-authors trace how polar ring galaxies grow old by comparing three of them at different life stages. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. In these odd galaxies, a ring of gas and stars circles over the poles of the main body. How the ring forms and fades is still debated.

The team fit the light of ring and host apart for each galaxy, a first for this class. Ultraviolet images from an Indian space telescope gave fine spatial detail. Ring stars proved younger than host stars in all three. The age gap shrank along the trio's order, and ring star birth slowed the same way. Gas shares lined up with the same three-stage story. The results sketch a shared life path for these rare systems.
arxiv-2503-03909:
Appelo and Cheng accelerate low-rank solutions of nonlinear matrix equations with a new Anderson method, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Such equations arise when nonlinear partial differential equations are discretized in space. Full solutions are huge, so low-rank forms are essential. Their method, lrAA, performs every step in low-rank form.

An adaptive tolerance schedule trims rank as residuals guide the process. A new cross approximation handles nonlinear terms with error control. It warm-starts each round from the last approximation for speed. Tests span Laplace, Bratu, Monge-Ampere, and Allen-Cahn problems. The method beats rivals on speed and accuracy across the set. It controls both rank growth and iteration counts well.
arxiv-2503-04009:
Marelli and co-authors unmask a new member of a rare class of flaring X-ray pairs from archive data, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Only about fifteen such supergiant fast transients are known. The source was picked for its odd swings in a timing catalog.

Its light twin reads as a far, dimmed blue giant star, the mark of a massive pair. In bursts it fires near nonstop flares for thousands of seconds, then sleeps about three fifths of the time. Swings top five hundred fold between sleep and flare. No giant outbursts are on record. The full pattern earns it a place in the rare class. Readers get a new flare star profiled from cold data.
arxiv-2503-05109:
Jiaying Liu, Yiheng Su, and Praneel Seth test whether AI can understand videos about mental health in this two thousand twenty-five study. Multimodal language models are increasingly used in computational social science, but mostly on text. The authors ran one of the first case studies of model-assisted video analysis, using a vision-language model to interpret abstract concepts in videos where people disclose experiences of depression. They analyzed hundreds of keyframes from over one hundred forty YouTube Shorts.

Four abstract concepts about video-mediated self-disclosure framed the task. By studying the model's self-generated explanations, the team found that how fully a concept was operationalized changed the model's interpretations. More detail, however, did not reliably improve agreement with human judgment. Concept complexity and the variety of video genres also affected alignment. The authors urge custom prompts per concept and more human-centered evaluation of AI research assistants.
arxiv-2503-05209:
Xiaokang Zhang and Bhargav Rallabandi study how two suspended particles act on each other in a uniform flow that shakes back and forth, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Over time, the push and pull between them comes from inertia and viscosity. The team builds a theory for the case where each swing of the flow is small.

The flow near both particles is set out with dual multipole expansions. A tool called the Lorentz reciprocal theorem then gives the time-averaged force between the pair. The results match data from past computer runs well. The team also gives simpler formulas for the force, for cases where the Stokes layers around the two do not overlap. The same approach works when the particles are free to swing and drift with the flow. It gives a fast way to work out these forces.
arxiv-2503-05309:
Rajini Makam and co-authors compare two neural networks that estimate speed for underwater robots from a Doppler log, in work from twenty twenty-five. Underwater craft cannot use satellite signals, so they rely on inertial sensors that drift. A Doppler velocity log, which bounces sound off the sea floor, is key to staying on course.

One network reads spatial patterns with a convolutional design. The other uses memory to read time patterns and handles biased, noisy data.
