Both trained and tested on real craft data from the Mediterranean Sea. Each beat the standard least squares method, cutting error by more than half with tighter spread. The memory model is put forward for noisy settings.
arxiv-2503-05409:
Sunit Ghosh, Younis Ahmad Bhat, and Jitendriya Swain sharpen uncertainty bounds for a fractional wave transform, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The bounds cap how tight a signal and its transform can both sit. Two gaps in past work are closed here.

The exact shapes that hit equality in older bounds are spelled out. A new bound of mixed-power type is proved for the fractional Dunkl case. At the square case, a still sharper bound follows. Terms for equality are given for both new bounds too. Readers in signal math get complete statements where past ones stopped short.
arxiv-2503-06109:
Keshu Wu, Xinyue Ye, Suphanut Jamonnak, and Xin Feng wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It recasts campus course timetabling as a mobility problem, and solves it with a digital twin of Texas A and M University.

A timetable is a movement policy: it sends thousands of students across campus in set waves. Hard rules on rooms and clashes must hold while soft aims on taste and fit are weighed. The frame joins two kinds of recommendation filters with a feedback loop that refines the picks. A score blends room use, travel span, travel time, and floor shifts. Real campus data show less travel friction and better room use than past plans.
arxiv-2503-08309:
Denis Brazke, Gianna Götzmann, and Hans Knüpfer study the limit shape of higher-order phase transition models. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. Such models blur a sharp border between phases by a small width set by a parameter. As that width shrinks to zero, the model should tend to a sharp-border form.

They prove that limit, in the gamma sense, for models of order two or more. A key value tied to the well shape and the order splits the tame case from the wild one. The proof leans on a new bound that ties high-order slopes to low ones, in the style of classic interpolation bounds.
arxiv-2503-10509:
Sahar Admoni, Omer Ben-Porat, and Ofra Amir present, in twenty twenty-five, a framework that turns an AI agent's policy into a plain text summary. Explaining reinforcement learning agents is hard, since their policies emerge from complex rewards and neural codes. Past tools show curated demos of local behavior, leaving users to infer the global strategy. Their framework, SySLLM, converts action trajectories into structured text. A large language model then writes a coherent summary of the agent's goals, exploration style, and decision patterns.

It scales to long, rich tasks with no task-specific tuning. Expert checks aligned well with human analyses. In a large user study, three quarters of participants preferred these summaries over the best demo-based explanations.
arxiv-2503-14809:
Jeff Jewett and Sandhya Saisubramanian teach control policies, in a 2025 preprint, by planning over sketches drawn by human experts. In complex continuous tasks, exact models are hard to write and trial-and-error learning is slow. Experts often can sketch the task's broad shape, though, even when details escape them. Older layered methods lean on such sketches mostly in discrete settings. They fail to carry learning across tasks too. The authors build a hierarchy that plans dynamically over the expert's sketch.

The planner sets subgoals, and a goal-conditioned policy learns to reach them. Sparse rewards are padded using the sketch's value estimates. Tests ran on suites of machine-generated continuous control tasks. The method beat rival hierarchical learners on learning speed and task completion. It also scaled to harder tasks. Policies from some tasks handled new ones with no extra training, a zero-shot transfer the authors stress.
arxiv-2503-15309:
The Euclid Collaboration releases its Quick Data Release Q1 study of galaxy shapes across cosmic time. The paper from twenty twenty-five fits Sersic profiles to galaxies in the new space telescope data. A Sersic fit gives a compact read of how a galaxy's light falls off from its core. With one form fit across eras, shape change over time can be charted fairly.

Euclid's wide, sharp view supplies the sample for this first quick release. Morphology trends with look-back time are the science target. Such trends test how galaxies assemble and settle into disks and spheroids. The author list spans the full collaboration, as survey papers do. The work marks an early science harvest from Euclid's sky survey. Later releases will widen the sample and deepen the fits.
arxiv-2503-15909:
Ankita and Arpita Chatterjee study how non-Gaussian entangled resources perform in continuous-variable quantum teleportation, under realistic conditions, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Three resources are compared through their characteristic functions. They are a two-mode squeezed vacuum, a photon-subtracted squeezed state, and a photon-added squeezed state. Past theory is extended to take in flaws seen in real experiments.

Photon losses and imperfect measurements are built into the analysis. Such flaws usually degrade teleportation. Even so, the photon-subtracted state beats the other two in the low squeezing regime. Its fidelity stays above the classical threshold. That suggests it is robust for practical use. The authors also examine Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen correlations of the three resources. The photon-subtracted state again shows the strongest correlations. The study ties modeling in theory to real flaws, for teleportation at high fidelity.
arxiv-2503-16209:
Moritz Moeller and Sebastian Neumayer lead a team showing that three sparse recovery decoders can rebuild a whole function from a sprinkling of random samples. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Reconstructing high-dimensional functions from few evaluations is a core sampling problem. Guarantees matter as much as algorithms.

Root-lasso, greedy pursuit, and a matching pursuit variant all earned the same style of guarantee. Their error tracks the best possible sparse approximation plus the cost of the search space. Sample counts need only grow with sparsity and mild log factors. A lower bound proves one log factor cannot be removed. That makes the guarantees instance-optimal in a precise sense. Numerical experiments found the bounds realistic in practice. Sampling widths for function classes follow as corollaries. The work unifies algorithms usually analyzed apart.
arxiv-2503-17409:
Minheng Xiao and Xian Yu tackle delayed rewards in reinforcement learning in a 2025 paper. In many tasks, feedback arrives only at the end of a long run, leaving each step unrated. Existing redistribution methods spread that final reward back over steps but usually treat steps as independent. Their method models the reward as drawn from a Gaussian process, which links steps through a kernel.

Fitting the model to the observed total return, with a leave-one-out trick over the whole trajectory, also adds a natural penalty on overconfidence. Paired with a standard off-policy algorithm, the spread-out rewards were denser and more informative. Benchmark tests showed better learning speed and final performance.
arxiv-2503-19609:
Jérémy Thibault, Joseph Lenormand, and Catalin Hritcu simplify, in a 2025 preprint, the hardest step in proving a compiler secure. A secure compiler must guarantee that attacks on the compiled code can be mirrored by attacks on the source. Showing that needs a back-translation: turn any attack on the target back into a source-level attacker. Their method records an attack's interaction as a set of call and return events. Those events form a tree. The tree is then rebuilt, step by step, as a source program that replays the same trace.

Each small step adds one piece of control logic to the rebuilt program. Every middle language gets its own semantics, with ghost state holding the bookkeeping. Correctness follows from several small simulation proofs. The whole construction is mechanized in the Rocq proof assistant. The authors say the nanopass style makes a formerly brutal proof manageable.
arxiv-2503-20709:
Farzad Milani builds a cosmology in which the universe bounces instead of beginning in a singularity, using a modified theory of gravity. The theory rewrites the gravitational action using three ingredients: ordinary curvature, a Gauss-Bonnet combination, and the trace of the matter stress-energy, with two scalar fields included. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Milani works in the standard flat expanding-universe geometry, derives the motion equations and the effective density and pressure. Extracts modified versions of the Friedmann equations that govern expansion.

At the bounce moment the expansion rate and scale factor reverse, removing the singular start. Five sample versions of the theory are reconstructed, and in each the effective equation of state crosses the phantom divide line, a crossing tied to the bounce. Numerical checks and plots back the construction, which the author presents as a generalization of several earlier modified gravity structures.
arxiv-2503-22109:
Seungjae Lee and five co-authors simulate pairs of black holes inside dense star clusters. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, places a mid-size black hole at the cluster core. Such holes may weigh from a few hundred to a few thousand suns. They can pair with much smaller black holes and spiral together.

Future space and ground detectors could catch these unequal pairs as waves in space-time. The team runs full star-by-star simulations on fast graphics hardware. They track how the pairs form, harden, and merge. The results show which pairs the next detectors are most likely to hear. The work ties cluster life to future wave finds.
arxiv-2503-22609:
Giuseppe Gaetano Luciano rebuilt a holographic dark energy model in twenty twenty-five inside a modified gravity theory. The model swaps the usual black hole entropy for Barrow entropy, which bakes in quantum corrections to a horizon's geometry. He places it in f(G,T) gravity and studies a flat universe filled with pressureless dust.

Using the Hubble horizon as the cutoff and a power-law expansion history, he tracks the equation of state, deceleration, and sound speed. With a conserved energy-momentum tensor, the model slides from quintessence-like behavior into the phantom domain, ending in a freezing pattern. Without conservation, it starts phantom-like and thaws toward a cosmological constant or quintessence state, with sound speed turning positive in the far future. The variants improve on the original holographic model's fit to cosmic acceleration.
arxiv-2503-23309:
Trifoi wrote in twenty twenty-five about fixed point theorems for a generalized class of mappings in Hilbert spaces. A fixed point is an input that a mapping leaves unchanged. Nonexpansive mappings never stretch distances between points. Trifoi extends known results for single-valued enriched mappings to multivalued ones. A new class, star-b-enriched nonexpansive mappings, is introduced. An existence theorem for its fixed points is established in Hilbert space.

Weak and strong convergence results follow for a classic iteration process. The Krasnoselskii iteration averages a mapping with the identity to home in on fixed points. Both mapping classes are covered by the convergence proofs. Such theorems underpin algorithms for equations and optimization problems. The paper is a technical contribution to nonlinear analysis. It widens the family of mappings with guaranteed iteration behavior.
arxiv-2504-00209:
Xiaowei Pang and Jun Wang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It gives a new iterated Tikhonov method for Fredholm integral equations of the first kind, a classic hard inverse problem.

Such equations are ill-posed: small noise in the data can wreck a naive solve, so a penalty term steadies it. The new iteration is proved to reach the best rate under a set prior guess. Numeric tests set it next to the classic iterated Tikhonov method and the Landweber iteration on the split form of the task. The new method holds up well on both soundness and speed. The paper is a compact methods note.
arxiv-2504-01809:
Cong Xu, Hong-Bo Jin, and Yue-Liang Wu test a quantum gravity idea in twenty twenty-five. Gravitational Quantum Field Theory tries to reconcile general relativity with quantum field theory. It makes a sharp prediction about gravitational waves. General relativity allows only two tensor polarization modes.

The new theory also favors a third mode, a massless breathing scalar mode. That extra mode is a clean target for testing quantum gravity. The authors build a model-independent response frame for space detectors like LISA and Taiji. It includes first-order orbital dynamics in the solar system frame. With it, they assess how well future detectors can split and spot tensor and scalar parts across the sky.
arxiv-2504-02209:
Haoyu Li and Zhi-Qiang Wang study sign changing solutions, called nodal solutions, for a set of linked curved equations in math physics. Each part of the system must cross zero a set number of times. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The linked system sits in a round bounded domain in two or three space dimensions. The link strength lies in the push apart range, where parts repel each other. The authors prove that many solutions exist with the nodal pattern set in advance, for both plain positive and sign changing cases. They also bound how the nodal counts of gaps between parts can vary, from above and below.
arxiv-2504-02809:
Christian Dioguardi, Antonio Iovino, and Antonio Racioppi test, in twenty twenty-five, a class of cosmic inflation models against the latest telescope data. Inflation is the burst of expansion thought to have set up the universe. Their models, called fractional attractors, arise from a variant of gravity theory known as Palatini gravity. Each model is defined by a scalar potential, an energy landscape for the field driving inflation. For certain choices of that landscape, the models predict two key numbers: the spectral index, which describes ripple sizes, and the tensor-to-scalar ratio, which gauges gravitational waves.

Both numbers fall inside the one-sigma band of combined ACT and Planck data, across a wide parameter range. They also give a numerical fit for two simple cases, quadratic and quartic fractional potentials.
arxiv-2504-05609:
Boris Mordukhovich, Yixia Song, Shangzhi Zeng, and Jin Zhang developed new solution methods in twenty twenty-five for a hard class of optimization problems. In these problems, the goal and the limits are written as differences of two functions, with no promise that either part is convex. Such forms show up in design and economics but resist standard solvers.

Their methods extend the sequential quadratic approach, solving a chain of simpler convex problems built from slopes and sub-slopes of the true functions. They prove the methods converge for wide families of functions, using a known curve condition. The framework also covers problems with variational inequality limits, recast through gap functions. Tests on network design problems showed the methods work well in practice.
arxiv-2504-06609:
Sujay Khandagale and five colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on InteractRank, a system for the pre-ranking stage of web-scale personalized search. Modern search engines refine billions of items through stages: retrieval, pre-ranking, full ranking, and blending. Pre-ranking must score hundreds of thousands of candidates down to a few thousand, fast.

Pre-rankers usually use two-tower models, which are efficient but miss the rich interactions between a query and an item that full rankers exploit. Adding cross interaction features to pre-ranking is hard because of the computational cost at that scale. InteractRank integrates those features into pre-ranking while keeping it efficient enough for production use. Better pre-ranking means the full ranker sees a stronger shortlist, improving final search quality.
arxiv-2504-07809:
Alban Bloor Riley, Marcus Webb, and Michael Baker show that a classic lift-and-project algorithm for inverse eigenvalue problems is secretly Riemannian gradient descent. Their paper from twenty twenty-five revisits the method of Chen and Chu, which fits selected eigenvalues of an unknown Hermitian matrix from an affine family. Each iteration lifts the guess onto the spectral manifold, then projects back to the affine subspace. The equivalence proof reframes both steps in one geometric language.

The insight buys a faster implementation and sharper global convergence analysis. Extra constraints bolt on naturally in the manifold view. Numerical tests show order-of-magnitude speedups for extreme or targeted eigenvalues. A neutron scattering problem on manganese, fitting sixteen measured eigenvalues of a huge sparse matrix, demonstrates the method.
arxiv-2504-08409:
Gerasimov and six co-authors look at sharp light peaks in flat sheets that guide light, and they call their shapes with machine learning. The peaks come from bound states that stay safe by same form, in gratings with flat same form. Rules for joined modes show two traits rule the shape of the line for light that goes through.

That rule set holds lopsided Fano shapes, plus Lorentz type and anti Lorentz type shapes. Marks where no light goes through show in all cases. Marks where no light bounces back do not show in the one mode short cut in most cases. A random forest model then calls peak shapes far more true than least squares fits. Its flaw is ten times less. The train set held near ten thousand cases. The work links base rules with data led design of light tools.
arxiv-2504-09009:
Tianyu Pan, Vivek Charu, Ying Lu, and Lu Tian tackle a subtle problem in clinical trials. Teams often study secondary outcomes only when the primary outcome shows a clear effect. They may also change course at interim looks. Standard checks control error rates. But they do not ensure that inferences made after such a choice keep their pledged traits.

A plain confidence interval, for one, can cover the truth at a rate far from its stated level once the choice process is counted. The team argues that validity given the choice is what uses in fact need. They build confidence intervals with correct coverage given that choice. The intervals rest on a pivotal value from the truncated normal distribution the choice creates. Theory and broad tests support the method.
arxiv-2504-09809:
Zhimin Li and five co-authors ran a sanity check in twenty twenty-five on whether multimodal models truly read charts when answering questions about them. Visualization question answering is used to grade chart understanding, by analogy with human literacy tests. The authors found models answer many test questions correctly with no chart shown at all, options or not.

Their explanation: the language model's stored knowledge lets it recall answers, bypassing the visual signal entirely. That undermines the test's meaning. They propose a sanity check framework — a rule-based decision tree plus a check table — that separates seeing from recalling in a model's responses. It can validate data sets and flag where vision helps, hurts, or is simply ignored.
arxiv-2504-11909:
Saswati Roy and four co-authors compute how much light bends passing a Kerr-Sen black hole, the rotating charged solution from heterotic string theory. Instead of following geodesics, they treat the curved spacetime as a material medium with a refractive index. That approach worked for the non-rotating Schwarzschild case once the metric was written in isotropic form.

Frame dragging in the Kerr-Sen geometry changes the local speed of light, from which the refractive index follows. In the far-field approximation they derive the deflection angle. Results are compared against the familiar Kerr and Schwarzschild deflections from general relativity. The comparison shows what the string-theory charge and rotation each contribute to the bending.
arxiv-2504-15109:
Three mathematicians wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on geometric inequalities for curved spaces. The results are of Heintze-Karcher type, which bound a domain's volume using the curvature of its boundary. The setting is a class of warped product spaces that are sub-static, a condition borrowed from relativity.

The new inequalities involve a shifted version of mean curvature. One covers domains in hyperbolic space whose boundaries need not bulge outward, a case earlier results missed. As applications, the authors prove uniqueness for surfaces that solve a family of curvature equations, pinning down their shape completely.
arxiv-2504-15409:
Peter Asenbaum and Chris Overstreet comment on a recent test that claimed to see the quantum equivalence principle for matter waves. In matter-wave interferometers, the phase shift that is worked out looks distinct under distinct choices of coordinates. It also looks distinct when a uniform gravitational field is added. The phase shift that can be seen rests on neither.

The two men find that the phase shift the test saw is a magnetic recoil phase shift. It is like the recoil phase shift in light-pulse interferometers. Recoil phase shifts vary in inverse proportion to inertial mass. They do not rest on gravitational mass. That split matters. A recoil effect cannot speak to whether inertial and gravitational mass are the same. The work stresses the gap between magnetic and gravitational effects in quantum mechanics.
arxiv-2504-16909:
Jean Dolbeault and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on a set of inequalities for spinors, the objects that model spin in quantum work. The weights in play are of a named type due to Caffarelli, Kohn, and Nirenberg. For plain functions, much is known about the best cases. For spinors, the picture is richer and less clear.

A key ask is when the best spinors show symmetry, and when that symmetry breaks. No trick to force symmetry is known in the spinor case, unlike for plain functions. The team maps a range of the weights where symmetry holds. Their tools lean on spectra, the sets of values a system can take. The work sorts where the symmetric view is safe.
arxiv-2504-18309:
Turzi and Mehrkanoon present a neural network for short term rain forecasts in twenty twenty-five. Such forecasts, called nowcasts, help with planning and safety. Classic weather models are complex and can be hard to adapt. Learning based models offer a lighter option for some tasks.

Their design, SSA-UNet, builds on an earlier small attention model. It adds a channel shuffling step to boost results while cutting complexity. They train it on Dutch rain data from twenty sixteen to twenty nineteen and French cloud data. The model can output one, six, or twelve forecast maps. A heat map method shows which parts of the input the model finds most useful. Code for the model is shared in public.
arxiv-2504-18509:
Shivam Duggal and nine co-authors grade generated 3D assets with a tool that explains its own scores. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Three-dimensional generators often produce warped or inconsistent objects. Existing metrics ignore geometry or lean on opaque judge models. Coarse verdicts tell builders little about what failed. A fine-grained, readable grader is the goal.

Their Eval3D scores assets across several distinct criteria. Semantic fit and geometric consistency sit at the core. Many desired traits, they note, can be checked directly. Checks replace black-box guessing where possible. Scores point to the exact weakness in an asset. Generation teams gain feedback they can act on. Three-dimensional content tools mature with honest grading.
arxiv-2504-18609:
Annika Morgenstern and a team of co-authors probe how spin states flip in light-emitting materials. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, studies three related emitters used in organic light diodes. These materials can turn triplet states back into light-giving singlet states. The open question is what drives that flip.

The team swaps light hydrogen for a heavier form in one emitter. The flip rate stays set by spin-orbit coupling, not by the weaker force from atomic nuclei. Magnet tests show how charges and triplets clash in each device. Math models back the reading. The results give clear rules for picking emitter traits.
arxiv-2504-20709:
Pyry Herva and Jarkko Kari study patterns of points in space in a mathematics paper from two thousand twenty-five. They look at Delone sets, point patterns where points are neither too close nor too far apart. The question is how local complexity, the variety of small patches, relates to whether the pattern repeats.

Their algebraic approach uses finite relations between shifts of a pattern. They show that any pattern with such relations has one of a simple product form. For patterns with limited local variety, the shift directions can be chosen in a clean way. They then prove when these relations force the pattern to be periodic, and link certain well known sets to low pattern complexity.
arxiv-2504-21409:
Peng Liu and colleagues study smart edge sensing in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Phones and sensors can now sense their surroundings and send data to base stations for heavy computing. Sending all raw data costs bandwidth and time. The authors propose a three-tier setup to share the work. Small devices, edge servers, and cloud servers each run part of one neural network.

Only mid-level features travel up the chain, which cuts the load on the links. The paper also covers how to split the network and aim the radio beams at once. Their design targets sensing tasks that need fast answers. It should interest engineers who build networks where sensing, radio links, and computing must work as one system.
arxiv-2505-01809:
Xiaoqi Li and six co-authors built a weak taught tool to find things in 3D scenes from words. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with visual grounding in point clouds. No box labels guide the learning. Two snags rule: fine kinds blur in sparse cloud form, and many same kind things crowd a scene and pull the eye. Their tool splits the task in two branch paths.

One branch sorts kinds with rich aids; the other picks the one instance meant. That split lets each snag be fought on its own ground. The output is a turned 3D box round the target thing. Readers in vision get a way to ground words in space with far less hand label work.
arxiv-2505-03609:
Ning-An Lai, Jie Shao, Zexian Zhang, and Yi Zhou prove that the skew mean curvature flow is well posed worldwide for small starts, in a critical function space, for mid dimension cases. This flow moves surfaces of codimension two by a twist of their curvature. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

With matched coordinates and a gauge fix, the flow turns into a wave like equation for complex curvature plus an elliptic system. The hard part is ruling frequency clashes at the critical level, where no spare smoothness helps. Two space time gauges, one from a new div curl lemma and one of Morawetz type, split that work. Curvature identities then close the proof.
arxiv-2505-07009:
Han Cheng, Avy Soffer, Zhao Wu, and Xiaohua Yao study when wave tools stay bounded for a higher-order form of a core quantum equation, in low odd dims. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The operator joins a power of the spread term with a fading field. The hard case sits at zero energy, where odd states can linger. The authors sort those states into kinds, with a key split point. Below that split, the wave tools stay bounded for all fine gauges. Past it, the range of gauges shrinks. They cover all odd dims in a set range, with sharp results.
arxiv-2505-10109:
Christopher Wareing, Alasdair Roy, Matthew Golden, Roman Grigoriev, and Steven Tobias compare two machine learning setups that rediscover fluid equations from model run data, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. The testbed is turbulent convection, including Rayleigh-Bénard flow and convective plane Couette flow.

The established SINDy algorithm recovers two-dimensional convection equations from laminar to fairly turbulent regimes, though diffusive terms get harder as turbulence grows. The newer SPIDER setup needs a much smaller term library and recovers equations across a wider range of settings. It also extracts the incompressibility constraint and boundary settings. The authors argue such tools can check numerical solvers, not just fit data.
arxiv-2505-13109:
Guangda Liu and seven co-authors speed up large language model serving in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Long inputs swell a memory store called the KV cache, which grows with context length. Shrinking that cache is vital for cheap deployment. Dropping parts of it hurts accuracy, while fetching parts back is slow. Their system, FreeKV, aims to keep accuracy and gain speed at once.

On the method side, it guesses which cache parts will be needed ahead of time, moving that work off the critical path. Small corrections then catch any misses. On the system side, it splits the cache layout between processor and graphics memory. The split removes a transfer bottleneck. The paper targets engineers who serve very long-context models.
arxiv-2505-14009:
Yuxuan Yao, Linqi Song, and seven co-authors merge language models by watching their inner activity. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, is called ACM. Merging blends skills from several tuned models into one, with no new training. Old merge methods treat every layer as equally key, which wastes the fact that layers do different jobs.

ACM sets a merge weight for each layer from how much its signals agree. Shared signals between the base and tuned models guide the mix. No gradient math or extra training is needed. Tests on long-to-short reasoning and general merges beat all rival methods. One trial on a mid-size model family shows clear gains.
arxiv-2505-15909:
Alex Kogan argues in a solo twenty twenty-five paper that the most simple way to shrink a large language model may be all we need. The method is called Round-to-Nearest, or RTN. It rounds each weight to the nearest low-precision value, which makes the model cheaper to run.

Newer methods claim to beat RTN on most counts, but Kogan pushes back. His tests, built on fast Marlin code, show RTN can match them on accuracy and even run faster. He also shows that raising the precision of just a few key layers lifts accuracy step by step. The claim is that RTN is a sound, low-cost choice for real use.
arxiv-2505-17209:
Huaiyuan Yao and colleagues introduce a self-driving motion planner that keeps learning from rare situations instead of staying fixed after training. Their system, described in twenty twenty-five, pairs large language models with a memory store that saves strategies from past scenes. It works in four stages covering sensing, scene encoding, strategy refinement from memory, and guided reasoning by the language model. The aim is to handle the long tail of uncommon road events that rule-based and standard learning planners often miss.

Tested on a public driving benchmark, the system beat static rule-based and learning-based planners on both common and rare scenes. Because it refines stored strategies rather than retraining from scratch, it can adapt as new cases appear. The authors present the design as a step toward planning that stays flexible in real traffic.
arxiv-2505-18109:
Juliane Haug and Fabian Wunder rewrite high-order formulas for semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering into one smooth form, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Past results split the answer into four zones of the motion plane, for both plain and spin cases. Such splits bloat use and invite seam errors.

By restating the hard parts with single-valued polylog functions, the splits vanish. One unified result now covers the whole motion range. Total formula length shrinks by a third to over a half. The work serves precision tests of the strong force at colliders. Readers in particle theory get cleaner, shorter formulas for a staple process.
arxiv-2505-18609:
Ashwin Sankar and co-authors release a giant speech dataset for Indian languages in a 2025 paper. Their collection covers twenty-three Indian languages plus English, with thousands of hours of speech. Rich text descriptions tag each clip with speaker, accent, emotion, style, and background conditions, drawn from tens of millions of annotations. The aim is speech synthesis that can be steered in fine detail.

Using the data, they built an open text-to-speech system guided by those descriptions. Tests showed it can copy named speakers, follow style descriptions, and hit requested traits accurately. Expressive traits also transferred within and across languages. The authors claim a new standard for this task.
arxiv-2505-20109:
June-Woo Kim and seven co-authors built a language-agnostic framework in twenty twenty-five for detecting suicidal risk in adolescents from speech. Existing detectors are tied to one language, limiting where they can be deployed. The team's pipeline sidesteps that by working through large language models.

Speech is transcribed by an automatic recognizer — in their study, Chinese speech — and language models answer prompted questions that extract risk-related features from the transcript. Features are kept in both Chinese and English for cross-linguistic analysis, then used to fine-tune pretrained language models. Performance matched models fine-tuned directly on the transcripts or on Chinese-only features. The authors present the approach as a route to risk assessment that travels across languages without retraining from scratch.
arxiv-2505-20509:
Tony Kim, Haotian Liu, Chiung-Ting Huang, Ingrid Wu, and Xilin Liu release OpenNIRScap, a cheap open-source cap that reads brain blood flow with near-infrared light. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that functional near-infrared spectroscopy is gentle and live, yet rigs are pricey and bulky. Clinic and lab walls have kept it in. Their cap aims at daily settings.

The build holds many custom sensor boards with dual-tone emitters and light detectors. A central control unit routes the signals through analog switches. A live pipeline turns raw light into blood-flow traces. Bench checks and pilot runs on volunteers caught brain responses to thought tasks. All hardware, software, and interface files are posted in public. The team pitches it as a low-cost on-ramp to portable brain tech.
arxiv-2506-00909:
Ming Hu and Tongwen Wu study booking revenue problems in a 2025 paper, motivated by train tickets and hotel rooms. Each request needs a resource for a run of consecutive days or seats, and requests arrive one by one with known odds. Managers must decide at once whether to accept each request or offer a set of options.

The authors design fast policies and prove how close their revenue comes to the best possible online policy. For fixed request types, their guarantees are constant factors, a big step up from prior non constant bounds. When request types are random, the guarantees shrink by a known factor but stay constant. The results cover both simple acceptance and choice based offers.
arxiv-2506-02509:
Jiajie Fu, Haitong Tang, Arijit Khan, Sharad Mehrotra, Xiangyu Ke, and Yunjun Gao cluster records with a language model instead of comparing them pair by pair. Entity resolution links records that name the same real-world thing, and pairwise checking grows ruinously expensive at scale. Models can cluster a set of records directly in context. The paper maps the design space of that idea.

Set size, diversity, variation, and record ordering all move clustering quality, the experiments show. Their system builds on those lessons, with machinery for merging clusters efficiently and resisting hallucination. Across nine real-world data sets it improved result quality substantially, up to one hundred fifty percent higher accuracy on the headline comparison. Application calls fell as much as fivefold at comparable cost. In-context clustering turns entity resolution into a reading task.
arxiv-2506-04209:
Jingfeng Yang, Ziyang Wu, Yue Zhao, and Yi Ma asked in twenty twenty-five whether image and text encoders really need joint training. Methods like CLIP train both together with contrastive learning, at great cost. Their alternative, LIFT, freezes a large language model as the text encoder and trains only the image encoder to align with it.

Across broad benchmarks and ablations, LIFT proved surprisingly effective. It beat CLIP in most scenarios involving compositional understanding and long captions, while using considerably less compute. The authors frame the result as a first systematic look at how language model embeddings can steer visual learning. The takeaway challenges a default assumption of the field and suggests cheaper routes to language-aligned vision.
arxiv-2506-04509:
Kishan Kumar Ganguly and Tim Menzies report a surprise in software engineering optimization: messy real problems collapse into very few distinct solution buckets. Across thirty-nine multi-objective problems, only a tiny fraction of the expected buckets were ever used, about one hundred out of thousands. They name this the BINGO effect.

Exploiting the collapse changes the economics of search. Their simple algorithms, LITE and LINE, use plain stochastic selection yet match heavyweight optimizers like DEHB. Optimization ran up to ten thousand times faster with comparable effectiveness. The authors explain when simple methods suffice: when the data occupy a small corner of the possible space. Code and data are public.
arxiv-2506-05109:
Tennison Liu and Mihaela van der Schaar argued in a 2025 position paper that truly self-boosting artificial agents must learn to think about their own learning. Today's self-boosting agents do get better with little supervision. But their improvement loops are rigid, transfer poorly between task areas, and may not scale as the agents themselves grow more capable.

Borrowing from human metacognition, the authors define built-in metacognitive learning through three parts: knowledge of one's own capabilities, tasks, and plans. Planning that decides what to learn and how. And testing that reflects on experience to boost future learning. Reviewing current agents, they find most rely on fixed, human-built outer loops instead. Their claim is that many parts for the built-in version already exist in current systems, and assembling them is the route to agents that keep boosting on their own.
arxiv-2506-05209:
Nikhil Kandpal, Brian Lester, and Colin Raffel lead a large team on this paper from two thousand twenty-five. It releases the Common Pile, a vast set of public domain and openly licensed text for training language models.

Most models train on text with no license, which draws legal and moral fire. Past open sets were too small or too rough to train strong models. The Pile draws from dozens of sources: papers, code, books, reference works, lessons, and transcripts. To prove its worth, the team trained two mid-size models on it. Both stand up well next to peers trained on closed text at like cost. The data, build code, and model saves are all public.
arxiv-2506-06409:
Dor Tsur, Carol Xuan Long, Claudio Mayrink Verdun, and a wider team wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It designs watermarks for text written by large language models, marks that prove where the text came from without spoiling it.

Watermarking is hardest when the model's next word is nearly fixed, as in computer code, leaving little room to hide a signal. The authors frame watermark design as a trade-off: raise the chance of detection while bending the text as little as possible. Their analysis yields two new marks, HeavyWater and SimplexWater, both adjustable along that trade-off. Either can be added to any model. On standard tests, both caught marked text reliably while barely changing its quality, above all in the hard, low-choice cases.
arxiv-2506-06709:
Lunrasri and Pongkitivanichkul link black hole heat rules to bounds on early universe inflation, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Their setup uses a three-form field, a cousin of the fields that drive inflation. Classic reasoning caps how heavy a black hole can be in an expanding space. Quantum gravity tweaks add small corrections to that cap.

They demand the tweaks raise entropy, which yields a strict bound. In a local heat cavity, the correction to the peak mass cancels out. So the classic bound is met exactly, not beaten. Applied to inflation, the large-field case gives a Higgs-like hill that fits satellite data. The small-field case fails space-based swampland rules. Heat rules bound the model more tightly than inflation alone.
arxiv-2506-09609:
Haoyu Liu and Zijie Zhuang present a study from twenty twenty-five on the shape traced by a random curve in the plane. The curve type, Schramm-Loewner evolution, is set by one dial. In the range they study, the curve crosses itself but does not fill the plane. The gaps it leaves form a patchwork of zones.

They prove that when the dial sits close to its top mark, the curve's trace holds a copy of a Sierpiński carpet shape. That shape is a square riddled with holes at all scales. A past result then shows the curve cannot be wiped by smooth warps of the plane. The link graph of the gaps is also split in this range.
arxiv-2506-09709:
Alexander Lobashev, Assel Yermekova, and Maria Larchenko wrote a 2025 paper on voice conversion, changing one speaker's voice into another's while keeping the words. Their method needs no training of its own. It improves an existing pipeline called kNN-VC, which normally requires a fair amount of reference audio from the target speaker.

Their version, Factorized MKL-VC, replaces the pipeline's nearest-neighbor step with a factorized optimal transport map, a mathematically principled way of shifting voice features. It works in the feature space of the WavLM speech model and handles uneven variance across feature dimensions. With only five seconds of reference audio, it converts voices across languages, preserving content better than the original on standard test sets.
arxiv-2506-11109:
Yile Chen and five co-authors teach language models geography in twenty twenty-five. Location-based services generate vast mobility data about how users move through cities. Language models could analyze that movement, but two limits block them. Locations are usually given as bare ID numbers with no semantic content. Mobility signals inside the model are also thinly trained.

Their framework, QT-Mob, fixes the location side first. A tokenization module learns compact tokens that carry rich meaning about each place. Those tokens stay compatible with language model input. Complementary fine-tuning stages then deepen the model's grasp of mobility. Readers get urban movement analytics where places mean something to the model, not just index numbers.
arxiv-2506-13509:
Xiaoyang Wei, Camille Kurtz, and Florence Cloppet propose a new way to score medical image search in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Judging retrieval systems usually needs hand-labeled ground truth, which is costly and often missing in medicine. Captions and case reports hold concepts that could serve instead.

Earlier attempts treated those concepts as isolated labels, ignoring how they relate. The authors use knowledge graphs to measure distances between medical concepts. From those distances they build an approximate matching score between concept sets, which stands in for image similarity. Tests on a public data set show the measure is workable and effective. The method lets retrieval quality be judged from text that already travels with the images.
arxiv-2506-15509:
Rindlisbacher, Rummukainen, and Salami measure two traits of the change between two phases of nuclear force in twenty twenty-five. The theory, called SU(N) gauge theory, models the strong force for a set number of colors. At a set heat, matter flips from a confined phase to a free phase. The team worked on a space time grid for up to ten colors.

They held half of each grid in each phase to watch the border between them. Ripples on that border gave the border's tension with fine precision. The heat soaked up at the flip came from a jump in the grid energy. Both traits grew with the square of the color count, plus set corrections.
arxiv-2506-17209:
Kathleen Fraser and three co-authors test what fine-tuning does to safety in twenty twenty-five. Adapting a general language model to a task is now routine. Yet fine-tuning is known to strip safety alignment, even when the new data is harmless. Most developers who fine-tune probably do not know they are shipping a less safe model.

The authors call this a critical failure mode of current models. Malicious users can exploit the same weakness deliberately. Progress requires safety evaluations that are reliable and reproducible. So the paper examines how robust a safety benchmark is to small changes in procedure. Random variation in evaluation setup turns out to matter. Readers get both a warning about fine-tuning and a caution about trusting safety scores too easily.
arxiv-2506-18409:
Assale Adje wrote a solo mathematics paper in two thousand twenty-five on finding the largest term of a number sequence. Given a sequence, the task sounds simple: find its supremum, the least upper bound, and an index where the biggest term occurs. For sequences with no neat formula, that task can be hard to make rigorous.

Adje builds upper bounds from pairs of shrinking sequences made of rising functions and scalars. Each pair yields whole numbers that can point to the index of the maximum. He proves such pairs always exist. He then tests the method on famous sequences, including the logistic, Fibonacci, and Syracuse sequences, and on peak problems in control systems.
arxiv-2506-19809:
Li and Zhu propose a shared way to check multipartite quantum states. Checking a state means proving the source made the state it claims. Their protocol uses Schmidt decomposition and mutually unbiased bases. It works for any multipartite pure state with local tests that adapt as results come in. They also prove a cap on the sample count that holds for all local sizes.

Tests with random states showed a flat sample cost across system sizes. That held even when the source could not be trusted at all. The authors add simpler variants that skip the Schmidt step. The simplest variant needs just two distinct tests to run. Both paths keep the high efficiency of the main protocol.
arxiv-2506-21909:
Justin Reinman and Sunwoong Choi present a test set for finding cracks in bridges and walls. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Crack checks keep roads and buildings safe, but training a vision model needs many labelled images. Real crack photos are slow to gather and hard to repeat.

Their set, CERBERUS, makes fake crack images and builds three-way scenes in a game engine. One scene is a plain wall fly-by, and one is an underpass with hard light and shapes. They test a known detection model with mixes of fake and real data. The mix does best on real images. The set is free for others to use and rerun.
arxiv-2506-22609:
Graham Todd, Alexander Padula, Dennis Soemers, and Julian Togelius set out Ludax. Ludax is a tongue to tell board games that builds to GPU sped code. Tongues that tell games let AI staff test plans through more than one game. They need not hand code each game. Learn by gains, in its turn, has been changed by speed from gear. Libs like JAX drive that speed.

Ludax joins the two thoughts. Write a board game once, and get a fast mock that runs in pairs. It plugs into deep learn paths. The text tells the tongue and the build steps in points. It gives speed tests and a show of train for bots that learn by gains. The frame and more than one game build are open source. They aim at games work from learn by gains to mind work.
arxiv-2506-23209:
Chia-Wen Huang, Haw Hwai, Chien-Chang Lee, and Pei-Yuan Wu build a learning network to sort CT scans by whether the appendix is inflamed. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Fast, right diagnosis of this illness keeps grave harm at bay, yet scan loads can swamp doctors. The network reads the full stack of slices and gives weight to the slices that count most. It learns with help from flat image sets, which sharpens its eye for small sores. A stacked scheme then splits plain cases from hard ones, using pre-trained flat models. The team reports clear gains over past work on both tasks.
arxiv-2507-05209:
Qian Hu untangles overlapping gravitational wave signals by peeling them off one at a time with neural help. The paper from twenty twenty-five looks ahead to third-generation detectors, where overlaps will be routine. Past reports warned that stepwise subtraction can grow errors. Joint fits are truer but cost too much compute. Hu shows the stepwise route can work after all.

Neural density estimators spit out posterior samples fast. That speed makes repeat rounds of subtract-and-refit cheap. With enough rounds, accuracy lands where it should. A likelihood-based resampling step speeds the settling further. The method adapts across source types and time gaps. Hu offers it as a general answer to the overlap problem that next-era detectors will face daily.
arxiv-2507-10409:
Amine Lbath and Ibtissam Labriji wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It weighs the energy cost of an AI receiver for fifth-generation networks, and then shrinks that cost by knowledge distillation.

The receiver, DeepRx, is a deep convolutional net that decodes radio signals. The team gauges its draw by work per watt and per clock, and checks the gauges against real use, where memory traffic shapes the bill. Training and live use are weighed apart. A small student net is then taught to mimic the big teacher, at tuned sizes and settings. The students show a lower error floor at each signal grade. Green AI for radio gear, the work shows, need not mean weak AI.
arxiv-2507-12309:
Ghaed Sharaf computed shape counts for singular spaces in this mathematics paper from twenty twenty-five. The spaces are links of isolated singularities inside compact toric varieties of real dimension eight. A link is the rim where a small sphere meets the space around the singular point. The author uses the cell structure of these links to find their Betti numbers.

Those numbers count holes of each dimension in the link. He also builds the intersection spaces tied to the links. A duality in those spaces shows the Betti numbers hold just one non-combinatorial parameter. The same held in dimension six, studied before. The final part extends the picture to link bundles over smaller toric bases.
arxiv-2507-13209:
Maximilian Stadelmaier rebuilds cosmic ray air showers with a universality model in a 2025 dissertation-style study from the Pierre Auger Observatory. When an ultra-high-energy cosmic ray hits the upper air, it spawns a vast shower of particles. Universality says showers sharing energy, angle, depth of maximum, and muon count should share the same particle spread along and across the shower.

A model built on cascade equation solutions, extended with hadronic parts, turns detector readings into estimates of those key parameters. Cheaper, principled work helps the observatory squeeze physics from every rare event.
arxiv-2507-13309:
Hanxiu Zhu, Ruijia Chen, and Yuhang Zhao designed FocusView for viewers with ADHD who watch informational videos. Their twenty twenty-five paper reports both the design and a user study. Videos carry much teaching and work information today. Yet moving images, music, and overlays can pull attention away from the main point.

FocusView lets viewers adjust parts of a video to suit themselves. Twelve participants with ADHD tested the interface. They found videos easier to watch, with fewer distractions. Views differed, since some found background music helpful rather than harmful. The authors warn that too many controls can distract users themselves. Future systems should keep choices limited and personal.
arxiv-2507-14409:
Max Gardenswartz and co-authors solve in 2025 a control problem where the node you must steer cannot be touched directly. In a network, friendly nodes can only push their neighbors, hoping the effect reaches a target whose behavior is unknown. The target must follow a set path anyway.

The team uses a graph neural network, whose message passing mirrors the network itself, so nodes learn the target's habits together in real time. On top sits a layered control design with a mathematical proof of stability. Computer simulations show the combined system keeps the target on course. The method suits settings like coordinated drones or networked machines where direct access is impossible.
arxiv-2507-14809:
Zhong, Zhang, and Li present Light Future, predicting robot action frames with an image editing model, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Forecasting what a robot will see guides safer decisions. Video prediction models are heavy and slow by contrast. Their method repurposes InstructPix2Pix for future frame generation.

One current image plus a text instruction is all it needs. The model forecasts the view one hundred frames, ten seconds, ahead. Fine-tuning adapts the editor to robotic tasks specifically. Image quality scores beat state-of-the-art baselines on a robot data set. Low compute and fast inference suit robotics and sports analytics.
arxiv-2507-17809:
Scholtz and a large team of co-authors report deep telescope observations in two thousand twenty-five of a galaxy seen as it was in the early universe. The galaxy, GS-z11-1, lies at a redshift of about eleven. The James Webb Space Telescope took detailed spectra of its light.

The spectra show several emission lines from carbon, oxygen, neon, and hydrogen. The pattern fits star formation, with a possible added role for an active galactic nucleus. The galaxy is very compact and low in heavy elements, yet rich in carbon compared with oxygen. That mix fits more than one path for early enrichment by stars. Unlike some compact galaxies, it shows no strong nitrogen lines linked to a second wave of stars.
arxiv-2507-18109:
F. M. Maccagni and P. Serra survey cold gas in galaxies of the Fornax cluster in a 2025 astronomy study. Cluster galaxies often stop forming stars, and losing their neutral hydrogen is a prime suspect in that shutdown. The MeerKAT telescope in South Africa is mapping that gas deeply and sharply across a wide patch centered on this nearby, low-mass cluster.

Most of the survey was complete when the authors wrote. Early analysis of the cluster center traces where hydrogen has been stripped away. Watching gas removal in a modest cluster shows environmental effects that also operate, more violently, in richer systems.
arxiv-2507-19709:
Hao Gao and Hanlun Lei hone the rules for flips of paths in three body sets that rank mild in tiers. A case is worlds in pairs of stars. In such sets the pull of the far body slow twists the in path. A named act can flip which way it leans. Bounds named for Brown, in the base count rules, are key for true long term calls.

The team grows Brown bounds to the next rank past four, an eight fold rank. They ease the join terms with free choice in set change rules. As tiers grow weak, zones that flip grow more lopsided. The bounds clear up that break in same form. Cuts named for Poincaré, small step rules, and a grown swing close guess all match well. They match most at high stretch of path.
arxiv-2507-19809:
Fang, Moon, Tang, and Meng wrote in twenty twenty-five about robust control for mean-field stochastic systems with extra affine terms. Mean-field systems couple each agent to the population average. The H2 and H-infinity criteria balance average performance against worst-case disturbance. Their setting runs in continuous time over a finite horizon. A mean-field bounded real lemma gives exact conditions for the disturbance bound. Forward-backward stochastic equations then characterize open-loop optimal strategies.

Closed-loop solvability reduces to solving several coupled equation sets. Riccati equations, backward stochastic equations, and ordinary equations all appear. State-feedback gains come directly from those solutions. Open-loop and closed-loop feasibility turn out to be equivalent. The results extend robust control theory to mean-field settings with drift terms. Large interacting systems, from finance to engineering, motivate the framework.
arxiv-2507-20709:
Clara Grassi and Giovanni Federico Gronchi test which sets of orbit rules can pin a first orbit from two short arcs of sky reads. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five, in the math of orbits.

The full set holds seven rules in four unknowns. With two help terms, it forms a nine-rule system with, in most cases, no answer at all. Past work found one part-set that is sound, and leads to a ninth-degree rule in one range. The team tries all the rest. They find two more sound part-sets, each with an eighteenth-degree rule in the same range. The rest clash. They give a way to tell the cases apart.
arxiv-2507-23209:
Du, Udagawa, and Tateno taught recommender models to mind the clock in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Most systems read the order of past purchases but ignore the gaps between them. Yet a weekly buyer and a yearly buyer with identical histories are different people. Their model, IntervalLLM, feeds those gaps into a language model alongside the items.

A special attention scheme weighs items and intervals jointly. The authors also judge cold-start performance from the interval angle, a new viewpoint. Across three benchmarks, scores rose by about four percent on average. The model led in both warm and cold scenarios. Interval-based cold starts, they note, hurt every method most, marking a research frontier.
arxiv-2508-00709:
Shubham Kumar Nigam and six co-authors build a system that forecasts court rulings in India. Their paper from twenty twenty-five is called NyayaRAG. Past tools in this space read only the case file itself. But Indian courts lean on statutes and past rulings, as common law systems do. The new system feeds those sources to the model too.

NyayaRAG pairs a case's facts with the laws that apply and with like past cases found by sense-based search. It then asks the model to predict the ruling and explain it. The team tested many mixes of inputs. Scores used word-match checks, sense checks, and a model-based judge. Adding the legal sources raised both accuracy and the quality of stated reasons. The setup aims to mirror real court work.
arxiv-2508-03209:
Xinwei Liu and co-authors present a defense in two thousand twenty-five against AI models that guess where a photo was taken. Vision-language models can infer a user's location from a public image with unsettling skill, threatening privacy. Tiny adversarial tweaks to images can fool models, but older methods falter on large photos and small tweak budgets.

Their system, GeoShield, works in three parts. One module separates location clues from the rest of the image content. Another pinpoints the spots that betray place. A third scales the tweaks across image sizes, tuning them globally and locally. In black-box tests the defense beat prior methods while barely touching image quality or meaning. The authors call it the first such shield aimed at modern vision-language models.
arxiv-2508-03509:
Seraj Al Mahmud Mostafa, Aravind Mohan, and Jianwu Wang teach a reinforcement learning agent to run cloud training jobs against deadlines and budgets at once. Static allocation either breaks service agreements or wastes hardware. Writing in twenty twenty-five, their framework balances training time, cost, and agreement compliance, with user preference tilting the mix. Two ideas stand out. Smart initialization from history or quick baseline runs removes the cold start, cutting early exploration overhead sharply. Dynamic weight adaptation then re-prioritizes goals as violation severity changes, making the system self-correcting.

Thirteen diverse workloads ran on production supercomputing infrastructure. Deadline jobs finished much faster, budget jobs cost much less, and overall compliance rose steeply against static baselines, by the authors report. The state description packs utilization, progress, and compliance into one view.
arxiv-2508-04309:
Wojciech Flieger studies Feynman integrals in a twenty twenty-five paper. Banana integrals are a family that appears in particle physics calculations. With generic masses, an integral with a given number of loops obeys differential equations. Flieger presents a small set of differential operators for the general case.

He proves those operators annihilate the integral under dimensional regularization. The count of operators grows only slightly with loop number. He also studies where the generated ideal becomes singular. That locus sits inside the Landau singularities of the first and second type. Using a matrix method, he computes the holonomic rank up to eight loops. The values match the known counts of master integrals. He conjectures the operators generate the full annihilating ideal.
arxiv-2508-08409:
Shober tests if meteorites come in streams in this two thousand twenty-five astronomy paper. If some meteorites share a parent asteroid breakup, their orbits should cluster in a way that stands out. The author sets forty-six meteorite falls, instrument-seen, and five hundred thirty-five meteorite-dropping fireballs off against catalogs. The catalogs are many thousands of asteroids from NEODyS-2 and NASA/JPL. Likeness is scored by a function built from four geocentric values stating each encounter geometry.

Weight was judged against synthetic groups built with kernel density estimation or randomized longitude, repeated for the three-sigma band for chance. The likeness spread showed no excess and no clustering that fits streams. If any meteorites do come in streams, they form under a tenth of a percent of all falls. Asteroid processes might shape meteorite features, but they are not making orbital families that can be told apart.
arxiv-2508-09209:
Kun Ming Goh compares plain and hybrid quantum-classical versions of generative adversarial networks, the paired models that learn to fake data. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. In these pairs, a generator tries to fool a judge. The judge's pushback trains the generator toward realism.

Goh swaps the generator's random seed source for small quantum circuits. Three variants used three, five, and seven qubits. All ran on a simulator with realistic noise, matching today's fragile quantum gear. The task was writing two handwritten digits. The plain classical model still scored best on image quality. The seven-qubit hybrid closed much of the gap late in training. The three-qubit one stalled early. Training time rose only modestly despite the quantum sampling.
arxiv-2508-09409:
Xiang Lv studies a broad random process tied to equations where the present state depends on past states plus noise, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The process extends the classic Ornstein-Uhlenbeck form to affine equations with memory. Core traits of the process are set out and proved.

The main use is a clean routine to show that random balance points exist and are unique for nonlinear versions. All pull-back paths are shown to be drawn to those points in several senses of closeness. Worked examples carry the main claims. The results sharpen and simplify earlier findings by Jiang and Lv. Readers in stochastic analysis get a tidier toolkit.
arxiv-2508-09909:
Gabriele Paolini and colleagues report on a twenty twenty-five shape analysis contest about relief patterns carved or molded onto three-dimensional surfaces. Earlier contests mostly asked systems to retrieve similar shapes. This track asked for two skills at once: first mark the regions of a surface that carry each distinct relief pattern, then find other surfaces bearing similar patterns. Test objects were computer-generated triangle meshes with patterns embedded on their surfaces. Teams submitted automatic methods, and the organizers compared how well each one segmented and retrieved.

Performance showed that the combined task is still hard and unsolved in general. The report reviews the submitted methods, points out where current techniques break down, and suggests directions for future work. All contest materials are posted on the track web page, so later researchers can rerun the comparison and try to beat the results.
arxiv-2508-10009:
Six researchers, Hojun Jin, Eunsoo Hong, Ziwon Hyung, Sungjun Lim, Seungjin Lee, and Keunseok Cho, present a new design for speech-to-text models. Their twenty twenty-five paper starts from a flaw in the usual design. When one model is trained for many tasks with shared parts, the tasks can clash and hurt each other.

Their design, called S-MoE, gives each task its own expert part. A special token routes each task to its expert, so no learned gate is needed. They use it for two tasks at once: writing down speech, and translating speech. It also takes in sound of mixed quality. Tests show a clear drop in word errors when the design is used in both halves of the model.
arxiv-2508-11209:
Fadhilla and co-authors set out a way to steer skyrmions with light, not charge flow. Skyrmions are small swirls in a spin field that can move as one part. A time-tied drive term comes from a Zeeman link with round-spun light. The team works the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert form to first order for the shift. A breath-form guess based on the Belavin-Polyakov shape tracks the swirl edge. That edge warps in a one-way breath mode as light acts.

The warp makes a skyrmion count flow that is not zero. In push space, the paths close in a loop by the read. Loop traits rest on field size, link strength, and the damp term. The team frames count flow as a low-loss stand-in for charge flow.
arxiv-2508-13609:
Karol Palka and Tomasz Pełka classify a family of algebraic surfaces case by case. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. It is the third in a series on del Pezzo surfaces of Picard rank one. The surfaces may be singular and live over any algebraically closed field. A number called height guides the sorting. Height counts how a resolution's fibers meet the exceptional divisor.

Earlier work settled heights up to two. This article completes the height three case. Height four is expected to cap the story, with small exceptions in low characteristics. The classification proceeds up to isomorphism. Algebraic geometers gain a fuller census of these surfaces. Singularity theory benefits from the explicit lists.
arxiv-2508-13809:
Omran Ahmadi and Hassan Norouzi extend a rank method for tensors in this 2025 paper. The slice rank lemma of Tao has proved many results in extremal combinatorics. The authors define triangular tensors, which generalize triangular matrices. They then prove a slice rank style lemma for the new objects.

With the new tools they give shorter proofs of known theorems on set intersections. The Frankl-Wilson and Snevily theorems, with modular constraints, are among them. One Snevily result is also improved in special cases. Further bounds follow for generalizations of the reverse odd town problem. Readers get both a new method and a set of cleaner arguments for classic results in the field.
arxiv-2508-15209:
Xijun Hu, Zhiwen Qiao, and Guowei Yu published a 2025 mathematics paper on orbits in the spatial Kepler problem, the motion of a body under gravity. They study what happens when a small extra force is added that respects two symmetries: rotation around one axis and reflection through the middle plane.

With total spin fixed, the system simplifies to two degrees of freedom. For small added forces and suitable energy, the authors show the motion lives on a surface shaped like a sphere. On each such surface sits one special symmetric brake orbit, linked with a flat orbit like rings in a chain. Under extra conditions, they prove infinitely many repeating relative orbits exist. The results apply to satellites around a squashed planet and to pyramid-shaped arrangements of masses.
arxiv-2508-15609:
Gang Li, Ying-Ying Li, Sida Lu, and Ye-Ling Zhou constrain a light right-handed neutrino within the minimal left-right symmetric model, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. That model offers an elegant, testable account of neutrino masses. The authors work in its type-II seesaw scenario without left-right mixing. They gather limits widely.

Collider searches, meson decays, supernovae, neutrinoless double beta decay, and cosmology all feed in. The double beta decay limits use an advanced effective field theory approach with updated nuclear matrix elements. The supernova cooling bound is refreshed with the latest simulations. New limits come from energy deposition and cosmic nucleosynthesis. One region survives every constraint. There the neutrino mass lies between seven hundred mega-electronvolts and one giga-electronvolt. The right-handed W boson sits just under twenty tera-electronvolts. Only future tonne-scale double beta decay tests can probe it.
arxiv-2508-15709:
Yifei Wang and five co-authors tackle position bias in long texts, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Models often read the start or end of a long text well, but miss facts in the middle. Past fixes changed the model build or needed costly training on huge sets of text.

Their method, Pos2Distill, moves skill from strong spots to weak spots inside the same model. One form fits search tasks, and the other fits tasks that need step-by-step thought. Both rest on the same thought: use the gap itself to close the gap. Tests show more even scores across all spots, plus gains that carry to new tasks.
arxiv-2508-16909:
Shifan Kang, Bingsong Long, and Hairong Yuan prove the hypersonic similarity law for steady flows past thin bodies. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. At hypersonic speed, a thin body stirs the air only a little, and a classic law says the flow turns on one combined value, not on shape and speed apart.

They work in a framework of measure-valued solutions to the Euler equations. Two cases are proved: flow past a long curved wedge, and flow past a long cone. As the body thins and speed grows with their product fixed, the true flow tends to a small-disturbance form. Plain shapes for those limit solutions make the proof go through.
arxiv-2508-17509:
Michael Podsiadly and Brendon Lay combine two self-supervised learning methods in a 2025 vision study. Training image models without labels saves costly annotation, and both parent methods work well alone. One uses a teacher and student network, while the other reduces redundancy in learned features. Each also has a weakness, from sensitivity to image changes to needing very large batches.

Their hybrid, DinoTwins, joins the two training objectives so each covers the other's gaps. The model trains on a large photo dataset and is tested with only a small share of labels. The aim is strong image features that need fewer labels and less computing power.
arxiv-2508-19109:
Weiqiang Yang, Sibo Zhang, Olga Mena, Supriya Pan, and Eleonora Di Valentino vary dark sector couplings in two thousand twenty five. Dark energy and dark matter may exchange energy as they evolve. The coupling strength is usually frozen as a constant. No deep reason forces that choice, they note.

Two time varying coupling forms are fit to fresh data. Planck cosmic microwave data and DESI baryon oscillation measures enter. Supernova samples add further constraints to the fits. One scenario shows a nonzero interaction beyond ninety five percent confidence. Other cases stay mild or inconclusive in their tests.
arxiv-2508-19609:
Zhuohang Zhu, Haodong Chen, Qiang Qu, and Vera Chung present a foundation model for forecasting financial series in a 2025 study. Markets shift patterns over time, differ across stocks, commodities, and futures, and arrive at resolutions from seconds to weeks. Models trained narrowly overfit and fail when conditions change.

FinCast aims at one model that handles that variety directly. A foundation design pretrains broadly so new forecasting jobs need less custom work. Stable forecasts support economic stability, policy choices, and investment planning. The study frames the three sources of pattern shift and builds the model to answer each of them.
arxiv-2509-00009:
Carla Feistner, Francesca Ziliotto, Barbara Wohlmuth, and Gabriele Chiogna compare ways to gauge which design choices drive mixing in chaotic flows in 2025. Pumps that inject and extract fluid can stir two species well, but gains vary a lot with pump rate, well site, and run time. Sensitivity analysis ranks those choices, yet the best method hinges on the system and its cost.

Their study tracks sensitivity over time in two flows of distinct complexity. One flow uses two settings, the other uses four. Choice of mixing gauge, such as plume area or peak concentration, also proves system-bound. The results guide teams that must pick a cheap, apt gauge before they tune a mixing design.
arxiv-2509-00109:
Theodor Stoecker, Samed Bayer, and Ingo Weber review bias fixes for recommender systems caught in AI feedback loops in 2025. Such systems retrain on user reactions to their own picks, so bias can grow and fairness can shrink over rounds. Most fixes are tested on one static split, which leaves their long-run fairness unknown.

The review screens hundreds of papers and keeps twenty-four core studies from 2019 to 2025 that test across many rounds or in live trials. Each is coded on six facets, from method and bias type to domain and task, and sorted into a taxonomy. The map gives industry a quick checklist for robust fixes. It also marks the most urgent gaps for researchers to close next.
arxiv-2509-00509:
Yasser Benigmim leads a team of seven authors on learning from black-box models. A black-box model works through an online service. It hides its weights, its training data, and its scores. The team asks how a local model can still learn from it. Access is limited to one-hot outputs. That means one chosen label for each image.

Such broad models outline objects in images. They do so best at a scale that varies by class. The team calls this snag the curse of resolution. Their ATGC method uses attention maps from DINOv2. The maps pick the best scale for each class. Those scales guide fake training labels. Tests show clear gains across several datasets.
arxiv-2509-00609:
Runcao Lyu, writing alone, studies a free boundary problem. The problem involves the fractional Laplacian. That operator captures long-range diffusion, where effects spread far. The unknown region has one phase. Its edge is a free boundary whose shape must be found. Earlier work by De Silva, Savin, and Sire proved a first level of smoothness for flat boundaries.

Lyu raises that smoothness to the highest level. In plain terms, the boundary is as smooth as it can be. The result covers the fractional range stated in the record. It extends a known finding for the half-power case. That finding was due to De Silva and Savin. Such results matter for a clear reason. They confirm that flat free boundaries hide no corners or rough spots at small scales.
arxiv-2509-01109:
Turning an image into tokens, small units a model can process, is usually done on a fixed grid that treats every region the same. Zhengqiang Zhang, Rongyuan Wu, Lingchen Sun, and Lei Zhang propose GPSToken, a method that adapts token shapes to the image itself. Areas with rich texture get different treatment from flat, plain areas.

First, a step driven by entropy, a measure of detail, splits the image into regions of like texture and varied size. Each region is then described by a two-dimensional Gaussian, a smooth hill shape that marks its place, spread, and content. A transformer tunes these shapes as it learns. The authors argue this flexible layout captures image structure better for both describing and generating pictures.
arxiv-2509-01209:
Scene graph generation turns an image into a graph of objects and the relations between them, such as a person riding a bike. Maelic Neau, Zoe Falomir, Cedric Buche, and Akihiro Sugimoto tackle the open-vocabulary form, where models must handle a wide range of relations, not a fixed short list. Current benchmarks use narrow vocabularies, so they judge such models poorly.

The team proposes a reference-free metric, a score that needs no gold labels, to judge relation prediction fairly. They also build high-quality synthetic training data through region-specific prompt tuning of vision-language models. Tests show pre-training on that new data improved how well models generalized. The work gives the field both a sharper ruler and better material to learn from.
arxiv-2509-01309:
Bjorn Schafer studies a family of C-star algebras, abstract systems that generalize both numbers and functions, built from two partitions of unity. The rules linking the parts are governed by a bipartite graph, a network split into two sides. These algebras extend both an algebra built from two projections and the hypergraph algebras of earlier authors.

Schafer finds alternative universal generators for these bipartite graph algebras and studies partitions of unity placed in generic position. The main result is a full classification: the algebras are pinned down by their one- and two-dimensional irreducible representations, the simplest ways they can act. That classification is presented as a first step toward classifying the wider class of hypergraph C-star algebras, a goal in operator algebra research.
arxiv-2509-01609:
Feeling heat or cold matters in virtual reality, yet real thermal hardware is bulky, power hungry, and limits movement. Yannick Weiss, Marlene Eder, Oguzhan Cesur, and Steeven Villa quantify thermal illusions, perceptual tricks where sight and sound cues shift felt temperature without any physical change. Such illusions had been shown to move subjective ratings, but not how far.

Two user studies followed psychophysical procedures. The first ordered and scaled the effects of varied visual and auditory cues across twenty participants. The second, with twenty-four, measured how well single and combined cues could offset real temperature changes. Illusions produced robust shifts in judgments, and auditory cues showed promise as an alternative channel. Weiss and the team give designers numbers, not just impressions, for faking temperature in immersive systems.
arxiv-2509-01809:
Youssef Chaabouni and David Gamarnik study when a sparse signal can be recovered from few noisy measures. A sparse signal has only a few nonzero parts among many slots. Their measures use sparse random matrices, where each row touches few slots. They find conditions on how many measures suffice for best likelihood recovery when noise is low.

Paired with known lower bounds, their result gives a sharp threshold for the needed sample count. One regime stands out: sparsity costs only a modest factor in samples but gains nearly proportional savings in computation. They also study thinning a dense design after data are taken. Even heavy thinning still allows recovery with a stated sample size in their proof.
arxiv-2509-02009:
