Wahei Hara and Michael Wemyss give a survey of ways to sort sphere like objects in a branch of algebra. The field uses sets with shift and triangle rules to hold rich data from math and physics. Sphere like objects act like spheres in that world and guide much of the work to sort them. A wider class called semibricks shares much of the same grip on the task.

The pair stress their own tools in low dimensions with finite settings. Work on a class of algebras with a silting base gets close care as well. Tools from other teams are summed up at varied depth in the survey. Clear worked cases show each strand of the field at work. The survey maps a fast field for new and old hands alike.
arxiv-2509-02209:
L O Castanos-Cervantes, Lorenzo M Procopio, and Tim J Bartley study blurred cause order in cavity quantum electrodynamics. Blurred cause order lets steps run in a blend of orders, a fresh source for quantum work. Most tests use light rigs, but their rig pairs atoms with two cavities. Light and matter play is the field on trial in this work.

Blurred order makes links between far cavity fields that at no point touch head on. From blank states in both cavities, it makes large links each time, which beats fixed order rigs. One light bit can swap from one cavity to the next with full chance while the atom stays the same. Fixed order rigs can not pull off that swap at all. The finds show gains in clean control of atom and field traits.
arxiv-2509-02709:
Cheol Woo Kim and three co-authors wrote a 2025 AI alignment paper. It tunes language models from human preferences. The preferences are noisy, and the stakes are public health. Their testbed designs reward functions that guide sequential resource allocation.

The proposed DPO-PRO algorithm builds on Direct Preference Optimization. It adds a distributionally robust layer. That layer allows for uncertainty about how preferences are distributed. Unlike earlier robust versions, it stays only mildly conservative. Evaluation uses a real maternal mobile health programme. The nonprofit ARMMAN runs it. Standard alignment benchmarks are also used. The method improved robustness to noisy preference signals over rival variants. It matched a self-reflection baseline on reward design, at far lower run-time cost.
arxiv-2509-03009: Shintaro Suzuki and Hiroki Takahasi wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on random continued fractions built from the Gauss and Rényi maps, two classic rules that generate such fractions. They study weighted cycles, meaning closed loops of a random dynamical system counted with weights. Using ergodic theory, thermodynamic formalism, and large deviation tools, they show those cycles spread out evenly with respect to a measure named for Gauss and Rényi. Results come in two forms: annealed, averaged over all random choices, and quenched, holding for a typical single choice.
arxiv-2509-03109: Paolo Cascini and Calum Spicer proved a 2025 algebraic geometry result about foliations, structures that slice a space into leaf-like pieces, of rank one. They establish a base point free theorem, a statement guaranteeing that certain divisor classes can be realized without fixed points, for log canonical foliated pairs. The setting is a three-dimensional projective space with mild singularities. They also prove abundance, a related existence claim, for numerically trivial pairs of this kind in any dimension.
arxiv-2509-03609:
A 2025 research paper by Shengkai Sun and five co-authors discusses self-supervised learning from skeleton data for action recognition. Skeleton sequences record body joint positions over time, without full video. Masked modelling hides parts of a sequence and trains a network to reconstruct them, a proven way to learn useful features.

Most such methods reconstruct raw joint coordinates, which wastes computation and captures limited meaning. Their General Feature Prediction framework instead predicts richer features, from local motion patterns up to global action semantics. A lightweight companion network generates varied teaching signals across space and time levels on the fly, avoiding precomputed features. Constraints keep those signals diverse and prevent collapse to trivial answers. On three standard benchmarks, training runs several times faster than standard masked skeleton modelling, and downstream action recognition reaches leading performance.
arxiv-2509-04209:
Mario Di Luca and eight co-authors measure fractional electric charges with a tiny engineered hill in a 2025 physics paper. In the fractional quantum Hall regime, current inside special materials flows in units smaller than one electron's charge. Spotting those quasiparticles usually needs complex interferometers, devices that split and recombine paths. An antidot, a raised potential bump inside a narrow channel, offers a simpler route through plain conductance readings.

Their antidot is carved by electric gates in bilayer graphene, two stacked atom-thin carbon sheets. Patterns in gate voltage and conductance slopes revealed charges such as one third and two thirds of an electron charge at several settings. One setting showed signs of two charges at once. Other layered materials could adopt the method.
arxiv-2509-04409:
Matthew E Hubbard and one co-author, Thomas J Radley, present a high-order method for problems whose boundary moves in a 2025 research paper. Moving boundary problems arise when a melting front or growing edge depends on the solution inside the region. Their one-dimensional finite element scheme drags its mesh along with the domain, using an arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian approach that respects conservation, the bookkeeping of quantities that must not leak.

Boundary speed comes from a high-order reading of a local conservation principle, which also drives a flow velocity inside. Mesh speed varies as a simple straight-line profile within each piece. The scheme keeps the fixed-mesh method's accuracy at any chosen order, needs only linear equation solves, and skips reference-domain mapping.
arxiv-2509-04909:
A damaged zone of fractures around a main fault may explain much of earthquake behaviour. M. Almakari, lead author with nine co-authors, build a fault volume digital twin in a 2025 geophysics paper. Their two-dimensional model surrounds a shear fault with off-fault cracks whose sizes and densities follow power laws, all governed by rate-and-state friction.

Despite uniform frictional properties, the simulations produce a natural continuum from slow to fast ruptures. They reproduce the Omori law, the Gutenberg-Richter scaling, and moment-duration scaling seen in real data. Seismicity localises toward the main fault before large events, and slow slip shows migration patterns resembling fluid diffusion.
arxiv-2509-05009:
Elementary symmetric polynomials behave in new ways when arithmetic happens in positive characteristic. Ian Orzel studies formula size and forms for those polynomials in a solo 2025 computer science paper. He first extends earlier work by proving formula lower bounds for the degree-d elementary symmetric polynomial over such fields.

Orzel then shows two zero-characteristic results fail in positive characteristic. Some polynomials cannot be written as linear projections of the elementary symmetric ones. The gap comes with quantitative lower bounds. Others cannot be computed by certain shallow border circuits with small top fan-in. The proofs use the geometry of points where the polynomial and its derivatives vanish. Those vanishing points carry the key structural clue.
arxiv-2509-05109:
Regularity of rings can be judged by finiteness conditions, and Rafael Parra studies several such notions in a solo 2025 algebra paper. His goal is to identify broad classes of rings that are K0-regular. That property is tied to algebraic K-theory. He revisits coherence and von Neumann regularity. He also establishes new characterisations of them.

Attention then turns to n-coherent regular rings, a recently introduced class. Parra studies their K-theory behaviour in detail. Applications at the end show how the methods produce concrete examples of such rings. That widens the territory where the property is understood.
arxiv-2509-05309:
Opening up protein language models so their inner features mean something is the aim of Xiangyu Liu and four co-authors in a 2025 paper introducing ProtSAE. Sparse autoencoders, small networks that expand a model's signals into clearer features, often mix several biological ideas in one unit.

ProtSAE guides training with annotation data and domain knowledge, rather than filtering features only afterwards. In tests, its hidden features align better with real biology and support more reliable probing of what the model knows. The system also rebuilds the original signals with high fidelity. The authors show it can steer protein models during generation tasks, a step toward models scientists can inspect and control.
arxiv-2509-05509:
Element 119, not yet made in any lab, has two key energy values worked out by A. R. Saetgaraev and seven co-authors in a 2025 chemistry paper. Its ionisation potential is the energy needed to remove an electron, and its electron affinity is the energy gained by adding one.

The calculation uses relativistic coupled cluster theory, a sharp method for electron correlation, carried to fourfold excitations. It also adds the Gaunt term between electrons and fixes from quantum electrodynamics. High-order correlation effects are studied closely. The recommended values tighten earlier estimates and give experimenters a benchmark for how the table's trends go on beyond oganesson, the heaviest known element.
arxiv-2509-05609:
Speech and text representations inside a recognition system should meet in the middle, Xugang Lu, Peng Shen, and Hisashi Kawai argue in a 2025 speech technology paper. Knowledge transfer for automatic speech recognition needs acoustic frames aligned with linguistic tokens, but the match is lopsided.

Many sound frames map to one token, some transition frames touch several tokens, and silence or noise frames match nothing. Their model treats alignment as a detection problem and uses an unbalanced transport method allowing soft, partial matches. Every token must anchor to at least one sound observation, while sound frames may stay unmatched. Experiments on a CTC-based recogniser with a pre-trained language model improved recognition performance.
arxiv-2509-06009:
A planet orbiting both stars of a binary system is reported in a 2025 paper led by Vito Squicciarini with eight co-authors. Direct imaging is the one technique that can catch wide-orbit giant planets and probe how disks and host stars interact. The COBREX project reanalyzed archival images from the SPHERE and GPI instruments with stronger post-processing, turning up new candidates.

Follow-up imaging confirms a companion to the young binary HD 143811, about sixty astronomical units out. A nine-year baseline gives a mostly face-on, low-eccentricity orbit of a few centuries. Spectrum and brightness measurements pin its temperature and imply a mass of about six Jupiter masses. The planet is only the second ever found by GPI and joins the small family of imaged circumbinary planets.
arxiv-2509-06109:
Currents that flow forever around a ring, carrying both charge and spin, are computed in a 2025 paper by Sourav Karmakar and two co-authors. Their ring follows the Hatano-Nelson model with ferromagnetic order, and its non-reciprocal hopping acts like a synthetic magnetic flux, driving a non-Hermitian version of the Aharonov-Bohm effect. Both real and imaginary persistent currents appear.

Using a current operator method in a biorthogonal basis, the authors track all three spin-current components, which the orientation of the magnetic moments selects. They map how currents change across topological regimes and with chemical potential, system size, and disorder. Strikingly, disorder can even amplify spin currents, a result the authors offer as a new lever for non-Hermitian spintronics.
arxiv-2509-06209:
Borrowed workspace that must be returned untouched is the strange resource of catalytic computing, and James Cook and Edward Pyne give it fast graph algorithms in a 2025 paper. Catalytic logspace lets an algorithm use a large memory filled with any data, provided it restores the contents exactly. Earlier work in this model lacked stated running times.

Their randomized algorithm settles s-t connectivity by pushing values along edges, one register per vertex; a non-random version runs slower but surely. A second algorithm simulates random walks, estimating where a walk ends within a set error by counting visits per vertex. Both carry concrete polynomial runtimes, making catalytic methods practical rather than mere theory.
arxiv-2509-06309:
Random tuples of operators hide a tidy moment structure, reveals James Tian in a 2025 paper. Averaging word moments over chance produces a positive kernel invisible to pointwise bounds. A single shift-positivity condition controls that kernel, and when it holds, the kernel admits a Cuntz dilation, realizing all mean-square effects inside one canonical isometric model.

Consequences include a mean-square free von Neumann inequality and a free functional calculus for random tuples. Tian then defines a ladder of higher-order defects of the kernel and proves their positivity matches a nested chain of projections inside one dilation. The decomposition splits the tuple into dissipative and unitary parts, Wold-style, with a curvature invariant measuring what never dissipates.
arxiv-2509-06609:
Spotting rare bad actors in network data, and making the detector work on new networks, is surveyed by Junjun Pan and three co-authors in a 2025 review. Graph anomaly detection flags malicious nodes or links in social media, shopping, and similar systems. Most methods assume training and test data look alike and are built for one job.

Recent work attacks that weakness two ways: transfer learning, which borrows knowledge from related domains, and foundation models meant to serve many applications at once. The authors trace how the field evolved, define the problem settings precisely, and build a detailed taxonomy from those settings. Every current generalized method is then reviewed against that map. The survey closes with open challenges and future directions for this young area.
arxiv-2509-06709:
A chemical reaction front crawling through stirred liquid is watched closely by Nihal Tawdi and two co-authors in a 2025 fluid dynamics paper. Thin flame speed in turbulence is still debated. A classic model says a front advances steadily while turbulence wrinkles it and speeds it up, but experiments often stray from that picture.

An autocatalytic reaction in water creates a thin front without combustion's heat effects, isolating turbulence's role. Oscillating grids stir a closed tank in two setups, one with decaying turbulence and one with nearly uniform turbulence in the middle. Velocity and fluorescence measurements reveal two regimes: the expected steady propagation, and a reactive mixing regime where turbulence carries products into fresh reactants and sparks many scattered reaction sites. Even a slight density contrast between the two liquids strongly shapes how the front moves.
arxiv-2509-06809:
Guaranteed-correct math problems for training language models are manufactured from theorem-proving archives by Valentin Quesnel and one co-author in a 2025 paper. Good reasoning data is scarce, and generating it with language models risks baking in errors. Decades of automated theorem proving offer a cleaner source.

Their engine runs the E prover in saturation mode over the TPTP axiom library, deriving a large corpus of theorems that are valid by construction, with no language model in the loop. Interesting results are filtered out and turned into three tasks with controlled difficulty: checking entailment, selecting premises, and reconstructing proofs. Zero-shot tests on frontier models show performance collapsing on tasks needing deep structural reasoning. The framework thus serves both as a diagnostic for that weakness and as a scalable supply of symbolic training data, released publicly.
arxiv-2509-06909:
Sequences that spread evenly, sampled along analytic curves, are the subject of a 2025 number theory paper by Vitaly Bergelson and one co-author. Uniform distribution results, going back to Weyl and Koksma, say most sequences of multiples fill a torus evenly. The authors prove multidimensional metric versions where the sampling points are parametrized by analytic curves.

One main theorem says that for any injective integer-valued sequences, the set of points whose scaled multiples are uniformly distributed in the torus has full Lebesgue measure inside any non-degenerate analytic curve. Full measure means the good points occupy essentially the whole curve, up to a negligible set. The results extend the classical theorems in several directions at once. Metric results of this kind tell researchers that even distribution is the typical behavior, not a lucky accident.
arxiv-2509-07109:
Sk Md Adil Imam and 1 co-author wrote a 2025 paper on the neutron star equation of state, the rule that links pressure and density inside a neutron star. They use Bayesian methods, which update beliefs step by step as new data arrive. Their data come from both Earth-based nuclear work and observations of real neutron stars in space.

Five candidate models for the equation of state are compared, and the data are added in stages. New radius measures for two pulsars from the NICER telescope join older data on nuclear matter, heavy ion collisions, and the gravitational wave event GW170817. The comparison favors the Skyrme model. For a typical neutron star, the authors find a radius close to 11.85 kilometers, with tight limits on key nuclear values.
arxiv-2509-07409:
Earth-like planets in the habitable zone sit at the very edge of what the Kepler telescope could detect. Jakob Robnik and Uroš Seljak recheck the claimed detections in a 2025 research paper. Judging a candidate real requires a false alarm probability, the chance that noise alone produced the signal. Older estimates came from flipping or scrambling the light curves, and the authors show both tricks are unsatisfying.

Their null signal template shifts transit times by small random amounts, keeping the statistics honest. Tests on simulations and real data show the method resists unmodeled noise. Applied to all known habitable-zone candidates, it leaves a smaller set with false alarm chances under one percent. Some famous candidates, including Kepler-186f, look marginal under the new test. The reassessment sharpens targets for future missions hunting life signatures.
arxiv-2509-07509:
Zexin Pan and 2 co-authors propose a new importance sampling scheme in 2025 for quasi-Monte Carlo integration over all of real space. Quasi-Monte Carlo replaces random points with carefully spread ones for faster integration, but over an unbounded domain the sampling adjustment can grow wildly at the boundary and ruin the speed. Importance sampling reweights the integrand to match where samples are drawn.

Their strategy designs the adjustment factor first, to have the regularity they want, then builds a tractable transport map that carries standard uniform points to the proposal distribution. The map damps the boundary growth of the adjusted integrand, restoring quasi-Monte Carlo effectiveness. Under stated conditions on the integrand, the method converges fast regardless of the dimension. Dimension-independent speed is prized for the high-dimensional integrals that arise in finance and uncertainty studies.
arxiv-2509-07609:
Yichen Xu and 3 co-authors extend capturing types in the Scala programming language in a 2025 paper. Capturing types track effects and resources with object capabilities. They give lightweight effect polymorphism with little extra notation. Their weak point was data structures. Capabilities hidden inside generic containers, like the standard collections library, could not be named in the system's box types. That blocked wider adoption.

System Capless, the new foundation, adds reach capabilities, a way to name what is inside the box. It refines the universal capability idea with existential and universal quantification over capture sets. The witnesses work inside generic types. They do not force existential capture types into the surface language. The full formal theory is mechanized in the Lean proof assistant. It includes proofs of type soundness and scope safety. The lightweight notation of the old system is preserved.
arxiv-2509-07909:
Arun Verma and 17 co-authors argue, in a 2025 position paper, that the rules governing large language model performance should be uncovered backwards. Scaling laws describe how model quality grows with data and computing power. Finding them by trial and error means training many huge models, which costs too much for most teams.

Inverse problems work the other way: start from measured results and infer the law that produced them. Sciences have used that trick to find fundamental regularities from limited observations. The authors propose the same route for language models, so builders can predict performance before spending on training runs. Cheaper discovery of scaling laws would make model development more planned and less like expensive guesswork.
arxiv-2509-08109:
Nicolas Nytko and 5 co-authors move hard shape problems onto neat grids in a 2025 paper on numerical methods. Fast solvers love grids with a block-like layout. Real shapes, like bent pipes or branched vessels, do not fit such grids. They need loose meshes, and building solver ladders for loose meshes is slow, hard work.

The team's frame warps the hard shape onto a plain one. A smooth change of coordinates does the warping. The fast grid solver then runs as if the shape were simple. Memory access stays neat, which suits graphics chips well. Heat flow, electric fields, and many other tasks rest on the same kind of equation. A warp that brings grid speed to wild shapes helps them all.
arxiv-2509-08209:
Genuine three-way entanglement gets a new detector in a 2025 quantum gravity paper by Ning Bao and 2 co-authors. The proposed signal builds on the entanglement of purification, a measure of how mixed-state correlations can be cleaned up. One version targets ordinary finite-dimensional quantum systems, and a twin version targets holographic systems described by gravity.

The signal is proved non-negative for tripartite entangled mixed states. Using the conjectured equality between entanglement wedge cross sections and purification in the semiclassical limit, the authors apply the measure to three-party entanglement in a three-dimensional anti-de Sitter setting. A generalisation to many parties is sketched. Such signals help map how quantum information is shared inside space itself.
arxiv-2509-08309:
Serving large language models in production often means mixing expensive high-end graphics cards with cheaper ones. Zizhao Mo and 4 co-authors present Hetis, a serving system for such mixed clusters, in a 2025 research paper. Older parallelization strategies divide models coarsely and statically. In mixed hardware that wastes memory on some cards and leaves compute idle on others.

Hetis parallelizes at a finer grain and adjusts the split dynamically. Compute-heavy operations get spread to cut latency. Attention work is dispatched to low-end cards at the level of individual attention heads. An online dispatching policy keeps rebalancing network delay, compute load, and memory pressure. In evaluations, Hetis raised throughput and cut latency compared with existing systems. The design matters as operators squeeze value from whatever hardware they already own.
arxiv-2509-08809:
Cheng Chen and 2 co-authors evaluate language model annotations without oracle feedback in a 2025 paper. Models can label data cheaply, but judging label quality is hard when no trusted answers exist. Dynamic, unsupervised settings make standard methods fail.

A student model works with a noisy teacher model to assess and refine labels. Voting based on user preference checks how consistent teacher outputs are. A new metric, the CAI Ratio, measures that consistency. Across ten datasets and four models, the ratio tracks true accuracy closely. It can also guide model choice in real settings where trusted feedback is scarce.
arxiv-2509-09009:
Marianna Nezhurina and 9 co-authors release open-sci-ref, open reference baselines for language model comparison, in a 2025 paper. Judging whether a new dataset or recipe is truly better needs shared baselines. Without them, scaling comparisons can mislead.

Dense transformers are trained at four scales on nine reference datasets with one documented procedure. Weights, checkpoints, logs, code, and evaluations are all released. Placing methods on a common compute axis reveals weak and strong reference points. One dataset leads the suite, matching a known model with far less compute. A case study shows how a weak small scale point can overstate scaling trends.
arxiv-2509-09209:
Jean Liénardy and 1 co-author study the open XXZ spin chain at a special anisotropy value in a 2025 paper. The chain has diagonal boundary fields depending on a parameter x and finite length. Its ground state vector is the central object.

In a natural normalization, ground state components are polynomials in x with integer coefficients. Their sum is shown to equal a generating function for weighted enumeration of totally symmetric alternating sign matrices. Those matrices are combinatorial objects with strong symmetry. Weights depend on the same parameter x. The result links a quantum spin chain quantity directly to a counting problem in combinatorics.
arxiv-2509-09309:
Dana Harari and 1 co-author show proactive AI adoption can be threatening in a 2025 paper. AI assistants in workplace tools increasingly offer help without being asked. Prior work blamed trust and expectation mismatches for low adoption, but mechanisms were unclear.

Two vignette experiments with hundreds of participants each test anticipatory versus reactive help. One study is preregistered. Anticipatory help raises self-threat, a feeling that one's competence is judged, and lowers willingness to accept help and future use. AI reactive help feels more threatening than human reactive help. Offering help differs from automatically providing it. Design implications are suggested for testing in real systems.
arxiv-2509-09509:
Pedro Miguel Bastos Soares and 5 co-authors introduce SMapper in 2025, an open-hardware platform for collecting data to benchmark robot mapping and navigation. Progress in simultaneous localisation and mapping depends on data sets that others can reproduce. Existing collections often lack sensing variety, cover few kinds of places, or rest on hardware setups nobody else can rebuild exactly.

SMapper joins synchronised LiDAR, several cameras, and inertial sensing, backed by a careful calibration pipeline that aligns readings in space and time. Units can be carried by hand or mounted on robots. The team also released SMapper-light, an indoor and outdoor data set with accurate reference paths and dense three-dimensional reconstructions.
arxiv-2509-09609:
The galaxy glows faintly in gamma rays up to enormous energies. That glow limits how much ultra-heavy dark matter can be hiding in it. Manuel Rocamora, Pedro De La Torre Luque, and Miguel A. Sánchez-Conde turn the glow into constraints in a 2025 research paper. Their dark matter candidates weigh as much as the highest-energy cosmic rays. New measurements from two ground observatories map the diffuse emission along the galactic plane.

The authors model both the direct gamma rays from dark matter decay or annihilation and the secondary light from its electrons and positrons. Absorption of the highest-energy photons is included. Adding realistic backgrounds sharpened the limits considerably. The newest data, especially one observatory's combined detectors, now rival or beat the strongest existing bounds on decaying dark matter. The authors also flag where the limits are least hostage to uncertainty about dark matter's spread.
arxiv-2509-09709:
Jing Ren and Weiqi Wang study, in a 2025 paper, how well ChatGPT can help write research proposals, and how that help can be checked. Two worries drive the work: proposal text is often judged only by subjective human reading, and language models sometimes invent references that do not exist. The pair propose two scores, one for content quality and one for reference validity.

On top of those scores they build an iterative prompting loop, where low scores feed back into new prompts. Their experiments report that the scores give a steady, quantitative way to grade the writing, and that the loop raised content quality while cutting wrong and fabricated references. That matters because fake citations are an ethics problem in academic work.
arxiv-2509-10009:
Zhiwei Liang and 6 co-authors extend a standard model of signal distortion in fiber-optic links in this 2025 paper. High-capacity systems use dual-polarization four-dimensional modulation and shaped constellations, and signals in neighboring channels disturb each other through inter-channel stimulated Raman scattering. A model that leaves that effect out can misjudge how a new format will perform.

The authors widen the four-dimensional nonlinear model so it includes the Raman interaction between channels. They then check its predictions against the split-step Fourier method, a slow direct simulation, and against the enhanced Gaussian noise model. Agreement with those checks supports the extended model as a faster, trustworthy tool for planning high-dispersion links with modern modulation formats.
arxiv-2509-10109:
Lorenzo Emer and 2 co-authors dissect the patent record of green AI in a 2025 study. About sixty-three thousand patents join AI methods to climate work. That work covers both adapting to change and cutting emissions. The authors ask who owns the patents. They ask where the patents cluster. They ask what the patents are worth. Topic models sort the mass into sixteen areas. The fate of each area is then tracked over time.

Focus is shifting in a clear way. It moves from engine technology toward data processing. It also moves toward microgrids and farm water control. Company ownership grows more focused over time. At the same time, the crowd of patenting firms swells. Some areas sway later inventions and hold strong market value. Others matter much for the climate but pay their owners weakly. That mismatch is flagged as a target for public support.
arxiv-2509-10209:
Kui Tuo and 6 co-authors combine simulation with machine learning in a 2025 complexity paper. Their subject is Wolfram's cellular automata. Each automaton follows a rule packed into eight bits. The rule decides a cell's next state from its two neighbours and itself. Tiny rules still grow rich patterns and fractals. Researchers use them to probe how complexity emerges.

The team tracks the density of live cells over time. They ask how the resting level of that density depends on its start. Supervised learners then name which rule made a given pattern. Unsupervised tools cluster patterns into groups instead. Those groups line up well with the simulated densities. The tools used include principal component analysis and autoencoders. Growth from a single seed cell is also explored.
arxiv-2509-10509:
Sai Teja Reddy Adapala, writing alone, reports a surprising result on models trained on their own output in this 2025 paper. The standard worry is model collapse: each generation trained on the last one's text gets steadily worse. Adapala adds a selective feedback step, filtering which outputs become training data, and reports that the pressure did more than slow decay.

In the reported experiments, a Gemma model improved on a hard summarization task across five generations under quality filtering, while unfiltered and random-filter controls got worse. A simpler classifier test did show the expected degenerative loop. The author presents the contrast as evidence that resilience can emerge in large models under selection, framed as a claim for others to test.
arxiv-2509-10609:
Lavinia Paiella and 4 co-authors ask where the heaviest black hole merger yet seen could have formed, in this 2025 paper. The event GW231123 joined two black holes of unusual mass and very high spin, a pairing that standard evolution of an isolated star pair struggles to explain. Star clusters offer another route, mixing ordinary stellar binaries with repeat mergers.

Using a semi-analytic population code, the team modeled young, globular, and nuclear clusters. Metal-poor settings produced the best matches. In nuclear clusters, many heavy black holes were themselves built by earlier mergers, while in other clusters the parts mostly came from stellar binaries with high birth spins. The modeled systems also merged soon after forming.
arxiv-2509-10709:
Shama Maganur and 3 co-authors survey feature-based ways of analyzing Android malware in this 2025 review. Android's openness lets sophisticated malware families slip into networks of connected devices, where they can steal data, disrupt services, or mount large attacks. Defenders analyze app features to catch them, and this review compares how those features are gathered.

The authors sort methods into static, dynamic, hybrid, and graph-based families. Static checks are fast but easy to dodge by disguising code. Dynamic runs resist disguise but cost heavily, a problem for light devices. Hybrid methods balance the two, and graph methods model behavior most richly. The survey ends with gaps in the field and a roadmap for more scalable detection.
arxiv-2509-11009:
O. V. Selyugin and O. V. Teryaev relate the sizes of particles to the quarks and gluons inside them in this 2025 paper. Protons, neutrons, and mesons have measurable electromagnetic radii, and a newer notion, gravitational radii, describes how their mass and energy are spread. The authors compute both kinds of form factors, split into quark and gluon parts, using generalized parton distributions from several research groups.

Their results draw a contrast. The gluon's gravitational radius for the nucleon comes out comparable to the proton's electromagnetic radius, while the quark gravitational radius is smaller than its electromagnetic counterpart. At high momentum transfer the gluon form factor also falls faster than the quark one. Such maps guide experiments that probe particle structure.
arxiv-2509-11509:
Kim Fook Lee and Prem Kumar propose a way to detect a classical state hidden inside a quantum light setup, in a 2025 optics paper. Their scene involves an entangled photon pair, where one photon, the idler, gets mixed with weak ordinary light of matched wavelength and polarization.

Quantum state tomography, a reconstruction technique, is performed on both the mixed idler and its entangled partner. The reconstructed state is modeled as a blend of two state types. Within that framework, the weak light effectively performs a local polarization measurement. An algorithm then identifies the classical state's density matrix from the reconstructed matrix entries. The approach could help classical and quantum signals coexist in future networks and key distribution systems.
arxiv-2509-11809:
Johannes Aspman, Daniel Mastropietro, and Jakub Marecek ask how resetting a wandering particle changes its arrival time. This 2025 statistical physics paper treats a diffusing particle of Langevin type. The particle is teleported back to its start at some rate. The question is the mean first passage time to a target. The reset rate may vary with position.

Quadratic and piecewise-quadratic potentials are studied. The benefit of resetting hinges on the drift-to-noise ratio. It grows as drift weakens against noise. When the target sits at a local optimum of the potential, a spatial strategy wins. Reset less often near the target. Reset more often far away. The folklore that resetting always helps gets refined.
arxiv-2509-12109:
Circuits can mix unitary gates with checks made mid-course. Near the snap between two phases, how is multiparty entanglement arranged? James Allen and one co-author chart that layout in 2025. These measurement-induced transitions differ from ordinary critical points. They carry true multiparty entanglement across long distances.

The authors picture the average spread of entanglement as clusters. From that picture they guess three general exponent rules. The rules cover classical dominance, monotonicity, and subadditivity. Weighted graphs then build such clusters in any circuit. For a one-dimensional measurement-only circuit, exact exponents follow. That circuit maps to percolation, and the values are checked numerically. A two-dimensional cousin maps to three-dimensional percolation. It yields its first exponents. The hierarchy runs over every party count from two up.
arxiv-2509-12209:
Fractional equations, whose derivatives involve memory of the past, resist the neat grids of standard numerical methods, especially when the grid spacing is uneven. Devank Mishra and two co-authors build a generalized non-standard finite difference scheme for them in 2025, tuned for non-uniform grids.

The scheme grows out of the fractional Taylor series for Caputo derivatives and uses specially chosen denominator functions in the time steps. The authors prove the method is consistent, stable, and convergent, the three properties a numerical scheme must earn. Comparisons against existing methods support their claims about accuracy and computing cost.
arxiv-2509-12409:
Ayesha Amjad and 6 co-authors uncover how virus-like particles can trap several cargo items at once in a 2025 paper. Virus shells can carry useful cargo such as small RNAs, enzymes, and light-emitting molecules, making them valuable for drug delivery and new materials. How many cargoes get enclosed during assembly was not well understood.

The team studied shell proteins assembling around ligand-coated nanoparticles that stood in for cargo. Electron microscopy could distinguish the stages because the metal particles stand out clearly. They found a certain assembly-line pathway, varied from earlier described mechanisms, in which intermediates form in sequence. The emerging model also explains the strong size selectivity observed for the nanoparticles, a point that matters for delivery applications.
arxiv-2509-12509:
Søren Smidstrup and 6 co-authors describe using machine learning force fields to model large atomic systems in a 2025 paper. Atomistic modeling supports development of superconducting qubits and sensors, but standard density-functional theory misses parts of the physics and cannot handle very large systems, especially for thermal traits.

The QuantumATK tool combines density-functional calculations with non-equilibrium Green's functions to study interfaces between superconductors and insulators and surface states of topological insulators. Machine-learned force fields extend it to thermal traits and real-life amorphous geometries at large scale. Modeling qubits as two-level systems also needs many-body physics for electron interactions. The paper demonstrates how these pieces together improve the fidelity of model runs for quantum devices.
arxiv-2509-13009:
F. Kummer and 3 co-authors study mergers in massive triple star systems in a 2025 paper. Heavy stars are commonly born three at a time, bound together by gravity. In such a triple, the pulls between the stars, and the ways stars affect each other, shape how the whole system ages. On one path, the inner two stars merge. What is left looks like an ordinary binary, but its past is different.

The authors set out to count how often such mergers happen. Their tool joins two codes. One code handles whole populations of triples, tracking how stars age, how pairs trade matter, and how gravity moves them. The other handles populations of binaries. With them, the team simulated one hundred thousand massive triples that stay dynamically stable. Each run began at the zero-age main sequence and ran through merger and beyond.
arxiv-2509-13309:
Zile Qiao and 15 co-authors present WebResearcher in a 2025 paper on agents that can do long research tasks on the web. Such agents aim to find facts on their own and build them into a clear report. Most past agents work in one long stream of text, which soon grows clogged and noisy as a task drags on.

WebResearcher treats research as a chain of choices. From time to time the agent pauses, sums up what it has found so far in a draft report, and then goes on with a clean slate. A mate tool, WebFrontier, makes training tasks of rising hardness with the help of tools. The authors find that data from this way of work lifts tool use even for plain single-stream agents.
arxiv-2509-13909:
Xavier Bonnetain and three co-authors close a gap in quantum collision search in a 2025 cryptography paper. Finding collisions in a random function, two inputs with the same output, is a basic attack primitive in cryptanalysis. For a single collision, quantum algorithms already match the proven lower bound; for finding many collisions at once, a range of cases stayed open.

Earlier chained quantum walk methods, building on the MNRS framework, reused the walk's state after each collision found. Bonnetain and colleagues extend that chaining to a regime where several collisions come out at each step while the walks themselves run a single diffusion layer. The new algorithm matches the lower bound up to a polynomial factor in both queries and, assuming quantum random access memory, in time.
arxiv-2509-14409:
Rafael Rangel, writing alone in 2025, asks whether each system that loses energy can be read as a gradient system, one that flows downhill on a potential. Some writers have claimed the two classes are one and the same. Plain changes of coordinates seem unable to settle the claim.

Rangel links a differential form to any such dynamics and splits it in two parts. One part comes from a potential, and the rest is a leftover part. When the leftover part is zero, the form counts as closed, which marks the gradient case. When it is not zero, no plain coordinate change can make it closed. A wider kind of coordinate change is then brought in to aim at a gradient form. The puzzle turns into a question about which changes are allowed.
arxiv-2509-14709:
Sándor Kisfaludi-Bak and Leonidas Theocharous study in 2025 when finite metric spaces can be built with obstacles in three dimensional space. Obstacles reshape distance: travel must go around them, which gives a geodesic metric in the free space. Flat cases are well known, higher dims far less so.

A space is near realisable if it embeds around obstacles with worst case distance warp as close to one as wished. Three obstacle traits are varied: convexity, disjointness and fatness. Dropping each trait changes which metrics can be built, and the pair work out those shifts. Motion planning and visibility in three dims rest on such results. They tell a designer which obstacle freedoms are a must before a target distance plan is promised.
arxiv-2509-14909:
Flor Ortiz and Eva Lagunas propose hybrid routing for next-generation satellite constellations in a 2025 communications letter. Satellites in low orbits move constantly, so routes between them keep changing. Pure reinforcement learning routers adapt well but can be complex, slow to settle, and unstable under heavy traffic.

Their design pairs precomputed routing tables with a learning-based fallback. Under normal conditions, traffic follows fast, deterministic table lookups. A Deep Q-Learning agent activates only when links fail or become congested, handling the exceptions. Simulations on large constellations show the hybrid beating a pure learning baseline on delivery ratio, delay, hop count, and throughput. The authors present the mix as a scalable, resilient option for delay-sensitive satellite broadband services.
arxiv-2509-15009:
Asmita Bhandare, Adnan Ali Ahmad, and Benoît Commerçon measure how well a newborn star sheds heat as it gains mass, in a 2025 letter. A protostar forms in two collapse steps, and each step makes a dense core. The second step sets two key numbers: the share of infall energy that is radiated away, and the rate at which mass lands on the star.

Those numbers set how bright young stars look, and surveys and theory still do not agree on that point. The team ran high-detail radiation hydrodynamics runs with two trusted codes. Their main result is that the radiated share climbs to one, the supercritical point, soon after birth. That quick climb backs cold accretion, where infall adds little heat to the star.
arxiv-2509-15209:
Gabriele Cugno and Sierra L. Grant report a carbon-rich disk around a planetary-mass companion in a 2025 astronomy paper. While giant planets finish forming, leftover gas and dust circle them in circumplanetary disks, the raw material for moons. These disks are faint and hug their hosts, so their chemistry stayed out of reach until the James Webb Space Telescope.

Webb's mid-infrared spectrograph now resolves the disk around the young companion CT Cha b. Seven carbon-bearing molecules appear in its spectrum, up to benzene-sized species, plus one isotopologue variant. The gas-phase carbon-to-oxygen ratio exceeds one, unlike the ratios typically measured in directly imaged giant planet atmospheres. A carbon-rich cradle for moons contrasts with the chemistry astronomers expected around such companions.
arxiv-2509-15409:
Yu Shee leads a team that plans how to build a target molecule from simpler parts. This backward planning, called retrosynthesis, guides computer aided chemical design. The common tree search method can blow up in cost as molecules grow. The team wanted a method whose cost grows far more slowly.

Their method, FragmentRetro, breaks the target with known cutting rules, then joins the pieces back in ways that match a stock of real building blocks. They give the first formal cost study of such methods and show theirs grows with the square of size, not far faster. Tests on three data sets show high success rates and good speed. The method solves some cases where tree search fails.
arxiv-2509-15509:
Xiaoshuang Wang, Yifan Lin, and Enlu Zhou plan choices under risk when the world's rules are partly unknown. Their setting is a chain of states and actions with a broad loss measure. They learn the unknown parts from data in a Bayesian way, then judge loss by a risk rule that respects that doubt. This setup breaks the standard step by step equations.

Since the usual tools fail, they build a method that follows the slope of the loss with respect to the plan. Key steps use a dual form of risk rules and a wider version of a classic theorem. They prove how fast the method settles. They also extend it to run in episodes, with global proof and bounds on the work needed.
arxiv-2509-15709:
Yicheng He leads a team that studies how wide the hidden codes in recommender systems should be. These codes, called embeddings, stand for users and items. Many builders assumed wider codes hurt accuracy, so growth efforts moved elsewhere. The root cause of that belief was unclear. The team test the claim at scale.

They run four classic model types across ten data sets of varied size and sparsity. Two surprise patterns appear as codes widen. One curve rises, falls, rises again, then drops: a double peak. The other climbs as a clean logarithmic curve. They trace why the double peak forms. They also prove how noise interacts with code width in these filters.
arxiv-2509-15809:
Mei-Sen Gao leads a team that proposes a new probe of a proton's inner spin structure. The trait they chase, called transversity, shows how a nucleon's spin lines up with the spins of its quarks. Past probes read it from the sideways drift of made particles, over a narrow range. Their probe uses energy patterns inside jets instead.

The tool, a one point energy correlator, is safe from two classic sources of noise in jet physics. In crashes of oppositely spun protons, it shows a clean wave like pattern tied to the spin angles. The method covers a far wider range of scales. It suits a running collider and a future electron ion one.
arxiv-2509-16409:
Standard cosmology grows the seeds of galaxies from quantum jitter during inflation, but Gabriela Barenboim explores a different source: noise from a decaying vacuum. In her model, an early de Sitter phase decays into radiation through quantum-thermal steps, and the noise of that decay stirs curvature ripples directly. Any horizon crossing is brief and not the main driver.

The tilt of the ripple spectrum comes from spatial links in the noise, while the statistics stay Gaussian. Starting from thermal balance handles the classic horizon and flatness puzzles. The model also predicts no primordial gravitational wave signal, a sharp test for future data.
arxiv-2509-16909:
Yijun Yuan and co-authors put robot mapping and tracking into one transformer in a 2025 paper. SLAM lets a robot map a place while tracking its own position in it. Classic systems split this into a frontend and a backend. Their model, SLAM-Former, houses both parts in a single transformer that runs them in turns.

Each part boosts the other as they alternate. Tests show scores that match or beat top dense SLAM methods. A single learned system could simplify robot stacks that now mix many hand-built parts. Simpler stacks are easier to train, ship, and debug across varied robots and scenes.
arxiv-2509-17009:
A. R. Nurmukhametov and co-authors study one-way light emission in a copper borate crystal in a 2025 physics paper. Emission that differs by direction is rare, since it needs broken time-reversal symmetry. Magnetic order inside the crystal can break that symmetry without an outside field. The team measure photoluminescence from copper ions in varied setups.

A quantum analysis of the ion states matches the data well. The one-way effect comes from interference between two kinds of transitions in ordered spins. The result confirms a subtle mechanism in an antiferromagnetic crystal. One-way emitters could one day shape optical isolators that protect lasers from back-reflected light.
arxiv-2509-17209:
Lourdes Moreno, Jesus M. Sanchez-Gomez, Marco Antonio Sanchez-Escudero, and Paloma Martínez describe a shared-task entry in a 2025 arXiv paper. The task, part of CLEARS 2025, asks systems to rewrite Spanish texts in plain language. Their team, HULAT-UC3M, tested language models trained on Spanish in two setups: prompting alone, and fine-tuning with a low-rank method.

The team scored rival setups on slices of the training data with two official measures, one for meaning kept and one for ease of reading. The winning system joined text cleanup steps, a Spanish chat model, and a prompt written for plain language. It placed first on keeping meaning but fourth on ease of reading. The authors also flag uneven training data and weak points in how the scores judge clarity and faithfulness.
arxiv-2509-17909:
Snjezana Maksimovic proves limit results for two fractional signal transforms. Her 2025 maths paper works with broad classes of signals called distributions. She links how such a signal behaves at extremes to how its Stockwell transform behaves, in both directions.

She also shows that the fractional wavelet transform, and its rebuild step, act smoothly on classic test spaces and their duals. A bridge between the two fractional transforms is set out in the paper. Limit rules for the wavelet form close the set of results. Such rules help read far-out or near-in traits from a transform.
arxiv-2509-18309:
Hand shapes carry core sound-like units in signed languages, and American Sign Language uses about fifty of them. Yet most computer systems for sign language barely model hand shape at all. Alessa Carbo and Eric Nalisnick tackle that gap in this 2025 paper. They build a graph neural network, a model that works on linked points, for hand shape recognition.

Their network keeps two things apart: how the hand moves over time and the still shape it holds. It uses the structure of the hand itself, plus a training method that pulls matching shapes closer together. The team also built the first test set for this task. Their model reached 46 percent accuracy across 37 hand shape classes, well above the 25 percent scored by older methods.
arxiv-2509-18409:
Erbium atoms inside a crystal can emit light at the wavelengths used for fiber communication. Mahtab A. Khan and five co-authors study erbium placed in alumina, a hard oxide, in this 2025 paper. The host could suit chips that route and boost light signals. The team asks where the erbium sits and which light transitions that site allows.

Computer models from first principles show the erbium site is stable. The local symmetry then sorts the erbium energy levels and yields rules for which light polarizations are allowed. Computed absorption spectra matched those symmetry rules well. The work links line strengths to a classic theory of rare-earth light emission. It predicts a clear absorption near the telecom band, useful for on-chip amplifiers. The authors offer the frame as a template for tuning other rare-earth dopants.
arxiv-2509-18709:
The newsvendor problem is a classic: stock enough for demand you cannot foresee, but not so much that the surplus rots. Xin Chen, Jiameng Lyu, Shilin Yuan, and Yuan Zhou study it when demand keeps shifting over time. Their 2025 paper handles both abrupt and gradual change. Demand data may also be censored, showing only sales, not true demand.

Their framework watches the demand distribution for change, then restarts learning when a shift is detected. Two efficient algorithms cover the open-data and censored cases. Neither needs to know how strong the shifts are in advance. The team proves matching upper and lower regret bounds, the theory's gold standard. Tests on nurse staffing and COVID test demand data show strong, robust results. Managers get a deployable method with guarantees, the authors argue.
arxiv-2509-19009:
Ed Bennett and six co-authors study how a Yang-Mills theory behaves when heated, using a lattice simulation method built for hard cases. Many such theories jump sharply between a confined phase and a free phase as temperature rises. If that jump happened in the early universe, it could have left a background of gravitational waves that detectors might one day hear. Standard sampling methods struggle to measure the jump cleanly.

The team applies the density of states method to a theory with the gauge group Sp(4). They map its first-order transition in very large volumes for two depths of the time direction, a step toward the smooth continuum limit. They confirm signs of a true sharp jump: coexisting states, lingering metastable states, latent heat, and surface tension. Several ways of locating the critical point agree with each other.
arxiv-2509-19109:
Timur Turatali and four co-authors release the first hand-labeled dataset for finding named entities in Kyrgyz, a language with few digital resources. Named entity recognition teaches software to spot names of people, places, and organizations in text. Their dataset, KyrgyzNER, covers about 1,500 news articles from the 24.KG portal. It holds nearly 11,000 sentences and about 39,000 entity mentions spread over 27 classes.

The team describes its labeling scheme and the hard cases met along the way. They then test several recognizers, from classic sequence labelers to large multilingual transformer models fine-tuned on the new data. All models struggled with rare entity types. A multilingual RoBERTa model struck the best balance between precision and recall, and close rivals suggest the approach generalizes. The dataset gives Kyrgyz language technology a first solid benchmark.
arxiv-2509-19409: J. P. C. Greenlees, writing alone, describes the space of conjugacy classes of subgroups of a compact Lie group, under the Zariski topology. That space splits into separate blocks that do not touch. Each block is governed by one subgroup whose Weyl group is finite. Inside a block, an integral representation of the governing subgroup's component group controls the structure. The abstract states this decomposition in a single dense sentence, and this summary stays close to it.
arxiv-2509-19509:
Social media posts often hint at science claims without naming the study behind them. Team AIRwaves, led by Cem Ashbaugh with four co-authors, built a search system that links such posts to the right papers. Their entry took second place in a shared task at the CLEF 2025 CheckThat! Lab. Short posts, sparse words, and field jargon make the match hard for plain word search.

Their pipeline first pulls candidates with a dual encoder trained on tough near-miss examples. A second model then re-ranks the list by reading post and paper side by side. Ranking scores rose from about one half with word search to about two thirds with the full pipeline. The team offers the design as a template for fact-check tools. Such tools need fast, sound links from claims to sources.
arxiv-2509-19609:
How well a system withstands shocks is called resilience, but many fields gauge it in ways that clash. Andreas Morr, Christian Kuehn, and George Datseris sort the main gauges into one shared form. They view each gauge through dynamics, the study of how systems change. They then give a fast method that works out many gauges side by side.

The method tracks the pull states a system settles into as its settings shift. That yields resilience curves for a whole range, not just near one point. Tests on sample systems show the gauges part ways in telling ways. Checks that look only near one state can miss broad weakness. New gauges can be added to the frame as they are coined.
arxiv-2509-19709:
Most quantum computing demos in chemistry chase the lowest energy state of small molecules. Alan Bidart and five co-authors review the wider frontier beyond that ground state. Chemists also need reaction paths, reaction speeds, and behavior at real temperatures. The review surveys algorithms and progress for those harder targets.

Shared hurdles include how to load molecular states and read answers out. Each target also brings quirks of its own. The authors weigh where quantum speedups might realistically appear and where classical methods will hold their ground. Reaction mechanism prediction could change how catalysts and drugs are designed. The review maps a field moving from toy problems toward questions working chemists actually ask.
arxiv-2509-20109:
Pengxiang Li and eight co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on self-driving cars. Modern driving systems often learn by copying human drivers. That copying struggles to teach the physical rules of the road. The authors propose ReflectDrive, a system that plans safer paths by reflecting on its own draft plan.

ReflectDrive first turns the driving space into a grid of action codes. A diffusion language model then drafts a goal-directed path from these codes. A safety-aware reflection step searches locally for unsafe parts and marks safe anchor points. The path is then regenerated around those anchors, with no costly gradient steps. On the NAVSIM benchmark, the system did well at safety-critical path generation. The authors present it as a scalable and reliable option for autonomous driving.
arxiv-2509-20409:
Can a purely symbolic system ever connect its symbols to the real world? Zhangchi Liu tackles that symbol grounding problem in a 2025 arXiv paper of formal philosophy and logic. He separates two notions: internal sense, which axioms can supply, and external reference, which ties a symbol to the world. His unified theory argues that genuine grounding must come from outside any fixed algorithm.

The argument proceeds in four stages. First, ungroundability for a purely symbolic system follows from its definition. Second, adding any finite static set of meanings does not help. Third, Godel-style reasoning shows such systems cannot fully define their own groundability. Fourth, new meanings require a meta-level update, which Liu identifies with physical transduction, following Turing's oracle machines. The paper concludes that embodied interaction is a logical necessity, not an engineering choice.
arxiv-2509-20609:
Mutual information gauges how much two things move together, but gauging it in rich data is hard. Longxuan Yu and four co-authors turn diffusion models into a gauge in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their method, MMG, grows out of a fresh link between denoising and information theory. The shared information equals half the gap in denoising error, with aid versus without aid, summed over all noise levels.

That link turns a hard gauge into a task of training denoisers and scoring them. The gauge passed self-checks the team devised. It beat classic gauges and past diffusion-based ones in their tests. Smart sampling keeps it fast on hard cases. It held up even where the true shared information ran high, a zone where many gauges fail.
arxiv-2509-20709:
Construction robots need site plans that reflect real hazards, not just design drawings. Mani Amani and Reza Akhavian fuse language guidance with building models in a 2025 paper on robot path planning. They treat a large language model as a sensor that scores danger.

Each obstacle in the building information model starts with a design-time repulsion value, modeled as a Beta distribution. The language model reads text descriptions and returns danger scores. Those scores update the distribution like new observations, a Beta-Bernoulli fusion. The updated values feed a potential-field planner that steers the robot. The result is a path cost that responds to context and wording, not only to plain distance.
arxiv-2509-20909:
A model that memorized a test will ace it without truly reasoning, and simple rewording can hide the cheating. Zirui He and four co-authors present LogitTrace, a 2025 method for detecting benchmark contamination in large language models. It watches how an answer forms inside the model, layer by layer.

Older detectors rely on surface overlap or final-answer likelihood, and they degrade when inputs are rephrased. LogitTrace instead tracks the trajectory of the model's preferences across its layers. Contaminated examples tend to show early commitment to the answer, while clean examples settle later and less steadily. By reading these internal dynamics, the method aims to flag memorization on benchmarks such as AIME and Math500 even after rewording.
arxiv-2509-21009:
Post-training a language model with reinforcement learning wastes expensive GPU time when a few very long answers hold up each batch. Wei Gao and thirteen co-authors present RollPacker in a 2025 systems paper. The problem is the long tail of rollout lengths in synchronous training.

Their strategy, tail batching, sorts the work instead of relaxing synchronization. Prompts likely to produce long responses are consolidated into a few long rounds. Most rounds then contain only balanced, short rollouts and finish quickly. Competing systems often loosen synchronization, which can cost training accuracy. Tail batching keeps the synchronous algorithm intact while removing most idle GPU bubbles. The authors report faster post-training for reasoning models as a result.
arxiv-2509-21109:
Two new facilities will soon watch the same violent galaxies in different light. Julian Hamo, Jonathan Biteau, and Julien Peloton preview that era in a 2025 conference paper from the International Cosmic Ray Conference. The facilities are the Rubin Observatory and the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory.

Both begin collecting data around 2026, with sensitivity reaching blazars at redshifts of at least two and a half. Rubin's monitoring, revisiting fields every few nights in rotating filters, will trace blazar light curves. Targeted deep observations from the gamma-ray array can then test models of particle acceleration and radiation. The authors use existing survey and satellite data to forecast the combination's power. Real-time processing of the flood of alerts is a central challenge they discuss.
arxiv-2509-21509:
Solving a drift diffusion equation on a quantum computer requires circuits shallow enough for real hardware. Ellen Devereux and Animesh Datta analyse circuit depths for one such algorithm in a 2025 paper. Their algorithm uses diagonalisation by the quantum Fourier transform. Five gate sets are compared, from an unconstrained set to native sets of named hardware platforms. Scenarios use up to twenty two qubits.

Scaling with spatial resolution matched theory in one dimension. Scaling with spatial dimension was less efficient than theorised, due to block encoding overhead. The Fujitsu STAR gate set was tested for a space time efficient design. Even minimal problem instances exceeded current hardware limits there. The analysis maps where quantum PDE solvers stand against present machines.
arxiv-2509-21609:
General vision language models describe disaster images in generic words that responders cannot act on. Md. Mahfuzur Rahman and 7 co-authors build a knowledge enhanced captioning system in a 2025 paper. Their system, VLCE, targets post disaster satellite and drone imagery. External knowledge comes from ConceptNet and WordNet, two public semantic networks. A domain vocabulary of many terms is extracted from those graphs.

A standard model first captions the image, conditioned on object detections from YOLOv8. A second, knowledge enriched model then refines the caption. Two designs are tested for refinement: a CNN-LSTM and a hierarchical cross modal transformer. Benchmarks cover satellite and drone disaster data sets with damage classes. Semantic alignment and informativeness metrics score the results.
arxiv-2509-21709:
Quantum circuit synthesis aims to use as few expensive non Clifford gates as possible. David Kremer and 2 co-authors apply reinforcement learning to that optimization in a 2025 paper. Unitaries exactly implementable by Clifford plus T, or Clifford plus CS, gate sets are the targets. Their system uses a channel representation of unitaries. Matrix steps then run fast with integers only.

Pruning heuristics and operator canonicalization reduce search complexity. Sharply larger unitaries are implemented in less time, with better success rates than previous work. Two qubit synthesis achieves close to optimal decompositions for up to a hundred T gates. That is far beyond earlier reinforcement learning results. Non Clifford count optimization matters because those gates dominate fault tolerant quantum computing costs.
arxiv-2509-22009:
Cehao Yang and eight co-authors present GraphSearch in this 2025 paper, a deeper way for language models to search knowledge graphs before answering. Graph-based retrieval grounds answers in structured facts, but current systems search shallowly and miss key evidence. They also use their pre-built graph data poorly. The authors aim for a search that reasons as it goes.

GraphSearch organizes retrieval into six modules that interact over several rounds, refining the search as partial answers form. It also runs two channels at once: meaning-based queries over text chunks, and relation-based queries over the graph structure. The two channels cover for each other's blind spots. Across six benchmarks that need multi-step reasoning over sources, the workflow improved both answer accuracy and generation quality over the standard strategy. The authors offer it as a promising direction for graph-based retrieval.
arxiv-2509-22109:
Philipp Gohlke, Marc Kesseböhmer, and Tanja I. Schindler study a family of measures built from the Thue-Morse sequence, a famous pattern that never repeats in blocks. The measures arise as Riesz products, and the authors show they serve as diffraction measures of generalized Thue-Morse sequences, possibly over an infinite alphabet. Diffraction describes how a structure scatters waves, so these measures connect combinatorics on words with a physical measurement. Their 2025 paper builds much of the analysis on a dynamical system driven by the doubling map.

That system carries an observable with a logarithmic singularity, which pushes beyond the standard formalism. The authors develop the extended formalism and obtain explicit formulas for two spectra: one for time averages along orbits, one for dimensions. From it they determine the Fourier and quantization dimensions exactly.
arxiv-2509-22409:
Loic Jegou and 5 co-authors watch a melt pool form inside metal as a part is printed. The process, laser metal deposition with powder, builds or repairs steel parts layer by layer. Pool shape shapes the final part's quality, yet it hides inside the metal. X-ray imaging can see through the part and show the pool by its density contrast.

The team filmed ten layers of stainless steel as they were laid down. The X-ray beam's mixed energies blurred contrast, so classic image methods failed. Neural nets trained on simulated heat and X-ray data found the pool instead. A VGG16-style net worked well, backing live X-ray checks in factories.
arxiv-2509-22609:
James Pearson and 3 co-authors review a project that bridges astronomy and particle physics in the hunt for dark matter. The two fields search in different ways and rarely share tools or language. Astronomers, in particular, can struggle to read what particle experiments mean for cosmic scales. The ESCAPE Dark Matter Test Science Project has spent years building tools to help particle physicists constrain dark matter traits.

This short review sums up the project's progress and its applications to current experiments. It also looks at how the work can foster collaboration with astrophysical observations. The need is sharp: all direct evidence for dark matter lies in astrophysics and cosmology.
arxiv-2509-22709:
Louise McCormack and 3 co-authors ask industry practitioners what trustworthy AI looks like in practice. The EU AI Act pushes firms to build AI that is human-centered and trustworthy. Adoption has outrun the frameworks meant to judge ethics and risk. The team ran structured interviews with fifteen industry professionals. Each key interview finding was then paired with a literature review.

Participants flagged tangled problems in risk management, compliance, and accountability. Unclear rules, rushed rollouts, and poor transparency made them worse. Worries ranged over model errors, security flaws, and overreliance on AI. Social and environmental harms, from energy use to inequality, also loomed. The authors call for a wider approach tied to local values.
arxiv-2509-22809:
Neeraj Bhatt and 6 co-authors probe how disorder shapes the electrons in a superconducting high entropy alloy. These alloys mix many elements at random, and that randomness drives their prized traits. The team studied an osmium-based alloy with ruthenium or rhenium, molybdenum, tungsten, and zirconium. Photoemission spectra and density functional theory traced its electronic structure.

Core level shifts tracked each element's electronegativity and valence electron count. Valence band data showed crystal structure plays a large role in the electronic makeup. Near the Fermi level, the density of states is strongly suppressed, in line with Altshuler-Aronov theory, a sign that disorder localizes charge carriers. Computed coupling and transition temperature matched experiments, backing phonon-mediated pairing.
arxiv-2509-23109:
Vision-language models hallucinate partly because image and text tokens sit far apart in sequence. Junyang Zhang, Tianyi Zhu, and Thierry Tambe close that gap with attention anchors. Their AttAnchor framework needs no new parameters. It inserts text tokens near the visual patches they match. Those placements act as semantic signposts for attention.

True content-based scores then guide the model to the right regions. Scores improved on thirteen of fifteen metrics and benchmarks tried. Reasoning gains reached about thirty-two percent, and hallucination scores rose too. A one-billion-parameter model beat much larger rivals on one test. Inference overhead stayed near zero.
arxiv-2509-23209:
Agents that adapt in context, with no weight updates, can swing wildly between runs. Wenhao Zhang and 4 co-authors explain that brittleness with a policy-gradient view. Trajectory-level return feedback gives high-variance updates when rollouts are few. Their fix borrows the actor-critic idea. An explicit context value estimates the return ahead, given state and history.

A value head writes its estimate back into the context as a token. TD-style targets then lower the variance of updates. Tests on Dark Room, Minigrid, and Procgen show steadier adaptation. Returns rose on tasks and environments alike. The team share code and data in public.
arxiv-2509-23409:
Networks with many relation types, like work plus family plus school ties, need link forecasts that read all layers at once. Devesh Sharma and 5 co-authors frame that task as multi-view edge classification. Each node pair yields one edge view per layer. Cross-layer self-attention fuses those views for the target layer. Two models fill the frame: a light transformer on static embeddings, and a graph-attention hybrid.

A union candidate pool and leak-free protocols keep tests fair and scalable. Six public multiplex data sets frame the trials. Both models beat strong baselines on macro F1 by consistent margins. The frame accepts precomputed embeddings or graph encoders alike.
arxiv-2509-23809:
Shrinking a language model's weights to three values, minus one, zero, or one, makes edge hardware happy and accuracy sad. Hong Huang and 9 co-authors trace the damage to what they call deadzone trapping. Many weights sit stuck at the deadzone boundary, fed only noisy gradients that cannot push them free. Their method, Tequila, reuses those trapped weights as dynamic biases instead.

Repurposed weights then carry a continuous signal forward and receive direct gradients backward, at nearly zero inference cost. Across five benchmarks Tequila beat leading ternary methods. On ARC it gained over four points on the best rival and nearly matched full precision, with a threefold inference speedup.
arxiv-2509-24209:
Rebuilding a moving person in three dimensions from a few uncalibrated cameras is a prized but hard trick. Yingdong Hu and 9 co-authors built Forge4D, a feed-forward model that does it in one pass and can also fill in new moments in time. Past methods were slow or could not synthesize unseen times.

Forge4D first builds static three-dimensional Gaussians from sparse views, then uses learned state tokens to keep them consistent over time. A motion module predicts dense movement for each Gaussian between frames, trained by matching points without ground truth. An occlusion-aware fusion step blends Gaussians at any chosen instant. Tests on in-domain and new data show the model works well.
arxiv-2509-24409:
Martino Borello and 2 co-authors study duality for subspaces over finite fields, in the spirit of Delsarte's classic work. They define weight and defect for a subspace relative to a smaller-field subspace, then analyze the sequence of maximum nonzero defects. A correspondence links subspaces of positive defect to their Delsarte duals, which yields explicit descriptions of those sequences.

The framework unifies several classes of subspaces from finite geometry. It also gives a new geometric reading of duality for linear rank-metric codes. The team characterizes which code classes stay closed under duality, including several MRD families and a new one. Applications to q-matroids close the work, including rank generating functions for sums of uniform ones.
arxiv-2509-24809:
Changtao Sheng, Huiyuan Li, Huifang Yuan, and Li-Lian Wang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It gives a fast finite element method for the nonlocal Laplacian on even grids, in any dimension.

That operator's stiffness matrix is hard to build on loose meshes, since its reach is wide and can be singular. On even grids the team links element bases to B-splines, whose blend traits cut the hard integrals down to balls with plain forms. The matrix then shows a block pattern that lets fast Fourier steps do the heavy work. As the reach shrinks to zero, the matrix falls back to the local one. A grid overlay trick stretches the solver to odd-shaped domains.
arxiv-2509-25709:
George Gui and Seungwoo Kim use language models to design better experiments before any data are collected. Blocking subjects into similar strata sharpens treatment effect estimates, but with many covariates the choice of strata becomes guesswork. Their generative stratification procedure has a model synthesize covariate data to guide the design.

Applied retrospectively to a set of real experiments, the method would have cut the variance of treatment effect estimates by ten to fifty percent versus simple randomization. It also stacks with standard stratification tools for further gains. The authors stress practicality: the simulation step is easy to implement. The paper speaks to the growing use of generative models inside the research design process itself.
arxiv-2509-26309:
Li, Wu, Zhang, Wang, and Yuan released a major software upgrade in this paper from twenty twenty-five. TBPLaS simulates electrons in materials with the tight-binding method. Exact solvers slow down steeply as models grow, blocking billion-orbital systems. The package instead propagates the state in time, which scales gently.

Version two rewrites the solvers in C++ for speed gains of several times or more. Modeling tools gained a matching C++ version, orders of magnitude faster. New features include spin texture maps, Berry curvature and Chern number tools, and targeted eigenstate solving. Graphics processor support joins the list as well. Benchmarks and refreshed tutorials accompany the release.
arxiv-2509-26509:
Raghul Saravanan and Sai Manoj P D present a new way to hunt bugs in chip designs, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Their tool, TargetFuzz, aims test inputs at chosen spots in a design rather than testing the whole chip at once. It uses a logic solver to steer the search and works at the real design level.

Tests on mixed chip blocks showed the tool could reach far more target spots than older fuzz tools. It reached full state cover in the tests and got to target states much faster. The gain in target cover was large when set against a standard cover-guided tool. Readers in chip testing get a method that scales to big designs.
arxiv-2510-00409:
Corey de Wit wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on the famous hat tiling and the system that generates it. The hat is a single tile shape that covers the plane only in non-repeating patterns. Smith and colleagues stunned geometers with its recent discovery. De Wit describes that aperiodic tiling as the output of an overlapping iterated function system.

An iterated function system builds a pattern by applying scaled copies of a rule again and again. The hat tiling's substitution rule is imperfect, so ordinary theory does not fit it directly. De Wit develops a theory of infinite sequences of such systems that converge uniformly, piece by piece. That theory then models the hat's substitution system faithfully. The paper connects a headline discovery in tiling theory to a classic fractal framework. It gives other researchers a new handle for proving facts about the hat.
arxiv-2510-00509:
