Their simulations follow non equilibrium chemistry, dust evolution, and cooling to very low temperatures, so atomic and molecular gas can be predicted directly.

For the present day universe the simulations reproduce the observed relations for both kinds of gas, including their scatter, which the team ties to stellar density, star formation intensity, and metal content. Looking back, the time galaxies need to use up molecular gas shrinks dramatically toward early epochs, mainly because early gas held fewer metals. Galaxies forming stars more intensely also hold more molecular gas and use it faster. Predictions match observations across a wide span of cosmic time.
arxiv-2512-11509:
Mohor Banerjee and fellow authors test whether methods that stop language models from hallucinating also dull their creativity, a trade off that matters for discovery in science. Assistants must be factually reliable, yet hypothesis generation needs divergent, exploratory thinking. The team weighed three popular fixes: a self verification method, a decoding method that contrasts internal layers, and retrieval augmented generation.

They tested several model families at sizes from small to very large on two creativity benchmarks. The three fixes pulled in varied directions. Self verification in fact enhanced divergent creativity, the decoding method suppressed it, and retrieval changed little. The findings give researchers concrete guidance: the right anti hallucination tool depends on whether the use case prizes being right alone or being right with creative range. Workflows in science, the authors argue, should choose on purpose rather than by habit.
arxiv-2512-11809:
Youssef Azouzi proves a completeness result for a family of function spaces built on vector lattices. Vector lattices, or Riesz spaces, order their elements like functions while allowing limits. The spaces Lp(T) arise when a conditional expectation operator T, an averaging map, supplies the size measure.

Azouzi first builds a general convergence theory that unifies order, norm, and weak convergence, with simpler proofs than before. With that frame he shows the Lp(T) spaces are strongly complete for all p, settling a question open for years. The universal completion is covered too. A final payoff is a new ergodicity result for systems that preserve the averaging operator.
arxiv-2512-12009:
Marc Uphues, Sebastian Thöne, and Herbert Kuchen draft a reference architecture for putting quantum software inside business systems. Quantum hardware can accelerate certain hard business problems, but enterprise software has strict needs for modularity and audit that quantum code rarely respects.

Their design splits the system into loosely coupled services. Some services are quantum free, handling business logic, while others wrap the quantum steps. An executable BPMN process model conducts the whole flow, giving a stable reusable pipeline. Two case studies from operations research, both combinatorial problems, show the pattern in action. The blueprint lets firms add quantum parts without rebuilding their core systems around them.
arxiv-2512-12109:
Allen Daniel Sunny and Ido Sivan-Sevilla build a framework that holds public sector AI to the law. Auto eligibility systems decide who gets vital benefits like CalFresh, California food aid program. Their stated reasons often drift from the statutes that authorize the decisions, leaving wronged applicants with little to contest.

The framework encodes eligibility rules from the state policy manual into a formal ontology. A pipeline turns statutory logic into checkable form, and a solver tests whether each system explanation obeys the law. Case studies show it catching explanations that break real rules and naming the rule broken. The goal is decisions that stay traceable and contestable by design.
arxiv-2512-12209:
Zahra Dehghanian and three co-authors present CineLOG in a 2025 paper on film style video generation. Text prompts give weak control over camera moves and genre, two things viewers notice at once. Old data sets also have uneven labels, noise, and a gap between fake and real footage.

CineLOG is a data set of 5,000 high quality, uncut clips with balanced coverage. It covers 17 camera movements and 15 film genres, each clip with scene notes and camera orders. A four stage pipeline builds the clips, plus a module that smooths joins between shots. Human judges rated its videos above top end to end models on following camera and script orders.
arxiv-2512-12809:
Junbo Jacob Lian and seven co-authors present OPAL, a system that learns an optimizer program for each black box problem, in a 2025 paper. Black box optimization tunes inputs when only outputs can be seen, and standard evolutionary algorithms vary wildly by problem. OPAL views an optimizer as a short program over a small set of search operators, like explore, restart, and local search.

A small design budget probes the landscape with a differential evolution baseline, and sampled points form a nearest neighbor graph encoded by a graph neural network. A meta learner then outputs a phase wise schedule of operators for that instance. On the CEC 2017 test suite, one meta trained policy was statistically competitive with top adaptive differential evolution variants, with modest overhead.
arxiv-2512-13409:
K. Decker French, Brenna Mockler, Nicholas Earl, and Tanner Murphey estimate how well the Vera Rubin Observatory will measure black hole masses from tidal disruption events. In such events, a star shredded by a black hole flares brightly. Rubin should find thousands per year, a flood compared with today.

They model how Rubin's sampling and noise affect fits to simulated light curves. Black hole masses in their tested range were recovered with typical errors of 0.26 dex, and early coverage removed the worst outliers. The disrupted star's mass proved hard to recover, tangled with accretion efficiency. Only 57 percent of cases correctly told full disruptions from partial ones.
arxiv-2512-13509:
Rodrigo F. Saliba and Raphael C. Drumond study the quantum Mpemba effect in open quantum systems. In this odd effect, a system far from balance can settle to balance faster than one that starts closer. Their 2025 paper looks at systems that lose memory of past states as they evolve, a case called Markovian.

The authors offer a cause based on parts of the system that stay free of decoherence. They show the decay rate can grow fast with system size, giving an extreme form of the effect. They also test strong forms through Davies maps and build a small model of the heat bath around the system.
arxiv-2512-13609:
Shweta Mahajan and co-authors introduce Do-Undo, a task and benchmark for action understanding in vision-language models. A model must show the outcome of a real-world action on a scene, then reverse it back to the first state. That forward and reverse demand tests true cause-and-effect grasp, not just style edits.

The team built a curated benchmark of reversible actions from real-world scenes. Their tests show current models struggle with reversibility in image generation. The gap shows why action understanding needs its own tests, apart from prompt-based editing scores. Do-Undo gives a plain testbed for judging and improving models that must reason about how the physical world changes.
arxiv-2512-13909:
Frank M. Abel and co-authors train machine learning models to predict magnetization of iron oxide nanoparticles from X-ray diffraction alone. High-throughput materials work needs property checks from a single measurement. Their route builds the training data from physics-based simulation rather than from large lab campaigns.

Simulated diffraction patterns, generated from crystallographic files and modulated, are linked to a simple magnetic model to give magnetization at a set field. Random Forest and Gradient Boosting models train on that simulated data. The team then synthesized real nanoparticles and measured diffraction and magnetization curves to tune the models. Best models reached an R squared above 0.9 for maximum magnetization at 2.8 T on five tuning samples, and predicted full magnetization curves reasonably well.
arxiv-2512-14009:
Yadikaer Maitiniyazi, Christof Wetterich, and Masatoshi Yamada discuss scaling solutions for gauge invariant flow equations in dilaton quantum gravity. Asymptotically safe gravity seeks an ultraviolet fixed point that keeps quantum gravity well behaved at very short distances. The dilaton version differs from the Reuter fixed point because the Planck mass depends on a scalar field.

They use the gauge invariant functional flow equation in a general approximation with up to two derivatives. That strengthens the argument that this fixed point exists. The quantum effective action from the scaling solution can describe inflation in early cosmology. It can also describe dynamical dark energy for late cosmology, linking one quantum gravity scenario to both ends of cosmic history.
arxiv-2512-14109:
Peter Athron and the GAMBIT Collaboration review global fits in a 2025 paper on the hunt for physics beyond the Standard Model. Global fits combine many experiments at once to test a theory against all the data, rather than one result at a time.

Early fits focused on simple supersymmetric models, which add partner particles to known ones. The review traces how fits grew to cover axion like particles, larger Higgs sectors, dark matter models, and effective field theories. It also covers the shift from hunting signals to judging whole models after null results. The authors close with machine learning, faster sampling, and shared software as next steps.
arxiv-2512-14409:
Michelle Döring, Jannes Malanowski, and Stefan Neubert study the River method, a newer voting rule related to Ranked Pairs. Both rules build a margin graph from voter preferences and remove majority cycles to pick a winner. Ties in the graph force a tiebreaker, which breaks neutrality because the rule then favors some options in advance.

Counting a candidate as a winner whenever any tiebreaker would elect them restores neutrality, but for Ranked Pairs that task is NP-complete. For River, the authors give a fast algorithm instead. Their Fused-Universe method runs all tiebreakings in one pass and produces certificates explaining each winner.
arxiv-2512-14509:
Andrei Tokovinin measures the orbits of twelve multiple-star systems, where stars orbit each other in nested pairs. He combines sharp speckle imaging with radial velocity data to pin down both the tight inner orbits and the wide outer ones. Masses and brightnesses of the individual stars are estimated along the way.

Four systems hold four stars arranged as a triple plus a distant single, while the rest are triples. Two triples turned out nearly flat, with similar-mass stars on mildly stretched orbits. One inner pair circles in just a quarter of a day, two stars nearly touching. Another compact system, first spotted by the Gaia mission, gained a newly confirmed wide companion.
arxiv-2512-14709:
Transformer language models reason well on many tasks, yet they stay brittle when a task needs stable handling of symbols. A vector-symbolic view is developed here to explain both sides of that behavior in one frame.

The reading treats self-attention and the residual stream as a rough form of vector symbolic architecture, a scheme where symbols are bound by vector operations. On this view, reasoning works when the binding stays clean and fails when it degrades. The view gives researchers a shared language for diagnosing transformer failures, and for building models that handle symbols with more care.
arxiv-2512-14809:
Tinglong Feng, Jesse Moes, and Tomislav Prokopec study how unstable quantum states decay over time. Such decay is mostly a steady exponential drop, but it starts with odd early behavior and ends with a slow tail. The team gives a full study of simple one dimensional models of this process, called resonance models.

They split the math into a pole part and a branch part, and use the split to define two key times. Dawn time marks when the steady decay takes over, and twilight time marks when the tail wins out. The twilight time has a neat closed form using the Lambert W function. Their formulas cover square and curved barriers, and the picture may extend to vacuum decay in field theory.
arxiv-2512-14909:
Wyatt Gibbons and five coauthors boost a quantum effect that lets current flow one way more easily than the other. The setting is a superconducting diode effect inside a SQUID, a loop device that is exquisitely sensitive to magnetic fields. The effect comes from interference between the wavy current patterns of the loop's branches.

Their device uses two loops, and each branch holds two gate tunable Josephson junctions in series. The gates let them tune both the shape and the strength of three interfering patterns on their own. With careful tuning, the diode efficiency passed 50 percent. Wiggles in the response as flux changed matched a simple model of the device well. Strong, tunable diodes of this kind are sought for superconducting circuits that waste less energy.
arxiv-2512-15309:
Kai Zhang and seven coauthors present GuangMing-Explorer, a four legged robot that explores on its own. Autonomous exploration fuses perception, planning, control, and motion, and it serves indoor search, mapping of extreme places, and resource scouting. Progress on single parts has been strong, but a full, practical system description covering hardware and software together is rare.

The paper walks through the whole platform: the hardware design, the software stack, how algorithms are deployed, and the experimental setup. Real world trials then show the robot carrying out exploration tasks effectively and efficiently. The authors aim to give builders a working blueprint, not just a lab demo. Their results suggest the platform can handle complex, unstructured environments, the kind where exploration robots earn their keep.
arxiv-2512-15409:
Hector Ariza, Carmen Fernandez, and Antonio Galbis study composition operators on weighted modulation spaces in a 2025 math paper. A composition operator reshapes a function by feeding its input through another function first. Modulation spaces measure a function by both its size and its frequency content, with weights that stress some parts over others.

The authors look at operators whose symbols are suitable small changes of the identity map. They study how these operators act between different weighted modulation classes. The work covers spaces built from tempered distributions and also spaces of ultradistributions defined with a subadditive weight. The results clarify when such reshaping stays well behaved across these settings.
arxiv-2512-15609:
Antonio Galvan and co authors test whether hadronic processes drive high energy emission in quasars seen by the Fermi space telescope in a 2025 paper. Most models credit leptons, such as electrons, for quasar gamma rays. Hadronic processes, involving protons, would also produce neutrinos, giving a cross check.

The team models the full spectral energy distributions of a sample of flat spectrum radio quasars with both lepton and hadron parts. The fits suggest a hadronic contribution is needed to explain the observed spectra. Even so, the share of the IceCube neutrino flux these quasars supply stays modest. The paper is accepted in Revista Mexicana de Astronomia y Astrofisica.
arxiv-2512-16109:
G Abellan, N Bolivar, and I Vasilev construct model universes from electric fields in an arXiv paper published in 2025. They ask how gravity responds when the only source is a classical electrostatic setup, like the field of a charged ball. Their spacetimes are static and spherically symmetric, written in Painleve-Gullstrand-like coordinates.

Inside each charged region the geometry comes out flat, while outside it is shaped by the field. The authors work through several cases: point-charge-like fields, screened Yukawa fields, dielectric layers, and a Hulthen-type field. For each they derive the pressures the Einstein equations require and test the classical energy conditions. They also check for singular behavior where regions join. The models offer a clean, solvable setting to study gravity from simple, well-understood sources.
arxiv-2512-16409:
Hao Tang and four co-authors generalize neural PDE solvers in an arXiv paper made public in 2025. Neural operators learn maps between functions, solving whole families of partial differential equations quickly. Most designs stumble on signals that do not repeat, on transient responses, and on domains with irregular shapes.

Their framework expands solutions in a pole-residue form enriched with exponential basis functions, which naturally captures aperiodic and decaying behavior. The Geometric Laplace Neural Operator then places that representation in the eigen-basis of the Laplace-Beltrami operator, extending it to curved surfaces of any shape without grids or periodicity. A companion network, GLNONet, makes the scheme grid-invariant in practice. Across PDE and ODE benchmarks and real-world data sets, the method proved more robust than leading rivals.
arxiv-2512-16509:
C Morin and seven co-authors demonstrate an elusive state of matter in research shared on arXiv in 2025. A supersolid is both a crystal, with atoms locked in a pattern, and a superfluid, flowing without friction. Real examples are rare and fragile, limited to weakly interacting gases.

The team confines dipolar excitons, bound electron-hole pairs with long-range interactions, in a lattice with long-range hopping. At fillings of one quarter, one third, and one half, crystals of about 100 sites form on their own, breaking the lattice's translation symmetry. Coherent hopping across the lattice gives the same crystals off-diagonal long-range order, the mark of superfluidity. Numerical calculations confirm quantitatively that supersolidity builds in the ground state. The framework reaches the strong interaction regime earlier work could not.
arxiv-2512-16709:
Didier Barret and Simon Dupourqué improve fast X-ray spectrum fitting with simulation-based inference, in the third paper of a series. The method learns likely parameter ranges from simulated spectra, giving near-instant fits for data from the future newAthena X-IFU instrument.

An auto-encoder first squeezes each spectrum into a small code, trained with a custom loss tied to fit quality. A density model then learns ranges from those codes over several rounds, each round zooming in near the observed data. A final importance sampling step corrects the learned ranges to exact ones. On test data the results match slow nested sampling, at ten times the speed on a laptop.
arxiv-2512-16809:
Davide Racco and Alfredo Stanzione revisit how dark matter froze out or froze in when the early universe went through supercooling, a stage of fast expansion during a phase switch. The changed expansion and the heat dumped at reheating can shift the final dark matter share.

Past work counted only a plain dilution factor. The pair show extra effects when dark matter making ends during supercooling itself. For WIMP-like candidates, zones once ruled out can open up for direct searches, and freeze-in candidates move closer to test reach. The linked gravitational wave background gains a distinct low-tone shape from a slow reheating stage, tying lab searches to wave astronomy.
arxiv-2512-16909:
Yuanchen Ju and coauthors introduce MomaGraph, a scene graph format for household robots that must both move and handle objects. A good scene record must say where things are, what they do, and which parts can be grabbed, and it must update as states change.

MomaGraph merges spatial and functional links with part-level detail in one task-aware graph. The team also built MomaGraph-Scenes, a large annotated data set, and MomaGraph-Bench, a test suite over six reasoning skills. Their 7 billion parameter vision-language model, trained with reward learning, predicts such graphs and plans from them. It hit 71.6 percent on the bench, 11.4 points past the best rival, and transferred to real robots.
arxiv-2512-17009:
João Barata and coauthors show how jet substructure can probe the first instants of heavy-ion collisions, when quark-gluon matter sits far from equilibrium and strongly directional. Those early stages set later flow, yet soft measures barely see them.

Using classical Yang-Mills runs and kinetic theory for the jet quenching parameter, they compute the energy-energy correlator for mid-rapidity jets in the BDMPS-Z frame. Split into celestial blocks, the result isolates terms that encode the directional shape of the young medium. A named observable couples straight to spatial anisotropy. Checks with the JEWEL Monte Carlo, tuned to a directional medium, agree in kind, and higher-point correlators could sharpen the view.
arxiv-2512-17209:
Keisuke Toyama and coauthors test whether foundational audio encoders understand music structure, the sections and repeats that organize a song. Such encoders, pre-trained on large audio corpora, lift many music tasks, but structure analysis was barely explored.

Eleven encoder types were compared, varying learning method, training data, and context length. Encoders trained by self-supervised masked modeling on music data proved best for structure analysis. Other mixes lagged, showing that what an encoder learned from matters more than size alone for this task. The findings chart how future encoders should be built and picked for music structure work.
arxiv-2512-17309:
Asil Kaan Bozcuoğlu and Ziyuan Liu revisit RoboEarth, an early project that let robots share what they know about actions, objects, and places through one shared knowledge graph. Engineers once wrote that knowledge by hand in a formal web language, a slow process that kept the library small. The authors ask whether a large language model can do much of that writing now.

Their planner, RecipeMasterLLM, takes a user prompt and drafts action descriptions that fit the RoboEarth format. The model was fine-tuned for that format, and at run time it pulls facts about the setting from the graph to ground its answers. The goal is a robot knowledge base that can grow on its own.
arxiv-2512-18309:
Harsh Rathva, Ojas Srivastava, and Pruthwik Mishra sketch a way to build safety into learning agents rather than bolting it on after. In multi agent training, guardrails usually come as outside rewards or late checks. Their ESAI frame grows an inner alignment signal inside each agent, a learned code that forecasts harm from roads not taken and steers updates away from it.

Four parts work together: soft what if penalties, attention weighted by alignment, a memory that links cause to later credit, and a graph spread that tempers bias. The authors prove when the inner codes stay bounded and weigh fairness against raw performance. No lab tests are included; the paper is a blueprint with open questions named.
arxiv-2512-18509: V. R. Shaginyan and A. Z. Msezane wrote this two-page comment, posted to arXiv in December 2025, answering an earlier paper on the future of the correlated electron problem (arXiv:2010.00584). They argue that some of the very difficult problems that paper raised have in fact been successfully solved, and that the field should focus on those resolved problems. Quoting the original authors' hope that their topics inspire progress, the comment concludes there is no need to mislead potential researchers about how open the problems remain.
arxiv-2512-18909:
Anshika Bansal, Jack Jenkins, and Daniel Winney refine predictions for rare kaon decays, prized tests of the Standard Model. The decays of a charged kaon into a pion plus a lepton pair, or a pion plus a neutrino pair, are described by nonlocal form factors that are hard to compute directly. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, builds dispersive representations grounded in unitarity.

The representations lean on the P-wave amplitude for kaon-pion scattering into two pions. That amplitude is parameterized in the Khuri-Treiman framework and pinned by data from kaon decays into three pions, plus the pion vector form factor. Relations from the operator product expansion tie the charged-lepton and neutrino modes together, adding constraints. The payoff is a sharper theoretical grip on the neutrino mode's spectrum and rate, exactly where new physics could hide.
arxiv-2512-19509:
Shangbo Yun, Xiaodong Gu, Jianghong Huang, and Beijun Shen sort programming languages into families, for the benefit of code language models. Trainers usually just pool code from every language together. Whether languages help or hinder each other, and which are truly kin, has gone mostly unasked.

Twenty-one linguistic traits, from variable definition to control flow, anchor the study. A model writes trait-matched snippets in nineteen languages, and embeddings of those parallel samples form a similarity map. Hierarchical clustering then reveals clear language families. The authors argue such kinship should shape how multilingual code data is mixed for training and inference, replacing blind pooling with structured sharing.
arxiv-2512-19609:
Route tracing on maps turns out to be a weak spot for multimodal language models, the systems that reason over images and text together. Artemis Panagopoulou and four co-authors note that models often break basic path rules, partly because pixel-accurate route annotations are costly to collect by hand. Their answer, MapTrace, generates that training data synthetically instead.

MapTrace builds synthetic map images and parses them at pixel level to produce exact path labels automatically. From it the team assembled 23 thousand path samples spread over 4 thousand maps, then fine-tuned open and proprietary models with the data. On the MapBench benchmark, success rates rose by up to 6.4 points and path-tracing error fell, showing spatial skills can be taught with synthetic supervision.
arxiv-2512-19809:
Shashwat Chakraborty and Taylor Hughes describe a skin effect that lives in state space, not in real space. In non-Hermitian systems, states can pile up at a boundary. Here the pile-up is across Fock space, the space of many-body setups. The stage is a quantum dimer model, where atoms pair up under strict rules. They name the effect the Fock space skin effect. They map it with both math and computer runs.

The payoff is state preparation. The effect can steer a system into a gapped quantum spin liquid state. Such states are prized for their long-range entanglement, and hard to make. A Rydberg-atom layout is shown to do the job. It uses blockade tricks to enforce the pairing rules. One-way reservoirs supply the non-Hermitian drive. The layout reaches an exact spin liquid ground state on a square grid.
arxiv-2512-20009:
Ahmed Elezaby and Artem Abanov bound how hot a superconductor near a quantum critical point can stay superconducting. At such a critical point, soft collective bosons mediate strong interactions that simultaneously create non-Fermi-liquid behavior and unconventional pairing, breaking textbook BCS and Eliashberg theory habits. Their playground is the gamma-model, where the effective interaction falls off as a power of frequency.

A recent reformulation recasts the Eliashberg equations as a classical infinite spin chain with nonlocal interactions, and free-energy Hessian analysis turns that picture into algebra. From it they derive rigorous closed-form lower and upper bounds on the transition temperature for every positive gamma. The new upper bound is significantly tighter than the literature's and converges quickly toward earlier numerical results, while their route independently confirms known lower bounds.
arxiv-2512-20209:
Ya-Min Quan and co-authors model the magnetic compound CoNb2O6 as a twisted Kitaev chain. Kitaev interactions are prized because they can host exotic fractional excitations, but they are hard to detect in real materials. The team fixes the model's twist angle by matching the measured specific-heat phase diagram of the compound.

They then predict what terahertz two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy should see in this material. The simulated signals show diagonal peaks and a grid of split rephasing peaks. A projection analysis traces these features to excitations made of two and four spinons. The message is practical: even weak Kitaev interactions should be visible with this spectroscopy, giving experimentalists a concrete detection route.
arxiv-2512-20309:
Xuegang Li and co-authors design a dark matter detector built from arrays of superconducting qubits. Light dark matter particles would deposit only tiny amounts of energy, far below what conventional detectors notice. The team's quantum parity detector aims to sense single phonons, the smallest packets of lattice vibration, with high resolution.

A two-chip layout reduces signal loss between the absorber and the sensing qubits. Full simulations of phonons and quasiparticles show the device catching energy deposits of roughly thirty milli-electronvolts with near-perfect efficiency. Projected sensitivity to dark matter scattering improves by orders of magnitude for both light and heavy mediators. Similar gains are expected for axion and dark photon absorption in a stated low mass range.
arxiv-2512-20409:
Junho Yoon, Jaemo Jung, Hyunju Kim, and Dongman Lee align room cameras with ambient sensors to recognize human actions. Wearable-based systems work, but they burden users, raise privacy worries, and scale poorly. Fixed exocentric video plus room sensors is a gentler alternative, provided the two streams can be aligned well.

Global alignment, the standard trick, washes out subtle motions and confuses actions with similar timing but different meaning. DETACH instead decomposes alignment into spatial and temporal parts. New sensor-spatial features, found by online clustering, ground the alignment in context. Mutual supervision sets spatial correspondence first; a weighted contrastive loss then handles time. On two public data sets, the method improves substantially over adapted wearable-based benchmarks.
arxiv-2512-20509:
Sanjay Pant, Himanshu Parihar, and Pradeep Kumar Sharma use holography to measure a subtle kind of quantum link. Entanglement negativity detects mixed-state links that entropy measures can miss. Their bulk setting is a deformed anti-de Sitter black hole, backreacted by a cloud of strings, dual to a hot gauge theory with heavy quarks.

The authors establish a first-law-like relation for the heat-like rules of entanglement at small backreaction, taking the zero-temperature black hole as ground state. Pen-and-paper expansions in cold and hot limits yield negativity for adjacent, bipartite, and disjoint regions. Backreaction enhances distillable links at both extremes of heat. Compared with the usual entropy measure and mutual information, negativity reads the tug-of-war between thermal and quantum correlations more sharply.
arxiv-2512-20709:
Władysław Sokołowski, Huma Jamil, and Karol Makuch extend a theory of diffusion to particles shaped like rods. In complex fluids, how fast a particle spreads resists the classic Stokes-Einstein rule. A fruitful line of work ties that spreading to the fluid's viscosity function, which says how thick the fluid feels at each length scale. The authors widen that line from round probes to long ones, using linear response theory.

Their test rod is a dimer, two beads joined as one. Neat closed forms give its spread rates along its axis and sideways to it, both read straight off the viscosity function. The same forms cover near-round wandering and strongly one-way, snake-like motion. For lab workers who track rod-like tracers in polymer solutions, the result is a handy tool, with its limits for gels stated plainly.
arxiv-2512-21009:
S. M. Shovan, Arindam Khanda, Sanjukta Bhowmick, and Sajal Das build the missing data structure for networks whose connections join groups, not pairs. Hypergraphs capture those higher-order interactions, and counting their triads reveals group patterns ordinary graphs miss. Real hypergraphs are large and constantly changing, and no specialized tooling existed for tracking them. ESCHER is a graphics-processor-centered structure designed to store an evolving hypergraph and update triad counts without recomputing from scratch.

The update framework trims redundant work for hyperedge-based, vertex-based, and temporal triads alike. On large real and synthetic datasets it outruns prior methods by factors reaching into the hundreds, with the largest gain above four hundred seventy times on vertex-based triads. Dynamic hypergraph analysis becomes something researchers can run interactively rather than overnight.
arxiv-2512-21109:
Chen Liang and Daniel Rakita speed up the derivative bottleneck inside a popular robot-control library. MuJoCo MPC plans robot motion by repeatedly rolling out the MuJoCo physics simulator and optimizing. It prices candidate actions with finite-difference derivatives, a costly nudge-and-measure routine. That routine scales badly with a robot's degrees of freedom. The authors swap in Web of Affine Spaces derivatives, a recent technique that reuses information across related derivative computations to produce accurate approximations faster and more stably.

The fit with predictive control is natural, since each planning step needs derivatives only slightly changed from the last. Across a suite of tasks and robot bodies, the new backend integrates seamlessly, runs up to twice as fast with gradient-based planners, and beats the library's sampling-based planners on efficiency and reliability. The integrated implementation is open source.
arxiv-2512-21809:
Vitthal Bhandari, in a term paper for a course on the societal impacts of language technologies, examines how researchers study cross-cultural bias in language models. Large models can adjust answers to cultural context, but they also overgeneralize across cultures. Bhandari's concern is methodological: evaluations of cultural bias often never involve the people who actually use the technology.

He reviews twenty papers on cultural bias in natural language processing published in 2025, building on earlier work about stakeholder engagement. From that literature he draws a set of observations meant to help future researchers define bias concretely rather than loosely. He also argues for evaluating the actual harms of biased output, not just measuring its presence on a benchmark. The paper advocates a robust assessment of societal impact as a standard part of bias research. It is a critique of evaluation practice itself.
arxiv-2512-21909:
Computing gradients of the CCSD energy, needed for geometry optimization, is expensive for large symmetric molecules. Luca Melega, Tommaso Nottoli, Jürgen Gauss, and Filippo Lipparini present a code built on Cholesky decomposition of the two-electron integrals with Abelian point-group symmetry.

The decomposition uses a symmetry-adapted two-step algorithm. Derivatives of the Cholesky vectors use symmetry-adapted nuclear displacements and are contracted on the fly with the CCSD density matrices. Tests on such systems with several hundred basis functions show the speed gains from using symmetry. The code targets the medium and large systems where standard gradient codes become the bottleneck. Each geometry search step needs them.
arxiv-2512-22009:
Graphical interface agents must act quickly on routine steps yet ground precisely when a task hinges on one small element. Sarthak Mehrotra and colleagues present iSHIFT, a lightweight agent with two modes. A fast mode uses global screen cues; a slow mode grounds in detail, guided by perception tokens and latent reasoning.

The perception control module decides both how the model reasons and where it attends on screen, adapting effort to the step at hand. At only two and a half billion parameters, iSHIFT matches state-of-the-art performance on multiple GUI benchmarks. The design targets the practical gap between heavyweight agents and the responsiveness real interfaces demand.
arxiv-2512-22209:
Haozhe Jia applies diffusion models to sharpen the blurry pictures from capsule endoscopy, the swallowable-camera exam of the digestive tract. Capsule cameras are limited by size, power, and transmission, so their images lack the fine mucosal detail doctors need for early diagnosis. Jia's system learns a probabilistic mapping from low-resolution to high-resolution images using the SR3 approach built on denoising diffusion models.

Trained and tested on the HyperKvasir dataset of gastrointestinal endoscopy images, the method beat bicubic interpolation and GAN-based rivals such as ESRGAN. With attention methods added, image quality reached a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 29.3 decibels and a structural similarity of 0.71 in the reported tests. Anatomical boundaries, blood vessel patterns, and lesion forms were preserved better than with the alternatives.
arxiv-2512-22409:
L. Landivar Scott and four co-authors measure how silver iodide films bend light nonlinearly, and how the answer depends on the crystal phase grown. Silver iodide's noncentrosymmetric lattice and direct band gap make it a useful nonlinear optical material. Films grown by physical vapor deposition can be steered into zincblende or wurtzite phases, arriving as triangular flakes or rod-shaped crystals respectively.

Using polarization-resolved second harmonic generation and two-photon light emission, the team found sixfold symmetric harmonic patterns from the flakes and twofold patterns from the rods, in both reading channels. Theory combining second- and third-order response strengths explains the shapes. After correcting for internal reflections and interference, they estimate the effective nonlinear coefficients for both phases, giving a careful method for thin films on substrates.
arxiv-2512-23009:
Rudraksh Sharma tests whether building the system's symmetries into a quantum circuit makes near-term quantum simulation more trustworthy. The target is the ground state of a one-dimensional antiferromagnetic Heisenberg spin chain, a standard model of quantum magnets. Variational quantum eigensolvers attack such problems with adjustable circuits, but on noisy hardware the choice of circuit shape, the ansatz, decides whether the result means anything.

Sharma compares a generic hardware-efficient ansatz against physics-informed circuits that preserve the system's symmetries, using the same resources. Against exact reference results and noiseless simulation, the symmetry-preserving circuits gave clearly better energy estimates, converged more cleanly, and resisted hardware noise better. The approach was then validated on real IQM Garnet quantum hardware. The conclusion is practical: for reliable simulation on today's noisy machines, circuits should be designed around the problem's symmetries, not the device's layout.
arxiv-2512-23109:
Paul Thompson asks how much data generative and vision-language models need before their predictions can be trusted uniformly, not just on average? In medical uses, a model can look accurate overall while failing badly on rare conditions, and ordinary calibration scores hide exactly that. Thompson studies predictors whose outputs vary by changing prompts or semantic embeddings inside a bounded representation space.

When outputs depend smoothly on a low-dimensional semantic representation, a premise backed by the spectral structure of text and joint image-text embeddings, classical uniform convergence theory gives finite-sample guarantees. The bounds cover accuracy and calibration for these classifier groups. The required sample size depends on the representation's dimension, not the ambient embedding size. Spectrum-dependent versions make the role of eigenvalue decay clear. The upshot is guidance on when today's dataset sizes suffice for uniformly reliable medical predictions.
arxiv-2512-23209: Swathi Shetty, B. R. Rakshith, and Sayinath Udupa study the ABS spectral radius, the largest eigenvalue of a graph's ABS matrix, a popular measure blending degree and edge structure. They settle which graphs in two small families push this value highest. Among bipartite unicyclic graphs, connected graphs with exactly one cycle, they determine the graphs attaining the largest value. Among bicyclic graphs, those with two independent cycles, they characterize the graphs attaining the largest and second largest values.
arxiv-2512-23509:
Mikhail Rybakov investigates the algorithmic complexity of non-classical logics. The focus falls on superintuitionistic and modal systems. His method studies whole logics through small fragments of them. A fragment keeps only a few variables or predicate letters. The question is when the full logic reduces to such a piece.

Propositional logics usually reduce to fragments with at most two variables. One-variable and even variable-free fragments often suffice. Predicate logics usually reduce to fragments with one or two unary predicates. Two or three individual variables cover those cases. Rybakov gives conditions that make such reductions work. He also gives examples where they fail. Non-reducibility is established there. New complexity bounds follow for several logics. Results on Kripke-incompleteness and analogues of the Church and Trakhtenbrot theorems round out the work.
arxiv-2512-23709:
Hau-Shiang Shiu and six co-authors make diffusion-based video upscaling fast enough for live streams. Diffusion super-resolution produces excellent quality, but ordinary versions peek at future frames and need many denoising steps, so they cannot run online. Stream-DiffVSR instead works strictly frame by frame, using only the past.

Three pieces make it work: a distilled denoiser that needs only four steps, a temporal guidance module that feeds motion-aligned cues into each frame's denoising. A lightweight decoder that sharpens detail while keeping consecutive frames coherent. On a high-end graphics card it processed high-definition frames in about a third of a second each, cut per-frame runtime by more than a hundredfold against earlier diffusion methods. Shrank the wait for the first frame from over an hour to a fraction of a second.
arxiv-2512-24209:
Sei Ban and five colleagues build detector hardware for a rare-decay search. Future experiments will hunt the muon decay into a positron and a photon. The target sensitivity reaches one part in a quadrillion. Their conversion spectrometer uses an active LYSO converter. Incident photons convert into electron-positron pairs inside it. The converter also records energy deposit and timing.

Simulations fixed the converter's thickness and segment size. Prototype segments were then fabricated. An electron beam at the KEK test facility measured them. The timing resolution reached twenty-five picoseconds. That beats the thirty-picosecond design goal. The light yield also exceeded requirements by a wide margin. Both results clear the bar set for the full instrument. The work supports precise reconstruction of the decay's high-energy photons.
arxiv-2512-24309:
Jessica López-Sánchez studies two cosmological tensions in one model. The tensions concern the Hubble constant and the clustering measure S8. Her setting is ultra-light dark matter with a quartic self-interaction. The interaction switches on briefly. During that episode the scalar field acts radiation-like. It then settles into matter-like behavior.

The framework stays perturbative and model-independent. The self-interaction's energy is a localized addition to the cosmic budget. Responses of key observables become weighted integrals over time. Distinct kernels encode when each observable is sensitive. The sound horizon responds to early times. The growth factor responds later. A simple analytic relation links the two responses. Correlated shifts in the Hubble constant and S8 follow. Their sign and size depend on the episode's timing. One brief change to expansion history thus touches both tensions at once.
arxiv-2512-24409:
Zhang Hangyue constructs an example in smooth dynamics. The system is partially hyperbolic, with stable, unstable, and central directions. It is also mixed and nontrivial in the technical sense. The author names its skeleton explicitly. The example shares features with the classical ones in the area.

Each physical measure of the system has striking support. Three fixed points lie inside it. Their unstable indices are all different from each other. Perturbing the skeleton then produces a variation effect. The count of physical measures changes only in one direction under small perturbations. Measures can merge or vanish, but not suddenly appear. The example tests the general theory of such mixed systems. It shows how delicate the count of physical measures can be.
arxiv-2512-24509:
A Bagci tests optimization methods that need no derivatives on a quantum chemistry problem. The task is minimizing Hartree-Fock-Roothaan energy functionals. The orbitals are Slater-type with noninteger order. Their parameters enter in a nonlinear way. Exact derivatives of the energy are not readily available. Derivative-free methods must therefore carry the work.

Four algorithms compete under identical conditions. Powell's method and the Nelder-Mead simplex represent the classics. A coordinate pattern search joins them. A model-based method builds radial basis surrogates. Tests start on the Powell singular function. That case is notoriously hard, with a singular Hessian at its minimum. Closed-shell atoms from the helium and beryllium families follow. Up to eight nonlinear parameters are tuned. The study is the first systematic comparison of this kind for noninteger orbitals.
arxiv-2512-24909:
Matthias Kaminski reviews non-balance motion in quantum chromodynamics through holography, the duality that maps a strongly coupled plasma to gravity in a higher-dimensional space. Plasma from heavy ion crashes starts far from balance, then settles toward hydrodynamic pattern. Direct QCD computing of the early stage is prohibitively hard, while holography gives access at strong coupling.

Three hydrodynamic methods and contrasts are reviewed as examples. Nuclear physics readers get an survey of how far-from-balance stages can be modeled at all. The review connects crash experiments, working hydrodynamics, and gravity dual accounts of the same changing plasma.
arxiv-2512-25009:
Sajad Salami determines the splitting field and generators for Shioda's elliptic surface defined by a cubic with a very high power term. That surface is famous for rank sixty-eight, the largest known for an elliptic curve over a function field. The splitting field is the smallest extension over which all rational points are defined.

A symbolic algorithmic approach, using the known decomposition of the Mordell-Weil lattice, produces the field and sixty-eight linearly independent generators. Arithmetic geometry readers get explicit control over a record-holding example. Explicit generators let others compute heights and intersections on a surface often cited only for its rank.
arxiv-2601-00009:
Lucas Arenstein and Michael Kastoryano price options that depend on several assets at once, a task governed by the Black-Scholes equation. Standard grid solvers grow impossibly fast as assets are added, so in practice they stop at about three assets. Traders instead rely on random sampling for complex multi-asset products. Their 2026 paper shows a compressed grid method can do better.

Using quantized tensor trains, a compact way to store large grids, the pair build solvers for European and American options. They compute full price grids and risk measures for basket and max-min options in three to five dimensions with high accuracy. The authors say the approach can reach ten to fifteen assets on ordinary hardware, with room to grow.
arxiv-2601-00309:
David Millard and coauthor Ali Baheri ask whether optimal transport can fuse reward lessons from a fleet of robots. Each agent works in a slightly different setting. All chase one shared high level goal. Pooling raw data is often blocked in practice. Dynamics differ, privacy binds, and bandwidth runs thin. Inverse reinforcement learning must therefore stay federated.

Each client runs a light maximum entropy learner at home. It infers a local reward function from behavior. Those functions then merge through a Wasserstein barycenter. The merge respects the geometry of the reward space. The authors prove it beats plain parameter averaging. Their estimate stays more faithful to the true shared reward. Communication stays light throughout the process. The frame suits fleets that cannot share raw logs. Heterogeneous agents gain one reward that travels across settings.
arxiv-2601-00509:
Code written by AI often has security holes, logic slips, and lines that will not run. Vidyut Sriram and four co-authors tackle that flaw in a 2026 paper. Their workflow lets one code-writing model fix its own work in rounds. Each round feeds it notes from three tools. One is the compiler, which flags lines that break. One is a security scanner, and one tests code paths with symbols, not fixed inputs.

The workflow also looks up past fixes that worked on like flaws. The team tested the setup on more than three thousand programs. The programs came from two open code models, one small and one larger. For the small model, security flaws fell by about ninety-six in each hundred. For the larger model, the share of code with grave flaws fell a lot too. Tool feedback, the study shows, can make AI code much safer.
arxiv-2601-00609:
Mehdi Heydari Shahna, Pauli Mustalahti, and Jouni Mattila design navigation and control for very large mobile robots working on loose, slippery ground. Such machines are complex multibody systems, and poor traction makes them drift from their intended pose. Their framework combines four modules to keep the robot stable and safe.

A vision module fuses stereo cameras and onboard sensors into a fast, accurate pose estimate. A high-level nonlinear predictive controller then corrects drift by updating wheel commands, while a neural network policy approximates the complicated behavior of the wheel actuation itself, backed by robust adaptive control. Learning-based control adds safety guarantees on top. The package targets heavy machines that must operate reliably where wheels slip.
arxiv-2601-00709:
Heng Yuan, Wenzhong Zhang, and Bo Wang compare two ways to compute the dyadic Green's functions of electromagnetism in layered materials. These functions describe how fields from a point source propagate through stacked media, and they underpin fast simulation methods for antennas, chips, and optics. One formulation, based on splitting fields into two standard polarization families, is well known in engineering.

The second, newer formulation uses a vector potential and a matrix basis, and the authors simplify its derivation considerably. They show the two formulations are equivalent, while the newer one's interface conditions decouple more directly and its basis separates out awkward non-symmetric factors. That makes far-field approximations easier, and the method extends to related tensor Green's functions.
arxiv-2601-00909:
Sheldon Paul and Izzat Alsmadi build one dashboard for judging how securely Linux servers are configured. Different auditing tools grade hardening differently, leaving administrators with incompatible scores. Working on the FABRIC research testbed, the authors set up three Ubuntu servers at baseline, partial, and full hardening levels, then audited them with three tools across many runs.

Their Unified Compliance Aggregator parses each tool's output, normalizes scores onto a common zero-to-one-hundred scale, and blends them into a weighted metric, with a rule engine for organization-specific policies. Full hardening raised one tool's compliance score from about forty to about seventy-two, and custom rule compliance more than doubled. The aggregator aims at clearer, reproducible security assessment.
arxiv-2601-01209:
Xin Tan and five colleagues build OrchestrRL, a system for training large language models with reinforcement learning at scale. Modern practice splits the work: one pool of machines generates text, another trains on it. That split creates two headaches. Generation loads swing wildly and fall out of balance, and the network traffic between stages keeps changing shape, straining a fixed network.

OrchestrRL adjusts both compute and network on the fly. Its scheduler reshapes how generation work is spread across machines as loads shift. Its fabric, RFabric, uses optical switches to rebuild the network layout for each phase, from training to weight updates. On a testbed of sixty-four high-end graphics processors, throughput rose by up to about forty-two percent over static setups. Simulations at larger scale show the reconfigurable fabric also wins on cost. The work targets the plumbing that increasingly limits AI training.
arxiv-2601-01309:
A very large team, led by Aleksey Lunkin and colleagues at Google and partner institutes, uses a superconducting quantum processor to watch a disordered quantum system evolve in two dimensions. The fate of such systems, whether they spread out or stay localized, is a famous open problem that classical computers struggle to simulate. Fast sampling lets the team picture the state as a network over its configurations.

Tracking how often the system returns to its starting pattern, they find heavy-tailed statistics and slow, glassy decay. As disorder grows, the spread of pattern probabilities widens into a power law spanning eight orders of magnitude. Analysis shows the state occupies only a finite fraction of its possible space, a signature of a multifractal, non-ergodic regime. The results rule out a direct jump from spreading to localized behavior. They also show quantum hardware can attack questions that stall classical simulation.
arxiv-2601-01409:
Six authors led by Chuyuan Tao study how a sampling-based controller should draw its trial moves when steering a legged robot. The controller, MPPI, tests many random control sequences, scores them, and blends the best into the next command. For a four-legged robot, naive random sampling wastes trials and produces jerky motion.

The team compares several sampling designs inside the same framework. Some draw each step independently; others build smooth spline curves through a few control points, which ties the steps together. Simulations on a quadruped platform measure smoothness, task success, robustness, and how many samples each design needs. The comparison shows sampling design is not a detail but a main lever on performance. The findings give practical guidance for deploying this controller class on complex legged machines, where every wasted trial costs stability.
arxiv-2601-01509:
Midooka, Mizumoto, and Ebisawa look for clumps of gas blowing out from the centers of bright galaxies. Seyfert galaxies host feeding black holes, and fast winds from them are well known. Less clear is whether slower, patchy clouds also move out at great speed and share the same origin.

Using past X-ray telescope records for twelve galaxies, the team fit changes in the spectra with a ratio method they built. Patchy, mildly charged clouds explained most soft X-ray changes. In three galaxies, speeds matched or beat known ultra-fast winds. Speeds rose with brightness, backing the idea that light from the center pushes both kinds of wind.
arxiv-2601-01609:
Albert Sadowski and Jaroslaw Chudziak combine language models with strict logic rules to judge text against written standards. Jobs like checking trial eligibility, court evidence, or science methods need flexible reading plus rulings that can be audited. Models read well but apply rules unevenly, while logic systems are steady but need structured input.

In their design, a model turns plain text into formal statements guided by expert-written definitions, then a rule engine checks them with firm guarantees. Trials across legal, science, and clinical tasks with eleven models beat ordinary prompting overall. Removing the logic check in a side test cut much of the gain, proving its worth.
arxiv-2601-01809:
G. Vilella Nilsson and M. A. Moore examine crystal defects, dislocations, vacancies, and interstitials, in a two-dimensional one-component plasma, where charged particles interact through a logarithmic potential on the curved surface of a cylinder.

Numerical results confirm a striking prediction: for vacancy-interstitial pairs, the Coulomb attraction and the elastic energy cancel at long distances, leaving a defect energy that stays bounded. Yet bound dislocation pairs behave in ways that depend on how they were prepared, a history dependence missing from the standard KTHNY theory of two-dimensional melting. Isolated dislocations can also be cheap enough to appear thermally, raising doubts about whether that theory, or any phase transition, applies to this plasma at all.
arxiv-2601-01909:
An early universe that expands at different rates in different directions is called a Bianchi I spacetime. Alex Giacomini, Chevara Hansraj, Genly Leon, and Andronikos Paliathanasis study such universes. Their setting is four-dimensional Einstein-Gauss-Bonnet scalar field theory. That is a modified gravity with an extra scalar degree of freedom.

The team rewrites the equations in dimensionless variables. They map the long-term behavior with both analysis and numerics. Some solutions speed up. In them, the scalar field and the Gauss-Bonnet term together act like a cosmological constant. Plain expanding and flat solutions appear too. Scaling solutions are ruled out. With three distinct expansion rates, Kasner-like solutions emerge in compact form. A new family also appears. Its geometry splits into two-dimensional pieces. That echoes behavior seen in higher-dimensional theories.
arxiv-2601-02409:
Longwei Wang, Ifrat Ikhtear Uddin, and KC Santosh attack two linked problems in medical image AI, too few labeled images and models whose reasons clinicians cannot see. Few shot learning copes with scarce labels but stays opaque, while active learning picks useful new samples without asking whether the model's attention makes sense. Their paired frameworks join the two concerns.

In the first, radiologist drawn regions of interest guide training through a loss based on Grad CAM attention maps, joined with prototypical classification, so the model looks where experts look. In the second, new samples are chosen for both uncertainty and attention mismatch, closing the loop. On brain MRI and two chest X ray data sets the guided methods beat non guided baselines, reaching their best accuracy on the brain tumor data.
arxiv-2601-02609:
Arjun S. Nair presents Chronicals, an open source framework that speeds up fine tuning of large language models by attacking memory use, the usual bottleneck. A seven billion parameter model can need far more memory for weights, gradients, and optimizer states than a strong forty gigabyte accelerator holds. Chronicals combines four optimizations that reinforce each other.

Fused Triton kernels cut most memory traffic by merging common operations. A cut cross entropy method shrinks the memory held by output logits from gigabytes to a small fraction. A LoRA variant uses theoretically derived learning rates that differ sharply between its two adapter matrices. Best fit decreasing sequence packing recovers most of the computing wasted on padding. On a standard test model the full fine tuning speed is more than three times that of the popular Unsloth framework, with a still larger gain for adapter tuning.
arxiv-2601-02809:
Wolfgang Woess surveys the later work of Alessandro Figà-Talamanca, the Italian mathematician who led his country's harmonic analysis school for many years and died in 2023. From the late nineteen seventies his research centered on harmonic analysis on free groups and trees.

Later he turned to diffusion processes on homogeneous ultrametric spaces, such as local fields and totally disconnected abelian groups, spaces closely tied to trees and their boundaries. In particular he built such diffusion processes from discrete time random walks on trees. Woess gives detailed comments on that part of his work and its abundant related literature, written for a volume of Figà-Talamanca's selected papers.
arxiv-2601-03209:
Wooyeon Kim, Jens Marklof, and Matthew Welsh verify a famous conjecture about the spectra of simple quantum systems. In 1977, Berry and Tabor predicted that the energy levels of a generic integrable system should be spaced like a Poisson process, essentially at random. The authors settle the two-point statistics case for a quantum particle in a three-dimensional box, under a Diophantine condition on the box's proportions.

The result extends earlier two-dimensional work by Eskin, Margulis, and Mozes, which rested on the quantitative Oppenheim conjecture for quadratic forms. Three dimensions are harder because the relevant indefinite forms must be studied in shrinking intervals rather than fixed ones. The proof recasts the counting problem through values of ternary quadratic forms and averages a theta function over expanding unipotent orbits, where Ratner's measure classification controls the asymptotics.
arxiv-2601-03309:
Jianke Zhang and nine co-authors ask a practical question about robots that see, read, and act: how much does the choice of the underlying vision-language model matter for the final policy? Vision-language-action models borrow a pretrained model's competence, and builders assume better general models make better robots. The authors introduce VLM4VLA, a minimal pipeline that converts general models into action policies with only a few new learnable parameters, enabling fair comparison.

Across three benchmarks, the simple pipeline proved surprisingly competitive with sophisticated designs. Vision-language initialization consistently beat training from scratch, but a model's general benchmark competence was a poor predictor of its control performance. The finding challenges a common assumption: broad vision-language skill looks necessary for embodied control, but it is far from sufficient.
arxiv-2601-03409:
William Ho and six co-authors build a tabletop demonstration of dynamic stabilization that students can watch with their own eyes. A permanent magnet hangs between two anti-Helmholtz coils driven sinusoidally, and the oscillating field traps it ponderomotively, the same principle behind Paul traps and the Kapitza pendulum. The magnet shows rapid micromotion layered over a slower secular swing, with the micromotion growing as the magnet strays from center.

Driving between twelve and eighteen hertz keeps the two timescales cleanly separated and visible. Video tracking, included with the article, quantifies the motion and finds a stability edge when the drive drops near six or seven hertz. From the measured separation of timescales, the team extracts the effective Mathieu parameter of the system. The setup turns an abstract stability theory into a bench-top exhibit.
arxiv-2601-03609:
Pratyush Jena and three co-authors work on reading ancient stone inscriptions in Indic scripts, where carved letters blend into weathered rock. The first step is binarization, turning a photo into clean black and white so letters stand out. Poor contrast, surface damage, stray marks, and wildly varying layouts make standard methods fail on these stones.

Their strategy cuts images into patches chosen adaptively, with character context guiding the choices, and trains an Attention U-Net network on them. Attention helps the model notice faint structural cues, while dynamic sampling teaches it to handle noise and irregular layouts. They also built a carefully annotated, pixel-precise dataset. Reliable binarization is the gateway to digitizing inscriptions before the stones erode further.
arxiv-2601-03709:
Sarah Spiekermann-Hoff and six co-authors argue that digital society needs an ethical compass as artificial intelligence accelerates. Popular visions of superhuman machines and seamless digital life, they say, hide real costs: surveillance, mental health crises, and other harms from technologies that surround daily life. Inspired by the durability of the biblical Ten Commandments, a European interdisciplinary group drafted Ten Rules for the Digital World.

The rules form a framework meant to help individuals and societies make prudent, human-centered decisions about powerful technology. The article presents that ethos as guidance rather than law, aimed at everyday choices as much as policy. Its appearance in a research venue signals a shift: technical communities increasingly treat shared norms as part of the design problem, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2601-03909:
Clara Bertinelli Salucci, writing alone, characterizes a tricky case in statistical testing: likelihood ratio tests where nuisance parameters also sit on the boundary of the allowed space. When parameters of interest are on the boundary, the test statistic's long-run distribution is known to be a chi-squared mixture whose weights come from the geometry of an associated cone. Much less was known once boring but necessary nuisance parameters are constrained too.

Salucci gives the first general characterization for arbitrary numbers of both kinds of boundary parameters. The analysis tracks how the cone geometry changes as parameters of interest are traded for nuisances, and the orthogonal case is worked out in detail. Boundary problems arise constantly in applications, from variance testing to mixture models, so a general answer replaces a patchwork of special cases.
arxiv-2601-04209:
Seokhwan Ko, Donghyeon Lee, Jaewoo Chun, Hyungsoo Han, and Junghwan Cho build a local search system to suggest research collaborators inside a hospital. Language models help with clinical, research, and office work, but strict privacy and network rules force sensitive data to stay on local machines. Their retrieval system must therefore run fully in-house.

The system recommends collaborators from PubMed papers written by members of one medical institution. It embeds text with PubMedBERT, a model tuned for biomedical language, and writes summaries with a locally run LLaMA3 model. The five authors show the pairing of a specialist encoder with a light local generator works in practice. Their study supports biomedical knowledge discovery under tight deployment limits, where cloud services cannot be used.
arxiv-2601-04509:
Peixin Huang and five co-authors give optimization solvers a new kind of neural backbone, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Mixed-integer linear programming is the standard language for hard planning and scheduling problems, but its NP-hardness makes big instances slow. learning-based helpers usually read a problem as a graph of variables and constraints, using graph neural networks whose local view limits what they can grasp.

The alternative proposed here is attention, organized around the elements themselves: variables and constraints each attend within their own kind, and cross-attend to the other kind, in parallel. Tested at three levels — judging whole instances, scoring individual elements, and reading the state of a solve in progress — the backbone consistently beat graph-network architectures. The authors present element-centric dual attention as a stronger foundation for learning-enhanced combinatorial optimization generally.
arxiv-2601-04609:
Rhea Kapur, Robert Hawkins, and Elisa Kreiss separate two qualities that image description systems routinely confuse, in a 2026 arXiv paper. A caption can be long and empty or short and sharp, yet evaluations for vision-language models. Increasingly the voice that describes images to blind users — often reward length as if it were information. The authors define specificity properly: a description is specific insofar as it picks its target image out from a contrast set of rivals.

They build a dataset that holds length fixed while varying information content, and confirm that people reliably prefer the more specific descriptions at any length. Model behaviour shows why the distinction matters: given the same word budget, how the words are allocated changes specificity, so no control for length alone can explain the differences. Evaluation, they argue, should score specificity directly rather than verbosity.
arxiv-2601-04809:
Caijun Xu's 2026 paper, written with 4 co-authors, introduces SCALER, a training environment meant to keep reasoning practice at the right difficulty. Reinforcement learning can improve large language models, but progress stalls when tasks are too easy or too hard for the model's current level. Training also suffers when a narrow set of problem patterns repeats too often.

SCALER answers with adaptive environment design and a scalable synthesis pipeline that creates fresh tasks. The environment adjusts as the model improves, keeping the learning signal informative instead of letting it fade. Better-matched practice could make reinforcement learning steadier and cheaper, since fewer training steps would be wasted on problems that teach the model nothing new.
arxiv-2601-05009:
Avik Dutta and 4 co-authors probe how language models fail on distorted tables in a 2026 paper. Tables in a standard format are subjected to semantic and structural distortions, small changes that a careful reader should notice and correct. The authors find that models show no built-in knack for spotting and fixing such distortions, answering as if the warped table were sound.

Given an explicit warning through a system prompt, models partly adjust their reasoning and fix some distortions, though only in part and not for every case. The team introduces a small expert-curated dataset for table question answering under distortion. The result matters for business and science users who paste real spreadsheets into models: silent table errors can pass straight into decisions unless the model is primed to check.
arxiv-2601-05509:
Yi-Ning Weng and Hsuan-Wei Lee show, in a 2026 paper, that routine exploration can break cooperation in shared-policy multi-agent learning. Many agents sharing one policy is a common way to scale reinforcement learning. In social dilemmas, stable and payoff-dominant cooperative outcomes may still exist.

Controlled experiments with shared Deep Q-Networks settled into persistent low cooperation. The cause was not misaligned rewards, noise, or short training. Partial observability plus shared parameters biased the common representation toward defection, and that bias spread across agents. The collapse held across network sizes, exploration schedules, and payoffs. It vanished when agents used separate policies or representations, giving designers a clear structural warning.
arxiv-2601-05609:
Nguyen Minh Phuong and 3 co-authors propose a 2026 pipeline that uses large language models to augment training data for legal information extraction. Extracting structured facts from legal text normally needs costly hand annotation. Their approach generates additional training material with model help instead.

The authors describe the method as simple and effective, reducing manual annotation effort while making extraction systems more robust. They also argue the same augmentation idea transfers beyond law to other natural language processing tasks. The clearest contribution is the overall design itself: language-model-driven data augmentation aimed at legal extraction and reasoning, with generality presented as a central feature.
arxiv-2601-05909:
Ayoub Ajarra and Debabrota Basu study in 2026 how fairness auditing can survive when the audited model keeps changing. Machine learning systems embedded in finance and other infrastructure get updated as environments shift. Those updates can alter the model class while preserving the property under audit, or quietly destroy it.

The authors ask two questions: which strategic updates preserve an audited property, and how few labeled samples suffice to estimate fairness reliably anyway. Their generic framework rests on an empirical property optimization oracle. For statistical parity they prove distribution-free bounds governed by a new combinatorial measure, the SP dimension, capturing the complexity of admissible updates. The framework extends to prediction error and robust risk auditing as well.
arxiv-2601-06309:
Long films cost a lot to teach to AI, and few long films come with good notes. Zane Durante and 8 co-authors take a fresh path in a 2026 paper: fix the data, not the model. Their tool, VideoWeave, builds long fake films from short real ones that have notes.

It splices short clips end to end, so one training film spans more time. The team tried ways to splice: at random, or by how clips look. They also tried rich versus plain notes for each clip. With the same compute time, models taught this way beat plain film training on film quiz tasks. The gain held when the test films were long. The work says smart data prep can be a cheap, wide path to strong film skills.
arxiv-2601-06409:
Hunting ultra-high-energy neutrinos means listening for radio pulses inside polar ice. Simon Chiche and 2 co-authors characterize the main background to that search in a 2026 paper: radio emission from cosmic-ray particle showers cascading in the ice. Experiments at the South Pole and in Greenland use deep antennas for both signals.

Using the FAERIE simulation framework, which couples air shower and particle transport codes, the team analyzed in-ice radio signatures. They examined polarization, timing, and radiation energy, and how each depends on shower parameters. Cosmic-ray showers are also the first in-situ detection target for in-ice cascades, so characterizing them validates the detection principle and aids calibration. The insights should help future experiments separate cosmic-ray events from the neutrino signals they seek.
arxiv-2601-06609:
Anup Kushwaha and Om Prakash study symplectic hulls over an unusual ring in 2026. Their ring is non-unital, generated by two elements, kappa and tau. Its relations set twice each generator equal to zero.

Squares of the generators give a further set of relations. Each generator squared equals itself in this ring's arithmetic. Cross products between kappa and tau also collapse onto one generator. Symplectic hulls arise in coding theory for quantum and classical codes. Studying them over such rings extends where code constructions can live. Algebraists get the hull structure for this specific non-unital case. The results feed into constructing codes with controlled hull dimensions. Small rings like this often model error behavior surprisingly well.
arxiv-2601-06709:
Tiffanie Ng and Sara Clifton show how the bystander effect can grow from lone minds in 2026. Folks help a person in need less when more folks stand by. That group fact has long drawn a list of group-based accounts.

Past accounts cite doubt on what is wrong and cues copied from peers. Blame spread thin and joint denial also get named as causes of the effect. Their work starts one step down, with the odds as one mind sees them. Put many such minds in one place and the group effect shows up. If lone rules suffice, group causes may count for less than thought. The work gives a base model that tests can check against live trials. A known group effect is thus recast in lone, countable terms.
arxiv-2601-06809:
Hong-Bae Jeon and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with RIS-aided ISAC with k k -Rydberg atomic receivers. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. The authors investigate a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS)-assisted integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) framework equipped with multiple Rydberg atomic receiver (RAR)-aided users.

By leveraging the reference-assisted reception mechanism of RARs. The authors develop a unified signal model that jointly captures downlink multi-user communication with RARs and monostatic radar sensing. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07009:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Shifa Sulaiman and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers sliding mode controller based on timoshenko beam theory developed for a Tendon-Driven robotic. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Development of dexterous robotic joints is essential for advancing manipulation capabilities in robotic systems.

The work presents a design and an implementation of a tendon-driven robotic wrist joint. Together with an efficient Sliding Mode Controller (SMC) for precise motion control. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07109:
A. J. Brizard and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers guiding-center dynamics in a screw-pinch magnetic field. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The guiding-center dynamics of charged particles moving in a doubly-symmetric screw-pinch magnetic field is investigated.

In particular, we verify that Kruskal’s adiabatic-invariant series expansion of the radial action integral associated with. The reduced full-orbit radial motion matches the perturbation expansion of the magnetic-moment gyroaction up to first order in magnetic-field non-uniformity. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07209:
Yu Guo and four co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how to strip glare from a photo. Glass both lets light pass and throws light back. That mix makes a photo through glass hard to clean up. The task is called single-image reflection removal, or SIRR. It must clean one photo at a time, with no second shot to help.

Good training data for SIRR is hard to get. Fake data made by code tends to look less than real. Real shots are true to life but too few in count. Guo and the team built a new way to make training data. It traces light paths through 3D glass shapes set over real scene photos. The team can vary the glass, the camera, and the final look of each shot. The aim is a large set of training pairs that still act like real glass.
arxiv-2601-07309: Research by Zhuoka Feng and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with ARM. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Interactive large language model agents have advanced rapidly, but most remain specialized to a single environment and fail to adapt robustly to other environments. Model merging offers a training-free alternative by integrating multiple experts into a single model. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07509:
Feiyu Deng studies how a deformation changes boundary conformal field theories, in a 2026 theoretical physics preprint. The deformation is known as T T-bar, built from the theory's stress tensor. Deng also uses holography, which links such theories to gravity in a higher-dimensional space. The approach here stays intrinsic, working from field theory itself.

By restating the deformation as a change to the asymptotic variational principle in AdS space, Deng avoids a finite radial cutoff. From that setup he obtains an exact quadratic trace relation for the stress tensor. He takes that relation as the basic definition of the deformed theory. The paper then pursues a geometric realization of boundary flow. Specialists in holography and deformed field theories are the readers.
arxiv-2601-07609:
