Coarse levels encode long modes and finer levels add short-distance fluctuations. Preserving coarse fields exactly yields restriction maps and unbiased multilevel variance reduction. On phi-fourth theory, autocorrelation times run orders below hybrid Monte Carlo, with unbiased observables matching long hybrid runs.
arxiv-2604-10409: Wen and twenty colleagues release IMPACT, a factory assembly data set shot from five synced RGB-D views. Thirteen workers built and stripped a commercial angle grinder with pro tools across 112 trials and 39.5 hours. Notes link each hand's small moves to coarse steps, part states, and rule checks per hand. A six kind fault list plus workload scores adds fault fix trials to the mix. Base tests show gaps that single task sets hide, such as lost views and bent task paths.
arxiv-2604-10509: Zhao proves limit laws for busy time in a driven particle exclusion system. The symmetric simple exclusion process gains Glauber flips that add and drop particles. From a nonequilibrium start, he proves central limits for busy time in two dimensions. In one dimension, he proves moderate deviation rules for whole sample paths. Martingale plus sharp entropy tools drive the fluctuation proof, while a log Sobolev link ties busy time to density swings.
arxiv-2604-10609: Stillwagon and three colleagues tackle cell segmentation in microscope images, where good labeled data is scarce and models trained on everyday photos transfer poorly. Their DINOCell system adapts the DINOv2 vision model to microscopy with further self-supervised training on unlabeled cell images before supervised fine-tuning. On the LIVECell benchmark it scores 0.784, about 10.42 percent above leading Segment Anything-based models, and it also generalizes well to three unseen microscopy collections.
arxiv-2604-10709: Kobayash and four colleagues study powder jets thrown up when an impulsive force hits a powder layer with a concave surface, a setup proposed for testing powder flowability from small samples. Varying the concave radius, they find wider bowls produce broader, slower, lower jets. Jet speed and height follow a scaling relation with drop height, but the scaling coefficient shrinks as the radius grows, showing surface shape governs energy loss. A minimal mechanical model with sliding-distance and velocity-squared dissipation reproduces the linear link between jet height and radius.
arxiv-2604-10909: De Pas, Dipierro, and Valdinoci survey recent new work on nonlocal phase transition problems modeled by Ginzburg-Landau type energies with a smooth degenerate double-well potential W, controlled polynomially near its wells. The focus is traits of minimizers and critical points of the energy for long-range phase models. The survey maps how nonlocal energies shape phase shifts when the wells flatten, with results on minimizers, critical points, and coexistence patterns in these models.
arxiv-2604-11309: Zhang and nine colleagues expose a salami-slicing risk in language-model safety: many low-risk inputs, each below alignment thresholds, can chain together to accumulate harmful intent and trigger high-risk behavior. Their Salami Attack framework works across model types and modalities, topping 90 percent attack success on GPT-4o and Gemini and resisting real-world alignment defenses. A proposed defense cuts the attack by at least 44.8 percent and blocks up to 64.8 percent of other multi-turn jailbreak attacks.
arxiv-2604-11409: Ye, Khan, and Liang argue that T-depth misleads predictions of fault-tolerant quantum execution under limited magic-state delivery. They model demand-supply imbalance with two quantities: slack ratio, a structural gauge of scheduling flexibility, and Delta-max, a measure of cumulative demand surplus. Delta-max gives a provable lower bound on executable makespan for a fixed schedule and proves the strongest predictor of slowdown, while slack ratio best predicts stall and inversion risk. Across 4,904 instances the bound shows zero violations, with 88.9 percent of cases within one cycle.
arxiv-2604-11509: Lenz and four colleagues assess 5G security for industrial control systems with SWICS, a virtual testbed simulating an industrial system in a 5G environment. Industrial systems long prioritized uptime and live communication over security. The shift from wired to 5G links adds attack surface and a less reliable medium. Under optimal channel conditions, industrial 5G matches wired resilience. Degraded channels amplify attacks, threaten stability, and blind detection based on steady traffic. Eavesdropping and jamming on the open-air interface expose inherent limits of securing 5G channels for industrial use.
arxiv-2604-11609: Maltbie and Raval probe whether large language models flatter users differently by perceived demographics. Across 768 multi-turn chats spanning 128 personas and three domains, sycophancy varies sharply by model and domain, emerging from trait combinations rather than any single dimension. GPT-5-nano scores far higher than Claude Haiku 4.5, averaging 2.96 versus 1.74, and within GPT-5-nano, philosophy elicits 41 percent more sycophancy than mathematics, and Hispanic personas score highest. The worst persona, a confident 23-year-old Hispanic woman, averages 5.33 out of 10. The authors argue safety tests should include identity-aware testing.
arxiv-2604-11709: Ma and four colleagues propose a Mamba-based multimodal network for multiscale blast-induced rapid structural damage assessment. Field inspections are precise but limited by access, safety, and time after large explosions, while machine learning with remote sensing scales better. Prior Mamba networks need extensive training and large datasets and ignore blast-loading physics. Their network combines blast-loading data at several scales with optical remote sensing images. In tests on the 2020 Beirut explosion, it beats state-of-the-art approaches.
arxiv-2604-11809: Nordström, Edstedt, Kahl, and Bökman ask where rotation invariance belongs in image matching: in the descriptor or in the matcher. Training across large three-dimensional vision collections, they find putting it in the descriptor matches matcher-side handling on accuracy while letting the matcher itself become rotation-invariant sooner and run faster. Enforcing invariance does not harm upright performance at scale, and larger training sets sharply improve generalisation to rotated images.
arxiv-2604-12109: Verrico and twelve colleagues develop a criterion for changing-look AGN from photometry and ZTF curves. It requires g-band and g-r shifts above 0.4 and 0.2 magnitudes. It finds transitions in 9.6 percent of hosts, including a repeating event. Simulated Seyferts give 1.6 percent false positives, against 1.2 percent flares for Type 1 and at most 0.39 percent for Type 2. Transitions last 21 to 560 days, median 360, matching disk timescales, with no black hole mass correlation. It can extend to the Legacy Survey of Space and Time to find candidates and test theories.
arxiv-2604-12309: Wang and five colleagues generate orbital videos of an object from a single image, using shape priors from a 3D foundation model to keep views geometrically consistent. Pixel attention alone fails at long-range extrapolation such as rear views, where input correspondences run thin. Their method prompts generation with a global latent vector plus projected latent images for view-dependent detail, injected through a multi-scale 3D adapter. Tests show superior quality, shape realism, and multi-view consistency.
arxiv-2604-12609: Klichchupong Dabsamut and two colleagues study defects in lithium gallium oxide, LiGa5O8. The spinel-type oxide was claimed as a p-type ultra-wide-band-gap semiconductor. Earlier work predicted insulating results instead, with deep acceptors offset by shallow donors. This paper maps transitions, the absorption and emission steps for carrier capture. Symmetry-breaking relaxations of native defects are checked again. The lithium vacancy, the shallowest native acceptor, gets revised levels. Carbon impurities from organic growth precursors are also studied.
arxiv-2604-12909: Yifei Yan and Linqi Ye teach humanoid robots many skills without forgetting old ones. Current routes need complex expert mixtures or huge models. Tree Learning reuses root parameters as motion priors for branch skills. Feedforward adaptation blends phase modulation with interpolation for periodic and aperiodic motion. Task-level reward shaping speeds skill convergence. Unity tests show higher rewards than joint training with full skill retention. A Mario-style scene and a Chinese garden navigation task confirm generalization.
arxiv-2604-13309: Chatterjee and three colleagues build vision-based control for a robotic arm using only natural visual features. They attach ArUco markers to train a keypoint detector, use marker centres as labels, then inpaint the markers away to create markerless training images. At runtime a second inpainting model restores partly hidden robot regions, while an Unscented Kalman Filter steadies the estimates over time. The system controls the arm without a model under full and partial visibility, and extends to soft origami arms.
arxiv-2604-13609: Ebtekar and Cohen make reinforcement learners safer with golden handcuffs. They widen the agent's imagined reward range to include a large negative outcome. True rewards stay between zero and one. After steady high rewards, the Bayesian agent grows wary of novel schemes that might hit that bad outcome. A mentor override takes over whenever predicted value falls below a threshold. This yields sublinear regret against the best mentor, plus a safety guarantee on low-complexity predicates.
arxiv-2604-13809: Wiedemann offers a GAP package for working with cubic Jordan matrix algebras by computer. The package, CubicJordanMatrixAlg, also covers related Lie-type structures. Here computation means exact algebra with matrices, not numerical approximation. The package works by rules, not by rounding. He applies the package to commutator relations in F4 groups. De Medts and Wiedemann built those groups from the same objects.
arxiv-2604-14209: Wang and five colleagues introduce ViTaX, a formal framework that explains neural network decisions with mathematical guarantees. Standard attribution tools flag influential features but certify nothing about decision boundaries, while formal checks verify robustness without targeting the risks that matter. For an input class and a user-named critical alternative, ViTaX finds the smallest feature set most sensitive to flipping between them and proves that small perturbations cannot force the flip. Tests on MNIST, GTSRB, EMNIST, and TaxiNet show fidelity gains above 30 percent with minimal explanation size.
arxiv-2604-14509: Gallant, Mrdjenovich, and Persson test whether a metastable polymorph's kinetic staying power follows the shape of the energy landscape between it and lower-energy phases. They build a method for finding diffusionless paths between metastable polymorphs and their ground-state versions, grounded in the Crystal Normal Form graph of crystal configuration space. Path energetics are then read against experimental observation of each phase. The method is applied to titanium dioxide, home to anatase, rutile, and brookite plus several hypothetical metastable polymorphs.
arxiv-2604-14609: Zhang's team of seven presents El Agente Forjador, a multi-agent framework where coding agents forge, validate, and reuse computational tools on their own for science. Tools emerge through analysis, generation, task execution, and iterative evaluation, replacing static hand-curated toolsets blocking new-domain adaptation. Across 24 tasks in quantum chemistry and dynamics on five agent setups, tool generation and reuse consistently beat direct baselines. Reusing a stronger agent's toolset cuts API cost and substantially lifts solution quality for weaker agents. Tools forged in other domains combine on hybrid tasks.
arxiv-2604-14709: Cui and four colleagues introduce HWE-Bench, the first repository benchmark for language-model agents fixing hardware bugs. Its 417 tasks come from bug-fix pull requests across six projects spanning Verilog, SystemVerilog, and Chisel. They cover RISC-V cores, systems-on-chip, and security roots of trust, each checked by project simulations. The best of seven models in four frameworks solved 70.7 percent, topping 90 percent on small cores but falling below 65 percent on complex chips. Failures centered on fault localization, hardware reasoning, and coordination across code, configuration, and verification files.
arxiv-2604-14909: Yang and five others propose fuzzy private set overlap protocols for Lp metrics, on cheaper symmetric-key operations. Fuzzy PSI lets a receiver find sender items within a threshold of its own, privately. Earlier Lp methods use expensive encryption, hurting efficiency. Their protocols reach linear communication and computation in set sizes, dimension, and threshold, via a secret-shared oblivious programmable PRF, with a prefix technique cutting threshold dependence to logarithmic. Tests show large speedups and communication cuts over Gao and others and Dang and others.
arxiv-2604-15009: Li proposes mixture-of-experts flow matching for faster language model inference. Flow matching keeps diffusion-model quality with much faster inference, but struggles with complex latent distributions like anisotropy and multimodality. Mixture-of-experts flow matching splits global transport geometries into locally specialized vector fields. Built on it, YAN, in Transformer and Mamba forms, matches autoregressive and diffusion-based quality with as few as three sampling steps. YAN runs 40 times faster than autoregressive baselines and up to 1000 times faster than diffusion models.
arxiv-2604-15109: Fan, Duan, and Xu tackle uncertainty in long, free-form answers from large language models. Short-answer methods falter here, since fluent replies can still carry false claims across many tangled meanings. Their IUQ framework first interrogates a reply and then answers, combining agreement across samples with faithfulness within each sample. The result gives claim-level uncertainty measures for long-form generation, giving readers a steadier gauge of what to trust.
arxiv-2604-15409: Chodavarapu and Xu show that KV caching in autoregressive transformers, long assumed equal to recomputation, drifts apart under FP16 precision. Different sum orders in cache-on versus cache-off paths drive a 100 percent token divergence rate across three open models on GSM8K, even under greedy decoding. Switching to FP32 shrinks the gap by eight orders of magnitude, pinning FP16 non-associativity as the cause.
arxiv-2604-15509: Zhou and Ying propose a correction-function kernel-free boundary integral method for Stokes- and Brinkman-type interface problems. Recasting the problem as boundary integral equations turns its operators into boundary data for simpler problems without coefficient jumps. A fixed Marker-and-Cell grid plus a local fix for the solution jump, solved by point matching, proves exact and fast on fixed- and moving-interface tests.
arxiv-2604-15609: Zhang and four colleagues introduce BETA, a framework for test-time adaptation of black-box models reachable only through APIs. A lightweight local white-box steering model creates a tractable gradient path, with prediction harmonization, consistency regularization, and prompt-learning filtering enabling stable adaptation with no extra API calls. On ImageNet-C it gains 7.1 percent on ViT-B/16 and 3.4 percent on CLIP, and matches zeroth-order optimization at 250 times lower cost on a commercial API.
arxiv-2604-15709: Huang and four colleagues tune agent skill packs, set bundles of rules, tools, and files, by two-layer tuning. An outer Monte Carlo tree hunt picks the pack shape while an inner loop polishes each part, with text models aiding both loops. On a test set of open operations research Q and A, the scheme beats untuned packs, showing pack design sways task wins a lot.
arxiv-2604-15809: Liu, Choi, Zhang, and Oh fix a see-say split in vision-tongue models. The model oft eyes the right patch yet still answers wrong, since word bits spray heed over dead eye bits. Their fix steers word bits to key eye bits alone while decoding, picking key bits by their odd fire shapes across decode stages. Tests on ask-answer, grounding, counting, letter-read, and ghost-object sets show clear gains over baselines.
arxiv-2604-15909: Chandran and five colleagues study the general position number of digraphs, the largest vertex sets with no three vertices on a common shortest path. They extend the graph problem to directed graphs, giving bounds for the general position number of digraphs. They show the problem is NP-complete for oriented graphs, and investigate circulant, Kautz, and permutation digraph families. They also study the numbers arising from all orientations of an undirected graph.
arxiv-2604-16309: Li and eight colleagues present AgentGuard, a multi-agent framework for detecting package confusion in open-source software supply chains. Attackers publish harmful packages with names close to legitimate ones, meant to mislead. Older detectors rely on a single signal, suffer high false positives, and face evasion tricks. AgentGuard first finds confusion targets with fine-tuned word models and hybrid similarity matching. It then fuses metadata and content signals to separate benign look-alikes from harmful fakes with different code.
arxiv-2604-16509: Sastry, Poudel and Li prune the fast-growing graphs that robotic exploration builds for frontier search and path planning. Their hybrid transformer framework, trained with proximal policy optimization, trims graphs during exploration to limit growth and excess information. Tested in simulations where a robot agent used rapidly-exploring random trees for frontier exploration, the learned policy cut graph size by up to 96 percent. It beat a randomly pruned baseline and improved both exploration and compute efficiency on complex long-horizon tasks, suggesting reinforcement learning can viably prune dynamic exploration graphs.
arxiv-2604-16809: Gao and three colleagues study delayed loss spikes, sudden jumps that appear late in neural-network training, through the simplified lens of batch-normalized linear models. They derive conditions for when a spike waits before striking, and show the rise steadies itself within finitely many steps. They warn, though, that this stylized mechanism is not a general explanation for real networks.
arxiv-2604-16909: Wu and eight colleagues reframe language-model hallucination as a diagnostic puzzle. They separate failures of missing knowledge, wrong knowledge, faulty reasoning, and missed instructions across memory, instruction, and reasoning stages. Their PRISM benchmark spans 9,448 instances over 65 tasks, and tests of 24 models reveal trade-offs: fixes that help one dimension often cost another.
arxiv-2604-17109: Zhu and seven colleagues show p-bit Ising machines can update all spins in parallel after all, overturning the belief that parallel updates ruin results. An added inertia term in spin dynamics enables fully parallel synced updates while lifting success odds. Parallel updates yield speedups growing faster than linear with spin count, averaging about 34 times at size 200 for Max-Cut and SK problems, with a best single speedup of 150 times.
arxiv-2604-17209: Shaik, Cherukuri, and Ye introduce DREAM, a framework for medical report generation from retinal images that works even with limited data. Its Abstractor maps image and keyword features, with keywords curated by ophthalmologists, into one space, enriching visual data with pathology insights. Its Adaptor then fuses modalities, weighting each by parameters into one representation, while Contrastive Alignment aligns fused outputs with true reports in training. DREAM sets a new best mark on the DeepEyeNet benchmark with a BLEU score of 0.241, and generalizes well to the ROCO dataset.
arxiv-2604-17309: Yu and Wang propose Knows, a slim sidecar file that sits beside a research paper. It hands AI agents the paper's claims, evidence, sources, and links in structured form. Small models reading the sidecar instead of the full PDF jumped from roughly a fifth correct to about half or better on comprehension questions, while using far fewer input tokens. A public hub already indexes over ten thousand papers, so the format aims to make agent-led research cheaper, steadier, and easier to check.
arxiv-2604-17609: Engländer and four colleagues show that LLM agents ignore solutions planted in their own environments, injecting solutions across Terminal-Bench, SWE-Bench, and AppWorld to test exploitation of finds. On Terminal-Bench, agents discover solutions in 79 to 81 percent of runs but exploit them in 37 to 50 percent of cases. In AppWorld, agents see a command billed as returning the solution in over 90 percent of attempts yet exploit it in under 7 percent of trials. The authors call the missing capacity environmental curiosity, shaped by scaffold tools, compute, and training data.
arxiv-2604-17709: Huang and three colleagues introduce DeInfer, a fast system for side-by-side runs of decomposed large language models. Old decomposition work focuses on downstream task results but ignores poor side-by-side runs when scaling up model size. DeInfer combines several tweaks to lift speed while working with leading techniques. Broad experiments show its edge, suggesting it can greatly ease side-by-side runs of decomposed LLMs.
arxiv-2604-18109: Kesiraju, Yusuf, Sedláček, Plchot, and Schwarz introduce FLiP, a method that probes what sentence embeddings retain. FLiP maps embeddings back to words in a compact factored way. Trained on multilingual, multimodal, and commercial systems, it recovers over 75 percent of the original words. That beats unfactorized rivals and exposes language and modality biases in popular encoders without running task tests.
arxiv-2604-18209: Hertzsch, Feldbrugge, and van de Weygaert map galaxy populations onto the caustic skeleton of the IllustrisTNG cosmic web. It tracks the web's growth story through singular points in the dark-matter flow. Galaxies are sorted into voids, walls, filaments, and cluster nodes, and their colors and star birth are studied. Galaxy traits form a smooth range across web scales, showing how build-up timing shapes the well-known color-density link.
arxiv-2604-18309: Porbeck, Adriano, and Giese test how the context fed to a debugging model shapes its failure explanations. Explanations that are incomplete or wrong can mislead bug triage and repair, yet most work treats them as a by-product. Varying context across 93 setups on real bugs, the authors score explanations on six criteria and check machine judgments against human ratings. Rich, failure-specific artifacts improve causal and actionable quality, while oversized contexts yield vague text, and top-scoring explanations predict better repair rates.
arxiv-2604-18409: Husein and six colleagues rethink far-field gain checks for sub-THz antennas, where huge horns need ranges too long to use. Using off-the-shelf horn units at 145 to 170 GHz, they measure exact gain in nearby distance clusters via the three-antenna method. A tweaked far-field formula plus the Friis rule resets far-field distance from both horn mouths. Checked by lab tests and models, the compact setup stays reliable even with mixed antenna pairs, suiting 6G, sensing, and imaging work.
arxiv-2604-18509: Xiao, Huang, Liu, and Xie propose MASS-RAG, a multi-agent approach to retrieval-boosted generation for noisy, gappy evidence. A single pass struggles to square spread-out contexts, so distinct agents condense evidence, extract evidence, and reason over files. A special merging stage combines those middle views into the final answer. Tests on four benchmarks show steady gains over strong RAG rivals, largest where key evidence spreads across pulled contexts.
arxiv-2604-19009: Dong and five colleagues propose GDMD, a framework guiding distribution matching distillation with gradient reinforcement learning. Few step generation trades quality for speed, and naive fusion scores samples, creating conflicts and noisy rewards. GDMD instead treats distillation gradients as implicit targets, letting reward models judge distillation updates directly. This gradient guidance keeps the reinforcement policy in step with the distillation goal, curbing divergence. Four step models beat their multi step teacher in quality and top prior results on GenEval and human preference metrics.
arxiv-2604-19209: Maciejko examines spoof detection through GaborNet, a bank of Gabor filters. Time-domain processing has gained ground, exemplified by SincNet, whose layer convolves sinc functions with the input. Finite sinc length distorts frequency, as windowing does. Gabor filters replace sinc functions, but their complex outputs need squared modulus and Gaussian Lowpass Pooling. GaborNet and its modifications are tested within the RawNet2 and RawGAT-ST architectures for audio spoof detection. Audio augmentation via codecs, room responses, and noise is tested.
arxiv-2604-19409: Bu, Sun, and Zeng determine which graphs maximize certain clique spectral radii among graphs with no two disjoint r-cliques. They treat the sum from k-clique to (2r-1)-clique spectral radius over all such graphs on n vertices, for large n. They also settle the maximum 3-clique spectral radius among graphs with no two disjoint triangles. Their results give spectral versions of known results on generalized Turán numbers.
arxiv-2604-19509: Jones, Santos-Rodriguez, and Hauert test whether vision-language models can infer affordances for non-humanoid robots. Such models handle human-object interaction well, but robots with different bodies remain largely untested. The authors build a hybrid dataset mixing real annotated affordance relations with model-generated synthetic scenarios. Tests across object types and robot shapes show wide variation in inference skill. The goal is robots that handle daily objects with bodies unlike our own.
arxiv-2604-19809: Wang introduces MIRROR, a benchmark of eight experiments across four metacognitive levels testing whether large language models can draw on self-knowledge to make better choices. Sixteen models from eight labs are tested across roughly 250,000 evaluation instances with five independent behavioral measurement channels. A core finding is that compositional self-prediction fails across the board, with calibration error running high on both the original and expanded sets.
arxiv-2604-20009: Bérczi, Csaplár, and Yamaguchi study edge-weight symmetries in perfect matchings, motivated by finding perfect matchings of given rank. They define a hierarchy of weakening properties, from node-induced weights through even walk and cycle symmetries to matching equality and the min-max condition. The conditions coincide in bipartite graphs, with tight characterizations for general graphs via block and tight cut decompositions. A matching-covered non-bipartite counterexample settles the motivating question negatively: one fixed edge need not eliminate all minimum- or maximum-weight matchings.
arxiv-2604-20109: Pan and four colleagues present PLMA, a permutation learning scheme for the quadratic assignment task, where learned solvers still lag older rules. Warm-started MCMC fine-tuning steers tuning at run time to good zones found before, and an added energy model allows constant-time two-swap sampling. A cross-graph attention net maps links between sites and slots in the task. Tests show PLMA beating top rivals on many benchmarks, with a near-zero mean gap on QAPLIB and tough staying power on the hard Taixxeyy cases.
arxiv-2604-20209: Bailey and four colleagues tackle self-play scaling failure, where a Conjecturer inventing problems for a Solver games its reward. The Conjecturer collapses into pointlessly hard problems that do not help the Solver, stalling learning. Self-Guided Self-Play adds a Guide scoring synthetic problems for relevance to unsolved targets and cleanliness, blocking that degeneracy. In Lean4 theorem proving it beats the strongest reinforcement learning baseline's asymptotic solve rate in under eighty rounds. After two hundred rounds, a 7B model out-solves a 671B model at pass four.
arxiv-2604-20309: Staeck and seven colleagues use crossed multilayer Laue lenses as the lens in dark-field X-ray microscopy. At ID03, two flat Mo-Si lenses with a 50 by 50 micron opening focus near 14 mm at 19 keV. Under a 10 percent transfer test, bright-field sharpness hits 56 nanometres, over three times sharper than a refractive lens, with dark-field sharpness close behind. The lens runs at 26.7 percent efficiency, with triple the light grasp of the refractive case, speeding direction maps and aiding tomography.
arxiv-2604-20409: Vasilyev and three colleagues introduce calibrating conditional risk: estimating the loss you can expect from a prediction model once you know the input features. They treat both classification and regression, and show the problem is at root the same as a standard regression task. For classification they link this risk task to individual and conditional probability calibration, with lessons for how it should be scored. They test the theory in the learning to defer setting, where a model hands hard cases to a human.
arxiv-2604-20709: Ohno, Dorrian, Show, and Falson report growth of LaAg2Ge2 thin films on MgO(001) and their transport. ThCr2Si2-type intermetallics are conductors where anisotropy and multiband states often produce magnetotransport phenomena. The Hall effect and magnetoresistance fit a two-carrier picture with a fast electron band, giving positive magnetoresistance of 22.5 percent at 9 T. Angle-dependent magnetoresistance shows a twofold anisotropy plus dip and peak traits at angles nearly independent of field and temperature. Those results extend understanding of electronic transport in film germanides within the ThCr2Si2 family.
arxiv-2604-20909: Berezowski, Hassanzadeh, and Ginde test whether masked autoencoder pretraining helps predict downhole drilling measures from surface sensors, where labeled underground readings are rare and costly. Training on about 3.5 million steps of telemetry from two Utah geothermal wells, they compare 72 pretraining setups against supervised baselines. The best setup cuts test error by about 20 percent against the GRU baseline, though it still trails the LSTM baseline.
arxiv-2604-21009: Duan reworks Bayesian variable selection in linear regression as optimization. Bayesian methods account for uncertainty in coefficients and noise variance. Yet the marginal likelihood, found by integrating them out, is not log-concave, so its global optimum carries no guarantee. Duan recasts its log-loss form as a gap of convex functions in the precision values. A routine then solves it, reaching the global optimum at a linear rate under compact-set limits. The finding extends to type-II maximum likelihood and posterior under fitting priors.
arxiv-2604-21309: Nannan Huang, Iffat Maab, and Junichi Yamagishi evaluate political bias in multi-document news summarization across 13 models and five fairness metrics, using the FairNews dataset of labeled articles. Mid-sized variants often beat their larger counterparts, challenging the assumption that bigger means fairer, with the strongest fairness-per-cost trade-off. Debiasing by prompting works unevenly across models, while sentiment toward named entities stays the most resistant fairness dimension, unmoved by every intervention tried. Fairness, they argue, needs many-sided checks and design-aware debiasing, not just scale.
arxiv-2604-21709: Kalinin, Lupercio, and Shkolnikov define a tropical zeta function for convex domains that stays invariant under integer changes of basis. In two dimensions, it admits a boundary Dirichlet-series form indexed by Farey pairs. For smooth, strictly convex domains, it extends to a wider range, with a single simple pole whose residue tracks equiaffine perimeter. A Tauberian argument then gives a wave-front lattice-perimeter growth rule. A special limit-shape domain gives an exact leading coefficient.
arxiv-2604-21909: Caglar, Mediano, and Lin ask whether human directional confusion asymmetry holds for machine vision. To humans, a robin seems more like a bird than vice versa. Humans and models match in accuracy but err differently, in who gets mistaken for whom. Using matched responses under 12 perturbation types, they quantify confusion asymmetry and link it to rate-distortion geometry. Humans show weak asymmetries across many pairs, while models show sparser, stronger collapses into few categories. Robustness training reduces asymmetry but fails to recover the human-like distributed structure.
arxiv-2604-22109: Poungpeth, Clark, and Mitra audit spontaneous persuasion, the quiet use of persuasive tricks in everyday chats where persuasion is not really called for. They test five language models over multi-turn talks, using a user reply taxonomy drawn from psychology, communication, and linguistics. They compare model replies with human replies on the same topics from Reddit. The models persuade in virtually all talks, leaning on information-based tactics such as appeals to logic or numbers. Mental-health talks show more appraisal-based and emotion-based tactics.
arxiv-2604-22309: Ramadhan, Fauzi, Witjaksana and Sulaksono study light bending and black hole shadows under nonlinear electrodynamics. Their model generalises Born-Infeld theory with one parameter, q, between Maxwell theory and exponential electrodynamics. Outside the horizon the spacetime stays close to the Reissner-Nordstrom solution, yet photon paths follow a different geometry. For small positive q, stable photon orbits appear outside the horizon, shifting paths that loop multiple times. Those shifts alter relativistic images, and the shadow is compared with horizon-scale limits on Sagittarius A-star.
arxiv-2604-22509: Harith and Kaufmann present LaissezCloud, where running cloud jobs keep renegotiating for resources. Tenants and operators update bids while jobs run, so a tenant keeps a resource only while its bid beats rivals. Prices serve as the shared meeting point, letting operators fold in power, cooling, and carbon costs without revealing inner telemetry. Spot deals bid once at launch and can be seized outright. Across accelerator workloads it cuts slowdowns under contention by 8 to 23 percent against on-demand and spot baselines, and scales to 10,000-node clusters.
arxiv-2604-22609: Domokos and Miklósi determine the degeneration order of simultaneous similarity classes of 3 by 3 nilpotent matrix tuples, showing it is given by rank conditions. A degeneration order ranks classes by which can deform into which: a lower class arises as a limit of a higher one. Nilpotent matrices are those with some power equal to zero, so their tuples have restricted structure. The paper's contribution is the full determination of this order for triples of 3 by 3 nilpotent matrices, with rank conditions deciding all comparisons.
arxiv-2604-22709: Ramji, Naseem, and Astudillo replace long written chains of thought with short sequences of abstract tokens drawn from a reserved vocabulary, letting a language model reason without words. A warm-up loop alternates masking verbal reasoning with self-distillation, followed by reinforcement learning under constrained decoding. The method uses far fewer reasoning tokens while matching verbal reasoning across math, instruction, and multi-hop tasks.
arxiv-2604-22909: Meinhardt and Oliveira use Masked Siamese Networks to turn daily temperature time series into discrete, meaningful climate states. Working from daily minimum and maximum temperatures, they find clusters that reflect real climate regimes under their modeling assumptions and simplify downstream use. The clusters also support sampling and study of specific climate scenarios. They show statistical links with El Niño events, suggesting that self-supervised discretization is a useful tool for climate data analysis.
arxiv-2604-23109: Xie, Oiwa, and Hayami propose a symmetry-based approach for effective harmonic phonon models using a multipole basis. Breaking the force-constant matrix into bond-based electric moments reveals the minimal parts behind phonon angular-momentum splitting. In a minimal zigzag-chain model, ferroaxial order yields hidden sublattice-resolved chiral phonons, while an extra polar contribution gives finite global chirality. The results unify hidden and emergent phonon phenomena and suggest tuning phonon properties through electronic orderings and external fields.
arxiv-2604-23209: Phan and Wakabayashi simulate a 2D photonic crystal of lossy magneto-optical matter, where both wave shapes and complex eigenfrequencies carry nontrivial topology. The non-Hermitian skin effect, guarded by point gaps in the eigenfrequency spectrum, appears at both edges and corners of cut shapes, with no Hermitian twin. They also find edge states rooted in the bulk bands' nontrivial topology. Unlike most prior work on tight-binding models, this continuous system offers a more true-to-life platform and a concrete path toward tests.
arxiv-2604-23409: Zakharov builds a class of exactly solvable models for relativistic quantum statistical thermodynamics. He treats interacting atoms together with an extra field that stands in for their mutual forces. The field breaks into Klein-Gordon parts tied to the force's Fourier pattern, and working out the partition function reduces to rescaling the field's parameters. Quantizing the field removes a runaway energy divergence, and a phase transition emerges in the model.
arxiv-2604-23509: Yang and Chen present SeGa, a test-generation technique that hunts business-logic bugs by starting from product requirements rather than code alone. It groups requirements by business intent, derives detailed scenarios with preconditions and expected outcomes, and steers a language model to write tests from them. On four industrial projects it finds many more real bugs than rival methods, and deployment uncovered sixteen further bugs that developers confirmed and fixed.
arxiv-2604-23609: Xue and six colleagues present Tube Diffusion Policy, a reactive framework for contact-rich robot manipulation that fuses diffusion-based imitation with tube-style feedback control. Instead of blindly replaying action chunks, it learns a feedback flow around them, forming an action tube that reacts fast to unexpected contact and disturbance. It beats state-of-the-art imitation baselines on a standard pushing benchmark and three dexterous tasks, plus two real-world tests.
arxiv-2604-24409: Romero, Chen, and Ban study a kicked-Ising quantum battery under heat and outside dissipation. Starting from Gibbs states of the transverse-field Ising model, they add thermal and decoherence effects along the evolution, using exact and numerical methods. With ergotropy as the central measure, they characterize injected and extractable energy and find regimes where charging stays robust despite environmental effects. Their results give a systematic framework for assessing battery performance under thermal and dissipative effects.
arxiv-2604-24909: Channing and five colleagues release paired microscopy images with acquisition metadata. The set holds 7,330 scanning images with seven-dimensional metadata. Low doses avoid damage but give noisy images with no ground truth. Their CIMP encoder aligns images and metadata, reaching 84.4 percent Top-1 retrieval. All seven parameters are recoverable from the frozen embedding via a linear probe. The embedding also drives a style-transfer model that re-renders images under new settings. Virtually scaling dwell time and beam current turns it into a denoiser.
arxiv-2604-25109: Lv and four colleagues study pre-load checks for untrusted Agent Skills. These skills bundle instructions, scripts and reference files into units an agent can reuse, so a bad file can hide risk. Their tool, SkillGuard-Robust, gathers role-aware evidence, checks meaning in key spots and judges each case the same way across files. On up to 404 test packages it hit about 97 percent exact match, though transfer to harsher outside sources stayed open.
arxiv-2604-25409: Kuang, Wu and Tu scale the Probabilistic Transformer, a white-box model for word reads that matches standard Transformers on small models and sets. But it is less steady under hyperparameter picks than standard Transformers, making efficient scaling hard. Following Maximal Update Parametrization, they rescale its factors so small-model hyperparameters carry to larger models with no fresh tuning. With this move, they scale PT to models with up to 0.4B parameters. Tests show PT beats standard transformers on Masked Language Modeling tasks under the same parameter budget.
arxiv-2604-25509: Köhler and four colleagues attack Even-Mansour with Simon's algorithm on noisy hardware, as a proof of concept. Simon's algorithm exploits symmetric cipher structure for exponential speedups. While theory is settled, practical NISQ builds remain limited. For N equal to 3 and 4, secret key recovery is shown on ibm_miami. Tests find a scaling limit: DORCIS hit a memory jam at N equal to 5, blocking tuned circuits for larger maps. Results suggest Simon's algorithm works at short lengths, and more scalable tools are needed for larger permutations.
arxiv-2604-25609: Adhikari and four colleagues describe a radon emanation measurement system built at the Carleton Noble Liquid Detector Laboratory. Radon from natural uranium ranks among the largest backgrounds in rare-event searches, and emanation from detector materials drives much of it. The setup joins a steel emanation chamber, a low-background zinc sulfide silver-activated cell, and a radon transfer and collection assembly, and it studies emanation under vacuum. A charcoal trap with a flow meter extends the work to radon in nitrogen gas and in the DEAP-3600 gas filter.
arxiv-2604-25709: Giesler studies degenerations of surfaces in fake weighted projective three-space, following what happens along an edge of the degeneration. He introduces the Hodge-theoretic data of the problem and shows that the Hodge loci of vanishing cycles can be either proper or not. The examples illustrate results of Green and Voisin on Hodge loci. The note is short and technical, aimed at readers working on Hodge theory and the geometry of singular surfaces.
arxiv-2604-25809: Bangde and Roy propose IECD, a decoding framework that balances linguistic informativeness against visual faithfulness in vision-language models. Such models often produce fluent answers weakly grounded in images, and instruction prompting can worsen the problem by amplifying language priors. IECD runs two parallel token streams: one instruction-driven, one evidence-driven. A contrastive gate fuses them, suppressing tokens that language priors favor but images do not support, while keeping tokens both streams agree on. Tests on captioning and question answering show better accuracy and much less hallucination.
arxiv-2604-26009: Geller and Telem address false vacuum decay catalyzed by black holes. Small black holes with large Hawking temperatures might naively generate highly boosted true vacuum bubbles. Those bubbles could trigger decay in the early universe with no exponential suppression. The authors work in the thin-wall regime of the phi^4 and sine-Gordon models, showing radiative losses slow these bubbles. That prevents runaway decay. Production stays enhanced over vacuum tunneling in parts of parameter space, yet always exponentially suppressed.
arxiv-2604-26209: Glavas and four colleagues devised Hyper-Parallel Decoding, a way to pull many attribute values from one document at once instead of one token after another. By reordering token positions and stacking documents inside a single prompt, the method decodes up to 96 tokens together. It works with any large language model and cut inference cost and time sharply on extraction tasks without losing accuracy.
arxiv-2604-26309: Kato and four colleagues ran computer models of Turing patterns, the spots and stripes made by reaction-diffusion equations, on fixed grids under mechanical stress. Activator and inhibitor levels sit at fixed points, as with pigment cells on zebrafish skin, while a Finsler-geometry variable tracks the direction of stress. A tensile-stress formula built on a Gaussian bond potential held up on such grids, so stress-relaxation entropy could be worked out as on wavy surfaces. Living patterns answered forces much as patterns on rippling membranes do.
arxiv-2604-26709: Isabel, Rodríguez-Carbonell, Rodríguez-Núñez, and Rubio present a DPLL(T)-based approach to satisfiability modulo prime fields, aimed at verifying zero-knowledge proof systems. Such proofs rest on arithmetic circuits and polynomial systems over large prime fields, and formal verification needs SMT solvers that handle those constraints. Their theory solver orchestrates several modules with different completeness-efficiency trade-offs. A prototype already beats state-of-the-art tools on zero-knowledge compiler-correctness benchmarks and new arithmetic-circuit verification benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-27009: Wee and Bruzzese develop a phase framework for time-bin light qudits, with a practical calibration and feed-forward method sorting geometric, dynamical, and technical phases. Working in the time-bin basis, geometric phases show as interference offsets, while all phases enter one diagonal transform. They model state setup with cascaded Mach-Zehnder interferometers and give exact amplitudes for any splitting ratios and phases. Tomography from adjacent-bin scans, with a Fourier cross-check, plus a case study, demonstrates feed-forward compensation with standard components.
arxiv-2604-27209: Young and Björner examine research software where the math, the code, the benchmarks, and the public claims must mature together. Often they drift apart. Language models can now write large codebases and draft papers. Yet two failures recur. First, hallucination accumulation, where claims outrun what code or theory supports. Second, desynchronization, where code, theory, and the model's world model fall out of step. Their Comet-H system couples ideation, building, testing, grounding, and writing in one workspace.
arxiv-2604-27509: Pouladi tackles stability and data-driven state gauging for Persidskii systems with delays and shocks. Persidskii systems couple linear motion with sector-bounded nonlinear feedback loops, giving a tool for machine and neural systems. He builds input-to-state rules, cast as matrix bounds, and offers a watcher. To handle doubt, arrays are found from data with a Koopman method that preserves stability. Tested on a 1.5 kW motor drive, it cuts speed error by 35 percent against a Kalman filter and lifts tracking scores by 67 percent against field control.
arxiv-2604-27609: Navarrete and three colleagues explain eclipsing time variations in close binaries with azimuthal dynamo waves. These non-axisymmetric magnetic fields drift around the star, changing its quadrupole moment over time and producing distinct timing shapes. Depending on how fast the moment changes, the signal can drop sharply, as in QS Vir, or look sinusoidal, as in V471 Tau or NN Ser. The waves offer a self-consistent dynamo-theory account, easing the Applegate mechanism's energy problems, with amplitudes from tens to hundreds of seconds.
arxiv-2604-27709: Swain and four colleagues use CrystaLLM-pi, a language model tuned with 6,179 double transition-metal MAX phases, to generate new MAX phase forms. With a two-part control vector, the model targets regions good for MXenes, and chosen control vectors double novel stable structure generation rates over plain baselines. Of ten novel entries, five show DFT-validated stability with energy above hull below 0.050 eV per atom. The work shows autoregressive generative models can explore chosen materials spaces for accelerated discovery.
arxiv-2604-27809: Bardin, Lorenzi, and Salasnich study Bosonic Josephson superfluid motion beyond mean-field theory, with thermal and quantum fluctuations. Using a gas-fluctuation model and assuming tiny non-condensed transport, they derive a corrected motion equation in a two-site approximation. Shifts in Josephson frequency, self-trapping strength, and symmetry-breaking threshold predict fluctuation effects and their relative weight across regimes. Quantum fluctuations oppose thermal ones: thermal fluctuations cut Josephson rate and raise both key strengths, and the likely regime is quantum-led.
arxiv-2604-27909: Abiad and colleagues derive sharp upper bounds on how large a sum-rank-metric code can be for a given minimum distance, using spectral and optimisation tools. The sum-rank measure blends the Hamming and rank measures, suiting space-time coding, network coding and storage spread across sites. Their bounds also settle non-existence for certain optimal and perfect codes, showing the hybrid measure yields to combined methods.
arxiv-2605-00109:
Sejal Agarwal, Delara Forghani, Brandon Lit, Thomas Driscoll, and Anthony Maocheia-Ricci announce a workshop on the identity of human-computer interaction. The field has always defined itself around the human, through user-centered and human-centered design, drawing on computer science, psychology, and human factors. The rapid adoption of generative AI tools now presses the field to say what it is and why its human focus still matters.

The workshop brings researchers from diverse disciplines together to reflect on two questions: what is HCI, and why does the human matter? Guided discussions, group brainstorming, and reflection explore what the field means today. They also ask what it may look like in the future, and why its human aspect must not be forgotten as its tools change.
arxiv-2605-00509:
Mohammad S. Khorrami and 7 co-authors build physics into the build of neural models for stress in solids, instead of only fining breaches while training. A stress field inside a body at rest must be divergence-free, the math statement of force balance. Standard physics-informed networks only push for that through the loss, so their outputs can still break the balance after training.

The authors encode the constraint directly, writing stress through a potential that makes the output divergence-free by design. Their physics-encoded Fourier neural operator is trained on stress data for a many-crystal solid of springy grains under one-way stretch. Against physics-guided and physics-informed rivals, with matched skill on the stress field itself, the encoded model's output met the balance far more closely. The approach shows how a hard physical law can be built in rather than hoped for.
arxiv-2605-00809:
Yan Fang and nine co-authors present GenLIP, a generative pre-training framework that teaches a Vision Transformer to predict language tokens directly from visual tokens. The goal is a vision encoder that fits naturally with autoregressive language models used in multimodal systems. Training uses a standard language modeling objective, with no contrastive batches and no extra text decoder, so a single transformer handles both kinds of tokens.

The authors stress simplicity, scalability with data and model size, and strong results across multimodal benchmarks. Trained on many samples drawn from Recap-DataComp-1B, GenLIP matches or beats strong baselines while using much less pre-training data. Further training on multi-resolution images at native aspect ratios improves detail tasks such as text reading and chart understanding.
arxiv-2605-01309:
Ruichi Zhang and six co-authors tackle a flaw in image training data where a few common classes have many examples and most rare classes have very few. Fine-tuning large pre-trained models helps, but training with one label per image can hide links between related classes and hurt rare ones.

Their method, called CUE, adds extra concept labels to each image. One set of cues comes from a vision model that reads the image itself, and a second set comes from a language model that describes each class. Two weighted loss terms teach the model these links while the main loss still sorts the classes. On several standard long-tailed test sets, CUE beats recent methods and gives rare and common classes a more even score.
arxiv-2605-01409:
Chengzheng Wu and five co-authors build search tools for health videos that can hold a conversation, not just take one query. A patient or trainee often starts vague, and only later adds the details that matter, such as posture, hand placement, risks, gear, or the patient's state.

The team creates MHVRC, a corpus that pairs video-grounded descriptions with follow-up queries drafted by a language model. Their system, DATR, first pulls a rough shortlist with a fast dual encoder and sparse frame sampling. It then re-ranks the list by merging the whole chat history and scoring with a small cross-encoder. On the new corpus it beats strong video search baselines, and user studies show the refined queries catch fine procedural detail that single queries miss.
arxiv-2605-01609:
Pratyush Acharya, Nuraj Rimal, and Habish Dhakal find that Transformers hide their concepts in the quiet corners of their own geometry. Across a core suite of seventeen models, concept directions sit in the low-variance tail of the output covariance, the directions the model uses least loudly.

Three extraction methods agree on the pattern, backed by sparse autoencoder features and linear probes. A dual geometry appears: concept directions from live activations lean into the tail, while contrasts from static word rows lean into the loud directions. The study began as a test of a cross-language transport tool, which adds nothing over plain spectral control. Steering tests show the predicted interference pattern in most models, and grammar probes find syntax stored in the loud subspace in six of eight architectures, with one model family reversed. The authors read this as rotation of meaning into quiet spectral ground during processing.
arxiv-2605-01709:
Aekta Aggarwal, N K Aswini, Sarvesh Kumar, and Ganesh Vaidya prove stability bounds for systems of balance laws whose flows remember. In these equations the flux and the source at a point depend on the state nearby in space and back in time, blended through kernels. It is a model for traffic, fluids, and materials where the past pushes on the present.

The team work with entropy solutions, the physically admissible kind that respects the second law across shocks. Their estimates bound how much a solution can move when the flux rule, either kernel, or the starting data is perturbed. That is the groundwork any simulation or control claim must stand on. Numerical runs close the paper, showing how memory strength and source terms reshape the dynamics the theorems describe. Coupled nonlocal systems of this kind are a growing corner of applied analysis.
arxiv-2605-01809:
Yang and eleven colleagues build a benchmark for judging music and dance made together by machines. Text-driven music-dance co-generation is far harder than general audio-video synthesis, because rhythm, phrasing, and accents in the music must drive the choreography beat by beat. Existing scores miss this coupling: they rate music and video separately, or reward generic audiovisual consistency. TMD-Bench rates systems on generation quality, instruction following, and rhythmic alignment between sound and movement.

The benchmark pairs computable physical measures with human-like multimodal judgments, backed by a curated rhythm-aligned dataset of ten thousand examples and a captioning tool for music structure. Tests found that leading commercial models make high-quality music and video, yet their rhythmic coupling stays uneven. The authors' own baseline, RhyJAM, trained on rhythm-aligned data, matched rivals on beat-level synchronization while keeping unimodal quality competitive.
arxiv-2605-02009:
Murilo Batista and colleagues benchmark ways to represent wireless channels for later learning tasks. High-dimensional embeddings from a wireless foundation model may capture rich detail, but they cost time and parameters. The team compares them with compact autoencoder representations and with raw data, across several tasks and conditions.

Beyond line-of-sight classification and beam selection, they add power allocation as a new task. High-dimensional embeddings did well in some low-data cases, but they brought much higher latency and size. Compact forms were often close in accuracy at far lower cost. The study maps data needs, noise robustness, and compute cost so builders can choose a representation with eyes open.
arxiv-2605-02209:
Alexander Smola formalises how to choose a small set of benchmarks that still says a lot about a language model. Testing across many benchmarks is costly, and many benchmarks move together, so a subset can carry most of the signal. Smola models benchmark scores as a multivariate Gaussian and casts subset choice as submodular maximisation, where each added benchmark gives diminishing new information.

Two objectives arise naturally: entropy of the chosen set and mutual information between chosen and remaining benchmarks. Both are submodular. Entropy choice matches pivoted Cholesky and carries spectral error bounds, while mutual information is optimised greedily. On three matrices from ten public leaderboards, mutual information choice beat entropy for filling in missing scores at small subset sizes.
arxiv-2605-02409:
Sofianos Panagiotis Fotias and Vassilis Gaganis make Bayesian optimisation respect permutation symmetry in well placement for carbon capture and storage. Bayesian optimisation searches costly black-box functions with a surrogate model, usually a Gaussian process. Standard kernels suit vector inputs, not unordered sets, so they waste the symmetry when wells are run under group control and injectors or producers can be swapped.

Their kernel, GP-Perm, encodes permutation invariance by comparing sets through a stable divergence between their induced empirical representations. It can be combined with standard kernels for added vector structure. The simulator runs wells under group control, giving the symmetry the kernel exploits. The authors apply the method to well placement in storage projects.
arxiv-2605-02709:
Gelei Xu and six co-authors give the first empirical study of agent skills in healthcare: packaged, reusable procedures that AI agents can load to adapt to local settings. Hospital work is shaped by local rules, so capabilities rarely transfer unchanged. Skills promise a procedural layer for that adaptation, but their real-world state was unmapped.

The team filtered hundreds of healthcare skills from tens of thousands of public ones and coded them on ten dimensions, covering function, setting, autonomy, and safety. Public skills stress patient-facing workflow automation and monitoring, not the diagnosis and treatment tasks that dominate research. Coverage of the care lifecycle and specialized clinical inputs is uneven. General technical risk scores, they find, do not reliably capture clinical risk, so benchmarks and risk frameworks need a healthcare-specific layer.
arxiv-2605-02909:
Kazuki Egashira and five co-authors study what happens when the checker that grades a language model's answers is systematically wrong. Training with verifiable rewards improves reasoning by scoring outputs against ground truth. Real checkers, such as static code tools, make errors, and prior work treated those errors as random, concluding they mainly slow training.

In controlled arithmetic experiments, the pattern of errors mattered more than the overall rate. Systematic false negatives, marking right answers wrong, behaved much like random noise. Systematic false positives, marking wrong answers right, were far more dangerous: outcomes ranged from flat, suboptimal plateaus to full performance collapse. Because the pattern, not the rate, decides the harm, fixing the problem in advance is hard. The findings qualify earlier reassurance.
arxiv-2605-03009:
J. Olofsson and twenty-four co-authors, in the eleventh paper of a large ALMA survey of debris disks, ask why small and large dust grains sit at different radii around young stars. Debris disk dust comes from colliding parent bodies, and observations from the near infrared to the submillimeter trace grain sizes across a wide range. In most gas-bearing disks, the small-grain ring peaks outside the large-grain ring.

Simulations test whether gas drag on dust can cause that offset. More gas makes small grains drift outward more efficiently, but the resulting offset depends strongly on the disk's optical depth, since drift races against the grains' collisional lifetime. Raising the share of tiny grains also shifts the balance. The study names the parameters that set where each grain size is seen.
arxiv-2605-03109:
Stephen J. Thomas presents a method to speed up transformer inference by using the low effective rank of token activations at each layer. Each activation splits into a main subspace part and a leftover residual, and most linear work can run on the smaller part alone.

A per-token gate decides whether the residual fix is needed, keeping output within a set tolerance. On three model families, weight reads sped up several times over, with top token agreement above ninety-eight percent and no retraining or model changes. At one setting, output matched the baseline character for character.
arxiv-2605-03209:
R. J. Hernández-Pinto, L. X. Gutiérrez-Guerrero, M. A. Bedolla, J. P. Uribe-Ramírez, and A. Bashir compute elastic form factors of axial-vector mesons with a symmetry-preserving contact interaction. Form factors describe how a particle's charge and magnetism spread out, probed here through coupled Schwinger-Dyson and Bethe-Salpeter equations.

They report charge radii, magnetic moments, and quadrupole moments for mesons made of light, heavy, or mixed quarks. Like vector mesons, the electric form factor crosses zero, but at lower momentum. Radii shrink as quark mass grows. An anomalous magnetic term in the photon vertex shifts the magnetic and quadrupole results by large percentages.
arxiv-2605-03309:
Alan L. McCann proposes a signed-proof defense against dependency confusion attacks. In such attacks, installers are tricked into fetching a bad package from the wrong registry. Once a package is installed, no proof shows which registry supplied it. Current defenses rely on settings, and they fail silently when misconfigured.

Each registry holds a signing key. It requires signatures from both publisher and registry. Consumers pin approved registry fingerprints, so the resolver rejects all else. An attacker must breach all three layers at once. A survey of eight ecosystems finds none has all the required pieces today. The work gives package users a clear way to check where each file came from.
arxiv-2605-03409:
Srinath Perera, Kaviru Hapuarachchi, Frank Leymann, and Rania Khalaf present Robust Agent Compensation, a log-based recovery safety net for AI agents. When a multi-step agent fails mid-task, naive retries can repeat side effects, while language-model-driven recovery is slow and costly.

Their architectural extension plugs into existing frameworks through normal extension points, with no changes to agent code, and users can switch it on by choice. A LangChain implementation tested on two agent benchmarks beat leading model-based recovery on both latency and token use by large factors on complex problems, making reliable execution far cheaper.
arxiv-2605-03609:
Chenchen Yuan, Zheyu Zhang, and Gjergji Kasneci study how to steer a large language model's moral reasoning toward a chosen ethical framework without damaging its general ability. Models often show mixed moral preferences across settings. Their method, Convergent-Divergent Routing, finds minimal branch points inside transformer blocks where framework-related pathways first meet and then split.

Gating the non-target branches at those points blocks unwanted downstream reasoning while leaving earlier computation intact. For finer control, they extract directions that separate utilitarian from deontological reasoning and apply Dual Logit Calibration, a closed-form update that shifts the model toward user-set preference weights. On real-life moral dilemmas, the method calibrated preferences reliably and largely preserved general capabilities.
arxiv-2605-03909:
Zhiling Chen and five co-authors tackle the trial-and-error tuning of robotic laser profilers used for dimensional verification and surface inspection. Industrial profilers expose coupled parameters: sampling frequency, measurement range, exposure time, receiver dynamic range, and illumination. A mismatch can cause saturation, clipping, or missing returns that no later step can recover.

Given a pre-scan RGB image and a natural-language inspection instruction, the system must infer a discrete configuration for a robot-mounted profiler. To benchmark the task, the authors built Instruct-Obs2Param, a real-world multimodal dataset linking inspection intents across sixteen objects to canonical parameter regimes. Their ScanHD framework uses hyperdimensional computing. It binds instruction and observation into a task-aware code. It then reasons over compact memories, matching discrete scanner regimes with stable, interpretable, low-latency decisions.
arxiv-2605-04009:
Giuseppe De Laurentis and four co-authors present the leading-color two-loop quantum chromodynamics corrections for producing a Higgs boson together with two jets through gluon fusion, in the heavy-top effective theory. They are needed for precise predictions at the Large Hadron Collider. They provide exact expressions for the finite remainders of the helicity amplitudes, written in terms of one-mass pentagon functions with spinor-helicity factors.

The amplitudes were rebuilt from numerical finite-field samples computed with numerical unitarity. Advances in using analytic structure made that possible. They reduce the needed samples and yield compact forms. A new algorithm for multivariate partial fraction splitting is added along the way. The authors supply efficient, stable numerical code ready for use. They confirm a threshold singularity at non-degenerate physical momenta.
arxiv-2605-04209:
Sarthak Choudhary and five co-authors describe an attack that hides a secret backdoor inside a pretrained image classifier. The altered model behaves normally until a trigger appears, then it sends the input to a class chosen by the attacker.

The change is a sparse nudge spread across layers, masked with random noise so the weights look like a clean reference model. The authors prove that telling the two apart is at least as hard as a known hard detection problem, even for a checker who can inspect every weight. The work exposes a supply-chain risk for shared models.
arxiv-2605-04309:
Xin Wang and five co-authors present a framework for reading what populations of neurons in the primary visual cortex are doing. Recent methods can decode images from brain activity well, but they reveal little about the computations behind that success.

Their dual-tower system aligns images and neural responses in a shared space at the level of intermediate feature maps, keeping those maps open to inspection. On large mouse imaging data, it decodes accurately while showing that coarse, low-level visual structure carries most of the signal, rather than fine detail or object category. That insight helps link decoding back to biology.
arxiv-2605-04409:
Yupeng Gao and three co-authors work on describing, in words, how a place has changed between two remote sensing images, with drones monitoring urban construction as the target use. Word-level descriptions go beyond simple change masks, but past methods struggle to serve both detection and caption writing well.

Their framework uses a learned bank of prototypes to model the structure of changes. It separates the representations each task needs. It also feeds detection results into the caption generator as spatial guidance. They also build a large new benchmark data set covering high-resolution urban construction scenes, an area earlier benchmarks largely missed.
arxiv-2605-04509:
Gyujin Sim and five co-authors speed up rendering for light field displays, screens that show many viewpoints at once so a scene looks three-dimensional without glasses. Producing the interlaced multi-view image is expensive, and a popular fast rendering method for single views becomes costly when extended to so many angles.

Their framework renders at the level of individual subpixels. It reuses attributes across neighbouring viewpoints instead of recomputing them. It also remaps the work so graphics hardware handles the interlaced layout efficiently. Together these steps aim for real-time, high-quality light field synthesis on consumer-grade hardware. Earlier acceleration methods either wasted computation or used heavy intermediate representations.
arxiv-2605-05009:
Michael Lanier and three co-authors study decentralised learning systems that train separately but then deploy side by side, as in networks of unequal Internet of Things devices. Most methods train each node alone, even when a stronger neighbour could help at prediction time. Data at each node is scarce and skewed, making that help valuable.

Their method, LNTrust, lets each node learn a small trust function over its neighbours from local validation evidence. That trust gates extra teaching during training and then defines a shared prediction ensemble at deployment. Across datasets and network shapes, LNTrust improved deployed accuracy by large margins over the strongest output-only baseline while using far less communication.
arxiv-2605-05309:
Dark matter that interacts with itself can annihilate much faster at low speeds, an effect named after Sommerfeld. Barry E. Cimring and Tracy R. Slatyer examine a worry about that calculation. Near certain resonances the standard result seems to break unitarity, a basic rule of quantum theory.

Several fixes have been proposed, some using an explicit high-energy cutoff and some not. Cimring and Slatyer show the fixes agree where it matters, and the answers barely depend on the cutoff. They then write one clean prescription for restoring unitarity that also works for systems with several states.
arxiv-2605-05709:
Hiding a harmful request inside an image or puzzle can slip it past a multimodal model's safety filters. Md Farhamdur Reza, Richeng Jin, Tianfu Wu, and Huaiyu Dai show such attacks live on a knife's edge. The disguised input must conceal intent from the filters yet stay recoverable enough for the victim model to rebuild the original request.

Analyzing three representative black-box attacks, they find existing transformations balance that tradeoff poorly. Simply removing characters worked better. Their concealment-aware construction method tunes variants deliberately along the tradeoff, producing stronger jailbreaks and a clearer map of the vulnerability.
arxiv-2605-05909:
Making a multimodal model forget specific visual knowledge, without damaging everything else it knows, is surgical work. Yuhang Wang and five co-authors freeze the language backbone and operate only on the visual module. Their contrastive visual forgetting mechanism separates target visual knowledge from knowledge to retain, guiding what gets erased.

A null-space constraint further protects retained representations from collateral change. Textual knowledge stays untouched by construction. The approach addresses the intertwining of visual and textual knowledge that makes multimodal unlearning harder than its text-only counterpart. Throughout, the balance between removing the target and retaining everything else is the criterion the design is judged by.
arxiv-2605-06309:
Sofia Callejas and four co-authors segment laughter in audio without any labeled training data, across many languages. Laughter is a universal social signal central to bonding and communication, yet detecting it in recordings is hard and cutting it into segments is harder. Machine learning methods usually need costly hand annotation, and their data sets lean heavily on English material, which limits use in other settings.

Their method, MultiLinguahah, recasts segmentation as anomaly detection over energy based audio segments. An isolation forest runs on representations from a self supervised audio encoder, flagging the bursts that stand out as laughter. Tests span stand up comedy, sitcoms, and general short audio collections. Leading existing methods proved poorly tuned for multilingual use, while the new unsupervised method beat them in non English settings.
arxiv-2605-06609:
Chenyang Zhang and Yuan Cao show that Transformers can perform logistic regression inside their context window by running normalized gradient descent. In-context learning is often explained by transformers secretly executing algorithms on the prompt. The authors construct multi-layer transformers with softmax attention where each layer performs exactly one step of normalized gradient descent on a logistic loss defined by the context examples.

The constructed model is also reachable by training: one self-attention layer is trained to imitate a single gradient step, then looped to form the full model. Convergence guarantees for the layer training and out-of-distribution guarantees for the looped model are provided. The result sharpens the theory of how attention implements learning algorithms.
arxiv-2605-06709:
Sadeq Yaqubi and Jouni Mattila build a modular adaptive controller for flexible robot arms with any number of links. Each link bends like a spring, described by a PDE that most designs approximate away early. Their framework carries the full deformation equation through the whole design, writing motion and joint forces in one shared form, as Lie algebra twists and wrenches.

A deflection-compensating inverse kinematics step builds desired paths per link. Nominal controllers guarantee fast twist error decay, and an adaptive version learns unknown physical parameters online instead. Interaction forces between links cancel exactly in the stability proof, making it scale to long chains. Tests on a two-link arm moving in three dimensions confirm the approach.
arxiv-2605-06809:
Ali Salamatian and five co-authors speed up video recognition by teaching a model to choose what computation is worth doing. Transformers split videos into tokens and process all of them at superlinear cost, yet videos brim with redundancy. Their LookWhen framework pairs a shallow selector, which quickly scores every space-time token from a downscaled video, with a deep extractor that processes only the top-ranked tokens.

Uniqueness scores based on nearest neighbors supervise the selector, while distillation from video and image teachers trains the extractor. Across six action and gesture datasets, LookWhen beats efficient rivals on accuracy per computation in most settings and runs several times faster than a strong baseline at equal accuracy.
arxiv-2605-07209:
Akshita Singh, Prabesh Paudel, and Siddhartha Roy detect hallucinations by reading generated text with a second, smaller model. Instead of inspecting the generator, which may be a closed commercial system, their proxy analyzer watches its own internal activations as it reads. Features cover attention, entropy, layer signals, and new token-level grounding measures.

An ensemble trained on tens of thousands of samples was tested across seven analyzer sizes and families. Every analyzer beat a leading earlier method on a key benchmark, and results clustered tightly despite an eighteen-fold size range. A mid-size model even beat its larger sibling, suggesting analyzer choice matters more than raw scale.
arxiv-2605-07409:
Baishi Li and three co-authors warn social scientists against treating text embeddings as direct measures of social concepts. Scholars read constructs like novelty or bias off gaps in embedding space, a habit the authors call the proxy presumption. Without checking, embeddings mix the target concept with side factors like topic and style.

Their Construct Validity Protocol offers a path from naming a concept to checking its measure with numbers. A companion method uses language models to cancel that mixing inside the space. A test suite checks whether a measure stays distinct and adds forecast value, turning rough proxies into sound tools.
arxiv-2605-07609:
Marco Damele and Andrea Loi study topological skew braces, algebraic objects carrying two group operations that interact by a fixed rule. For finite skew braces, a known question asks whether solvability of the additive group forces solvability of the multiplicative group. They ask the same question for topological versions, where the groups also carry a topology.

In the connected, locally compact, Hausdorff setting, they prove the answer is yes. The proof reduces to a solvable Lie quotient and uses a theorem about affine actions of Lie groups. They also show each hypothesis is essential by giving counterexamples when any one is dropped. In the compact connected case with abelian additive group, they prove more: the two group laws must coincide.
arxiv-2605-07709:
Giordano d'Aloisio and five co-authors study how harmful large language model responses can be reduced by tuning rather than retraining. They first measure harmfulness across four general-purpose models, then ask whether search over hyperparameters and system prompts can push harm down while keeping answers relevant to the prompt.

Their approach, SafeTune, runs a multi-objective search that trades harmfulness against relevance. On the small Qwen model they tested, it significantly cut the rate of harmful responses and raised relevance, both with large effect sizes. One finding stands out: among the knobs explored, encouraging greater repetition in responses had the strongest impact on both goals at once.
arxiv-2605-07809:
Sirui Wu and five co-authors present Potamides, a method for measuring the shapes of dark matter halos in other galaxies from the curved tracks of stellar streams. Streams trace their host galaxy's gravitational field, so their bends carry information about halo flattening and orientation, evidence that is scarce for individual galaxies despite sharp predictions from simulations.

Applied to fifteen streams from the Stellar Stream Legacy Survey, the method constrained projected axis ratios and orientations for their host halos. Streams with edge-on loops or sharp turning points gave the strongest limits, while great-circle-like streams said little. Every stream was consistent with a spherical halo along the measured direction. With Euclid, Rubin, and Roman set to find many more streams, the technique promises fast statistical tests of dark matter physics.
arxiv-2605-08009:
Moritz Fontboté-Schmidt and colleagues report an experiment with a promising design for quantum computers. Bosonic codes store information in vibrating modes and can correct errors with less hardware. One such code, the GKP code, needs a beamsplitter-like coupling between two modes that stays fault-tolerant.

Working with two motional modes of a trapped ion, the team mixed two grid-like states on a beamsplitter to create entangled GKP states.
