They produced all four Bell states with an average fidelity of sixty-nine percent. They then used error correction to extend how long the entangled state lasted, completing a key set of operations for this approach.
arxiv-2605-08609:
Josh Gibson borrows sheaf theory from pure mathematics to keep complex engineering designs consistent. Large cyber physical systems are viewed through separate electrical, thermal, mechanical, and software lenses, and keeping those views in agreement usually rests on informal habit. Gibson builds a space whose points are pairwise interfaces between domains, with each view holding its own local design options.

A formal equivalence shows global agreement across all views reduces to checking pairwise overlaps alone. Compatible local designs then join into exactly one global design. The whole chain is machine checked in the Lean proof system with a worked three view example. Systems engineering gains a precise, verifiable meaning for design consistency.
arxiv-2605-08809:
Yan Sun and nine coauthors add a similarity regularizer called SimReg to the pretraining of large language models. Next token training leaves token representations scattered within each class and overlapping across classes, slowing representation learning. SimReg pulls representations sharing the same true label closer within each sequence while pushing different labels apart through a contrastive term.

Analysis ties the gain to widened classification margins. Across dense and mixture of experts architectures, training converges more than thirty percent faster and zero shot downstream scores rise modestly on standard benchmarks. Tuning studies round out practical guidance. Pretraining gains a cheap add on that organizes the embedding space from the start.
arxiv-2605-09009:
Minmin Zhang, Sina Aghaei, and Soroush Saghafian ask whether large language models can learn to make good choices step by step, not just answer questions. They study settings where an agent sees full, partial, or unclear information about its world, and they train models on examples labeled by an expert.

Fine-tuning, they show, lets a model copy good policies from past records rather than rely only on examples shown in the prompt. Their theory links part of the trained model to estimates of the best long-term value of each action. In tests, fine-tuned models came much closer to the best possible results than prompt-only ones, above all on long and partly hidden tasks.
arxiv-2605-09109:
Yann Berthelot, Philippe Preux, and Riad Akrour compare methods that let a learning agent ask an existing controller for help while it trains. Many control problems come with a decent but imperfect controller, yet each help-using method was tested alone, on its own benchmark, with a flawless expert assumed.

The team lines the methods up on one shared backbone with common tuning rules and many random seeds, then degrades the expert in set ways. Three failure modes appear that single studies miss, including a blind spot that makes help hurt when the expert is already strong. No method wins everywhere. The authors turn the pattern into a practical rule for picking a method before training starts.
arxiv-2605-09209:
Masiha and three colleagues study optimistic bilevel optimisation where the lower level has a non-isolated manifold of minima. The upper level must then choose among many lower-level solutions, so smooth derivatives may fail. Under a local Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition, smooth derivatives need only a unique optimistic selection, not a single solution set. That yields a clear pseudoinverse hyper-gradient formula going beyond the classical singleton result.

Non-degeneracy along the manifold gives local smoothness. Failure of uniqueness creates many rough points, and failure of non-degeneracy destroys all positive Holder regularity. Their HG-MS method pairs clear optimistic selection with fast pseudoinverse hyper-gradient math. Despite the nonconvex selection problem, it converges to a still point with cost set by inner dimension, not outer dimension. A working HG-MS variant for matched-budget LLM source reweighting takes the best GSM8K and MATH scores across tested backbones.
arxiv-2605-09509:
Matsuda develops an empirical Bayes method for predicting missing entries in a binary matrix, a task called one bit matrix completion. Binary matrices arise in recommendation, where a system records only whether a user touched an item, and in social networks, where links are present or absent. Standard completion tools assume continuous values and handle such yes or no data poorly. They also demand fiddly tuning and give no natural measure of uncertainty.

His method adapts the Efron Morris estimator, which shrinks singular values toward zero, and exploits the low rank structure of binary matrices. It draws a parallel with multidimensional item response theory. Simulations and real data tests show a better balance of prediction accuracy, calibration, and speed than existing methods. Practitioners gain a principled tool for binary completion with honest uncertainty attached.
arxiv-2605-09609:
Dao and Rodriguez disprove a conjecture about minimal polynomial neural networks, models whose activation raises each input to a fixed power. Fixing input and output widths, the minimal unimodal conjecture claimed every minimal filling architecture has hidden layer widths that rise then fall, never dipping in the middle. The authors found a counterexample through a frontier search, a systematic hunt across candidate architectures, and certified it with recursive dimension arguments plus symbolic checks.

Notably, several smaller architectures inside their example show large defect, a measure of slack in the architecture, in contrast with the mostly small defect behavior of earlier examples. The counterexample is concrete, not merely existential: it is exhibited and checked. Minimal filling architectures, the paper shows, can break the unimodal pattern that researchers had expected to hold universally.
arxiv-2605-09709:
Ymai and five colleagues designed a rotation sensor built from ultra-cold atoms with electric dipoles, trapped in four wells. Their design reads rotation from a simple imbalance in how atoms sit across the wells. The trick behind it is superintegrability, a property where a system holds more conserved quantities than usual.

Using that property, the team reports sensitivity past the Heisenberg limit, a benchmark for quantum measurement precision that ordinary methods cannot reach. Quantum sensors of this kind could sharpen navigation and other tools that depend on exact rotation readings. The paper frames superintegrability as a fresh route to better quantum sensing, not just a math curiosity.
arxiv-2605-09909:
Wang addressed a failure mode of variational quantum eigensolvers (VQEs). When strong correlation splits the molecular energy landscape into rival basins, the first state may select a non-ground-state basin before tuning even begins. The paper offers a shape-based preconditioner constrained by SE(3) symmetry of the Hamiltonian. It maps nuclear shape into circuit settings inside the correlated ground-state basin.

That basin localization shifts gradient stats from concentration-led to curvature-led. In statevector tests on six stretched cases, the preconditioner cut Hartree-Fock start errors by factors from 38 to 6250. It reached sub-milliHartree starts in CO, LiH, and H8, and placed N2, H2O, and BeH2 in the milliHartree-scale correlated basin. In messy H10 chains, equivariant basin aiming plus stochastic escape reached unit success odds at a fixed tuning budget.
arxiv-2605-10009:
Cai and three colleagues address image retrieval when queries arrive in unfamiliar styles: sketches, artworks or low-resolution previews. Large vision-language models like CLIP retrieve well in general but stumble when query style shifts. Their lightweight framework, Hystar, adapts model weights to each query's style on the fly, using a hypernetwork, a small network that generates weights for a larger one.

The hypernetwork perturbs singular values in attention layers per input, while fixed singular-value offsets on feed-forward layers keep cross-style stability. A contrastive loss called StyleNCE, weighted by optimal transport, emphasises hard negatives across styles to cut semantic confusion. Across multi-style retrieval and cross-style classification benchmarks, Hystar beat strong baselines with state-of-the-art performance, staying parameter-efficient and stable across styles.
arxiv-2605-10409:
Adi Rosenthal and three colleagues trim photos without turning them into cartoons. Past tools usually rely on cartoon-style rendering, producing stylized sketches or paintings that sacrifice true-to-life looks. Their 2026 paper explores the reverse direction: reducing scene complexity while keeping each intermediate image a plausible natural photo.

The method pairs scene understanding with smart editing. Vision-language models pick and rank elements for removal, and a learned verifier checks lifelike looks and fit throughout. An iterative Select-Remove-Verify pipeline produces high-quality trim paths, later distilled into an image-to-video model that predicts coherent sequences from a single input. Beyond cleaner pictures, the approach enables content-aware decluttering, layer splitting, and hands-on editing.
arxiv-2605-10909:
Alex DeWeese and Guannan Qu revisit policy gradients for restricted policy classes, which often stall at myopic local optima. Standard gradients improve a policy using only the one-step action-value function, so they cannot see gains that need several coordinated steps.

Their k-step policy gradient couples randomness across a k-step window, escaping those traps with a guarantee: performance lands exponentially close to the best deterministic policy as k grows. Projected and mirror descent variants reach that guarantee in a standard iteration count, assuming only smoothness, and dodge the usual distribution-mismatch penalties. The method opens state aggregation and partly observed cooperative multi-agent problems that resisted near-optimal solutions.
arxiv-2605-11009:
Qian Chen and six colleagues present ACSAC, an actor-critic method that adapts its action-chunk size to the state. Long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks punish single-step temporal-difference learning, since bootstrapping errors pile up across Bellman updates, and action chunking helps by shortening the effective horizon.

Fixed chunk sizes force a trade-off: large chunks blunt responsiveness to new observations, small chunks produce incoherent motion, and tuning stays task-specific. ACSAC uses a causal Transformer critic to score expected returns for different chunk sizes and picks the best at each chunk boundary. The team proves its Bellman operator contracts to the adaptive policy's action-value function. OGBench experiments show state-of-the-art results on long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks. Reinforcement-learning practitioners get chunking that adapts itself.
arxiv-2605-11309: Nitin Vaidya and Lewis Tseng study consensus in networks modelled by directed graphs. They assume messages carry authentication, such as digital signatures, to verify integrity. They pin down necessary and sufficient conditions for the directed graph for two problems to be solvable. The first is exact consensus in synchronous systems. The second is approximate consensus in asynchronous systems. The paper gives a full answer for both timing models, so readers can tell at a glance whether a given graph lets its nodes agree.
arxiv-2605-11509: Yan and six colleagues propose a language-model control framework for HAPS-assisted UAV networks, tuning flight and connectivity. Multi-UAV motion and connectivity stay hard to tune together. They model a three-dimensional aerial highway as a layered decision process under partial views. A language-model controller on a high-altitude platform plans load balance and handovers. Each UAV pairs a slow language model for spatial thought with a fast learning agent for link and motion control. It lifts transport efficiency by 14 percent and telecom throughput by 25 percent.
arxiv-2605-11809: Huoren Yang and nine colleagues rethink how vision-language-action models command robot arms. Most action heads predict commands in a fixed world frame. Their MCF-Proto head, by contrast, predicts a rotation each step. It builds actions from prototypes in the resulting local frame and returns them to the world frame. The learned frames line up with real end-effector motion without directional labels, and the design proved sturdier under geometric disturbances.
arxiv-2605-12109: Ali Tahaei, Ahandeep Manna, and Marko Popović ask whether living tissue shows the mass avalanches seen in passive glass-like solids. They model a flat tissue where cell splits act as plastic events. Splits make the tissue flow below the passive yield point, yet keep its marginal stability when changes are slow. Splits also strongly damp system-wide waves of cell shifts, unlike passive solids. The cause is energy balance: split energy lets tissue flow below yield, but caps how much shifting can happen.
arxiv-2605-12609: Moenter and three colleagues examine how physics education research gathers and reports neurodiversity data. Current practice often demands official labels rather than letting people name themselves. That blocks true voice for crossing selves and hurts trust in data and reading. Mixed reports across studies further hurt use. Through a review of neurodivergent student lives, they document a wide spread in how data are taken and shown. They call for self-naming and clear write-ups.
arxiv-2605-12709: Dądela and three colleagues introduce the Spectral Energy Centroid, a metric for spectral bias in implicit neural representations. Such models use multi-layer perceptrons to model smooth signals in compact, smooth form. Yet those nets carry a low-frequency bias that blocks learning of small details, so it must be tuned through the embedding layer. Prior tuning before training ignored model depth. The centroid gauges target image frequency and model spectral bias, clarifying how it, depth and scores relate.
arxiv-2605-12909: Bui, Daneshpajouh and Karasev study the cross-index of free group posets, a combinatorial analogue of the equivariant topological index. They show its union behaviour splits sharply by group. For two-element groups the sharp bound mirrors the classical topological inequality, while for every other group that bound fails and only a weaker estimate holds. The gap between cross-index and topological index can grow without bound, clarifying the combinatorial analogue's role.
arxiv-2605-13009: Ravasio and six co-authors study conditioning, a minimal route to reliable behaviour in growing populations. Instead of micromanaging errors with molecular machinery, conditioning destroys attempts that fail a coarse criterion, leaving no physical record. In a socks-before-shoes model where n actions must finish by a threshold time to replicate, resets impose hierarchical temporal order for free when disorder carries a time penalty. Save points that preserve verified progress let the strategy scale to complex multi-step processes.
arxiv-2605-13209: Thüring, Strack and Pflüger present multi-vendor, heterogeneous CPU-GPU versions of the conjugate gradient method and Cholesky decomposition using SYCL, tackling linear systems with symmetric positive-definite matrices. GPU-only plans waste powerful modern CPUs, so their code uses CPU and GPU at once. Against GPU-only versions on large matrices, the mixed code runs up to 32% faster for conjugate gradient and up to 29% faster for Cholesky. The Cholesky version also runs at least 12% faster across systems with NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs.
arxiv-2605-13409: Carlos Baiget Orts argues that comet 1P/Halley takes part in a 1,151-year planetary quasi-period. He draws on historical perihelion records covering 2,225 years and thirty apparitions. Fifteen Halley orbits fit the period with an angular residue of just 1.43 degrees. That residue is the smallest of any body examined. No other Halley-type comet joins in. Statistical tests point to Jupiter acting through phase-dependent modulation and Saturn through distance-dependent modulation. Cumulative deviations reach only 9.4 percent of a random-walk expectation.
arxiv-2605-13509: Yongjae Oh, Euijoon Kwon and Yongjoo Baek propose a large-scale deep-learning method for gauging stochastic information flow from time-series data. Unlike usual symmetric ensemble measures, it tracks flow at the trajectory level. Hard maths has blocked its use. The method is tested on an exactly solvable two-particle model, Kuramoto oscillators, and paths of interacting motile cells. The tests show it works as a data-driven sign of cooperative structures.
arxiv-2605-13609: Rohan Abeyaratne, Roberto Paroni and Marco Picchi Scardaoni show volume growth can be framed as an optimisation-driven process in linear elasticity. At each step, shift and growth fields meet balance, mass-balance and one-way rules, while a goal measure encodes the drive. Finite element meshing turns the problem into a finite constrained smallest-value problem in the growth values alone, read as a cast gradient flow. Tests show the framework.
arxiv-2605-13709: Qian Shen and five colleagues fine-tune three 8B-parameter language models for children's English reading story generation with controllable difficulty and safety. Using an expert-designed reading curriculum plus stories from GPT-4o and Llama 3.3 70B, the team tests fine-tuning designs for compact affordable models. With apt fine-tuning, 8B models beat zero-shot GPT-4o and Llama 3.3 70B on difficulty metrics, with almost no visible safety issues. Such fine-tuned models could serve teachers, parents and children at school and home.
arxiv-2605-13809: Władysław Wachowski considers the 'metric-affine-like' generalisation of Yang-Mills theory, mal-YM, first proposed earlier by the author. Here the connection is no longer assumed compatible with the Hermitian form in the fibres. Alongside the usual Yang-Mills potential A_a and field strength tensor F_ab, it contains non-trivially interacting fields B_a, h, G_ab and N_a.
arxiv-2605-13909: Zhang and seven co-authors build TERMS-Bench, a testbed for economic reasoning in multi-turn strategy, aimed at negotiation agents. Old tests lean on model-versus-model chats or blunt scores like deal rate, which hide why agents fail. TERMS-Bench turns the setting itself into the judge, fixing the other side's hidden type, policy and payoff shape in a Bayesian game frame. It is first tried on two-sided price haggling, where the other side's traits stay hidden.
arxiv-2605-14009: Gologlu and Kolsch build new commutative semifields from maps of the Desarguesian plane. A classic theorem says a finite semifield three-dimensional over its center must be a field or an Albert twisted field. That result ties quadratic homogeneous maps of the projective plane to Dembowski-Ostrom monomials. The paper instead gives a large class of semiquadratic homogeneous maps that match no such monomial. Those maps yield many commutative semifields unlike fields or twisted fields, and hence many non-Desarguesian semifield planes.
arxiv-2605-14609: Sztamborski, Perez-Gonzalo and Agudo introduce Deep Discriminant Analysis, a loss function for image segmentation that sharpens edges by shaping learned features. It raises between-class variance while lowering within-class variance, so features form compact separable groups. No extra cost is added at inference time. Tested on the DIS5K set across several nets, it is claimed to lift segmentation accuracy, edge sharpness and model confidence time and again.
arxiv-2605-14709: Liu and team tackle two bottlenecks in unified multimodal models that turn any input into images. One is attention entanglement in blind planning for complex prompts. The other is weak visual refinement from unstructured feedback. Their framework lets a model switch on its own between direct generation for simple cases, self-review for quality fixes, and multi-step planning for complex scenes. A data pipeline with over fifty thousand samples and a two-stage training strategy support the switch. Gains over baselines are claimed.
arxiv-2605-14909: Botond Oreg and four colleagues use cold atoms to make hidden charge patterns in a Fermi-Hubbard system easier to see. A rapid boost in interaction strength turns delocalized pairs into doublons, compact markers of each pair's center. The gain is strongest where pairing stretches across sites. Reading atom-level spin and charge correlations after the ramp separates an unpaired Fermi liquid from a pseudogap phase of preformed pairs, and the method may expose stranger pair orders elsewhere.
arxiv-2605-15309: Mehdi Esmaeilzadeh and three others argue that one pass is not enough for generative models. FID, the leading metric, mixes fidelity with coverage and nears a ceiling, so mode-narrowed models can still score well. Their Recursive Latent Refinement swaps single-pass latent mapping in style-based makers with repeat polishing. Joined with hidden maximum likelihood estimation, which tunes breadth by design, it hits the highest precision and recall among current methods at rivaling FID across image and few-shot benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-15409: Sylvie Bronsard and Charles S. Peskin model a buoyancy-driven air-to-air heat exchanger from first principles. Inflow uses a conservative boundary condition from the compressible Bernoulli formula, while outflow uses a lossy rule from pressure continuity. Steady-state behavior solved by computer and at limits agrees well between the two methods. The model lets the authors study the tradeoff between efficiency and airflow, with lessons for optimal unit design where buoyancy alone drives circulation.
arxiv-2605-15909: Anić and Felder introduce a Hopf algebra graded by the double groupoid of commutative diagrams of a finite groupoid. Its finite-dimensional representations form a rigid monoidal category with a fibre functor to graded vector spaces. The leading example comes from restricted quantum groups behind certain statistical mechanics models, including the Andrews-Baxter-Forrester and Jimbo-Miwa-Okado families.
arxiv-2605-16309: Hakim and five colleagues show that ReAct and Reflexion recover episode by episode, yet fail 72 to 100 percent of holdout tests on recurring faults. The operator schemas, preconditions, and constraints behind each fault were never fixed. Their ANNEAL turns repeat failures into governed symbolic edits to a process knowledge graph, leaving model weights untouched. Its Failure-Driven Knowledge Acquisition step finds the responsible operator and drafts a typed patch, validated before commit. Across four domains and 27 runs, ANNEAL alone commits lasting repairs, cutting recurring-fault holdout failure to zero.
arxiv-2605-16609: Magalhães, de Almeida and Alexandropoulos tackle channel estimation for wireless links aided by a fluid reconfigurable surface, whose reflecting parts can shift position on a dense grid. Their method uses a two-timescale setup, orthogonal pilot signals, and tensor models to estimate each user channel together with motion-driven phase errors. Numerical tests show strong performance even when element positions drift from their assumed spots.
arxiv-2605-16709: Guo and colleagues study multi-bit watermarking for non-autoregressive language models, where the encoder sees token distributions within each block but not causally. They build a theory-based model inspired by diffusion language models and pin down its non-causal capacity exactly, using Gelfand-Pinsker and channel synthesis coding. The hiding is tuned across blocks with a constrained Markov process, and a polar-code algorithm implements it. Tests on LLaDA check error rates and total variation against key randomness.
arxiv-2605-16809: Han and colleagues observe that graph structure learning often expands edge count dramatically, because similarity-based construction links highly similar neighbors and adds redundant structure. Their Informative Graph Structure Learning method, InGSL, jointly weighs similarity and diversity in edge construction through mutual-information-guided learning. InGSL works as a plug-in module for existing graph structure learning frameworks. Across six representative methods, InGSL improves performance while using fewer edges.
arxiv-2605-17109: Wu and three colleagues rethink Muon, a popular way to train large language models, by reshaping its update spectrum. Their theory weighs local curvature, gradient noise, and training stage to choose how strongly each direction counts. Positive shaping helps early by stressing steep directions, while mildly negative shaping helps late by rescuing weak but useful ones. Their DynMuon schedule cuts steps to a target loss by roughly eleven to twenty-seven percent.
arxiv-2605-17409: Krishnan and colleagues give time-dependent coupled-cluster theory a chemical reading by expanding its left and right functions in Slater-determinant bases. That yields configuration weights over time for tracking populations. It also splits the dipole moment and autocorrelation, linking absorption peaks to orbital transitions. Tests assign valence lines in four ten-electron molecules and core excitations in three, validated against equation-of-motion theory. Pump-probe and X-ray Raman cases show the method.
arxiv-2605-17609: Dughmi, Haghifam and Kalayci frame pipelines pairing cheap rewards with an expensive verifier as active search: a policy samples options and pays for labels until one passes. For one prompt, generator and reward induce a score distribution. With both known, optimal policy follows from dynamic programming. With both unknown, ADAP raises samples and verifications. Under monotonicity, higher scores pass no less often, so ADAP costs stay near optimum. Lower bounds via a star number show score-label assumptions matter. Experiments on math and programming validate the advantage over fixed baselines.
arxiv-2605-17709: Baoli Hao, Kamrun Mily, Annalisa Quaini, and Ming Zhong model home burglary with police who react to crime reports only after a delay. Extending a known agent-based model, they derive a continuum system. It links criminal density, neighborhood attractiveness, a delayed crime signal, and deployment. Their analysis shows delays can destabilize calm states through Hopf bifurcations, producing pulsing, moving, splitting, and merging hotspots. Their simulations suggest faster crime data matters more than simply adding officers.
arxiv-2605-17809: Chun-Hsiung Tseng and four colleagues present PuppyChatter, a framework for building AI applications with less vendor lock-in. Vendor APIs demand fiddly manual request building, while vendor SDKs tie code to one provider. Model abstraction layers ease that tie but add complexity and security worries of their own. PuppyChatter keeps the easy feel of a vendor SDK while staying vendor-neutral, aiming for a simpler and more flexible way to build. The paper frames it as a usable middle path for developers working with large language models.
arxiv-2605-18309: Yuhan Huang's 2026 paper builds a unified account of why language-model alignment breaks under fine-tuning. The authors define a tractable alignment score with a closed-form update, splitting updates into two competing forces. A rebound force, set by present alignment and distribution narrowness, pulls back toward prior alignment. A driving force, set by how data lines up with posteriors over aligned and non-aligned completions, pushes toward new data. Narrower posteriors strengthen reversal, and prior alignment leaves an imprint that speeds re-alignment on re-exposure, called rehearsal priming.
arxiv-2605-18409: Hengyan Huang and seven co-authors present EnvTriCascade, an environment-aware system for the ESDD2 2026 challenge on audio deepfake detection at the component level, where speech and background sounds may be faked separately. A mix-consistency detector first flags manipulated mixtures, then two five-class detectors combine speech representations through an attention-gated classifier. Trained only on the official CompSpoofV2 set, the system scores 0.8266 Macro-F1 and ranks second in the challenge.
arxiv-2605-18609: Sachin Garg and Michał Dereziński develop, in a 2026 analysis, a general theory of momentum acceleration for mini-batch stochastic gradient methods on quadratics. Classical schemes like Polyak's heavy ball already speed large-model training, yet mini-batch behavior was poorly understood. Their analysis covers heavy-ball and Nesterov-style momentum at any batch size under minimal noise assumptions. Acceleration grows directly with gradient mini-batch size up to a natural saturation point, enabling perfect parallelization. The theory also yields a simple momentum choice that works well in practice.
arxiv-2605-18709: Yongliang Sun and five co-authors propose, in a 2026 paper, a deep image prior method for dynamic MRI reconstruction. Learning methods need large sampled datasets and work poorly. Training-free prior methods adapt per scan but miss temporal structure and overfit. Their framework models space-time links through a low-rank plus sparse split, using two fresh networks jointly optimized by accelerated ADMM. The mix joins deep image prior rules with classical interpretability and convergence analysis. Across speedup factors, it beats classical, supervised, and unsupervised rebuilds.
arxiv-2605-18809: Zuyuan Zhang, Sizhe Tang, Mahdi Imani and Tian Lan steady multi-agent learning by splitting each joint update into group improvement and cyclic churn. Their Hodge-projected method, HPML, projects the stacked update field onto its closest metric-gradient component and follows only that direction. The projected dynamics admit a Lyapunov potential that falls steadily, with bounds on the remaining equilibrium gap. Controlled tests confirm the geometry, and centralized-training benchmarks show better stability and returns when HPML plugs into existing pipelines.
arxiv-2605-18909: Ahmed Gamal Eldin draws a line between two kinds of uncertainty in systems that compress the world into finite representations. Descriptive uncertainty merely colors outputs, while regulatory uncertainty feeds back into optimization and reshapes behavior. He proves current transformers are stuck with the descriptive kind at inference: without real energy cost, errors and correct derivations dissipate alike. Tests on three locally run language models find token entropy flat across tasks even as accuracy swings from zero to perfect, at every model size.
arxiv-2605-19009: Saurav Ghosh, Abdou Sow and Luke Zhang stress-test SPARK humanoid safety filters beyond scores. Safety filters adjust actions that might violate collision-avoidance constraints, but standard scores hide harder-setting behavior. The authors replicate a SPARK case in MuJoCo and evaluate six filter methods under controlled seeds, converting logs into goal, distance and collision metrics. Goal tracking is tighter for some methods, while others cut collision steps more effectively. Safety behavior shifts under crowded obstacles, noisy distance estimates and late obstacle updates, arguing for evaluation exposing failures before deployment.
arxiv-2605-19209: Manohari Goarin and two colleagues combine a graph focus planner with a local nonlinear forward unit for multi-robot open motion planning. The planner supplies middle subgoals through multi-robot teamwork, while the unit keeps safety under bent motion and drive limits. Recent graph neural methods offer scalable local answers but rely on simple motion and sim runs, missing what is doable and message limits. Tests in sim and drone trials show better reach to larger teams, toughness to delays up to 200 ms, and workable local on-board runs.
arxiv-2605-19409: Lin and Kang make continual model merging steadier by treating each merge as a path, not a jump. Fixed merge rules give little control over how much old knowledge survives, so long task streams degrade. Their ODE-M method builds a barrier-aware path through parameter space, with light feedback from a small set curbing loss-raising moves. Picking a point along the path balances old knowledge against new skill, and tests beat strong baselines across backbones and stream lengths.
arxiv-2605-19909: Mbrice and Liu test fairness plans for Aurora, a deep reinforcement learning congestion controller. Systems trained on single flows may not share bandwidth fairly when several flows compete. Three plans keeping Aurora design are tested in a choke point sim on Jain's fairness index: reward shaping, observation augmentation and loss sensitivity tuning. Modest reward shaping gives the best fairness while keeping total throughput, won by sharing out, not cuts. Loss tuning proves most TCP friendly against CUBIC, while the watching plan stays most stable as flows enter and leave.
arxiv-2605-20009: Vy Bui and four colleagues replace trial-and-error learning-rate choice with a theoretically derived rate from two opposing Bayesian processes. Their double-Bayesian framework treats the learning rate in stochastic gradient descent as a decision problem, yielding an optimal value from the interaction of the two processes. Experiments across classification, segmentation and detection tasks support the practical value of the derived rate for training neural networks.
arxiv-2605-20109: Duy Ho studies Hermitian hull-variation for vector rank-metric codes. Apart from one parameter pair, a code's Hermitian hull dimension can drop to any smaller value in its class, and every such code matches a Hermitian LCD code in equivalence. He addresses maximum rank distance codes with a chosen Hermitian hull dimension. A trace-self-dual basis of a field extension, existing always, lets him construct Hermitian self-orthogonal Gabidulin codes for every prime power. With that theorem, this yields maximum rank distance codes attaining every Hermitian hull dimension.
arxiv-2605-20309: Runyuan Cai and three co-workers set out Tiny-Engram, a trigger-indexed table for frozen image and video makers. Adapters or weight tweaks teach new ideas, with scant say over when they return. Stored slots, keyed to n-gram phrases, steer text encoder states just where the phrase sits. Elsewhere the base model runs unchanged. A rare cue phrase can call up a target face while the rest of the prompt shapes the scene. In video it also works, though a face may drift on new prompts.
arxiv-2605-20409: Douthitt, Israel and Kennard define the three-cosystole, a matroid invariant tied to higher cogirth for weighted matroids. They prove an optimal upper bound for it among regular matroids of rank at most six. The proof shows the invariant grows under matroid extensions, then bounds it for each maximal simple regular matroid of rank at most six. The argument thus reduces the general bound to checking the maximal cases.
arxiv-2605-20809: Kon Woo Kim, Jin-Dong Kim, and Akiko Aizawa propose reusing and refining annotation guidelines as an alignment tool for language-model tagging. Models do well at zero-shot annotation yet struggle with the special rules of gold-standard benchmarks. Their iterative moderation design mimics the early phases of annotation projects and tests three claims: rule integration helps, reasoning-tuned models help, and moderation works with little supervision. Tests across biomedical entity tasks with three model families confirm all three claims.
arxiv-2605-21109: Zhenjiang Mao and colleagues tune confidence scores for camera-based safety calls in self-driving race cars. Such predictors grow too sure of themselves when light or control shifts. Their tool needs no retraining: it mixes a sight score from image errors with a motion score from doubt and control data. On a small real car in dark, blurred, biased, and delayed runs, error fell by about thirty-seven percent from the best rival.
arxiv-2605-21209: Anna Aksamit, Małgorzata M. O'Reilly, and Zbigniew Palmowski give the first response study of stochastic fluid models. They derive rules for how key steady and time-based values respond to setting changes. Worked cases show the method at work in queues, including wearing systems and risk processes in insurance. The work sets a base for response studies of wider models that generalize these fluid models.
arxiv-2605-21309: Abhishek Dinkar Jagtap and co-authors present Hyper-V2X, a hypernetwork method for doubt in cooperative vehicle perception. Shared sensory data build one environmental view, but doubt in multi-agent fusion is largely unexplored. Their scheme conditions a Bayesian hypernetwork on fused multi-agent features to generate weight spreads for bird's-eye-view segmentation. Both epistemic and aleatoric doubt are estimated with little added cost. The method fits modern cooperative backbones such as CoBEVT.
arxiv-2605-21409: Yoontae Hwang models portfolio preference elicitation in institutional crossing markets. Traders value trades as bundles, but liquidity search is organized around single stocks. The platform first uses price-led demand queries to search the bundle space. It then checks chosen bundles through value queries. Final deals are chosen from gathered reports, so the learning model steers queries without setting welfare, and demand queries give only cautious welfare evidence unless bundles are checked.
arxiv-2605-21709: Josien, El Hachimi, and Ramiere design a solver for linear elliptic equations with patchy coefficients that handles fine meshes. It works in two and three dimensions, using quantized tensor trains whose exponential compression tames the data volume. The solver recovers solutions and their gradients accurately, at up to twenty orders more degrees of freedom than classical solvers. A penalized gradient equation, solved in Fourier space, plus an error estimator, keeps it stable at any mesh. A microstructured-material test reaches ten to the thirty-seventh virtual degrees of freedom.
arxiv-2605-21809: David Osten presents a Cartan-geometric framework for generalised geometries ruled by a differential graded Lie algebra. Unlike the usual Cartan case, the tangent bundle is extended, with both a global duality group and a local gauge group. The method constructs generalised connections with their torsion and curvature tensors for these geometries. It also reviews how these structures appear on the phase space of branes in M-theory.
arxiv-2605-22309: Toda and Gómez-Valent test modified gravity against a dynamical dark energy background on linear scales. Data from the microwave background, baryon acoustic oscillations and supernovae hint the accelerating component may change over time. They let the effective gravitational coupling depart from Newton's constant below a scale, in two redshift bins. To suppress structure growth at low redshift while fitting microwave background data, the scale must sit below about 150 megaparsecs. The best fit lands near 40 megaparsecs, inside the range probed by galaxy surveys.
arxiv-2605-22409: Khakimov, Prokhorov and Teryaev test entanglement viscosity for higher-spin fields. The Minkowski vacuum looks thermal to a fast-moving viewer through the Unruh effect. For lower spins, the medium's sticky flow hits the KSS bound. Spin-3/2 viscosity in RSA theory comes out negative. Entropy density from modular Hamiltonian expansion is also negative, so the ratio still hits the bound. A Zubarev density operator approach instead gives positive entropy. The theory also shows many features of a conformal field theory.
arxiv-2605-22509: Tarvirdians and team study an agent that helps with high-stakes personal choices by fitting the user's thinking style. Most support tools target thinking alone, not feelings and gut sense as well. The agent nudges users to blend thought types. In a study with 128 people, it led to broad, rich thinking, more personal thinking paths, and more joined-up thinking language. Users felt it gave stronger help for joined-up reflection. The plain tool, by contrast, gave samey sets full of thinking-only language.
arxiv-2605-22609: Ianconescu and Vulfin derive exact forms for voltage induced into a twin shielded line by a one-color flat wave from any way, at set polarization. The line's cut of wires and shield stuff may be any shape, if its size is much smaller than wave length, so field waves meet the quasi TEM rule. Voltage down the line is worked out by math for end loads and set against HFSS model runs. The math uses wave flow from such a line, from past work, and give-and-take.
arxiv-2605-22709: Yocam and Vaidyan design TriSweep, a framework for a four drone swarm that hunts electromagnetic side channel leaks from embedded microcontrollers at standoff range. Three collector drones specialize in full spectrum capture, mask register loading and masked cipher output, feeding a stationary accumulator drone combining signals for about 5 decibel gain. On real masked AES data sets, the swarm reaches key rank 18 at close range, and alignment tricks cut single drone rank from 89 to 21 under timing jitter. No hardware exists yet; a prototype is planned next.
arxiv-2605-22909: Bentsen and four coauthors offer a sample-efficient benchmark for shallow all-to-all random quantum circuits, where sampling looks classically hard but no existing test separates noisy quantum hardware from classical spoofers. They show nonlinear cross-entropy cleanly separates noisy quantum machines from state-of-the-art spoofers, even under depolarizing noise. A heavy-output classifier built on the same idea needs only logarithmically many samples at short depth. Exact analytics and simulations support both claims.
arxiv-2605-23009: Beretta and Kogelbauer give a full Sturm-Liouville spectral study of the Constant Elasticity of Variance operator used in finance. By turning its Fokker-Planck form into a generalized Laguerre operator, they pin down its extensions, edge rules, spectra, and eigenfunctions across all elasticity regimes. They then link these spectral traits to arbitrage. Edge patterns and positive harmonic functions separate attainable-boundary cases from bubble regimes.
arxiv-2605-23109: Agarwal and twelve coauthors present Inductive Deductive Synthesis, an approach to generating verified systems with AI. Formal verification guarantees properties like read write consistency under every interleaving. Yet it demands months to years of expert effort. State of the art coding agents solve only 2 of 7 key-value store specifications. Their agentic system synthesizes implementation and proof, learning from failures. It achieves 7 of 7 in 6.8 hours and 106 dollars each. That is 200 times faster than effort and 17 percent cheaper than agents. Its implementations run up to 3 times faster than verified systems.
arxiv-2605-23209: Crawford and six coauthors present the population study of variability in extreme helium stars, hydrogen-deficient stars from white dwarf mergers. Using TESS curves for all known such stars, they update curves for two pulsators, V652 Her plus BX Cir, and discuss possible pulsators. Most show low-frequency variability, power rising toward low frequencies, rather than oscillation peaks. Gaussian regression with a damped kernel measures timescale, amplitude, and quality per star. They run 0.5 to 10 days, tracking density. Convection zones may drive it, but theory is needed.
arxiv-2605-23309: Kumagai and seven coauthors present U-FlowPET, a self-taught physics-informed setup joining light-stress scans with the ruling laws of fluid flows. It rebuilds the full 3D stress tensor without fixed guesses or tagged training data. Rather than learning from labeled known stress fields, the method finds nature-valid stress fields meeting motion balance and flow while staying matching with seen optical views. In round-pipe flow with an exact answer, all six stress parts are rebuilt with scaled mean absolute errors below 4 percent.
arxiv-2605-23509: Kumar, Lahiri, and Seshadhri shrink the random seed for partition oracles on bounded-degree minor-free graphs like planar graphs. These oracles reveal the component of any vertex with query counts independent of graph size, coordinated through a shared seed. Yet every prior oracle used a seed of linear size, implying linear setup time. Polynomial-query oracles run with a seed of polynomial length times log n. They also prove that for cycles, with labels from a larger universe, any partition oracle needs more than a constant number of bits.
arxiv-2605-23909: Michael and three colleagues test how well large language models judge their own certainty across varied tasks. In a preregistered study, the models, like people, proved overconfident on average, with confidence running ahead of accuracy. The gap grew on hard tests yet flipped on easy ones, where models showed marked underconfidence. To measure this pattern across difficulty levels, the team built LifeEval, a new test of model calibration.
arxiv-2605-24109: Demeter and Fu sharpen the decoupling exponent for functions whose spectra sit in AD-regular arc collections on the parabola. They fold recent Szemeredi-Trotter-type estimates into the bootstrapping argument of an earlier work, tightening how wave packets on such arcs can be split and recombined. As a payoff, their bounds complement and in places beat earlier results for arithmetic Cantor sets, showing the new estimates bite on concrete fractal spectra.
arxiv-2605-24709: Noah Farr and others close a streaming reinforcement learning gap: agents learn one sample at a time with no replay buffer. Partial observability stayed out of reach even as full observability scaled to deep networks. Truncated backpropagation collapses to a one-step horizon, while exact recurrent learning costs too much. Their recurrent trace units form a design enabling exact real-time learning with linear time and memory. On a MemoryChain diagnostic with chains from 2 to 128, it holds up where baselines collapse. On POPGym and masked MuJoCo it rivals batched methods.
arxiv-2605-24809: Minseok Choi and co-authors compute native defects and erbium impurities in calcium tungstate with hybrid density functional theory. Oxygen and calcium vacancies form most readily without doping, though interstitials can also enter, while tungsten-related defects look unlikely. Modeled optical levels trace observed absorption and emission peaks mainly to oxygen-related defects. Migration barriers show calcium interstitials, oxygen vacancies, and oxygen interstitials move readily even when cold. Erbium takes the calcium site easily, but complexes with vacancies would switch it off.
arxiv-2605-25009: Huangsen Cao and colleagues reframe fake image detection as structured forensic reasoning, not bare yes or no calls. Their framework pulls out perceptual clues, picks the best forensic skill, and uses that skill to gather evidence and decide. To support the approach they build ClueAegis-Bench, which splits detection into annotated forensic skills. The full ClueAegis system chains skill choice with evidence guided reasoning through skill based toolchains. Tests report top performance, stronger cross domain generalization, and clear reasoning traces with structured evidence.
arxiv-2605-25809: Haas, Giles and Nakatsukasa present a layered sketch-and-solve method for overdetermined least squares. Sketch-and-solve shrinks least squares problems by random sketching, and averaging sketch solutions improves accuracy. Their layered version combines small-sketch samples with correction terms from larger sketches. Correction-term variance falls faster than the simple estimator's on each level. Yet the layered framework costs slightly more than the simple average estimator, so naive layered use looks unattractive.
arxiv-2605-25909: Gridusov, Popov and Kolyubin present R5DGS, a unified 4D Gaussian splatting method joining physical grounding with meaning awareness. Early warping models fill training frames but fail at future prediction, while meaning methods lack physics fit. Their rigid-body constraint predicts motion for a single anchor Gaussian per labeled object, moving the rest by relative transforms. This speeds novel views past a plain baseline, while giving object-accurate prediction and intuitive meaning interaction.
arxiv-2605-26109: Yenphraphai and eight colleagues present Helix4D, turning video into moving four-dimensional meshes. Current video-to-4D methods falter on shape changes, see-through materials, thin parts and inner surfaces. Helix4D builds on Trellis2, moving it from still-image 3D to video-driven 4D. Cross-frame attention in sliding windows shares data across frames while keeping prior skill on rare cases, anchored on the first frame. Time data enter a three-dimensional position code without breaking prior skills, and tests on complex motion beat baselines.
arxiv-2605-26209: In 2026, Hao Fu and eleven colleagues model how early galaxies built up their stars between redshifts five and twelve. They feed observed ultraviolet brightness counts into a data-driven scheme that skips uncertain cooling and feedback physics. The model matches the stellar mass census, galaxy clustering, and the star-forming main sequence. It predicts bursty growth with efficiency peaking near nine-tenths above redshift nine, while dust lifts rates lower down and a top-heavy stellar mix cuts them two- to threefold.
arxiv-2605-26709: In his 2026 paper, Faulhuber proves a barrier for the Wirtinger criterion, a tool proposed for studying which lattices support Gabor frames, systems of time-frequency shifts used in signal analysis. The criterion cannot settle the frame set conjecture for the first Hermite function, and more generally it cannot identify frame-set regions of density below two for any odd function. The result closes off one route to resolving the conjecture for odd functions.
arxiv-2605-26809: Kurz and Tzimoulis define canonical extensions for categories enriched over a quantale. They build on two well-known prior theories, one for canonical extensions and one for enriched categories. From those sources they set out the new idea and prove its basic traits, moving a classical tool into a new setting. The result gives enriched categories a toolkit of their own for this kind of extension.
arxiv-2605-26909: Kanzow and Lehmann study optimization of nonsmooth upper-C2 functions over submanifolds, where the classic descent rule needs a new form. With projectional subdifferentials, they show the descent rule carries over from flat spaces to curved ones. They propose a nonmonotone subgradient method and prove accumulation points settle, with rates under Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz. Tests cover difference-of-convex functions and clustering on manifolds.
arxiv-2605-27009: Zhang and eight co-authors present SCENT, a system that predicts human smell perception from mass spectra instead of chemical structures. Structure-based methods need the real structures at test time, which practical sensors lack. SCENT aligns mass-spectrum vectors with ready-made chemical embeddings through contrastive learning, needing only spectra at inference. It beats mass-spectra-only baselines, matches structure-based models, and works on real lab spectra too.
arxiv-2605-27209: Chen and co-authors train agents under noise so they hold up in messy real settings. Their NoisyAgent frame adds two kinds of trouble: vague or shifting user input, and tool calls that fail or act oddly. Noise hits only some training runs at first, then grows harder as the model adapts. Tests show steadier behavior under noisy and shifting conditions, and the noise-trained models also gain on clean benchmarks. The authors read this as evidence that controlled exposure to flaws builds more general reasoning.
arxiv-2605-27409: Shuhan Ye and colleagues improve data-free distillation from artificial networks to spiking networks. Their STARS method adds two objectives to standard synthesis: one preserving relational consistency between teacher and student, and one regularizing threshold-relevant tail probabilities. The synthetic batches stay teacher-valid yet teach spiking students better, with gains on CIFAR benchmarks. The work targets settings where training data cannot be shared.
arxiv-2605-27509: Elizabeth Moreno-Hilario, Hui Li, and Luis Martinez-Medina reconstruct the globular cluster initial mass function from present-day systems. The present-day turnover near 200,000 solar masses motivates the work. Working mass loss back from dynamical evolution with a model that varies by setting, they map observed masses to birth values without assuming a set form. The recovered functions shift to higher masses with power-law high ends, and their slopes rise with host halo mass.
arxiv-2605-27609: Zeyu Zhou, Maxim Sukharev, Abraham Nitzan, and Joseph Eli Subotnik study Raman scattering near metal interfaces in the strong-coupling regime. Between mirrors, the cavity traps the field and boosts excited-state population, while the metal surface adds damping and line broadening passed to cavity polaritons. Clashes between incoming and reflected light further shape the spectrum, with Rabi contraction effects matching Raman itself in size.
arxiv-2605-27809: Qiyuan Wang, Yao Li, and Raymond K. W. Wong study backdoor attacks, hidden triggers that make a trained model misbehave on chosen inputs. They show triggers work best, and survive cleanup, when poisoned examples sit in sparse, low-density corners of the clean data's distribution. Their construction method kept attack success above ninety-nine percent before defenses and resisted fine-tuning and pruning far better than rivals.
arxiv-2605-28009: Ha and colleagues stop long-term AI memory from mixing facts, events, and rules into one soup. MemGuard labels each stored item with a clear functional role at save time and draws proof only from job types the task needs. On tests of made-up facts and long chats it raised trust scores by up to twenty-eight percent while pulling far fewer stored tokens.
arxiv-2605-28309: Gjorgjieva and colleagues learn to tell good run-count guesses from bad ones for random optimizers. They train sorters on traits from a hundred thirty-two thousand test runs to flag shaky guesses, with strong catches of wrong guesses inside fixed optimizer setups. Narrow trait variety inside each setup still caps how far the sorters reach.
arxiv-2605-28409: Mingze Wu and three colleagues test offline reinforcement learning, which trains on existing code datasets instead of live model rollouts, as a cheaper post-training route for code-generating language models. Their experiments show it improves performance, with the largest gains for smaller models and harder coding problems. The work argues that reusing logged code data can replace much of the costly inference and verification demanded by online reinforcement learning.
arxiv-2605-28709: Domonkos Czifra and four colleagues improve the bound for the double cap conjecture on the unit sphere. Witsenhausen asked in 1974 for the densest measurable set on the sphere with no pair of orthogonal vectors, and the double cap of two opposite caps is thought optimal. Combining harmonic-analytic arguments with the geometric fractional chromatic number of finite graphs, the authors reach about 0.295 for three dimensions, beating the prior bound. A 33-element set found by large-scale computer search yields the bound, and the method may improve bounds in higher dimensions.
arxiv-2605-28909: Clement Etienam and colleagues build sequential surrogate models for three-phase black-oil flow in the Norne reservoir, using Fourier neural operators and their physics-informed variant. Their theory covers well-posedness, covariate shift growth, spectral stability under physics constraints, and bias decay in truncated gradient training. Tests over the full 3298-day history fit oil, gas, and pressure strongly, with water improving over time. A thousand-member ensemble runs in under a minute, far faster than a standard simulator.
arxiv-2605-29009: Matt Gorbett and Hossein Shirazi propose Cross-Model Entropy, a label-free reward for post-training language models with reinforcement learning. It scores a response by mean log-likelihood under a separate verifier model, so unsurprising responses count as likely correct. Because verifier and generator are independent, the signal cannot be gamed through self-consistency. Built into GRPO unchanged, it extends label-free learning to open-ended instruction following. On UltraFeedback prompts judged on AlpacaEval 2.0, it beats the untrained base across four model families and three regimes.
arxiv-2605-29209: Xiangyu Zhang and colleagues expose the WER trap: low word error rate tokens need not preserve what synthesis needs. High-frequency tokens succeed via leakage, while pure semantic tokens at low frame rates strip articulation and micro moves. Fixed downsampling cannot reach compression without wrecking word error rate. The authors build a dynamic tokenizer aligning them with meaning edges, reaching ultra-low frame rates at low word error rate. Using those pure tokens, with durations, yields blurred articulation and unintelligible speech, arguing for decoupled representations.
arxiv-2605-29509: Mingshu Cai and five colleagues propose KGEdit, a control method sharpening training-free video generation and editing from written prompts. Vague wording, wrongly bound concepts, and flickering consistency across frames still trip existing methods. KGEdit first turns a prompt into an ambiguity-aware knowledge graph separating identity, relations, attributes, and negative constraints. An injection step feeds those signals into key layers of the video diffusion model, while a timing step schedules them across generation steps. Tests report better editing precision and steadier frame-to-frame behavior than existing methods.
arxiv-2605-29609: Maksim Lednev and three colleagues show that recoil heating in floating optomechanics is not fixed at its free-space value. Photon scattering heats matter and limits quantum moving states. Cavity rigs in the coherent scattering setup lacked a heating theory, since small-change methods fail near optical peaks. The authors prove the field setting shifts the heating rate through the Purcell effect, cutting it a lot in chambers for motions. Their system joins large-scale quantum field theory with few-mode quantum methods for matter near any field shapes.
arxiv-2605-29809: Leyi Qi and four colleagues certify ownership checks for text-to-image diffusion models. Backdoor mark methods assume a faithful checker that can query a suspect model and receive a clean watermark, yet adversaries can damage watermark signals. Their method, Cert-LAS, embeds watermarks with image classifiers and layer-tuned noise, then checks ownership by testing whether the suspect model answers watermarks far more strongly than unwatermarked references. Under stated conditions it stays reliable even against removal attacks. Experiments confirm Cert-LAS works and its resistance to new attacks.
arxiv-2605-29909: F. Acero and the Fermi-LAT team hunt gamma rays from superluminous supernovae, rare blasts far brighter than plain core-collapse events. Sixteen years of Fermi-LAT data yield just one firm signal, SN 2017egm, fifty to one hundred sixty days post-blast. Its curve and spectrum fit a fast-spinning magnetar engine, while shell impact fits brightness but not timing. A gamma-to-optical ratio near one breaks shell-impact models. Mock runs show a like event would stay visible to CTAO to 140 Mpc in the magnetar view.
arxiv-2605-30309: Valery V. Ryzhikov shows how deviations of ergodic averages can be structured: they tend to zero almost everywhere, and are asymptotically almost invariant under the action due to averaging. Hence the distribution of deviation values becomes a meaningful question. For any free ergodic action of integer lattices, these distributions can sit weakly close to any given distribution if the scale is changed. The article gives short proofs of the ergodic theorems of von Neumann, Birkhoff and Wiener, and Rokhlin's lemma, for integer-lattice actions with an invariant measure.
arxiv-2605-30509: Cohen, Kontorovich, and Livshitz tighten the mathematics of estimating a discrete probability distribution when error is judged by the worst single probability. They give improved minimax bounds in expectation and high-probability tail bounds, answering open questions from an earlier paper by Kontorovich and Painsky. Among the advances are a fully empirical version of the tightest earlier risk bound and a description of the worst-case distribution that attains it. Tests back the new bounds.
arxiv-2605-30709: In a 2026 measurement, the MicroBooNE collaboration characterizes energy resolution in the MicroBooNE liquid argon time projection chamber at the MeV scale. Using monoenergetic signals from gamma rays of thallium-208 decays undergoing pair production, they measure resolution near one and a half MeV. The resolution found is about seven and a half percent, consistent with the simulation prediction near ten percent at under two sigma. The study is the first of its kind at the MeV scale and opens a path for monoenergetic calibrations in future argon detectors.
arxiv-2605-30809: In a 2026 study, Kalamadi and colleagues diagnose internet inequality with 170 million Ookla tests and Census demographics across six regions. After fixing sampling bias, Random Forest regression finds speed and latency drivers. Population density dominates, but this is a scale artifact. Once areas are stratified into density bins, its influence fades in denser neighborhoods. After controlling for density, income and racial composition emerge as drivers, with income shaping upload speed and racial composition shaping download speed most. Inequality is locally set, and policy demands region-specific action.
arxiv-2605-31109: Anton and colleagues extend the scattering-kernel formalism for gas hitting rough surfaces. Standard kernels lump all gas-surface effects into one operator, hiding the scales at which they act. The new roughness-based version lifts a local kernel to larger scales. It uses single- and multi-reflection operators tied to surface shape statistics. The authors derive conditions under which the lifted kernels keep reciprocity, normalisation and non-negativity. They also establish composition laws for combining roughness contributions recursively.
arxiv-2605-31309: Chen and Maguluri survey Lyapunov-based tools for finite time analysis of random iterative algorithms, also called stochastic approximation. These solve fixed-point equations with an operator known only through a noisy oracle. First, a shrinking operator and independent same-way noise, where broad Moreau covers serve as all-norm tools. The framework then yields settling bounds for random gradient descent, linear random approximation, and reinforcement learning like Q-learning. Extras cover linked noise, semi-norm shrinkage and leaky operators, and high-probability bounds.
arxiv-2605-31409: Sagaseta and colleagues map the dials for best single-ion spin kicks in fast trapped-ion gates. Fast Raman pulses allow entangling gates quicker than the trap period. Good fast gates need good spin kicks. The team charts Raman frequency gap, pulse timing, Lamb-Dicke value and heat. Pulse length, not trap motion, drives most error: for nanosecond kicks it beats trap-motion error by far. Errors below one-thousandth are within reach with at least 10 evenly spaced picosecond pulses. These yield rules for sub-microsecond work.
arxiv-2606-00009:
Candelieri and Bliek speed up offshore wind farm design by teaching an optimizer to ignore turbine ordering, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Bayesian optimization is a method for expensive black-box problems, where each evaluation is costly and the objective has no formula. Placing identical turbines is one, but ordinary algorithms waste effort: swapping two identical turbines changes nothing in energy output. Their method, PIBO, builds that permutation invariance into the optimizer using optimal transport theory, which measures distances between point arrangements.

The authors prove the approach finds better wind farm layouts than vanilla Bayesian optimization on their test case. It also cut run time in half, a substantial saving when each layout test requires simulation. The paper frames this as search over layouts, where only the set of positions matters. Sensor placement and facility location share the symmetry, so the technique should transfer beyond wind energy, the authors argue.
arxiv-2606-00209:
Matsumoto and Piran weigh why a torn star near a black hole glowed so faintly. The event, TDE2025aarm, sits close by in cosmic terms. Its early radio and X-ray light fell far below past such events. The pair test if plain wind and disk tales can fit.

Radio light near day 40 proves too weak for a round disk wind. It fits a thin jet of loose star scraps far better. X-ray light is also oddly faint for months. A veiled disk would need a clear patch far too small to stay steady. The same shock that makes the radio glow can make the X-rays too. That route fits by shine or by bounce of light off fast bits. More views will split the two tales.
arxiv-2606-00409:
Cui and co-authors mine a vast stock of solids for odd magnets with split spin bands. Such magnets hold no net pull, yet their bands split by spin. That mix suits spin-based gear in a fresh way. Finds so far came case by case from a scant pool of known forms.

The team screen more than 37,000 magnets from the Materials Project. Physics-led cuts, swap math, and a shape test thin the pool. Some 189 flat-line anti-magnets stay at the end of the sift. Shape reads name 36 as altermagnets and 11 as a paid-back kin type. Most of those are fresh finds, not past lore. Tests say the set can host spin Hall marks and tune-by-dope spin flows.
arxiv-2606-00909:
Mussabayev and Mussabayev build a microscope for multimodal models in this 2026 paper. Their system, MLLM-Microscope, inspects the hidden states inside multimodal large language models. It measures three traits of token embeddings across layers: linearity, intrinsic dimension, and anisotropy. Two top models, LLaVA-NeXT and OmniFusion, face the probe on the ScienceQA dataset.

Both streams, main and residual, act in highly linear ways across layers, they find. That holds for tokens of both senses. One split shows: image tokens in LLaVA-NeXT lose a bit of linearity with depth, while OmniFusion's stay steady. OmniFusion's image tokens also keep higher dimension across layers. Its anisotropy stays low throughout. The lesson is that how senses fuse before the language core shapes all later behavior. The tool gives designers a way to see those inner patterns and tune fusion with proof, not taste.
arxiv-2606-01009:
Camargo rebuilds the ear of neural audio models as one matrix product in this 2026 paper. Audio models run on chips whose peak speed comes from dense matrix math. The classic front end is a poor fit: a Fourier stage plus a sparse Mel pooling stage, in many steps. Vendor specific FFT code carries the load.

His front end, MelT, precomputes Mel spaced non uniform Fourier bases once. Each audio frame then maps to Mel features in a single general matrix multiply. The design frees the step from vendor FFT quirks. In the compact sizes neural front ends use, it still wins. Latency and active energy both fall by up to about three times, from an Apple phone chip to a top NVIDIA card. All gains are within platform tests. Word error rates on frozen Whisper models stay level with the native front end.
arxiv-2606-01109:
Foppiano and Boulanger dig citations out of footnotes in this 2026 paper. Citation tools are built for the tidy reference lists of the sciences. Law and humanities writing cites in footnotes instead. There, reference data mixes with commentary and cross references, in many languages and styles. Gold standard data for that world was scarce.

Their dataset, FOSSIL, holds 96 annotated scholarly articles with over 7,600 footnote references. It is openly licensed and multilingual. A web annotation tool and a seven annotator workflow come with it. So does a Grobid variant tuned for footnote citations. In end to end tests, micro F1 rises from 0.36 up to 0.72 with the specialized pipeline in use. Recall drives most of the gain. Cross references and mixed content notes still leave much headroom. The authors flag the work as in progress, with parsing and cross reference resolution still open.
arxiv-2606-01209:
Atar studies large Jackson networks when traffic is heavy. A Jackson network is a set of queues with routing. Here each of n stations has one server. When a job ends at one station, it may move on. It goes to a new station with a small chance, or it leaves. Atar looks at the joint limit as n grows and load nears full.

He proves a form of chaos propagation for queue lengths. Idle time counts also fit the same limit. The limit is a nonlinear reflected Brownian motion. Its form has a drift term and a reflection term at zero. The proof couples the network to a Brownian particle system.
arxiv-2606-01309:
Ma and co-authors frame a multiagent matroid upgrading problem. The setup models shared resource allocation tasks. Many agents each hold a set of assigned elements. Each element has a default cost and a lower upgraded cost. Upgrading an element drops its cost to the lower value. Each agent also has its own matroid constraint. Each seeks a minimum-cost basis under that constraint.

At most k elements can be upgraded in total. The aim is to pick which ones to upgrade. The objective is a convex function of the agents' basis costs. It is non-decreasing in each agent's cost. This form captures both efficiency and fairness goals. The title reports that a greedy approach proves fair and efficient here.
arxiv-2606-01409: Flores-Alfonso, Lopez-Monsalvo, and Rubio-Ponce cast the Gödel universe as a superconductor. The Gödel universe is an exact solution of Einstein's field equations. Materials can mimic effective gravitational fields. Spacetime metrics can also model physical media in return. Optical, acoustic, and viscous media already have such analogs. None had captured the hallmark traits of superconductors. Their work shows the Gödel universe fills that gap. It serves as the gravitational analog of a superconducting medium. The medium sits in its Meissner state in this mapping.
arxiv-2606-01509:
Zhao and co-authors make mixture-of-experts routing differentiable via probability. MoE models activate only a few experts per token. Top-k routing is discrete and blocks gradients, though. Gradient estimators for expert choice remain an open problem. ProbMoE models selection as a distribution over subsets. The subsets are constrained in cardinality by design. Routing becomes probabilistic inference in that discrete space. Exact-k routing samples k-expert subsets in the forward pass.

Backward gradients flow through each expert's exact marginal probability. That gives a tractable surrogate for the true gradient. A dynamic-k variant adapts expert counts per token. Training and inference share the same cardinality range there. Tests show strong performance against competitive baselines. Expert utilization and routing diversity both improve.
arxiv-2606-01609:
Adams, Ionov, Mason-Brown, and Vogan prove Arthur's unitarity conjecture in general. Arthur packets are sets of representations of a real reductive group. Arthur conjectured their existence in the 1980s. Adams, Barbasch, and Vogan later defined them via microlocal geometry. A longstanding conjecture says all members are unitary. Their main new idea is a Jordan decomposition for Arthur packets. A canonical two-step process realizes any packet. It uses real parabolic and cohomological induction from a unipotent packet.

The Levi subgroup for that packet is chosen by the process. Unitarity then reduces to the unipotent case. That case was already known from prior work by many authors. The same methods prove Jiang's conjecture for real reductive groups. Wavefront sets get an upper bound from that result.
arxiv-2606-01809:
Das and co-authors give a fast method for path lengths in flat graphs. The graphs are planar and directed, with weighted edges. Edge weights change over time in this task. Queries ask the gap between any two points. Known methods need more time per update or query.

The new method works when all updates are known upfront. It runs in near square-root time per step. That matches known lower bounds up to log terms. The key step speeds up dense distance graphs. An online variant also handles added edges fast. The work narrows a long-standing gap in this field.
arxiv-2606-02009:
Wilkens and co-authors assess automated essay scoring for French language certification. Scoring benchmarks have fostered narrow evaluation habits. Broader frameworks urge multidimensional checks of such systems. High-stakes language tests need that wider view most. The team enhance an argument-based validation framework for use.

Fairness analysis joins the practical version of the framework. Correlations with linguistic features are included too. Prediction error and model agreement are also measured. Eight model architectures are compared on French essays. The main corpus holds 27,000 exam essays. Each essay carries scores from two raters. A generalization corpus adds 961 essays with more raters. The study shows what broad validation reveals about systems.
arxiv-2606-02209:
Moirangthem Singh studies how to help two sides reach a deal when they bargain. Old tools search a fixed set of deals that are split into discrete steps. That search can fail when no deal in the set is fair to both sides at once. Such tools also miss the hints about what each side wants that are buried in the talks. The new framework, called Conditional Graph Diffusion, works in a smooth space of deals instead.

A graph based encoder learns how the wants of the two sides compare, with attention that shifts as the talks go on. Those learned features are fused with features from the text of the talks, taken from a transformer model. The fused context then guides a diffusion model that builds deal proposals step by step. A guidance term, worked out in closed form, nudges each step toward terms both sides can accept.
arxiv-2606-02309:
Jin and co-authors study when generative priors can be trusted in inverse problems. Generative models serve as priors for such problems widely. Their realistic outputs create a basic trust problem. A plausible reconstruction may come from the measurements. Or the prior may have filled in unobserved directions. That distinction matters most in medical imaging.

Acquisition operators there face scan time, dose, and calibration limits. The central question is one of measurement geometry. Can a fixed operator distinguish nearby plausible images? A local compatibility measure is introduced for that question. It quantifies how well the operator observes prior relevant directions. The measure can guide better measurement design. Trustworthy reconstruction is the end goal of the work.
arxiv-2606-02409:
Alvarez-Gavela writes a short note in symplectic geometry, on Lagrangian homotopy spheres. A homotopy sphere looks like a sphere to algebraic tests. Its smooth structure may still differ from the round sphere. The note asks how far that difference can go. The spheres sit as Lagrangian submanifolds in cotangent bundles.

The argument joins two known results. One is a derivative map result by Bökstedt and Waldhausen. The other gives generating functions for nearby Lagrangian spheres. Together they bound the smooth difference of the two spheres. The difference must be a multiple of the Hopf element. It is therefore 2-torsion in the quotient group. One sharp case follows. A homotopy 8-sphere embedded in the cotangent bundle of the round 8-sphere must be diffeomorphic to it. The note gives a concise path through a special case of joint work.
arxiv-2606-02509:
Karacan and co-authors mine Turkish teacher narratives for ADHD signals that rating scales miss. Diagnosis blends clinician judgment with standard scales. Parents and teachers both report. The Conners' Teacher Rating Scale gives structured scores. Teachers also write open-ended narratives. Those texts may hold signals the scores drop.

The team studies de-identified Turkish forms from clinical ADHD reviews. Each form holds scale scores plus narrative text. Models built on each source are compared head to head. Some cases split the sources. Scales fail to separate ADHD from non-ADHD students there. Narrative models catch clear behavior patterns in the same cases. The missed-case sets barely overlap. A language-model theme pipeline then interprets the split. It finds attention, behavior, and family themes. Narrative text, the authors argue, complements standard screening tools.
arxiv-2606-02609:
Bauer and co-authors improve Activation Oracles, tools that explain neural network activations in words. Oracles read residual stream activations and describe them. Current versions face real flaws. They hallucinate and stay vague. Text-inversion confounds also cloud their evaluation. The team improves the training regime in four ways.

Training uses on-policy rollouts. The conversational dataset is improved. More layers feed the oracle. The injection formula is revised. Capability gains are marginal, the authors admit. Quality of life gains are substantial. The team also open-sources AObench. It is the first comprehensive evaluation suite for oracle quality. The work aims to set a foundation for scalable, end-to-end interpretability. Future oracle builders get both a better recipe and a shared yardstick.
arxiv-2606-02709:
Masiero and co-authors dissect a minimal flavor-deconstructed model in the lepton sector. The study uses effective field theory. Flavor and CP violation are the twin foci. Starting from the ultraviolet completion, the team derives the effective Yukawa structure. A systematic spurion expansion goes beyond leading order. Dominant sources of flavor and CP violation are identified.

At leading order, dipole effects align roughly with the Yukawa matrices. Next-to-leading terms generically break that alignment. Physical CP-violating phases appear. The low-energy theory is then built. Charged lepton flavor violation, universality tests, and electric dipole moments are analyzed. Future muon-to-electron conversion searches can probe multi-10 TeV scales. The electron EDM reaches similar scales under natural assumptions. Precision lepton measures, the authors argue, probe flavor scenarios beyond collider reach.
arxiv-2606-03109:
Pathak and co-authors use a quantum circuit to find equilibria in games of incomplete information. In Bayesian games, each player has a hidden type. The joint space of types and actions grows fast with player count, so direct linear programming gets costly. The team seeks Bayes correlated equilibria with a hybrid quantum-classical method.

A parameterized quantum circuit stands for the joint action distribution. For eight players and depth two, it needs just 48 trainable angles. Training boosts social welfare while fining any break of the obedience rules. Tests use a Bayesian congestion game with two, four, six, and eight players. The circuit found valid answers with higher welfare than two classical baselines. All runs were valid up to six players, and four of five at eight.
