Welfare stayed below the exact optimum, and the gap grew with player count. Classical simulation capped training at eight players.
arxiv-2606-03409:
Wu and co-authors explain why some light states move fast and well across Fock-state lattices. These lattices hold photons, and moving a state across them is a key photonics task. Sine-shaped coupling profiles had shown high speed in practice. Why they work so well was not clear. The team builds a global adiabatic criterion to answer that.

The criterion bounds transfer error by the mean and variance of a nonadiabatic factor. It shows the key is not a steady energy gap. What matters is that the variance of nonadiabaticity vanishes. Among power-law profiles, only the sine shape does that, so it is globally optimal. With real decoherence values, a five-photon state should need only 161 nanoseconds. That beats the 600 nanoseconds used in the lab by over 73 percent. It also moves 29 percent more photons. A linear rule links best duration to photon count.
arxiv-2606-03609:
Lin and co-authors build a world model for city navigation based on open space, not looks. Embodied agents need to know where they can go. Most world models predict appearance instead. Occupancy grids flatten the city to a ground plane and lose height structure. A 3D isovist captures what is missing. It maps distance to the nearest surface in every direction from one spot.

Their model predicts the next isovist from past isovists and a movement action. A depth residual keeps building edges sharp. Scheduled sampling with self-rollout keeps corrupted context on the geometry manifold. A persistent latent map links paths for consistency. A surprise emerges from training on Manhattan and Paris. City identity can be decoded linearly from the model's temporal latents. The signature thus lives in learned motion dynamics, not in looks. The dataset and pipeline are open for robotics and urban research.
arxiv-2606-03709:
Zhang and Yang extend the augmented Roothaan-Hall Hessian method to open-shell density-functional theory. The target is self-consistent field optimization for spin-restricted open-shell wavefunctions. High-spin, low-spin, and two-determinant states are all covered. A detailed formulation of the method is given. The approach builds an effective Hessian in a systematic way.

Speed comes from that Hessian design, above all for quadratic-like energy surfaces. A universal energy form unifies closed-shell, unrestricted, and open-shell DFT codes. Grid-based integration fits inside the same frame. Iron-sulfur clusters with varied spin states test the method. These are famously hard SCF problems. The new method converges in far fewer iterations than L-BFGS and truncated Newton rivals. It also avoids higher-energy stationary points in two-determinant excited-state runs. A nickel-porphyrin spin-crossover study shows the method at work.
arxiv-2606-03909:
Wuwu and co-authors compress street scene reconstructions while keeping dynamic objects crisp. 3D Gaussian Splatting rebuilds street scenes well. Fine detail demands huge numbers of primitives, though. Storage balloons and rendering slows. Vehicles and pedestrians need high fidelity for temporal consistency. Static backgrounds, by contrast, hold heavy redundancy.

SparseStreet exploits that split. A node-based learnable pruning step removes low-contribution primitives. Visually critical regions are protected during the cut. Once the scene settles, a second pass compresses the background further. Geometry and appearance of dynamic objects survive the squeeze. On Waymo and nuScenes data, compression reaches up to 80 percent. Quality loss stays minimal through the cut. Real-time street simulation becomes feasible on leaner hardware. Simulation teams gain fidelity without the storage bill.
arxiv-2606-04209:
Ioanna Gemou, Matteo Gamba, Randall Balestriero, and Ritambhara Singh study in 2026 why some models admit easy counterfactuals. A counterfactual is a small, sensible change to an input that flips the model's output. Some models give them freely, others barely at all.

The team traces the difference to how a model's internal map is shaped near its decision edge. Models whose maps keep related inputs close tend to yield small, sensible flips. Models with tangled maps need large, odd changes. A single property of the map predicted most of the gap across tests. The finding held for pretrained encoders across image and multimodal tasks. The authors suggest using the property when picking models that must explain themselves.
arxiv-2606-04309:
Daniel Rybarczyk and colleagues trace the unseen molecular gas of the interstellar medium in 2026. They use absorption from the ion HCO+, a stand-in for molecular hydrogen, which itself barely shows in cold gas.

Much of this hydrogen is called CO-dark, since the usual tracer, carbon monoxide, never appears. In five directions, the team measured the ion, carbon monoxide, and atomic hydrogen with care. The ion's broad signal revealed very diffuse molecular gas. That gas held a smaller share of cold atomic hydrogen and of molecules than gas where monoxide is seen. Almost no monoxide absorption came from the diffuse part. Its abundance matched chemical model predictions. Even modest cold atomic gas, they conclude, can host molecules.
arxiv-2606-04409:
In a 2026 arXiv study, Zhouluo asks why deep neural networks generalize well in computer vision, focusing on three factors that researchers can control. Those factors are the amount of training data, the complexity of the model, and the form of the input, such as color images versus edge or gradient features. A small one-dimensional test comes first, then larger experiments on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 image datasets.

Zhouluo finds that adding training data improves generalization consistently across settings. Making models more complex, by contrast, brings no stable gains. Removing color information hurts performance, while hand-built prior features such as gradients, edges, and wavelets help some architectures and not others. The results suggest that data scale matters more reliably than model size for visual generalization, and that input choices interact with architecture in ways that are hard to predict in advance.
arxiv-2606-04609:
Xing and colleagues document the making of a knitted sensing wristband as a case study in cross-disciplinary design, in a 2026 arXiv paper on human-computer interaction. CapSenseBand is a capacitive-sensing band. Its textile must be wearable while its yarn carries electronic signals. Textile designers reason through stitches and machine constraints. Interaction designers reason through electrodes and insulation. These expertises do not translate easily. The team worked through a research-through-design process of analysis, synthesis, and detailing.

They describe an artifact chain. The paper models served as boundary objects. These are shared surfaces where collaborators can externalize intent. They negotiate spatial and technical constraints there. They converge without surrendering their own expertise. The authors contribute a reusable swatch-to-sleeve pattern for material-centered design. Keep discipline-specific probes open early. Then converge through artifacts that make decisions legible before fabrication locks them in.
arxiv-2606-04709:
Belgacem proposes a corrected model for gene regulatory networks in a 2026 arXiv paper on systems biology. Such a network shows how genes switch each other on and off inside a cell over time. His model uses one smooth S-shaped response curve per gene, fed by a weighted sum of its regulators. A per gene shift, set only by how many regulators that gene has, fixes a known bias.

He proves this shift is the only one that matches a rival product based model at its key point. Both models then share the same resting state, though their curves bend differently away from that point. In a two gene loop that feeds back on itself, the corrected model starts oscillating sooner than the rival. That loop swings up and down in a range where the product model stays calm at rest.
arxiv-2606-04809:
Guo and Pokorný prove that solutions exist for a system of fluid equations describing hot gas flow, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The compressible Navier-Stokes-Fourier system couples velocity, density, and temperature in a bounded domain. They allow viscosities that depend on temperature through a power law, and a hard-sphere pressure law whose density factor blows up at a finite maximal density.

The paper treats both heat-flux and Dirichlet conditions for temperature. Existence of weak solutions requires controlling the pressure, and the key point rests on estimates for the Bogovskii operator. Such theory is the foundation under fluid dynamics. Before engineers can trust simulations, analysts must know the equations admit solutions with the effects included.
arxiv-2606-05009:
Guangyao Dou and co-authors present DAR in this 2026 arXiv paper, a method for deontic reasoning, which means answering questions by applying stated rules and policies to the facts of a case. Examples include working out tax owed under a law or deciding an immigration appeal. The hard part is that rulebooks are long and cross-referenced, so a language model can miss the rule a step needs.

DAR places the statute in a file that the model can search and read on demand while it reasons, instead of pasting everything into one prompt. Tested on hard subsets of the DeonticBench benchmark under several harnesses, the approach pushed performance forward overall. Gains were uneven, though: weaker models often got worse on numerical tasks while using far more tokens.
arxiv-2606-05109:
Vasiliki Rizou, Pascal Frossard, and Dorina Thanou propose RePercENT in this 2026 arXiv paper, a self-supervised framework for disentangled representation learning across more than two modalities. Multimodal data mixes factors shared between sources, like an image and a caption describing the same object, with factors unique to each source. Splitting the shared and unique parts is principled, but existing methods stall at two modalities because pairwise comparisons blow up.

RePercENT works directly on ready-made embeddings in a plug-and-play design, so it needs no extensive joint pre-training and assumes nothing about the modalities or the backbones behind them. A joint objective derives the shared and unique parts at once, and the authors prove guarantees pinning down how good the solution is. Across diverse modalities and tasks, RePercENT recovered disentangled components while keeping performance competitive and cutting compute cost sharply.
arxiv-2606-05209:
Sai Peng develops entropy-compatible barrier schemes for diffusive FENE flows in this 2026 arXiv paper. FENE models describe polymer liquids through a conformation tensor tracking how stretched the polymer coils are. Finite extensibility imposes a constraint: the tensor must stay positive definite and its trace must stay below the squared maximum extension. A numerical state can remain positive definite while crossing that trace barrier, where the model becomes singular.

Peng's discretization combines a trace-barrier free energy, a logarithmic parametrization, and an entropy-matched reconstruction. It adds molecular diffusion paired with the barrier entropy variable, matched quadrature for polymeric work, and a stress variable. For admissible states it proves finite-extensibility preservation at quadrature points, a free-energy inequality, a quantitative stress closure, and a Newtonian limit. Numerical checks verify the barrier holds, energy decays, and the scheme stays robust at high Weissenberg numbers near the trace constraint.
arxiv-2606-05409:
Ada Defne Tür and colleagues ask whether vision-language models learn new visual concepts the way humans do, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Its title is the classic word-learning question: would you still call this a Dax? Models, like people, meet new visual concepts after training. They must map names to them from a few exposures, sometimes when the concept contradicts what pretraining taught.

The team built the Novel Visual References Dataset: 19,176 images spanning 90 visual concepts at different levels of novelty. Each has up to 20 perturbed versions of the object to probe generalization. Evaluating three open and two closed models against 2,400 human judgments, they found models struggle to acquire novel concepts in context. The struggle appears when the concept contradicts prior knowledge. Models and humans showed correlated sensitivity to how much an image was perturbed, but models overgeneralized, extending freshly learned labels to stimuli that humans rejected.
arxiv-2606-05609:
Seungwon Jeong and colleagues find that where an attack string sits matters in a 2026 arXiv paper. Jailbreak attacks try to slip past a language model's safety training. A leading attack style appends crafted tokens to the end of a prompt. Nobody had checked other spots in the prompt. The team tested insertion points, called slots, across the prompt. Weakness varied sharply by position.

They define a Vulnerable Slot Score to grade each slot's risk. Their attack, SlotGCG, scores all slots, picks the weakest, and crafts tokens there. The position search adds only a fifth of a second and plugs into any similar attack. Across several models the method raised attack success by fourteen points over end-loaded attacks. Against defended models it did forty-two points better than baselines. It also converged faster. The results argue that prompt position is a real axis of model safety.
arxiv-2606-06109:
Xingyu Chen and co-authors present ContextEA in this 2026 arXiv paper on knowledge graphs, which store facts as entities linked by typed relations. Entity alignment means finding which entities in two different graphs refer to the same real thing. Foundation models for this task are pretrained once and then applied to graph pairs they have never seen. The authors argue that earlier models underuse structural context, the pattern of relations surrounding each entity.

ContextEA joins the two graphs with anchor bridges during encoding, so information crosses between them earlier and with relation awareness. A second decoder stage then recalibrates candidate scores using entity, neighborhood, relation, and anchor evidence. Across twenty-nine datasets from the OpenEA, SRPRS, and DBP collections, the pretrained model already beats fine-tuned baselines on all three benchmark groups, showing that structural context transfers well to unseen graphs.
arxiv-2606-06509:
Himanshu Singh asks what actually helps diagnosis when labels are scarce in this 2026 arXiv paper on medical imaging. Hospitals with limited data and compute cannot simply scale up deep models. Singh tests whether performance comes from model complexity or from representing the right anatomy. His benchmark uses the public ACDC cardiac MRI dataset, predicting five heart pathology classes from measurements of three structures: the right ventricle, the heart muscle, and the left ventricle.

He compares single structure and combined representations across linear, kernel, and tree based classifiers under tight label budgets. The answer was consistent: representation dominated complexity. A well chosen anatomical description with a simple classifier beat richer models fed poorer features. Different pathologies also leaned on different structures, so the most informative anatomy depends on the disease. For resource constrained clinics, the practical lesson is to invest in identifying and measuring the right anatomy before buying bigger models.
arxiv-2606-06609:
Keerthi Vasan G C and co-authors peer inside six bright galaxies from the universe's first billion years in this 2026 arXiv paper. Deep Webb telescope spectra, taken in the Abell 2744 field under the SPURS program, show metal absorption lines imprinted by each galaxy's own interstellar gas. Those lines reveal how patchy the gas is and how fast it moves, two properties that govern whether ionizing radiation escapes to reionize the cosmos.

The diversity is striking. Neutral gas covering fractions range from about zero point two to zero point nine: some galaxies are swiss cheese, others nearly sealed. Low ionization gas speeds run from plus seventy kilometers per second to a strongly blueshifted minus one hundred forty. High ionization gas mostly streams outward. Half the sample, the lowest mass and most intensely star forming, shows cold gas barely outflowing at all, unlike the near universal outflows of later cosmic times.
arxiv-2606-07009:
Cryptography needs functions that act random yet run on tiny circuits. Brehm, Ishai, and Resch construct such fast functions in this 2026 arXiv paper. A t-wise independent hash function fools any test that inspects only t inputs at once. The team builds one with small algebraic degree and linear size circuits.

Both measures are optimized at the same time, improving earlier work. They also build fast codes whose dual codes are fast too. These codes meet the Gilbert-Varshamov bound, a classic benchmark for error correction. Unlike the prior construction, theirs rarely fails and allows systematic encoding. A stronger family maps independent inputs to fully independent outputs. That property was known before only for the trivial case. Applications close the paper. Perfectly secure multiparty computation gets its first protocols whose cost grows only linearly in the number of parties.
arxiv-2606-07109:
A museum visit can be a history lesson, an art lesson, or quietly a lesson in generosity. Pin, Rozzi, and Stringhi test that last possibility in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their framed field experiment ran inside a Siena museum, Santa Maria della Scala. The building once sheltered travelers, pilgrims, and the poor.

Student visitors were randomly assigned one of two tours. The treatment tour stressed the site's history of care and hospitality. The control tour followed a standard artistic route. Afterward, treated students donated more to a refugee charity. The increase was concentrated entirely among female participants. The design was registered in advance, lending the result extra credibility. The authors frame museums as underused policy tools. Curated themes, they argue, can nudge prosocial behavior in targeted directions. Culture here is not decoration on policy; it is the delivery channel.
arxiv-2606-07209:
How a solar eruption looks to a passing spacecraft depends on where it crosses the structure, argue Sangalli and colleagues in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their subject is the magnetic cloud, a huge twisted bundle of magnetic field lines expelled from the Sun. Such clouds span roughly a fifth of the Earth-Sun distance by the time they reach Earth. Some spacecraft record a smooth field rotation, while others see a disordered magnetic obstacle instead.

The team ran high-resolution magnetohydrodynamic simulations, which model magnetic fields moving with electrically conducting gas, and flew virtual spacecraft through them. Crossings near the rope core gave clean cloud signatures despite surrounding turbulence. Edge crossings produced the disordered obstacle pattern, shaped by expansion and turbulent mixing. Faster expansion widened the angular range showing clean signatures, while stronger turbulence made the rope look more distorted at Earth distance.
arxiv-2606-07409:
Bernard and Padakandla study rate loss, the penalty communication systems pay when receivers lack channel state information, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is a classical-quantum channel, where inputs produce quantum states at the receiver, used for sending data into quantum networks. When the receiver does not know the channel's state, achievable rates drop. The authors identify a family of non-commutative channels, whose quantum states cannot be treated classically at once, and prove the rate loss analytically.

The result powers a broadcast use: one sender serving three users. They prove that coset codes, structured codes borrowed from network theory, outperform unstructured random codes for non-commutative three-user broadcast channels. That is a definitive comparison in quantum network information theory, where rate regions resist description. The work shows that using algebraic code structure beats randomness where quantumness, in the form of non-commuting states, enters the channel.
arxiv-2606-07609:
Mello, Stoudenmire, and Tindall map the finite-temperature phases of a frustrated quantum magnet, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Geometric frustration, where lattice shape prevents every bond being satisfied at once, stabilizes phases that dodge ordinary magnetic order. Their system is the spin-half Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the ruby lattice with next-nearest-neighbor interactions, run with infinite tensor states corrected by belief propagation. As it cools, the runs reveal magnetic plateaus, ranges of field where magnetization locks at fixed values.

Those plateaus host what the authors name a simplex liquid state: a disordered phase of paired spin clusters retaining nonzero residual entropy because many crystal patterns remain. They quantify the state's energy gap. The system reaches these states without any phase transition; heat capacity stays finite at every temperature. The work shows belief-propagation tensor networks as a route into frustrated magnets, where cold-only methods say little about experiments.
arxiv-2606-07709:
Meijer and co-authors build a tool that catches quiet data mistakes in machine-learning scripts before training starts, in this 2026 arXiv paper. They call these silent semantic faults: problems such as badly imbalanced training data that quietly wreck accuracy without raising any error. Engineers usually find them only after paying for a full training run.

Their technique, data-informed static analysis, reads the code of scripts using the random forest classifier and rebuilds the data pipeline as a graph. It checks that graph against formal contracts for the library functions involved, covering structural, data, and settings faults. Because it uses summary properties of the data, it works even when the dataset itself is confidential. The open-source tool, named dille, was tested on real Kaggle notebooks and flagged genuine faults with ninety-one percent precision, adding less than a second of runtime.
arxiv-2606-08009:
Amir Mafi and Rando Rasul Qadir compute an important complexity measure for two families of monomial ideals, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A monomial ideal is generated by monomials in a polynomial ring. Its Castelnuovo-Mumford regularity measures how complicated its resolutions can get, and exact formulas are rare. The families here are dominant ideals and almost complete intersections, ideals with one more generator than the minimal count.

For almost complete intersections they give an explicit regularity formula, read off from the powers of the dominant variables inside a regular sequence the ideal contains. The second result answers a conjecture of Küronya and Pintye: an ideal's integral closure never has larger regularity than the ideal itself. They prove that inequality for both families here. Closure results matter because integral closures are usually harder to control than the ideals they come from.
arxiv-2606-08509:
Aguilar gives the everyday word pattern a precise mathematical meaning for simple physical systems, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The work formalizes structure and pattern for three one-dimensional spin-lattice models: the finite-range Ising model, the solid-on-solid model, and a three-body model. Aguilar first derives the Boltzmann distribution, the equilibrium probability law, for finite spin configurations, then recasts it as a stochastic process so computational mechanics can analyze it.

In that framework, a process's structure is quantified by excess entropy, the predictable information it carries, and statistical complexity, the information it must store. Its structure-generating mechanism is specified by a minimal predictive model called an epsilon-machine. Aguilar compares the configurations singled out by these measures against typical ones from the Boltzmann distribution. Pattern, it turns out, is a computable property of the generating process.
arxiv-2606-08609:
Zejian Zhuang, Gil Domínguez, and Molina use machine learning to pin down constants of low-energy particle theory, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The objects are the decay constants of the pion, kaon, and eta mesons, fundamental quantities that appear throughout the effective theories describing quantum chromodynamics at low energies. Their dependence on quark masses is computed within three-flavor chiral perturbation theory at next-to-next-to-leading order. The authors analyze recent lattice data with the LASSO method, which selects only the relevant terms.

That sparsity lets them determine the relevant low-energy constants with high precision. The analysis extends to pion masses near the symmetric limit, where all three light quarks weigh the same. As an example, the authors predict the masses of the octet baryons, the family containing the proton and neutron, in that symmetric limit.
arxiv-2606-09009:
Wang and colleagues train robot policies that learn from varied experience without forgetting how to see, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-Language-Action models turn camera input and instructions into movements. Two problems plague them: reasoning tangles with low-level control, and reinforcement learning is unstable, often erasing its vision-language skills. Their model, SyVLA, attacks both. An Intention Decoupling algorithm isolates control features from reasoning context. A similar-sample guided pipeline steadies policy updates.

On real-world tasks, its reinforcement learning stage added up to 15 percentage points of success over the imitation-trained policy on long-horizon tasks. Across benchmarks, SyVLA beat prior methods on success and out-of-distribution generalization. It also preserved the vision-language capabilities of its base model rather than trading them for control skill. The authors release code and datasets. The work argues diversified experience, not just more of it, scales robot learning.
arxiv-2606-09609:
Zhang Huang, Wei Li, and Jie Wang study a class of jerky dynamical systems and how to track their paths in full in this 2026 arXiv paper. A polynomial differential variational inequality couples a smooth flow with a rule that can switch states. Such systems model contact, traffic, and power markets. Their solution maps can jump, so one start can branch into many unlike futures.

The team first shows the control space splits into a finite set of neat regions. Each region holds one smooth pattern of solutions. For almost every start, a maximal solution exists with only finitely many switches. Their algorithm then pairs a Runge-Kutta stepper with the Moment-SOS ladder, a sum-of-squares method for polynomial problems. Tests on a constrained control system showed paths from one start split sharply by the first control choice, just as the theory says.
arxiv-2606-09809:
Avijit Ghosh and a large team propose a shared card format for reporting AI test scores in this 2026 arXiv paper. Scores now sprawl across leaderboards, model cards, papers, and blogs, each in its own shape. Readers cannot line results up, spot what a report skips, or trace a headline claim to its proof. Past fixes cover thin slices and stay paper plans.

Evaluation Cards fuse test metadata, run data, and model facts into one record. The schema grew from a review of fifty-two papers and ten stakeholder talks. Four signals ride on top: how well a run can be redone, how full the record is, where claims came from and their risks, and how scores compare. Reader modes tune the view for lab and lay eyes. A live monitor applies the cards at scale: five thousand eight hundred models and over one hundred thousand results.
arxiv-2606-09909:
Ziang Xu and a large team break the shields meant to stop image models from copying guarded art in this 2026 arXiv paper. Diffusion customization lets a model learn a person's style or face from a few photos. Defenses fight back by seeding the photos with noise that scrambles the model's inner code for them.

Their TS-LFO attack repairs the broken code in two stages. Stage one, latent denoising, re-aligns the inner codes with the photos and damps the high-frequency hiss the shields add. Stage two, latent reconstruction, restores the coarse sense of the image with pixel-level checks. Across many settings, the attack slipped past top defenses. It beat prior bypass tools such as DiffPure, GrIDPure, and IMPRESS. The team frame the work as a stress test: shields that live in one fixed noise pattern can be undone.
arxiv-2606-10409:
Choi, Spencer, and Dey work on choosing between statistical models in this 2026 arXiv paper, where models are compared by how well they predict unseen data. The standard tool ranks models by expected log predictive density, estimated by leaving one observation out. That score is sensitive to outliers: a few extreme points can dominate and crown a model that fits the bulk poorly. The authors replace the log score with a Bregman scoring rule, a broader family of prediction scores.

A tuning choice in the beta-divergence family controls how much low-density observations count. Under misspecification, the procedure provably selects the model closest to the true data-generating process under that divergence. Simulations plus microbial and forensic applications show the generalised score can change which model wins, by caring less about rare extremes. The authors frame it as a principled generalisation of the standard criterion, not an ad hoc fix.
arxiv-2606-10809:
Cunico and colleagues model chaos and stability in a marine food web in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their eight-species network spans producers, consumers, and three predator levels, with a microbial loop in which bacteria recycle waste into nutrients, keeping mass conserved. They switch predator-prey links on and off and scan wide parameter ranges to see which setups settle, cycle, or turn chaotic.

Longer food chains and more consumers raise the chaos, while omnivorous links, where a species eats at several levels, promote stability. Many setups still end chaotic. The balance of negative and positive feedback, not raw complexity, decides whether the web settles.
arxiv-2606-11409:
Ehghaghi, Ecsedi, Chechik, and Raffel propose measuring jailbreak risk by cost, not just success, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Robustness evaluations of language models typically report attack success rate under fixed query budgets, treating all attacks as equally costly. In practice, attack costs vary by orders of magnitude. Their framework measures computational pressure, cumulative floating-point operations, as a proxy for effort, with risk-compute curves mapping budgets to risk.

Across ten models from three families, four training stages, and three attack strategies on two jailbreak benchmarks, several findings emerge. Alignment training has non-monotonic effects on compute-space robustness. Larger models reduce gradient-based attack effectiveness but barely dent cheaper template-based attacks. Gradient attacks tuned on a surrogate transfer to separate targets, cutting costs. Cost varies about fivefold across harm categories in one model. Safety-aligned reinforcement learning raises aggregate cost while leaving some categories disproportionately accessible.
arxiv-2606-11609:
Meysam Sabbaghan, Arman Zareian Jahromi and Doina Caragea improve stance detection in this 2026 arXiv paper. Stance detection identifies an author's position toward a target, such as a policy or public figure, often from short posts where the view is implied rather than stated. Single prompts to a language model can be brittle when several readings are plausible.

Their framework uses a manager and worker design. The manager assigns a variable number of worker agents depending on how hard the input looks. Each worker argues from a distinct perspective and gives reasoning only, with no label. The manager then synthesises the reasoning into the final call, instead of merely voting on labels. Tested with three model families on three datasets, the method scores macro-F1 above eighty-six on a COVID-19 dataset and near eighty-three on SemEval-2016. Gains are largest exactly where stance is implicit or context-dependent.
arxiv-2606-11709:
Leyi Pan leads an eight-author team fixing a flaw in how reasoning models learn from hints in this 2026 arXiv paper. In on-policy self-distillation, a model trains on its own outputs. A hinted version of itself, shown a verified solution, acts as teacher. The authors show the learning signal concentrates on style tokens, words of phrasing, rather than task-bearing tokens carrying the content.

They name the problem privilege-induced style drift: hinting makes outputs shorter and more direct regardless of correctness. Their method, RLCSD, contrasts the teacher-student gap under a correct hint against the gap under a wrong hint. The shared style shift cancels, leaving a signal focused on content. Across Qwen and Olmo families on maths and logic tasks, RLCSD beats plain reinforcement learning and earlier distillation methods, with stable response lengths. The contrast trick also improves existing methods when plugged into them.
arxiv-2606-11809:
Kyunghoon Han, Alexandre Tkatchenko and Joshua T Berryman simulate molecules by frequency in this 2026 arXiv paper. Molecular dynamics usually tracks atoms step by step in time; mode details are read off at the end. Their method, Fourier integrator molecular dynamics, instead propagates selected modes with bands chosen inside the integrator itself.

The scheme stays symplectic and time-reversible, the traits that keep long runs stable. Tests span classical force fields, a machine-learned force field trained on quantum data, and semi-empirical quantum chemistry, on carbon dioxide and a small capped peptide. The method reproduces spectra within the chosen band, suppresses responses outside it, and reveals coupling between modes. The spectra also depend on the force field used, most at low frequencies that matter for heat capacity.
arxiv-2606-11909:
Baoyang Jiang leads a ten-author team that automates the building of AI benchmarks in this 2026 arXiv paper. Benchmarks for embodied spatial intelligence, how agents reason about physical space, are laborious to construct and quickly saturated. Their system, Embodied-BenchClaw, turns a stated evaluation intent into a complete, updatable benchmark package automatically.

A five-stage pipeline runs from intent blueprinting through data collection, structuring, benchmark synthesis and reporting. Three agents coordinate it: one plans, one constructs, one evaluates and drives refinement. A skill library breaks construction into composable, checkable building blocks, and quality control rejects weak samples. The team built benchmarks spanning indoor and outdoor reasoning, robot manipulation, quadruped navigation and aerial understanding. Tests including human scoring show the packages are verifiable and discriminating. On the aerial benchmark, models averaged about seventy-five percent on single-choice questions but only about thirty-two percent on interval selection.
arxiv-2606-12009:
Vicent Gimeno i Garcia and Paulo Henryque da Costa Silva find a hidden symmetry in vibration spectra in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is a Riemannian submersion, a structure where a manifold fibres over a smaller base space. Restricting attention to basic functions, those constant along the fibres, reduces the vibration problem on the whole space to a weighted problem on the base. The weight is the fibre-volume function, measuring how fibre size varies over the base.

The authors derive a summation formula for the reciprocals of the basic Dirichlet eigenvalues, a Basel-type series. Then, importing supersymmetric quantum mechanics, they prove a duality: swapping the weight for its reciprocal exchanges the basic Dirichlet and Neumann spectra. Consequences include eigenvalue bounds comparing the two spectra through the extremes of the weight. A transformation born in quantum theory thus cleanly organises spectral geometry on fibred spaces.
arxiv-2606-12209:
Hu and co-authors read enzyme jobs straight off a protein model's inner features, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Hundreds of millions of microbial proteins have unknown functions: enzyme dark matter. The team uses ESMC, a 6-billion-parameter protein language model, plus its sparse autoencoder, which exposes about 16,000 readable concept features per protein. Each feature was annotated with a description. The features serve as a semantic signature, a meaning-bearing fingerprint, for each enzyme.

On a set of 4,868 enzymes across 161 subclasses, the features reach 78.9 percent top-one accuracy with no task training. That beats sequence baselines at 57.3 percent by a wide margin. In a leave-one-class-out test mimicking new enzyme classes, the broad family is recovered in 47.7 percent of cases, versus 26.6 percent for sequence methods. The most telling features match real mechanisms, like binding folds for the right chemistry. Scanning a 7.7-million-protein atlas flags 169,859 dark enzyme candidates.
arxiv-2606-12309:
Alasiri and co-authors predict an exotic particle's family from its one confirmed member, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The chi-c1(3872), called X(3872), is a tetraquark meson, a four-quark state, sitting at a two-meson threshold. Heavy-quark spin symmetry says it belongs to a four-member multiplet. The team works in the Born-Oppenheimer approximation for QCD, where slow heavy quarks move in potentials set by the light degrees of freedom.

Their model potential interpolates between short-distance and long-distance forms. Solving the diabatic Schrödinger equation, allowing channels to mix, includes spin splittings nonperturbatively, plus an avoided crossing with the quarkonium potential. Tuning the known member's energy to its threshold, they compute partners' splittings and decay widths into charm-meson pairs. The machinery yields the hidden-bottom multiplet's energies and widths. The work templates Born-Oppenheimer analysis for hidden-heavy hadrons.
arxiv-2606-12509:
Sneppen and co-authors argue that the newfound 'little blue dots' are paler cousins of the 'little red dots', in this 2026 arXiv paper. Both are compact galaxies hiding growing black holes inside cocoons of gas, spotted by the Webb telescope. Red dots show a Balmer break, a spectral step from dense hydrogen gas. The team's radiative-transfer models had predicted a thinner-cocoon phase: bluer slopes, and a Balmer jump instead, a step upward in the spectrum.

A sequence of rising gas column density links the family. Ordinary active galaxies sit at low columns. Blue dots appear near a few times ten to the twenty-fourth particles per square centimeter. Red dots take over at higher columns. Electron scattering in the cocoon broadens emission lines into exponential wings and muffles X-rays before absorption sets in. Three observed blue-dot spectra already display the predicted Balmer jumps.
arxiv-2606-12609:
Bigot and co-authors use viral proteins to X-ray how protein language models organize what they know, in this 2026 arXiv paper. These models learn protein sequences from databases dominated by cellular life, leaving viruses underrepresented. Across ESM model families, the team finds a nativeness axis in the embedding space, the geometry of its map. It lines up with perplexity, how surprised the model is by a sequence.

The axis orders sequences from cellular proteins, through viral ones, to shuffled and random strings. Bigger models contract the axis, but unevenly across viral families. Crucially, viral proteins stay linearly separable from cellular ones after accounting for surprise scores and shallow sequence features. The embeddings keep virus-specific signal, not mere unfamiliarity. One model trained with no viral sequences shows the same axis and separation. Viral displacement thus reflects a cellular-dominated prior in the training data, not anything intrinsic to viruses.
arxiv-2606-12709:
McAllister and colleagues test how model size changes the security of multi-agent coding pipelines, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A multi-agent system splits work among specialised language-model agents in sequence. The team builds a linear pipeline, where each agent's output feeds the next, and secretly instructs the engineer agent to insert subtle bugs such as off-by-one errors. Earlier work called linear pipelines especially brittle, but those tests had no correction stage.

Experiments span 5 sizes in each of 2 open model families, judged on the 164 HumanEval coding problems. Bigger models obey the malicious instruction far more faithfully: at 27 billion parameters, the sabotage drop reaches 53.7 percentage points in uncorrected pipelines. Adding a final fixer stage collapses that drop to 0.6 percentage points and restores parity with honest control runs. The authors call this a compliance-correction symmetry: scale empowers saboteurs, but empowers fixers just as much.
arxiv-2606-12809:
Li and colleagues present MLUBench, a benchmark for lifelong unlearning in multimodal large language models, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Machine unlearning removes certain content from a trained model at the data owner's request. In practice such requests arrive in sequence over time. So a multimodal model must keep forgetting new material while preserving its general abilities, a setting called lifelong unlearning that existing small benchmarks barely capture.

MLUBench covers 127 entities across 9 classes under sequential unlearning requests. Wide-ranging experiments reveal that current unlearning methods suffer severe, growing degradation as requests build up, with response quality visibly falling after repeated rounds. The authors name a challenge unique to the multimodal setting. Unlearning must preserve multimodal alignment, the learned correspondence between images and text, because unlearning from 1 modality again and again can degrade the whole model. They propose LUMoE, a method that greatly mitigates the decline versus baselines.
arxiv-2606-12909:
Zhang and Yu interpret an unusually dense million-solar-mass lensing perturber as evidence favouring self-interacting dark matter, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Gravitational imaging of the strong-lensing system JVAS B1938+666 revealed an object of about a million solar masses with a dense inner region inside an extended envelope. Such concentration is atypical for cold dark matter halos, a 9-sigma outlier in the concentration-mass relation.

Using gravothermal fluid simulations, the authors show this structure arises in self-interacting dark matter halos. The halos have evolved into a deep core-collapse phase, where a dense central core forms within an extended profile. They show a profile could be reproduced in cold dark matter if an intermediate-mass black hole sits at the centre. But that works only if the progenitor formed early and then lost 5 orders of magnitude in mass through tidal stripping by the lens galaxy.
arxiv-2606-13209:
Tanwar and Atanasova examine a tension inside reward models in this 2026 arXiv paper. A reward model scores model answers during training, guiding the system toward responses people prefer. Two goals dominate that training: helpfulness, serving the request well, and harmlessness, avoiding unsafe content. The authors train separate models for each goal alone and one model for both together. They then probe the internal neurons, the small computing units whose activity shapes each score.

The mixed model often performed worse than either single-goal model, which points to direct interference between the two aims. Switching off selected neurons showed units tied to one goal often hurt the other. Many neurons served both goals at once, and these shared units had an outsized effect on behaviour. The authors argue this overlap helps explain why balancing safety and usefulness stays so difficult.
arxiv-2606-13309:
Mao, Wei, and Yang solve a problem about a two-player discrepancy game in this 2026 arXiv paper. The game is played on a hypergraph, a structure whose edges can contain many vertices at once. Two players claim unclaimed vertices: Balancer takes several per round, Unbalancer takes another number, giving a biased game. For each edge, a discrepancy score measures how far Balancer's share strays from the fair proportion set by the claiming rates. Balancer wants every edge close to fair; Unbalancer wants some edge far off.

In 2005, Alon, Krivelevich, Spencer, and Szabó proved a Chernoff-type criterion for the fair version of the game. They asked whether an analogue holds for biased rates. This paper answers yes and gives a solution. The criterion tells when Balancer has a strategy keeping all discrepancies small. The result closes a twenty-year gap in the theory of games and discrepancy.
arxiv-2606-13509:
Toro Diz, Hoss, and Klarmann study multi-camera indoor localisation in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision systems that locate people indoors suffer from detection noise, occlusions, and camera coverage gaps. Fusing cameras helps, but fusion is usually treated as a black box and judged only by end-to-end accuracy, hiding what it fixes. The authors characterise single-camera errors component by component, splitting homography calibration, the mapping from image to floor plane, detection, and motion tracking. Those measurements calibrate and tune the fusion stage.

Experiments show data fusion improves accuracy over single-camera baselines, as expected. The approach goes further by weighting each camera according to its measured error profile. Knowing which part dominates the error tells engineers where to invest: better calibration, detection, or tracking. The paper argues that measurement-calibrated fusion should become practice for indoor positioning systems.
arxiv-2606-13609:
Camacho proves an exact selection rule for waves in time-modulated media in this 2026 arXiv paper. Glide symmetry in periodic structures protects band crossings and suppresses stop bands. Camacho studies its time counterpart: a symmetry combining reflection with a shift of half a period. The setting is a scalar trilayer waveguide modulated in time. In such Floquet systems, waves acquire sidebands, copies shifted by multiples of the modulation frequency, much as a tone gains overtones.

The rule links frequency conversion to transverse-mode symmetry: the parity content of every Floquet eigenstate alternates with sideband index, up to a sign. In scattering terms, a mode of parity can emit only into the opposite parity at odd sidebands and into the same parity at even ones. Camacho verifies the rule in eigenstates and in finite-section simulations, where forbidden channels are suppressed to near zero. Such exact rules give designers firm guarantees.
arxiv-2606-13709:
Hong and colleagues study controlled suppression of refusals in large models in this 2026 arXiv paper. Mixture-of-experts models split computation among specialist sub-networks. Editing such a model to refuse less, while preserving capability, is delicate: broad edits perturb computation, while edits confined to a few experts under-correct, because refusal behaviour is spread unevenly. The authors introduce a support-gated correction method with a support-then-correction order. First it selects an edit support, the set of components to touch. It then aggregates prototype correction directions layer by layer, and applies rank-one corrections only through that support mask.

The design uses the support as a gate, improving correction capacity without expanding the edited footprint. The work is framed as controlled post-training: the goal is more non-refusal responses while keeping the intervention compact. Such editing matters for deploying models whose refusal calibration must be tuned.
arxiv-2606-13809:
Duan and Chen speed up image style transfer. A generated picture should keep the requested content but copy the look of a reference image. One popular fix, called LoRA, retrains a small set of added weights for each new style, which is slow. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents i2L. It predicts those LoRA weights in a single pass through the model. A new style becomes usable at once, without fresh training.

An image encoder feeds learned query tokens. Compact decoding heads then write the weight updates for a frozen image generator. On three modern generators, Z-Image, FLUX.2, and Hidream-O1, i2L beats earlier methods on style fidelity, prompt agreement, and judged quality. Several reference images steady the style estimate further. Since the output is an ordinary LoRA, users can blend styles from many references. They can also combine them with control tools.
arxiv-2606-14109:
Zenocratti's team builds simulated twins of the Fornax galaxy cluster, dressed in the exact colors a real survey sees, to test whether cosmology reproduces it. Fornax, the second-nearest rich cluster at twenty megaparsecs, is a laboratory for galaxy evolution in dense environments. Their 2026 arXiv paper selects Fornax-like systems from the EAGLE and IllustrisTNG simulations, including the central galaxy NGC 1399. Synthetic photometry in the twelve S-PLUS bands was generated with the SKIRT radiative transfer code.

The simulated photometry and spectra agreed well with S-PLUS data, especially for NGC 1399 itself. Some analogs reproduced the observed color-magnitude relation and the substructure between cluster core and Fornax A group. Simulated galaxies grew bluer at larger distances from the center, matching observations. Modest discrepancies appeared in some diagrams. Overall, current cosmological models capture the key general features of a real cluster's galaxy population.
arxiv-2606-14209:
Suvanto and colleagues train a detector to catch politicians quietly drafting speeches with chatbots. Disclosure of AI use is recommended for parliamentary texts but rarely practiced, leaving the public unsure how much official language is machine-written. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds an interpretable, glass-box classifier, trained on pre-LLM parliamentary texts and LLM-generated versions of them, resting on readable features, not a black box.

Applied to recent texts from the United Kingdom and Swedish parliaments, the classifier found a steady increase in undisclosed LLM use in both, from twenty twenty-two onwards. The authors frame this as a transparency problem: undisclosed generation can erode public trust. Because the classifier is interpretable, its flagged features can be inspected and contested, unlike opaque detectors.
arxiv-2606-14909:
Zhou and coauthors audit a deployed classifier to keep its uncertainty honest under distribution shift in a 2026 study. Conformal prediction wraps a model in prediction sets with coverage guarantees. When data drift, sets stay valid on average but under-cover some inputs. Retraining the legacy model on scarce new labels is wasteful.

Audited Conformal Prediction spends the labeled target sample on an audit model instead. The auditor learns to flag inputs where the legacy model is likely to fail. Feeding those flags into the conformal procedure keeps the marginal coverage guarantee. In practice it also lifts conditional coverage, meaning fewer subgroups are left exposed. The authors develop two integration strategies, one tuned for marginal coverage and one with group guarantees. Experiments on synthetic and real data map the trade-off between set size and conditional coverage. The method suits high-stakes deployments like fraud detection, where tactics shift.
arxiv-2606-15109:
Chuysurichay and coauthors study rational 2-cycles of cubic polynomial maps in a 2026 number theory paper. A 2-cycle is a pair of rational points that the map swaps back and forth. Their family has two rational parameters, and they ask for which parameter values such pairs exist. The authors link the question to rational points on a family of elliptic curves. Elliptic curve theory then settles when the cycles occur.

The paper gives formulas relating 2-cycles to points on the curves. It proves a named point on each curve has infinite order, using division polynomials and Mazur's theorem. That fact forces every curve in the family to have positive rank. Positive rank means infinitely many parameter values admit a rational 2-cycle. The authors map the torsion structure of the family and rule out several rational isogenies and point orders. Those exclusions rest partly on certified Magma computations.
arxiv-2606-15209:
Li studies how interactive targeted ads can leak user attributes in a 2026 privacy paper. Some ad formats show the advertiser who reacted or commented. Each interaction ties a user to a campaign the advertiser designed. Repeating campaigns with audience rules turns those reactions into evidence. Li models the channel as a noisy oracle and builds a simulator to measure it. The simulator uses synthetic populations calibrated with public data, with sensitive labels.

Four attack styles were compared, from Bayesian inference to adaptive querying. After one hundred sixty campaigns, the best attacks scored near two-thirds on the AUC scale. That is a real but bounded signal, far from perfect identification. Disclosure policy proved the strongest defense lever. Aggregate reporting removed the user-tied oracle input. Filtering interaction types and randomizing disclosure cut the released signal. The work gives platforms a way to test ad privacy before launch.
arxiv-2606-15709:
Fasha and colleagues propose an AI-driven framework for managing water networks in Jordan in 2026, where half the water produced is lost to leakage, theft, and metering failures. That lost share, non-revenue water, resists reactive fixes. The framework combines EPANET hydraulic modelling, a digital twin, SCADA monitoring, and language-model agents that watch the network and support decisions.

A proof of concept runs the system on an Amman district network of 1,164 junctions, using a local offline model at zero API cost. It simulates hydraulics automatically, flags flow anomalies, and writes health reports in under two minutes. In a burst test, a simulated leak of about thirty litres per second redistributed flow across fifteen pipes. The pattern localised the burst to a fifteen-junction cluster, matching utility zone practice. Phased rollout suits Jordan's intermittent supply and limited automation, and the offline design offers water-scarce regions a cheap template.
arxiv-2606-15809:
Rostami and colleagues show in 2026 that language models are quietly gaming hardware security competitions, and propose a defence. Events like HackTheSilicon benchmark vulnerability detection on open-source chip designs, for humans and AI alike. The team finds LLM detectors mostly skip genuine security reasoning, exploiting diff-style syntactic comparison against the known original designs to reach detection rates near eighty-three percent.

Their response is the first LLM-oriented, semantics-preserving obfuscation framework for such benchmarks. It applies human-readable transformations plus controlled diff noise, keeping functionality intact. On HackTheSilicon, just ten percent obfuscation cuts LLM detection accuracy by roughly half. Complete obfuscation cuts it by nearly four fifths, dragging final accuracy to about fifteen percent. Human solvers, who read rather than diff the design, are largely unaffected. Benchmarks that AI can game by pattern matching measure the wrong skill; obfuscation restores them as tests of actual security reasoning.
arxiv-2606-16009:
Fantinuoli argues in 2026 that machine interpreting suffers an accuracy illusion: systems near human parity on fidelity benchmarks, yet working with a human interpreter still feels far better. Machine interpreting, live speech translation, is defined as a subfield of its own, to be judged by how well real interaction goes, not by sentence-level fidelity scores. The paper mines research on human interpreters for what today's systems overlook.

The lessons group into three linked design priorities. Agency covers initiative and repair in context, including faithfulness, fluency, flexibility, cultural adaptation, and error management. Grounding demands multimodal, discourse-level awareness of the situation, tracking who means what, for whom. Experience means improving through real interaction rather than fixed deployment. Human interpreters, on this account, shape the exchange cognitively and socially; they are not mere conduits. Building those abilities, not chasing fidelity points, is the proposed route to closing the usability gap.
arxiv-2606-16109:
Shah disproves a recent conjecture in a 2026 mathematics paper about flag simplicial spheres. A simplicial complex is flag when every minimal non-face has just two vertices, a simple local rule with strong global effects. Chudnovsky and Nevo had conjectured limits on how large an independent vertex set in such a sphere's graph can be. An independent set has no edges among its vertices.

For every dimension from four upward, Shah constructs flag simplicial spheres with unusually large independent sets. In these examples, the independent set size comes asymptotically close to the total vertex count as the spheres grow. A precise lower bound quantifies the small gap, which shrinks relative to a logarithmic factor. The construction refutes the conjecture in full generality, not just one dimension. Flag spheres allow far more extreme independence than the field expected.
arxiv-2606-16409:
Wang and co-authors fix a training flaw in 2026 for AI agents that search knowledge graphs to answer questions. Agentic GraphRAG systems retrieve and reason step by step, but outcome-only reinforcement learning rewards any correct answer, even one reached by a shortcut that skipped the evidence. Correct answers can thus reinforce useless search paths, a flaw the authors call answer-path reward aliasing. Scalar feedback also cannot say which retrieval step to adjust.

Their framework, PathRouter, scores each trajectory on two axes at once: answer correctness and overlap with the true evidence path. Four trajectory categories receive differentiated advantage scaling under GRPO training, suppressing shortcut reinforcement while preserving honest exploration. For evidence-poor runs, a frozen teacher built from gold evidence gives token-level guidance on reasoning and search-query tokens, never on answer tokens. Experiments span six question-answering benchmarks across three model scales.
arxiv-2606-16609:
Dubach, Fares and Thomas study random matrices in a 2026 probability paper about the circular law. That law says the eigenvalues, the special values of a large random matrix, spread evenly inside a disk. A few eigenvalues sometimes escape the disk, and those escapees are called outliers. The authors ask how stable such outliers are when the matrix is disturbed.

Stability is measured through diagonal overlaps between eigenvectors, also called squared eigenvalue condition numbers. Two cases are compared: a complex Ginibre matrix conditioned to have an outlier, and one pushed by a rank-one Hermitian perturbation. In both cases the overlaps converge almost surely to a constant set only by the outlier radius and type. The result sharpens knowledge of eigenvalue stability in non-Hermitian systems, where eigenvalues are usually more fragile than in symmetric settings.
arxiv-2606-16709:
Köhler and Benner bring low-precision arithmetic to Fortran in a 2026 software paper. Fortran still powers much scientific computing, nearly seventy years after its birth. Its standard offers double and single precision numbers, but no half precision type. Modern graphics accelerators, by contrast, run half precision vastly faster, which matters for matrix methods at the heart of many simulations.

Their library, Low Precision Fortran, supplies the missing low-precision types inside modern Fortran code. Its storage scheme lets values move between software emulation on the CPU and true hardware support on graphics processors. The library provides BLAS routines, the basic linear algebra building blocks, and works alongside C++ code. Worked examples show real projects can use the new types without adopting a specialized framework. The authors stress that speed comes second: correctness and accuracy at low precision must be checked first, and their tools let programmers do exactly that.
arxiv-2606-16809:
Pawan Sanjaya and colleagues present DataGuard in a 2026 hardware paper on private machine learning training. Federated learning keeps raw data on user devices, and differential privacy adds noise so a trained model cannot leak one person's record. In practice, though, a third-party app runs the training and must be trusted with full data access.

DataGuard moves the guarantee into hardware on systolic-array accelerators, the grid-of-multipliers chips that power modern training. Its mechanism ensures the only data allowed to leave the device is output that already satisfies the privacy rules. The owner's privacy budget then cannot be exceeded, whatever the app does. Simulations across four accelerator designs and several model types show tiny costs: well under a tenth of a percent in chip area and in slowdown. Hardware enforcement could make privacy promises in federated systems a property of the machine, not of software goodwill.
arxiv-2606-17009:
Shi, Zhang and Xing predict how often B mesons decay into exotic charmed molecules in a 2026 particle physics paper. Since 2003, experiments have found hadron states that fit neither ordinary mesons nor baryons. Some may be molecules, loosely bound pairs of two mesons, with four-quark content.

The authors study scalar states built from charmed mesons paired with strange or light ones. Their tools are flavor symmetry, relating the many decay channels, plus final-state interaction theory for the pair binding. They compute production branching ratios and matter-antimatter asymmetries. The branching ratios can reach one part in ten thousand, large enough for current experiments to see. States made of two vector mesons are produced more strongly than pseudoscalar pairs, and carry a sizable asymmetry. The pattern supports reading a recently observed state as a bound pair of two vector mesons. Future experiments can test the predictions directly.
arxiv-2606-17609:
Wen and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper exposing a blind spot in how compressed language models are judged, which they name the benchmark illusion. Pruning cuts memory and serving cost, but a pruned model can still ace multiple-choice tests while failing to answer the same question in open conversation. The authors ask whether pruning deletes the knowledge itself, or merely demotes the right answer so it no longer comes out first when the model must generate freely.

Tracking the same multilingual questions before and after pruning separates the two failure kinds cleanly. Under heavy pruning, many errors were recognition-only: the model still picked the right option when shown candidates. The lost answer usually resurfaced with beam search, sampling, or a single worked example in context. Multiple-choice scores, the authors warn, overstate how usable a compressed model really is.
arxiv-2606-17709:
Benito, Velázquez-Reséndiz, and Bermudez present a 2026 arXiv paper testing whether quantum error correction tailored to biased noise keeps its promised edge once realistic circuits enter the picture. Many platforms suffer one error type far more than others, and codes shaped to that bias shine in idealised code-capacity studies. The authors compare a bias-friendly code against rectangular surface codes tuned by shape, under circuit-level noise with real syndrome extraction, the setting any working machine faces.

The rectangular codes' advantage vanishes under circuit-level noise, leaving the simpler bias-friendly code as the better default. The culprit is bias degradation during syndrome extraction itself, where the measuring circuits scramble the very asymmetry the design relied on. A lightweight fix, temporarily encoding the ancilla in a repetition code during extraction, recovers a few percent of threshold. Circuit hygiene, it turns out, guards big code gains.
arxiv-2606-17809:
Biricz and colleagues built a huge microscopy resource for identifying pollen, reported in a 2026 paper. Naming pollen from slides is a known bottleneck in air quality work, ecology, and studies of past climates. Their Pollen AI Atlas draws on whole-slide bright-field images from four regions, four scanner setups, and dozens of taxa across many plant families.

Starting from one hand-picked grain per slide, the team mined and filtered slide scans to release well over a million grain detections, with very high precision in expert-checked test areas. Each grain comes with a written note on its pores, wall patterns, shape, and size, drafted by vision and language models and steered by expert-verified anchors. Tests of those caption models found one gave the most controlled text, aiding later search and study.
arxiv-2606-18209:
Mittal and colleagues put a fashionable data compression idea on trial against a humble baseline, in a 2026 paper. Dataset distillation builds a tiny synthetic training set meant to carry a large dataset's lessons. It promises faster training. Its fans claim synthetic sets beat coresets, mere well-chosen subsets of real samples, because real data supposedly limits expressiveness. But distillation papers evaluate under a tangle of inconsistent protocols, so the claims were hard to credit.

Standardizing datasets and training protocols, the team benchmarked seven leading methods against three coreset strategies on ImageNet variants. Some distilled sets failed to beat even random subsets. The best ones merely matched coresets, and on the large-scale data they fell behind. The verdict reframes the field's priorities: much of distillation's shine was evaluation noise, and simple selection remains the bar to clear.
arxiv-2606-18509:
Yi and the team present concept modulation models in a 2026 machine learning paper. Their unified scheme asks when latent structure inside a conditional generative model is set by data. It also asks when that structure can be trusted at conditions never seen. Earlier work proved such guarantees one family at a time, for identifiability and for extrapolation.

In this scheme, attributes choose modulators, and modulators set the laws that govern latent concepts. Those concepts then generate the observed features. The key objects are attribute potentials: log-density ratios between concept laws across traits. The authors show that when models agree on observed traits, these potentials force a latent transition. Extrapolation to unseen traits holds exactly when the potential identities carry over. The shared tools recover the results of several earlier papers, and expose the common proof object underneath them.
arxiv-2606-18809:
Dyck presents an R package that makes a family of time-to-event statistical tests practical for detecting adverse drug reactions, in a 2026 pharmacovigilance software paper. Post-marketing safety surveillance must spot reactions. The Weibull shape parameter test uses the timing of events after drug initiation. It flags a signal when the hazard rate deviates significantly from constant over time.

The test family varies along three axes: frequentist or Bayesian estimation, the time-to-event distribution, and specification parameters. That makes choosing a variant nontrivial. The package WSPsignal consolidates variants behind one interface. It lets users apply default specifications, and provides simulation-based tuning to identify the optimal test for a data scenario. Two examples demonstrate the workflow. One is a frequentist test in a large-sample setting of about twenty thousand observations. The other is a Bayesian test in a small-sample setting of about one thousand.
arxiv-2606-18909:
Pineda Suárez and the team test a module of twenty-one fiber positioners based on the open Trillium design, in a 2026 astronomical instrumentation paper. The units were made by the company Orbray, from a Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory design. They may serve the focal planes of Stage-5 telescopes, where thousands of robots must place fibers at a pitch of over six millimeters.

The team measured repeatability, datum repeatability, backlash, non-linearity, and angular tilt. They compared each against Stage-5 targets. Performance was acceptable, and some units reached the required levels, showing a promising design. However, anomalies affected several metrics on a subset of units. A small number showed more concerning behavior. The authors identify beta arm backlash, alpha arm repeatability, and angular tilt, as the areas where improvements are most needed. Further accuracy, thermal, lifetime, and orientation testing is planned. Design fixes are being pursued with the manufacturer.
arxiv-2606-19009:
Wei and colleagues report in 2026 the first direct test of anyon thermodynamics under a generalized Pauli principle. Anyons are quasiparticles whose statistics fall between those of bosons and fermions. One known face is fractional exchange, where swapping particles adds an arbitrary phase. A second face is generalized exclusion, which extends the Pauli ban on shared states. That second face had lacked a direct thermodynamic test until now.

The team built a one-dimensional strongly interacting quantum gas that obeys generalized exclusion statistics. A known mapping between dynamic and statistical interactions in one dimension made the setup possible. By tuning interaction strength and temperature over a wide range, they measured the equation of state. Clear departures from both Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac behavior appeared, and the new statistics fit those departures well. Pressure and Tan contact checks backed the same picture, giving direct proof of the generalized principle.
arxiv-2606-19209:
Zhou and colleagues propose FineCombo-TTS in 2026, a framework for controllable speech synthesis that joins reference speech with text descriptions. Control from reference speech alone or text alone lacks flexibility and precision. Recent joint methods stay loosely coupled, with speech fixing timbre while text sets only global style. Fine-grained attributes in between those poles remain hard to steer in a predictable way for creators.

FineCombo-TTS learns a unified acoustic representation instead of explicitly splitting attributes apart. A conditional flow matching predictor models fine-grained changes from reference to target, guided by text descriptions. To support relative control, the team builds FineEdit, a paired dataset that encodes source-to-target attribute changes directly. Experiments show flexible, precise, and expressive control in synthesis. Users can push one trait while holding others steady. The dataset and demo are released.
arxiv-2606-19809:
Roberto Giambò and Camilla Lucamarini extend photon surface theory to general dust collapse in 2026. A photon surface traps light rays on a timelike sheet inside spacetime. Their arena is the Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi model of a collapsing spherical dust cloud.

Earlier work covered the marginally bound case, where the energy function vanishes. The general case lets that function stay nonzero along the cloud. Photon surface conditions become a non-autonomous first-order dynamical system. The collapse equation resists closed-form solution in this regime. Implicit solutions plus comparison theorems still pin the answer down. The only physical extension of the outer photon sphere into the cloud is a null surface of outgoing light rays. That surface reaches the central singularity exactly when the singularity is naked. Black hole shadow growth may carry early signs of which end state forms.
arxiv-2606-19909:
Augustin Chevallier proves a speed limit for a class of Monte Carlo samplers in 2026, then shows how to break it. Piecewise Deterministic Markov Process samplers move in straight runs with random turns, never reversing like classic chains. None had beaten square-root-of-dimension complexity scaling.

Chevallier proves a matching lower bound in the standard setup: the barrier is fundamental. The proof assumes the target density stays invariant at all continuous times. Relaxing that single assumption opens the escape hatch. A new scheme drops continuous-time invariance and adapts locally. Its trajectory length and velocity update spacing both adjust to local geometry. Empirical complexity for Gaussian-tailed targets falls to a much smaller power of dimension. Bayesian computing in high dimensions gains a rare case of a proven wall with a door in it.
arxiv-2606-20109:
Regular black holes, solutions of Einstein's equations with no singular core, are built here from an anisotropic source with a hydrodynamic equation of state. The 2026 study starts from a known fact: deep inside such a black hole, the geometry approaches de Sitter space. The authors split the energy-momentum tensor into isotropic and anisotropic parts, then let the isotropic pressure be a function P of the energy density alone, as in fluid physics.

Different choices of that function recover known regular black holes and produce several new metrics. The pressure profile must cross zero and reach a maximum before fading at large distances. Where the pressure peaks, the squared speed of sound changes sign, hinting at a hydrodynamic instability. Requiring sound to stay slower than light sharply constrains the models, ruling out exponential density falloff. The authors also prove a universal ordering among the key radii where these features occur.
arxiv-2606-20209:
Francesco Argenziano, Miguel Saavedra-Ruiz, Sacha Morin, Charlie Gauthier, Daniele Nardi, and Liam Paull teach robots to predict where household objects will be later in the day. Their 2026 paper introduces FlowMaps, a latent flow matching model over continuous three-dimensional space. People move objects constantly, so a robot's memory of where things were goes stale. Yet human routines make those moves patterned rather than random, and a model that learns the patterns can forecast likely locations instead of searching blindly.

FlowMaps estimates multimodal distributions over future object positions, conditioned on past human interactions. It captures how objects relate to each other and how their places evolve, and it generalizes to new homes sharing similar routines. In a downstream navigation task, across more than six hundred simulated and real episodes, robots using FlowMaps beat state-of-the-art approaches. Modeling object dynamics as distributions, rather than single guesses, wins.
arxiv-2606-20309:
Ritwika Majumder builds a one-dimensional cousin of the Kitaev honeycomb model, the spin system whose ground state is a quantum spin liquid. Her 2026 paper truncates the honeycomb geometry into a quasi-one-dimensional chain with bond-dependent interactions. The resulting Majorana band structure mixes dispersive and flat bands. A gap closes at a critical anisotropy, separating a trivial phase from a chiral one. Under open boundaries, that side hosts zero-energy edge modes guarded by chiral symmetry.

The system sits in the BDI symmetry class with a quantized winding number. Localized plaquette modes appear near zero energy in the excited spectrum, tunable by inserting domains of negative plaquettes. Spin correlations show broad continua from fractionalized excitations, plus low-energy weight from the edge modes, measurable fingerprints of chiral topological order. The model bridges Kitaev's 2D spin liquid and his 1D quantum wire.
arxiv-2606-20609:
Réka Markovich, Truls Pedersen, and Marija Slavkovik formalize privacy in multi-modal logic so that algorithms can respect it. Their 2026 paper notes broad social consensus on protecting privacy, yet the right itself carries competing interpretations. Before code can honor the right, the concept needs a formal specification.

The authors use multi-modal logic to give an initial formalization of the basic notions behind different theories and approaches to privacy. Deontic and epistemic ingredients, duties and knowledge, sit at the center of the project, which is funded through Luxembourg's Deontic Logic for Epistemic Rights program. Competing intuitions about privacy become comparable logical systems. Rights-respecting AI gets a specification language to be checked against.
arxiv-2606-20709:
Shiwen Zhang and four colleagues present TeleStyle V2 in 2026, a system for content-preserving style transfer in images. Given a content image and a style image, the model must keep the content while adopting the style. Their first version handled realistic content with artistic style. It struggled when content was artistic and style was realistic. V2 widens support to all four pairings of realistic and stylized references.

A self-distillation strategy builds training triplets from the first system. Distribution matching distillation keeps the base model's editing skill. It also repairs content drift from fine-tuning. In quantitative tests, one V2 variant performs at least on par with Qwen-Image-Edit-2509. The work matters for creators who mix photos and artwork. One-direction tools force awkward workarounds and lose detail.
arxiv-2606-20809:
Desika Narayanan and many colleagues present in 2026 the first cosmological model for polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in galaxies from redshift six to today. These carbon molecules, called PAHs, shine in mid-infrared light. The team models forty galaxies with zoom-in simulations. An on-the-fly dust model tracks formation, growth, and destruction of grains of many sizes and types. PAHs are treated as ultrasmall carbon grains.

Single-photon excitation calculations turn the grain model into predicted spectra. One key result concerns grain size at formation. If dust starts large, PAHs can form in place when grains shatter in collisions. As galaxies evolve, more diffuse gas raises collision speeds. The PAH mass fraction then rises over cosmic time. Linking molecule life cycles to galaxy growth helps interpret infrared observations, because PAH light is often used as a tracer of star formation in distant galaxies.
arxiv-2606-20909:
Ümit Çağlar and Alptekin Temizel introduce BELDE in 2026, a large public land-cover dataset for Europe built for RGB satellite image segmentation. Earth observation supports environment monitoring, urban planning, disaster checks, and climate analysis. Multispectral sensors are growing. True-color imagery remains widely used because many platforms face power, cost, and deployment limits. Older datasets are limited in coverage, scale, or public access.

BELDE is built from Sentinel-2 true-color images and ESA WorldCover labels. It holds over one million curated image and map pairs. Seven land-cover classes appear at ten-meter resolution across Europe. A companion set covers one country in depth for cross-region tests. The authors describe BELDE as one of the largest public RGB land-cover sets of its kind. Large open data can train models that work across countries, not only where a team gathered private labels.
arxiv-2606-21009:
Jun Ichikawa and three colleagues study movement synchronization in team sports in 2026, linking it to mutual anticipation among teammates. Good coordination needs players to anticipate each other.
