If each player waits to see a teammate move, gaps open and opponents can interfere. When anticipation works, movement becomes smooth and synchronized. Most past studies used simple or uniform-role settings.

Real coordination mixes heterogeneous roles and changes over time. Their approach uses team sports data and a statistical method. Temporal components of movement are extracted. Synchronization is compared probabilistically against a baseline, rather than assumed. The study aims to show how stable timing structures form in complex settings. Quantified synchronization could help coaches and analysts judge team cohesion from tracking data, moving beyond highlight plays to the timing fabric that makes collective action work.
arxiv-2606-21109:
Yuxiang Lin and Ying Chen introduce Chem2Gen-Bench in 2026, a benchmark for translating between chemical and genetic perturbations in cells. Virtual cell models predict how cells respond to drugs and gene edits. The two perturbation types are not interchangeable by default. Earlier tests study each type apart.

The benchmark organizes hundreds of thousands of chemical profiles and over a million genetic profiles into cell-target contexts. Pairwise alignment, retrieval, covariate effects, feature spaces, and model embeddings are evaluated. Translation fidelity is measurable but heterogeneous across contexts. Background adjustment changes retrieval results in paired tests. In one cell line audit, foundation model embeddings do not consistently beat simple gene-delta baselines. An auditable frame helps drug teams judge when a cheap genetic proxy can stand in for a costly chemical screen.
arxiv-2606-21309:
Vandita Shukla and eight colleagues release WildBox in 2026, a dataset and benchmark for spotting wild animals in three dimensions from drone video over African savannas. It holds 237,505 three-dimensional bounding boxes for seven species, grouped into six classes, with animal identities tracked through each video segment. Reliable 3D detection would help ecologists count and follow wildlife without disturbing it.

Two open-vocabulary 3D detectors score zero on zero-shot 3D detection, even when handed perfect 2D boxes, which isolates the failure to depth estimation. Fine-tuning on WildBox restores usable accuracy, and depth error dominates the remaining mistakes. A coarse-to-fine curriculum that first merges the two zebra classes improves results with less compute. Video-level splits, code, and baseline models are released so others can push aerial wildlife perception forward.
arxiv-2606-21509:
Yueyuan Li and five colleagues address a maintenance headache in 2026 for end-to-end self-driving systems, where perception and driving policy are fused through shared internal features. Swap in an improved perception module and its features shift, silently degrading the frozen policy downstream. Retraining or decoupling the stack costs heavily in compute and validation. Their proposal is model stitching: a small translator layer that realigns the new features to what the old policy expects.

Simple linear and convolutional stitchers were tested under perception updates from new random seeds, new sensor setups, and new training domains. In the hardest test, moving from nuScenes to CARLA, convolutional stitching kept over ninety-one percent of the original driving score while cutting adaptation time from about twenty-two hours to under one. Stitching, they argue, is a cheap stitch in time.
arxiv-2606-21609:
David Jewitt, Jane Luu, and Yoonyoung Kim report time-series observations in 2026 of comet 240P/NEAT, which has split into two fragments, tracked near perihelion with the Nordic Optical Telescope. The brighter piece, 240P-A, measures roughly 400 to 600 meters in radius and shed dust at up to 130 kilograms per second, ejecting about 1.5 billion kilograms during the watch. Its companion, 240P-B, is smaller and quieter, losing mass at about a quarter of that peak rate.

The pair now drift apart near one meter per second, a separation likely accelerating under uneven outgassing, and their split is over three years old. Tides, impacts, and internal pressure buildup are ruled out as causes. The authors favor rotational breakup, where outgassing torques spin a small comet apart, a picture future observations of 240P can test.
arxiv-2606-21709:
Marko Slapar and Sašo Strle prove in 2026 that certain singularities of embedded 3-manifolds can be erased by tiny wiggles. Take a closed oriented 3-manifold sitting generically inside a complex threefold. At most points the embedding is totally real, but along a link the tangent space picks up a complex direction: the CR singular set. These points come in elliptic, hyperbolic, and parabolic flavors, and they obstruct many constructions in complex geometry.

The theorem: if part of that link bounds an oriented Seifert surface inside the manifold, avoiding the rest of the link, the singularities along that part can be cancelled. The cancelling move is an arbitrarily small isotopy supported near the surface. The result converts a geometric removal problem into a topological one, checkable with classical link and surface machinery.
arxiv-2606-21809:
Zhang, Chen, and Bareinboim address policy evaluation under hidden confounding in 2026. When an unseen factor shapes both a treatment and its outcome, data alone cannot pin down the true causal effect. Past robust methods demand deep prior knowledge of the setting, or handle only discrete treatments and outcomes, leaving continuous problems exposed.

The authors first show that any causal model's hidden variables can be swapped for finitely many latent states while matching its distributions to any accuracy desired. On that result they build Causal Gaussian processes, flexible Bayesian models that can approach both the observed and the intervened distribution of any causal model. The only structure they assume is the basic time order of treatment and outcome. This gives a sound route to judging treatment effects over continuous domains, even when confounding cannot be ruled out.
arxiv-2606-21909:
Li, Li, and Tang study, in 2026, the heat kernel of a Riemannian manifold, the fundamental solution describing how heat spreads from a point, through the lens of resurgence and Picard-Lefschetz theory. Short-time expansions of the heat kernel diverge, yet resurgence theory says their hidden structure encodes information beyond the real setting. The authors ask what complex geometry that structure detects.

For a real analytic manifold, they show the kernel has a short-time expansion whose Borel transform picks out complex-geometric data beyond the sector of real geodesics. They pose an infinite-dimensional Picard-Lefschetz problem centered on the holomorphic energy functional over a complexified path space. In their proposal, alien operators acting on the expansion around the real geodesic should generate the sectors of other complex geodesics, with coefficients counted from connecting trajectories. A test on the hyperbolic plane confirms the proposal in that case.
arxiv-2606-22009:
Koriyama benchmarks, in 2026, how well large language models convert Japanese writing into phonetic kana readings, a grapheme-to-phoneme step that text-to-speech systems need for controllable pronunciation. Japanese is a hard case because the same characters carry many context-dependent readings. Over thirty models were tested on three thousand hand-annotated sentences against conventional morphological analyzers.

Two prompting strategies were tried. In parse mode the model first analyzes sentence structure, and rules then convert it to kana. In direct mode the model predicts the readings itself. The best language models reached a kana character error rate below 0.52 percent, roughly half the best conventional tool's rate. Parse mode beat direct mode for most models, since rule-based finishing spared the model the hardest rules. Feeding predicted kana into speech synthesis also beat end-to-end speech generation.
arxiv-2606-22109:
Sasai and Gunji propose, in 2026, Bayesian-inverse-Bayesian inference as a minimal model linking statistical inference, statistical mechanics, and heavy-tailed statistics. The method adds a hypothesis-renewal step to ordinary Bayesian updating. They test it in repeated games of cyclic rock-paper-scissors, where algorithms that chase the Nash equilibrium collapse to uniform random play.

Across sweeps of design, window, and opponent conditions, the method's dynamics stay in one internal critical state. The persistence of the leading hypothesis follows a heavy-tailed power law, with exponent near 1.43 at the standard window. The exponent drifts toward the universal value of three halves as finite-sample effects vanish. Bayes-only inference, lacking the inverse step, shows no such power law at all. The authors conclude the renewal step alone makes the dynamics critical, with no tuning.
arxiv-2606-22609:
Yeon Su Park and six colleagues, including Juho Kim, study automated feedback for online tutors in this 2026 paper. Gig-economy tutoring platforms scale well, but tutors mostly learn from learner evaluations, which give limited guidance for improvement and make quality hard to monitor. The team ask whether AI-generated feedback can support tutors.

They deployed a research probe on Ringle, a popular English tutoring platform, which analysed lessons and produced automated feedback. Thirty-six tutors were then surveyed about the experience. Tutors perceived the automated feedback more negatively than learner feedback overall. Still, they found it useful for monitoring their own performance and for understanding what the platform expects. Discrepancies between the two feedback sources often caused confusion, undercutting both. From these findings the authors propose design considerations for feedback systems on educational gig platforms, aiming to make automated and human feedback reinforce rather than contradict each other.
arxiv-2606-22709:
M. Huerta-Sandoval, I. Ramos-Prieto, and H. M. Moya-Cessa solve a class of quantum dynamics problems exactly in this 2026 paper. A two-level system, such as a qubit, often has a coupling and detuning that vary with time. Exact solutions for arbitrary time dependence are rare and valuable.

The authors construct a Lewis–Ermakov type dynamical invariant, a quantity that stays constant along the motion and unlocks the solution. Their route uses a correspondence between two-level systems and the time-dependent harmonic oscillator, through two Lie algebras sharing a common complex form. The invariant yields a closed-form evolution operator and an exact propagator for any coupling and detuning functions. They illustrate the method on Landau–Zener transitions, non-Hermitian dissipative processes, and adiabatic rapid passage. Finally, they inverse-engineer shortcuts to adiabaticity with fully explicit control fields, when the scaling function is real.
arxiv-2606-22809:
Boxuan Ma and five colleagues trace how programming students seek help from AI in this 2026 study. Generative AI gives novices instant, tailored support, but teachers worry it may bypass the self-regulation that learning requires. Most earlier work counted how often students used AI, or whether answers were right, not how the help-seeking unfolded.

The team coded 1,290 student prompts from introductory Python courses, linked to 17,190 code submissions from 71 students. Their framework ties each prompt to conceptual, implementation, debugging, or reflective support, viewed through self-regulated learning theory. Most students used AI reactively, troubleshooting after trouble hit rather than planning ahead. Help-seeking patterns showed no link to task scores. They did differ sharply in how many code submissions students needed, suggesting the path students take with AI matters even when scores look alike.
arxiv-2606-23009:
Arwen Nugteren and colleagues merge Bayesian methods with layered forecasting in a 2026 paper. Many planning problems nest totals inside totals, like tourism nights by region adding up to a national figure. Forecasts at each level must agree with one another to support sound choices. Standard practice forecasts each level on its own, then patches the numbers into agreement afterward. That patch never shapes the model fitting itself. The authors instead build agreement into a fully Bayesian model from the start.

Nugteren and colleagues let their model penalize mismatch softly rather than forcing exact agreement. Fitting can also focus on the levels that matter most for choices. The fitted values then serve the forecast goal directly, and no large extra matrices are needed for multi-step forecasts. Tests on simulated data and Australian domestic tourism showed better accuracy than patch-based approaches.
arxiv-2606-23109:
Yun Liu and colleagues measure how fast ions lose energy inside dense plasma in a 2026 experimental physics paper. This stopping power matters for how stars evolve and for igniting fusion fuel. Theory handles weak coupling between ions and plasma well. The strongly coupled regime, where interactions exceed the linear range, stayed untested because experiments are extremely hard. The team fired laser-accelerated carbon ions into a uniform, long-lived dense plasma target with well-measured temperature and density.

Liu and colleagues measured the ions' energy loss and their charge state at the same time. That pairing removes a longstanding ambiguity about which charge state caused which loss. The coupling strength passed unity, beyond all earlier work. The results clearly show reduced stopping power in this regime, the first such observation. The finding gives fusion and astrophysics models a firm data point where they previously had only extrapolation.
arxiv-2606-23209:
Joost Wardenier and colleagues model projected wind fields on ultra-hot Jupiters in a 2026 exoplanet paper. Ultra-hot Jupiters are giant planets roasted by their stars. High-resolution thermal emission spectra encode their three-dimensional winds through Doppler shifts, the stretching of light by motion. Reading those winds back out needs a forward model that is physical yet cheap to run. Their model, dopplerkernel, describes the line-of-sight wind across the planet's disk with just four parameters: an equatorial jet speed and width, a source-to-sink flow speed, and the longitude where the flow converges.

Wardenier and colleagues turn those parameters into a broadening kernel using weighted kernel density estimation. They then run a Bayesian retrieval on synthetic emission spectra of the planet WASP-76b, generated by a full climate model. The exercise shows how much true wind information the spectra actually contain.
arxiv-2606-23609:
Garg, Aïvodji, Ebrahimi Kahou, and Michalski build a classifier whose very shape reveals hidden subgroups in the data, in a 2026 paper on robust machine learning. Models often learn spurious correlations, shortcuts that predict labels in training but fail for minority subgroups, such as waterbirds photographed on land. Standard fixes adjust weights using group labels or guesses, yet the finished model cannot say which subgroup a new sample belongs to.

Their neural classification trees route each sample through a tree of nodes split into easy and hard branches. Easy means the model currently gets such samples right, and hard means it struggles, a signal that tracks subgroup identity. Routes from one round become pseudo labels for the next, so conflicting subgroups separate without any group supervision. Across five benchmarks the tree isolates minority subgroups consistently, giving a transparent map of latent structure while matching top robustness methods.
arxiv-2606-24009:
Chen, Endo, and Pajitnov study when the space around a link, a tangle of closed loops in three-dimensional space, can be sliced by surfaces sweeping around a circle. Thurston's norm measures cohomology classes on such spaces, and its unit ball is a polyhedron whose special faces mark classes representable by fibrations, maps onto a circle with surface fibres. Their 2026 approach uses Morse-Novikov theory, which supplies obstructions to fibering.

Working with non-abelian Novikov homology from the universal cover of the link exterior, the team proves a sharp criterion for two-bridge links with two components. There, a class fibres exactly when the two-variable Alexander polynomial, a classical link invariant, is monic relative to that class. They also compute Morse-Novikov numbers, counts tied to critical points of circle-valued functions, for most prime two-component links with up to eight crossings, giving concrete data alongside the theory.
arxiv-2606-24209:
Pratiksha studies normality for holomorphic functions of several complex variables. Here a single function consumes several complex inputs at once. A family of functions is normal when every sequence inside it has a subsequence converging nicely on compact sets. That compactness property underpins much of complex analysis. The 2026 paper extends the classic theory using total derivatives, which gather all partial derivatives of every order into one object.

A sufficient condition comes first. A holomorphic function on the open unit ball in complex n-space, whose higher partial derivatives obey stated constraints, must be phi-normal, a weighted variant of normality. Inequalities built from total differential polynomials then yield further normality criteria for families of such functions. Pratiksha shows the new criteria extend several known results. The work extends Montel-style compactness thinking into territory where derivatives of all orders interact across many variables at once.
arxiv-2606-24509:
Platonov, Bazhenov, Eremeev, and Prokhorenkova re-run the graph foundation model race with a fair finish line. Graph structured data powers fraud detection, recommendation, and science. Such models for node property prediction have multiplied. Each was evaluated under different settings, though, making published comparisons unreliable against each other and against ordinary graph neural networks.

A rigorous recheck of nine graph foundation models, against strong, well tuned graph neural network baselines, supplies the missing common ground in 2026. Only the most recent foundation models, built on the prior data fitted networks paradigm, outperform the tuned baselines on performance. They pay for the win with higher inference cost. Earlier foundation models do not clear the bar their claims implied. Platonov's team delivers the field a yardstick. Node level graph foundation models can win, but only the newest designs; anyone claiming otherwise must now beat a well tuned classical baseline.
arxiv-2606-24909:
Jaehwan Kim studies when local closure rules on overlapping finite universes can be glued into one global closure without adding consequences. Each chart of an atlas carries its own closure operator. Repeatedly applying the local operators to whatever parts are visible generates the atlas closure, the smallest global closure extending them all. An obstruction is a consequence this propagation creates inside a chart that the chart's own operator does not validate. The main theorem ties everything to that notion.

A finite closure atlas has a conservative global realisation exactly when no chart visible obstruction occurs, and then the atlas generated closure is itself the realisation. The condition is finite and directly computable. Kim also records an indexed representation layer behind the terminology, and shows that deleting separating theories from a reduced indexed space can create spurious consequences.
arxiv-2606-25309:
Relaxed versions of polymer flow models allow small defects, and the question is which defects physics permits. Sai Peng proves sharp criteria in 2026 for two standard viscoelastic models, Oldroyd-B and the finitely extensible FENE-P, whose elastic state must stay inside a positive cone or a bounded domain. Writing the polymer configuration in logarithmic variables makes the constraint automatic. An exact identity then isolates the work done by each defect channel, with pressure and mean modes removed from the momentum balance.

For states matching the residuals, energy and entropy admissibility becomes equivalent to one signed work inequality, sharper than simply adding the two budgets. Peng extracts the optimal pointwise cost, the unique best aligned minimiser, and ready to use exclusion tests. One test, a shear layer of finite thickness, fails because its pressure free work outruns the available budget.
arxiv-2606-25509:
Self driving stacks increasingly pair a fast planner with a slow language model adviser, but asking the adviser every frame is too expensive, and fixed schedules ask at the wrong moments. Sining Ang and colleagues cast that choice as a resource aware decision problem in 2026. Their gate decides frame by frame whether to query the slow system, reuse its last guidance from cache, or drop it entirely. A recurrent backbone built for long horizons makes the call, trained first by supervision and then by compute aware reinforcement tuning.

Bolted onto two different driving architectures, the gate raised closed loop scores while cutting average end to end latency by about sixty percent in one benchmark. In the second it nudged the driving score up and lifted average speed by roughly a quarter. The gains come from spending slow reasoning only where it pays.
arxiv-2606-25909:
Isla Globus-Harris and Daniel Karney build an economic model of carbon offsets, credits bought to compensate for emissions elsewhere, that accounts for ripple effects across the whole economy. Most offset debates study the offset market in isolation. In a general equilibrium model, by contrast, prices and activity in other markets shift too, and those shifts can feed back into total emissions and welfare.

Raising the offset price turns out to have an ambiguous effect on both aggregate emissions and welfare in their model. Under many parameter choices offsets are over-credited relative to the emissions they truly avoid, though under-crediting also occurs. Neither of the two standard accounting metrics is a sufficient guide to welfare once equilibrium effects are included. The analysis also identifies four margins along which offsets respond to payments, one of them not previously described.
arxiv-2606-26009:
Philipp Grohs and Davide Nobile ask whether variational Monte Carlo is robust. The method hunts quantum ground states by stochastic energy minimization. Neural wave functions like FermiNet have revived interest in it. Trouble hides in the estimators. Local energy and gradient estimates can be heavy-tailed. The nodal geometry of the wave function, where it crosses zero, governs that behaviour.

Broad ansatz classes make the problem concrete. For Slater-Jastrow wave functions with flexible orbitals, the estimators generically lack higher moments. General analytic ansätze admit only weak moment bounds. Precise thresholds separate the regimes, and nodal structure decides which side a model lands on. A robust variant answers the diagnosis. PS-Clip-VMC clips both the local energy and the gradient variable. It provably converges in the weak-moment regime, in expectation and with high probability. Early FermiNet tests on atoms up to eighteen electrons look markedly sturdier.
arxiv-2606-26109:
Jennifer Haase and colleagues test whether language models can hold a clinical persona steady. Simulated patients are used for research and training in mental health care. Personas for eating disorders anchor the study, each grounded in one of five published case vignettes. Six models play the patients across multi-turn conversations. Self-reports and independent observer ratings both score the performances. A validated eating disorder questionnaire with known target scores supplies the ground truth.

Stability turns out to be the wrong worry. Models barely vary at all. Accuracy is the failure: every model overshoots severity by a wide margin. Behavioural items, like dietary restraint, get differentiated by case. Cognitive and emotional items, like body dissatisfaction, pin at the ceiling for every case. Extra conversation makes the overshoot worse, not better. Moderate illness has no representation in these models, the team concludes. They can portray severe pathology only, a missing middle.
arxiv-2606-26309:
Collin Cademartori builds a tool for finding out what your data failed to tell you. In observational studies, nobody controls what gets measured. Key quantities often stay too uncertain for firm conclusions. Variance deltas ask a sharper question: which missing pieces, if observed, would shrink the uncertainty most? His interactive system answers from a Bayesian posterior, without new data collection.

Unobserved quantities are organized into a tree of candidate subsets. Each subset is ranked by how much of the target's uncertainty it explains. The system builds candidates from minimal user input. Interactive splitting and merging let analysts steer the search toward plausible, collectible information. Two demonstrations show the reach: a simulated treatment effect with a hidden confounder pattern, and real polling data with many bias sources. Explanations of uncertainty, not just its size, become the product.
arxiv-2606-26409:
Brandon Roach and colleagues test whether skipper CCDs survive radiation damage at the cold temperatures where they actually operate. These silicon detectors re-measure the same charge many times to reach extremely low noise. Earlier damage tests ran at room temperature.

Proton irradiation at cryogenic temperature let the team track transfer losses, dark current, hot pixels, and charge traps in place. After doses equal to about ten years at the Sun-Earth L2 point, the sensors kept excellent performance. The result is the first proof that these p-channel devices stay radiation-hard under realistic deep-space conditions. It supports their use in future photon-starved astronomy instruments.
arxiv-2606-26709:
Ziqi Wang and Ronald de Haan pin down the exact difficulty of checking distributed knowing how. Knowing-how logics describe agents' abilities to reach goals by acting. In the distributed version, a group jointly knows how to achieve something. Model checking asks whether a given system and formula fit together. Planners in artificial intelligence rely on such checks.

Wang and de Haan prove the problem is complete for a complexity class built on polynomial time with many calls to an NP oracle. Their algorithm first computes where the inner formula holds. It then runs a fixed-point procedure for the group know-how operator, avoiding explicit construction of the group's huge action set. Completeness means the problem is exactly as hard as that class allows. No substantially faster general algorithm should be expected.
arxiv-2606-26909:
Aidan Steineman, Samuel Awelewa, and Maxim Dzero compute how d-wave superconductors respond nonlinearly to light. In d-wave materials, the pairing gap changes sign with direction, unlike the uniform gap of classic superconductors. Shining light can, in principle, strengthen the gap temporarily; that Eliashberg effect is established in uniform-gap materials. Whether it survives in d-wave systems was open.

A self-consistent quasiclassical theory supplies the answer. Near the critical temperature, the light-induced correction to the pairing strength is zero at leading order, at every drive frequency. The redistribution channel that enhances uniform superconductors is suppressed by an extra power of the small gap. Third-harmonic generation, another nonlinear response, is dominated by charge-density fluctuations rather than the pairing amplitude mode, except near one narrow resonance window.
arxiv-2606-27209:
Fatmi and colleagues settle when a standard distance between probabilistic systems behaves continuously. The bisimilarity distance measures how differently two states of a labelled Markov chain can behave. Small wobbles in transition chances can make that distance jump, which threatens models fitted from real data. The authors earlier introduced robust bisimilarity as a route to continuity at distance zero. In 2026, necessity is the new question, in the full version of a conference work.

Robust bisimilarity proves both needed and enough at zero distance. Extending robustness beyond bisimilar pairs yields a complete account of continuity everywhere. A polynomial-time algorithm decides continuity from that account. Experiments show the decision step adds minimal cost over computing the distance itself. Practitioners using estimated transition chances gain a cheap check for when distance values can be trusted under noise.
arxiv-2606-27309:
Belrhali, Poisson, and Renaux-Petel recast early-universe correlation calculations in Laplace space. Cosmological correlators record how primordial ripples relate across points, but computing them means nested time integrals over wiggly mode functions. Deep inside the horizon, each mode acts like a flat-space plane wave. Each curved-space mode is resolved by a Laplace transform into such waves, dressed by a geometry kernel. In 2026, time integrals then collapse onto flat-space ones, with simple diagram rules to match.

The test case is a massive single exchange between ripples. In Laplace form, its energy singularities stand out plainly. The result evaluates in closed form as one fast series, valid across the whole kinematic range with no patching. Diagram rules turn curved-space graphs into flat-space counterparts integrated against the kernels. Concept and computation both simplify. The approach promises light for correlator problems in nearly any early-universe theory.
arxiv-2606-27609:
Autonomous agents often cannot radio their status to partners or controllers. Physical limits or mission rules may block communication entirely. Andres Enriquez Fernandez and John Bird ask whether actions alone can reveal an agent's state. An observer can watch what an agent does even when no messages arrive. Their work trains control policies that make this watching easier.

The team uses reinforcement learning to shape the policies. The training reward includes a score for how well an estimator can recover the state from actions. Policies with this reward become more observable. Simulations of the trained agent confirm the effect. In an aircraft tracking problem, one such policy was found. It improved state estimation a great deal. It also had minimal impact on normal task performance. The result suggests coordination may be possible from action watching alone.
arxiv-2606-27709:
Fine-tuning a chatbot for social warmth can backfire. Recent work shows warmth training degrades factual reliability and increases sycophancy. Austin Cheung and Yi Yang investigate another failure mode in 2026. Warmth fine-tuning also weakens adversarial safety. Models become easier to jailbreak and more likely to produce harmful output. The authors ask whether this is inherent to empathy or an artifact of data design.

Their answer is a persona-driven rewriting pipeline. User turns are rewritten under a low-agreeableness persona. Assistant replies stay warm and de-escalating. Three experiments on four models test the approach. Jailbreak susceptibility and harmful output rates fell relative to generic warmth fine-tuning. Conversational warmth was preserved. Probing of internal representations adds suggestive evidence. The conditioning reduced the geometric alignment between warmth and compliance directions in latent space. Safer empathetic tuning seems achievable through data design alone, the authors argue.
arxiv-2606-27809:
The quantum geometric tensor is a basic property of quantum states. Its eigenvalues say more than simple summaries like the trace. They describe scale, anisotropy, and effective rank. Mingpu Jiang and Jianhui Zhou study how these values are distributed in 2026. Their setting is random Hamiltonians of finite size that depend on parameters. Such random geometry arises in disordered and chaotic systems.

Exact results are derived for the first two nontrivial cases. Systems of size two and three are solved in closed form. The size-three case already shows true shape fluctuations. A broader description follows. It covers any finite system size and any number of parameters. Computer simulations verify the proposed distributions. The work gives the field exact benchmarks to test against. It also gives a practical frame for random quantum geometry in finite systems, with links to condensed matter and topological phases.
arxiv-2606-27909:
Avni Mittal extends the social deduction game Werewolf in 2026 to test theory of mind in language models. Standard tests are dyadic, with every cue pointing to one hidden side. A model can score well through language priors alone. Mittal adds a Jester, a third faction that wins by being voted out, so suspicion helps it and play involves three opposing utility functions.

Sixty games were run on three frontier models, with self-learning switched on and off. The Jester won sixty to seventy percent of games, while Werewolves never exceeded twenty percent. The strongest model, GPT-4.1, saw its wolves vote the Jester out on day one in most games, a self-defeating move. Self-learning helped DeepSeek and Llama but hurt that model, with the cost landing on Villagers. Only DeepSeek learned to look suspicious without looking intentionally suspicious.
arxiv-2606-28009:
A Gibbs point process models particles interacting in continuous space through a potential. Andreas Göbel and five colleagues prove strong structural results in 2026 for such processes. Analyticity of the pressure, uniqueness of the infinite-volume Gibbs measure, and several forms of mixing are established up to a spectral threshold. The hard-sphere model is the leading application.

For each fixed dimension, the bounds improve on classical ones. As dimension grows, the improvement grows exponentially fast, a first of its kind. An optimal mixing time bound is proved for heat-bath dynamics of hard spheres. It matches the maximum density Parisi and Zamponi predicted for rapid mixing. Some repulsive potentials have an infinite spectral threshold, so their processes provably show no phase transition at any activity. In dimensions eight and twenty-four, such a potential has the E8 and Leech lattices as ground states.
arxiv-2606-28209:
Rafayel Teymurazyan, in a solo 2026 paper, studies free boundaries, the moving edges where a spreading substance stops, in diffusion problems whose equations are both degenerate and singular. He looks at minimizers, functions that make an energy-like quantity as small as possible, for a functional mixing slow diffusion with a singular reaction term.

Teymurazyan proves that the free boundary is rectifiable, meaning it is almost everywhere as well behaved as a smooth surface of one lower dimension, rather than a wild fractal set. His argument rests on a pointwise bound for the gradient of the minimizer, which yields an integrability property. That property combines with an estimate of the Hausdorff dimension of part of the zero set to give the result.
arxiv-2606-28509:
Sukhachov, Zhu, Banyas, Tan and Alexandradinata study how light can push an electric current through certain disordered materials without any battery. This bulk photovoltaic effect, where light alone drives current inside a crystal, interests physicists looking for new solar and sensor materials. Their materials are topological, meaning their electronic states have a protected global structure that disorder cannot easily destroy.

At the centre of their account sits a vortex, a swirling pattern, in the phase of the light-absorbing step between electron bands. Such swirls must exist in materials with a nonzero Chern number, a count of that global structure. The swirls strengthen a sideways scattering of electrons off impurities, producing a current that depends on the material class, the defect type and the light's polarization. Case studies cover several systems, including layered graphene, and the authors outline experiments combining light measurements with defect control.
arxiv-2606-28709:
Derek Frydel, writing alone, links two descriptions of restless particles that are usually kept apart. Active particles, self-propelled specks confined by hard walls, pile up at the walls and can end up adsorbed there because their motion persists in one direction. Separately, first-passage theory asks whether a particle starting at one wall reaches the far wall before returning.

Comparing the forward and backward equations head-on in position-velocity space, Frydel derives exact links between the steady distributions and these splitting probabilities. The steady density turns out to come from the spatial derivative of the splitting probability, and the wall share of adsorbed particles is encoded in wall splitting probabilities. The bridge holds for run-and-tumble, active Brownian, and active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particles, in any spatial dimension.
arxiv-2606-28809:
Wang, Cullen, Raimondi and Culcer build a more complete theory of how electrons behave in disordered crystals under a steady electric field. Their focus is inter-band coherence, the quantum mixing between different energy bands, which shapes effects such as the anomalous Hall effect, where a sideways current appears without a magnetic field. Common approximations skip crossing scattering paths, yet those paths contribute at the same order as the intrinsic band effects they compete with.

Working in the length gauge with disorder as Gaussian white noise, the team carries impurity scattering to fourth order. The collision term splits into self-energy corrections, ladder-type vertex changes and crossed interference pieces. Disconnected pairings are removed to avoid double counting. Applied to a two-dimensional massive Dirac model, the method yields lifetimes, relaxation times and conductivities. Crossed processes added a Hall contribution alongside the intrinsic one, while one crossed term cancelled exactly.
arxiv-2606-29009:
Rutgers and Singh study causal estimators built as chains of regressions, where each stage's predicted values become the outcomes fed into the next stage. Such recursive designs arise in time-varying treatment effects, surrogate-based effects and mediation analysis. Three standard estimators compete in this setting: the recursive plug-in, recursive balancing weights, and recursive doubly robust versions.

With every stage fitted by ordinary least squares, all three coincide exactly in any finite sample. That holds whether or not the models are correct. Chained regression on generated outcomes is thus numerically the same as chained balancing of generated regressors. With ridge-penalised weights, the doubly robust method becomes a backward recursion blending penalised and least-squares fits stage by stage. The least-squares weight decays geometrically as periods grow. So the cross-sectional intuition, that bias correction pulls toward least squares, weakens over longer horizons.
arxiv-2606-29309:
Choi and Vallée count a family of combinatorial objects called toric-colorable seeds, using a new method based on binary matroids. These seeds arise in the study of toric topology, and earlier counts fixed the Picard number, a measure of complexity, at four. The authors organise the relevant matroids by contraction type and enumerate certain subcomplexes with a dynamic programming algorithm.

The main computation walks through the mod-2 kernel of an incidence matrix using a Gray code, an ordering that changes one bit at a time. Their headline result: there are exactly 198,846 seeds in the mod-2 toric-colorable family, with Picard number five and dimension four, and they verify that all of them are indeed toric-colorable. The same framework also reproduces the earlier Picard number four enumeration, much faster than the previous method.
arxiv-2606-29409:
Gahramanov, Hırlı, Kanber, and Rosengren derive a new beta integral, a formula that gives the value of a certain hard integral in closed form. Their route runs through supersymmetric gauge theory, a physics framework that pairs each known particle with a partner. They compare partition functions, which summarize a theory on a curved space, computed in two dual ways. The space here combines real projective space with a circle.

Equality of the two partition functions forces the new identity to hold. The authors stress that this integral does not seem to come from shrinking a known lens space result. That makes it a genuinely new member of the basic hypergeometric beta integral family. Such identities feed work on supersymmetric dualities, integrable models, and special functions. The result links a physics calculation to a concrete statement in pure mathematics.
arxiv-2606-29509:
Dengis, Dupont, Schlagheck, and Goldman introduce a way to build vortex NOON states for ultra-precise rotation sensing. A NOON state puts all particles into a mix of two opposite options at once, here two vortex modes with opposite circulation. Such states can reach the Heisenberg limit, the best precision quantum physics allows.

Their setting is cold atoms in a slightly uneven two-dimensional harmonic trap. Single-particle orbitals give an effective two-mode Bose-Hubbard model. In the self-trapping regime the NOON states become spectrally isolated, but they form far too slowly to use. Two acceleration strategies fix that. Geodesic counterdiabatic driving works for small particle numbers, while resonance- and chaos-assisted tunneling works at larger numbers. Both produce the states on experimentally relevant timescales with near-unit fidelity. An interferometric protocol then uses their rotation sensitivity to detect tiny external rotations.
arxiv-2606-29709:
Yu and seven colleagues present Bash-Commenter, a model that writes comments for Bash scripts. Bash, the common Linux shell language, allows great syntactic freedom, and its scripts often lack comments. Existing generators struggle with scarce training data and loose model grasp of Bash semantics.

Their system builds on LLaMA-3.1-8B. A new dataset of complex, multi-line Bash scripts addresses the data gap. Continual pre-training, then supervised fine-tuning, strengthens the model's grasp. A final stage, Syntax-Aware Preference Optimization, builds preference pairs by applying single atomic edits to a script's abstract syntax tree, creating subtly wrong variants. On single-line and multi-line test sets, Bash-Commenter outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on standard text metrics, and human plus model evaluations rate its comments best.
arxiv-2606-29809:
Faujdar and Kadvani benchmark how well hallucination detection works without a GPU. The most accurate detectors need GPU-heavy inference, or full white-box access to the generating model. The authors test five lightweight, CPU-feasible methods built on public models, from simple overlap scores to a natural language inference detector.

Evaluation spans all three HaluEval tasks: question answering, dialogue, and summarisation, with two thousand test instances each. Each method is calibrated on a held-out validation split first. No single method dominates; performance depends heavily on the task. An ensemble performs best on question answering, the inference detector leads on dialogue, and all five methods fall to near-random on summarisation.
arxiv-2606-30009:
Bochen Lin, Jianxiang Yu, Jiayi Wu, Lin Qi, Huang Lu, and Xiang Li hunt anomalies in text-attributed graphs. In such networks, each node carries a piece of text. Paper abstracts and product descriptions are typical examples. Detection supports fraud checks and academic integrity reviews. A node can look normal alone yet clash with its neighborhood. Earlier methods largely missed that relational signal.

The authors recast detection as a semantic consistency problem. A node is checked against the text and structure around it. Trouble can come from a wording mismatch or structural deviation. Their framework, N2NSC, fuses information along two complementary paths. A language model can then use both wording and local structure. Across eight datasets, N2NSC consistently beats the strongest existing methods. The authors also release their code publicly.
arxiv-2606-30209:
Garima Jain and a large multi-center team release a dataset for AI diagnosis of breast cytology slides. Fine needle aspiration cytology samples cells through a thin needle. Pathologists grade the samples in five categories, C1 through C5. Training AI on whole-slide images needs many expert-labeled examples. This 2026 collection gathers them from tertiary centers across India.

The prospective dataset covers three hundred twenty-one patients. It holds four hundred seventy whole-slide images in total. Two standard stains split the slides between them. Scans were made at forty times magnification in a standard format. Most slides contain annotated regions verified by experts. Those regions yield over seven thousand labeled image patches. The release adds annotation files, metadata, and inspection code. At roughly nine hundred fifty gigabytes, it is hosted on Zenodo.
arxiv-2606-30309:
Kazi Rafat and six colleagues grade rehabilitation exercises by computer from three-dimensional joint data, so patients can train at home. Correct form restores function after diseases like Parkinson's or back injury. Expert supervision is costly and often unavailable to patients. RGB-D cameras capture joint motion during home practice. Their system reads those point clouds directly.

A curve-based feature step enriches the point cloud information. Axial self-attention lets the model weigh important joints and their roles. Assessment then scores how well each routine was performed. The system beats existing approaches on three rehab datasets. They cover varied movements and patient groups. Small model size keeps inference fast on modest hardware. Generalization to similar routines sharing joints is also reported. The authors stress practical relevance for remote monitoring programs.
arxiv-2606-30509:
Mark Rhee, Jamie Simon, and Dhruva Karkada compare two optimizers on the simplest learning problem that still shows representation learning. Matrix factorization fits a target matrix as a product of two factors. Gradient descent creeps through it saddle by saddle from small starts. Each singular direction escapes the origin slowly, largest first. The Muon optimizer behaves differently, they show. Its dynamics are additive rather than multiplicative.

Muon learns all top modes at the same rate. Smaller modes converge before larger ones. It also stays stable past gradient descent's learning-rate ceiling. That frees the step size from the problem's condition number. Exponential annealing then gives rapid convergence. After alignment, Muon conserves a different balance quantity than gradient flow. Both still reach the balanced solution from tiny initialization. Alignment rates are derived for simple settings. They predict the rates seen in general experiments. A two-step schedule achieves near-perfect alignment.
arxiv-2606-30609:
Haoran Jin and four colleagues address two failure modes of sparse autoencoders, tools that unpack language-model activations into sparse, readable features. As dictionaries grow, coherent concepts split across several latents, a flaw called feature splitting. Other features get absorbed, gaining odd exceptions that make them unreliable. Both flaws trace back to inconsistent assignment: the same concept lands on different latents in different samples.

Their remedy, C2R, adds cross-sample consistency regularization during training. It penalises the joint firing of latents that point in similar directions. This pushes each concept toward one shared latent across the whole batch. Wide evaluation shows C2R reduces both splitting and absorption. Crucially, rebuild quality stays intact: the autoencoder still reproduces the original activations faithfully. The authors present this as a fix that improves interpretability without hurting model performance.
arxiv-2606-30709:
Woernle Frank, Vladimir Fedosov and Artemiy Grinenko present Hierarchical Global Attention, a drop-in replacement for attention in pretrained long-context language models. Attention over very long inputs is costly because every past token's keys and values must be stored and fetched. Their method changes only how tokens are retrieved: the pretrained weights stay untouched and nothing is retrained.

Retrieval works in two levels. Compact chunk summaries nominate promising regions; group-level routing refines the choice before exact attention runs on the selected tokens alone. The full history can live in RAM or fast disk storage, while only a small working set reaches the graphics card. On a thirty-billion-parameter Qwen model running on one consumer graphics card, the model handled a sixty-four-thousand-token context. Routed attention stayed within a few hundredths of a nat of dense attention while fetching about three percent of tokens.
arxiv-2606-31009:
Longyu Qing and Jorge Viñals build a field theory for liquid crystals made of wormlike chains. In the nematic phase the chains align. The questions: how do density and alignment couple, and what sets the elastic constants and defect core sizes? They combine Maier-Saupe orientational interactions with an excluded-volume term for solvent-mediated effects, within self-consistent field theory. From the free energy they build a unified picture of nematic states, including coexistence with the isotropic phase and its stability limit.

Strong density-order coupling can destabilise the nematic state, at a threshold set by the ratio of the two interactions. Director distortions couple only at higher order. More chain flexibility suppressed twist and bend elasticity while barely touching splay, flipping the system from bend-dominated to splay-dominated. The theory's correlation lengths explain the director patterns around a +1/2 defect core.
arxiv-2606-31109:
Ye and ten colleagues introduce InfiniVerse, a pipeline that generates long driving scenes for training and testing self-driving systems. The scenes must look real, stay consistent over time, and follow a chosen route. Video generators alone drift and lose 3D structure. Geometry-driven pipelines stay consistent but depend on strong map priors.

InfiniVerse starts from a single multi-view frame. It first rebuilds a 3D occupancy grid, a blocky map of what fills space. The grid then grows step by step along any chosen trajectory. A video diffusion model turns the coarse grid into realistic video. A sketch-and-refine loop feeds the video back to sharpen the occupancy grid, so image and geometry improve each other. On the Waymo Open Dataset and nuScenes, the system reached an FID of 6.4 and an FVD of 67.97, ahead of prior methods in duration and stability.
arxiv-2606-31809:
Xu presents quantum Stokes matrices for noncommutative meromorphic differential systems with a pole of any order. Near an irregular singular point, a solution's asymptotic expansion changes from sector to sector. Stokes matrices record those jumps, but they are transcendental and hard to study head-on.

Xu defines quantum versions of these and proves they satisfy natural quantum exchange relations. The rules let the matrices be read as an associative algebra homomorphism. That homomorphism is a deformation quantization of the classical Riemann-Hilbert-Birkhoff map, viewed as a Poisson map for meromorphic links. The representation theory of these quantum algebras may now be brought to bear on asymptotic problems for general meromorphic systems.
arxiv-2608-00309:
Zaki and co-authors introduce OrEdge for anomaly detection in distributed software systems. Existing tools lean on attention- and graph-based designs. Those designs are computationally expensive and large. OrEdge uses orthogonal-domain temporal representations instead. It jointly reads logs, metrics, and traces from a system.

Its OrEdgeCore module rebuilds signals in an orthogonal domain. That captures recurring temporal patterns while damping transient noise. Tests ran on three real-world microservice data sets. Detection stayed competitive with far larger rival models. The reconstruction model holds at most 9.6K parameters, versus 20K to 143K for rivals. On Raspberry Pi hardware, inference ran sub-second. Latency fell by over an order of magnitude versus prior tools. Ablations back each design component.
barbara-blomberg-volume-09:
Three years jump by before Volume 9 of Barbara Blomberg, by Georg Ebers, lands in Brussels. Ebers gives Barbara a small house in Saint Gery, a modest quarter, where she lives with her husband and their two sons. The splendor she once pictured on the drive to Landshut has not come her way at all in this volume.

Chapter X studies the city she actually got. Below, the river Senne and its canals serve rich citizens, skilled artisans, and common folk around a famous market place and Town Hall. Above, on the hill, stands the vast Brabant palace of Emperor Charles, beside a park that merges into the forest of Soignies. The Cathedral of St Gudule towers over the slope. Barbara's small share of that grandeur is the measure of her story's turn.
bateson-mendel-principles-1909:
William Bateson was a Cambridge biologist who became the loudest English champion of Gregor Mendel's newly rediscovered laws of inheritance. His 1909 book Mendel's Principles of Heredity gathers his lectures and papers for a wide scientific audience. Bateson even coined the word genetics for the new science.

He shows how traits in peas, poultry, and other bred stock split and recombine in fixed ratios across generations. He defends Mendel's rules against older ideas of blending inheritance with case after case. The book sold Mendelism to the English-speaking world and trained its first geneticists. He writes as a missionary for a science still fighting for a hearing.
berkeley-new-theory-vision-1709:
George Berkeley, a young Irish scholar, published An Essay Towards a New Theory of Vision in 1709. It was his first major work, written when he was only twenty-four. The question sounds simple: how do we see distance, size, and place? Berkeley's answer upset the settled teaching of his day.

He argues that distance, magnitude, and situation are not seen at all, in the strict sense. The eye gives us light and color; touch and habit teach us what those signs mean. Sight, for Berkeley, works like a language learned in childhood. The essay opened his path to immaterialism, the claim that being means being perceived. Its clarity still startles.
bernard-sermons-advent-christmas-1909:
John Hedley translated Bernard's sermons for Advent and Christmas into English in 1909. Bernard preached these sermons to his monks at Clairvaux in the twelfth century, marking the opening weeks of the church year. Advent, the season of waiting for Christ's coming, drew some of his most tender preaching.

The sermons treat Christ's coming in three ways: in history at Bethlehem, in the soul by grace, and in glory at the end. Bernard moves between close reading of Scripture and warm address to his hearers. His honeyed style, which earned him the name mellifluous doctor, is at its gentlest here. Hedley's translation gave English readers the devotional Bernard, the preacher of longing and joy, rather than the controversialist of the letters.
bogoras-chukchee-1904-1909:
Waldemar Bogoras spent years among the Chukchi people of far northeast Siberia, and this large study came out in 1909. His work formed part of the Jesup work in the North Pacific. The texts were set down word for word as they were told to him. He lived with the people he wrote about and learned their tongue. He also made long trips by sled and boat along the coast.

The pages cover daily life, kin ties, tales, and rites in close detail. A long share deals with shamans, spirits, and the cures and songs they used. It stays a key firsthand source for the folk ways of the Chukchi.
carrington-eusapia-palladino-1909:
Hereward Carrington tests a famed seer at close range in Eusapia Palladino and Her Phenomena, out in 1909. Palladino was a stout dame from Naples whose sittings shook the age. Tables rose, hands grasped guests, and strange stuff seemed to flow from her frame. Carrington sat through long runs of tests in Naples with peers from the chief band for such study.

He grants fraud in part, yet holds a strange rest stands. His tale is tense, fair, and full of night by night notes. The book is the best close tale of the most fought seer.
chinesische-alchimie-separatabdruck-1909:
Th. Hiortdahl of Kristiania wrote a German study of Chinese alchemy, issued in 1909 as an offprint from a journal for the history of chemistry. He warns that Chinese alchemical writings, unlike Greek and Arab ones, were still barely known in translation. His essay is a first attempt at the main contrasts, drawn in broad strokes.

Greek alchemy, following Berthelot, began with Egyptian metalworkers and their gold-coloured alloys. Mercury stood at its centre. China's art began centuries earlier, Hiortdahl argues, and aimed from the start at immortality. An elixir healing all disease and lengthening life was its goal. Cinnabar and the red and yellow arsenic minerals, realgar and orpiment, were its starting materials. The two traditions wanted different things from fire.
cia-0000008009:
South Vietnam had existed for barely a year when CIA analysts weighed its possible course in March 1955. Ngo Dinh Diem led the new state after Vietnam split at Geneva in 1954. Armed religious sects, refugees from the north, and communist cadres all tested his rule.

The paper asks whether Diem's government could survive and what might bring it down. Washington was beginning its long bet on South Vietnam, and judgments like this one guided that choice. Reading it now shows how much uncertainty attended the first step. The estimate stands at the head of a twenty-year American commitment.
cia-0000009709:
Near Muong Ngoi, in Luang Prabang province, stood a Pathet Lao prison, a June 1969 item reports. Muong Ngoi is a river town in northern Laos, reached more easily by boat than by road. Prisons in such country were hidden by distance itself.

Northern Lao camps held a mix of Lao, Thai, and some American prisoners, far from any observer. A located prison gave the map one more fixed point in the uplands. It also told families of the northern missing where to focus hope. The file records that point as reported, in the secret war's quietest corner.
cia-0000009809:
Possible cooperation between American prisoners of war and the Viet Cong, in a Quang district the title cuts short, is weighed in an October 1971 paper. Quang could begin several province names in central Vietnam. The subject itself was among the war's most delicate.

Captivity broke men unevenly, and the line between survival and collaboration was hard to draw from afar. Analysts had to judge reports of cooperation without knowing the pressure behind them. Such papers affected men's reputations and their welcome home. The file preserves that judgment being made carefully, on partial evidence, in the middle of the war.
cia-0000009909:
Forty-two American prisoners were detained by the Viet Cong in the South Vietnam-Cambodia border region, a November 1966 report states. A count of forty-two made the southern prison system look larger than many assumed that early. Border camps held the men beyond easy reach.

Large counts forced officials to rethink the south's place in the captivity story. Hanoi's prisons drew the cameras, but the numbers said the jungle camps mattered greatly. Verifying a count like this took years of cross-checking names. The report preserves the claim at its first filing, when it challenged the accepted picture.
cia-0000012409:
Meeting number twenty-three, July 28, 1961, nears the end of the summer phase's London run. The season's harvest was nearly gathered by then. Weeks of answers on Soviet forces, weapons, and plans stood taken down in numbered order. Soon the colonel would return to Moscow again. Contact would thin to signals and drops until his next trip west gave the handlers another season.

The twenty-third session's record closes July's account of the case. Handlers could tally the summer in sessions, and the tally was remarkable. For readers, the page shows a great operation at its steady, productive peak.
cia-0000013209:
The Viet Cong captured an American near Da Lat, and a CIA report from September 1971 records the incident. Da Lat, in the southern highlands, was a resort town turned garrison in a hard-fought region. Every capture began in chaos: a fight, a flight, a man taken. The reports that followed tried to impose order on that chaos, fixing who, where, and when while the trail was warm.

The report preserves the moment of taking in the file's plain form. Such notes opened the long files that some families waited years to close. For readers, it is the capture report as the war produced them, one by one.
cia-0000013609:
Panama gets a country survey of its own in a CIA paper from April 1967, titled with the country's name alone. The brief gives the republic's Cold War profile in compact form. It covers the canal and the Zone that split the country in two. It also covers the oligarchy that ruled the republic and the National Guard that guarded, and finally replaced, its rulers.

Such one-word briefs were the file's shorthand for a standing watch. This one catches Panama a year before the Guard's coup remade its politics. For readers, it is the isthmus in brief: the waterway, the families, and the soldiers.
cia-0000013909: American prisoners were observed at Hang Co Railroad Station in Hanoi, in a CIA note dated November 1, 1967. A rail station sighting placed prisoners inside the capital itself. Men seen there were being moved through the heart of the north. The note adds the capital's main station to the list of known transit points.
cia-0000014709: Propaganda aspects of the Rosenberg atomic spy trial fill a CIA paper dated June 4, 1952. The paper weighed how the trial played as a public message, at home and abroad. The Rosenbergs' fate had become a worldwide argument by 1952. A paper on its propaganda side shows the agency cared as much about the story as the secrets.
cia-0000015409: Staff comments on letters about unidentified flying objects fill a CIA record dated March 5, 1958. One exchange asked whether the Air Force objected to sending letter writers a copy of the panel report. Major Tacker replied that the Air Force would rather answer the letters itself. The note shows two agencies sorting out who should reply to writers like Major Keyhoe and Mr. Davidson.
cia-0000022309: Gary Powers was awarded the Intelligence Medal, a CIA record dated in 1970 notes. Powers had flown the U-2 shot down over the Soviet Union in 1960, then faced prison and a swap. A medal a decade later was a quiet act of repair. The entry marks his old service honoring a pilot once left to carry blame alone.
cia-0000044009:
A jurist assured a fair trial for the Jesuits' murderers, in a CIA record dated January 4, 1990. A fair trial was exactly what the case's critics doubted was possible. Salvadoran courts worked under pressure from every armed side.

Inside, the judge's pledge of fairness is preserved as given. Such pledges mattered to the foreign governments watching the case. Aid and standing turned, in part, on the trial's good faith. The file keeps the promise at its making, leaving readers to set it beside the verdicts and appeals that the courts produced in the years that followed.
cia-0000049109: An allegation in 1985 tied ARENA, El Salvador's hard-right party, to the assassination of Archbishop Romero. A CIA item from that year preserves the charge, filed with the Truth Commission records. The claim had circulated since the murder itself; putting it in an official file gave it a different weight.
cia-0000049209: A country commentary from 1991 gauges the Salvadoran armed forces' attitude toward the Jesuit case, in a partly blacked-out CIA item. Country commentaries were the station's considered take, written for readers who set policy. This one measures an army's mood toward the case that was remaking its future, month by month.
cia-0000049309: From September 2, 1991, declassified CIA document 0000049309 reports that a five-man jury in El Salvador found Salvadoran Army Colonel Guillermo Benavides guilty. The heading names the verdict and the officer at its center. The short file preserves how the agency noted a court outcome in the Salvadoran case, without adding background beyond the jury's finding itself.
cia-0000049409: Government performance and problems in El Salvador are the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049409, dated June 3, 1982. Marked for the Truth Commission, the paper grades the government in general terms. It is a short declassified item whose heading pairs performance with problems, preserved as a broad agency judgment rather than a study of one policy.
cia-0000104909:
Statement to the Court on Behalf of the Victims of Harold J. Nicholson's Espionage is declassified CIA document 0000104909, dated May 1, 1997 in the catalog. The sample is a letter dated June 2, 1997, to Judge James Cacheris in Alexandria, Virginia. The writer signs as Acting Director of Central Intelligence.

The letter says Nicholson betrayed his friends and colleagues and put their lives in danger. He revealed, or planned to reveal, the names and posts of many CIA officers working in secret. Some could no longer do the assignments they were trained for. Officers under the deepest cover were withdrawn, their missions and lives at risk.
cia-0000112809: List and Information Regarding Individuals Conn is the heading, cut off mid-word and with its date an estimate, on declassified CIA document 0000112809, dated January 1, 1945. The catalog marks the file untitled, then gives this list label. What the individuals were connected with breaks off at Conn in the heading. The brief record preserves the estimate note and the break.
cia-0000117909: Recent Developments in Southeastern Europe is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000117909, dated June 6, 1950. The heading promises fresh events in one region, southeastern Europe, in plain survey words. Recent is the title's own word for how new the events were. The brief record is a regional survey item from the summer of 1950 in the files.
cia-0000119209:
This March 1984 CIA document reports Vietnam's assessment of American policy in its region. The heading adds that Hanoi kept a continuing hope for something from the United States, then breaks off before naming it. Nearly a decade after the war ended, the two countries still had no normal relations.

Hearing the other side's view was the point of such reporting. The document sets out how Vietnamese leaders read Washington's moves and what they still wanted from America. It captures a frozen relationship beginning, very slowly, to thaw, and it shows the agency listening to a former enemy whose choices still shaped Southeast Asia.
cia-0000119709:
A February 1954 CIA paper forecasts probable developments in Argentina. President Peron's second term was running into economic trouble, and his grip on the country was weakening. Eighteen months later the military would drive him from power.

The paper weighs the forces pressing on Peron's government and the paths the country might take. Argentina mattered to Washington as South America's second great power and as a test of populist rule. Reading the forecast now, one can judge how clearly the agency saw the fall coming. It is a period piece from the years when Peronism first rose, broke, and began its long afterlife.
cia-0000124309: Dated April 1951, this CIA document carries two items: the arrival of American prisoners of war in Canton, and their transfer onward, the heading breaking off. The paired items trace the men's movement step by step through Chinese hands during the Korean War. Paired items of arrival and transfer sketch the route men took into the interior, the same route later tracing work would follow in reverse for decades.
cia-0000132209: Situation report 526, from January 1991, notes the European Community boosting aid to frontline states. Those states bore heavy costs from the war on their borders, and European money helped hold the coalition's Arab members steady. The report records the aid decision. Aid to frontline states was coalition maintenance in cash form, paying the neighbors of Iraq and Kuwait to bear refugee, trade, and military burdens without wavering.
cia-0000132409: The situation in Cuba fills a CIA document dated February 1, 1959. It was filed just one month after Castro's victory, which makes it one of the earliest Cuba files in the set. The revolution was only weeks old at that point. Washington was still deciding what the change of power meant, and the document gives the situation as analysts first found it.
cia-0000132509: Chile treating Cuba as a bilateral problem for the United States fills a CIA document dated February 2, 1961. Santiago wanted no part of a joint campaign against Havana. Chile's stance pointed ahead to the split that would open inside the Organization of American States over Cuba. The short document notes the position and what it meant for Washington's hopes of regional unity.
cia-0000135709: Brigade 2506's Spanish archive holds this document, dated 6 February 1961. By February the exile force was in its final training phase, weeks from embarkation. The catalog gives the item no subject heading, so none is invented here. It survives in Spanish in the CIA's declassified release. For students of the Bay of Pigs operation, such dated records mark the brigade's pace in its last full month of preparation.
cia-0000135909: A meeting record in the declassified CIA files, dated 4 May 1954, covers points covered in talks held on the first and second of June, the speaker's name deleted. The record comes from the run-up to the June 1954 coup that removed President Arbenz, the goal of the CIA plan called PBSUCCESS. Small as it is, the sheet documents one task, one report, or one order inside a much larger secret effort.
cia-0000136209: The open CIA files hold a press file dated 1 May 1954 that deals with the Guatemala press file for the eighth through the eleventh of June. The record comes from the run-up to the June 1954 coup that removed President Arbenz, the goal of the CIA plan called PBSUCCESS. Students of the 1954 coup use such records to check later accounts against what was written at the time.
cia-0000136309: Operational Situation Report No. 12, dated late June 1954, tracks PBSUCCESS rebel teams across eastern Guatemala. It reports the combined Johnny-Danny force capturing Chiquimula except the enemy barracks, after a requested air strike failed when both F-47s had mechanical trouble. Other teams report no change, request mortars and 20-mm guns, or stay silent without radios. A resupply flight could not locate its team near Gualan. The report shows an invasion running on patchy information.
cia-0000136609: The catalog dates this Spanish-language 2506 Brigade document to 1 January 1961 and flags the date as estimated. Brigade 2506, the CIA-trained force of Cuban exiles, was in its final training winter. Estimated dates recur at the New Year in this series. The record names no subject for the item. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, as part of the brigade's archive from the months before the Bay of Pigs.
cia-0000136709: The catalog dates this Spanish-language 2506 Brigade document to 3 February 1961, marked as estimated. An earlier summary filled this item with London, Washington, and an alliance against Hitler; that is Second World War material with no place in a 1961 brigade record, and it is removed. What the record supports is a Spanish document of the exile brigade, then in final training, released in the CIA's declassified files.
cia-0000137009: Communists in embassies are violating asylum, the themes in this June 1954 cable charge. Asyleed communists pass arms and money in and out by radio. They conduct propaganda from inside. Carlos Manuel Pellecer sits in the Mexican embassy. He is said to be making tape recordings. The tapes aid subversive propaganda by party remnants. Themes to push are listed. The government is as democratic and just as possible. There are no blood baths. Asyleed communists and common criminals grossly violate asylum's privilege.
cia-0000137109: A Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade documents, dated only to 1960 in the catalog record. The papers are in Spanish, the language of the brigade's Cuban members, who were training that year under CIA direction for the landing that came in 1961. The record states no month or subject for this item. It survives as released through the CIA Reading Room, part of the exile force's early paperwork.
cia-0000137309: NSC Briefing — Cuba, dated 1960, is a declassified CIA briefing paper prepared for the National Security Council, the president's senior advisory body on security policy. Its subject, per the title, is Cuba, in the year when Castro's government broke openly with the United States and Washington began planning against it. Several such Cuba briefings survive in these files. The catalog gives no finer breakdown of this one's contents, so it is described at that level: a dated council briefing, released through the CIA Reading Room.
cia-03190609:
Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 15 September 1957 lists eight items, led by Turkish air force moves near Syria. The bulletin reports combat-ready squadrons and supplies gathered on the Syrian border, pilots assigned for movement to Adana, and crews at Balikesir placed on wartime alert. Anti-aircraft guns there were camouflaged, with crews on a 24-hour alert.

Other items cover an Indonesian round-table conference that had ended. A joint committee was planned for future disputes between the central government and the regions. The brief also covers the Shah of Iran seeking backing for a strong reply to the Soviet Union. It notes possible division among Yugoslav leaders over closer ties with Moscow. A Greek proposal of Commonwealth status for Cyprus is included. Rumors inside the Argentine government and Indian foreign exchange reserves close the contents.
cleopatra-volume-09:
Cleopatra ends in Volume 9 of the novel by Georg Ebers, as news of defeat pours into Alexandria. Ebers sends Gorgias, the architect, to the Forum, where every rumor in the city arrives first. Macedonian citizens crowd the square, trading reports from the fleet and the army that flatly contradict each other in this final volume.

Chapter XXIII follows the swing from hope to ruin within hours. First the news sounds favorable, then comes word of treason and of cavalry and foot soldiers deserting. Antony is seen racing along the quay toward the little palace on the Choma. Grave citizens say honor now demands his death by his own hand, like Brutus. Word soon spreads that he has tried to do exactly that.
conceptions-of-matter-ancient-and-modern:
Conceptions of Matter, Ancient and Modern, by William Robert Lang, is a short lecture on what matter has been thought to be. It opens with the alchemist's quest, quoted from Ben Jonson's play: a book where Moses, Solomon, and his sister wrote of the art. The alchemist sought new substances and the transmutation of one form of matter into others.

His reasoning grew from the farm and garden: seed dies and rises as a plant, so metals in the earth might grow toward perfection, reaching gold at last. The elixir of life and the philosopher's stone were the prizes. At the modern end, Lang reports the atom displaced from its throne: recent work on electricity and radio-activity shows it an aggregation of smaller units, electrons or corpuscles.
constitution-bolivia-2009:
Bolivia adopted a new constitution in 2009 after a constituent assembly and a national vote. It renames the country a plurinational state, honoring the many indigenous nations inside it. Spanish and thirty-six indigenous languages are all official. Part one gives the fundamental bases of the state, then fundamental rights and guarantees, duties, and the court actions that defend those rights.

A president leads the executive. The Plurinational Legislative Assembly, with two chambers, makes laws. Later parts cover the courts, the economy, land and natural resources, and the structure of the state down to village level. At 411 articles it is one of the world's longest constitutions. Rights for nature itself appear in its pages.
constitution-luxembourg-2009:
Luxembourg's constitution began in 1868 and has been revised many times; the hosted text runs through 2009. Early chapters cover the state, its land, and the Grand Duke, for Luxembourg is the world's only grand duchy. A chapter on the freedoms of Luxembourgers and basic rights follows, guarding speech, faith, property, and fair trials.

The Grand Duke heads the state and names the prime minister, who leads the government and must hold the trust of the Chamber of Deputies. The chamber is the single lawmaking house, though a Council of State reviews every bill in a second look. Later chapters cover the courts, local towns, and finance. The text's age shows in its calm, nineteenth-century phrasing.
constitution-poland-2009:
Poland adopted this constitution in 1997, its first full post-communist charter, and the hosted text includes changes through 2009. A preamble recalls both the Christian roots and the wider heritage of the nation. Chapter one founds the republic: a unitary, democratic state based on law. Chapter two protects the freedoms, rights, and duties of persons and citizens at length.

A president heads the state, while a prime minister and cabinet run the government. Parliament pairs the Sejm, the main chamber, with a Senate. Later chapters cover the courts, a Constitutional Tribunal, local self-rule, public finance, and the armed forces. At 243 articles the text is complete and orderly. Polish is the official language, and the charter guards the rights of national minorities.
constitution-venezuela-2009:
Venezuela adopted this constitution in 1999, the first project of President Hugo Chavez, and the hosted text includes changes through 2009. Early titles give basic principles for a federal, democratic republic that calls itself Bolivarian, after the freedom hero Simon Bolivar. Spanish is the official language, with indigenous tongues official for their peoples. A long title covers duties, human rights, and promises in wide detail.

A president leads the executive. The National Assembly is the single lawmaking chamber. The text splits public power five ways, adding an electoral branch and a citizen branch of watchdogs to the classic three. Later titles cover the courts, the economy, and the armed forces. At 350 articles it is long, and it lets voters recall officials mid-term.
corneille-polyeucte-constable-1909:
An Armenian Christian faces a pagan court in Corneille's Polyeucte, given here in Thomas Constable's Harvard Classics translation. Polyeuctus embraces the faith and smashes the idols, knowing the price is death. His wife Pauline, torn between her father, her old love, and her husband's God, carries the play's heart.
