French classical tragedy reaches its religious summit in this drama of conversion and sacrifice. Duty and grace argue in high, ordered verse, as Corneille loved to stage them. The translation joins the library's Le Cid, letting English readers meet both faces of France's first great tragedian.
croce-aesthetic-1909:
Aesthetic as Science of Expression and General Linguistic, published in English in 1909 in Douglas Ainslie's translation, is Croce's foundational work on art. It opens his Philosophy of Spirit, the system that made him Italy's leading philosopher.

Art, Croce argues, is intuition given expression: not copying nature, not decoration, but the mind's first form of knowledge. From that claim he rebuilds the history and theory of aesthetics, treating language and art as one activity. The book's learning is vast and its tone magisterial. It set the terms of Italian criticism for a generation and traveled worldwide.
croce-philosophy-practical-1909:
Philosophy of the Practical, published in English in 1909, is the second volume of Croce's Philosophy of Spirit. After art and expression comes action: this book treats the economic and the ethical as the two practical forms of the spirit.

Croce distinguishes useful action, aimed at single ends, from moral action, aimed at the universal good, and shows how each corrupts the other when confused. Politics, law, and history are drawn into the scheme. The argument is abstract, but its stakes are conduct itself. With this volume, Croce's system covered both knowing and doing in one design.
crowley-777-1909:
Aleister Crowley built a master key to his magic in 1909 and called it 777. The book sets out tables that match gods, planets, signs, and symbols to the thirty-two paths of the Tree of Life. Crowley was then shaping the system he would teach for life.

Row by row, the tables let a student pass from a god to a scent, a stone, a plant, or a verse. The scheme rests on the Jewish Kabbalah as the Golden Dawn had taught it. Workers in the Thelemic line treat 777 as their standard desk book. Few tables of symbols have been thumbed so hard for so long.
crowley-equinox-vol-1-no-09:
Number nine of The Equinox came out in March 1913, the journal's fifth year of life. Crowley's twice-yearly numbers had built a shelf of white volumes by now. The spring issue carries the work of the order into its next phase.

First printings of rites and teachings fill the number, as in each issue before it. The pages show Crowley's school at work in rite, song, and argument. Each number locks one season of that work into the lasting record. Number nine locks the spring of 1913 in its place. One more number would close the great first volume.
davies-mythology-british-druids-1809:
Edward Davies, a Welsh cleric, set out his grand scheme of British druid lore in this book of 1809. He wrote in the Romantic age, when old British roots drew much public zeal. His aim was to trace the druids back to the dawn of faith.

Davies tied the druids to Noah, the flood, and the ark of the Bible. He read old Welsh verse and stone works as proof of one vast rite scheme. Grand and flawed, the book fixed what druidism meant for a whole age of readers. Few books show the age's hunger for old roots so well.
ernest-maltravers-volume-09:
Volume Nine of Ernest Maltravers opens Book the Ninth, the last, of Edward Bulwer Lytton's novel on a fine December afternoon. Lumley Ferrers turns from Lord Saxingham's door, where the knockers are muffled and sickness is in the house. He repents aloud: if ever he loved a woman, he loved Florence, and his lover's stratagem has ended in effects he could not foresee.

Government has offered the place he wanted to Maltravers instead; Lord Vargrave is cross with him; his star is not in the ascendant. In the sickroom, Florence's love turns grateful and clinging, her thought mellowing into religion as the shadows close. A Sophocles motto heads the book: I go, the bride of Acheron. The novel ends its course in this volume.
essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volume-09:
Volume nine of Michel de Montaigne's Essays opens Book Two, in Charles Cotton's translation edited by William Carew Hazlitt in 1877. Montaigne begins with the inconstancy of our actions. Men contradict themselves so strangely, he writes, that judges cannot build a steady character from their deeds. Nero, cruel beyond measure, once wept at signing a death sentence.

Drunkenness gets the second chapter, treated as a gross and brutish vice. A custom of the Isle of Cea, where old men ended their lives at a banquet, follows. Conscience and habit close the set of six chapters. Montaigne tests every moral rule against human variety. Readers get Book Two's opening in full, with the essayist doubting constancy itself and finding practice, not nature, behind most of what men call character.
eucken-life-spirit-1909:
Philosophy itself is the problem at the heart of Rudolf Eucken's introduction, first printed in German and Englished by F. L. Pogson in 1909. Eucken refuses to treat philosophy as a fixed set of facts to hand over. Instead he presents it as work the human spirit must keep doing.

Across a few clear leading lines, he traces how that work went on through the centuries. Doubt and conflict mark the path, since spiritual life rests on no safe, given base. The book asks readers to take part in the search themselves. It served many newcomers as their first door into Eucken's thought.
eucken-problem-human-life-1909:
Great thinkers from Plato onward have each formed a view of what human life is and should be. Rudolf Eucken gathered those views in Lebensanschauungen grosser Denker, a German survey of life views held by major minds. W. S. Hough and W. R. Boyce Gibson translated the work into English in 1909.

Eucken walks through the answers given across the ages, from Greek thought to his own century. He compares each view, notes what it grasps and what it misses, and builds toward his own position. The survey shows how one deep question kept changing shape. It also gives readers a guided tour of Western thought.
europmc-pmc10154209:
Therriault and colleagues model Alzheimer's disease stages from brain scans in a 2023 study, using a staging system first built from autopsy tissue. The Braak system ranks how far tau tangles have spread through the brain. The team applied it to living patients using PET scans with a tau tracer, in a group of more than three hundred people.

They then modeled how blood and scan markers change across those stages. The model links marker shifts to disease progress in life, not just after death. That link helps trials pick patients and track whether drugs work.
europmc-pmc10329209:
Aiken led a large 2023 survey of doctors and nurses who work in US hospitals. The US Clinician Wellbeing Study Consortium backed the work. The team asked 15,738 nurses and 5,312 doctors about stress, burnout, and plans to quit. Burnout means deep work fatigue that harms health and care.

Aiken found that burnout was high and spread across hospital staff. It linked to staff quitting and to worries about patient safety. Staff had low trust that bosses would fix care problems. They ranked more staff and a better work setting above wellness classes for their own health. The team urges bosses to act on staffing and work design first.
europmc-pmc10406609:
Ashuach and colleagues built MultiVI in 2023, a model that joins two kinds of single-cell data. One kind reads which genes a cell has switched on. The other reads which parts of its DNA lie open for use. Each view alone gives a partial picture of the cell.

MultiVI merges both views into one shared profile for each cell. It can even fill that profile for cells where one view is missing. Ashuach built it as a chance-based model that learns from the data. Users can then group cells, spot subtypes, and chart how cells differ. The tool is free through the scvi-tools site. It aims to sharpen work on cheaper, single-view data sets too.
europmc-pmc10501909:
Lu led a vast team in 2023 to build ageing clocks that work across all mammals. The clocks read methylation, small tags on DNA that shift with age. Past clocks fit one species or a few tissues. The team pooled 11,754 samples from 185 mammal species and 59 tissue types.

Their clocks guessed tissue age with very high accuracy, a score above 0.96. Lu found that gaps from true age track death risk in humans. The same gaps shift with calorie limits and with growth gene faults in mice. Age-linked tag sites cluster near genes for growth, cancer, weight, and long life. The work hints that ageing is an old, shared program tied to development.
europmc-pmc10767809:
Rauluseviciute and co-authors marked 20 years of JASPAR in 2024, a free data bank of transcription factor binding profiles. A profile sums up where a factor, a protein that switches genes, grips DNA. JASPAR staff curate each profile by hand and keep the set free of repeats. This is the tenth release of the bank.

The CORE set gained 329 new profiles, a 20% rise. Three old profiles were updated, and 72 past drafts gained firm backing. Rauluseviciute adds a trim step that cuts low-value edges from profiles. Binding site tracks were rebuilt for eight organisms. A new tool lets users pull predicted sites that cross their own genome zones.
europmc-pmc10837209:
Wu, Wu, Chen, and Li review two signal families that build and maintain bone and cartilage in this 2024 paper. Cartilage is the smooth tissue that caps joints. The TGF-beta and BMP families send growth signals that guide bone-forming and cartilage-forming cells. Their signals pass through relay proteins inside the cell, and small shifts in those relays change the outcome.

BMP signals promote bone and cartilage growth at all stages, the review says. TGF-beta signals act in a more stage-dependent way and help keep the bone cell network intact. The two families pull in opposite directions for joint cartilage balance. The authors map the many control layers that tune these signals. They also list human diseases and mouse models tied to faulty signalling, in hopes of guiding bone drugs.
europmc-pmc11111409:
Zuntini and hundreds of co-authors rebuild the family tree of flowering plants from nuclear genes in this 2024 study. Flowering plants, called angiosperms, anchor most land ecosystems and human livelihoods. Past trees rested mainly on the plastid genome, the small genome of the cell's food-making parts. Sampling of species and genes was limited and biased, weakening trust in those trees.

The team built the tree for almost 8,000 genera, about 60 percent of all such groups, using 353 nuclear genes. That is a 15-fold jump in genus sampling over prior nuclear studies. Many older relationships held, but key groups, above all rosids, changed. Dated with 200 fossils, the tree shows explosive early branching that produced over 80 percent of living orders. Bursts returned in the most recent era.
europmc-pmc11180609:
Roohani, Huang, and Leskovec present an AI method that predicts how cells respond to gene tweaks never tried before in this 2024 paper. Testing gene perturbations, meaning switching genes up or down, is central to cancer and regenerative medicine work. The number of possible multi-gene combos explodes far past what labs can test. The team built a predictor to cover that gap.

Their method, GEARS, fuses deep learning with a knowledge graph of gene relationships. It trains on single-cell data from perturbation screens. It can predict outcomes for combos of genes that were never perturbed in any experiment. On a combinatorial screen it scored 40 percent higher precision than prior methods at sorting four interaction types. It also flagged the strongest interactions twice as well. The authors offer it as a guide for designing perturbation experiments.
europmc-pmc11742009:
Jomova, Alomar, Nepovimova, Kuca, and Valko review heavy metal toxicity and human health effects in this 2025 paper. Heavy metals occur naturally in the Earth's crust and persist as pollutants in the environment. People take them in by breathing air and dust, and by eating or drinking tainted food, water, or soil. Their build-up in the body can damage many tissues and organ systems.

Toxicity depends on the metal's properties, dose, route, and duration of exposure, the authors explain. The main harm route is interference with antioxidant defences. Metals bind glutathione and the sulfur groups of defence enzymes such as superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione peroxidase, disabling them. Arsenic is thought to bind thiols directly at critical sites, the sulfur sites on proteins. Alternative routes that generate hydrogen peroxide are also postulated. The review maps effects organ by organ.
europmc-pmc1270009:
Haycraft and co-authors studied two gene switches and cell antenna proteins in 2005. Cilia are tiny hair-like structures built by transport proteins. Those proteins also serve the Sonic hedgehog signal pathway. Gli2 and Gli3 are the switches that pathway controls.

Both switches were found located at cilia themselves. A transport protein called Polaris proved needed for their processing. Without Polaris, Gli3 processing went wrong in mouse limb buds. That failure lifted repression on a target gene, Gli1. Yet Gli1 activity itself stayed intact at molecule level. Haycraft shows transport proteins tune specific switch steps.
europmc-pmc1797809:
Salazar and colleagues tracked in 2007 how dengue virus type 2 moves through the mosquito Aedes aegypti after an infected blood meal. To reach a new human host, the virus must infect the gut, spread through the body, and enter the saliva glands. The wait between meal and possible spread is the extrinsic incubation period.

They used a newly colonized mosquito strain from Chetumal, Mexico. Gut virus levels peaked between seven and ten days after infection, then viral protein and live virus fell while viral RNA stayed stable. Spread from the gut tracked with virus appearing in the trachea, the insect breathing tubes. Virus showed in saliva glands of over a third of mosquitoes by day four, and it built up in nerve tissue throughout the wait.
europmc-pmc1878509:
Aid, Timmusk and co-authors redrew the map in 2007 of a key brain growth gene in mice and rats. The gene makes BDNF, a factor that supports neuron development and the plasticity behind memory, learning, and addiction. Rodent versions of the gene were heavily studied, yet their structure stayed incompletely known.

The team found several new transcript forms with previously unknown starting sections. Both the mouse and rat genes hold eight alternative first exons, meaning start pieces, plus one shared protein-coding final exon. Each transcript splices one of the eight starts onto that coding end. Each start version also shows its own pattern across brain regions and body tissues. Seizures induced by kainic acid, plus shifts in cell calcium and gene-tag removal, tuned the starts differently, showing fine-grained control.
europmc-pmc1892109:
Stahlhut, Swan and co-authors asked in 2007 whether everyday plastic chemicals track with obesity and insulin resistance in American men. Phthalates, used to soften plastics, can block male hormones in rodents and lower testosterone in men. Low testosterone in turn goes with more belly fat and diabetes risk.

The team used a national survey of adult men from 1999 to 2002, measuring six phthalate breakdown products in urine. They modeled those levels against waist size and a standard index of insulin resistance, adjusting for age, race, diet, activity, smoking markers, and kidney and liver function. The abstract frames the study as the first population test of this chain. Its title reports the direction found: higher metabolite levels went with larger waists and stronger insulin resistance in these men.
europmc-pmc1994709:
Caicedo and co-workers mapped DNA variation in domesticated rice in 2007. Rice, Oryza sativa, is among the oldest crops and feeds more people than any other plant. The team compared rice with its wild ancestor, Oryza rufipogon. They sequenced 111 randomly chosen gene fragments across varieties. Their aim was to infer how domestication shaped the rice genome.

They found, genome-wide, an excess of high-frequency derived variants, a pattern not reported in other crops. A simple bottleneck model, where numbers crash during domestication, could not explain the pattern. Models adding selective sweeps, where favoured genes spread fast, fitted better. So did models with population subdivision and gene flow. Strong selection may thus mark variation across the whole genome.
europmc-pmc2065909:
Hoshida and co-workers introduced SubMap in 2007, a method for matching disease subtypes across separate gene studies. Gene expression profiling can reveal molecular subtypes of a disease. But subtypes found in one data set often fail to match those in another, especially across platforms. Supervised models trained on one set can miss real structure in a new set. SubMap instead compares both data sets in both directions.

The method defines a score for how well subtypes correspond, and tests whether that match is significant. It builds on the team's earlier gene set enrichment work. Applied to cancer data sets, SubMap found shared breast cancer subtypes tied to estrogen receptor status. It also found a lymphoma subgroup with similar survival patterns. That match improved the accuracy of a clinical outcome predictor.
europmc-pmc2124509:
Philip Hanson Hiss, adjunct professor of bacteriology, tackled a bench problem in 1905: pneumococcus and streptococcus can look and grow too much alike to tell apart. The usual test, the pneumococcus capsule, fails both ways, since some streptococci carry marked capsules and some pneumococci show none, on artificial media. Hiss looked instead for differences in what the two germs do to their food.

Pneumococci slowly make acid in the alkaline serum. Streptococci do not share that habit in the same way. The study also gives methods for staining capsules. His inulin medium needs care, since spores in the inulin can survive ordinary heating and call for the autoclave. Readers get an advance in telling two dangerous germs apart, won from their feeding habits rather than their shapes.
europmc-pmc2125009:
Alfred E. Cohn asked in 1912 whether the heart's two vagus nerves do the same job, and answered with dog experiments. They do not. Stimulating the right vagus usually arrests every chamber of the heart outright. The left vagus tells a different story.

On the auricles the left nerve's slowing effect is only moderate. Its real power is over conduction between auricles and ventricles. In some dogs it merely stretches the delay between their beats. In others it produces incomplete heart-block. In still others it blocks the path fully, so the auricles beat on while no impulse reaches the ventricles. Rarely, the left nerve blocks the heart's own pacemaker signal. Readers get the two brake pedals of the heart shown to work on different wheels.
europmc-pmc2125209:
Peyton Rous and James B. Murphy of the Rockefeller Institute examined immunity to transplantable chicken tumors in 1914. Resistance in fowls, natural and acquired, behaves strikingly like resistance to transplanted mammalian growths. Nothing in it, they stress, suggests the tumors have a cause outside the tissue itself.

Two resistances must be kept apart. One aims at the tumor cells, foreign tissue to be rejected. A fowl whose tumor has shrunk away holds both. The anti-agent resistance is largely specific: it gives little protection against the agents behind other chicken tumors. Blood passed from resistant fowls into tumor-bearing ones did nothing to the growths. Dried tumor with its agent weakened by heat could not protect against the simple sarcoma. Readers get tumor immunity split into its two strands, a decade before viruses entered the story.
europmc-pmc2125409:
Laura M. Stryker of the Rockefeller Institute hospital grew virulent pneumococci in their own immune serum in 1916 and catalogued how the organisms changed. Five alterations are listed: they clump differently, they lose virulence, they stop forming capsules properly, they become easier for phagocytes to take with normal serum, and their absorption and antigenic behavior shifts.

The changes are real but not permanent: passage through an animal restores the original type. That reversibility speaks to an old dispute. Stryker's virulence tables make the contrast concrete. A subculture carried through normal serum still killed at a millionth of a cubic centimeter, while its immune-serum twin failed to kill at a full cubic centimeter. Readers get bacterial adaptation under immune pressure, documented trait by trait and then undone by one animal.
europmc-pmc2128209:
John W. Churchman and Morton C. Kahn, of Cornell's hygiene department, showed that bacteria act differently in company than alone. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1921. Using a dye-fast strain of Bacillus coli on gentian violet agar, they planted single cells and counted groups side by side and compared what each could do.

A single bacterial cell's behavior toward gentian violet differs at the root from a small group's. Thirty cells planted together grew where single cells could not. The explanation is not simple arithmetic: thirty cells accomplish much more than thirty times what one cell can accomplish. Something in the grouping itself, a communal activity, changes the outcome against the dye. The finding matters wherever laboratory tests on sparse bacteria are used to predict how dense infections will answer a drug.
europmc-pmc2131009:
Jacques J. Bronfenbrenner and Charles Korb measured how fast alcohol destroys the bacteriophage, in the second paper of their series. It appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1925. Precipitating the lytic principle with alcohol is a natural purification step, so its cost in activity needed knowing.

At room temperature, alcohol-precipitated phage loses activity steadily and is totally destroyed between six and twenty-four hours. Precipitated in the cold, it dies much more slowly, and measurable traces survive even four weeks in alcohol. Most activity sits in the precipitate, but the alcohol above it carries some active principle for several days. In all cases the surviving activity remained transmissible in series, as true phage should be. The authors never saw the non-transmissible action d'Hérelle had ascribed to an enzyme. Alcohol inactivation of phage, they conclude, behaves like the alcohol inactivation of certain enzymes and toxins.
europmc-pmc2131109:
Franklin A. Stevens and A. R. Dochez sorted the hemolytic streptococci of erysipelas and scarlet fever into families by their serum reactions. Their paper is the fifth in a streptococcus biology series, in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1926. Strains from each disease were tested for clumping in immune sera raised against the other.

Erysipelas strains clumped in high proportion in erysipelas sera, and a strain reacting with one such serum usually reacted with all. Erysipelas sera caught scarlatinal strains less often, and strains from mixed pus infections only rarely, in one or two sera at most. Strains reacting alike are not necessarily identical, though identical strains occur within each group. The verdict is two compact families: erysipelas strains form one closely related group, scarlatinal strains another, the two related to each other and more distantly to the pyogenic crowd. Diseases that look distinct keep distinct germs.
europmc-pmc2140309:
Jacques Loeb wrote part three of his amphoteric colloids series in 1919, on how acid changes the physical behavior of gelatin. Gelatin solutions swell, thicken, and build osmotic pressure as acid is added. Loeb measured how much bromine from hydrobromic acid the gelatin binds, after washing away the excess acid, and set that count beside the physical curves.

The bromine bound by the gelatin rose and fell in parallel with osmotic pressure, viscosity, and swelling. Acid thus acts by forming gelatin bromide molecules: at its isoelectric point gelatin barely dissolves, while the salt form dissolves freely. The bromine number counts the gelatin molecules made soluble, and so gives the shared root of the physical changes.
europmc-pmc2265709:
Bello, Izergina, Caussinus and Reichert found in 2008 a new mode of brain cell production in the fruit fly Drosophila. In mammalian brains, neural stem cells amplify their output through intermediate progenitor cells that keep dividing. Whether fly brain neuroblasts, the stem-like cells there, do the same was unknown. Using lineage tracing and genetic markers, the team examined remarkably large neuroblast lineages in the dorsomedial larval brain.

These neuroblasts divide asymmetrically to renew themselves, but unlike others they do not pass the differentiation factor Prospero to their smaller daughters. Those daughters keep neuroblast markers and divide repeatedly, acting as intermediate progenitors. Their divisions look symmetrical but are molecularly asymmetrical, segregating fate determinants into one daughter only. This amplification mirrors mammalian neurogenesis, suggesting deep conservation of neural stem cell biology between insects and mammals.
europmc-pmc2289809:
Rafailidis, Mourtzoukou, Varbobitis and Falagas systematically reviewed severe cytomegalovirus infection in 2008 in people with apparently normal immunity. This virus is well known for harming transplant recipients, HIV patients and unborn babies. Its toll on immunocompetent adults had received little attention. Searching major databases for 1950 to 2007, the team gathered reports of severe infection in such patients and examined where it struck and whether antivirals were used.

They found 89 articles covering 290 immunocompetent adults with severe disease. The gut, mainly colitis, and the central nervous system, including meningitis and encephalitis, were the commonest sites. Other manifestations included blood disorders, vessel clots, eye inflammation and pneumonia. Reported practice reserved antiviral treatment for the most severe brain, eye and lung involvement. The authors conclude severe complications in healthy hosts may be less rare than assumed.
europmc-pmc2323709:
The START Trialists' Group reported Trial A in 2008, a UK trial of radiation treatment after surgery for early breast cancer. The standard plan gave 50 gray of radiation in 25 small daily doses. Gray is the unit for absorbed radiation dose. The trial tested whether 13 larger doses could work as well.

Over 2,236 women at 17 centres took part between 1998 and 2002, split among three dose plans. After about five years, cancer returned near the treated site in 3.6% of the standard group. The higher of the two new plans gave 3.5%, a difference the data showed was tiny. The lower new plan, 39 gray, caused fewer late changes in breast appearance. The authors concluded breast tumors respond to dose size much like normal tissue does.
europmc-pmc2360509:
Lloyd and colleagues measured how the UK public values life with metastatic breast cancer in 2006. Metastatic means the cancer has spread beyond the breast. Health economists use utility scores, where 1 is full health and 0 is death, to compare treatments fairly.

The team wrote plain descriptions of disease states, from stable cancer on treatment to cancer growing again, plus six side effects. One hundred members of the public rated each state using the standard gamble, a choice task that reveals how much risk people accept to avoid a state. Stable disease scored 0.72 on the utility scale, and a good response added 0.07 to that value, while progression cut 0.27 from it. Side effects cost between 0.10 and 0.15, with fever from low white cells the worst.
europmc-pmc2397409:
Perez-Iratxeta and Andrade-Navarro built a web tool to read protein shape from light in 2008. The lab method is circular dichroism spectroscopy, which shines twisted light through a protein solution. The way the protein absorbs that light betrays how much of it is coiled into helices or folded into flat strands.

Their method, K2D2, learns from spectra of proteins whose shapes are already known. It arranges those spectra on a self-organised map, a grid where similar spectra sit together, and ties each spot to known shape contents. A new spectrum is placed on the map, and its spot gives the estimate. The free web server returns the shares of alpha-helix and beta-strand, the two main shape elements, plus an error estimate for the prediction.
europmc-pmc2515109:
Rosa and Everaers used computer simulations in 2008 to explain why chromosomes keep to their own territories inside the cell nucleus. When a cell is not dividing, its chromosomes loosen, yet microscope images show each one still occupies a distinct region. Many had assumed some scaffold or protein anchors must hold them apart.

The simulations show no scaffold is needed. A plain model of loosening chromosomes, built only from polymer physics with no fitted values, reproduced the territory shapes seen in human, fruit fly, and yeast cells. The territories persist because long chain molecules stay tangled with themselves and cannot pass through each other. Confined random motion plus these topological limits, meaning the chains cannot cross, is enough to keep chromosomes apart.
europmc-pmc2612009:
Arvidsson, Kwasniewski, Riaño-Pachón, and Mueller-Roeber presented a tool called QuantPrime in 2008 for designing PCR primer pairs automatically at scale. Quantitative PCR measures gene activity, but each assay needs a specific primer pair, and designing hundreds by hand is slow and error-prone. QuantPrime automates the choices, checking specificity against ready-made transcriptomes.

The tool ships with data for 295 species, from model organisms to crop plants, and uses gene structure information such as exon borders and splice variants to place primers well. Parameters are highly customisable, and it runs online or locally. Tests in the model plant Arabidopsis, in barley, and in a green alga gave success rates above 96 percent for designed primer pairs. The framework also extends to probe design for related techniques.
europmc-pmc2631809:
Dowell proposed in 2001 a fresh explanation for the seasonal cycles of infectious diseases: the susceptibility of the host population itself may rise and fall with the seasons. Standard explanations blame weather, how common or strong the pathogen is, or human behaviour. Dowell lists observations those ideas struggle to fit, including outbreaks igniting simultaneously across wide regions at the same latitude.

Pathogens can also be detected during the off-season, yet no epidemic follows. Seasonal timing stays consistent despite wide variation in weather and behaviour. Dowell points instead to the annual light-dark cycle. It acts through the hormone melatonin, whose release pattern tracks day length. Light-driven body change is well documented in mammals. Some is documented in humans too. If such change governs resistance for much of the year, finding and shifting it could prevent and treat a great deal of illness.
europmc-pmc2657209:
Brownlie and co-authors reported in 2009 a hidden benefit that a common insect bacterium, Wolbachia, may give its hosts. Wolbachia lives inside many insects and spreads by bending their reproduction in its favor. Some strains cannot do that trick, yet still spread, which hinted they must pay their hosts something in return.

Fruit flies carrying Wolbachia laid more eggs when their food held too little iron, or too much. Iron is a nutrient both flies and bacteria need, and the bacterium's genes suggest it can handle iron for the host. The team also measured iron in wild-caught flies. Wild levels matched the low-iron lab diets, so the benefit likely matters outside the lab too. A supposed parasite, the authors argue, may often act as a quiet nutritional partner.
europmc-pmc2659709:
Brooks and colleagues warned in 2009 that the flushed face many East Asians get after drinking alcohol marks a hidden cancer risk. About 36 percent of Japanese, Chinese, and Korean people inherit a weak form of an enzyme, ALDH2, that clears a toxic alcohol byproduct. Their faces redden, and they may feel sick and race in the chest.

Because the byproduct lingers, these drinkers face a far higher risk of cancer of the esophagus. That is the tube carrying food to the stomach. Drinkers with the normal enzyme face no such added risk. This cancer is among the deadliest, with low survival rates on every continent. The authors aim their warning at doctors: a flushing patient shows a sign of the flaw. Asking about flushing, they argue, is a cheap way to spot patients who should be urged to drink far less.
europmc-pmc2728709:
Thring, Hili, and Naughton tested in 2009 extracts from twenty-one plants for anti-aging effects on skin enzymes and for antioxidant power. Elastase and collagenase are enzymes that break down elastin and collagen, proteins that keep skin firm, and their activity rises with skin aging. Plant extracts are widely sold for skin care, but few are tested side by side.

White tea topped both enzyme tests, blocking each by close to nine tenths, and also held by far the most phenolic compounds, plant chemicals tied to antioxidant effects. Sixteen extracts blocked collagenase and nine blocked elastase, with green tea, cleavers, and burdock root among the stronger ones. All extracts showed antioxidant activity in at least one assay.
europmc-pmc2790509:
Somm and colleagues tested whether contact with bisphenol A before birth and during nursing changes how rat pups store fat. Bisphenol A, or BPA, is a chemical used in plastics that can disturb hormones. Pregnant rats drank water with a low dose from early pregnancy through the end of nursing in the 2009 study.

At weaning, female pups exposed to BPA carried about three times more fat around their reproductive organs than unexposed pups. Their fat cells were larger, and genes that build fat ran at higher levels in both fat and liver tissue. Later weight gain depended on sex and diet, while food intake stayed the same across groups.
europmc-pmc2820409:
Balsitis and colleagues built the first mouse model in 2010 of dengue disease made worse by antibodies from a prior infection. Dengue comes in four types, and catching a second type after the first can turn deadly, because cross-reactive antibodies help the virus enter immune cells instead of stopping it. No animal model had captured that worsening before.

Giving mice dengue antibodies before infection reproduced the human danger signs: low platelets, leaking blood vessels, high cytokine levels, and heavy virus loads. High doses of type-matched antibodies protected, but lower or cross-reactive doses worsened disease. One rebuilt antibody that cannot grip cell receptors both prevented and treated the lethal course, pointing to a safer antibody design.
europmc-pmc2838909:
Bayoh and colleagues traced a forty-year shift in 2010 in which malaria mosquito dominates western Kenya, following the spread of insecticide-treated bed nets. Two close mosquito species share the region: Anopheles gambiae, which prefers human blood and rests indoors, and Anopheles arabiensis, which feeds more on cattle. Records from 1970 onward plus new sampling along a transect gave the long view.

The indoor species made up about eighty-five percent of house catches until the late nineteen nineties. As net ownership rose after 2004, its share crashed to about one percent by 2009, while its sibling took over almost completely. Infection and breeding rates also fell where nets were common, a population-level effect of the nets.
europmc-pmc2846909:
Aulchenko, Struchalin, and van Duijn introduced ProbABEL in 2010, a software package for genome-wide association studies built on imputed genetic data. Imputation fills in unmeasured genetic variants with probabilities rather than certainties, and simply treating the likeliest guess as fact biases results. Ordinary tools built for directly measured variants cope badly with such guesswork.

ProbABEL folds the uncertainty straight into its tests, covering measured traits, yes-or-no outcomes, and time-to-event outcomes under the matching models. A fast two-step score test handles related samples, such as families and isolated populations, without crushing computing time. The authors offer it as a usable way to hunt complex-trait genes across the whole genome from imputed data.
europmc-pmc2857309:
Deaths tied to a gut germ were rising fast in the United States, and Redelings, Sorvillo, and Mascola measured the trend for 1999 to 2004 in this 2007 study. The germ is Clostridium difficile, a spore-forming bacterium that often strikes older patients after antibiotic treatment. It can cause severe diarrhea, colon inflammation, and blood infection.

Using national death records, the team found the death rate rose more than fourfold across the six years. It climbed from under six deaths per million people to nearly twenty-four per million, and the rise held through the whole period. Rates ran higher in white patients than in other groups. The authors link the surge in part to a newer, stronger strain then spreading in hospitals.
europmc-pmc2858209:
Repeated miscarriage may reflect a womb lining that fails to screen embryos, Salker and colleagues propose in this 2010 study. Recurrent pregnancy loss means three or more miscarriages in a row. The lining cells must change into a state called decidual each cycle, and that change should let the lining sense embryo quality.

Biopsies from women with repeated loss showed too little prolactin, a marker of the decidual state, and too much of a signal that invites implantation. Cells grown in the lab repeated the same faulty pattern and ignored signals from the embryo. Paradoxically, the women conceived again very quickly, which fits a lining that accepts embryos too easily, including weak ones it should reject.
europmc-pmc2948509:
Yao and colleagues tested a short stretch of ribosomal DNA called ITS2 as a universal barcode for telling species apart, in a 2010 study. A good barcode needs standard primers, easy copying, and enough variation to separate close relatives.

They downloaded tens of thousands of plant and animal ITS2 sequences from a public bank and measured length, base makeup, and variation within versus between species. Between-species gaps generally beat within-species spread. Naming success at species level ran from roughly two thirds in conifers to over nine tenths in animals, varying by family. The folded shape of the segment added extra clues.
europmc-pmc2988709:
Simarro and colleagues built an atlas of human African trypanosomiasis, sleeping sickness, in a 2010 mapping effort led with world health bodies. Charting where cases occur guides the push to end its standing as a public health threat.

The atlas covers twenty-three of twenty-five affected countries for the decade to 2009, with two still being processed. Records combine active screening of over two million people with cases found at clinics, totalling tens of thousands of cases across thousands of localities. Village coordinates anchor the maps. The database gives control programmes a shared, detailed picture for targeting.
europmc-pmc3037909:
Woodruff and colleagues reviewed in 2011 the causes, models, and treatment attempts for ischemic stroke, where a blocked vessel starves part of the brain. Stroke kills more people worldwide than almost any other condition and leaves many survivors badly disabled. Few treatments exist to limit tissue death after onset, so better models and targets are urgently needed.

The review walks through how brain tissue dies, then details animal and cell models used to copy the injury in the lab. It judges the strengths and flaws of the best mouse models and the lab practices they demand. Past single target drugs protected brains in animals yet failed in every human trial so far. The authors urge work on targets with broad, multi sided effects instead. They frame the review as a guide for the next round of research.
europmc-pmc3053509:
Jain, Gautam, and Naseem reviewed in 2011 the proteins the body floods into the blood within hours of infection, injury, or trauma. These acute phase proteins are made mainly by the liver after alarm signals arrive from the damage site. They help trap microbes, clear cell debris, neutralize harmful enzymes, and tune the immune response while repair gets under way.

Because their levels rise and fall with illness in predictable ways, the proteins double as diagnostic tools. The review lists veterinary and medical uses, from cattle lung infections and pig diseases to prostate cancer and blood cancers in people. In farm practice, a blood test for these proteins can flag sick animals before clear symptoms show. The authors present them as a cheap, early window on animal health that complements hands on examination.
europmc-pmc3237409:
Patrick Schloss, Dirk Gevers, and Sarah Westcott worked out how to clean up errors in gene-based surveys of microbial communities, in this 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Studies that read the 16S ribosomal gene to profile microbes were plagued by sequencing mistakes and by chimeras, hybrid sequences created during amplification, which invent species that do not exist.

The team sequenced ninety identical mock communities built from twenty-one known species, so every error could be spotted against the truth. They tested ways to flag bad reads, trim poor-quality regions, and correct bases, cutting the error rate sharply; one established algorithm gave the best balance of accuracy, length, and yield. Chimeras made up a notable share of raw reads and drove most fake diversity, but filtering plus a detection program reduced them to about one percent. The pipeline still left batch effects to watch for.
europmc-pmc3278109:
Gunther Eysenbach asked whether tweets can predict which papers will be heavily cited, in this 2011 paper in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Citations are the standard measure of scientific impact but accumulate slowly. Eysenbach mined every tweet linking to articles in his own journal over more than three years and built metrics of social attention, then compared them with later citation counts.

Most tweets arrived on publication day or the day after, then decayed fast. Tweet volume correlated moderately with later citations, and a combined model using timing and tweets explained a meaningful share of citation variation. Articles in the most-tweeted group were about eleven times more likely to end up highly cited than the least-tweeted. Top-cited papers could also be flagged from tweet data with high specificity. He proposes a twimpact factor to capture social impact alongside citations.
europmc-pmc3315009:
Moore and Fletcher reviewed how people come to feel that they caused their own actions, in a 2012 article. This feeling, called the sense of agency, helps people learn from outcomes and take responsibility for what they do. Older theories split over whether the feeling comes mainly from inside signals tied to movement, or from outside clues in the situation.

The authors argue that both kinds of clues matter and are weighed together, much as the senses combine sight and sound. They adapt a statistical framework from perception research to explain how the brain merges these cues. The review then applies that lens to disorders where the feeling of control breaks down. Delusions of being controlled by outside forces are one example. The authors also note where the framework still falls short.
europmc-pmc3320609:
Smith and co-authors revisited the classic mathematical theory of mosquito borne disease, in a 2012 article. The framework is usually credited to Ronald Ross and George Macdonald, two pioneers who modeled malaria spread. Tracing publications across seventy years, the authors show that many scientists added pieces, and that Ross built two models while Macdonald built a third.

What textbooks call the Ross Macdonald model is really a family of models sharing a core set of assumptions. Around the math grew a wider theory covering how transmission is measured and how mosquito control cuts it. Its key measure, vectorial capacity, and the main field methods were all settled before the nineteen sixties ended, as the worldwide malaria eradication campaign wound down. The authors argue the theory still anchors research and control strategy for mosquito borne diseases.
europmc-pmc3374609:
Abubucker and a large team introduced HUMAnN in 2012, a method to read what a microbial community can do from its DNA. Shotgun sequencing of mixed samples yields short reads from hundreds of species at once. Piecing those reads into whole genomes is slow and often impossible.

HUMAnN instead counts gene families and pathways directly from the short reads, along with their abundances. Tests on fake communities recovered both big pathways and small modules with high accuracy. Applied to hundreds of Human Microbiome Project samples from seven body sites, it found a core set of modules present nearly everywhere. Other pathways marked single niches, such as sugar breakdown in the gut.
europmc-pmc3378609:
Basu and colleagues systematically reviewed in 2012 whether private or public health care serves poorer countries better. The debate had grown heated as tight budgets pushed governments toward private provision. Both camps accused the other of cherry-picking friendly case reports, so a full evidence check was overdue.

Reviewing the comparative studies, the team found the evidence mixed and often thin. Private services tended to cater to wealthier patients with fewer medical needs, an unfair pattern seen across many settings. Claims that private care is simply more efficient or effective did not hold up consistently. The review urges policy built on measured performance rather than ideology.
europmc-pmc3394709:
Kueider, Parisi, Gross, and Rebok systematically reviewed in 2012 whether computerized training sharpens the minds of healthy older adults. Their net caught studies of people averaging at least fifty-five, free of dementia and mild impairment. Of more than one hundred fifty reports found, thirty-eight met the bar.

Programs fell into three families: classic training tasks, therapy-style software, and video games. Nearly all reported gains after training, with effect sizes ranging from tiny to very large. Most studies also found that seniors did not need prior computer skill to finish or benefit. The gains matched or beat paper-and-pencil training, at far less labor, making the digital route attractive.
europmc-pmc3444709:
Bady and colleagues built a prediction model in 2012 for glioblastoma. It reads the methylation status of the MGMT gene from chip data, a status that forecasts benefit from certain chemotherapy. Whether the gene is silenced by methylation depends on exactly which spots in its promoter carry the tags, which makes classification tricky. The team mined a chip reading well over a hundred spots in and around the gene.

Two promoter regions carried nearly all the signal for silencing and for patient outcome. A two-probe model built on them classified tumors about as well as the standard lab test in a training set, and held up in an independent patient group. Methylation patterns also shifted with tumor grade and a broader methylator state. The model lets researchers mine existing chip datasets for treatment-resistance clues.
europmc-pmc3474909:
Barrett, Fletcher, and Wilton reviewed how the non-coding parts of genes control gene activity, in Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences in 2012. Sections of a gene that never become protein were once dismissed as junk. The review argues the opposite: those regions hold much of the control system that lets complex organisms time and place gene activity with great precision.

The authors walk through the regions before and after each gene's coding part, the stretches cut out of messages, and the many non-coding RNAs copied across the genome. Together these elements fine-tune output through many layered interactions. Barrett's team ties the growth of such control regions to the rise of complex body plans. Variation in them, they note, helps explain differences between people and species.
europmc-pmc3527209:
Fruit flies from Africa carry the species' deepest history, and John E. Pool and eleven colleagues sequence 139 wild-derived strains in 2012. The samples span 22 sub-Saharan populations plus one European group, most read at over 25-fold coverage from haploid embryos.

Non-African ancestry turns up inside many African populations, more in urban samples than rural ones. Its share also varies along the genome in peaks and valleys, suggesting the mixing was not neutral drift alone. Flies from one location can differ sharply in ancestry, hinting at isolating mechanisms close to home. After stripping admixed segments, southern African populations hold the greatest diversity. The team supplies a new admixture detection method with the data.
europmc-pmc3552709:
Heart scars can hide against bright blood, and W. Patricia Bandettini leads a ten-author clinical validation of the MCODE imaging method in 2012. Standard late gadolinium enhancement scans show infarcted heart muscle, but weak contrast between blood and scar can mask damage that hugs the inner wall.

MCODE acquires a T2-weighted image together with the enhancement image, giving readers a second contrast for the same slice. In 73 patients scanned at 1.5 tesla, MCODE and standard imaging matched on transmural infarctions, but MCODE found more subendocardial ones and measured a greater extent of damage. The paired images, the study concludes, sharpen detection where ordinary scans are weakest.
europmc-pmc3593009:
Takayuki Miki and colleagues reviewed diabetic cardiomyopathy in Heart Failure Reviews in 2013. Four decades ago doctors first described heart muscle disease caused by diabetes itself, apart from clogged arteries. Since then the mechanisms have come into focus. In the diabetic heart, fat burning rises while sugar burning falls, and signaling inside cells shifts. Each step from electrical trigger to muscle contraction works less well, wasting energy and inviting damage when blood flow returns after a blockage.

Small vessels dwindle and the scaffolding between cells stiffens, adding to the weakness. Sensitive ultrasound methods and magnetic resonance scans can now catch the condition early and tell it apart from other heart diseases. The authors stress that silent cases are common in patients who feel well, yet no proven prevention or treatment plan exists. Their review lines up the open problems that management research still must solve.
europmc-pmc3599009:
Saurabh Shrivastava, Prateek Shrivastava, and Jegadeesh Ramasamy argued the case for self-care in diabetes in the Journal of Diabetes and Metabolic Disorders in 2013. Diabetes, a long-running disorder of blood sugar, affected over 346 million people by the World Health Organization's count, with numbers set to double by 2030 without action. Drugs alone cannot carry that load; the daily work of control falls on patients themselves.

Seven habits predict good outcomes, the authors write. They are healthy eating, regular activity, checking blood sugar, taking medicines as agreed, solving problems as they arise, coping well with stress, and cutting risks such as smoking. Each habit tracks with better sugar control, fewer complications, and better quality of life, yet long-term follow-through is poor everywhere. Social support and income matter, but the review stresses the clinician's role in coaching and motivating. A joined-up, many-sided push is their prescription.
europmc-pmc3692109:
Wang and colleagues report the 2013 update of WebGestalt, a web toolkit that interprets long gene lists by testing which biological categories they enrich. Gene lists from genome-scale experiments mean little until they are matched against known functions, pathways, and disease links.

The toolkit now supports eight organisms and draws identifiers from many databases and platforms. Its holdings grew to more than seventy-eight thousand functional categories, spanning Gene Ontology terms, pathways, network modules, and associations with phenotypes, diseases, drugs, and chromosome locations. New interactive views, including pathway maps and network displays, help users read the enrichment results rather than just receive them.
europmc-pmc3694309:
Chhor and colleagues catalogued what happens when microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, are pushed into their different activation states in culture. Microglia can take a classic attacking state, or several other states tied to repair and immune control. Drug screening needs reliable ways to tell these states apart.

Working with primary microglia, the team induced each state with its known triggers and measured the surface markers, released factors, and capacity to harm neurons that came with it. The resulting catalogue is offered as a shared reference. It lets labs tell the states apart and screen candidate brain drugs against defined immune states rather than a mixed cell population.
europmc-pmc3784509:
Scott Kennedy, Jesse Salk, Michael Schmitt, and Lawrence Loeb reported a study in PLoS Genetics in 2013 on mitochondrial DNA mutations and aging. Mitochondrial DNA was long thought to be highly exposed to damage from reactive oxygen species. Rare mutations in it were nearly impossible to measure accurately until a technique called Duplex Sequencing, which can find one mutation among over ten million normal molecules.

Applying it to human brain tissue from young and old people, the team found that point mutations rise about fivefold over 80 years of life. Most changes were transitions of a kind that points to copying errors or spontaneous chemical decay. The G-to-T changes that are the hallmark of oxidative damage did not rise with age. The authors argue against oxidative damage as a major driver of aging.
europmc-pmc3798909:
Surangi Thilakarathna and H. P. Vasantha Rupasinghe wrote a review in Nutrients in 2013 on flavonoid bioavailability. Flavonoids are plant compounds with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and cholesterol-lowering effects seen in cell, animal, and human studies. Yet the body absorbs them poorly, which can limit or even cancel their health effects.

Of the six common food flavonoid classes, flavonols are found in nearly all plant foods, while isoflavones concentrate in legumes. Because absorption decides how much good a flavonoid can do, researchers are testing ways to raise it, from processing changes to delivery systems. The review surveys those attempts and the evidence behind them. The authors call for more work on bioavailability as the determining factor in flavonoid activity.
europmc-pmc3893509:
Toshihiro Kawamoto leads a large team in setting out a birth cohort design in BMC Public Health, with the record dated 2014. The Japan Environment and Children's Study follows children from before birth to judge how surroundings shape health and growth. Concern over chemical and other hazards to children drives the work.

Recruiting began in 2011, aiming for about a hundred thousand expecting mothers in set study areas. Children will be tracked to their teens. Exposure reads come from blood, urine, hair, and milk samples, home measures, air data, and surveys. Key outcomes span birth issues, birth defects, brain and behavior, immunity, and hormone-linked health. Gene, income, and lifestyle factors are logged alongside, so hazard effects can be told apart.
europmc-pmc3903109:
L. Desbonnet, G. Clarke, F. Shanahan, T. G. Dinan, and J. F. Cryan report a mouse behavior study in Molecular Psychiatry, with the record dated 2014. Gut microbes sway brain and behavior through the gut-brain axis. Altered gut mixes have been reported in autism, yet whether early-life microbes shape social growth was untested.

Mice raised with no microbes at all were tested as adults in a three-chamber social choice setup. Microbe-free mice showed clear social deficits next to normal mice, shunning social contact and novelty in ways the test is built to catch. Past work with such mice found altered stress responses, brain growth factors, and transmitter levels, often stronger in males. The findings cast early gut microbes as needed partners in social development.
europmc-pmc3920909:
Anu Rahal and six colleagues review the balance between oxidants and antioxidants in the body in BioMed Research International in 2014. Reactive oxygen species are made during normal cell activity, and enzyme systems keep their levels low. Oxidative stress names the state where prooxidants gain the upper hand over the antioxidant defenses that normally contain them.

The review explains how these reactive molecules are produced and cleared, and what markers show when they damage tissue. It gathers genetic and protein-level evidence tying oxidative stress to chronic and some acute diseases, to cancers and autoimmune disorders, and to weaker defense against bacterial, fungal, and viral infection. Dietary antioxidants from plant foods get attention as one line of protection the body can draw on.
europmc-pmc3971609:
Leopoldo N. Segal and colleagues link the lung's microbial mix to quiet inflammation in Microbiome in 2013. Healthy lungs often harbor microbes from the mouth, probably breathed in during sleep, and smoking diseases involve the same micro-aspiration, but whether those mouth microbes inflame the lung was untested. The team washed the lower airways of 29 symptom-free adults, nine never-smokers and the rest former or current smokers, and sequenced the bacteria found there.

The airway communities fell into two patterns, which the authors call pneumotypes. One resembled background; the other was rich in mouth-typical bacteria such as Veillonella and Prevotella. People with that second pattern had more white blood cells in their lung washings and more nitric oxide in their breath, signs of subclinical inflammation. Smoking status did not decide which pattern a person carried.
europmc-pmc3977509:
Yanyan Yang and colleagues review the p38 MAPK pathway in inflammation. Their paper appeared in Mediators of Inflammation in 2014. Macrophages run much of the innate immune response. The MAPK enzyme family relays the signals that set their behavior. The p38 branch is a key driver of inflammatory output. It switches on messengers such as tumor necrosis factor alpha. It also switches on COX-2, an enzyme behind pain and fever compounds.

The review lays out how p38 is switched on. It shows what p38 controls inside macrophages. It follows the pathway through the inflammatory response step by step. Then it turns to therapy. Blocking p38 in macrophages is an attractive idea for inflammatory diseases. The authors weigh the inhibitor proof with care. Some drugs in this line have struggled in trials. The pathway's promise as a target is judged against that record.
europmc-pmc4031209:
César de la Fuente-Núñez and five co-authors report a peptide that breaks up bacterial biofilms, in PLoS Pathogens in 2014. Biofilms are sticky cell cities that cause two thirds of infections. Inside them, bacteria shrug off standard antibiotics at many times the normal dose. No approved drug targets biofilms as such.

The peptide, numbered 1018, worked across a wide set of major pathogens, both major bacteria classes included. At low doses it scattered film cells and stopped new films. At high doses it wiped out mature films and killed their cells. The peptide acts on a stress signal inside the cells, forcing its breakdown within minutes. Mutant bacteria that cannot make that signal behaved as if treated. Raising signal output made cells harder to treat, which backs the claim. The authors propose signal targeting as a new route against film-based drug resistance.
europmc-pmc4046109:
Thomas S. Blacker and six colleagues separate two look-alike energy molecules inside living cells, in Nature Communications in 2014. NADH and NADPH drive different work: the first feeds energy production, the second building tasks and defence against oxidative harm. Both glow under light, but with identical colours, so standard imaging cannot tell them apart.

The team used fluorescence lifetime imaging, which times how long the glow lasts. Genetic and drug tweaks showed the two decay at different rates. Changes in fuel use alone did not explain the timing shifts. In cancer cells, altered lifetimes likely track a changed balance between the two molecules. A maths model turned the timing data into relative amounts per cell type. Applied to the inner ear, it found cell groups rich in NADPH. The method opens live redox mapping in tissue.
europmc-pmc4052509:
Medha Raina and Michael Ibba review the second careers of transfer RNAs, in Frontiers in Genetics in 2014. These small RNAs are famous as adaptors that carry amino acids to the ribosome during protein building. That role, it turns out, is only part of their working life.

Loaded tRNAs also serve as raw material elsewhere. They help build cell walls, tag proteins for disposal, alter membrane fats, and assemble antibiotics, all without a ribosome. Free tRNAs act as signals that tune gene expression and metabolism under stress. Small fragments snipped from tRNAs have lately joined the list, with regulatory roles of their own. The review gathers these cases across bacteria and higher organisms. It argues that tRNA should be read as a general-purpose tool the cell reaches for in many pathways, not a one-job part.
europmc-pmc4074809:
Richard L. Carpenter and Hui-Wen Lo reviewed the genes switched on or off by STAT3, a transcription factor tied to many human cancers. Their review appeared in Cancers in 2014. STAT3 helps control growth and development, and its gene targets can push tumours to form, grow, and spread.

Working alone or with partner factors, STAT3 raises some genes and lowers others, shaping cell survival and stem-like traits. Oddly, it can also switch on genes that hold tumours back, acting as a suppressor in some settings. Effects seem to depend on cell context and tumour type. The authors catalogue validated cancer-linked targets and argue that fuller knowledge of the pathway is needed as STAT3-blocking therapies enter early clinical testing.
europmc-pmc4145409:
Paolo Pelosi, Immacolata Iovinella, Antonio Felicioli, and Francesca R. Dani reviewed the soluble proteins that carry chemical signals in arthropods. Their overview appeared in Frontiers in Physiology in 2014. In both insects and vertebrates, such proteins, packed into smell organs, bind scent molecules and somehow activate receptors.

Insects use two protein families for this courier work, while vertebrates use one structurally unrelated family. The same proteins often appear where pheromones are made, likely helping release them. Checking other arthropods, the authors find the insect binding families barely extend beyond insects. They propose that lipid-transporter proteins of the Niemann-Pick type C2 family may have been recruited to fill the same role elsewhere.
europmc-pmc4198209:
Ammar W. Ashor, John C. Mathers, and four co-authors pooled exercise trials in PLoS ONE in 2014 to see which training softens stiff arteries. Arterial stiffness, measured by how fast a pressure wave travels, predicts heart disease. Wave reflection gives a second index of vessel health.

Across 42 trials with 1,627 adults, aerobic exercise lowered pulse wave velocity and the reflection index clearly. The gain was biggest in people whose arteries were stiffest at the start, and harder aerobic work cut the reflection index further. Resistance training alone changed neither measure, and neither did combined programs in the trials pooled. The authors conclude that aerobic training is the reliable route to more supple arteries, at least over trial lengths of four weeks or more.
europmc-pmc4207909:
Juliane Léger and seven co-authors issued European consensus guidelines on congenital hypothyroidism in the Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism in 2014. Babies born with too little thyroid hormone face stunted brain development unless treatment starts fast. Practice varied across countries, so the European Society for Paediatric Endocrinology gathered 32 experts from six societies to agree on shared rules.

The guidelines back screening every newborn, then quick work to find the cause and severity. Treatment with levothyroxine should start at once, with frequent checks to keep hormone levels in range. Children suspected of a passing form should get a trial off treatment later. Regular checks of development and hearing, plus parent education, complete the plan. The document harmonizes care across the societies involved.
europmc-pmc4245909:
Noelia Urbán and François Guillemot compared brain cell birth before and after birth in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2014. The embryo builds the brain from neural stem cells at full speed. In adults, new neurons still arise, but only in small niches, from stem cells that spend most of their time asleep.

Many of the same switches run both programs, yet they act differently in the two settings. The BMP signal, for example, keeps embryonic stem cells dividing, while in the adult hippocampus it enforces rest so the pool is not spent early. The review walks through the shared transcription factors and signals, then marks where adult control has no embryonic counterpart. The hippocampal niche gets special attention as the best-mapped case.
europmc-pmc4284309:
Meng-Chuan Lai, Michael V. Lombardo, Bonnie Auyeung, Bhismadev Chakrabarti, and Simon Baron-Cohen map the research on sex and gender differences in autism. Their review appeared in the Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry in 2015. Autism is diagnosed far more often in males, and studies on the gap range from clinic patterns to brain biology and causes.

The findings do not line up neatly, so the authors propose a four level frame to sort the questions: rates, presentation, biology, and the social side of diagnosis. They searched the literature to September 2014 and mark which questions stay open. The frame is meant to help design cleaner studies of why the sex gap exists and what it means for care.
europmc-pmc4296509:
Jennifer T Wang and ten co-authors studied how worm embryos build and dissolve RNA granules, droplets that store RNA and proteins. Their study appeared in eLife in 2014. In the worm C. elegans, granules in germ cells behave like liquid drops, and a family of loose, serine rich proteins called MEG proteins helps control them.

An enzyme adds phosphate tags to the MEG proteins and another removes them. Tagging pushed granules to break apart; untagging let them form. Live imaging with a new light sheet microscope showed MEG protein coating and threading through each granule. The work names a chemical switch behind granule dynamics in a living embryo.
europmc-pmc4362409:
Aristeidis Kritis, Eleni Stamoula, Krystallenia Paniskaki, and Theofanis Vavilis reviewed how glutamate harms nerve cells, in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2015. Glutamate is a key signal chemical in the brain, but too much of it outside cells overexcites neurons until they die, a process called excitotoxicity. Labs study that harm in many cell lines. The review compares how the harm unfolds in each line and which route dominates.

Excess glutamate can flood cells with calcium through its receptors, stir harmful oxygen byproducts, strain mitochondria, and drain protective stores. In cell lines with glutamate receptors, receptor overdrive leads the damage. In lines lacking those receptors, oxidative stress does the harm instead. Most lines carry both systems, so the damage adds up from several routes at once. Knowing which route a line uses shapes how results should be read.
europmc-pmc4383909:
Kristian Gray, Bethan Yates, Ruth Seal, Matthew Wright, and Elspeth Bruford reported on the HGNC gene naming resources in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. The HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee assigns each human gene a unique symbol and name, a standard that major databases from Ensembl to UniProt follow. By then the committee had named over 39,000 genes, adding more than 5,000 in two years, most entries hand-curated with help from specialists in each gene family.

Their website, genenames.org, was redesigned with faster, stronger search. A tool for mapping gene names across species, HCOP, was greatly improved, and a programmatic REST service widened machine access. Consistent names sound mundane, yet they prevent a common failure: two labs studying the same gene under different labels and missing each other's work.
europmc-pmc4387509:
Giulio Tononi and Christof Koch set out a theory of consciousness in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B in 2015. Brain research had mapped many correlates of experience, yet correlates cannot say why the cortex yields consciousness while the cerebellum, with even more neurons, apparently does not. Nor can they judge hard cases: infants born early, animals, patients with little working cortex, or smart machines. The authors present integrated information theory as a principled answer.

The theory starts from five axioms about experience itself, such as that it exists for the subject and is unified. From these it derives what a physical system must be like to host experience, and a calculus for how much consciousness a system has and of what kind. It claims to explain many clinical and lab findings and makes testable predictions.
europmc-pmc4415409:
Fernando Santos-Beneit reviewed the Pho regulon, bacteria's answer to phosphate scarcity, in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2015, in a solo article. Inorganic phosphate is essential yet usually scarce in nature, above all in soil, where microbes compete fiercely. Bacteria sense that scarcity through a two-component system that switches on the Pho regulon, a network of genes for scavenging and economizing. It is among the most sensitive and efficient regulatory systems known in bacteria, Santos-Beneit notes.

The review gathers three decades of findings: the DNA signal box that marks regulon genes, the signaling pathway itself, and the full starvation response. New members of the regulon keep appearing in species after species. Its reach extends into nutrient cross-talk, the production of secondary compounds such as antibiotics, and even virulence, tying a hunger circuit to medicine.
europmc-pmc4423209:
Jonathan Lefcheck and nine co-authors tested whether richer ecosystems do more jobs at once, in a 2015 analysis in Nature Communications. Past work often checked one service at a time, such as plant growth, which can miss trade-offs. The team built a database of experiments that changed species counts and measured several functions together.

Across ninety-four manipulations, spanning plants, herbivores, and other levels in water and on land, richer groups kept more functions at higher levels. Effects grew stronger as more functions were counted, and herbivore diversity mattered even more than plant diversity in their data. Trade-offs existed, but the overall pattern suggests earlier single-function studies understated what species loss can cost.
europmc-pmc4474809:
Audrey Gustin and nine co-authors, including Thomas Kufer, asked which mouse brain cells can fire a key inflammatory machine, in PLoS ONE in 2015. The machine, the NLRP3 inflammasome, assembles inside cells and releases IL-1 beta, a powerful inflammatory signal involved in brain reactions to infection, injury, and protein clumps. Both microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, and astrocytes, its support cells, were candidates.

Only microglia, the team found, held all the machine's parts and released IL-1 beta when triggered by classic activators such as ATP. Astrocytes neither secreted the signal nor expressed the full set of components. Microglia also released two related inflammatory factors. A Parkinson's-linked protein, alpha-synuclein, did not trigger release in their tests. The results assign this inflammatory pathway to one brain compartment, sharpening ideas about its role in brain disease.
europmc-pmc4476709:
Luke Chang, Peter Gianaros, Stephen Manuck, Anjali Krishnan, Tor Wager, and Ralph Adolphs built a brain signature for negative emotion in PLoS Biology in 2015. Brain imaging had found many regions that react during emotion, but none that could predict how strongly a given person feels. The team used machine learning on brain scans of people viewing unpleasant pictures to find such a pattern.

The resulting signature predicted each person's reported intensity of negative feeling with high accuracy in both the training group and a fresh test group. It did not respond to physical pain, and it separated emotion from pain well, showing it is not just arousal. The pattern spans several brain systems at once, and no single region, including classic emotion areas such as the amygdala, explains it. The work offers a brain-based measure for sorting emotional processes apart from pain.
europmc-pmc4489809:
Danilo Carvalho and eight co-authors, including Ken Olson, reported suppressing a wild mosquito population with engineered males in Brazil, in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2015. The mosquito Aedes aegypti spreads dengue, and traditional control programs have struggled against its rising burden. A self-limiting strain, OX513A, carries a gene that kills offspring before adulthood, so releasing males, which do not bite, can crash a local population as they mate with wild females.

In a suburb of Juazeiro, Bahia, sustained releases ran for more than a year. They cut the target population steeply compared with a nearby no-release area. Both adult trap catches and egg trap measures showed the drop. The released males competed for mates about as well as in an earlier Cayman Islands trial, despite different conditions and target strains. The authors conclude that sustained release of such males can suppress a field population effectively.
europmc-pmc4490509:
Adriano Sofo, Antonio Scopa, Maria Nuzzaci, Antonella Vitti, Ann Cuypers, and Tony Remans reviewed two peroxide-cleaning enzymes in stressed plants in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2015. Hydrogen peroxide is made constantly by plant metabolism. At low levels it works as a signal guiding photosynthesis, growth, and stress responses. But drought and salt push its production up. Then the excess damages molecules and can kill cells.

Plants keep it in bounds with several enzymes, of which catalase and ascorbate peroxidase stand out. Catalase, housed mainly in peroxisomes, splits it without needing a helper chemical. Its partner enzyme binds it more eagerly and works in chloroplasts, cell fluid, mitochondria, and peroxisomes alike. The review covers how the two enzymes' activity and genes respond to drought and salinity, and how their balance decides whether peroxide signals or harms.
europmc-pmc4502609:
Khalid Alfarouk and eleven co-authors argued for a wider view of chemotherapy resistance in Cancer Cell International in 2015. Cancer cells that evade chemotherapy, whether from the start or after acquiring resistance, are among the most pressing problems in cancer therapy. Most research blames tumor-specific factors, above all pump proteins that expel drugs from cancer cells, such as P-glycoprotein.

The authors propose widening the frame to the whole journey of a drug in the body: absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion, the ADME steps, all governed partly by the patient's own physiology. A drug that never reaches the tumor at effective levels fails just as surely as one pumped out of a cell. They review resistance mechanisms from host and tumor together and set out a platform for modifying drug response that treats the patient, not only the tumor cell, as part of the problem.
europmc-pmc4520009:
Justin Jagosh leads a ten-author team evaluating research done with communities, not just on them, in BMC Public Health in 2015. In community-based participatory research, scientists and local partners share control of a project aimed at better health. A 2012 review had found long-term effects but could not fully explain what made partnerships work.

The team interviewed 24 people, researchers and community members, from 11 long-running partnerships kept from that review. Using realist methods, they asked what settings spark synergy, the state where joint work beats solo effort. Trust building stood at the center, and gains rippled outward: ties lasted, skills grew, and solutions stuck. The paper draws out what helps such partnerships hold together over years.
europmc-pmc4522109:
Nabil N. Dagher leads an eight-author team testing a microglia-blocking drug in Alzheimer's model mice, in the Journal of Neuroinflammation in 2015. Microglia, the brain's immune cells, need signals from the CSF1 receptor to survive. Blocking that receptor can clear nearly all microglia from the brain. The question was what dose does, and whether partial clearing helps or harms.

In normal mice, high doses of the blocker PLX5622 wiped out most microglia, while a dose 75% lower held removal near 30%. Neither clearing nor low doses hurt behavior or thinking. In aged Alzheimer's model mice, six or twelve weeks at the low dose improved learning and memory, and kept microglia from clustering on plaques.
europmc-pmc4531509:
Chika Kasai leads an eleven-author team comparing gut microbes in obese and lean Japanese adults, in BMC Gastroenterology in 2015. Obesity is a growing problem in Japan, and gut microbes have been tied to it elsewhere, though the exact link stays unsettled. The team collected stool from 23 lean and 33 obese adults before a colon check.

A fingerprinting method showed obese subjects carried fewer Bacteroidetes, one major gut group, and a higher ratio of Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes, the other main group. Ten samples then went through deep gene sequencing for species-level detail. The pattern matches reports from other countries, suggesting the shift is not unique to Western diets. The authors stop short of claiming the microbes cause the weight gain.
europmc-pmc4551309:
Laura Hobley and four co-authors review the scaffolding that holds biofilms together, in FEMS Microbiology Reviews in 2015. Biofilms are microbe cities stuck to surfaces, useful in sewage treatment and plant growth, harmful in chronic infections and industrial fouling. The cells sit inside a matrix they build themselves from proteins, sugars, fats, and loose DNA.

That matrix gives the city its strength, shields it from attack, traps nutrients, and helps control gene activity. The review gathers recent findings on how the sugar and protein parts are built and woven, and how the three-dimensional layout works. Knowing the matrix in depth, the authors argue, is the route to both fighting harmful biofilms and harnessing helpful ones.
europmc-pmc4682109:
Ramona Schrage, Anna-Lena Schmitz, Evelyn Gaffal, and dozens of co-authors studied a plant compound called FR900359 in Nature Communications in 2015. Cells receive many signals through receptors that switch on G proteins inside the cell. One family, Gq, had no clean, cell-friendly blocker, which made its roles hard to test. The team set out to show that FR900359 could fill that gap.
