Careful tests showed the compound blocks Gq family proteins while leaving other G protein types alone, and the team worked out how it does so. In melanoma cells, blocking Gq shut down many traits that make the cancer dangerous. The authors compare the compound to pertussis toxin, the standard tool for a sister protein family. Their work hands cell biologists a sharp new tool and points to a possible route for drug design.
europmc-pmc4726509:
David Lamparter, Daniel Marbach, Rico Rueedi, Zoltán Kutalik, and Sven Bergmann presented Pascal, a tool for scoring genes and pathways from genetic study data, in PLoS Computational Biology in 2016. Genome-wide studies give each DNA variant a significance value, but biology speaks in genes and pathways. Combining variant scores upward adds power and meaning, yet existing tools were slow or loose. Pascal computes gene scores fast, using either the strongest or the average signal per gene.

For pathways it uses a modified Fisher method that avoids arbitrary hit-list cutoffs. Tests on summary data from dozens of large studies showed more power with strict error control, and hits that made better biological sense. The tool turns flat variant lists into ranked genes and processes, the level at which drug ideas live.
europmc-pmc4743009:
Alsafadi and eleven colleagues investigate how hotspot mutations in SF3B1, a core splicing factor mutated in about 20 percent of uveal melanomas, corrupt the way cells splice RNA. RNA sequencing of tumours shows the mutant protein shifts a subset of junctions to alternative 3-prime splice sites.

Experiments in cell lines prove the pattern depends strictly on the mutant protein and the sequence around the splice site. Removing or overproducing the normal protein does not reproduce it, so the mutations change the protein's function rather than weaken it. Mutating predicted branchpoints confirms the mechanism: mutant SF3B1 forces the splicing machinery to use alternative branchpoints.
europmc-pmc4761709:
Alexandra Bernadotte, Victor M. Mikhelson, and Irina M. Spivak review cell aging markers in Aging in 2016, with a focus on telomere shortening. Senescence is the state in which a cell stops dividing for good while staying alive and active. Cells in this state share a set of signs, and scientists need firm signs to spot them in tissue and in the dish.

Telomeres are the caps of repeated code at chromosome ends. They shrink a bit with each cell division, which makes them work like a clock for a cell's past. The review weighs the theory and lab data behind using that shrinkage as a senescence marker. It also sets the marker among the wider changes that mark an aged cell, from shape shifts to altered chemistry.
europmc-pmc4822009:
Ji-Sen Li leads nine authors in Nature Communications in 2016 building a platinum-free catalyst for making hydrogen from water. Splitting water is a clean route to hydrogen fuel, but the best catalysts are rare, costly platinum. Molybdenum carbide behaves much like platinum, and the team married it to graphene, the one-atom-thick carbon sheet that conducts superbly.

The hybrid came from a layered precursor built around a metal cluster compound. In acid tests it drove hydrogen production with the best activity yet reported for a non-noble catalyst and held that performance over long runs. Computer modeling located the working sites: certain nitrogen atoms in the graphene and their neighboring carbons. The authors present the recipe as a design route for a wider family of catalysts.
europmc-pmc4869309:
M. Alexis Kirk and co-authors reviewed in 2016 how a popular health framework, CFIR, has been used since its 2009 launch. The Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research lists factors that help or block new practices in care settings. The review searched two databases for studies citing the source paper and kept 26 of 429 that used the framework in a deep way.

Use spread wide across topics, but depth varied: some studies used the full factor list, others picked slices. Few tied findings back to shared measures that build the field. The review urges fuller, more standard use so lessons add up. A shared map only helps if travelers mark the same landmarks.
europmc-pmc4879409:
Anna E. Sheppard and co-authors traced in 2016 how a last-resort drug resistance gene, blaKPC, races through a hospital's bacteria like nested dolls. Carbapenems are last-line drugs against a common germ family, and blaKPC defeats them. The team sequenced 281 resistant isolates from one hospital over five years with short and long reads.

The gene spread at every nested level: strains passed between patients, plasmids carrying it jumped between strains and species, and its transposon hopped between plasmids, often at one favored site. Short-term outbreak spread is thus far more mobile than case counts suggest. Control must target the gene's vehicles, not just single strains.
europmc-pmc4921909:
Jun Chen leads a large team comparing gut bacteria in multiple sclerosis patients and healthy controls. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports in 2016. Multiple sclerosis is an immune disease of the brain and spinal cord. Genes play a part, but the environmental triggers are still unclear, and gut microbes are one suspect. The team sequenced bacterial genes from stool samples of 31 relapsing remitting patients and 36 matched controls.

Patients carried a distinct gut community profile. Pseudomonas, Mycoplana, Haemophilus, Blautia, and Dorea were more common in patients. Parabacteroides, Adlercreutzia, and Prevotella were more common in controls. The authors say the pattern fits the idea of gut dysbiosis in the disease. They stress that more work is needed to learn whether these shifts help cause the illness or follow from it.
europmc-pmc4967609:
Suzanne M. Garland leads a large team reviewing ten years of real world results for the quadrivalent HPV vaccine. Their systematic review appeared in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2016. The vaccine covers four human papillomavirus types, including the two that cause most cervical cancers. Trial efficacy was high, but population impact depends on coverage and timing. The team gathered studies of infection and disease rates since the vaccine entered use.

Large reductions followed in infections with the covered types, in anogenital warts, and in cervical lesions. Gains were greatest where girls were vaccinated routinely before exposure to the virus. Catch-up programs for older teens sped the benefits. Still, preventable HPV disease persists in many places. The authors urge wider programs with high coverage before exposure. They frame the decade as proof that the vaccine works at population scale when delivery is strong.
europmc-pmc5010409:
Colleen E. Reid, Michael Brauer, Fay H. Johnston, Michael Jerrett, John R. Balmes, and Catherine T. Elliott review the health effects of wildfire smoke in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2016. Wildfires are expected to grow in many regions as the climate warms, and their smoke carries many harmful air pollutants. The team weighed studies on death and on lung, heart, mental, and pregnancy health.

The strongest and steadiest finding was harm to breathing, above all worse asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Evidence is also growing for more lung infections and for higher overall death rates after smoke exposure. Heart effects stayed mixed, with only some studies finding links. Too little work exists to name which groups are most at risk. The authors call for more study to guide health planning before future fire seasons.
europmc-pmc5037809:
Xi-Feng Zhang, Zhi-Guo Liu, Wei Shen, and Sangiliyandi Gurunathan review silver nanoparticles in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2016. Silver particles at nanoscale size kill microbes and show effects against inflammation, blood vessel growth, and cancer, which makes them a focus of nanomedicine. The review gathers how they are made, how they are measured, and what they can do.

Three making routes are compared: physical, chemical, and biological, the last using living extracts as a greener path. The particle traits that matter, size, shape, surface, and charge, decide how they behave in the body. Against cancer, the particles appear to harm tumor cells through stress and damage pathways, and they can boost standard drugs. The authors list the hurdles before clinic use: safe dosing, where particles settle in the body, steady supply, and targeting the right cells.
europmc-pmc5105309:
Tung Gia Phan and nine co-authors reported a new pig virus in Virology Journal in 2016. Three pigs had heart and body-wide inflammation but tested negative for known pig viruses, including porcine circovirus 2, a costly pathogen in pork farming. The team searched tissue samples with deep gene sequencing to find the cause.

They pieced together the genome of a third pig circovirus, named PCV3, only distantly related to the two known types and closer in part to a virus found in bat droppings. All three pigs shared heart muscle inflammation and inflamed heart arteries, and viral RNA sat inside the damaged heart cells. Other viruses turned up in single animals, so the authors say PCV3's role in disease needs more study.
europmc-pmc5188409:
Mark Messina, writing alone, updates the evidence on soy foods and health. More than 2,000 papers on soy appear each year, and claims about it often outrun the data. He reviews the clinical and population research on soy protein and isoflavones. The evidence links soy intake with lower risk of coronary heart disease and of breast and prostate cancer. Soy also eases hot flashes for many women. Most safety worries, he notes, grew out of animal studies rather than human ones.

Messina gives weight to the European Food Safety Authority's conclusion that isoflavones do not harm the breast, thyroid, or uterus in postmenopausal women. He separates what trials show from what headlines claim, and he is candid about where results conflict. The overall picture he draws is of a food that is safe for most people and modestly protective, not a cure and not a hazard.
europmc-pmc5190009:
Xiang Ying and seven co-authors trace a signal that ovarian cancer cells send to macrophages. Epithelial ovarian cancer cells release exosomes loaded with the microRNA miR-222-3p. When macrophages take up these vesicles, they shift toward the tumor-associated, M2-like state that helps cancers grow. The pathway runs through SOCS3 and STAT3: miR-222-3p targets SOCS3 directly, and lower SOCS3 levels come with stronger STAT3 activation.

Forcing miR-222-3p into macrophages reproduced the M2 shift in the lab. The microRNA could also be detected in exosomes from patients' serum, and its levels tracked with the cancer. The authors propose exosomal miR-222-3p as both a regulator of tumor-promoting macrophages and a possible biomarker for epithelial ovarian cancer. They frame the work as a step toward interrupting the conversation between tumor and stroma.
europmc-pmc5223809:
An unsigned editorial in The Hospital dated January 20, 1912 took up the rheumatic diathesis, the old belief that inborn body types predispose people to particular diseases. Until the late nineteenth century, doctors widely accepted diatheses such as the rheumatic, the scrofulous, the bilious, and the nervous. Each was said to carry bodily signs marking its bearers before any illness appeared.

The editorial argues that bacteriology broke that habit of thought. Once the tubercle bacillus was shown to cause tuberculosis, blaming a scrofulous constitution looked empty. Many victims showed none of its supposed signs, and many marked people stayed healthy. New work on immunity, from Wright's opsonic index to the studies of Ehrlich and Metchnikoff, swung attention back to the patient's own constitution, the soil as well as the seed. The piece weighs whether the old signs might regain meaning in that new light.
europmc-pmc5294809:
Remco R. Bouckaert and Alexei J. Drummond presented bModelTest, a Bayesian way to choose DNA substitution models, in BMC Evolutionary Biology in 2017. Rebuilding family trees from DNA with Bayesian methods gives sound math and honest uncertainty. But each analysis needs a site model: which substitutions happen at which rates, and how rates vary. Picking one fixed model in advance, by a separate likelihood test, was the usual awkward step.

bModelTest removes the pre-step. Inside the running analysis, a trans-dimensional sampling method hops between substitution models and weighs the options automatically. These include gamma-shaped rate variation, a share of unchanging sites, and unequal base frequencies. The inference runs jointly with the tree itself, over the full set of time-reversible models or two leaner subsets the authors introduce. The tool ships as a package for BEAST 2, open source, so the model is inferred and averaged, not guessed.
europmc-pmc534809:
Paul W. K. Rothemund, Nick Papadakis, and Erik Winfree made DNA compute a pattern in PLoS Biology in 2004. Algorithms guide shape in both machines and living things. Their aim was to build a fractal by rule: a Sierpinski triangle, the sieve-like pattern of nested triangles. The rule at its heart is a simple either-or logic step called XOR.

DNA tiles, small crossed pieces of DNA, stood in for the tiles of a cell game. Long starter strands seeded the growth, and the tiles then clicked in place by rule as the crystal grew. Under a fine microscope, clear Sierpinski patterns showed, with one to two hundred tiles in right spots. Slips ran between one and ten per hundred tiles. Faults aside, the growth proved that DNA assembly can run any cell game rule, and in time any set program.
europmc-pmc5405509:
S. Ryder and seven co-authors review the burden of Duchenne muscular dystrophy in a 2017 paper in the Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases. The disease is a fast, fatal muscle disorder present from birth that strikes almost only boys. The team searched studies from 2005 to mid 2015 on how common it is, how it unfolds, what care patients get, and what it costs families and health systems.

Birth rates ran near sixteen to twenty cases per hundred thousand live births, though rates by country varied widely. Most boys lose the power to walk at about age twelve, and breathing support starts near age twenty. Care such as steroids, spine surgery, and therapy differed much between countries. Costs climbed steeply as the disease advanced. The authors flag thin proof on quality of life and costs.
europmc-pmc5424009:
Johnstone reports a curious loose body found during surgery in a woman's pelvis. The case paper appeared in the Transactions of the Edinburgh Obstetrical Society. The patient was 32 and had borne one child. She felt something coming down and had sharp pain on her right side. X-ray films showed an oval mass in the pelvis. A second film showed it had moved. That mobility puzzled the team.

At surgery, a hard stony mass lay free in the Pouch of Douglas. It was about the size and shape of a large Brazil nut. The left ovary was missing. The mass looked like a dried, calcified ovary. Under the microscope its core showed no clear tissue. Surface patches resembled ovarian lining. Johnstone then reviews other loose bodies in the belly. Most were fibroids or twists of fatty tags on the bowel. The patient recovered fully.
europmc-pmc5442809:
Park and co-authors report a seven-year follow-up of a stem cell product for worn knee cartilage. Their clinical trial report appeared in Stem Cells Translational Medicine. Cartilage barely repairs itself. Osteoarthritis care mostly eases pain. The product, called Cartistem, mixes two parts. One is stem cells from donated umbilical cord blood. The other is a hyaluronic acid gel. Surgeons applied it to deep cartilage defects.

Seven patients joined the trial. All had grade 3 osteoarthritis with full-depth defects. A scope check at 12 weeks showed maturing repair tissue. Pain and knee function scores improved by 24 weeks. The gains held across seven years. Tissue samples at one year looked like true hyaline cartilage. Scans at three years showed the repair persisted. Only five mild to moderate side effects appeared. No bone overgrowth or tumors formed. The authors urge larger trials to confirm the result.
europmc-pmc5447909:
Bleakley and Hayes review algae as a future source of protein for people and animals. Their review appeared in Foods. World population may grow by 2.3 billion by 2050. Food output must rise by about 70 percent. Land and fresh water are tight. Algae need neither farmland nor fresh water. Seaweed yields 2.5 to 7.5 tons of protein per hectare yearly. Microalgae yield 4 to 15 tons. Soy and wheat yield far less.

The review profiles algae that people already eat. It judges their protein quality and digestibility. It then walks through extraction methods. Enzymes, chemicals, and physical force are the old routes. Ultrasound, electric pulses, and microwaves are newer ones. Dairy-style enrichment could lift value further. Algal protein could yield health peptides and pigments. Uses span human food, farm feed, and fish farms. Harvest rights, seasons, and costly isolation still block scale.
europmc-pmc546409:
Johnston and co-authors demonstrate direct links between cerebrospinal fluid and nasal lymphatic vessels across mammals. Their study appeared in Cerebrospinal Fluid Research. Brain tissue contains no lymphatics. Textbooks credited arachnoid projections into veins for fluid absorption. Sheep experiments challenged that view. They suggested nasal lymphatics carry the major load. Whether humans share the route was untested. The team injected yellow Microfil into the spinal fluid compartment. Seven species were examined after death.

The species ran from mice to monkeys and humans. Human material was studied within seven hours of death. In every species the tracer pooled around the olfactory bulbs. It crossed the cribriform plate along olfactory nerves. It then entered rich lymphatic networks in the nasal lining. The pattern was the first direct human evidence. The authors propose a universal mammalian pathway. Some fluid disorders may reflect lymphatic absorption failure.
europmc-pmc5487809:
Scatteia, Baritussio, and Bucciarelli-Ducci present a review in Heart Failure Reviews on strain imaging with cardiac magnetic resonance. Ejection fraction is the standard measure of heart pump function. It often changes only late in heart disease, though. Judging wall motion by eye is also error-prone. Strain imaging measures muscle deformation directly and may catch damage sooner.

The review defines strain and strain rate in plain terms. It then surveys the scan methods used to measure them. Tagging and feature tracking are among the main tools. Each method's strengths and limits are compared. Clinical uses across heart diseases close the survey. Cardiologists and imaging staff are the target readers.
europmc-pmc5488109:
Bassett and co-authors present a review in Sports Medicine on step counting. Steps per day offer a simple, objective gauge of walking activity. Pedometers spread in research after 1995, and wearable trackers boomed after 2010. Yet step values vary from day to day. Sound measurement rules are therefore essential, the authors argue.

Valid estimates need three to seven days of wear, they report. Devices worn at different body sites each carry trade-offs. Cross-sectional studies link more daily steps to better health markers. Programs using step counters raised inactive people's counts by about 2,500 steps a day. The authors call for shared testing standards. Dose and response links need firmer data.
europmc-pmc5526809:
Perski and co-authors present a systematic review in Translational Behavioral Medicine on digital health tools. Apps and websites that coach behavior change are called DBCIs here. Whether they work seems to depend on engagement. Yet fields define engagement in clashing ways. The team searched four databases and kept 117 relevant articles.

Engagement has two faces, they conclude: experience and behavior. One field treats it as absorbed flow, another as simple usage time. Their framework links engagement to the tool, its context, and the target behavior. Mechanisms of action sit between the tool and its effects. Shared definitions would sharpen future trials, they argue.
europmc-pmc5559609:
de Ávila and co-authors present a research article in Nature Communications. They built tiny motors that swim through stomach fluid and carry a drug. The cargo was clarithromycin, an antibiotic. The target was Helicobacter pylori, a bacterium that infects the stomach in mice.

The motors are made of magnesium and move on their own in gastric fluid. That motion helped the drug reach the stomach lining. Treated mice showed a sharp drop in bacteria, with no clear toxicity. The motors matched free drug given with an acid-blocking drug. They worked without that extra drug, since their motion uses up protons. Readers see a first live-animal test of motor-based delivery.
europmc-pmc5567209:
Wu and colleagues report a long-term follow-up study in Scientific Reports. They recruited 25 people who recovered from SARS. The patients were seen twelve years after their infection. Many had since faced lung, heart, or blood sugar problems.

Blood tests compared the survivors with healthy controls. Their body chemistry differed in clear ways. Levels of certain fat-related molecules were broadly raised. The pattern matched effects seen in other patients given high-dose steroid pulses. The authors suggest those steroid pulses may cause lasting systemic harm. Readers get rare evidence on the long shadow of both the disease and its treatment.
europmc-pmc5574709:
Chakravorty and co-authors report a lab and clinical test of a new tuberculosis assay. The work appeared in mBio. Their Ultra version of the Xpert test aims to find Mycobacterium tuberculosis in sputum. It also aims to spot resistance to rifampin, a key drug. The older Xpert test missed cases when sputum held few bacilli. It also gave some false resistance calls.

The team spiked sputum with known amounts of bacteria to set detection limits. Ultra found far lower levels than Xpert did. On clinical sputum samples, Ultra reached higher overall sensitivity. Its gain was largest on smear-negative samples. Both tests kept the same high specificity. Ultra also caught all tested resistance-linked mutations in the rpoB gene. It gave no false resistance results. The authors say Ultra should help most in patients whose sputum holds very few bacilli.
europmc-pmc5590809:
Grossmann and co-authors probe what radiomics measures in eLife. Radiomics turns tumor scans into numbers. Those numbers predict outcomes in lung cancer. What biology sits beneath them was unknown.

Two patient cohorts anchor the study. One held 262 North American patients. The other held 89 European patients. Imaging features lined up with molecular pathways in both. Features tied to immune response and inflammation also tracked survival. Tissue staining backed the imaging signal. Some features predicted single pathways with fair accuracy. Texture spread predicted one protein-breakdown pathway best. Prognosis improved when three data kinds combined. Radiomic, genetic, and clinical data together beat each alone. Readers see scans read as a noninvasive window on tumor biology.
europmc-pmc5605509:
The GBD 2016 Disease and Injury Incidence and Prevalence Collaborators report global estimates of non-fatal health loss in The Lancet. Death rates have fallen for decades in most of the world. Years spent in poor health have not fallen at the same pace. This study measures that quieter burden for nearly every country.

The team estimated how common 328 diseases and injuries were in 195 countries, from 1990 to 2016. Each case was weighted by how much it limits daily life. Low back pain caused the most lost healthy years. Migraine, hearing loss, iron-deficiency anaemia, and major depression followed. Rates adjusted for age fell only a little overall. Raw totals rose as populations grew and aged. Women carried higher rates than men. The spread between countries was far smaller for poor health than for early death. Planners get a shared ledger for the care needs of ageing societies.
europmc-pmc5695209:
Wick and co-authors show how long-read sequencing can finish bacterial genomes. Their research article appeared in Microbial Genomics. Short reads cannot resolve genome structure. That gap makes it hard to track resistance genes. The team used a small MinION device from Oxford Nanopore. Twelve Klebsiella isolates shared one flow cell.

Mixed assembly worked best in their tests. Long reads plus short reads resolved each genome. The tool they used needed little manual help. Long reads alone resolved fewer genomes. Error rates stayed higher despite fixes. The authors advise a two-step plan. Start with short reads first. Add long reads when structure matters. They call these runs a fast, high-volume finishing tool.
europmc-pmc5705709:
Shadrin and co-authors build a platform for growing mature human heart tissue. Their system, called Cardiopatch, cultures heart cells made from pluripotent stem cells. Such cells are used for drug tests and disease models. Methods to make large, working heart tissue for therapy have been lacking.

After five weeks, the patches showed strong electrical and mechanical coupling. Their structure gained features of adult heart muscle, such as T-tubules and M-bands. Output rose toward adult heart values during culture. Patches scaled to a clinically useful size kept uniform traits. In mice, host blood vessels grew into the patches. On rat hearts, patches engrafted well and did not raise abnormal rhythms.
europmc-pmc5769309:
Engstrand and co-authors study liver spread in colorectal cancer patients from Stockholm. Their cohort covers people diagnosed in 2008 and followed for five years. The team pulled records from a national quality registry and patient files. They compared spread patterns and survival by the side of the first tumor.

Liver spread appeared in 272 of the 1,026 patients. Left sided tumors spread to liver and lung more often, yet right sided spread was wider once present. Patients with left sided disease lived longer after liver spread. Added lung spread did not change survival in their adjusted tests.
europmc-pmc5781309:
Hackshaw and co-authors pool cohort studies on light smoking and heart disease and stroke risk. Many smokers cut down rather than quit, hoping risk falls in step. The team gathered 141 cohort studies from 55 reports. They modeled risk at one, five, and twenty cigarettes a day against never smokers.

Light smoking carried a large share of the excess risk of heavy smoking, they find. That share sits far above what a straight line from zero would predict. The pattern held for men and women and for both diseases. Cutting down alone leaves much of the risk in place.
europmc-pmc5794709:
Farzi, Fröhlich, and Holzer review the two way talk between gut microbes and the body's stress axis. That axis, run from brain to adrenal glands, steers many body processes under stress. Disorders of the gut brain link often come with a mis-set stress axis. The review maps how the two sides signal each other.

Routes include the immune system, gut and brain barriers, and microbial products. Gut hormones and nerve paths also play roles. Early life stress models and germ free mice supply much of the proof. Probiotics, prebiotics, and antibiotics shift the talk in tests.
europmc-pmc5796209:
Seca and Pinto review plant compounds that fight cancer, focusing on trial successes. Natural products inspire a large share of approved drugs. The review covers alkaloids, terpenes, and polyphenols with strong anticancer promise. Each case is chosen for reaching clinical trials or real use in care.

For each compound, the authors give its plant source and discovery path. They set out its targets in cancer cells. Chemical tweaks that raise its power are also traced. Paclitaxel and homoharringtonine stand as drugs in use. Curcumin and ingenol mebutate show the trial stage.
europmc-pmc5799609:
Bradbury and co-authors test the diet questions used in UK Biobank. UK Biobank follows 500,000 adults across the United Kingdom. At joining, each person answered brief food questions on a touchscreen. Later diet studies rely on those answers.

The team checked repeat answers from about 20,348 people after four years. They also compared answers with detailed 24-hour diet recalls. Most people gave the same or a near food category again. The brief questions ranked people well by intake. Readers get proof that short diet questions can support large studies. Agreement was strongest for fish and meat items.
europmc-pmc5811909:
Heintz-Buschart and co-authors compare nose and gut microbes in Parkinson's disease. Gut microbe shifts have been tied to Parkinson's before. A sleep disorder called RBD often comes first. The team asks if microbe shifts show that early.

Stool and nasal samples came from 76 patients and 78 healthy people. Another 21 people had the sleep disorder. Gut microbes differed in Parkinson's, with more Akkermansia among the changes. Most shifts also appeared in the sleep disorder group. They tracked nonmotor symptoms like mood and smell. Nasal microbes showed no strong gaps. Readers see gut change as a possible early sign.
europmc-pmc5819709:
Page and co-authors count registrations in PROSPERO, the review registry. PROSPERO logs planned systematic reviews before they run. Preregistration curbs hidden mid-study changes and wasted repeats. The registry opened in February 2011.

By October 2017 it held 26,535 registered reviews. Monthly sign-ups grew tenfold over the period, rising from 63 to 800 each month. The site drew over 1.75 million views in one year. A hand-checked sample of 150 records showed most tackle treatment questions. In 29 percent, key outcome details were left vague. Readers get a clear health check on a registry built for research honesty.
europmc-pmc5830209:
Norris reports a case of fungoid disease in a man of 59. A mole had sat on the man's lower belly since birth. In 1816 the skin around it darkened. A tumor then grew from that very spot.

The mass reached half a hen's egg in size. It felt firm and fleshy, with a raw, foul surface. Norris removed it by knife, and the wound healed well. Within six weeks the tumor grew back from the scar. Dozens of dark nodules spread like a bunch of grapes. Groin glands swelled as the mass kept spreading. Readers get an early, grim record of a recurring skin cancer.
europmc-pmc5845209:
Keshtkar, Azarpira, and Ghahremani review healing vesicles shed by mesenchymal stem cells. Their review appeared in Stem Cell Research & Therapy. Stem cell benefits seem to flow less from the cells themselves. Their secreted packages do much of the work.

These extracellular vesicles ferry microRNAs, messages, and proteins between cells. Animal studies credit them in kidney, liver, heart, and nerve repair. A cell-free therapy would dodge tumor and rejection risks of live cells. Doses are also easier to store and standardize. The authors call the vesicles a new frontier in regenerative medicine.
europmc-pmc5900009:
Silva and co-authors review bacteriocins and protective cultures for dairy food safety. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. Bacteriocins are peptides made by bacteria that kill other bacteria. Most producers are lactic acid bacteria with long safe use. Buyers now distrust chemical preservatives in food. Dairy firms still need longer shelf life and less spoilage.

The review covers use in milk, yogurt, and cheeses. Bacteriocins can be added pure or through live cultures. They can also sit in films and coatings on packaging. Human gut enzymes break them down with ease. That trait supports their safety case. Readers get options, limits, and recent progress in one place.
europmc-pmc5916809:
Gao and co-authors survey driver gene fusions across human cancers. Their article appeared in Cell Reports. They studied 9,624 tumours across 33 cancer types. Multiple calling tools found 25,664 fusions in total. About 63 percent passed validation checks. Fusions join two genes into one altered unit.

Fusions drove about 16.5 percent of cases, they report. In over 1 percent, a fusion was the sole driver. Cancer-gene fusions tended to raise expression levels. Suppressor fusions tended to lower them. Druggable fusions appeared in 6 percent of cases. Some fusions may also yield immune therapy targets. Readers get the scale of fusion-driven cancer.
europmc-pmc5979509:
Peach and co-authors review the molecular pharmacology of VEGF-A isoforms at the VEGFR2 receptor. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. VEGF-A is a key driver of new blood vessel growth. It signals mainly through VEGFR2 on vessel lining cells. Splicing of one gene yields many isoform variants. They differ in availability and in partner binding. Yet they bind the receptor with similar strength.

How isoforms signal so distinctly is the central puzzle. The review re-checks the pro-growth label of the classic form. It covers control by other membrane and matrix proteins. Better grasp of isoform action may guide future drugs.
europmc-pmc5979609:
Kong and co-authors review the emerging roles of VCAM-1 in immunological disorders and cancer. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. VCAM-1 is an adhesion molecule on vessel walls. The cytokine TNF alpha switches its expression on. It guides white blood cells across the vessel lining. Macrophages and T cells use it during inflammation.

New evidence links VCAM-1 to many disorders, the authors report. Rheumatoid arthritis, asthma, and transplant rejection are among them. Cancer progression also tracks with its activity. The review covers its role in inflammation in detail. It highlights VCAM-1 as a possible drug target.
europmc-pmc6046409:
Chen and co-authors review PTEN as a tumor suppressor and metabolic regulator. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Endocrinology. PTEN is an enzyme with two kinds of activity. It removes phosphate groups from proteins and lipids. Its lipid action lowers a key growth messenger.

That messenger carries signals from growth factors and insulin. Lowering it restrains cell growth and survival pathways. PTEN also works inside the cell nucleus. The review covers how PTEN itself is regulated. It then follows PTEN into sugar and fat metabolism. Mitochondrial energy work is included as well. Oddly, PTEN effects can cut both ways. Insulin sensitivity and tumor growth pull in opposite directions. Readers get a map for future cancer and diabetes work.
europmc-pmc6060609:
Hanzlikova and co-authors show that a DNA repair enzyme patrols normal replication. Their research article appeared in Molecular Cell. The enzyme system, called PARP, was known for sensing random DNA breaks. Yet most of its product appears in healthy cells during S phase. That is the stage when DNA gets copied.

The team traced the signal to unjoined Okazaki fragments. These short pieces form on one strand during copying. Blocking their formation erased the PARP signal. Disturbing their joining proteins raised it over ten-fold. PARP activity then calls in the repair protein XRCC1. Cells lacking these factors suffer when joining falters. Readers get a new day job for a classic repair sensor.
europmc-pmc6111409:
Dias and Paulo Silva Cunha wrote a review in Sensors on wearable health devices that track vital signs. Such devices help people follow their own health and fitness. They also give clinicians more data, which can support earlier diagnosis and better treatment choices.

The review lists the state of the art in wearable sensing for vital signs. It covers system designs and the specs that matter for each sign. Shrinking electronics have made the devices more reliable and easier to adapt. The authors discuss the main signs used to judge health and how each one is sensed. Readers get a map of a fast-growing field in home and remote care.
europmc-pmc6175909:
Mahn and co-authors present a research article in Nature Communications on better tools for silencing neurons with light. Optogenetic silencing lets researchers switch off chosen neurons at chosen times. Existing tools need strong light or disturb the cell's ion balance. A family of light-gated channels, GtACRs, looked promising but reached the cell surface poorly.

The team retargeted these channels to the cell body, the soma. The soma-targeted versions silenced neurons efficiently with modest light. They allowed wide silencing across the mouse cortex without killing cells. Sustained inhibition worked over long experiments. The advance widens what brain circuit studies can test, especially where large populations must be quieted at once.
europmc-pmc6195709:
Murata wrote a review in Environmental Health and Preventive Medicine on inflammation and cancer. Infection and inflammation account for roughly a quarter of cancer-causing factors. Inflamed tissues show mutagenic DNA lesions, chemical damage that can start cancer. The author reviews evidence gathered across many studies.

Examples link fluke infection to bile duct cancer and a bladder parasite to bladder cancer. Stomach bacteria, papillomavirus, and Epstein-Barr virus feature as well. Non-infectious triggers include asbestos and some nanomaterials. Murata highlights damage in cancer stem-like cells, which may explain aggressive disease features. Reactive oxygen and nitrogen species drive much of the harm. The review supports preventing chronic inflammation as cancer prevention.
europmc-pmc6258509:
Bien and co-authors built a deep learning system that reads knee MRI scans. Their study appeared in PLOS Medicine. The system is called MRNet. Knee MRI is the standard test for knee injuries, but reading it is slow. Reads also vary between doctors. The team trained the system on 1,370 scans from Stanford. Three specialist radiologists set the reference labels by majority vote.

MRNet flags general problems and two named injuries. Those are tears of the front cruciate ligament and tears of the meniscus. Scores on the home test set were strong for all three tasks. The system was then tried on a public set from Croatia with no extra training. It still found ligament tears well on that foreign set. The authors also measured how its advice changed expert reads. Such tools could triage urgent cases first.
europmc-pmc6262009:
Yu and co-authors built a tiny coated reactor that attacks tumours which have spread. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Light based therapy works well on surface tumours. It fails on deep spread tumours because light cannot reach them. The team packed a light drug into porous silica particles. An enzyme that eats glucose was added to the same particle. A cancer cell membrane coat wrapped the whole unit.

Chemical energy, not light, switches the light drug on inside deep tumours. The enzyme turns glucose into peroxide, which feeds that switch. Starving the tumour of glucose adds a second attack. The membrane coat helps particles stick to matching cancer cells and dodge immune patrols. Tests in cells and animals showed strong effects. The design could extend light therapy to spread disease.
europmc-pmc6298009:
Davis and co-authors present decontam, a tool that flags contaminant DNA in sequencing data. Their paper appeared in Microbiome. Microbe surveys often pick up DNA that was never in the sample. Stray DNA creeps in from lab reagents and kits. It can badly skew results in low-biomass samples.

Decontam is a free R package built on two simple patterns. Contaminants show up more often in weak samples. They also appear in blank control samples. The tool sorted a human oral dataset well. It matched what microscopes and past reports showed. It also cut technical noise in dilution tests. Applied to past data, it backed doubts about a placenta microbiome. It reframes some preterm birth signals as contamination too.
europmc-pmc6340809:
McCarty and Ledesma-Amaro review tools for engineering microbial communities. Their review appeared in Trends in Biotechnology. Microbe groups already ferment food and treat waste. Synthetic biologists now design such groups on purpose. They aim at medicines, fuels, and materials. Cheap carbon sources could feed those processes.

The review covers tools to build and program consortia. It explains how groups divide labor between species. It also covers signals that let species talk and coordinate. Case studies show what is already possible. Obstacles include stability and competition within groups. The authors point to new tools that can tame those risks. The piece gives bioengineers a map of a fast-moving field.
europmc-pmc6403009:
Bi and co-authors review artificial intelligence in cancer imaging, in CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians. Cancer care needs hard calls based on layered data. Scans are read by eye, and those readings can vary between doctors.

AI tools promise sharper detection and tracking of tumors, the review says. They can mine scan features that eyes cannot see. Yet clinical use faces hurdles, from weak validation to data that does not travel between hospitals. The authors sort current uses of AI in cancer imaging. They also name what must improve before routine care adopts it.
europmc-pmc6497709:
Yue and co-authors combine sound-activated therapy with checkpoint immunotherapy in mouse tumors, aiming to get the reach of ultrasound with the staying power of immune memory. Their liposomes, built entirely from clinically approved parts, co-carry a sonosensitizer, hematoporphyrin monomethyl ether, and the immune adjuvant imiquimod; focused ultrasound triggers the sensitizer to attack tumor tissue noninvasively.

Adding anti-PD-L1 antibody arrested primary tumors and sharply cut lung metastases, leaving 5.6 nodules on average against 30.8 in controls, and cured animals resisted tumor rechallenge, evidence of durable immune memory. Neither ultrasound therapy nor checkpoint blockade alone matched the pairing across the multiple tumor models tested, making the case for combination design.
europmc-pmc6588209:
Carhart-Harris and Friston propose REBUS, a unified model of how psychedelics act on the brain, writing in Pharmacological Reviews. The brain, on their account, runs on predictions: high-level beliefs rain expectations down, and sensory signals climb up only when they surprise. Psychedelics, they argue, loosen the grip of those top beliefs — relaxed beliefs under psychedelics — while raising the brain's entropy.

With priors relaxed, bottom-up signals, especially from the limbic system, flow freely and can rewrite entrenched expectations. The model merges the free-energy principle with the entropic brain hypothesis. Its therapeutic claim follows directly: mental illnesses rest on overweighted priors, locked in too tightly, and a psychedelic session may loosen them enough for revision to occur.
europmc-pmc6624409: Nallanthighal, Heiserman, and Cheon authored this article in Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology. Its subject is the extracellular matrix and its role in cancer stemness. The matrix is the scaffold of proteins around cells. Cancer stemness names the stem-like traits of some tumor cells. The hosted text pairs the title and byline with a long reference list. Its citations span work on matrix signaling, hypoxia, and stem-like tumor cells.
europmc-pmc6661709:
Du and co-authors track US adults' adherence to federal aerobic activity guidelines from 2007 to 2016. Their cross-sectional study appears in JAMA Network Open. Data came from the national NHANES surveys. The sample held 27,343 adults. Guidelines call for 150 weekly minutes of moderate activity. Work, transport, and leisure activity all counted here. The weighted adherence rate barely moved overall. It went from 63 percent to 65 percent. That change was not statistically significant.

Sedentary time, by contrast, rose significantly. It climbed from under six hours to about six and a half hours daily. Nearly every subgroup sat more over time. Adults both inactive and highly sedentary grew too. Their share rose from 16 to 19 percent.
europmc-pmc6693809:
Hughes and co-authors argue that filling in missing data is not always the answer. Their guidance paper appears in the International Journal of Epidemiology. Missing data threaten bias and precision in studies. Filling in is widely backed over complete case analysis. The authors show that preference is conditional. Complete case analysis stays unbiased in set situations. The key is whether completeness hinges on outcome. Covariates can account for that link. Even some not-at-random patterns qualify. Filling in under an at-random assumption can bias there.

Causal diagrams depict each missing-data scenario. Bias and efficiency are compared across them. Filling in wins when extra variables inform values. A real growth study example shows the choice. Method choice must follow why data went missing.
europmc-pmc6720009:
Xu and co-authors reviewed hydrogels held together by Schiff base links for medical use. Hydrogels are soft, water-rich materials that mimic the setting around cells. A Schiff base is a bond that can form and break again under mild conditions. That reversibility lets such gels heal themselves after damage.

The bond also reacts to acidity, a signal found in the body. Different Schiff base types give gels tuned strength and stability. The review covers how these gels are designed and made. It then surveys uses in drug delivery, tissue repair, wound healing, adhesives, bioprinting, and biosensors.
europmc-pmc6769509:
Al-Ishaq and co-authors review flavonoids and their anti-diabetic effects. Flavonoids are plant compounds found in fruits, vegetables, and fungi. They share a 15-carbon skeleton with two aromatic rings and fall into six subclasses. Diabetes, marked by high blood sugar, is a growing global burden. Lab and animal studies suggest flavonoids can help.

The review maps the pathways flavonoids act on. These include glucose transporters, liver enzymes, and the AMPK, PPAR, and NF-kB pathways. Through them, flavonoids may improve how diabetes develops and how its complications unfold. One compound, chrysin, eased nerve damage in diabetic rats and lowered inflammatory signals. The authors call flavonoids a promising support for blood sugar control.
europmc-pmc6787009:
Alves and co-authors propose an improved anatomical model of the brain's default-mode network. This network, the largest in the brain, hums during rest. Most research has focused on the cortex alone. Its resemblance to the old limbic system model hints that deeper structures matter too. The authors argue that subcortical parts have been underappreciated.

Their model adds the basal forebrain, cholinergic nuclei, and key thalamic nuclei to the network. Diffusion imaging tractography showed the thalamus and basal forebrain are central connectors. These chemically diverse nuclei help reconcile imaging results with findings from diseased brains. The model also raises the chance of finding a matching network in other mammals. That would let animal studies speak to human resting brain function.
europmc-pmc6827209:
Zhu and co-authors review a cell-surface receptor called AXL in Molecular Cancer. AXL belongs to the TAM family of receptors. Its partner protein, GAS6, switches it on. In many cancers AXL is overactive. That activity helps tumours grow, spread, and survive treatment.

The review lays out AXL's structure, its normal roles, and the signals it sends. Those signals aid invasion, new blood vessel growth, and the shift of cells into a mobile state. They also help cancers resist drugs and hide from the immune system. The authors then survey attacks on AXL now in study, from small-molecule blockers and antibodies to aptamers and natural compounds.
europmc-pmc6876109:
Bell and co-authors review DNA methylation ageing clocks in Genome Biology. These clocks read chemical marks at chosen spots in DNA to estimate a person's age. They track chronological age closely in humans and other vertebrates. Hopes run higher: that they measure biological ageing itself, and so can test treatments meant to slow it.

The authors lay out what still blocks that use. The drivers of age-linked mark changes are not fully known, and results vary by tissue and disease. They recommend work in single cells, in diverse and long-followed populations, and in non-human models. Ethical issues in forensic age estimation also get a warning.
europmc-pmc6904909:
Gleizer and co-authors report a feat of metabolic engineering in Cell. Life divides into autotrophs, which build themselves from carbon dioxide, and heterotrophs, which eat organic carbon. The workhorse bacterium Escherichia coli is a heterotroph. Turning it into a CO2 feeder had resisted all attempts, despite hopes for sustainable food and fuel production.

The team installed the CO2-fixing enzymes Rubisco and phosphoribulokinase, plus an enzyme that harvests energy from formate. They then evolved the strain in the lab, cutting its sugar pathways step by step. The result: bacteria drawing all their biomass carbon from CO2. Formate supplied only energy, and it can be made electrochemically from renewable power.
europmc-pmc6979009:
Huang and co-authors show that a circular RNA shipped in tiny vesicles boosts liver cancer spread. Their study appeared in the Journal of Experimental and Clinical Cancer Research. Exosomes are small parcels cells use to talk. Their cargo can push cancer growth, movement, and invasion in neighbours.

One cargo molecule, circRNA-100338, ran high in aggressive liver cancer cells and their exosomes. Raising it made cancer cells more invasive; lowering it did the reverse. Passed to blood vessel lining cells, it sped their growth and new vessel formation, and raised leakiness. In animals, it promoted tumour spread. In patients, blood levels that stayed high after surgery marked risk of lung spread and poor survival. The circle, the authors say, could warn of relapse and guide follow-up.
europmc-pmc7026709:
The GBD 2017 Inflammatory Bowel Disease Collaborators chart inflammatory bowel disease across 195 countries and territories in The Lancet Gastroenterology and Hepatology. The disease burden is rising worldwide, but at very different speeds in different places. Knowing where it climbs fastest helps health systems plan prevention and care.

The collaborators modelled deaths with a cause-of-death ensemble method and non-fatal burden with a Bayesian meta-regression tool fed by studies, hospital discharges, and claims data. In 2017 there were 6.8 million cases worldwide. The age-standardised prevalence rate rose from 79.5 per 100,000 people in 1990 to 84.3 in 2017. The report also tracks years of life lost and years lived with disability, showing a heavy load in high-prevalence regions and fast growth in newly industrialised ones.
europmc-pmc7067809:
Fares and co-authors revisit metastasis as a hallmark of cancer in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. Metastasis, the spread of cancer to distant sites, causes the greatest number of cancer deaths, yet it remains poorly understood. New research paradigms have begun to expose the molecular machinery behind it. The review gathers those advances into a fresh account of how spread happens.

A travelling cancer cell must interact with proteins and cells along its route, survive the tissue it lands in, and colonise it. Communication with the tumour microenvironment helps it overcome stromal defences and settle. Genetic and epigenetic changes inside the cell, and signals from its surroundings, drive its mobility and plasticity. The authors also ask whether surgery itself can sometimes aid dissemination, as dormant cells wake after a primary tumour is removed. Pinning down these mechanisms matters because each step offers a therapeutic window.
europmc-pmc7145509:
Karagkouni and co-authors present version 3 of DIANA-LncBase, a database of experimentally supported microRNA targets on non-coding transcripts, in Nucleic Acids Research. MicroRNAs steer gene activity by binding RNA molecules, including long non-coding RNAs whose functions are still being mapped. Claims about these bindings need experimental backing.

The new version holds about half a million entries, covering roughly 240,000 unique microRNA and long non-coding RNA pairs specific to tissues and cell types. Data came from hand-curated papers and more than 300 high-throughput datasets across 243 human and mouse cell types and tissues. New features include variant information on over 67,000 target sites, expression profiles, and interactive plots. The database was rebuilt from the ground up.
europmc-pmc7163409:
Rhee and co-authors measure antibiotic resistance in sepsis and the costs of mistargeted first treatment, in JAMA Network Open. Their cohort covered 17,430 adults with culture-proven sepsis at 104 United States hospitals. Guidelines urge immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics for suspected sepsis, but how often resistant bacteria are truly present was unclear.

Broad-spectrum drugs were given to 67.0% of patients, yet resistant Gram-positive organisms appeared in only 13.6% and resistant Gram-negative ones in 13.2%. Both missing the true organism and covering resistant organisms that were not there were tied to higher mortality after risk adjustment. The authors argue for faster diagnostics to aim the first dose better.
europmc-pmc7175209:
Mijit and co-authors review how the protein p53 helps control cellular senescence. Their article appeared in the journal Biomolecules. Senescence is a lasting stop to cell growth. It can follow DNA damage, worn telomeres, or strong growth signals. The authors place p53 at the center of the choice a stressed cell makes. A cell may pause and repair damage, enter senescence, or die.

The review explains how damage signals switch p53 on. It covers the ATM and ATR routes and the p53 and p21 path to growth arrest. It also describes traits that mark senescent cells. These include changed shape, altered chromatin, and a mix of secreted factors. Those secretions can inflame nearby tissue and harm its function. The authors link these processes to aging and disease. Readers get a clear map of how cell stress responses guard against cancer yet can also drive tissue decline.
europmc-pmc7200009:
Drew and co-authors describe rushing a mobile symptom app into service for real-time COVID-19 tracking. Their report appeared in Science. Lab testing was too slow to follow the virus's spread. The team updated an existing health app and invited cohort members to report symptoms daily. Recruitment reached about 2 million users in the United Kingdom and the United States.

Users shared symptoms, background details, and work exposures. Reports of fatigue, cough, and diarrhea were widespread. Loss of smell appeared less often but proved distinctive. Maps showed how symptom patterns varied by region. Health care workers were among the participants. The authors argue such apps can guide responses between test results. Population symptom data becomes an early-warning system.
europmc-pmc7217909:
An and co-authors show that danger signals from injured liver cell mitochondria directly switch on the cells that scar the liver. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Mitochondria descend from ancient bacteria, so their parts look bacterial to the immune system. When liver cells die, these signals spill out. Their role in fibrosis was unknown before this work.

Using mouse strains that resist or accept liver scarring, the team traced the chain. Mitochondrial DNA was the main active ingredient in the spilled signals. The signals woke hepatic stellate cells, the liver's scar builders. Those cells then drove further scarring. Cleanup of dying cells by other cells controlled how much signal escaped. Liver macrophages, notably, did not respond to the same signals. The study names a new driver of liver fibrosis.
europmc-pmc7226809:
Wang and Xu profile single cells from human testes to ask whether the tissue can be infected by SARS-CoV-2. Their study appeared in Cells. The virus enters cells through the ACE2 receptor, the same door used by the earlier SARS virus. Evidence had hinted at infection routes in lungs, gut, and urinary organs. The reproductive system remained an open question.

Sequencing individual testis cells mapped where ACE2 is switched on. The receptor concentrated in spermatogonia, the stem cells that start sperm production. It also appeared in Leydig and Sertoli cells, which support hormone production and sperm development. Other cell types, from sperm precursors to immune cells, were charted as well. The pattern marks the testis as a possible viral target. The authors call for care in fertility-related follow-up of patients.
europmc-pmc7245409:
Duncan and co-authors present GUIDED, a consensus checklist for reporting how health interventions are developed. Their study appeared in BMJ Open. New programs are often described too thinly for others to judge or copy them. The team built the guidance through expert consensus. Two parallel online Delphi exercises ran for three rounds each.

One panel held 26 intervention developers. The other held 18 wider stakeholders, including funders, editors, and public members. A workshop then settled the final items. The items grew out of earlier systematic reviews and interviews. They ask developers to report their aims, evidence, theory, and changes made along the way. Journals and funders can use the list to demand clearer accounts. Better reporting should make good programs easier to repeat.
europmc-pmc7290409:
Parasa and co-authors pool the evidence on gut symptoms and fecal shedding of virus in COVID-19. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in JAMA Network Open. They gathered 23 published and 6 preprint studies of patients with SARS-CoV-2 infection. Breathing symptoms dominate the disease's image, but the gut is involved more often than first thought.

About 12% of patients reported gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhea, nausea, and vomiting. Liver enzyme levels outside the normal range appeared in 15% to 20% of patients. Viral RNA was found in the stool of up to 41% of patients. That shedding raises the possibility of a fecal-oral transmission route, the authors note, and argues for including gut symptoms in case finding.
europmc-pmc7293209:
Chen, Liu and Tao review how chemical modifications made after production control three great tumor suppressor proteins. Their review appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. The proteins, Rb, p53, and PTEN, work together to restrain cell growth. Cells switch them on and off by attaching small chemical groups, in processes such as phosphorylation, acetylation, and SUMOylation.

Most of these modifications are reversible, so healthy cells use them like switches between resting and dividing. When the switching goes wrong, abnormal growth and tumors can follow. Modifications on one suppressor also affect the others, forming a network rather than three separate lines. The authors close by judging current cancer therapies that aim at these proteins as targets for prediction, prognosis, and treatment.
europmc-pmc7305609:
Li and co-authors review why tumors stop responding to PARP inhibitors, a class of cancer drugs that exploit faulty DNA repair. Their review appeared in Molecular Cancer. Tumors lacking working BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes cannot fix DNA properly, so blocking the PARP enzyme kills them while sparing normal cells, a trick called synthetic lethality.

Resistance, though, is nearly universal. More than 40% of patients with BRCA-deficient tumors never respond, and others lose their response over time. The main escape route is restoring the tumor's homologous recombination repair. Backup protection of DNA replication forks, reversion mutations that fix the original gene faults, epigenetic changes, and drug handling changes also contribute. The authors summarize strategies to overcome resistance or restore sensitivity.
europmc-pmc7381609:
Kim and co-authors report a drug combination that beats resistant ovarian cancer in Nature Communications. Ovarian cancers almost always learn to resist platinum chemotherapy and PARP inhibitors, two mainstays. Resistant cells, the team found, lean harder on a damage-response pathway run by the protein ATR.

Blocking ATR alone hurt resistant cells, but pairing an ATR blocker with a PARP inhibitor hit far harder. The combination stalled DNA copying forks, piled up double-strand breaks, and drove cell death across many resistance types, including tumors that had repaired their BRCA genes. In patient-derived tumor grafts in mice, the pairing gave complete, durable responses and longer survival. A way around a dead end, the authors argue.
europmc-pmc7391009:
Ji and co-authors build a multi-layer atlas of skin squamous cell carcinoma in Cell. They combined single-cell gene sequencing, spatial gene mapping, and ion beam imaging on human tumors and matched normal skin. The aim was to define which cells the cancer holds and where each type sits.

Tumors contained four cancer subpopulations. Three mimicked normal skin states, but a fourth, tumor-specific keratinocyte group appeared only in cancer and settled in a niche rich in fibroblasts and blood vessels. Those cells acted as a communication hub. Suppressive features showed too, with regulatory T cells parked beside killer T cells in walled-off stroma. Screens in tumor grafts found gene networks each subpopulation needs to grow.
europmc-pmc7395209:
Monaghesh and Hajizadeh systematically review telehealth during the COVID-19 outbreak in BMC Public Health. Remote care promised treatment without the infection risk of a waiting room. Searching five databases for studies from the outbreak's start, the authors kept 8 studies out of 142 search results.

The evidence shows telehealth serving prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and disease control at once. For providers and patients in self-isolation, remote visits clearly cut exposure risk. Video and phone follow-up handled much routine care while clinics were dangerous places. Quality was checked with a standard appraisal checklist. The review is early and small, as the authors note, but it marks telehealth as a standing tool for outbreaks, not a novelty.
europmc-pmc7454409:
Atkins and co-authors test which prior conditions truly raise COVID-19 risk in older adults. Hospital patients often have hypertension or heart disease, but those traits are common at older ages anyway. The team used the UK Biobank community cohort.

The cohort held 269,070 participants older than 65 years. Of them, 507 became hospital inpatients with confirmed COVID-19, and 141 died. After full adjustment, dementia, type 2 diabetes, lung disease, prior pneumonia, depression, atrial fibrillation, and hypertension stood as clear risks. The first five also predicted death. Kidney disease and asthma raised risk in women but not men. The authors warn against simple age-based targeting. Specific conditions mark the older people most at risk.
europmc-pmc7486909:
Benjamens, Dhunnoo, and Meskó catalog artificial intelligence devices cleared by the United States Food and Drug Administration. Hopes for AI in medicine run high. Rules and approval paths, though, shape what reaches clinics.

Cross-checking all approvals, the team found 64 AI-based devices and algorithms. Only 29 of the official notices named any AI or machine learning terms at all. Most devices cleared through the 510(k) path. Radiology led the fields, then cardiology, then internal medicine and general practice. The team launched a free, open database of these tools. It will update as new approvals land. The authors urge regulators to state plainly when a device is AI-based.
europmc-pmc7576409:
Kreps and co-authors survey US adults on factors tied to COVID-19 vaccine acceptance. A survey study used a national sample of adults. A hypothetical vaccine was described to respondents in detail.

The sample held 1971 US adults in total. Vaccine traits shaped which product people would choose. Efficacy, side effects and protection length all mattered. Approval process and vaccine origin also shaped choices. Endorsements by public figures had an effect too. Willingness to vaccinate linked to health care habits. Partisanship, age, sex and race also played roles. Results may help campaigns address vaccine hesitancy. Herd immunity was estimated to need about 70% coverage.
europmc-pmc7650109:
Grefkes and Fink review recovery from stroke, current ideas and future paths for care. Stroke is a leading cause of lasting disability worldwide. Acute care has improved, yet most patients stay disabled.

Survivor numbers will grow as societies age further. Better rehabilitation plans are needed for those survivors. Neural reorganization is the key driver of recovery. Brain imaging shows how networks rebuild after stroke. Some changes after stroke hinder recovery instead. Brain stimulation paired with imaging clarifies these shifts. Together they show how plasticity can be steered. New technology may tailor treatment to each patient. Limits of current models are also set out. Future work should target network repair, the authors argue.
europmc-pmc7684009:
O'Connor and co-authors track mental health in UK adults through the first lockdown weeks. They surveyed a national sample in three waves. The first wave ran from March 31 to April 9, 2020. In all, 3077 adults took part at the start.

Suicidal thoughts rose across the waves, a trend the authors call concerning in young adults. Anxiety eased, as did feelings of defeat and entrapment. Depression levels held steady, well-being rose, and loneliness did not change. Women, young people, poorer adults, and those with prior mental illness fared worst on most measures. The authors warn that harm may last long past lockdown.
europmc-pmc7778909:
Kooistra and co-authors update GPCRdb, a database for a major drug target family. G protein-coupled receptors form the largest family of membrane proteins. They mediate the action of one-third of medicines. The database serves more than 4,000 researchers each month with reference data and design tools.

It holds all human non-olfactory receptors, plus more than 27,000 counterparts in other species. Drug records top 2,000 agents, with nearly 200,000 ligands and their activity data. All published receptor structures are listed and refined. Models cover each human receptor in three states. New tools help spot key residues and design mutations for lab work.
europmc-pmc7795409:
Panizo and co-authors review fibrosis in chronic kidney disease. Fibrosis is a buildup of excess matrix after tissue injury. It can defend tissue at first. Left unchecked, it turns into lasting organ damage.

Many signals start and drive kidney fibrosis. The authors give special weight to inflammation. They cover the renin-angiotensin system and parathyroid hormone. FGF23, Klotho, and microRNAs all play roles. The vitamin D hormone system is covered too. These factors harm both kidney and heart. The review maps the core pathways for researchers and clinicians. The process can affect the skin, lungs, liver, heart, and pancreas as well as the kidney.
europmc-pmc7806509:
The IHME COVID-19 Forecasting Team models future paths of the pandemic in the United States. The team used case and death data from February 1 to September 21, 2020. Their model sorts people into susceptible, exposed, infectious, and recovered groups. Projections run state by state.

The forecast window covers September 22, 2020 to February 28, 2021. Inputs include pneumonia season patterns, travel, and testing rates. Mask use and distancing rules enter as driving factors too. The team tested how non-drug measures change the course. Their scenarios show what easing or holding measures could bring. The work was built to guide state-level planning through winter.
europmc-pmc7820109:
Fancourt and co-authors trace anxiety and depression week by week during lockdown in England. Concern about mental health under COVID-19 was widespread. Early studies suggested a broad decline. How symptoms moved over time was unclear. The study followed adults through enforced isolation.

The team used repeated surveys from the same people. That design shows paths, not just snapshots. Some people stayed well throughout the lockdown. Others started low and recovered at different speeds. A smaller group stayed highly distressed. The authors stress that averages hide these splits. Knowing the paths helps target help at those who need it most. It also informs how easing rules may lift or strain mood.
europmc-pmc7821609:
Abers and co-authors find a blood signature that predicts death in COVID-19 patients. Immune overreaction drives severe disease. Which immune markers best forecast outcomes was unclear. The team studied 175 patients in Italy. Illness ranged from mild to critical.

The team measured 66 soluble markers in blood. They also read gene activity signatures in whole blood. A wide inflammatory pattern stood out. Twelve markers tied to higher death risk on their own. The list includes IL-6, ferritin, IL-15, and IL-10. Repeat measures over time refined that list. Four markers stayed high in patients who died. They were sST2, sTNFRSF1A, IL-10, and IL-15. Such a panel could help sort patients early.
europmc-pmc7826709:
Izzo and co-authors review sarcopenia in people with type 2 diabetes. Diabetes weighs heavily on older adults. About 25% of people over the age of 65 years have it. Sarcopenia means loss of muscle mass, strength, and function. It now counts as a diabetes complication in old age.

The authors update what is known about its frequency. They list the traits that travel with it. Age, sex, body weight, and disease length all matter. Blood sugar control and vessel complications are covered too. Diet and glucose-lowering drugs enter the picture as well. Spotting sarcopenia early could protect quality of life. The authors urge doctors and dietitians to screen for it.
europmc-pmc7857409:
Schoof and co-authors build a synthetic nanobody that locks the SARS-CoV-2 spike in its off state. Standard antibodies need mammal cell factories. They also need vein delivery. Nanobodies can be brewed in microbes. Their small size and toughness suit new delivery routes.

The team's nanobody grips the spike with great force. It holds the spike shut in its inactive form. A closed spike cannot grab the cell receptor. Virus entry stops at that point. Linked copies of the nanobody hit even harder. The design stayed potent in lab virus tests. Spray delivery into the airways is a stated aim.
europmc-pmc7878809:
Sato and co-authors present a research study on predicting how RNA molecules fold. The shape an RNA strand folds into shapes what it can do in the cell. Computer models can predict that shape, but learning-based models often overfit their training data.

The authors built a method called MXfold2. It joins scores learned by a deep neural network with the classic Turner energy rules for RNA folding. A training step keeps the learned scores close to the physics-based free energy. In tests on newly found non-coding RNAs, the authors report the most robust and accurate predictions among the tools compared. The method kept its speed while gaining reliability. It offers a practical route to better RNA structure prediction.
europmc-pmc7909709:
Christensen and co-authors present a CDC surveillance report on autism spectrum disorder among children in the United States. The data come from the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring Network. The network tracks children aged 8 years at 11 sites across the country. This report covers the year 2012.

Staff first screened records from schools and health services. Trained clinicians then reviewed the records to decide which children met the case definition. That definition rested on behaviours matching the diagnostic manual then in use. The report gives prevalence figures for the network as a whole and site by site. It also describes the children's traits, such as age at first diagnosis and co-occurring conditions. Such figures guide services and policy for affected families.
europmc-pmc7911109:
Arroyave-Ospina and co-authors present a review of oxidative stress in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. The disease begins with fat build-up in the liver and can progress to inflammation and scarring. Oxidative stress is a major factor in that progression. It grows when oxidants overwhelm the body's antioxidant defences.

Strained fat handling harms the organelles that manage energy and lipids. The result is cell stress, lipid damage, and signals that drive inflammation. Scar-forming pathways switch on as the damage builds. A defence system called the Nrf2/ARE pathway fights back and helps restore balance. The review explains these links in detail. It then surveys treatments built on antioxidant effects. Their targets and early promise are weighed for use in prevention and care.
europmc-pmc7932109:
Koenig and co-authors report a research study on nanobodies that block SARS-CoV-2. Antibodies are a key weapon against COVID-19, but full-size ones are costly and hard to make in bulk. Nanobodies are single-domain antibodies, far smaller and easier to produce. They might even be given by inhalation. The team set out to build strong ones guided by structure.

They describe four nanobodies that bind the virus spike and stop it infecting cells. Structures showed the four aim at two distinct sites on the spike. Joining several nanobodies into one molecule made them far more potent. Linked forms that hit both sites also blocked the rise of escape mutants. The work points to a cheap, stable class of antiviral agents. It also shows how design can stay ahead of viral change.
europmc-pmc7938609:
Dries and co-authors present a software toolbox called Giotto for spatial gene expression data. New methods can now read gene and protein activity while keeping each cell's place in the tissue. That spatial view can reveal how cells act in their true setting. But the data are complex, and analysis tools lag behind. Giotto aims to close that gap.

The toolbox covers the full workflow in one package. Its analysis side characterises tissue make-up, spatial patterns, and cell-to-cell interaction. Single-cell data can be folded in to enrich cell-type calls. The display side lets users explore results and images side by side. The team tested Giotto on datasets from many platforms to show its range. The package is open source. It gives labs a single home for a fast-growing kind of data.
europmc-pmc8114409:
Hevey offers health psychology researchers a hands-on tour of network analysis. A network draws variables as nodes and their links as edges. The picture can expose a system's core at a glance. The tutorial walks from first concepts to a worked example. The example uses survey data on the theory of planned behaviour. A group of 200 people answered questions about regular exercise.

Attitudes, social norms, perceived control, and intentions formed the item pool. The estimated network split into three distinct communities of items. One node sat at the center of the whole web. It was the affective attitude item, how exercise feels. The author draws the practical moral with care. If feelings about exercise bind the system together, target feelings. Bigger samples would steady the estimates, he warns. Replication is owed before clinics act on the map. The method itself earns a clear, friendly case.
europmc-pmc8262709:
Xiong and co-authors announce ADMETlab 2.0, a platform that predicts drug-like traits of chemicals. Poor absorption or toxicity kills many drug candidates late. Judging those traits early can save years of work.

The platform predicts absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity. Its endpoints now number about twice the old version's count. Models were rebuilt for wider and sharper coverage. Chemists can screen leads online before synthesis. The tool supports design choices while change is still cheap. It sits beside lab tests, not in place of them. The redesign rebuilt the server from the ground up.
europmc-pmc8543909:
Zhao and co-authors review fresh gains in selective photothermal therapy for tumors. This treatment turns light into heat to burn cancer away. Agents that make the heat spread through the whole body, though. Missed laser aim can then harm normal tissue.

The review sorts plans that make the therapy pickier. One path packs more agent into the tumor site. Another gives agents a self-regulating heat switch. Both aim to raise survival and cut side effects. Lab and early results for each plan are weighed. The authors close with the challenges of clinic use. Selective heat may widen this therapy's safe reach.
europmc-pmc8653609:
Hellenbrand and co-authors review the timeline of inflammation after spinal cord injury. Trauma first harms the cord directly. A second wave of harm then builds over hours and can last more than six months. This wave kills more cells and widens the damage. No current treatment restores lost function well.

The review uses rodent studies to map immune cell entry over time. It sorts the roles of key cytokine signals in the second wave. Rats and mice differ in some parts of the response. Knowing which cells act, and when, can guide new treatments. The authors see precise timing as the key gap in the field.
europmc-pmc8766409:
Chen and co-authors review strategies and technologies for isolating and purifying exosomes. Exosomes are tiny vesicles that almost all cells release. They carry cell-specific cargo to other cells. That cargo gives them value in diagnosis, prognosis, and even therapy.

Clean, intact samples are the first step for any such use. Common separation methods are complex, slow, and often impure. They also need large sample volumes. The review first covers exosome traits, origins, and jobs. It then weighs standard methods and their clinical limits. New routes, led by microfluidic chips, close the survey with strong early results.
europmc-pmc8785409:
Vangeel and co-authors test whether three antiviral drugs stay active against Omicron and other variants of concern. The drugs were remdesivir, molnupiravir, and nirmatrelvir, plus their parent compounds. Tests ran in infected cells treated with a range of doses. The ancestral virus and all five variants of concern were covered.

All compounds blocked each virus at near equal strength. Their targets, the viral copying enzyme and its main protease, change little across variants. That matches the flat results seen in the assays. The authors conclude these drugs should keep working as variants shift. The finding supports their use while vaccines face immune escape.
europmc-pmc9106709:
Eskandari and Eaves review the puzzling double life of caspase-3, a protein best known for cell death. Caspase-3 cuts target proteins and helps carry out apoptosis, the ordered death of cells. Yet in living cells it also shapes protein quality, growth, and cell specialization. In some settings it can even aid tumor growth.

The review covers how caspase-3 is built, switched on, and controlled by gene signals. It weighs proof for its roles beyond death, in both normal tissue and cancer. The authors show why the same enzyme can protect cells in one case and kill them in another. Readers get a careful account of a protein whose full job is still being mapped.
europmc-pmc9233709:
