In 1693 Belilhos gave a memorial sermon for his father-in-law, a famed rabbi, which survives in manuscript. His printed sermons came out at Amsterdam that same year. A larger Hebrew poem of his, telling the history of Adam in Paradise, also survives only in manuscript. His printed sermons were issued by the Amsterdam printer Moseh Dias in that same year of 1693.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ben-sira-alphab:
Alphabet of Ben Sira names a small book built on two sets of twenty-two proverbs, one in Aramaic and one in Hebrew, set in alphabetical order. A later commentary in Hebrew explains each saying and adds fables and legends. The entry lists the Aramaic proverbs in full, from honoring a physician to keeping one's own counsel.

Only a few of those sayings can be traced to known sources, and two match proverbs of Aḥiḳar closely. The entry argues the sayings are old Jewish adages, not the work of Ben Sira himself. It then turns to the commentary and its tales.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bender-johann-h: Johann Heinrich Bender, a German jurist, was born at Frankfort in 1797 and died there on Sept. 6, 1859. He studied law at Giessen, where he also lectured from 1819 to 1823. In 1831 he moved to Frankfort to practise law. Five years later he joined the executive committee of the tariff commission and held that post until his death. The entry lists his legal works, including a history of German law, a study of oral procedure in criminal cases, and a two-volume work on commercial law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bensheim-simon-: Simon Bensheim sat in the grandducal Oberrat, the upper house of Baden. He was born at Mannheim on Oct. 14, 1823, and died there on Oct. 26, 1898. In congregational and charitable work he stayed very active all his life. His synagogue council elected him year after year without a dissenting vote, and in time he became its president. The grand duke marked his worth with an order of the second class. In the upper house he won the respect of people of all classes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernal-isaac-ma: Isaac Marcus de Almeyda Bernal, a Spanish martyr, was born in Montilla in 1633. He was burned at the stake at Santiago de Compostella in March 1655, at the age of twenty-two. A nephew of Abraham Nuñez Bernal, he had been thrown into the Inquisition prison at Valladolid at only seventeen, in 1650. A printed volume of praises tells the tale of his death in full. It adds poems in his honor by eight writers and a sermon by Jacob Abendana.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beth-jaazek-320: Beth-Jaazek is known only from the Mishnah. It was a large court. There the Sanhedrin awaited news of the new moon. The Palestinian Talmud explains its name. The calendar's calculation was settled there, it says. The entry is only a few lines long. It gives no location for the court. It names no events beyond that waiting. A single Mishnah passage is its source.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bing-albert-330:
Albert Bing was an Austrian physician. He was born at Nikolsburg, Moravia, in 1844. His birth date was September 20. He studied medicine at the University of Vienna. He finished his course in 1870. Doctorates in medicine and surgery followed. In 1871 he joined the Vienna General Hospital staff.

Bing specialized in diseases of the ear. He assisted the otologists Politzer and Gruber. He held ear clinics at Gumpendorf from 1878. He also served as otologist to the royal guard. Over twenty-four monographs came from his pen. His lecture book on ear diseases appeared in 1890.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blood-money-340:
Blood-money is ransom paid for a murder. The killer pays the victim's avenging kinsmen. Among Anglo-Saxons it had a lawful price scale. Roman law never allowed it for murder. Roman murder always drew the death penalty. Biblical law is stricter than Roman law. Numbers forbids ransom for a murderer's life. It also bars buying a fugitive's return home.

One narrow exception stands in Exodus. An ox's owner may ransom his own life. His beast killed, but he did not kill directly. Accidental killers get no such option. They must serve their full refuge term. The Talmud reasons through each case carefully.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bondavin-bonjud: Bonjudes Bondavin was a physician who lived at the end of the fourteenth century and the start of the fifteenth. He practiced at Marseilles from 1381 to 1389. In 1390 he settled at Alghero in Sardinia. The Jewish community of Cagliari chose him as rabbi for his Talmudic learning. The king confirmed the choice and extended his rule over all Jews of Sardinia. He traded scholarly letters with Isaac ben Sheshet.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-box-tree-hebrew:
Box tree is the rendering of a Hebrew word found only in that tongue. Isaiah names it among the trees of Lebanon promised for the Temple. A second Isaiah passage joins it with fir and pine in the desert.

Ezekiel's version, on a new reading, gives boxwood from the isles of Kittim. Ancient translators guessed at the word in varied ways. Some renderings give cedar, others pine. One line of tradition points to a Lebanon pine called sharbin. Another points to the true box, Buxus sempervirens, by way of the Targum. With so little material, the entry says, no firm choice between the two is possible.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brieli-judah-le:
Judah Leon ben Eliezer Brieli, also called Briel, was a rabbi in Mantua. He was born about 1643 and died in 1722. Great Talmudists of his day asked his view on questions of law.

Brieli also cultivated the secular sciences with zeal. Amsterdam's Sephardic leaders asked his help against Hayyun and his cabalistic claims. Brieli, opposed to the Cabala in general, condemned Hayyun in many letters. Hayyun struck back by calling him a Latinist who knew no Cabala. Brieli wrote a Hebrew grammar, printed at Mantua in 1724. His other works stayed in manuscript, among them attacks on Christian books and a study of miracles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-buk-3809: Buk was a town in Prussia, in the province of Posen, which passed under Prussian rule in 1793. As an old episcopal town it had kept Jews out before then. Jews began settling there after the partition, and many lived there by 1820. A nursing and burial society founded that year was still active at the time of the entry. The synagogue was built in 1846 and 1847. In 1848 a Polish uprising wrecked it and killed several Jews. It was rebuilt fully in 1894. About 250 Jews lived in Buk in 1902.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-calah-3909:
Calah was a city named in Genesis among the chief places of Assyria, set beside Nineveh and Resen. The entry says the verse holds a sound tradition: the Assyrian empire grew as an offshoot of Babylonia. The mound of Nimrod, between the Tigris and the Upper Zab, marks the site. Layard began digging there in 1845.

Diggers found a vast platform of sun dried brick faced with stone. It measured 600 yards by 400 yards. Remains showed palaces and repairs by a string of Assyrian kings, from Shalmaneser the first to Esarhaddon. The entry credits Shalmaneser, about 1300 B.C., with rebuilding the city into importance. Calah served at times as a royal residence. It never grew as populous as Asshur or Nineveh.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chajes-or-chaja:
Zebi Hirsch Chajes, a Talmudist, literary historian, and rabbi, was born at Brody on November 20, 1805. He died at Lemberg on October 12, 1855. His father was an educated banker. The boy received a good Jewish education and a good secular education at home. He learned French, German, Italian, and Latin. Rabbinical lore, though, was his chief study.

Chajes received his diploma as rabbi at twenty-two. A year later he took charge of the community of Zolkiev, where he served twenty-four years. There he formed a close friendship with Nachman Krochmal. In 1846 he passed a university examination at Lemberg and took a doctorate in philosophy. He later served as chief rabbi of Kalisch, in Russian Poland. His works include thirteen treatises on Talmudic tradition, printed in 1836, and an examination of the Targumim and Midrashim, printed in 1840.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chernigov-4309:
Chernigov, as a government of Little Russia, or Ukraine, held 114,630 Jews in 1897. They formed nearly 5 per cent of its 2,298,834 people. In 1881 they had formed only 2.5 per cent. The entry then gives the Jewish count district by district, with each district's total and its share.

Mglin district held 10,014 Jews, and Surazh held 10,078. Nyezhin held 9,987, and Starodub 9,975. Chernigov district itself held 12,006, the largest district figure. A second table lists towns and villages with their total and Jewish populations for 1897. Chernigov town shows 11,000 Jews out of 27,006. Nyezhin town shows 10,000 Jews out of 32,108. History for the government is left to other entries, the entry states, under Little Russia and the separate cities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-carlos-da: Carlos David Cohen was a writer living in Hamburg in the seventeenth century. The short entry ties him to one book from 1631. In that year he either rendered the Song of Songs into Spanish himself or rewrote a Ladino version of it. The older Ladino text stood in Hebrew letters. His version put it into Latin characters. Its title reads Cantares de Selomoh Traduzido de Lengua Caldayca en Espagnol, printed at Hamburg. Kayserling's bibliography of Spanish-Portuguese Jewish writing is the sole source named.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-conrad-cuntze-o: Conrad, called Cuntze of Winterthur, was burgomaster of Strasburg during the Black Death in 1348. A mob, sure that Jews had caused the plague by poisoning wells, demanded Jewish lives. Conrad stood against them. With two councilors he refused a citizens' deputation that pressed for arrests. When the men demanded a share of his protection money from the Jews, he arrested the whole deputation. The stand cost him dear. He was deposed, stripped of property, and barred from the council for ten years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-court-jews-4709:
Court Jews, also called court factors or chamber agents, served at the courts of the Austrian emperors and German princes. Their age ran from the seventeenth century into the early nineteenth. Most were wealthy business men, not scholars. Rulers valued their trade skill and adaptability. The same rulers treated them as favorites one day and whipping-boys the next. Rivals denounced them, and crowds hated them.

In war they supplied armies and handled state funds. They answered to the court marshal, wore no Jews' badge, and could live where the court sat. Their help to fellow Jews lasted only while their favor lasted. Many fell through court intrigue, and their fall brought fresh harm on the Jews at large.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-curacao-4809:
Curaçao is an island of the Dutch West Indies, taken from Spain in 1634. Jews from Holland were likely among its first Dutch settlers. They came in numbers in 1650. Twelve Jewish families won leave from Prince Maurice of Orange to settle there. The governor was told to grant them land, horses, cattle, and tools. Their district, on the north edge of Willemstad, is still called the Jodenwyk, the Jewish quarter.

Early years brought hard limits all the same. In 1653 the settlers were barred from buying more slaves for their farms. The article follows their growth through tombstones and synagogue records. The earliest readable stone dates to 1670. A Lopez da Fonseca stone of 1671 hints at an early reader or ḥazzan serving the young community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-daroca-4909:
Daroca is a town in the Spanish province of Saragossa, once part of the ancient kingdom of Aragon. It held an old Jewish community with its own privileges, like the nearby community of Calatayud, and it mostly shared that town's fortunes. In 1264 the community paid an annual tax of seven hundred and fifty dineros.

Many wealthy Jews lived at Daroca, among them Don Abraham Maquatel, a contemporary of Isaac ben Sheshet. A number of Jews there were baptized in 1413, including the wealthy Alfonso Reus and members of the Ram family. Don Astruc ha-Levi represented Daroca at the disputation of Tortosa and wrote a circular letter to the community of Gerona.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-day-of-the-lord:
Day of the Lord names the future time when God judges the world, bringing punishment and also blessing. The prophets call it "that day," "those days," or simply "the day." The entry traces the idea from early hopes of blessing for Israel to a sterner prophetic teaching.

Amos, in the eighth century B.C., warned that the day would not spare Israel itself. It would be darkness and not light. Isaiah likewise pictured wrath on Israel and Judah for their wrongdoing, with earthquake and fire. Yet Isaiah also saw the nation purified and restored through that judgment. The article follows this theme through the later prophets in detail.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-diocletian-5209:
Diocletian was Roman emperor from 285 to 305. The entry notes that he was the son of Dalmatian slaves and rose by his own ability. Rabbinic sources add that he had been a swineherd in his youth. They also say Jewish schoolboys in Palestine mocked him before he came to power.

Much of the entry follows his time in Palestine. It tells of a hard command laid on the patriarch Judah III at Tiberias, which Judah still managed to fulfil. It recalls building work at Paneas and an edict ordering sacrifice to the national gods everywhere. The Jews alone were exempt from that edict. Christians, the entry notes, suffered heavily under it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-drama-yiddish-5:
Yiddish drama is, by the entry's measure, the least independent branch of Yiddish letters. Fewer than fifty Yiddish dramas had been printed. The whole recorded stock hardly passes five hundred plays. At least nine-tenths of them are translations or adaptations.

The earliest Yiddish plays came from Germany, led by Baerman Limburg's Sale of Joseph, printed in 1711. Bible stories, above all Esther, filled the next two centuries. Aksenfeld's work opened the Russian Yiddish drama, bent on spreading enlightenment. The entry then follows stages at Warsaw, Odessa, London, and New York. Goldfaden's Esther plays win a rare word of praise.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eberty-george-f:
George Friedrich Felix Eberty was a German jurist and author born in Berlin on Jan. 26, 1812. He studied at the universities of Berlin and Bonn. In 1849 he became a privat-docent at Breslau, in natural and criminal law. He rose to associate professor in 1854. He died at Arnsdorf on July 7, 1884.

Eberty's best-known book links the stars with world history. It appeared at Breslau in 1846 and reached a third edition in 1874. He also wrote a seven-volume history of the Prussian state, printed from 1866 to 1873. Lives of Walter Scott and Lord Byron, each in two volumes, followed. De le Roi lists Eberty as a convert to Christianity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elam-5509:
Elam was a land on the great plain north of the Persian Gulf. It lay east of the lower Tigris river. Hills closed it in on the east and north. Babylonian and Assyrian texts call it Elamtu. Greek writers call it Elymais, or Susiana after its capital, Susa. It matches the later region of Khuzistan. The entry says the name may first have meant the east country.

Much of the entry traces wars between Elam and the lands of the Tigris and Euphrates. In the twenty-third century B.C. Elam took Larsa and ruled all Babylonia for a time. In the eighth and seventh centuries B.C. Elam held out long against Assyria. Assurbanipal ended that fight by taking Susa in 645 B.C. Later the Medes and then the Persians took Elam over. The entry closes with the Bible's many mentions of the land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliezer-ben-isa: Eliezer ben Isaac ha-Gadol was a German rabbi of the eleventh century. Men called him Eliezer the Great. He learned under his cousin Simon ha-Gadol of Mayence. He also learned under Gershom, the Light of the Exile. One late writer calls him the teacher of Rashi. Rashi cites him but never says that, the entry notes. That shift led some to split him into two men. A famed ethical will bears his name in some views. Most ascribe that work to Eliezer ben Hyrcanus instead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eltekeh-or-elte: Eltekeh was a town given to the tribe of Dan. The Book of Joshua names it twice in its lists. With its outskirts it went to the Kohathite Levites. They made their home in the town by lot. Assyrian records call the place Altaqu in their tongue. Sennacherib wrecked it on a march through the region. He was on his way to Timnah and Ekron at the time. That blow came after he beat the Egyptians in the field.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ephraim-veitel-:
Veitel-Heine Ephraim was a German financier who died at Berlin in 1775. His name means Veitel, son of Heine, son of Ephraim. He served as jeweler to the Prussian court. He was also mint-master under Frederick William I and Frederick the Great. Both kings held him in high esteem.

His money work helped Frederick the Great in his wars. When charges of cheating were later raised, the king blocked any inquiry. Ephraim pledged 150 thalers a year to the Berlin congregation for his brother-in-law, Rabbi David Frankel. He also founded a Berlin study house about 1774. It became the Veitel-Heine Ephraim'sche Lehranstalt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-europe-5909:
Europe's first Jewish settlements are obscure, and this long entry starts where records start. In 163 B.C. envoys from Judas Maccabeus sealed a friendship pact with Rome. By Cicero's time Rome held a fair-sized Jewish community. In 4 B.C. some 8,000 Roman Jews backed a commission to Augustus. Province settlements grew as well, and Jews gained citizenship in 212.

Tolerance ended, the entry argues, when Constantine and the Church tied civic rights to Christian faith. Later sections follow Jews under the migrating nations, in Spain, and under Muslim rule. Spanish Jews mastered every field of learning, the entry says. Then Church pressure forced them into separate quarters and marked clothing. The entry carries the story forward country by country from there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-famine-6009:
Famine is a broad lack of food, brought by drought, war, hail, flood, or insects. The entry lists the famines named in the Bible in time order. Canaan suffered again and again, and famine is often paired with pestilence and the sword. When David could choose among the three, he picked pestilence as the least dreadful, the entry notes.

Abraham's famine opens the list, then Isaac's, then Jacob's seven-year famine, first felt in Egypt. A ten-year famine falls in the days of the judges. David's lasted three years, and Elijah's drought brought three more. Under siege in Samaria an ass's head sold for eighty shekels, and mothers ate their children. Joel's locust famine closes the grim roll.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fidanque-jacob-: Jacob ben Abraham Fidanque was an English scholar who died at London in 1701. The short entry calls him one of the first Jews after the Return to take up the study of rabbinic writings. He wrote notes on Isaac Abravanel's commentary on the Earlier Prophets. Those notes were printed with the text at Hamburg in 1686. He also revised and issued a second edition of a Hebrew work by Solomon ben Melek at Amsterdam in 1685.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-foa-pio-6209:
Pio Foa was an Italian pathologist born at Sabbionetta on Jan. 26, 1848. He studied medicine at Pavia and took further courses at Turin and Heidelberg. As a pupil in pathologic anatomy he rose step by step at Modena. He became professor there in 1881. In 1884 he took the chair of pathological anatomy and bacteriology at Turin. In 1868 he had served as a volunteer in Garibaldi's campaign against the Southern Tyrol.

Foa's many works treat the marrow and bones, the red blood cells, and the spleen. Others treat the doctrine of tuberculosis and the gains of modern science. He wrote also for medical journals in many countries. Learned academies in Rome and Turin took him as a member. In 1900 he was elected president of the Università Popolare of Turin. One short source line closes the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankfurter-ber: Bernhard Frankfurter was a German teacher and writer born at Herdorf on March 15, 1801. He died on August 13, 1867. He was a son of Rabbi Moses Frankfurter. In 1822 he became a teacher in the Jewish elementary school at Nordstetten in Württemberg. Among his pupils was Berthold Auerbach. The two stayed close friends until Frankfurter's death. Auerbach honored his teacher in a tale of his Black Forest village stories. Frankfurter had supplied much of the material for that tale. One short source line closes the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ganzfried-solom:
Solomon Ganzfried, a Hungarian rabbi and author born at Ungvar about 1800, died there on July 30, 1886. He tried trade at Homona and Ungvar without success. In 1830 he took the rabbinate of Brezovica and held it until 1849. He then became a judge in his home town and stayed in that office for life. In 1869 he sat as a delegate at the Budapest Jewish congress.

His writing was vast, chiefly on ritual law. His short form of the Shulhan Aruk won wide fame. It was reprinted fourteen times in Hebrew and Yiddish. Other works treat slaughter law, the writing of scrolls, and the spelling of names in divorce bills. A prayer book of his also saw many printings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gerondi-jonah-b:
Jonah ben Abraham Gerondi, a Spanish rabbi and moralist of the thirteenth century, died at Toledo in November 1263. He came from Gerona and was a cousin of Nahmanides. As a pupil of Solomon of Montpellier he signed the 1233 ban on Maimonides books. He was blamed for the public burning of those books at Paris that year.

When Talmuds were burned at the same place in 1242, Gerondi owned his error in open synagogue. He vowed to beg pardon at Maimonides grave, but never made the trip. He taught at Toledo and quoted Maimonides with honor. His fame now rests on moral works. Gates of Repentance and kindred books became set texts of Jewish ethics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-glogauer-abigdo: Abigdor ben Simḥah ha-Levi Glogauer was a German Hebrew scholar of the eighteenth century. He published "Dabar Ṭob," a basic Hebrew grammar with paradigms, printed together with Moses ibn Ḥabib's "Marpe Lashon" at Prague in 1783. He also issued "Iggerot," a set of Mendelssohn's letters, at Vienna in 1794. Three years later came "Ḥotam Toknit," Hebrew poems whose appendix holds another edited series of Mendelssohn's letters. The entry is brief and leans on Steinschneider's catalogue and Zedner's British Museum catalogue of Hebrew books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gordin-jacob-ja:
Jacob Gordin was a Yiddish playwright and reformer. He was born May 1, 1853, at Mirgorod in the Poltava government. He wrote for Russian papers from 1870. In 1879 he founded a rational sect, the Bible Brotherhood, at Yelisavetgrad. It broke with dogmatic Judaism and had a short life. He emigrated to New York in 1890.

There he turned to the Yiddish stage and raised its standing. His first play, "Siberia," appeared in 1891. About sixty dramas and vaudevilles followed. The entry judges some of them poor but others among the finest of the Jewish stage. It names "The Yiddish King Lear," "Mirele Effros," and "Kreutzer Sonata" as his best. He also wrote Yiddish sketches, some moving and some comic.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-grunhut-karl-sa:
Karl Samuel Grünhut was an Austrian jurist. He was born at Bur-St. Georgen, Hungary, on Aug. 3, 1844. In 1872 he became associate professor in the law faculty at Vienna. In 1873 he published a work on expropriation law. He also founded a quarterly journal on private and public law. In 1874 he rose to professor of commercial law.

His later books dealt with bills of exchange and notes. His two-volume "Wechselrecht" appeared in 1897. Shorter treatises and a textbook followed in 1899 and 1900. He held the title of imperial councilor. Since 1897 he sat as a life member in the Austrian House of Lords.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ha-shahar-the-d:
Ha-Shaḥar, meaning "The Dawn," was a Hebrew monthly printed at Vienna from 1869 to 1884. P. Smolenskin was both its publisher and its editor. It was modeled on the German "Monatsschrift." Its pages held essays, life stories, tales, and studies, plus general Jewish news.

Smolenskin wanted to spread the Hebrew tongue, teach his readers, and fight dark, closed thinking. Lack of funds stopped the presses more than once. Even so, the monthly shaped the Haskalah movement, most of all in Russia. There, boys in the yeshibot read it in secret. Writers such as Brandsteter, Leon Gordon, David Kahana, and Solomon Rubin wrote for it, and Rubin helped edit it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hadid-7009:
Hadid was a town named with Lod and Ono in Ezra and Nehemiah. From Nehemiah it looks like a Benjamite town, though Joshua's list of Benjamin's towns omits it. In I Maccabees it shows up as Adida, walled with gates and bars by Simon the Maccabee. The Mishnah says Hadid, like Lod and Ono, had walls since Joshua's time.

The entry places the town at modern Al-Ḥadithah, not far from Lydda. Eusebius knew it as Adatha or Aditha, east of Diospolis. So the short article ties one small town across Bible, Maccabees, Mishnah, and the modern map.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hallel-lit-prai:
Hallel, meaning praise, is the name the Talmud gives to Psalms cxiii to cxviii read as one work. They are called the Hallel of Egypt, against Psalm cxxxvi, the Great Hallel. Signs in the text point to a late date and a day of thanks after war. The entry holds the psalms were likely written for Ḥanukkah, where they are still sung each morning.

Hallel is sung at the Passover night service, on the first day of Unleavened Bread, at Pentecost, and at Booths. On some days only a half Hallel is said, with set verses dropped. The entry traces the blessing said before it, which Rashi and Maimonides fought yet which kept its place. It also notes the old custom of the crowd answering the leader with the first verse alone, and closes with Hallel tunes and settings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herrera-alonzo-:
Alonzo de Herrera, also known as Abraham Cohen de Herrera, was a Cabalist born in Spain who died in Amsterdam in 1631. He served the Sultan of Morocco at Cadiz. Captured by the English there, he later moved to Amsterdam. In that city he openly confessed Judaism and took the name Abraham.

Herrera learned Cabala from Israel Sarug. He knew Cordovero, Vital, Plato, and Ficino well. The entry says he mixed Lurianic teaching with Neoplatonic ideas, changing the Cabala he taught. His Spanish works were never printed in his life. They were later translated into Hebrew in 1665 and partly into Latin in 1677.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hiller-eduard-7: Eduard Hiller, born at Frankfort-on-the-Main on April 14, 1844, was a German philologist and nephew of Ferdinand Hiller. Educated at Bonn and Göttingen, he took his doctorate in 1865. He taught at Bonn, became a lecturer there in 1869, and professor at Greifswald in 1874. Two years later he moved to Halle. His major works edited Eratosthenes, Theon of Smyrna, and Tibullus. He also edited Theocritus, Greek lyric poets, and a lyric anthology. He died at Halle on March 7, 1891.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirsch-levin-jo:
Levin Joseph Hirsch, born at Schottland, near Danzig, in 1758, was a German physician set by his parents for commerce. He clerked three years in a small firm while studying privately under great hardship. In 1785 he entered the University of Königsberg.

Hirsch took his medical degree in 1791 with a thesis on bone necrosis. He became prosector in 1793 and a lecturer in 1795. In 1805 he directed a midwifery teaching institute at Königsberg. When French invasion seized its funds, he paid to keep it alive. War service brought him a royal title in 1808 and a diamond ring. He died at Königsberg on May 29, 1823.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hottinger-johan:
Johann Heinrich Hottinger was a Swiss Christian Hebraist born at Zurich on March 10, 1620. He drowned in the Limmat on June 5, 1667. He studied Oriental languages and theology at Geneva, Groningen, and Leyden. In 1642 he became professor of church history at Zurich. Later chairs covered Oriental languages, rhetoric, and Old Testament study at Heidelberg.

Hottinger returned to Zurich in 1661 and became rector of its university the next year. His books serve Hebrew students most. They include a work on the Samaritan Pentateuch in 1644, a Hebrew grammar in two books, a philological key to Scripture in 1649, and an Oriental library printed at Heidelberg in 1658. A seven-language lexicon appeared in 1661.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-nunez-jacob: Jacob ibn Nunez was physician to King Henry the Fourth of Castile and his chief judge. He also calls himself a rabbi. In 1474 the king charged him at Segovia with dividing the yearly tax owed by the Jewish communities of the realm. The tax lists he produced were first printed from a Madrid manuscript by the historian Rios. Ibn Nunez did not gather the money himself. Royal tax collectors did that work, on his application to them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-infancy-legal-a:
Infancy, in legal terms, is grouped with deafness and unsound mind: infants are not liable for torts, not punishable for offenses and not competent as witnesses. A boy over thirteen and a girl over twelve are of age if signs of puberty exist. What a child may validly do depends on the kind of contract and on whether he has a guardian.

A child without a guardian may buy and sell movables; the word "pe'uṭot" covers children between six and ten, judged by business capacity. An infant cannot dispose of land or appoint an attorney. Before twenty he cannot sell land that came by descent or deathbed gift. Money borrowed for necessaries binds him; other borrowing is disputed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-b-gershom:
Jacob b. Gershom ha-Gozer was a German Talmudist of the twelfth century. He was a nephew of Ephraim b. Jacob of Bonn, with whom he kept a scholarly correspondence. He also dealt closely with Eliezer b. Joel ha-Levi. As far as is known, Jacob was the first man to write a whole book on circumcision.

A caution follows at once. The book printed in 1892 from a Hamburg manuscript, the "Kelale ha-Milah," was composed not by Jacob but by one of his pupils. It opens with a sermon in the German preaching style of the day. Then it sets out the three acts of the rite and the rules for circumcision on the Sabbath, and for days past the eighth. The entry values it as a store of facts on the liturgy and customs of German Jews. How much of it is Jacob's own, no one knows.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-james-david-dav: David James was an English comedian born at Birmingham in 1839. As a child he made his start in ballet at the Princess' Theatre in London, then acted in burlesques. His best early part was Mercury in a Burnand piece at the Royalty. In 1870 he helped manage the Vaudeville Theatre. His great success was Perkyn Middlewick in Our Boys, a part he played more than thirteen hundred times in a row. He died in London on Oct. 3, 1893, and left his large fortune to charity, mainly Jewish causes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jethro-jether-i:
Jethro was a priest of Midian and the father-in-law of Moses. In the marriage account in Exodus he is also called Reuel. Moses had shielded Jethro's daughters from rude shepherds at a well, and in thanks Jethro gave him his daughter Zipporah. After the crossing of the Red Sea, Jethro brought Moses his wife and two sons and heard all that God had done for Israel.

Jethro then praised God as greater than all gods and offered sacrifices. He also gave Moses sound advice: appoint deputies to judge the people and lighten the load. Then he went home. Rabbinic writing in the entry puzzles over his many names, lists seven of them, and tells that he once warned Pharaoh against harming Israel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joel-manuel-870:
Manuel Joel was a German rabbi born on Oct. 19, 1826, at Birnbaum in Posen. He studied word science and thought at Berlin and took his doctorate at Halle in 1854. That year he joined the Breslau seminary as a teacher. In 1864 he followed Abraham Geiger as rabbi of the Breslau congregation, and he died at Breslau on Nov. 3, 1890.

His love was the philosophy of religion, where he did pioneer work. He showed that Ibn Gabirol's great book is a text of Greek-style thought with little that is new, and he traced how Maimonides fed later Christian schoolmen. He also dug out two near-forgotten Jewish thinkers and showed Spinoza's debt to Jewish sources. Sermons and essays fill out a long list of works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-abra: Joseph ben Abraham was a liturgical poet whose name appears on seven prayers in the prayer book of Avignon. Zunz took him to be the same man as Joseph of Monselice. That Joseph wrote a penitential prayer for the seventeenth of Tammuz, kept in the rite of Carpentras. The entry adds that Saul ben Joseph, whose poem stands in the same rite, may have been this poet's son. No dates or places of life are given beyond these links to the prayer books of southern France.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joshua-bruno-89: Joshua Bruno was a doctor and scholar of Treves who lived in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. He treated Bruno, archbishop of Treves from 1102 to 1104. The archbishop let him wear knightly dress, a rare honor. The two men held frequent talks on religion. Those talks ended with Joshua accepting Christianity. At his baptism he took the name Bruno, after his patron. The entry is very short and rests on a register of documents and a book on medieval Jewish towns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kabos-eduard-91:
Eduard Kabos, a Hungarian writer and journalist, was born on Dec. 2, 1864, at Nagy-Karoly. He went to the University of Budapest to study modern philology and planned to teach, but he chose journalism instead. He soon won posts as a parliamentary reporter and feuilleton writer for leading Budapest papers.

By 1898 Kabos was editing the parliamentary column of the "Budapesti Napló," and in 1902 the Petöfi Társaság, a leading literary society, elected him a member. The entry lists his books year by year, from the story collection "Elzüllöttek" in 1885 through novels, dramas, farces, and comedies to the novel "A Verebek" in 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kara-menahem-be: Menahem ben Jacob Ḳara was a Bohemian scholar at Prague. He worked in the first half of the fifteenth century. He was a close kinsman of Abigdor ben Isaac Ḳara. He calls that scholar "my brother" in his writing. All his works survive only in manuscript. One comments on chapter thirty of Proverbs, at Abigdor's request. Others treat works by Enoch al-Ḳusṭantini and by Ghazali. One covers parts of Maimonides' guide. He spent eighteen months in prison.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-landau-adolph-y: Adolph Yefimovich Landau, a Russian journalist and publisher born at Rossienny in 1841, died at Berlin on July 21, 1902. He moved to St. Petersburg in 1862 and studied law there. Teaching at Kovno and newspaper work followed. His aim was to show the public the life of the Jewish masses. From 1871 his Biblioteka served for ten years as the organ of Russian Jewish writing. In 1881 he launched the monthly Voskhod and built it into a leading voice. Failing health forced him to give up its editorship.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-leeuw-jacob-hey: Jacob Heymann de Leeuw, a Dutch Talmudist born at Leyden in 1811, died at Amsterdam on Sept. 15, 1883. He moved to Amsterdam in 1874 and became rabbi at the bet ha-midrash there. Five Talmudical works carry his name. The first, dated 1848 at Leyden, bears a rose title. Two more Leyden books followed in 1852 and 1853. Rotterdam gave the last two, in 1857 and 1858. No teaching posts or family facts are stated in the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levi-carlo-9809: Carlo Levi, an Italian physiologist, was born at Genoa on March 26, 1866. He took his medical degree at the University of Modena in 1889. He became a tutor there, then assistant professor of experimental physiology. In 1893 he took charge of classes in special physiology. In 1897 he took the classes in histology at the veterinary college tied to the same school. In 1904 he became editor of "L'Idea Sionista." He also serves as vice-president of the Modena chapter of the Dante Alighieri Society.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-simon-9909: Simon Lévy, a French rabbi, was born in 1829 at Lauterbourg, Alsace. He died at Bordeaux on Nov. 29, 1886. He studied under Solomon Ulmann and at the Rabbinical School at Metz. He left that school in 1853 to take the pulpit at Lunéville. In 1864 he was called as chief rabbi to Bordeaux, and he stayed there until his death. He wrote a pamphlet on Renan and the synagogue. His book "Moïse, Jésus, Mahomet" came out after he died.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lipovetz-10009: Lipovetz was a town in the government of Kiev, Russia. In 1897 it had 6,068 people, of whom 4,500 were Jews. Many Jewish artisans made a new kind of footwear worn by peasants and by richer buyers. When yearly and weekly fairs were ended, trade fell and poverty grew sharp. In 1900 a crowd asked officials for bread and for the fairs to return. Schools included 25 small religious schools and a Talmud Torah founded in 1898. The town had also suffered in attacks in 1768.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lopez-rodrigo-1:
Rodrigo Lopez was court physician to Queen Elizabeth, born in Portugal about 1525. He settled in London in 1559 and joined the College of Physicians. By 1586 he was chief physician to the queen, who gave him a monopoly on importing aniseed and sumac in 1589.

Lopez dealt with Don Antonio, a claimant to Portugal's crown, and later intrigued with Spain. Captured men and coded letters about the price of pearls pointed to a plot against the queen. On the rack he confessed he had entertained offers to poison her for 50,000 ducats. He was executed on June 7, 1594, saying he loved the queen. His trial caused a great sensation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-margoliuth-mose:
Moses Margoliuth, a Polish-born convert who became an English clergyman, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in Suwalki on December 3, 1820, he came to Liverpool in 1837. There he met a convert named Lazarus and the Reverend H. S. Joseph. Joseph baptized him in April 1838. He died in London in 1881.

The article follows his church career. He entered Trinity College, Dublin, in 1840 and became a curate at Liverpool in 1844. Many appointments followed, ending as vicar of Little Linford from 1877. Erlangen gave him a doctorate in 1857. In 1847 he founded a Hebrew-Christian monthly, The Star of Jacob. His books include a history of the Jews of Great Britain, judged meritorious in its last two volumes. He also served among the revisers of the English Old Testament. The entry records a convert who spent his life between two faiths.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-melun-hebrew-or:
Melun is a town in Seine-et-Marne, France. It held one of the notable Jewish communities of medieval France. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn give its history in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Talmudic school mattered by the twelfth century. Its scholars sat in the synod at Troyes about 1160. Rashbam and Rabbenu Tam led it. Meshullam ben Nathan, come from Narbonne in 1150, won fame there.

The documents then turn grim. At Melun in December 1230, Saint Louis and his barons issued a decree. Jews could make no contracts. They were the property of their barons. They could be dragged back if they fled. They would lose uncollected debts too. The Jewish quarter, "La Iviferie," with its school, appears in deeds of 1206 to 1311. The town library keeps a fourteenth-century festival prayer-book of the French rite. In 1306 Philip the Fair expelled Melun's Jews for good.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshershaya-bar: Meshershaya bar Pakod, a Babylonian amora of the sixth and last generation who lived at Sura, is recorded in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Solomon Schechter and A. S. Waldstein in two sentences, both about his death. In the persecution of the Jews under Perozes, Firuz, king of Persia, he was imprisoned and executed, in 469 or 470, together with Amemar bar Mar Yankaï and the exilarch Huna Mar. The entry's sources are Sherira Gaon's responsa and Heilprin's chronology, Seder ha-Dorot.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-joshu:
Moses ben Joshua of Narbonne, called Maestro Vidal Blasom, was a French philosopher and physician born at Perpignan. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He began philosophy at thirteen under his father and went on to study medicine. The search for learning took him to Toledo, Soria, and Valencia in Spain.

During the Black Death persecutions a mob at Cervera drove him out, and he lost his books and all he owned. Moses was an eager admirer of Averroes, and most of his many works comment on Averroes, on Avicenna, or on Ghazali. He also wrote on free will against Abner of Burgos and commented on Maimonides' Guide. He died some time after 1362.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mulhausen-11209:
Mülhausen, a city in Alsace, had no Jews at all in 1784. Gotthard Deutsch and F. Blum wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on its young community. Jews were tolerated only from 1798, when the city became French. By 1830 the congregation counted seventy-six families and elected its first rabbi.

The article follows the building of a temple in 1849 and an organ in 1892, played on Sabbaths but not on Yom Kippur. It lingers on two charities. One is an infirmary for the aged of Upper Alsace, on ground given by Captain Dreyfus's father. The other is a trade school for poor Jewish children. By 1904 the city held twenty-four hundred Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naphtali-greek-:
Naphtali was the second son of Jacob and Bilhah, and Dan's younger full brother. The Jewish Encyclopedia article is by its editorial committee and J. F. McLaughlin. His name means my wrestling, from the rivalry of the sisters Rachel and Leah. He had four sons when the family went down into Egypt.

Jacob's blessing calls Naphtali a hind let loose who gives goodly words. The article reads that as alertness, freedom of spirit, and a gift for speech. The Targums make him a swift runner who first told Jacob that Joseph lived. He was also, they say, one of the five brothers Joseph presented to Pharaoh.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nebuzar-adan-11:
Nebuzar-adan was captain of Nebuchadnezzar's bodyguard. The entry was written by the Editorial Board's Executive Committee, Schulim Ochser, and Louis Ginzberg for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In 586 B.C. he entered fallen Jerusalem. He burned the Temple, the palace, and great houses. He razed the city walls as well.

He carried off the Temple's brass pillars and vessels. Priests and chief men were taken to Riblah and killed. Five years later he deported 745 more Jews. Rabbinic tales give him axes that broke at Jerusalem's gate. A voice from heaven told him to leap, and it opened. They also tell of a slain prophet's bubbling blood. At last, moved, he fled his king and turned to Judaism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-newman-selig-11:
Selig Newman was a German teacher of Hebrew in England. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Posen in 1788. He died at Williamsburg, New York, on Feb. 20, 1871. He was educated in his native Posen.

In 1814 Newman went to England for work. Plymouth took him as its congregation's minister. He taught Hebrew at Oxford at the same time. His faith alone barred him from a professorship there. Distinguished scholars, Christian and Jewish, sat among his pupils. In London he debated Christians on messianic prophecies boldly. Late in life he sailed for America and taught in New York. His Challenge Accepted, of 1850, stages that same debate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-novgorod-volhyn:
Novgorod-Volhynsk is a town in Russia's Volhynia government. Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Of 16,873 people, some 9,000 are Jews. That count comes from the census of 1897. Jews lead the town's commerce by a wide margin.

Export trade is their chief line of business. Butter alone ships out at 100,000 rubles yearly. Skins, eggs, and furniture follow in the trade. Salt and dried fish move with Astrakhan and Tzaritzyn. In 1899 the town counted 102 Jewish merchants. Petty traders and artisans ran into the thousands. A Talmud Torah teaches 130 pupils there. The handbook of 1904 lists one synagogue. Twenty-two houses of prayer stand beside it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-omer-sheaf-1050:
The Omer was a sheaf of grain brought at harvest time. The board and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Israel was told to bring it after taking Canaan. A priest waved it as a gift to God. The rule stands in the book of Leviticus.

The sheaf had to be brought and waved on one day. That day was the morrow after the Sabbath. A lamb was burnt with the gift that day. Flour with oil and wine went with the lamb. No new grain could be eaten till this was done. From that day, men counted seven full weeks. The fiftieth day was the Feast of Pentecost, or Weeks. The count is still kept, though the sheaf gift has ceased.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-onderwijzer-abr:
Abraham Samson Onderwijzer was a Dutch rabbi at Amsterdam. Isidore Singer and E. Slijper wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Muiden, near Amsterdam, in 1863. He read at the rabbis' school and the town university. He took his first degree in the year 1884.

In 1888 Onderwijzer was named rabbi of the Amsterdam flock. He put the five books of Moses into Dutch. He added the notes of Rashi to that work. It came out at Amsterdam in the year 1895. That same year he founded a Jewish work union. It was named Bezaleel, and he led it with honor. The union cared for the faith needs of its men. Most of its two hundred men cut diamonds for a living.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottinger-eduard:
Eduard Maria Öttinger was a German writer from Breslau. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born on November 19, in 1808. He died at Blasewitz, near Dresden, in 1872. In 1828 he became a Catholic by his own choice.

Eduard worked as a newsman in town after town. He ran comic sheets in Berlin, Munich, and Hamburg. He ran sheets in Leipzig and in Paris as well. He wrote a great mass of works in his life. They held novels, verse, and keen mocking tales. They held works on the past and on books too. His book of lives held facts on some 200,000 souls. It was the seed of his famed Moniteur des Dates.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-parenzo-cesare-:
Cesare Parenzo was an Italian senator and lawmaker. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Rovigo in the year 1839. He died at Nervi, near Genoa, in 1898. His death fell on April 15 of that year.

Cesare read law and took his degree in that field. In 1860 he chose to serve with Garibaldi in war. He went with that chief to Sicily on his great march. He went with him to Aspromonte in 1862 as well. He went with him to Tirol in the year 1866. Voters sent him to the chamber for Rovigo more than once. He then gave his time to the press and to law. He ran the paper Diritto for a time in Rome. In 1889 he was made a senator of the realm.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-penso-joseph-kn:
Joseph Penso was a merchant, poet, and giver to charity. He was born at Espejo, in Spain, about 1650. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died at Amsterdam in 1692, his home for most of his life.

His father had escaped the Inquisition's dungeon in Spain. He then kept a vow to live openly as a Jew. Joseph wrote a Hebrew drama at eighteen. He led a Spanish literary academy in Amsterdam. His Confusion de Confusiones still stands as an early book on the stock market.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phillips-barnet:
Barnet Phillips was an American journalist with the New York Times. He was born in Philadelphia on November 9, 1828. Cyrus Adler and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He graduated from the University of Pennsylvania in 1847.

After college Phillips crossed to Europe for study. He worked at journalism there before coming home. Back in America he joined the Times staff. That tie lasted more than thirty years in all. He also published two books of his own. Their titles were The Struggle and Burning Their Ships.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pletsch-solomon: Solomon Pletsch was a Jewish city surgeon at Frankfort. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He came from Regensburg to the post in 1394. The city paid him thirty-six gulden a year. It gave him uniform cloth like the Christian officials. Only his oath differed, sworn in the Jewish form. He treated council members and hospital Jews for free. Citizens paid him moderate fees for his care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-posner-solomon-:
Solomon Zalman Posner was a Polish rabbi born at Landsberg about 1778. The Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His father, Joseph Landsberg, was rabbi of Posen. Solomon died at Loslau in 1863. At his wish his sons set a wooden stone over his grave.

Posner left several works in handwriting, none printed in his life. One defends Talmud study against the young who scorn it. One is a set of moral letters for sons. The letters guide boys who leave home for the yeshivah. A third work gives notes on the whole Pentateuch. The entry names these books and their themes one by one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-psalms-12409:
Psalms is the name of the great song book of the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name comes from a Greek word for string playing. It first meant the music made on strings. Then it meant the song sung to that music. Greek translators use a like word for a big stringed tool.

Those Greek words render the Hebrew mizmor and tehillim. The root and sense of mizmor are not clear, he says. Tehillim means songs of praise in plain terms. The article traces the book's name and its making. It asks who wrote the psalms and when they were joined.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabinovich-rabb:
Osip Aaronovich Rabinovich was a Russian Jewish author and journalist. Herman Rosenthal and George D. Rosenthal wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Kobelyaki in 1817. He died at Meran in the Tyrol in 1869. His father held a post in the state liquor trade. That post set the house apart from its neighbors.

His father spoke Russian with ease and fluency. Most Jews of the southwest had but slight Russian then. Aaron took great care with his son's schooling. The boy learned Hebrew under a named teacher, Meïr Emde. He learned the tongues of his land as well. That rare mix made him a bridge between two worlds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-real-estate-126:
Real estate means landed property in Jewish law. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The entry contrasts land with movable goods, called chattels. It sends readers to many related articles for details.

The article stresses one point about inheritance. Land and goods pass to heirs under the same rights. That rule differs sharply from English common law. It agrees with Roman law instead, the writers say. A sick person's gift could pass land as a deed does. Sales and gifts by healthy owners used different forms. The entry maps how land moves between people under Jewish rules.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-roman-jacob-ben:
Jacob ben Isaac Roman was a bibliographer of Spanish descent born about 1570. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Constantinople. He died at Jerusalem in 1650.

The article says he knew the whole Mishnah by heart. Conforte reports that feat of his learning. He knew Arabic and understood Turkish and Latin. On a journey he was captured and later ransomed. Through a physician friend he met Anton Leger of Geneva. Leger recommended him to Johannes Buxtorf in Basel. Buxtorf used his bibliographic knowledge for a famous appendix. Their letters were later published in a French journal. Roman also planned a Hebrew press for Constantinople. No Jewish press then served the East, he noted.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rothschild-1290:
Rothschild is the name of the most famous family of financiers of the nineteenth century. Its named authors were Joseph Jacobs, Isidore Singer, Frederick T. Haneman, Jacques Kahn, Goodman Lipkind, J. de Haas, and I. L. Bril. The name comes from a red shield on a house in Frankfort's Judengasse.

The family's earliest known member, Moses Rothschild, was born about 1550. Its founder was Mayer Amschel Rothschild, born at Frankfort about 1743. As a boy he changed money for his father's small banking business. That work sparked his lifelong interest in coins and finance. The long entry follows the house from that Frankfort shop to European fame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sajo-aladar-130:
Aladár Sajó was a Hungarian author born at Waitzen on September 8, 1869. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was educated for the law at Budapest, and wrote novels alongside.

Sajó served as a lieutenant in Bosnia from 1892 to 1894. That service gave him his great subject: army life in barracks and field. His books Among the Soldiers and Secrets of the Barracks made him popular. Recruits and Other Soldiers and the novel Ezredes Boriska followed in 1897. He also wrote for the Budapesti Hirlap, a leading daily paper.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-jaco: Samuel ben Jacob of Capua was an Italian translator of the late thirteenth century. Richard Gottheil and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He may have been father of the physician Solomon of Capua, if Steinschneider guessed right. Samuel turned into Hebrew a work of Mesue the Elder, written first in Arabic. It treats the choice and correction of purgative medicines for doctors. The translation, in two parts, still survives only in manuscript copies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-midrash-:
Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the Midrash to Samuel. The work, Midrash Shemu'el, retells the Books of Samuel with stories and moral teaching. Rashi quotes it as early as his notes on First Samuel. It also went by the name Agadat Shemu'el. Printers once gave it the wrong title, Shoḥer Ṭob, by mistake.

The book holds thirty-two chapters of homilies. Each one opens with a verse from some other part of the Bible. The compiler gathered his material from the Mishnah, the Talmuds, and many older midrash collections. Almost every sage named in it lived in Palestine. Zunz dated the compiler to the first half of the eleventh century. The article closes with the book's printing history, from Constantinople to Buber's edition of 1893.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sarsino-sarcino:
Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Jacob ben Joseph Sarsino. He was an Italian rabbi of the seventeenth century. Sarsino studied under Ẓebi Hirsch ben Isaac in Cracow. He became a rabbi in Venice. There he worked alongside Leon of Modena. Much of his labor went into the printed books of his day.

Sarsino corrected several books printed at Venice. He supplied them with notes of his own. He printed the notes of his teacher Ẓebi Hirsch on Jacob Weil's rules for slaughtering. He added his own notes to that work. In 1692 he published Seder ha-Niḳḳur at Venice. That book gives the rules for porging, the removal of forbidden fat and sinews. It is said to be only an extract. The full work belonged to his teacher.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schott-schottla:
Isidore Singer and Abraham Lewinsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Benedict Schott. He was a German educationist. Schott was born in Danzig on March 11, 1763 or 1764. He died at Seesen on July 21, 1846. Orphaned early, he wandered Germany as a young scholar. In Berlin he tutored in the home of Herz Beer, Meyerbeer's father.

In 1804 Schott joined the new Jacobsonschule at Seesen as a teacher. Two years later he became its director. In 1806 Jacobson sent him to Paris. There he urged Napoleon's Sanhedrin to back better schooling for Jews. He retired on July 1, 1838, in his seventy-fifth year. His books include a reader for Jewish schoolchildren. He also wrote an open letter on a Jewish consistory for Westphalia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-semahot-joys-13:
Semahot, meaning Joys, is the soft name for Ebel Rabbati, a tract on mourning for the dead. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. The tract counts among the small, later treatises printed after the fourth order of the Babylonian Talmud.

Much of the entry asks whether this tract matches an older collection cited in the Talmud. The authors compare quoted lines and note that only some match well. They also report an early gaon's account of a large and a small version. Readers get a careful lesson in telling similar rabbinic texts apart.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shatzkes-moses-:
Moses Aaron Shatzkes was a Russian Hebrew author born at Karlin in 1825. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He had both Hebrew and general schooling and chose literature. Writing earned him little, and he lived in straitened means.

His chief work, Ha-Mafteah, applied modern inquiry to Talmudic tales. Printed at Warsaw from 1866 to 1869, it stirred Orthodox readers with bold views. It marked a fresh turn in Hebrew writing at the time. Shatzkes also wrote a satiric sketch of Jewish life in Judeo-German. That piece was reprinted often for common readers. He spent his last twenty years at Kiev and died there in 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shomron-kol-tit:
Shomron Kol Titten is a dramatic elegy by Solomon ibn Gabirol for the fast of Ab. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the poem. Polish ritual sings it at the close of the lamentations. It is sung at both evening and morning services.

Samaria and Jerusalem appear as two faithless sisters in it. Ezekiel's image of sister cities stands behind the poem. The sisters take turns bewailing their sins and punishments. Verses two and three give each her grieving voice. In verse four the poet begs pity for both. He prays for their Lord to return in forgiveness. Sephardim add the poem to prayers for the fast of Tebet. The entry shows two ruined cities speaking their sorrow aloud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-ben-nano:
Simeon ben Nanos was a tanna of the second generation, peer of Ishmael and Akiba. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He often debated points of law with those two giants. He is often mentioned simply by the name Ben Nanos.

Simeon won high fame for knowing Jewish civil law deeply. Ishmael said whoever would study civil law should learn from him. Several of his civil law sayings survive in the Mishnah. They appear in Bava Batra and Shebu'ot among other tractates. Opinions of his on other legal topics survive too. Neither his teachers nor his pupils are known today. The entry honors a specialist whose subject was money, property, and fairness between neighbors in daily life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-small-and-large:
Small and large letters are odd-sized letters in the Masoretic Bible text. Crawford Howell Toy and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. About one hundred such letters occur in all. Many of them stand in the Pentateuch. Scribes always copied them with care. Printed editions still show them today.

Examples include the cut waw in the word peace in Numbers. An inverted nun appears in nine passages in all. Large letters often point to a Talmudic or midrashic teaching. They also guard the text against copying errors. The first letter of Genesis must be large, the lists say. The waw in gahon is the middle letter of the Pentateuch.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-somekh-abdallah:
Abdallah Abraham Joseph Somekh was rabbi of Bagdad, born there in 1813. Joseph Jacobs and N E B Ezra wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was educated by Jacob Joseph ha-Rofe and Moses Hayyim. He was looked on as spiritual head of Bagdad Jewry. His legal decisions were accepted as conclusive across Asia.

Through his influence about twenty yeshivot were founded. The Sassoon family and Calcutta Jews helped fund that work. He left a work on ritual in manuscript at his death. Parts of it were published at Bagdad in 1900. It bore the title Zibhe Zedek, sacrifices of righteousness. A riot broke out at his funeral over his burial place.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steinberg-joshu:
Joshua Steinberg was a Russian Jewish writer and educator born in Wilna in 1839. Herman Rosenthal and Julius Gottlieb wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. Steinberg trained at the rabbinical school in Wilna and served briefly as a rabbi at Byelostok. In 1861 he was called back to Wilna as a rabbi.

Steinberg became head teacher of Hebrew and Aramaic at the Wilna rabbinical seminary in 1867. He later served as its inspector until 1904. His efforts led the Russian government to open seven elementary city schools for Jewish children in 1863. From 1863 he also worked as censor of Jewish publications. He wrote major dictionaries, including a complete Russian-Hebrew dictionary in 1880. His work shaped Jewish schooling across Russia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sulzer-salomon-:
Salomon Sulzer was an Austrian cantor and composer born in 1804. Isidore Singer and Alois Kaiser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born at Hohenems, Tyrol, on March 30. His family had moved there from Sulz in 1748. He died at Vienna on January 17, 1890.

Sulzer trained for the cantorate and traveled with his teachers. In 1820 he became cantor at Hohenems and added a choir. Vienna called him as chief cantor in 1826. There he kept old chants but harmonized them anew. His two-volume Shir Zion set models for synagogue music. It covers Sabbaths, festivals, weddings, and funerals. Nearly every synagogue in the world adopted parts of it. The entry honors the man who modernized Jewish song.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tallage-14209:
Tallage was a tax a ruler could impose at will. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. The whole community owed the entire sum together. English kings levied it on Jews again and again. The 1100s and 1200s saw the heaviest demands.

The Saladin tallage of 1189 demanded 60,000 pounds. Its stated purpose was a crusade against Saladin. King John tallaged the Jews for 60,000 marks in 1210. Henry the Third levied smaller sums in 1225 and 1270. Edward the First added repeated tallages of his own. These came atop fines, fees, and many other claims. One claim says losing Jewish income changed royal tax rights. Edward then gave up tallaging Englishmen in general. The entry shows a tax used as a royal squeeze.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-temple-the-seco:
The Second Temple in Jerusalem, from ruin to rebuilding, is traced here. George A. Barton wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Nebuchadnezzar had burned Solomon's Temple in 586 B.C. The site stayed a place of worship through the Exile.

Cyrus let the Jews return and rebuild in 538 B.C. Little building seems to have happened at first. Real work began under Darius in 519 B.C. The preaching of Haggai and Zechariah stirred the people. Within three years the new Temple stood finished. The article tests the Book of Ezra against other evidence. It shows how scholars weigh claims about Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-title-page-1440:
The title-page of Hebrew books grew out of the printer's colophon. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Early Hebrew books, like manuscripts, carried titles in colophons. The Soncino Berakot of 1483 followed that pattern. Kimhi's grammar of 1491 set its title on page one.

By the early 1500s titles moved to the first page. Bomberg's Talmud of 1520 gave its title five small lines. Soon titles filled whole pages with rich borders. Flowers, angels, deer, and Bible heroes framed the words. Prague printers copied the look of lit manuscripts. Temple gates formed a favorite design. Amsterdam's 1666 Tikkun used a fully engraved title-page.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trier-ernst-joh:
Ernst Johannes Trier was a Danish educator who founded a famed folk high school. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born at Copenhagen in 1837, he died at Vallekilde in 1893. He took his theology degree in 1863. He fought in the war with Germany in 1864.

In 1865 he became a follower of Grundtvig. At Grundtvig's urging he founded a school at Vallekilde in 1866. It soon led all Danish schools of its kind. Courses covered navigation and branches of trade too. It first brought Swedish gymnastics into Danish schools. His memoirs of twenty-five school years stayed unfinished. Overstudy hastened his death, the article says. Trier was a convert to Christianity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-urim-and-thummi:
Urim and Thummim were objects in the high priest's breastplate used as a divine oracle. Emil G. Hirsch, W. Muss-Arnolt, Wilhelm Bacher, and Ludwig Blau wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Greek translators rendered the names as revelation and truth. Others gave lights and perfections instead. The Bible itself gives no basis for those renderings.

Exodus describes the breastplate as four-square and double. Twelve stones sat on its outside, not inside. Moses placed the Urim and Thummim within it at Aaron's consecration. Deuteronomy blesses Levi with God's Thummim and Urim. First Samuel shows Saul asking God through the oracle. Wellhausen and Driver restored that passage from the Greek text. The article weighs every clue to a lost practice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-virtue-original:
Original virtue, in Hebrew zekut abot, means the merit of the fathers. Joseph Jacobs wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The term was coined as a contrast to original sin. It names a Jewish idea about ancestors. God rewards children for the goodness of their parents.

The doctrine rests on Bible verses. The second commandment promises mercy to thousands of generations. Isaac was blessed because Abraham kept God's commands. The first blessing of the daily Amidah prayer recalls the fathers. The entry adds a key limit. The merit helps only when children keep their parents' piety. It ties family memory to present duty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weaving-14809:
Weaving was a basic craft of ancient Israel. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In the nomadic age, families spun camel and goat hair. Sheep's wool served the same purpose. From these they wove rough cloth for tents and clothes. Their looms were simple sticks and threads.

In Palestine the methods grew somewhat better. Egypt's weaving was praised as highly developed. Yet Egyptian looms stayed primitive too. Herodotus says Egyptians wove at an upright loom. They began their work at the bottom, unlike others. Stone carvings show horizontal looms as well. The entry compares tools, terms, and cloth across the region.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wieniawski-jose:
Joseph Wieniawski was a Russian pianist and composer. Isidore Singer and Julius Gottlieb wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Lublin on May 23, 1837. He was the brother of Henri Wieniawski. He studied at the Paris Conservatoire under Zimmerman and Alkan. Harmony teachers included Marmontel and Leccoppey.

After 1850 Joseph often toured with his brother Henri. In 1856 he studied under Liszt at Weimar. He later studied theory under Marx in Berlin. In 1866 he settled in Moscow as a professor. He then opened a private piano school there. His works include two orchestral overtures. A string quartet and a piano concerto followed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-woolf-albert-ed:
Albert Edward Woolf (born 1846) was an American chemist and maker of new tools. Cyrus Adler and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in New York, he was schooled in its public schools. He also studied at the College of the City of New York.

His best work dealt with clean water and clean wounds. In 1876 he brought in a bleach for fine feathers. That same bleach served as a germ wash as well. In 1889 he found a new germ kill in sea water. Electric force split the sea water to make the wash. Town crews used it on water, waste, and sewage. In 1899 it helped fight yellow fever at Havana. He held seats in two learned groups in two lands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhak-ben-ze-e: Yizhak ben Zeera was a scholar of Palestine in the fourth century. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He read one verse of the Psalms in a rare way. The set sun, he said, is like a drop of blood. That drop is no more wide than a seed of mustard. One note on the Song of Songs bears his name too. Some books give a like name in its place there. The short entry rests on the tale study of Bacher.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zuzim-15309:
The Zuzim were an ancient people named once in Genesis, east of the Jordan. Emil G. Hirsch wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Genesis says Chedorlaomer smote them at Ham. The storyteller seems to assume readers already knew the name well.

Greek and Syriac translators read the name as a word meaning the strong or the mighty. On that reading, the Zuzim match the Rephaim, giants of the district. The Ammonites called those giants Zamzummim, a name close to Zuzim. The entry weighs whether the two names are one, split by copyists' errors. Sayce even traced the split to alike letters in Babylonian writing.
journal-of-discourses-vol-09:
War's middle years fill Volume Nine of the Journal, issued in 1862. The Saints prosper in their valleys while the Union fights for life. Young presses self-sufficiency in nearly every discourse of this span.

Home industry, grain reserves, and new settlements lead his public counsel. Converts keep gathering from Europe to swell the kingdom's towns. The discourses build Zion's workshops as Babylon tears itself apart. That sharp contrast gives Mormon Utah its odd, proud edge here. Faith, thrift, and defiance blend in the Tabernacle's weekly public voice. The volume shows prosperity preached as proof of divine favor.
kawaguchi-three-years-in-tibet-1909:
Ekai Kawaguchi lived in Tibet disguised as a Chinese pilgrim, and Three Years in Tibet, from 1909, tells how he did it. Kawaguchi, a Japanese Zen monk seeking true texts of his faith, spent 1897 to 1903 reaching Lhasa and studying in its great monasteries. Detection meant death, and his road ran through years of cold, hunger, and fear.

His account, the first by a Japanese traveler, shows daily life in the closed capital as few books ever have. Temples, markets, medicine, and monks all pass under his patient, observant eye along the way. The narrative stands as a primary witness to the old Lhasa on the edge of change.
kepler-astronomia-nova-1609:
Johannes Kepler published Astronomia Nova in 1609, the fruit of his long war with the orbit of Mars. No public-domain English translation exists, so the text stands here in Latin. Kepler worked from Tycho Brahe's superb records, the best naked-eye data ever gathered.

From those numbers Kepler forced out his first two laws of planet motion. Planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus. They also sweep equal areas in equal times. The laws broke the ancient rule that heavenly motion must be circular. Kepler told the story of his false starts in the book itself. It stands as a founding work of modern astronomy.
khunrath-amphitheatrum-sapientiae-1609:
Heinrich Khunrath was a German physician and Hermetic philosopher whose Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae appeared in 1609. The title means Amphitheater of Eternal Wisdom, and the book is built like its title: a theater of engraved visions. It is the great Christian-kabbalistic alchemical emblem book.

Nine large engravings show the alchemist at prayer and at the furnace, angels, gates, and the stone as Christ-like figures of renewal. Khunrath joins laboratory work to devotion, holding that the adept must be reborn along with his matter. Collectors prize the plates, and scholars mine the book for the period's union of faith and furnace.
kropotkin-great-french-revolution-dryhur:
Peter Kropotkin told the French Revolution from below in his history of 1789 to 1793. N. F. Dryhurst translated the work for Heinemann in 1909. The full English text runs to sixty eight chapters. Kings and assemblies share the stage with the Paris sections and village communes.

Peasant risings against feudal dues drive much of Kropotkin's story. He argues that common people, not leaders, made the Revolution's real gains. His anarchist sympathy shapes the telling without hiding the facts he gathered. The work rests on years in French archives. It remains a standard anarchist history of the event. Readers get the Revolution as a people's movement.
kuprin-yama-1909:
Yama, also called The Pit, is Alexander Kuprin's novel of life in a brothel district of a southern Russian city. Kuprin published the first part in 1909, and Bernard Guilbert Guerney translated the book into English in 1922. Kuprin called it the first and last honest book on its subject.

Inside the houses of Yama, Kuprin follows the women, their keepers, their clients, and the students who debate their fate. He shows routine, humor, cruelty, and sudden violence without flinching. The book was banned in places, devoured everywhere, and argued over for years. Kuprin meant it as protest, not titillation, and its frankness still startles.
les-sept-livres-de-l-archidoxe-magique-t: A 1909 French printing presents the Seven Books of the Magic Archidox, a work ascribed to Paracelsus, the Swiss physician and alchemist who died in 1541. The title page says these books were translated for the first time in this edition. The hosted sample survives only as garbled scan marks, so nothing beyond the title facts can be checked here. The entry is kept brief for that reason.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
The February 1875 Lippincott's concludes Following the Tiber. Six Months Among Cannibals offers rougher travel reading. Mary E. Blair tells of an American girl and her lovers. W. E. Griffis describes a Japanese marriage in high life.

William Black's Three Feathers advances through chapter twenty-five. Not the last word ends that installment of the serial. H. C. Wood Jr. writes a medical piece on fever. Trollope recalls sculptor Hiram Powers from personal recollection. Corn, by Sidney Lanier, and Gentleman Dick vary the number. A singular family and the lost baby complete the fiction.
lister-collected-papers-vol1-1909:
Joseph Lister was a British surgeon who changed hospital care by fighting wound infection. He built on Pasteur's germ theory and began treating wounds with carbolic acid in the 1860s. His key papers were gathered after his death, and this first collected volume appeared in 1909.

The papers set out the antiseptic principle: kill germs in and around a wound, and patients stop dying of hospital gangrene. Lister reports operations, compares results before and after his method, and answers his critics. Death rates in his wards fell sharply. These writings mark the start of safe modern surgery.
lister-collected-papers-vol2-1909:
Joseph Lister, the British surgeon behind antiseptic surgery, published research across a long career. His collected papers were issued in two volumes in 1909. This second volume holds his later scientific work rather than the first antiseptic reports.

The papers study inflammation, the clotting of blood, and related questions in surgery and physiology. Lister describes experiments on animals and patients, and he refines the methods behind his wound care. Readers can watch a careful scientist test each claim step by step. Together with volume one, the set records how modern surgery was built, step by tested step, over one working lifetime.
lodge-ether-of-space-1909:
Oliver Lodge, an English physicist, gave the ether its last great public defense in this book of 1909. He wrote for lay readers, in clear and warm terms. By then the new work of Einstein had made the ether look like a needless prop.

Lodge sets out what the ether does in his scheme, from light to the pull of worlds. He holds that space must be full of a real stuff that bears all waves and forces. The book shows the old view at its peak, just as its age came to a close.
lodge-survival-of-man-1909:
Oliver Lodge, a chief of the science of waves and wires, made his case for life past death in The Survival of Man, out in 1909. Lodge held high posts in the schools of Britain. He turned their tools on the dark room: notes, tests, and checks for fraud, weighed with a calm, fair hand through years of sittings.

He claims some notes from the dead pass all fair tests. His rank gave the claim a weight no mere fan could match. The book took the theme to the heart of science. Its calm tone is its force.
london-martin-eden-1909:
Jack London published Martin Eden in 1909, his tragic Künstlerroman of a working-class sailor who educates himself. A sailor educates himself into a famous writer, then discovers success is hollow, in London's most bitter novel. He protested that Eden was an individualist, not a socialist, and that the book indicted Eden's creed, not society's alone.

Martin loves Ruth Morse, a bourgeois student, and remakes himself by savage study in Oakland libraries. Rejection slips pile for years until the magazines suddenly pay fortunes for the work they once returned unopened. The same world that starved him now begs his company, and he sees the welcome is for fame, not for him. Ruth returns too late, and Martin sails for the South Seas and slips, at last, into the sea. The novel is the classic anatomy of literary success in America.
lorentz-theory-of-electrons-1909:
Hendrik Antoon Lorentz, a Dutch sage, gave these talks at Columbia in New York, and they came out in book form in 1909. His theme is the electron, the tiny charged part he had helped to place at the heart of physics. The talks sum up his life's work.

Lorentz shows how swarms of electrons can give light, heat rays, and the split hues of the Zeeman effect. He sets out the shrink of fast bodies that bears his name, tied to a still ether. The book is the old scheme in its last strict, fine form, by its chief maker.
macauliffe-sikh-religion-vol1-1909:
Max Arthur Macauliffe spent years in India studying the Sikh faith with Sikh scholars. His six-book account, printed in 1909, was the first full one in English. The first book gives scripture in English dress beside the lives of the Gurus. It opens with Guru Nanak, the founder.
