Morris and colleagues published a rapid review in twenty twenty-three of what works for hiring, keeping, and training the professional care workforce. Health and social care face deep shortages and high turnover, with fuzzy career paths making both worse.

The review searched two major databases for comparative studies from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-two and kept thirty studies. Most covered nurses, doctors, and allied health staff. Eleven studies tackled education alone, while others mixed training with hiring or safety efforts. Overall study quality was modest. Four lessons stood out: early rural support keeps workers in rural posts, managing workload protects well-being, learning must fit the job's real setting, and each profession needs its own tailored strategy. The authors say the evidence is a starting point, and a joined-up workforce plan is urgently needed.
pmc-10724809:
Sun Young Shim and Hyeonkyeong Lee examine how social conditions shape cardiovascular health among Mongolian adults, in a two thousand twenty-three cross-sectional study. Education, income, and insurance are suspected drivers, but their effects may differ by sex and age.

Nearly five thousand seven hundred adults from a national risk-factor survey were scored on a modified Life's Simple Seven scale. Among the lowest-income group, having under twelve years of education or no health insurance was strongly associated with poor cardiovascular health. The links were sharper in women and in adults under forty-five. The authors call for strategies that close education and insurance gaps to protect heart health.
pmc-10731209:
Ho-Young Jung and colleagues report ankle and toe weakness caused by a calcified cyst in a spinal ligament, a first documented case. Their 2023 case report concerns a sixty-six-year-old man with two weeks of leg pain and walking difficulty.

Examination found weakness lifting his left ankle and big toe. Scans showed spinal narrowing with a calcified mass pressing on the nerve sac at one lower back level. Surgeons removed part of the bone and the firm nodule, adding a fusion procedure. Tissue study suggested a calcified pseudocyst without a lining. After surgery, the man's ankle and toe strength gradually recovered.
pmc-10737209:
Rebecca Lassell, Abraham Brody, and six co-authors build a nature activity plan with Hispanic and Latino adults. The adults live with memory loss, from mild trouble to mild dementia. Their plan, from twenty twenty-three, is called Green Activity Prescription. A work therapist helps fit outdoor tasks to each person's home and area.

The team held five group talks and two solo talks in the Bronx, New York. Outdoor pros, patients, care partners, and health staff all took part. They shaped both the twelve-week plan and how it will be tested. The goal is care that fits the culture and daily life of each family.
pmc-10737909:
Prince Okrah, Shafer Tharrington, Isaac Shin, Aaron Wagoner, Katelyn Woodsmall, and Deborah Jehu review risk factors for mild brain injury from falls in older adults in two thousand twenty-three. Mild brain injuries often go undiagnosed, which delays care. About four in five such injuries in older adults stem from falls, yet the drivers were unclear.

The review kept only forward-looking studies of adults aged sixty and up. Searches ran across six databases plus grey sources in late two thousand twenty-two. Two reviewers screened each paper, with a third to settle disputes. Outcomes spanned injury risk, fall rates, and counts of fallers with and without injury. The work sets a base for spotting who needs fall checks most.
pmc-10741209:
Olga Shaprova and a large team of co-authors probe old blood samples for signs of early immunity, in a paper dated twenty twenty-three. The samples came from 799 people across Siberia in late twenty nineteen, before COVID-19 reached the region. The team tested them for antibodies against parts of the new virus.

They checked both how specific the antibodies were and whether they could block the virus. The samples came from a flu study of healthy donors. Sites sat near wild waterfowl routes. The work asks whether past colds left shields that shaped how hard the pandemic hit.
pmc-10744209:
Zhang and a large team hunt gene loci for resistance to Gibberella ear rot in maize with a kernel assay, in a study from twenty twenty-three. The fungus cuts yield and poisons grain with toxins. Genetic resistance is the cleanest defense, but its basis was poorly mapped. The team scores disease on kernels in the lab across time points.

They scan three hundred three diverse maize lines genome-wide. Three statistical models run in parallel to cross-check hits. Four significant markers emerge, each explaining a small share of variation. The top marker appears in all three models at the same spot. Twelve candidate genes sit near that peak, several tied to disease defense. The assay aids selection of resistant breeding stock.
pmc-10745409:
Benjamin Bertin, Benoit Foligne, and Delphine Ley lead a team reviewing whether breastfeeding shapes a child's later risk of inflammatory bowel disease. Their overview appeared in two thousand twenty-three. The first thousand days of life program much of later health. Gut microbes settling in during that window are prime suspects in lifelong gut disease.

Animal experiments encourage the idea that early feeding protects the bowel. Human studies, however, disagree with each other, partly because their designs vary so much. How long breastfeeding stays exclusive may decide whether any effect lasts. The authors weigh the experimental and clinical records side by side. They suggest early microbe-directed foods could mimic protection if the link firms up. For now the honest verdict is promising but unsettled. Standardized studies are the missing piece.
pmc-10753409:
Sund, Dargan, Archer, Blundell, and Wood surveyed vapers in the United Kingdom for this study in twenty twenty-three. Lung injury linked to vaping had raised concern, above all for cannabis-based liquids. The team asked current vapers about symptoms and health care use over the past year. An online survey drew close to two thousand five hundred replies.

About four hundred respondents currently vaped. Symptoms ranged from cough, reported by nearly a third, to blood in sputum, which was rare. People who vaped cannabis-based products reported more symptoms and more visits for care. Doctors reportedly never named a vaping-related illness as the cause. The authors suggest milder vaping illness may be missed in the United Kingdom.
pmc-10753809:
Bassey and coauthors solve the superstructure of a sodium battery cathode material. The layered cathode swaps magnesium into a manganese oxide frame. Fine structure drives how sodium ions hop in the cathode. That hopping sets battery speed and life in use.

Heat-varied NMR and resonance tests probed local structure. X-ray and neutron scattering revealed the superstructure. Computer models matched the spectra and hopping barriers. Local charge balance proved to drive the pattern. Sodium hops link in chains, not as lone jumps. The work may guide design of better sodium cathodes.
pmc-10809809:
Witkowska and four co-authors tell how a care-caused tear in a heart artery, reaching the aorta, was healed with no surgery, in a case report from 2024. Such a tear, an iatrogenic coronary dissection, is rare but can risk a life in heart tube work. A 62-year-old woman had tube work for unstable angina, with bad tight spots in her arteries. As the guide wire went in, it tore the right coronary artery into the aorta.

Three drug-eluting stents sealed the tear's mouth in a rescue move. The tear in the ascending aorta ran to the brachiocephalic trunk, and the aorta had not stretched wide. No pericardial effusion sat around the heart, and the aortic valve worked as it should. The team picked conservative management over rush surgery on the aorta. The case can guide patient-by-patient calls, where no set rules exist.
pmc-10868409:
S Cruz Rivera and fellow members of the SPIRIT-AI and CONSORT-AI groups present SPIRIT-AI, a reporting guide for trial plans that test treatments with an AI part. The hosted text is this guideline, in a Spanish edition with an English abstract. It was published in twenty twenty-three.

Trial plans need full, clear reporting so new care can be judged fairly. AI tools add fresh risks, since their gains must be proven in forward trials, not assumed. The guide extends a known plan reporting list with AI specific items. It was built in stages through a search of past work and expert talks that yielded candidate items. A twin guide covers trial reports.
pmc-10903309:

pmc-10909109:

pmc-10948409:

pmc-10994609:

pmc-11089909:

pmc-11533309:

pmc-11534209:

pmc-11570109:

pmc-11571209:

pmc-11574909:

pmc-11596209:

pmc-11599609:

pmc-11606209:

pmc-11608309:

pmc-11611509:

pmc-11636309:

pmc-11640209:

pmc-11640309:

pmc-11640409:

pmc-11642909:

pmc-11643309:

pmc-11644009:

pmc-11644809:

pmc-11645009:

pmc-11648209:

pmc-11656909:

pmc-11658209:

pmc-11669809:

pmc-11680209:

pmc-11684009:

pmc-11689109:

pmc-11690009:

pmc-11692109:

pmc-11692209:

pmc-11710909:

pmc-11888709:

pmc-12039709:

pmc-12663209:

pmc-12673109:

pmc-12686109:

pmc-12696209:

pmc-12699809:

pmc-12706909:

pmc-12710909:

pmc-12714109:

pmc-12715209:

pmc-12715709:

pmc-12721109:

pmc-12730409:

pmc-12731609:

pmc-12734909:

pmc-12735009:

Beatrice Murawski and a large team co-design a digital tool to cut cancer risk through lifestyle change. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. A large share of cancers could be stopped by healthy habits, yet support for change is hard to find and use. The tool, Lifestyle6, also backs early spotting of cancer.

A panel of community members shapes the tool through a run of group and solo workshops. Blocks they name span scarce cancer-specific help, too much generic advice, and doubts on truth and fit. Time, cost, and drive also hold people back. For the test build, they put access, range of voices, ease of use, and personal fit first. A tailored feel is the core ask.
pmc-13115509:
Elsokkary and two co-authors test grit as a bridge from edge traits to death thoughts in students in this twenty twenty-six study. Edge traits mark wild mood, self harm risk, and frail self worth in youth. Death thoughts rise with those traits, yet what sits in the path was dim.

Inside, more than two hundred fifty students filled forms on traits, grit, and thoughts. Edge traits went with more death thoughts and with less grit in the checks. Grit did not shift the trait-thought link when both were in play at once. Yet grit did sit in the path, as traits cut grit and low grit fed thoughts. The link held when age, sex, and past care were weighed in.
pmc-13120209:
Hasuk Nam and five co-authors tell of a Bengal cat with a lump at a past vaccine site that proved to be a rare plasma cell tumor. Their case study appeared in twenty twenty-six. The six-year-old male cat first had the lump cut out at a local clinic, where it was read as a T-cell skin cancer. Scans at the referral hub found left tumor at the cut site plus a fresh chest lump.

Both lumps were cut and probed with stain tests. The cells failed to stain for T-cell, B-cell, and skin marks but lit up strong for MUM-1, a plasma cell mark. The team read the growth as a plasmacytoma with fierce spread.
pmc-13136209:
Rachel Chambers and co-authors tackle content validity reviews of patient questionnaires in this 2026 paper. Content validity asks whether a questionnaire truly covers what patients experience. It is the most important measurement property and the hardest to judge. COSMIN guidance sets the standard method for such reviews.

The authors gathered challenges from an umbrella review and from expert consultation. Seven recurring problems are listed with practical fixes and examples. Feasibility of running a full quality review opens the list. Better reviews help clinicians pick questionnaires that measure what matters. The paper is a field guide for a fiddly but vital task. Patient voice in measurement starts with getting this step right.
pmc-13136609:
Shahla Shafaati Laleh, Sevil İnal, Mohammadbagher Hosseini, and a wider team wrote this clinical trial report, published in 2026. It tests whether a baby's scent and video can ease the strain on mothers whose infants are in intensive care.

Separation in the neonatal unit fuels anxiety and can cut milk supply. Seventy-eight mothers were split into three groups for five days. One group watched video of their baby while smelling a hat the baby had worn. A second watched video only. The third smelled a plain hat. Both video groups showed clear drops in anxiety compared with the control group, and the scent group gained most on some scores. The study also tracked stress, milk volume, and bonding. The authors present scent-plus-video as a cheap comfort hospitals could offer.
pmc-13150909:
Lindsay Stark and co-authors review, in twenty twenty-six, how infectious disease outbreaks affect violence against women and girls in low- and middle-income countries. Outbreaks are growing more frequent with climate change, urban growth, and land use change. Response measures can raise risk factors for violence. The team searched for studies from any outbreak since twenty fourteen. Nearly all hard evidence, though, covered the COVID-19 pandemic, and only three studies split results for women versus girls.

The synthesis points to increased violence in the first pandemic year versus before. Five mechanisms drove it: income loss, movement limits, changed access to services, fear of infection, and mistrust of health systems left by past outbreaks. The authors draw lessons for future outbreak responses.
pmc-13152209:
Hui-Ying Yu and fifteen co-authors built a new mosquito line for dengue control in Taiwan, reported in twenty twenty-six. Dengue is spreading as trade and a warming climate widen the range of the mosquito that carries it. Spraying and cleanup have not held the disease back, so new tools are needed.

The team placed a helpful bacterium, taken from a local mosquito type caught in Kaohsiung, into the dengue mosquito line. The germ passes from mother to young and can block the virus inside the insect. The paper checks the line's health, breeding, and virus-blocking strength, steps needed before such mosquitoes can be freed to cut dengue spread.
pmc-13153509:
Flores and six co-authors tested a remote exercise program for Hispanic and Latino adults with multiple sclerosis in twenty twenty-six. Evidence for remotely delivered exercise in this population was limited, though home programs could widen access. Their FERLA MS study delivered training at home with remote support.

Of three hundred forty people contacted, thirty-three enrolled and twenty-six finished, a retention rate of eighty-seven percent. Adherence averaged eighty-one percent in the exercise group. No serious adverse events occurred. The exercise group improved its physical activity, and walking scores improved by about ten points, beyond the threshold considered clinically meaningful. Higher education correlated with better compliance and lower anxiety. The authors conclude the approach is feasible and safe, and merits a larger trial.
pmc-13157809:
Poelhekken and van der Bent asked Dutch skin doctors in twenty twenty-six what they think of long, multi-step skin care habits. Such habits, pushed by social media and ads, are now common in teens and young adults. Proof that they help sound skin is still thin.

Most of the one hundred sixty-eight doctors who replied said they worry about these habits. Most also see skin harm from them often, such as sore rash, spots, or allergy rash. Strong creams and acids were named most. Yet most saw some gains too, like more care for sun wear. Almost all backed daily sun cream, and few backed long routines.
pmc-13162009:
Sandeep Kumar Yadav and co-authors measure, in twenty twenty-six, spine bone dimensions at the thoracolumbar junction in western India, to guide safe screw placement. Pedicle screws fix the spine through the bony bridges of each vertebra. Size data for Indian patients were limited, despite ethnic variation. The team prospectively scanned two hundred adults with back pain but normal imaging, at a tertiary center. One hundred ten were men. They measured pedicle width, spacing, cortex depth, and screw angle at four levels, from the eleventh thoracic to the second lumbar vertebra.

Pedicle width grew steadily down the levels, and was larger in men at two levels. Spacing and angle also rose downward. Cortex depth peaked at the first lumbar level. The values give safe screw size ranges for this population.
pmc-13177909: Michael Edwards, Alexandra Lee, and Simon Thompson discuss federated data linkage in a 2024 article. Federated systems let analysts work securely across several institutions without moving sensitive data, using trusted research environments. Real-world linkage across such systems is still early, and sharing the information that shows two records match, while preserving privacy, is hard. The article examines these challenges for population-scale linkage, including how links shift as providers join or leave, and explores privacy-preserving approaches across multiple research environments and their governance needs.
pmc-13179309:
Nwaopara and Woolery-Lloyd wrote a review in twenty twenty-six on lifestyle factors in skin aging. Skin aging mixes inner biology with daily habits built over years. The review gathers human studies, trials, and lab models across six habit areas. Plant-rich, antioxidant-heavy diets link to fewer wrinkles and better moisture. Sugar- and salt-heavy diets speed cell aging in lab models. Exercise thickens skin and supports collagen while calming inflammation. Stress and poor sleep slow barrier repair and cut collagen genes.

Tobacco, heavy drinking, and stimulants tie strongly to early aging. Social isolation links to body-wide inflammation, an indirect skin risk. Cause and effect still need long studies to settle. The authors frame lifestyle medicine for dermatology.
pmc-13183709:
Abdallah and seven colleagues test two cytokines as markers in familial Mediterranean fever in twenty twenty-six. The disease causes periodic inflammatory attacks with quiet inflammation between them. That hidden inflammation can damage organs over time. Midkine and pleiotrophin rise in many inflammatory conditions.

Blood from thirty patients and thirty controls was compared. Gene expression of both cytokines was higher in patients. Blood midkine levels were about four times the control level. Pleiotrophin ran higher too, but not significantly. Midkine expression tied inversely to a standard inflammation marker and positively to anaemia. The authors propose midkine as a tool for tracking hidden inflammation. Pleiotrophin may instead reflect acute flare activity.
pmc-13189909:
Gokhan Taskin and six co-authors ask whether daily physical activity levels predict outcomes in older patients with acute coronary syndrome. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. Patients were gathered in the emergency department, where the care path begins.

Two hundred and seven older volunteers with the syndrome took part. Patients who suffered major cardiac events had lower activity levels than those who did not. Events found later, within thirty days, also clustered in the low-activity group. Standard risk scores ran higher in the event group, which supports the activity reading as a real signal rather than noise. The authors suggest that asking about activity could help sort elderly chest pain patients faster and more safely.
pmc-13195809:
Hirotsugu Kurobe and colleagues reported a successful aorta repair case in two thousand twenty-six. The patient was a man in his late sixties. His aorta had split in the descending section. Blocked kidney flow caused acute renal failure. Scans showed the tear entry near the arch. The false channel squeezed both kidney arteries.

Surgeons placed a stent graft urgently inside the aorta. One branch artery was deliberately covered during repair. Urine output rose and kidney function recovered afterward. Early follow-up scans showed no leak or enlargement. Vessel shape remodeled favorably over time. Five years of follow-up are reported. Endovascular repair rescued both aorta and kidneys.
pmc-13197109:
Chidimma Doris Azubuike and colleagues describe a 2026 protocol called MOMitor for blood pressure after birth. High blood pressure after delivery affects about one in five women. Phone-based checks could catch rises early in this risky window, so the team set out a tracking plan.

Enrolled women answer brief phone prompts over the first six weeks after birth. Prompts ask whether pressure topped a set limit and whether warning symptoms are present. A subset also reports home pressure readings. The team will model change within and between women across the six weeks. Data gathering ran from late 2021 to mid 2025. Results are not yet reported, since analysis was still to come.
pmc-13198509:
Daniel Verscharen and colleagues review electron travel in tangled magnetic fields in a 2026 paper. Space magnetic fields are rarely smooth; plasma flows and turbulence twist them. Electrons spiral along field lines, so their measures can map how fields connect across space.

The review lays out the basics of that travel, then covers how turbulence tangles fields in the first place. It treats trapping in field dips, escape from traps, and drift across field lines. Waves hitting particles can speed or scatter electrons too. No single tool can untangle the full picture. The authors call for joint use of spacecraft data, remote views, theory, and simulation.
pmc-13199209:
Seyit Bilal Ozdemir and Busra Ozdemir tested how heat aging affects the X-ray visibility of tooth fillings in a 2026 lab study. Fillings must show on X-rays at least as clearly as tooth tissue, so dentists can spot gaps and decay. Heat cycling in the lab mimics years of hot and cold drinks.

Seven universal filling materials were shaped into discs at two thicknesses. X-ray brightness was measured against an aluminum scale. All materials met the standard minimum at the thinner size. Thicker discs read brighter across the board. After ten thousand heat cycles, two materials lost brightness at the thicker size. Material type and thickness both shaped readings, a point for dentists judging old fillings.
pmc-13201009:
Abdulrahman Alaseem and five co-authors counted the cost of limb amputations at a major hospital in Saudi Arabia over ten years, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Amputation carries heavy physical, mental, and social costs, and rates are rising where diabetes and vessel disease are common. National cost data, though, were scarce.

Records covered hundreds of operations and patients across the decade. Diabetes complications caused about two-thirds of cases and most of the total cost. Emergency operations cost more per patient than planned ones. Leg removals were most common, and removal above the knee cost the most per patient. Longer hospital stays drove costs up. The authors stress prevention as the cheapest path.
pmc-13207009:
Lin and five co-authors test antibody-drug conjugates that target a protein on new blood vessels in mouse tumors, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The protein sits on both tumor vessels and tumor cells and is taken inside the cell. Prior work showed conjugates can shrink tumors by hitting vessels or cells. Here the team isolates the vessel effect with a growth factor model.

A virus drives fresh vessel growth in mouse ears as a tumor stand-in. A gentler conjugate homes to those new vessels within hours. One dose breaks up growing vessels within two days. Repeated doses cause striking local tissue death with no harm to normal vessels nearby. The approach offers a fresh anti-vessel strategy for solid tumors.
pmc-13211209:
Siying Pan leads a team on a peptide that links salt and disease in poplar. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with a hybrid poplar tree. RALF peptides guide plant stress response in many species.

Their roles in woody species were still poorly defined. The peptide sparked a fast burst of reactive oxygen in leaf discs. Partner receptors from poplar let a test plant respond too. A gene cut line kept rooting at high salt levels. It also grew better than wild type under salt. Disease risk is the other side of its role.
pmc-13212909:
Kui Zhou and co-authors unveil in 2026 a compact spectral camera that works in longwave infrared, the band suited to spotting gases, minerals, and heat patterns. Existing instruments are bulky and rigid, which keeps them off small drones and field kits.

Their imager uses a programmable micro-mirror-scale filter chip placed in front of a modular lens system, keeping the whole unit near one kilogram. Software can switch between broad scans, fine scans of chosen bands, or custom band mixes for each task. Channel selection and image fusion help identify targets precisely. The small, adaptable design suits pollution monitoring, mineral prospecting, and security work in the field.
pmc-13213009:
Jianning Li, Agniva Sengupta, and Stefan Zachow develop in 2026 a neural network that rebuilds missing skull shapes while honestly reporting how unsure it is. Surgeons need plausible reconstructions for implants, yet any partial scan admits several reasonable completions.

Their Bayesian version of a standard three-dimensional network samples many completions instead of giving one answer. Tested on cranial rebuilding, face reconstruction, and sharpening low-resolution skull scans, it matched a conventional network's accuracy. The spread among its answers fell mainly in bone thickness, matching real anatomy. Tasks with tighter constraints produced lower uncertainty. Knowing where a reconstruction is shaky could help clinicians judge implant designs more safely.
pmc-13213609:
Michał Kazanowski and co-authors document in 2026 bleeding from the ear arising during robotic bowel surgery, an odd complication of operations done head-down with gas inflating the abdomen. Two patients at their centre developed it under only moderate tilting.

A 74-year-old woman bled from one ear during sigmoid colon removal, and scans plus ear examination found blood in the canal with eardrum injury. A 63-year-old man bled from both ears while waking after rectal surgery. Both recovered with conservative care and ear follow-up, keeping normal hearing. Earlier reports came mostly from bladder and gynaecology surgery under steeper tilt, so colorectal teams should know the risk too.
pmc-13213709:
Yijia Wang leads a large team surveying in 2026 wild rodents in Liaoning Province, China, for two hantaviruses that cause a serious kidney fever in people. Forest and farmland in the province shelter many rodent species, keeping the viruses circulating.

Testing 403 rodents collected during 2022 and 2023 found nineteen carrying virus. Standard tests caught most positives, clustered around three cities. Deep sequencing, though, spotted virus in one district that standard tests missed, because the local strain had drifted where the test primers bind. The team designed new primers from the recovered sequences and confirmed four more cases. Local rodent strains closely matched those infecting people nearby, sharpening prevention targets.
pmc-13215009:
Nima Parvaneh leads a large team reporting in 2026 two Iranian patients with a rare inherited variant that leaves an antiviral signal permanently switched on. The variant, traced to a sixteenth-century founder, causes life-threatening brain inflammation and lung failure, and many patients die young.

Both patients carried two copies of the same STAT2 gene change, which blocks the off-switch for interferon signalling. Early genetic recognition matters, the authors stress, because high-dose JAK inhibitor drugs can damp the runaway pathway. Their cases add clinical detail on presentation and treatment response. The report argues this devastating condition belongs on the treatable list when spotted fast enough.
pmc-13216109:
Megan Watkin-Bennett and Helen P White present a 2026 exploratory study of how fear of being sued affects ultrasound specialists in the United Kingdom. Litigation against imaging staff is rising while the workforce already faces burnout and shortages.

Six National Health Service sonographers took part in online interviews, and their accounts formed four themes covering emotional burden, changed practice, workplace pressures, and support. Fear of claims pushed defensive habits, especially in how reports were written, and short appointments plus confusion about the sonographer's role raised the perceived risk of error. Participants still valued openness and accountability. They asked for clearer guidance, learning opportunities, and stronger backing from employers.
pmc-13217909:
Aarón Espinosa-Jaime and co-authors present a 2026 methods paper, SiteCELL, for readying immune cells for single-cell sequencing where there is no proper lab. Standard blood cell purification needs machines and power, which is one reason rural and global-south communities are missing from immune atlases.

SiteCELL purifies and freezes the blood's mononuclear immune cells at the collection site with minimal gear and no electricity. In matched tests it performed as well as the standard density-gradient method, in both laboratory and rural field conditions, recovering cell type proportions well. It also reduced cell stress signatures and batch variability between countries. The authors offer the method to multi-country projects that want to include underrepresented ancestries in cellular atlases.
pmc-13218109:
Magaly Brodeur and colleagues set out a 2026 protocol for a five-year Canadian study of gambling habits among sexual and gender minority adults. Most people gamble without harm, but a minority develop problem gambling with serious effects on mind, relationships, and finances. Minority populations carry high rates of mental health disorders, yet how their gambling develops over time is unknown, since earlier work captured only snapshots.

The study runs in two phases. First, an online survey of 2,500 adults identifying as sexual or gender minorities who gambled in the past year will be repeated annually for three years. That design lets the team model gambling trajectories and find factors tied to problem gambling. Second, about 40 respondents showing problem gambling will take part in semi-structured interviews about their experiences. With ethics approval in place, the team expects findings to support prevention and harm-reduction programs shaped to this population.
pmc-13218309:
Jung Hwa Park and colleagues compare two DNA sequencing strategies for profiling microbes under the gumline, in a 2026 study of periodontitis patients. Periodontitis is an inflammation driven by a disturbed bacterial community, and researchers can survey it either by sequencing one marker gene or by shotgun sequencing the DNA. The approaches had rarely run side by side on matched samples.

Plaque from 28 patients was analyzed both ways. Shotgun sequencing produced more reads and finer species-level detail, but the share of microbial reads varied because human DNA dominates these samples. The marker-gene method gave steadier yields and caught low-abundance organisms that shotgun missed, while core genera appeared at similar levels in both. Functional predictions overlapped on pathways yet diverged elsewhere, with shotgun profiles swayed by depth. The authors offer the comparison as guidance: both methods capture the core community, and the choice depends on the resolution needed.
pmc-13219709:
Marco Porta and colleagues test whether deep learning reconstruction can sharpen musculoskeletal MRI while shortening the scan in a 2026 study. MRI faces a trade-off among speed, sharpness, and noise, and reconstruction promises to break it by cleaning images. The team built the method into a 1.5-tesla scanner protocol for joints.

Thirty-nine examinations of knees, shoulders, ankles, and hips were analyzed twice: once as sequences and once as higher-resolution sequences rebuilt with deep learning. Three readers, blinded to the version, rated the visibility of structures, and a fourth measured signal and contrast in bone and muscle. The deep learning versions used smaller pixels and finished faster, readers agreed more when scoring them, and every structure was rated visible or better. Measured signal and contrast held steady rather than dropping. The authors conclude the reconstruction buys resolution and time in joint imaging without paying for them in quality.
pmc-13219809:
Munjuri Akter and colleagues test local and imported honey sold in Dhaka for minerals and toxic metals in a 2026 study. Honey reflects the environment bees foraged in, so it can serve as a sentinel, and buyers assume it is wholesome. Twelve samples, six local and six imported, were analyzed by atomic absorption spectrophotometry for iron, zinc, and manganese plus cadmium, chromium, and lead.

Imported honey carried more iron and manganese, while zinc matched between groups. The finding was cadmium: four of the six local samples and all six imported ones exceeded the allowable limit. Chromium and lead stayed within bounds everywhere. Risk indices still came out below the level of non-cancer concern, but cadmium contributed most of that risk in local honey. The authors call for monitoring and quality control, and for research tracing where the cadmium in honey originates so it can be stopped at the source.
pmc-13221009:
William B. Mair and Ines Alvarez-Garcia introduce a 2026 collection of articles on the biology of aging in PLOS Biology. The editors note surging public interest in longevity, fueled by real progress in aging science alongside inflated claims from wellness influencers. Whether aging itself can be slowed remains an open question.

Contributors examine why longer lives may reflect better survival of disease rather than slower aging. Other pieces cover brain stem cells and memory, early-life interventions with lasting effects, and nutrient signaling pathways. Together, the collection sets out what proof a true aging therapy would need, and why healthy years matter more than extra years alone.
pmc-13221409:
Jack McGrath leads a ten-author team tracing metals from e-cigarette liquid into mouse lungs, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. Vapes are marketed as safer than tobacco, yet evidence of metal exposure keeps growing. Where those metals land and accumulate in lung tissue was poorly understood.

Four mass spectrometry platforms characterized the liquid, its aerosol, and exposed tissue. Mice inhaled nicotine e-cigarette aerosol at three puff doses, twice daily for four days, with air-breathing controls. Multiple toxic metals and organometallic compounds were found along the chain. The study maps distribution rather than just presence. Such detail matters for judging what short-term vaping deposits in the respiratory system.
pmc-13222509:
Krzysztof Sosnowski, Chloe Jordan, and Charles M Malata present a late breast implant complication triggered by blunt chest trauma, in a 2026 case report. Seventeen years after cosmetic augmentation, a low-speed blow produced both implant rupture and a blood collection around the implant. The patient also had severe capsular contracture, the tightening scar shell that complicates revision surgery.

Management required complex single-stage revision. Late bleeding around implants is rarely reported, and its causes remain debated between direct injury and tiny capsule fractures. Silent rupture adds diagnostic difficulty, since the implant can fail without clear symptoms. The authors advise checking implants after chest trauma even when the impact seems minor.
pmc-13222609:
Jing Ren and co-authors build a nanoplatform that delivers boron into breast tumors for neutron capture therapy, in a 2026 study. The therapy needs boron loaded into tumors and traceable during treatment. Their polymer particles carry a boron-rich compound called carborane, use porphyrin units that fluoresce, and wear a stabilizing surface coat.

The particles held a high boron share and stayed stable in suspension. Breast cancer cells took them up efficiently and kept them. In mice, fluorescence imaging confirmed tumor localization after injection. Combined with thermal neutron irradiation, the platform suppressed tumor growth by about seventy-three percent against controls, without significant body-wide toxicity on tissue checks. Imaging and therapy arrive in one package.
pmc-13224009:
Cody C Diezel and colleagues map a 2026 mouse study of the ventral tegmental area, a brain region involved in reward and mood, during chronic nerve pain. Combining protein, phosphorylation, and fat-molecule measurements with behaviour tests, the team tracked how the region changes over time. An early phase involved shifts in energy use.

Later, a less healthy state emerged, marked by altered energy metabolism and structural remodelling inside cells. Potassium channel parts changed in proportion, and a cannabis-like molecule called 2-AG ran low as animals showed passive coping. Supplying 2-AG or boosting those potassium channels reversed the passive behaviour, marking both systems as possible treatment targets.
pmc-13225009:
Jiayi Chen and colleagues analyse a 2026 surveillance report on foodborne illness in Shengsi County, an island area of Zhejiang Province, China, covering 2019 to 2024. Sentinel hospitals reported cases into the national monitoring system, letting the team chart which germs, foods, and seasons drove illness. Seafood features heavily in local diets, so marine products drew particular attention.

Across 2,173 cases, illness peaked in summer and most eating happened at home. Marine animals and their products formed the largest suspected food group. A bacterium called Vibrio parahaemolyticus dominated throughout, but Salmonella positivity jumped sharply in 2024 after years near zero. The authors urge tighter seafood safety and closer watching of the Salmonella rise.
pmc-13227109:
Daniel Betancourt and four co-authors published an enzymology study in twenty twenty-six on how a DNA repair polymerase works while chemically handcuffed to the DNA it fixes. Human polymerase beta fills single-letter gaps during base excision repair, apparently before its tether to the strand is released. Because the untethered enzyme falls off in seconds, the crosslinked dance was hard to watch.

The team built an active crosslinked complex and ran precise kinetic, thermodynamic, and structural tests. Chemical bond-making limited the speed for wrong letters but not right ones. Pulse experiments revealed a hidden intermediate before the chemistry step. The barrier involved small local rearrangements, not big domain swings. Their mechanism is the first complete account of accurate building by this tethered enzyme.
pmc-13229209:
Yuchen Guo, Matthew O. Jackson, and Ruixue Jia assemble a 2026 historical dataset on West Point cadets who had to choose between the Union and the Confederacy in the American Civil War. Classmates faced the same rupture with life-or-death stakes, making the episode a rare window on peer influence under extreme polarisation. Newly gathered records were paired with modern causal inference methods.

Cadets' choices were strongly shaped by who their classmates were, even with their home states' political and economic forces taken into account. The authors also trace how peer influence interacted with those wider forces and with cadets' other experiences. Peer effects, the study concludes, stay powerful precisely when decisions carry the heaviest personal and moral weight, a finding with modern echoes.
pmc-13230309:
Thomas Fabian reports in 2026 a study comparing eye jumps during reading with eye jumps during shape scanning. Participants read texts and also scanned rows of geometric shapes matched in layout to the text. Saccades are the quick eye movements that shift gaze from one spot to the next.

Jumps forward were more alike in length, one after another, during reading than during shape scanning. Jumps backward showed no such difference between the two tasks. Tighter control during reading may reflect how language guides where the eyes go next. Measuring the relative lengths of successive jumps offers a task-free way to study reading. The method could also help compare gaze control across many other activities.
pmc-13231009:
Zhong Dan and colleagues trace in 2026 how small RNA switches help cucumber fruit cope with heat while they grow. A heat-sensitive cucumber line was profiled across four growth stages under normal and hot conditions. The team measured fruit shape, plant hormones, gene activity, and the small RNAs that tune genes up or down.

Heat threw two hormones, jasmonic acid and a gibberellin form, out of balance across fruit regions. Ninety-two small RNAs changed with heat, and eleven that fell steadily paired with twenty-four target genes. Those pairs help keep hormone levels and signals steady, guiding shape under stress. The network offers breeding targets for cucumbers that hold their form in hotter greenhouses.
pmc-13231409:
Izquierdo Pretel, Uchiyama, Sadri, and Sharma evaluate a resident led ultrasound course in twenty twenty-six. Point of care ultrasound is now seen as a core clinical skill. Residents as teachers offer a scalable way to teach it. The team ran two identical five hour workshops at a medical school in Florida.

Learners and instructors filled paired surveys before and after the workshops. Nine learners showed clear gains in confidence for clinical use of ultrasound. Confidence in image interpretation also rose significantly. Mean confidence increased across all domains measured. Eight instructors began with high confidence and showed no significant change. The authors conclude that resident led teaching improves learner confidence. They present the model as scalable for other programs.
pmc-13232309:
David Jurnecka and colleagues show in 2026 that the tail end of a whooping cough protein is what lets the germ grip airway hairs. The huge surface protein normally gets trimmed before use in current vaccines. During contact with human nasal cells, the team found the protein stays mostly whole instead.

Deleting the tail left the protein folded, shipped, and displayed normally, yet the bacteria could no longer stick to ciliated cells. Mice carrying the tail-less germ failed to settle in the nose, which blocks spread to new hosts. Close imaging showed the protein reshaping on contact, as if the tail crosses the hair membrane to anchor. Future vaccines may gain from including that tail piece.
pmc-13232609:
Jose Miguel D Robes and Aaron W Puri review in 2026 a flipped labeling trick for tracing how living things build natural products. Normal labeling feeds organisms a marked building block and watches where the mark lands. Marked blocks are sometimes impossible to buy or make, which stalls the detective work.

The flipped method grows the organism on fully marked food, then adds the building block in its normal unmarked form. The unmarked piece stands out sharply against the marked background in lab readings. Uses covered range over pathway mapping, structure solving, and matching genes to the products they build. Cases where the trick adds little are also flagged, so researchers can pick the right tool.
pmc-13234109:
Linda Kalski and colleagues published a 2026 cross-sectional study of what midlife health checkups uncover. Just over a thousand adults aged forty-five to fifty-nine received preventive examinations combining medical history, records, and laboratory tests for cholesterol, blood pressure, blood sugar, and thyroid function. A finding counted as a suspected new diagnosis when it crossed standard clinical thresholds.

Forty-one percent of participants left with at least one previously undocumented suspicion. Raised LDL cholesterol led the list at twenty-eight percent, followed by hypertension at nine percent. Men faced higher odds of any finding and of hypertension specifically, and body mass tracked with blood pressure. A recent prior blood test lowered the odds of surprises. Family history of lipid disorders predicted high cholesterol. The authors argue checkups pay off most for midlife adults with little prior healthcare contact.
pmc-13234709:
S. Janssens and colleagues tracked in 2026 colorectal cancer and its precursor growths in younger adults in Belgium. Cancer registry data and insurance records covered incidence, detection, and deaths, with close attention to ages twenty to forty-nine. Rates were calculated by age and sex, and trend changes were estimated over time. Diagnostic procedure use in the forty-something group helped explain the patterns.

Invasive cancer stayed stable among people aged forty to forty-nine across two decades. Growths and very early cancers rose in that group alongside more stool testing and colonoscopy, suggesting earlier detection. Mortality there stayed stable or fell over the period. A different picture emerged for people in their thirties, where early and advanced cancers both rose. The authors see no case for lowering the screening start age, yet they urge vigilance for symptoms in younger adults.
pmc-13235509:
Jinlin Li and colleagues tested in 2026 a perilla leaf extract as a natural preservative for refrigerated snakehead fish fillets. Snakehead is a valuable freshwater fish whose flesh spoils quickly, developing fishy and putrid odours within hours. Chemical, microbial, and fat-profiling analyses tracked fillets through twelve days of cold storage. Treated and untreated fillets were compared on flavour compounds, spoilage organisms, and key fats.

Extract treatment cut the share of a main spoilage bacterium by more than eleven percentage points. Spoilage markers linked to nitrogen waste and fishy amines stayed far lower in treated fillets at day twelve. Certain delicate fats that oxidize into odour compounds were better preserved under treatment. Pleasant aroma compounds from the perilla leaves themselves lifted sensory acceptance in the tests. The authors describe three cooperating pathways behind the preservative effect.
pmc-13237809:
Bhuiya and colleagues lay out a plan to strengthen prevention of respiratory syncytial virus in young children. The virus is the leading cause of serious chest illness and death in children under five, with the heaviest toll in poorer countries. In 2023, two new shields were approved in rich countries: a vaccine given in pregnancy and a long-acting antibody for babies.

Using Bangladesh as the model case, the authors map how low and middle income countries can actually deliver such tools. Cold chains, cost, clinic reach, and parent trust all decide uptake. A blueprint that faces those barriers gives health ministries a route from approval on paper to protection in villages.
pmc-13237909:
Berg-Warman and colleagues review the first six years of Israel's dental reform for older adults. In 2019, dental care for seniors entered universal health coverage, aiming to open access, cut money barriers, and narrow gaps in who gets treated. Such reforms are often announced loudly and then tracked poorly, leaving their real reach unknown.

The study examines how dental care among elderly Israelis changed across those six years. It asks who gained visits and treatment, and whether old inequalities shrank or merely shifted. The findings give policymakers a rare long look at a national dental reform, useful far beyond Israel as populations age everywhere.
pmc-13238709:
Chen and colleagues model a slow-motion mismatch between an oil crop and the wild bees it depends on. Camellia oleifera, a woody oil plant native to China, cannot pollinate itself and relies wholly on insects to set seed. It flowers from late October into December, when cold already keeps most bees home, leaving two specialist bees to do nearly all the work.

Those bees, Colletes gigas and Andrena camellia, are its most efficient pollinators. The team's ensemble models project how crop and bees shift range as the climate warms. If the plant moves one way and its bees another, harvests fail without any field being ploughed. Naming that risk early gives growers and conservationists time to respond.
pmc-13238909:
Virginia Filippini and colleagues reported in 2026 a 14-year-old girl whose ureteral stump syndrome surfaced eight years after her left kidney and part of its ureter were removed. She arrived with left flank pain, and ultrasound first found nothing, then spotted a tubular structure wrongly blamed on the colon. The remaining ureter stump, left behind at her 2017 operation in her home country, had swollen into a megaureter.

MRI showed the dilated stump filled with dense fluid, plus a multi-chambered abscess where the kidney had been. Doctors placed an anterograde drain to empty the abscess, judging it more effective than a stent, and antibiotics then brought prompt improvement. The authors warn that stump complications, though rare, present confusing pictures across specialties. Partial records from the original surgery made the puzzle harder.
pmc-13239709:
Jiang and colleagues find a way to make breast tumours more visible to the immune system. Triple-negative breast cancer cells wear a surface signal, CD47, that tells macrophages 'do not eat me'. Drugs blocking that signal can restore the attack, but tumours often evade them. So the team hunted for what controls the signal itself.

The effect held across cell lines and mouse models. Pairing the two blockers could give immunotherapy a firmer grip on a stubborn cancer.
pmc-13240009:
Muhammad Ibrahim Shah and co-authors report heart failure appearing at the end of pregnancy in a 2026 case paper. A 27-year-old woman at just over thirty-seven weeks showed a sharply weakened heart, with both ventricles dilated and pumping poorly and several valves leaking.

Her condition fitted peripartum cardiomyopathy, a rare failure of the heart muscle arising late in pregnancy or soon after delivery without another clear cause. Treatment adapted standard heart failure medicines to her situation. The detail the authors underline is family history, since her older sister had died of the same condition. They present the case as a warning that inherited risk deserves attention in pregnancy care.
pmc-13240409:
Lisa-Marie Mai and colleagues move teeth safely in a mouth with advanced gum disease in a 2026 orthodontic case report. A 60-year-old woman had stage four periodontitis, protruding upper front teeth with a large overjet, crowding, and deep vertical bone loss, a combination often judged too risky for braces.

Treatment used a small segmented upper appliance anchored to the skeleton rather than to weakened teeth, keeping forces light and precisely directed. Over nine months the front teeth were drawn upward and backward, a side gap closed, and the overjet shrank. Function and appearance improved without further loss of gum support. Planning around lip and incisor position guided the movements.
pmc-13240809:
Swasti Shetty and co-authors present a 2026 cross-sectional study of mouth-breathing children aged six to twelve. The group examined tooth and jaw problems, dental injuries, and attention symptoms in the same children. A pediatrician confirmed attention diagnoses suggested by standard criteria.

Among the children studied, nearly half showed hyperactivity symptoms and about a third showed inattention. Most had one common bite pattern, and large shares had protruding front teeth and lips that did not close fully. Front tooth injuries appeared in a notable share of the group. Inattention was significantly linked with dental trauma. The authors argue that breathing, dental development, and attention should be assessed together in this age group.
pmc-13241409:
Liakouli and the Italian GIRRCS network measured metabolic syndrome inside a large systemic sclerosis cohort. Six hundred thirteen patients from eleven top centers enrolled at one point in time. Under nine percent met the syndrome bar, a modest share. Those patients skewed older, with far more active disease and mild lung restriction. Heart involvement, lung pressure, and advanced nailfold capillary damage all ran higher. Active disease and lung stiffness stayed linked after adjustment. Hypertension was the commonest single part.
pmc-13241509:
Bråhn and co-authors at Linköping University compare experiences of public violence among Swedish youths with and without a refugee background. Young people helped shape the questionnaire used in the study. Responses came from seventy-nine youths with refugee backgrounds and one hundred five Swedish-born peers. Data collection ran from 2019 through 2022 across Sweden.

About one third of all respondents reported facing violence in public places in Sweden. Direct exposure did not differ significantly between the two groups. Refugee-background youths, though, felt less safe and restricted their daily lives more. Participants suggested more education, more surveillance, and a stronger adult presence in public spaces.
pmc-13242109:
Fadaei and colleagues in Tabriz handed stroke nurses a phone app and timed the race to thrombolysis. Sixty emergency nurses implemented the Code Sama mobile decision-support tool. Sixty stroke patients treated with the app were compared against sixty routine-care patients. Trained observers clocked every milestone around the clock.

Door-to-needle time fell from about forty-eight minutes to forty-three after the app arrived. The effect size was very large by conventional standards. Baseline times had matched almost exactly between the two groups. Fadaei calls for a randomized trial to confirm the workflow gain.
pmc-13242409:
Bohye Kim and Ju Young Yoon studied how health literacy shapes quality of life for adults with physical disabilities in South Korea. Their paper appeared in Quality of Life Research in 2026. They analyzed survey data from 441 adults in the 2021 Korea Health Panel. Using a model that links personal, social, and health-system factors, they traced direct and indirect paths between literacy and well-being.

About forty-four percent of participants had inadequate health literacy, and another share had problematic skills. Needing more care was tied to both lower literacy and lower quality of life, while having a job and stronger literacy were tied to better quality of life. Unmet health needs also pulled scores down. Literacy partly carried the effect of care needs onward. The authors argue that services and jobs matter as much as teaching individuals.
pmc-13242509:
Gerard Breaden Madden and colleagues surveyed orchestral musicians about breathing problems and the cleanliness of their instruments. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports in 2026. Wind instruments can harbor microbes that players inhale again and again, and case reports link dirty instruments to lung trouble. The questionnaire went to players in German orchestras and other professional institutions, covering 245 wind players and 43 string players as a comparison group.

Asthma and diagnosed respiratory disease were reported far more often by the wind players than by the string players. Symptom patterns otherwise overlapped, and playing time and smoking did not explain the gap. The authors name microbial contamination of instruments as one plausible cause worth direct testing. They also found hygiene habits and hygiene teaching inconsistent across the profession. Standard cleaning routines, they argue, should become part of musical training for woodwind and brass players alike.
pmc-13242809:
Zeynep Gürbüz and co-authors present a 2026 observational study of two abdominal wall nerve blocks and lung function after gallbladder keyhole surgery. Pain after abdominal surgery makes patients breathe shallowly, which weakens lung measures. Both blocks numb nerves across the belly wall, but their lung effects were compared directly.

About a hundred patients were grouped by the pain technique they received, with a no-block comparison group. Lung volumes fell after surgery in everyone, yet the fall was steepest without a block. One block preserved a key predicted breathing measure better than the other at the first hour. Pain scores and opioid use were lower, and recovery quality higher, in both block groups. The authors endorse either block.
pmc-13242909:
Rivera, Munoz, and Dunaway tell of TB spread wide with no lung ill in sight. Skin TB, called scrofuloderma, creeps from deep parts to the skin. It is a rare face of TB past the lungs in hosts. Brain sac TB at the same time is more rare and more dire. A man of 69 came in with sore, hard skin spots up top. Spots sat at the neck bone and front chest in his case.

Those spots broke to sores that wept thin pus in time. Low heat spells came next, then a slow brain slide. Mind haze, head pain, sleep pull, and wobble marked the slide. Ward checks found low salt, a known brain TB mate mark. Spine fluid showed cell floods, low sugar, and high part counts. Brain scans showed a wrap flare and a fresh dead zone.
pmc-13244509:
Yong Zhang and co-authors traced how a sulfur-handling enzyme defends the heart against iron overload. Their study appeared in Redox Report in 2026. Iron overload cardiomyopathy kills patients whose bodies accumulate iron, largely through oxidative damage. The enzyme CSE runs a pathway that produces cysteine and hydrogen sulfide, the raw materials of the cell's antioxidant shield. The team deleted or boosted it in mice and in heart cells bathed in iron.

Mice lacking the enzyme suffered worse heart enlargement, weaker pumping, and more scarring under iron overload. Their cells imported less cysteine, made less glutathione, and silenced a chain of protective genes. The authors nominate it as a drug target for iron-loaded hearts.
pmc-13245409:
Macesic, Harris, and Mo review carbapenemases, the enzymes that defeat medicine's last-line antibiotics, in this 2026 JAC-Antimicrobial Resistance article. Bacteria carrying these enzymes now span the major Gram-negative groups, their genes hitchhiking worldwide on plasmids inside high-risk clones. Naming the exact mechanism early guides both infection control and drug choice. Treatment is organized by mechanism, with newer combination drugs central for some enzyme types. Harder workarounds are needed for the metallo-enzymes, whose rise the authors flag as the landscape's most worrying shift.
pmc-13246709:

A neural network fed a trimmed feature set won on the test set with strong accuracy. Hormone therapy, one liver enzyme, and lymphocyte count led the predictor list. Patients the model flagged as high risk died at far higher rates.
pmc-13247309:
Ruiou Chen and co-authors rank acupoint therapies for multiple sclerosis in a 2026 network meta-analysis. The disease inflames the central nervous system and leaves fatigue and disability in its wake. Needling, pressure, and heat at body points are all used as add-on care, with no clear winner before now.

The team pooled 23 randomized trials with 1,384 patients and eight stimulation methods. Electric needling plus point injection led on nerve function scores. Simple finger pressure led on fatigue relief. The same electric pairing also led on daily living scores. Rankings rest on indirect links between trials, so the authors frame them as guides for head-to-head tests.
pmc-13247809:
Amir Tahoun and co-authors report a heart case where a misrouted artery was squeezed from outside in a 2026 case report. The patient, aged 56, also had a vessel disorder that causes abnormal vessel tangles and bleeding. He was waiting for a heart transplant after earlier heart attacks and severe pump failure.

He arrived with chest pain, breathlessness, and heart failure signs and was found to have a heart attack pattern. A stent placed in the odd-route artery clotted early. Light-based imaging inside the vessel showed the artery was compressed by nearby structures, which explained the clot. The team presents it as the first such case documented with this imaging.
pmc-13247909:
Yanjanani Banda leads a large team that maps malaria risk in Malawi. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with Nsanje District in the south. Malaria stays a top health threat in that region.

Heat, rain, height, slope, and river range set hazard levels. Health post range, road range, and crowd density set weak points. Land use maps came from satellite views with a classifier tool. Weights from a rank method joined all layers into risk maps. A check showed which traits drove the map most. Risk maps can guide scarce control work.
pmc-13248009:
Anders Handrup Kverneland worked with seven others in two thousand twenty-six to test ways to read the proteins in blood plasma. Plasma holds hope for clues to disease. But a few proteins are so rich in it that they drown out the rest. That makes the set hard to read by mass spectrometry.

Labs cope in two ways. Some pull the rich proteins out, in Top14 depletion or with acid precipitation. Some pull rare bits in, with beads or by ultracentrifugation. The team tried top ways of each type on three blood sample types. The two ways read distinct sets. The pull-in ways read more, and more truly, but may be less steady in big groups. Ten routine lab tests were checked. Some, like C-reactive protein, matched well. Others, like albumin and transferrin, matched poorly. The way must fit the aim.
pmc-13248109:
Rodgers and Pace report a single unusual case in Case Reports in Urology in 2026. Their patient was a healthy fifty-year-old man who tore the lining of his penis during sex, an injury doctors treat as an emergency. Standard care calls for surgery at once, but the man also tested positive for COVID-19.

Because operating carried extra risk, the team waited ten days until he tested negative, then repaired the tear. At checks four and twenty months later he had no scarring or bending, and his erections were normal and painless. The authors argue that a short delay to make a patient safer can still end well.
pmc-13249709:
Feiteiro and colleagues review how a brain injury can end up harming the heart, in a 2026 Metabolic Brain Disease article. Against that chain, the authors weigh physical exercise as therapy. Exercise can calm inflammation, restore autonomic balance, and support brain rewiring, all at once. What nobody yet knows is the right dose: when to start, how hard, and how long. The authors call for standard protocols tested in trials.
pmc-13250109:
Sender and co-authors test whether lung artery CT scans can use far less radiation without losing image quality. Their 2026 Scientific Reports paper compares a new low-dose protocol, rebuilt with deep learning software, against standard-dose scans using an older reconstruction method. A phantom study, using model bodies of two sizes, came first.

In the phantom, deep learning reconstruction allowed dose cuts of up to about seventy percent at equal image clarity. The team then reviewed scans from just over three hundred patients treated before and after the switch. Patient dose fell by roughly two fifths, while image quality in the main lung artery improved. The authors conclude the low-dose approach is not worse than standard care.
pmc-13250809:
Kyle A. Watson and colleagues report 2026 experiments on how guaiacol behaves inside a zeolite catalyst called ZSM-5. Guaiacol is a molecule released when plant biomass is heated, and zeolites are used to upgrade such oils into fuels. Until now, direct evidence of how the molecule sits inside the catalyst's pores was missing.

Using magnetic resonance spectroscopy, the team separated guaiacol trapped inside the pores from guaiacol sitting outside them. The two groups differed in their chemical signals, relaxation behavior, and the temperatures at which they escaped on heating. By enriching the zeolite framework with a rare oxygen isotope, the researchers could also map close contacts between the molecule and the pore walls. The results show where guaiacol lodges and how it reacts, which should guide the design of better biomass catalysts.
pmc-13251009:
Radwan and co-authors test two cell-death genes as early warning markers in acute myeloid leukemia. Their 2026 BMC Cancer study compares samples from one hundred newly diagnosed patients with forty healthy volunteers. Five-year survival in this leukemia stays poor, and relapse often grows from cells that dodge normal death programs.

One gene, NFS1, ran high in patients, while GSDMD ran low, and both patterns reversed after treatment. Worse starting patterns, high NFS1 with low GSDMD, marked patients with poorer outlooks and lower one-year survival. The genes tie to two newer death routes, ferroptosis and pyroptosis, that cancer cells often suppress. The authors propose the pair as diagnostic and prognostic markers and as possible treatment targets.
pmc-13251709:
Pooveshni Govender and colleagues scope the use of platform trials in anesthesia and perioperative medicine in a 2026 review. All nine ran at multiple centers, mostly in wealthy countries, and nearly half were still in the planning stage when reviewed. Together they tested twenty-four interventions, with surgical site infection prevention the commonest focus. Every trial used adaptive features that let the design shift mid-course, and Bayesian statistics predominated. The authors call platform trials an early, uneven practice here. They ask for shared standards on naming, governance, and methods so the design can deliver its promised efficiency.
pmc-13253609:
Amirhossein Zarei, Marsa Gholamzadeh, and Fatemeh Asadi review digital twins in chronic disease care in this 2026 paper. A digital twin is a live virtual copy of a patient that can simulate how an illness will unfold, promising earlier and more personal treatment.

Training and education led the uses, ahead of personalised care and drug development. Clinicians were the top audience, then patients. Data analytics and machine learning powered most twins, with body modelling and sensors behind. The authors see the field moving from theory into clinics.
pmc-13253909:

Step-by-step filtering cut 2,052 proteins down to 11 strong candidates backed by several lines of computer evidence. Six had traits suited to deeper structural study. The candidates included enzymes and proteins tied to stress survival and host contact. The authors offer the workflow for other bacteria, not firm claims about protein jobs.
pmc-13254309:

Flood water left standing after floods gives mosquitoes ideal breeding grounds.

About 12 million people diagnosed with Plasmodium falciparum malaria were exposed to flooding, one-third of all flood-affected people. Flood exposure stood out as a main driver of malaria burden in these zones, guiding hotspot targeting.
pmc-13254509:

pmc-13255209:

pmc-13255309:
Kiana Kiani and co-authors interview key actors about patient involvement in health research in a 2026 study. Five themes covered culture and power shifts, clear structures, role expectations, trust and communication, and shared understanding. Different actors read the same barriers and aids in clashing ways, creating tensions that must be negotiated. The authors suggest grounding involvement in a person-centered ethic of partnership and shared responsibility.
pmc-13255409:

pmc-13257809:

pmc-13258009:

pmc-13258109:

pmc-13258409:

pmc-13258709:

The design held up well under timing noise and small placement errors. Comparisons with an information based design favored the new layout. Monitoring teams get a practical recipe for cheaper, more reliable damage tracking.
pmc-13259109:

Including separation moved the peak to a shallower curve, then force fell steadily with more curve. Layer separation governed total damage in the fuller model. Least separated area appeared at a mid high curvature. Aircraft panel designers learn that model choice changes the best curvature.
pmc-13259909:

pmc-13260109:

pmc-13260609:

pmc-13261009:

pmc-13261309:

pmc-13261409:

pmc-13262609:

pmc-13262709:

pmc-13264309:

pmc-13278909:
Zihao Wang and colleagues test a side-lying scan position for finding clots in the heart's left atrial appendage, in a 2026 study. Standard two-phase CT lying on the back doubles radiation exposure before ablation procedures. Ultrasound through the food pipe served as the reference check.

One hundred fourteen patients with atrial fibrillation were split evenly between the two scan protocols. Lying on the left side filled the appendage tip far better with contrast and cut early filling defects sharply. The single-phase side-lying scan matched the two-phase method's accuracy while nearly halving radiation dose. Clots were confirmed in about one in nine patients. The authors call for larger prospective validation before routine adoption.
pmc-13279009:
Xiaojing Zhu and colleagues published a 2026 study of engineered nanovesicles built to treat glioblastoma, the most aggressive adult brain tumor. Their platform fuses a rabies-virus targeting piece onto tiny bubbles shed by bacteria, then loads the chemotherapy drug paclitaxel inside. The design aims to cross the blood-brain barrier, a protective filter that keeps most drugs out of the brain.

Dendritic cell activation roughly doubled in laboratory tests, and tumors recruited about twice as many killer T cells as untreated controls. Mice gained durable tumor control and lived longer. pmc-13279209:
Christian Saal and colleagues published a 2026 study measuring how defensive formations change the physical workload in elite handball. Using a fixed positioning system during the 2023/24 German Handball-Bundesliga season, they analyzed 11,863 positional defense phases involving 316 players from 18 clubs. An algorithm sorted each phase into one of four formations, from the deep 6:0 to the aggressive 3:3. The team then counted accelerations, decelerations, and distance covered per phase for attackers and defenders alike.

More aggressive shapes raised distance covered and the number of sharp speed changes for both teams. Defenders in the advanced shapes showed most strong rises in deceleration events, though the most aggressive 3:3 shape appeared too rarely to judge confidently. Average distance climbed steeply as defenses pushed higher up the court compared with the 6:0 baseline. Coaches can use these numbers to set drill intensity so training loads mirror the shape a team actually plans to play.
pmc-13279309:
Chang Liu and colleagues published a 2026 study building a value assessment framework to help Chinese hospitals decide whether to adopt renal denervation. The catheter procedure calms overactive nerves near the kidneys to lower stubborn blood pressure. Four such products have been approved in China, and hospitals lacked a structured way to compare them. The team used multi-criteria decision analysis: a literature review, expert focus groups, a Delphi round, and a weighting exercise with clinicians and hospital staff.

The finished framework has seven top-level domains with 16 criteria and 30 sub-criteria. Efficacy carried the largest weight at about 23 percent, followed by safety at about 22 percent, while cost accounted for only about 6 percent of the total score. Suitability of the hospital and patient value also ranked high. The authors present the tool as a basis for procurement reviews, so adoption decisions weigh clinical benefit and hospital fit rather than price alone.
pmc-13279409:
Wencheng Hong and colleagues published a 2026 paper presenting Tea-DETR, a detection model that grades tea leaves in open fields. Sorting leaves by grade is hard outdoors because backgrounds are cluttered, light shifts, and leaves overlap. The model thus focuses on the leaf regions that separate one grade from another.

They built a dataset of 6,542 images of Anji white tea from Zhejiang Province and split it for training, validation, and testing. The model reached 92.2 percent accuracy and a detection score of 82 percent while trimming its parameter count to 14.65 million, about 27 percent fewer than the baseline design. Training also converged more steadily. The authors offer it as a non-destructive, real-time option for growers who grade harvests by eye.
pmc-13279509:
Chin-Hee Song and colleagues published a 2026 study charting how stomach bacteria change after Helicobacter pylori is eradicated in patients with gastric cancer. The bacterium is a leading cause of stomach cancer, yet cancer arises without it, and little is known about the other microbes. The team sampled tissue from 35 cancer patients treated endoscopically, some followed for more than ten years, and sequenced bacterial genes to profile the mixes by infection status, sex, and cancer subtype.

Samples without the bacterium held more diverse, distinctly structured mixes, with species enriched, including some able to make urease or reduce nitrates. Successful eradication reshaped communities over time, though unevenly, while failed eradication left a stable bacterium-dominated profile. One species, Actinomyces naeslundii, rose only in the successfully treated group. The authors propose that non-pylori mixes may feed cancer growth through their own routes, and that eradication leaves a microbial signature.
pmc-13279609:
Enver M Oruro and colleagues published a 2026 perspective proposing that neuroscience treat the shape of neurons as an emergent level in its own right. Complex systems thinking locates emergence at circuits or behavior. The neuron counts as a simple building block. The authors argue that a neuron's branching form emerges from interactions among growth processes, neighboring cells, and synaptic contacts. That form then shapes what networks can do.

They develop the argument through three arenas: how neuron shape diversity influences circuit function, how mother-infant relationships unfold, and how epilepsy intertwines with psychiatric comorbidity. Examples draw on animal models and human data, organized around structure, function, and behavior. The piece aligns with an international digital campus effort on complex systems the authors cite as a collaborative home. Their aim is to give morphodynamics, the study of changing form, a firmer place in how brain science explains emergent function.
pmc-13280309:
Burcu Soyak and Nejat Ozgul compare a 2026 study of spread and survival in two womb cancers. Uterine carcinosarcoma is a rare, mixed cancer with gland and flesh type cells. Grade three endometrioid cancer is a high grade gland cancer of the womb lining. The team contrast clinic traits, spread patterns and survival, with focus on node spread and full surgical staging worth. Records covered 2000 to 2016 at one large centre.

One hundred five patients fit: forty three with carcinosarcoma and sixty two with the gland cancer. A high quality subgroup of eighty had full pelvic and para aortic node removal. Carcinosarcoma patients were older on average. They showed less deep muscle invasion, about forty four versus sixty eight percent, yet far more positive belly wash tests. Node spread rates were alike in both groups. Five year progress free survival ran much lower for carcinosarcoma, near thirty six versus sixty three percent.
pmc-13281809:
Chuanqi Pan and colleagues made a filter material that traps mercury vapor in a 2026 study. Mercury gas escapes from coal smoke and drifts worldwide, then settles into soil and food. Trapping it in factory gas is hard, since sulfur gases in smoke crowd most traps. The team joined zinc sulfide with a carbon web called graphdiyne. A crafted bond between them shuttles electric charge. That charge wakes up sulfur defect spots that grab mercury.

In tests the material stripped nearly all mercury from the gas stream. It kept working even when sulfur gas ran very high, a common trap killer. Coated onto a glass fiber filter sheet, it still caught most mercury in dusty, sulfur-rich gas. Such sheets fit the bag filters factories already use. The authors say bond crafting at surfaces is a broad recipe for better traps.
pmc-13282309:
Aline Silveira Gonçalves and co-authors report a 2026 mouse study on bacteria-based products as possible treatments for depression and anxiety. Postbiotics are inactivated microbes and their useful parts, avoiding risks of live bacteria. The team used a Lactobacillus strain in three forms: live, inactivated, and inactivated enriched with selenium, a nutrient that supports antioxidant defence. Male mice received one form, a standard antidepressant, or a control for fourteen days.

All three bacteria forms eased depression-like behaviour and lowered a stress hormone.
