It also switched on gut pathways tied to cell growth and antioxidant defence. The authors highlight inactivated products as stable and safe candidates. Human use would need clinical trials, since mouse behaviour tests only hint at benefit.
pmc-13282709:
Enrique Blanco-Carmona and co-authors present a 2026 paper introducing SCpubr, an R software package for making publication-ready charts from single-cell gene data. Single-cell sequencing, which reads gene activity cell by cell, is now a core way to study mixed cell populations. Standard workflows produce many output types, each needing tailored plots. Existing tools chart some of them but leave heavy customisation to users, who spend long hours polishing figures to journal standards.

SCpubr wraps common single-cell visualisations in concise function calls, producing high-quality figures with little code. The package is free on the standard R archive, with source code, tutorials, and a full online book openly available. The manuscript's own analysis code is also published, so every figure can be reproduced. The authors position SCpubr as a time-saver that raises figure quality without demanding deep graphics expertise from bench scientists.
pmc-13283209:
Slow brain waves shared across four disorders anchor Paul Theo Zebhauser's 2026 plea for cross-diagnosis EEG markers. Brain-wave tests are cheap and easy to scale in clinics. Disease-specific signals have shown weak clinical value so far in practice.

Proof from 176 EEG studies covered chronic pain, migraine, fatigue, and depression. Slow brain-wave activity rose most often across all four conditions in the review. Lack of disease specificity does not kill its value, the authors argue. It may flag shared brain faults tied to mood, thought, and body symptoms. Such shared markers could guide prevention, tracking, and brain stimulation across disorders. Care can target shared processes, not labels alone.
pmc-13283409:
Reprogramming tumor macrophages with nanoparticle cargo is the strategy Jin-Ming Zhang and fellow reviewers map for 2026. These macrophages help tumors hide from immune attack and keep growing. Tiny drug carriers may reprogram them and lift that immune shield.

Strategies include flipping macrophage state, blocking their signals, and boosting their eating of cancer cells. Other paths cut macrophage supply, drain their energy, or block checkpoint signals on them. Carrier designs span mineral crystals, soft polymers, and hybrid systems for delivery. Some carriers act like Trojan horses built from body-friendly materials. The review weighs surface targets and signal paths for each approach. Gaps in safety and targeting are also covered.
pmc-13283709:
How strong is a graft built from only half of an ankle tendon? Christopher Kleimeyer and colleagues tested that question in a 2026 lab study for knee ligament repair. Surgeons increasingly use this tendon, yet half-grafts in short four-strand form lacked strength data.

Tendons came from both legs of seven donated bodies for paired testing. Half ankle grafts broke at notably lower loads than full hamstring grafts beside them. The gap was large and statistically firm in this small lab set. Surgeons should be careful when splitting the tendon for two grafts. A full tendon may be the safer choice for this graft style.
pmc-13284009:
Reward can pull attention to a chosen memory item even when color pop-out is removed, show Allison N Marino and colleagues in 2026. Working memory holds a small focus in a highly active state. Earlier proof always used red for the high-reward item, inviting doubt.

Four colors rotated as the high-value tag across participants in random assignment. A probe recognition task measured memory for list positions after cues. The priority benefit appeared for whichever position carried high reward value. Color salience alone did not explain the gain in these tests. Visual pop-out may help, but reward focus is real on its own. Findings refine how motivation steers memory.
pmc-13284109:
Hongyu Zhao and a large team reviewed in 2026 how the microbiota-gut-brain axis may drive depressive disorders. Depression involves far more than low mood, bringing thinking problems, sleep shifts, appetite change, and gut complaints. The review gathers evidence on gut microbe patterns in depression, with stress on the loss of bacteria that make short-chain fatty acids and the rise of pro-inflammatory types.

Signals travel both ways between gut and brain through barrier leaks, low-grade inflammation, the stress hormone axis, the vagus nerve, and chemical messenger routes. Key metabolic paths covered include tryptophan handling, bile acids, and a compound called TMAO. Diet change, tailored probiotics, and stool transfer show some antidepressant promise in selected groups, though effects stay modest and studies vary a lot.
pmc-13284509:
Ning Feng and co-authors report a 2026 blood study in primary angiitis of the central nervous system, a rare illness with severe brain vessel inflammation. Aromatic amino acids in blood have been tied to inflammation, but their pattern in this disease was unclear. Serum from 18 patients, 35 healthy controls, and 17 patients with other nerve diseases was tested by mass spectrometry.

Tyrosine and phenylalanine levels were higher in patients than in both control groups, while tryptophan did not differ in the authors report. Phenylalanine also rose with several inflammation markers. Tests suggested the two amino acids could help tell this disease apart from controls. The authors call the work exploratory and urge larger multi-center checks.
pmc-13284609:
Maciej M. Mrugala and Michelle Monje introduce a 2026 special issue on thinking problems that follow modern cancer treatment. Better therapies have raised survival, yet many survivors face lasting trouble with attention, memory, speed, and planning, often called chemo-brain. The issue gathers four articles from leaders in this field.

Editors note that harm was once tied mainly to brain radiation and classic chemotherapy, but immune therapy now shows like effects as well. Up to a third of survivors may be affected, with real costs for work and daily life. Causes likely mix direct nerve harm with immune shifts, oxidative stress, and mitochondria faults. The editors hope new mechanism work will lead to prevention and care.
pmc-13285709:
Qi Xiao, Chen Wang, and Chuang Yang present a 2026 pharmacovigilance study of drug-linked gum disorders. Working from the United States FAERS database, they scan two decades of adverse event reports for signals tied to gum swelling, bleeding, and overgrowth. Their aim is to flag which drugs deserve closer watch in dental care.

The team gathered 34,354 relevant reports filed from 2004 to 2024, most of them for women. Signal tests, followed by regression models, marked 43 drugs as associated factors, among them cancer drugs, immune suppressants, and blood thinners. The median time from drug use to gum problems was 35 days, though timing differed by drug. The signals offer an early guide for monitoring, and the authors note that further work must confirm them.
pmc-13285909:
Ghazunfer Abbas leads a 2026 study of a family planning push in urban Pakistan, run with government health departments. The Challenge Initiative backed high-impact steps in city districts of Punjab and Sindh from 2022 onward. Using monthly service records, the team weighed client numbers in program districts against matched districts without the program.

Records ran from mid-2020 to mid-2025, drawn from the national supply tracking system for contraceptives. The gap-in-gaps method found about 3,673 extra monthly clients tied to the program across the sites studied. Health department sites alone showed an even larger net gain, and trend checks agreed with the main result. Client counts kept rising where the program ran while they slid in control districts, a case for folding the steps into public budgets.
pmc-13286909:
Viviane Schuch and colleagues expose placental immune cells, called Hofbauer cells, to HIV and cytomegalovirus at different stages of pregnancy. The 2026 study isolates the fetal macrophages from early, middle, and full-term placentas and reads their gene activity after a day with each virus. How these guardians change across gestation was poorly known.

The cytomegalovirus additionally shut down energy, fat, and structural pathways and disturbed a growth signaling route. HIV instead preserved growth and antigen-display programs. Earlier in pregnancy, gene-level changes were subtler, showing mainly at pathway level. The authors link the term pattern to placental vulnerability.
pmc-13287009:
Soumyadeep Mukherjee and colleagues review how pattern-sensing receptors, the immune system's tripwires for microbial and damage signals, shape tolerance training inside the thymus. Their 2026 review explains that young T cells must pass filters in the thymus that delete self-attacking clones while sparing useful ones. What these pattern signals do to those filters was unclear, despite drugs for autoimmunity targeting them.

The review traces how pattern signals act both through antigen-presenting cells and inside developing T cells themselves, tuning the checkpoints that decide survival. Inflammation and self-tolerance, usually treated as opposites, appear deeply intertwined here. Understanding that partnership could let clinicians repurpose existing immune drugs with finer aim, the authors suggest.
pmc-13288209:
Shanghao Yang and co-authors evaluate a seven-day camp program for teenage gaming disorder in a 2026 report. Internet gaming disorder means gaming that a person cannot control despite harm. Controlled trials support talk-based treatments, but short residential formats have little published evidence. The camp gave twelve adolescents a tightly structured week of activities and therapy. Routine service records supplied entry and exit measures.

All twelve teens finished the camp, attendance reached near 99 percent, and no serious adverse events occurred. Scores on two gaming disorder scales fell sharply by exit, with large effect sizes. Craving ratings also dropped, and the share of teens in the high-risk band fell from two thirds to none. Impulsivity and depression scores improved as well, while anxiety scores did not. The authors present the pilot as early feasibility evidence, not proof of lasting change.
pmc-13288509:
Weiwei Liao and co-authors test heart MRI measures of the left atrium in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, in a 2026 study. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy thickens the heart muscle and often stiffens its filling. Ultrasound is the usual tool for judging that stiffness, but MRI lacks the flow measures guidelines rely on. The team asked whether atrial size and stretch from MRI could fill the gap. Two centers contributed 248 patients and 70 healthy controls.

Atrial stretch measures worsened step by step as filling pressure rose, while atrial volumes grew. One stretch measure, reservoir strain, detected raised pressure with high accuracy on its own. Pairing it with a minimum volume index pushed accuracy higher still. Both measures also predicted later heart failure events and new atrial fibrillation in follow-up models. The authors say atrial MRI markers can support risk sorting when ultrasound data are incomplete.
pmc-13288609:
Ngoualem Kegah Franklin and Ndjouenkeu Robert review starch in yoghurt in 2026. Most past work just added starch to milk. Few studies swapped milk fat for starch. Low-fat yoghurt leads shop sales worldwide. Claims for its health edge lack firm proof.

Added starch raised carbohydrate in yoghurt. It lowered moisture at the same time. Mineral, fat, and protein effects went all ways. Thickness rose and whey loss fell. Acidity also rose with starch. Taste and texture peaked near a two percent dose. That held for all starch sources. In storage, acidity kept climbing. Taste held steady and flow traits stayed the same.
pmc-13288909:
Chengwei Shao and colleagues scan virus changes for antibody escape. Their 2026 study maps the JN.1 Omicron line and its child XEC. They test each single change in the spike tip. Safe lab virus copies stand in for the real virus. Two strong antibodies anchor the escape tests.

pmc-13289009:
Eva Hernandez-Garcia and colleagues plan a 2026 trial series on clean bedroom air. The BREATHS trials deal with cancer survivors. These adults face high heart risk from past treatment. Dirty air can raise body-wide swelling. Night filters can cut fine dust in air.

Each person will serve as their own control. Trials will run in Valencia, Spain, in winter. Each cycle pairs real and sham filter use. Each phase lasts 14 nights in bed. Blood swelling marks lead the outcomes. Blood sugar and blood pressure will also be tracked. Air monitors will log dust in and out. Non-responders will move to open filter use.
pmc-13289309:

Findings needing more workup appeared in 34 athletes, and Holter caught more fleeting rhythm events than the resting tests alone.
pmc-13289409:
Isabelle Pearson and a large team offer a 2026 scoping review on protecting migrant workers from climate-driven job health risks. Two databases were searched for peer work from January 2000 to March 2025 in any language. Studies had to address climate, work health, and migrant workers together, not just general climate health. Two reviewers screened records on their own, with a third path for disputes. The map shows where programs exist and where blind spots remain for worker safety planning.
pmc-13290109:
What living with acne feels like, drawn from posts by users in the United States and United Kingdom, is examined by John Barbieri and colleagues in 2026. Acne mostly strikes teenagers and young adults but often persists, affecting self-esteem, body image, and mental health.

The team collected public posts from 2024 and processed them with natural language processing, machine learning, and topic modeling. From 646,809 messages by 432,234 users, the biggest topics were skincare routines and product advice, acne scars, and general treatment information. Just over half of users described at least one quality-of-life impact, most often symptoms, social functioning, mental health, and cost. Annotated messages pointed to unmet needs, above all working answers for hormonal acne and clearer guidance on triggers.
pmc-13290609:
Adults with hearing loss who lack vitamin D face notably higher depression risk over the long term, Wan-Jung Cheng and colleagues report in 2026. Hearing impairment already raises depression risk, and the team asked whether vitamin D status, a fixable factor, adds to it.

Using the TriNetX network, they followed adults whose vitamin D was measured between 2010 and 2023 and matched 48,184 deficient patients with 48,184 sufficient ones. Deficiency came with a hazard ratio of 1.57 for new depression over 12 years, with similar elevations for depressive episodes, recurrence, self-harm, and death. Milder insufficiency also raised risk somewhat, tracing a gradient, while a control outcome showed nothing. Cheng and colleagues stress that observation alone cannot prove that correcting the deficiency would prevent depression.
pmc-13291009:
Public fitness facilities in China, and why some regions supply far more than others, are studied in a 2026 policy analysis by Ziwen Zhang, Shun Wang, and Xunling Wang. Instead of judging single policies alone, the team asked which mixes of policy tools tend to go with a high level of provision.

No single tool proved necessary on its own for high supply. Comparative case analysis then found three working paths, grouped into a model pairing guidance with smart building, and a model centered on public services with many parts acting together.
pmc-13291209:
Joyce Rops and colleagues expose a dilution trap in counting tiny cell vesicles by flow cytometry, in 2026. Extracellular vesicles float in blood plasma among far more numerous lipoprotein particles. Samples must be diluted so the detector sees one particle at a time. Dilute too far, though, and labeled vesicles sink below the fluorescent background noise. The team varied dilution and spiked lipoproteins to map the conflict.

For some samples the two demands clash, which the authors name the dilution paradox. No dilution then yields sound scatter and fluorescence counts at once. In two past clinical studies, they judged thirty and sixty-five percent of measurements unreliable, depending on the label used. Fixes include triggering on fluorescence at a fixed dilution and stripping non-vesicle bits first. Cleaning fluorescent grit from staining reagents also helps. The authors urge that past vesicle counts made without these safeguards be rechecked.
pmc-13291609:
Yao Li and colleagues attach a polymer brush to a gene-silencing drug for myotonic dystrophy in a 2026 study. pmc-13292009:
Yusuf A Rajabally and colleagues check whether nerve tests normalize when a chronic nerve disease remits, in 2026. The disease, CIDP, inflames peripheral nerves and can quiet down off treatment. The average gap between test pairs ran near sixty-three months.

All patients met demyelination criteria at first, yet only fourteen of twenty-four still did later. The authors say serial testing may earn a place in monitoring and prognosis.
pmc-13292109:
Abdallah Al Ghnaimat and a large team weigh a 2026 question in a systematic review and meta-analysis: can diabetes drugs called SGLT-2 inhibitors drain ascites in liver cirrhosis? pmc-13292309:
Huanhua Wu and co-authors pair a 2026 genetics method with clinic data to probe whether frailty helps cause diabetic kidney complications. A separate dialysis cohort of 100 patients let the team compare frailty in kidney failure with and without diabetes.

In the clinic cohort, diabetic patients scored more frail than others, medians 2.0 against 1.0 on their scale. Machine learning flagged dialysis time, grip strength, and activity as top classifiers. pmc-13292509:

Planned data include resident surveys, focus groups, stakeholder interviews, air quality readings, site visits, and observations of walking, cycling, and green space use. Municipal records will add population and health indicators. A difference-in-differences analysis should separate plan effects from background change. The authors aim to guide municipalities on whether these bundled plans deserve institutional backing.
pmc-13293809:
Reduced watering plans go on trial in a 2026 field study by Luciana Gentili and colleagues, set in a young super high-density olive orchard in western Argentina. Dense hedgerow orchards yield early and suit machines, yet thirst heavily and suffer under long water stress in dry regions.

Steady watering at 70% of full need saved 30% of water, a saving the authors report, kept tree water status balanced, and lifted fruit and oil yield by the third season. Timed harsher cuts saved more water but knocked yield down in the second season.
pmc-13294109:
Celia Brown and coauthors track ethnic patterns in UK medical specialty destinations in a 2026 repeated cross-sectional analysis. Groups compared were White, Asian, and other ethnicities among UK-qualified doctors.

Samples held 64,995 doctors at entry and 62,380 at completion. Gaps appeared in nearly every year and grew over time at both stages. Asian doctors were over-represented in ophthalmology at both levels, while White doctors were over-represented in acute care and emergency medicine at set points. Systemic influences on choice and selection need study.
pmc-13294409:
Sandra Fuest and colleagues test a glass solder coating for zirconia dental ceramics in a 2026 lab study. Alumina toughened zirconia samples were grit-blasted and spray-coated, then exposed to mouse fibroblasts and human dental pulp cells in direct and indirect contact. Live-dead staining, growth checks, bone-forming differentiation, and whole blood tests covered safety angles.

No toxic effects appeared for coated or plain samples in any assay. Bone-forming steps proceeded normally, and blood tests showed no red cell bursting or shifts in standard counts. Cells spread and grew well on the coating. The layer looks suitable for improving implant surfaces, pending animal work.
pmc-13294909:
Muhammad Noman and co-authors model a thin mineral layer that could lift perovskite solar cells, in a 2026 simulation study. The added layer lined up the energy steps at the back face, made the inner electric field stronger, and helped charges part. Output rose for all three absorbers in the models, with the all-inorganic cesium cell gaining most in relative terms. The changed cells also stood wider swings in thickness, doping, heat, and flaws before output sagged. The authors propose the layer as a broad fix.
pmc-13295309:
Diyi Feng and Liqin Ge review heat-based cancer platforms built from metal-organic frameworks in a 2026 article. Simple frameworks offer stable, tunable shells, while metal-rich versions add chemical attack, magnetic response, and energy handling. Pairing heat with chemotherapy, immune therapy, or imaging guidance helps against regrowth and heat tolerance in tumours. The authors stress that standard making rules, breakdown behaviour, metal safety, and heat dosing must be settled before clinic use.
pmc-13295509:
Michael Kainz and colleagues combine printed frames with self-building peptide gels for cartilage repair in a 2026 study. Two printed materials were used, one stiff light-cured network and one flexible silicone, both with linked pores near a millimetre wide. Gels named RADA16 and IEIK13 assembled inside the pores into fibre nets resembling natural tissue surroundings. Both gels improved cell settling and growth, with RADA16 best at supporting cartilage-like matrix formation in the hybrid builds.
pmc-13295909:

pmc-13296109:

pmc-13296209:

pmc-13297609:

pmc-13298109:

pmc-13299409:

pmc-13299509:

pmc-13300109:

pmc-13300309:

pmc-13300609:

pmc-13301709:

pmc-13302909:

pmc-13303909:

pmc-13305509:

pmc-13306009:

pmc-13306509:

pmc-13306809:

pmc-13307309:

pmc-13308309:

pmc-13310409:

pmc-13310909:

pmc-13311109:

pmc-13311309:

pmc-13311709:

pmc-13311809:

pmc-13312109:

pmc-13312809:

pmc-13316109:

pmc-13319009:

pmc-13320709:

pmc-13320809:

pmc-13320909:

pmc-13321009:

pmc-13321309:

pmc-13321509:

An American trial had found that offering induction to first-time, low-risk mothers cut cesarean births. Whether that travels to French maternity care is unknown. Half will wait for labor to start on its own.

The main measure is cesarean birth after enrollment, for any reason. The trial is sized to catch a drop from fifteen percent to twelve. Mother and baby health, plus care costs, are tracked on the same definitions the American trial used. The authors stress this is a design paper: no results yet, only a test being built.
pmc-13321809:
Jin Lin and a large team design a light driven catalyst for hydrogenation in a 2026 chemistry study. Frustrated Lewis pairs can turn inert supports into active sites, but their random placement and weak hydrogen activation limit use. The team anchored single rhodium atoms on cerium oxide to create ordered interface sites.

The catalyst hydrogenated styrene at 35 percent per hour, far above plain cerium oxide at 2.74 percent per hour in the report. Interface sites split hydrogen into reactive parts, and light pushed those parts toward pair sites while also creating fleeting new pair sites on the surface. Similar boosts appeared on other semiconductor supports, which suggests a general design route.
pmc-13322909:
Lijiao Wang and Tingshu Jiang present an advanced case of follicular dendritic cell sarcoma in a 2026 report. Their patient was a 51-year-old woman with six months of cough, sputum and chest tightness, worse breathlessness over the last month, and sharp weight loss.

Scans found a mass in the mediastinum, between the lungs, with spread to multiple sites and enlarged lymph nodes. Such tumours arise from follicular dendritic cells and are rare, hard to diagnose and often aggressive in course. Care combined immune therapy and targeted therapy in an integrated plan. The authors draw lessons from the diagnostic difficulty and the mixed treatment approach for clinicians who may meet this uncommon cancer.
pmc-13323509:
Yirui Dai and colleagues report a spinal cord disorder mistaken for mental illness, in a 2026 case report on subacute combined degeneration. A 39-year-old man had nine months of tingling, dizziness and emotional distress, with normal brain scans and electrical tests at first checks.

Doctors diagnosed somatic symptom disorder and anxiety, and several psychiatric drugs failed as leg weakness and unsteady walking grew. Specialist review found absent knee reflexes and lost vibration sense, and blood tests showed critically low vitamin B12, with spinal imaging changes running from neck to mid-back. B12 replacement plus escitalopram for leftover distress brought strong recovery, and at five months he walked fully with near-normal test scores.
pmc-13323809:
Argen Mamazhakypov and team review the case for osteopontin as a driver and marker of atrial fibrillation. Their 2026 paper starts from a familiar gap: atrial fibrillation is the most common sustained heart rhythm disorder, yet treatments stay limited because its mechanisms are not yet fully known. Atrial inflammation and fibrosis, triggered by pressure or volume overload, heart attack, and metabolic change, remodel the atria and sustain the arrhythmia.

Osteopontin, a protein with many roles in the tissue around cells, has emerged in recent studies as a mediator of that remodeling and of arrhythmia itself. Human studies link its circulating levels to the rhythm disorder and its progression, making it a candidate biomarker, while laboratory work points to roles in that damage and ion channel change. The review argues that mapping it fully could open causative targets, moving therapy beyond symptom control toward the disease process itself.
pmc-13324309:
Dong Ruan and co-authors build a smart alloy scaffold that treats infected bone defects in timed stages, in a 2026 biomaterials study. Lasting bacterial infection over-fires the immune system and blocks bone growth, so single-target grafts often heal such defects poorly.

Their scaffold answers acidity changes in sequence. During the infection phase it releases copper ions for strong antibacterial action plus plant-derived vesicles that calm the early cytokine storm. Later it switches to steady magnesium release with low vesicle output, drawing stem cells in, speeding bone differentiation, improving the immune setting and growing blood vessels. Pathway checks point to blocking of the AGEs/RAGE/NF-kB route as part of the joint effect.
pmc-13324509:
Yoonsuk Huh and co-authors test whether scout images alone can predict a patient body outline for radiotherapy setup in a 2026 study. Surface-guided breath-hold treatment needs a free-breathing outline for baseline matching, which today means an extra CT scan.

The team trained a deep learning model on 173 chest CT simulation cases with front and side scout views. Test results on 26 held-out cases matched the true outlines closely, with a Dice score of 0.979 on average. Surface error averaged about 1.05 mm across the test group. Larger, more even torso shapes predicted best. Skipping the extra scan could cut dose and time, though live clinic checks must come first.
pmc-13325109:
Rizwan Rafique and co-authors study light resonances in bare silicon nanowires in a 2026 physics paper. Earlier work covered wires wrapped in an oxide shell, which itself bends the local light field.

Conical and cylindrical wires of varied length, stripped of any shell, were probed with electron energy-loss spectroscopy inside a scanning transmission microscope. Wires sat in vacuum or on carbon film. Every group showed periodic signals, and the resonance energy tracked wire length far more than surroundings. A strong sideways resonance appeared in all cases. The results suggest wire shape alone can tune these resonances, which eases design of silicon light devices.
pmc-13325309:
Qianqiao Liu and team worked out how the Borrelia burgdorferi protein BmpA selectively binds thymidine. Their 2026 study addresses a nutrient problem for the Lyme disease agent, a germ with limited fuel use that relies on salvage pathways rather than building blocks from scratch. The team solved the crystal structure of BmpA at 2.6 angstrom detail, showing a conserved binding-protein fold with a deeply buried pocket for its target.

Binding assays showed high-affinity binding to it, followed by cytidine and adenosine, with no binding found to ribose, guanosine, inosine, or uridine. Mutating either of two matching aromatic residues, Phe27 or Phe176, abolished all binding, proving both essential for recognizing it. A structural homology search found related proteins across bacteria and archaea sharing the fold despite low sequence similarity. The work shows how shared scaffolds enable selective nutrient uptake in reduced genomes.
pmc-13325909:
Kurt S. Schultz and team tested whether hydration changes iliac vein narrowing seen on MRI in fasted, symptom-free adults. Their 2026 prospective, within-subject, analyst-blinded study ran at a single tertiary academic hospital from August 2022 to April 2024. People fasted after midnight, then underwent MRI immediately before and after intravenous normal saline at 1.0, 1.5, or 2.0 liters, with two independent reviewers measuring the widest and narrowest vein areas.

Iliac vein stenosis appears in up to 30% of asymptomatic people, suggesting it may often be a normal variant rather than disease. The authors argue that pre-imaging hydration protocols could reduce misclassification of physiological narrowing as pathological stenosis, curbing overdiagnosis of nonthrombotic iliac vein lesions. The take-home message is practical: hydrating fasted patients before imaging may spare them a disease label, and possibly intervention, for a narrowing that fluids alone can ease.
pmc-13326509:
Kaijie Zheng and team removed two polyphenol enzymes from Nicotiana benthamiana to improve recombinant protein making. Their 2026 study tackles a real bottleneck. Leaf injection of this plant is widely used for molecular pharming, but enzyme browning and native protein clumping during extraction can damage protein health and cleaning rate. The team made genome-edited lines lacking two oxidase genes and tested them under gentle extraction.

Oxidase-deficient plants browned less and crosslinked less, preserved own proteins at their predicted weights, and showed increased enzyme activity. They also achieved much higher recovery and improved purity of a briefly expressed lab-made protein. The authors identify oxidase-driven oxidation as a major block in that step, and present oxidase depletion as a simple route to cleaner, higher-yield plant-made proteins.
pmc-13327009:
Qianxi Wang and team compared two surgery routes for breaks of the shoulder blade neck and body outside the joint. Their 2026 look-back study covered 40 people admitted from July 2021 to September 2023. Of these, 18 had the reverse Judet route and 22 had the changed Judet route. The reverse route was built to cut tissue harm, but how it stacked up was not yet well known.

The reverse route gave smaller cuts and less tissue harm, with good room to set the break. It leaned toward less surgery time and blood loss, though neither gap was firm. Scores for use of the arm did not differ much between groups. Neither group had failed healing, implant harm, or nerve or vessel harm. The team calls the reverse route a fuller choice for back shoulder breaks, with like healing and better looks, while urging bigger studies to tune flap design.
pmc-13327109:
Daniela Ortiz-Muñoz and team widened the map of von Economo neurons in the middle front cortex. Their 2026 study used stain imaging and size measures in postmortem tissue. It mapped where these big two-poled relay cells sit, how dense they are, and their shape across seven brain zones. Until now, these cells were thought to live only in front cingulate and front island cortex. Fresh reports added upper-middle zone 9 and front-pole zone 10.

The cells were far more packed in rough-zoned areas than smooth-zoned areas. Denser packs and bigger bodies sat on ridge tops and in the right brain half. On average they were 55% bigger than near pyramid cells. Pack density rose with cell body size. The team argues these cells fill a wider front brain web tied to gut sense, drive, and social thought. They act as link hubs for brain and mind disorders.
pmc-13327609:
Furong Chen and colleagues reveal a two-way role for a bacterial toxin pair in a 2026 study. In Pseudomonas bijieensis strain 2P24, the toxin Fic-1 blocks DNA copying by adding an AMP mark to the gyrase subunit GyrB, and its partner AntF normally restrains it. Few enzymes known can remove such marks.

Joined together, the pair itself removes the mark, returning gyrase to its plain state, and lab and gene tests pinpointed one AntF residue, Glu28, as vital for that cutting action. AntF thus both brakes the toxin and helps it undo its own work. The finding adds a fresh control scheme for toxin systems and hints at how multi-part enzymes evolve.
pmc-13327909:
Jose Eric Mella Lacsa writes a 2026 letter to the editor on the hidden wounds of veterans. He responds to a recent review of the polytrauma clinical triad, the linked trio of chronic pain, post-traumatic stress disorder, and traumatic brain injury in military patients. The letter praises that work's joined-up treatment picture, then widens the lens.

From Seoul to São Paulo, he argues, veterans fight a second war at home: pain that outlasts the battlefield, trauma returning in dreams, and brain injury quietly eroding memory, balance, and identity. Care split into silos cannot meet that mix, so pain, brain, mental health, and rehabilitation teams must act as one under a whole-person approach. How societies answer, he writes, tests compassion as much as science.
pmc-13328509:
Jiayue Wu and co-authors compare two closely related melon lines in a 2026 study of fruit quality. One line, called 109, differs from its sister line 108 in firmness, sweetness, acidity, and other traits. The team measured basic fruit traits and used wide-ranging chemical profiling to map small molecules in the fruit.

Line 109 was firmer and had more soluble solids and acidity, but a lower sugar to acid balance than line 108. Profiling found 2,101 compounds, with 246 differing between the lines. Changed groups included sugar-related, acid-related, and amino-acid-derived compounds. Pathway checks pointed to sugar handling and terpenoid building routes. The results give breeders candidate compounds for better melon quality.
pmc-13328809:
Morris and colleagues analyzed in 2026 what drives dietary self-management in chronic kidney disease, where eating rules are strict and hard to keep. Rather than run a new survey, they reworked a published synthesis of 92 studies covering 2,924 adults in 23 countries. They sorted its themes into a standard framework of behavior domains and a wheel that links those domains to intervention types.

Twelve of fourteen domains played a role, showing that diet control rests on knowledge, skills, emotion, social life, and setting, not facts alone. Clashing advice and thin practical guidance were key barriers, while trust in professionals and learning by doing supported adherence. Two domains, optimism and intentions, were absent. Judged for cost, ease, and fairness, education and enablement ranked as the most workable intervention routes, while training and system changes scored as harder. The authors urge multi-part diet support that builds skills and confidence.
pmc-13330109:
Yanrui Cai and co-authors test automatic measurement of brain ventricle size after bleeding around the brain in a 2026 study. The Evans index guides choices about fluid drainage, but hand measurement is slow and varies by reader. Admission scans from 364 patients with sudden bleeding were read by an open deep learning pipeline and by two experts.

Repeat runs by the program agreed almost perfectly, and expert readers agreed closely too in the reported values. Program and expert readings matched well overall, and better once cases with frontal blood were removed. The program flagged more cases above the set cut point than experts did. Its scores also tracked drainage choices and stayed linked after adjustment.
pmc-13330409:
Michela Deiana and team gave the first experimental proof that Strongyloides stercoralis sheds extracellular vesicles. Their 2026 study took infective larvae from fecal samples of a patient with strongyloidiasis and kept them in vitro for up to 48 hours. These vesicles are a key route for host-pathogen crosstalk, and many helminths shed vesicle-like structures carrying small RNAs with effects on target cells, yet this parasite's release had never been shown.

Transmission electron microscopy and nanoparticle tracking analysis found two-layer sacs about 120 nm wide. Small RNA sequencing found many vesicle-linked small RNA types, including microRNAs, only partly shared with those of related species, with likely host gene targets. The team presents the findings as filling a gap in how this parasite talks to and shapes its host, opening a route to studying how vesicles shape immunity in strongyloidiasis.
pmc-13330609:
Chiara Maria Calvanese and colleagues hunt gut bacteria that might support mental health in a 2026 study. The team screened gene data from 1,185 fermented foods for genes that make brain-active compounds. That screen guided lab isolation of new lactic acid bacteria strains from the foods.

In total, 73 fresh strains were isolated. Genome comparisons flagged three species as likely candidates for psychobiotic use in the reported analysis. Lab tests for brain-active output then confirmed four strains as the most promising, spanning four species. The authors propose them for supplements or new fermented foods aimed at mental health support. Gene-first hunting can speed strain discovery, they argue.
pmc-13331709:
Shan-Shan Hu and Wei-Hui Liu describe a 2026 technical innovation report in which two bile duct procedures, normally done in separate sessions, were combined into one. Their patient was a 58-year-old man with pancreatic head cancer that could not be removed and had blocked bile flow.

Standard drainage through the duodenum had failed because the tumor invaded it, so the team drained bile through the stomach wall under ultrasound guidance. Straight away they passed a very slim 6.5-French camera scope through the fresh opening, confirmed the cancer narrowing by direct view, and threaded a wire across it. Both drainage routes were then stented in a single 35-minute session with no leakage or bleeding, and bilirubin returned to normal within 9 days.
pmc-13333109:
Yasir Radhi and colleagues report a 2026 case of fixed drug eruption settling preferentially over a cosmetic lip tattoo. Fixed drug eruption is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction in which lesions recur at the same site after re-exposure to an offending drug. Localization over tattooed skin is rare and can mimic tattoo allergy itself. The patient was a 27-year-old woman with recurrent burning, swelling, oozing, and progressive darkening mainly affecting cosmetically tattooed lips, starting about a year after tattoo placement.

She reported episodic use of trimethoprim-containing drugs, ibuprofen, and ciprofloxacin before several flares. Her latest episode also produced a solitary dark buttock patch. Examination showed violaceous-gray darkening of the tattooed lips plus a well-defined buttock patch consistent with healed fixed drug eruption. The course favored drug eruption localizing to an immune-altered skin district created by tattooing. Clinicians should weigh drug causes before blaming tattoo ink alone.
pmc-13333309:
Daniela Antolová and colleagues report the first gene-confirmed finds of two rat tapeworms in wild Slovak rodents, in a 2026 survey. Both Rodentolepis nana and Hymenolepis diminuta can infect people, yet their presence in free-living rodents in Central Europe was poorly documented.

Between 2020 and 2025 the team examined 881 small mammals of 10 rodent species from the city of Košice and protected parts of the Tatra National Park. Worms were identified by ITS1 and mitochondrial nad1 sequences. R. nana appeared only in urban brown rats, in 7 of 97 animals, a rate of 7.2 percent. H. diminuta was confirmed in 10 animals overall, 1.1 percent, mostly brown rats at 9.3 percent plus one striped field mouse. The authors say the records extend the known map for both parasites in Central Europe and underline the city rat as the key local host.
pmc-13333409:
Lingling Wu and colleagues compared rival measures of blood sugar swing in a 2026 meta-analysis asking which one best predicts how critically ill patients will fare. Sugar variability, not just average level, tracks with death in intensive care, but clinics track it with different formulas and nobody knew which deserved the most trust.

Searching four databases to June 2025, the team pooled 31 studies covering 98,946 patients and three measures: coefficient of variation, standard deviation, and mean amplitude of glycemic excursions, called MAGE. High variation by any measure predicted more deaths and more major heart events. MAGE showed the tightest link to 30-day death, with a hazard ratio of 1.50, while standard deviation and MAGE reached 2.45 and 2.12 for heart events. The variation penalty at 30 days ran slightly larger in patients without diabetes, at 1.40, than in those with it, at 1.32. The authors back watchful dynamic monitoring while noting MAGE studies are still few.
pmc-13333509:
Rongjuan Jiang and colleagues describe how a giant chest tumor strangling a man's airway and chest vein was removed without a biopsy, in a 2026 case report. Imaging pointed to Castleman disease, but the diagnosis, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, only emerged after surgery, and waiting for tissue proof risked suffocation.

The 37-year-old arrived with a week of breathlessness, inability to lie flat, and morning facial swelling from superior vena cava compression. A multidisciplinary team planned around the dangers. Three-dimensional reconstruction mapped the surgery, and feeding vessels were embolized the same day to drain the hypervascular mass without starving it too long. He was intubated awake with a fibreoptic scope while tilted toward the tumor side, then rolled to relieve the vein. Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery removed the mass, decompressing him and delivering the diagnosis in one move. The authors offer the sequencing as a template for perilous mediastinal tumors.
pmc-13333709:
Yali Zhou and co-authors gathered qualitative studies in a 2026 systematic review of screening for cervical cancer in women living with HIV. These women face higher cancer risk yet reach screening services less often than HIV-negative women.

Four databases were searched for studies from January 2000 to December 2024, and ten articles met the criteria. Using a meta-aggregative method, the team sorted findings into two themes and six sub-themes. They counted 27 factors that help women attend screening and 79 that hold them back. Barriers specific to living with HIV stood out across the accounts. The synthesis gives program planners concrete targets for raising screening uptake in this vulnerable group.
pmc-13334309:
Ithar M Beshtawi and colleagues study 2026 adherence to daily single-use contact lens replacement among lens wearers. The cross-sectional study included 144 daily single-use lens users, eighty female, with mean age about twenty-eight years. Wearers answered a standard survey covering patient mix, lens history, replacement habits, self-reported side effects, risky wearing behaviors, and care instructions. The study aimed to evaluate adherence, identify factors behind non-compliance, and assess related risk behaviors.

Lens reuse was reported by eighty-three wearers, about fifty-eight percent, and was significantly linked to gender, age, and wear duration. Reuse was mainly driven by cost-saving in thirty-five participants and belief in reusability in twenty-four. Only thirty-seven wearers followed proper cleaning steps. Common risky behaviors included napping with lenses in and skipping follow-up visits.
pmc-13334609:
Chunxiu Du leads a team of seventeen authors who link a metabolic enzyme to the epigenetic changes that scar kidneys. In chronic kidney disease, fibrosis advances while the triggers that link metabolism to gene control stay murky. Proteomics of histones in mouse fibrosis models found one mark, acetylation at a specific histone site, selectively increased.

Profiles of metabolites showed citrate piling up. That pointed at the enzyme ACLY, which makes the acetyl groups histones consume. Injured kidneys showed more ACLY, more acetyl-CoA, and more of the mark. When ACLY was deleted in tubules, all three fell back and scarring dropped. The same signatures showed up in human kidney samples and tracked worse function. Drugs that already block ACLY reproduced the anti-scarring effect, which hints at a path to repurpose them.
pmc-13335009:
Yusuf Ahmed and colleagues compare 2026 Navitor and Sapien valves in transcatheter aortic valve implantation. Transcatheter aortic valve implantation is now a standard treatment for severe, symptom-causing aortic stenosis, above all in older patients. The meta-analysis compares the latest generations of self-expandable Navitor valves from Abbott Structural Heart with balloon-expandable Sapien valves from Edwards Lifesciences. The authors combed PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library for studies comparing the two valves.

The search turned up four studies covering 4,828 patients in total. The two groups did not differ in a statistical sense on device and technical success, 30-day all-cause death, stroke rate, or major vessel problems. Permanent pacemaker implantation was more common with Navitor valves, with a risk ratio of 2.16. The review gives heart teams a head-to-head safety and efficacy comparison for valve choice.
pmc-13336009:
Dezhi Chen and colleagues present 2026 a clear machine learning framework for Nb-Si based alloy design with enhanced fracture toughness. Flight materials need alloys with desired working traits for higher heat and lower weight. This improves aero-engine fuel use and cuts harmful exhaust. Nb-Si alloys can operate at higher heat than current nickel-based super-metals and have lower weight.

The authors develop a machine learning-driven design framework for Nb-Si based ultra-high temperature alloys using a three-step feature plan to break the 20 MPa·m1/2 fracture toughness barrier. Their model forecasts fracture toughness with error below 7 percent, and SHAP and PDP checks guide alloy design. Five alloys with silicon content ranging from 3 to 15 atomic percent were made to test model forecasts. Sample 5 achieved a fracture toughness of 22.791 MPa·m1/2, beating the typical range below 20 MPa·m1/2.
pmc-13336609:
Giuseppe Lapadula and colleagues examine hidden hepatitis B in a 2026 narrative review focused on people living with HIV. The virus can persist in the liver even when a surface test reads negative. New HIV plans that drop drugs active against hepatitis B have revived worry that the virus could flare again.

Drawing on case reports, cohort studies, and switch trials, the authors find flare-ups are real but uncommon after such switches. Risk clusters where HIV is poorly controlled, protective antibodies are absent, or surface antigen was lost during past treatment. People with steady viral control and healthy CD4 counts face low risk. The review supports checking risk before any switch.
pmc-13336809:
Wenfeng Zhuo and colleagues mapped in 2026 how lactate links pancreatic cancer cells and nearby stellate cells to help tumours evade immunity. Lactate reshapes the tumour surroundings, but whether it drives talk between these two cell types was undefined. The team found cancer cells are the main lactate source, and lactate switches on stellate cells through a chemical tagging process tied to autophagy.

Activated stellate cells then raise PD-1 on killer T cells, blunting immune attack. Blocking lactate transport with the drug AZD3965 made pancreatic tumours in animals more sensitive to PD-1 blockade. The lactate axis thus offers a combined treatment target: starve the immune suppressing signal while releasing the T cell brake.
pmc-13336909:
Bianca Peña and colleagues studied how nursing affects healing of pelvic floor muscle after birth injury, in a 2026 rat experiment. They used pregnant rats given a simulated birth injury, then compared animals that nursed their young with animals that did not. The work centers on the muscles that support the bladder and bowel, which are often hurt during vaginal birth.

Nursing rats mounted a fast immune response to the injury, with early shifts in immune cells inside the muscle and a fall in genes tied to swelling. Their muscles also showed more genes that calm swelling and grew larger new muscle fibers, which stayed larger after weaning. The authors read this as evidence that nursing brings forward the calming phase of healing, letting muscle regrow sooner and stronger.
pmc-13337009:
Wei Zheng and colleagues cloak gene-silencing particles in cancer cell membrane to beat drug resistance in a 2026 study. Their particles wrap a threose nucleic acid, a sturdy DNA-like strand, aimed at the AKT2 growth gene.

Coats taken from the same tumor subtype made particles fuse directly with matching cancer cells, skipping the bubble trap. Silencing reached about 70% protein knockdown, beating standard transfection tools in the reported tests. In drug-resistant mouse tumors the particles piled up, cut AKT2, and shrank tumors through a death pathway without body-wide toxicity. Borrowed identity could carry nucleic acid drugs past two barriers at once.
pmc-13337209:
Ankita Ojha, Banshi Mohan Rathi, and Sara Faiz present a 2026 case where supposed chronic kidney disease turned out to be amyloidosis. A 47-year-old man from Mexico, working as a roofer, arrived with stage 3 kidney disease plus heart and vessel history. He described tiredness, aching joints, and unintentional weight loss of 12 lb over 3 months without a clear cause.

Blood tests gave few clues: kidney function had slid, urine held modest protein at 352 mg over 24 hours, and no monoclonal protein appeared. A kidney biopsy settled the question, showing amyloid deposits staining strongly for LECT2 in the glomeruli, interstitium, and vessel walls. The case warns that bland, unexplained kidney decline deserves tissue answers.
pmc-13337309:
Ashraf T. Soliman leads a 2026 systematic review of testosterone therapy for boys whose growth and puberty run late. Constitutional delay tops the list of causes of delayed puberty in boys and drives most endocrine referrals for it. Short, low-dose testosterone courses have been used for over 5 decades to speed puberty and growth, yet the evidence stayed scattered.

Searching PubMed records dated January 1, 1986 through March 10, 2026, the team gathered 20 original studies covering 1,329 boys with this condition or closely related self-limited delay. Outcomes spanned height speed, puberty progress, bone age, predicted adult height, and safety, with formal bias checks and an exploratory pooled analysis where data allowed. A single synthesis helps clinicians weigh benefit against risk.
pmc-13337409:
Feng-Xian Ni and co-authors argue that a lytic cell death program sits at the center of asthma in a 2026 review. Asthma was long framed as an allergy-type immune disorder, yet that view poorly explains chronicity, airway remodeling, and steroid failure in some types. Necroptosis, a regulated bursting death run by RIPK proteins and MLKL, may fill the gap.

Allergens, viruses, and pollutants can trigger this death in airway lining and immune cells. Bursting cells spill danger signals that amplify type 2 inflammation, build a neutrophil-rich steroid-resistant setting, and scar airways directly. The review links necroptosis with sister death programs under the PANoptosis umbrella and weighs biomarker-guided patient sorting plus new inhibitors, while noting most proof is still preclinical.
pmc-13337709:
Giulio Calcagni, Flaminia Pugnaloni, Paolo Versacci, and Bruno Marino wrote a 2026 commentary on mitral valve development and disease. They respond to a review by Wang and Zhou that linked early valve formation to three problems. Those were rheumatic stenosis, congenital stenosis, and myxomatous prolapse.

Agreement with that synthesis is paired with a plea to add valve problems seen in genetic syndromes. Such cases show how altered signals in development shape the tissue between heart chambers and the final valve form. The dorsal mesenchymal protrusion and Sonic Hedgehog signaling get special attention, notably for Down syndrome. Including syndromic cases, they argue, would complete the developmental picture.
pmc-13338609:
Yufei Xue and colleagues reported a rare breast tumour case in 2026, tall cell carcinoma with reversed polarity. The tumour looks much like a tall cell variant of thyroid cancer, which can confuse diagnosis and risk mistaking a breast primary for thyroid spread. Stains and molecular tests are therefore essential to prove breast origin.

The patient was a 62 year old woman whose breast mass showed the hallmark microscopic pattern and stain profile. Despite a triple negative stain pattern, the tumour type tends to behave indolently. Accurate sorting of such cases matters, since treatment and outlook differ sharply between breast and thyroid disease.
pmc-13339009:
Sarah E. Miller and colleagues present a sticky gel for stopping bleeding after childbirth in a 2026 study.
