Lab tests showed stronger adhesion than controls in shear and burst checks. The gel could be pushed by hand at up to 5 mL per minute as reported and showed short-term safety with cells and blood. Tests in a rat bleeding model and a bench womb model placed the results in body-like settings.
pmc-13339809:
Patrick M. Schlievert and colleagues test a fatty germ killer in petroleum jelly in a 2026 lab study. Glycerol monolaurate, a food-approved fat product, kills staphylococci and calms swelling. Earlier carriers caused unwanted effects, so jelly was tried as a gentler base.

Among related fat products, the laurate form killed staphylococci best as reported. In jelly it killed drug-sensitive and resistant Staphylococcus aureus plus related skin species at 500 micrograms per milliliter in the reported tests. That dose sits a hundred times below earlier human use levels. Other streptococci also died, and rabbit skin tests confirmed killing, supporting skin use.
pmc-13340109:
Ian Windham and co-authors characterize bacteria taken from traumatic wounds in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Two groups dominate such infections and are known for drug resistance. The team sampled wounds at a university hospital and examined twenty-four isolates in depth.

Whole genome reading showed isolates from different patients were genetically distinct. Repeat samples from one patient were near-identical, suggesting lasting colonization by a single strain. Surprisingly, only two isolates counted as multidrug resistant. All isolates formed biofilms, though at different speeds and amounts. Most resisted killing by human serum when free-floating. The authors say these differences should shape treatment choices.
pmc-13341709:
A natural compound's target in disc degeneration pain is pinpointed by Hai-E Liu's team in a 2026 multi-omics study. Orientin, used for pain control, was matched against disc degeneration genes through network pharmacology, yielding 368 shared candidates.

Machine learning crowned CYP1B1 as the hub gene, with a diagnostic AUC of 0.95. Docking energies below −9.5 kcal/mol and stable simulations supported a tight orientin-CYP1B1 fit. Single-cell data showed the gene raised in diseased disc fibroblasts, and cell tests under inflammatory pressure showed orientin protecting cell survival. Immune infiltration, however, showed no link to the gene after correction.
pmc-13343509:
Maurício Portiolli Franco, Giovana Vitiello Teixeira, and André Luiz Barboza Formiga model ruthenium catalysts for turning carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide in 2026. Swapping one ring of the standard bipyridine ligand for five other nitrogen donors changes how the catalyst accepts electrons and grabs CO2, and the team computed each variant's path in solvent.

Pyrrole, pyrazole, and carbene variants took both electrons onto the main ligand and shifted the second step to harder potentials, while triazole and oxazole versions split the electrons across ligands. Losing the solvent molecule cost between 12.9 and 19.0 kilocalories per mole depending on the donor. Product shape ratios tracked a distortion measure, offering a quick screen for selectivity.
pmc-13343609:
Youguo Tan and Hui Fan tracked close to forty thousand Chinese teens over three years to see how long-term excess weight links to low mood and worry. Weight load was summed across yearly checks. In the last year, the team also scored sleep quality, sad mood, and anxiety with standard question sets.

A higher weight load went with more sad mood in a straight-line pattern. Poor sleep carried part of that link, about a tenth of it. Teens with both high weight load and poor sleep were far more likely to report anxiety. The authors point to sleep care as one path to ease the mental load of excess weight.
pmc-13343909:
Yao Ma and colleagues found an ensitrelvir resistant SARS-CoV-2 mutant in 2026 using a safe, weakened glowing virus lacking ORF 3a and 7b proteins. Ensitrelvir targets the conserved main protease Mpro, yet Mpro gene changes can confer resistance. Finding resistant mutants and their routes guides antiviral choice. The team isolated a resistant mutant carrying an Mpro G23 deletion.

That mutant showed about 1,000 fold resistance to ensitrelvir in lab tests, a dramatic loss of drug activity. Resistance maps of this kind warn doctors and drug makers where protease drugs may fail. The weakened virus system enables resistance studies without handling fully virulent SARS-CoV-2.
pmc-13344409:
Published in 2026, this notice from the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine records a routine review of its guidance documents across 2024 and 2025. Rather than presenting new research, it states which older documents were withdrawn, which were replaced by newer versions, and which were reaffirmed as still current.

Withdrawals covered guidance on cervical length screening, cervical pessary use, and patient safety roles, while twin transfusion guidance and cell-free DNA screening guidance were replaced by updated consult series. Several older consults, including those on vasa previa, chromosomal microarray, and ultrasound use, were reaffirmed. Clinicians and librarians can use the list to retire outdated advice and point readers to the guidance that now governs practice.
pmc-13346009:
Michael W. Mikula and Ezra Baraban review repeat genetic changes in epithelial tumors of the chest center in 2026. Thymic tumors dominate this family, and molecular testing keeps carving out types that look alike under the microscope yet behave very differently, knowledge surgical pathologists now need at the bench.

A hotspot change in GTF2I marks most type A and AB thymomas, and the review maps schemes tying gene patterns to outlook and therapy across thymoma and thymic carcinoma. It closes with two fierce look-alikes defined by their genetics. One is NUT carcinoma. The other covers tumors missing parts of the SWI/SNF complex, including the SMARCA4-deficient chest tumor. Stain clues can catch them before their aggression surprises clinicians.
pmc-13346109:
David M. Emms and co-authors set out in 2026 a major upgrade to OrthoFinder, a widely used tool for gene kinship across species. True gene kinship underpins studies of evolution. It also lets researchers move knowledge from model species to others. Yet speed and accuracy get harder as genome sets grow.

Better tree-based sorting of gene groups raised accuracy by about seven percent in relative terms. A new gene assignment method cut memory use sharply with no loss of accuracy. The latest version is free online. For labs that weigh hundreds of genomes, the upgrade means faster, leaner, and more trusted gene family maps. Later evolution and function work rests on those maps.
pmc-13346209:
Ziyi Ying and colleagues review short-chain fatty acids in ulcerative colitis. Their 2026 synthesis covers how these gut products are made, moved, and used. Named transporters in the colon wall get close attention. So does the idea of fuel priority for colon cells. Routes that carry the acids beyond the gut are also traced.

Later sections weigh roles in immune control and barrier strength. Effects on oxidative stress and gut movement are covered too. A testing section follows next. There, acid patterns may act as changing markers of disease state. Delivery is the hard problem. The authors stress targeted carriers and microbe-based plans. Each plan would be tuned to the patient, not given as a plain supplement.
pmc-13347209:
Juan Ma and co-authors train deep learning models to grade HER2 staining in breast cancer slides, in a two-centre study published in 2026. The set held 135 whole-slide images from 118 patients scored as 1+, 2+, or 3+. Two pathologists marked the tumour areas. The areas were cut into small patches for training. Splits were kept at patient level.

All six models graded well on the held-out test, and AlexNet led with a macro-AUC value of 0.971 in the reported results, just ahead of VGG16. Most mistakes fell between neighbouring grades, the hardest calls in routine practice, and heat maps pointed to strongly stained tumour zones. Outside-centre checks are stressed as vital before clinic use.
pmc-13348409:
Maximilian F. Mayerhofer-Rochel and colleagues present the draft genome of an anthrax strain found on a Vienna mail sack in 2001, in an announcement from 2026. Air drawn through filters at the United States embassy during the Amerithrax scare grew suspect colonies that were confirmed by light-based tests and banked. Early checks suggested natural fabric contamination rather than attack material.

Family typing placed the strain in group A.Br.081, highly alike the Ames Ancestor reference in the reported comparison, a placement that separates background finds from crime strains. A public genome for a scare-era isolate sharpens forensic baselines for telling real threats from harmless environmental cousins.
pmc-13348709:
Laura Fumanelli and co-authors modelled in 2026 how school-based steps affected SARS-CoV-2 spread. They weighed infection control against high social costs. Distance learning, reactive class quarantines, and periodic screening each carry trade-offs. Population-level proof is key for pandemic planning.

An individual-based model of spread in homes, schools, and the wider town was tuned to full contact tracing data from Reggio Emilia, Italy. Data came from March and April 2021, when the Alpha variant ruled under strict town rules. The model scores how each school step changed spread. Its results help policy makers pick school rules that curb spread with no needless disruption for children and families.
pmc-13348809:
Ruth Abeles and co-authors report a pilot study from two thousand twenty-six on a game-like workshop that teaches preoperative assessment to medical residents. Judging a patient's risk before surgery is a key skill, but training in it is uneven and many residents feel unsure. The workshop borrows the cooperative Jigsaw method and an escape-room theme.

The session ran for three hours at one California medical center in two thousand twenty-five. Residents worked through four areas: heart risk, medication management, blood thinner choices, and special populations. A comparison group learned through routine rotations and general lectures. Surveys before and after measured knowledge and confidence. Given the small sample, the authors report effect sizes rather than formal significance tests.
pmc-13349409:
Roman Pauli and co-authors replied in 2026 to comments on their pitch for work exposure limits for psychosocial hazards. They argued that perfection must not block progress. Critics had raised concept and method snags in moving limits made for chemical and physical hazards to psychosocial risks such as workload, control, and social backing.

The authors thanked their critics and welcomed shared worries about unsure measurement. Yet they argued that psychosocial risk checks have grown far more nuanced than the critique implied. Their first paper mapped what is known and unknown, not a finished standard. The reply backs step-by-step, proof-based limits as a workable step toward guarding workers from hazards that already cause wide ill health.
pmc-13349509:
Madoka Sano and colleagues studied in 2026 whether cardiorenal anaemia syndrome worsens outcomes in atrial functional mitral regurgitation, a valve leak that mainly affects older patients. The leak causes venous congestion and reduced forward output, which can accelerate kidney disease and anaemia, yet high-risk subgroups needing closer follow-up were unclear.

From the multicentre REVEAL-AFMR registry, patients with moderate-to-severe disease enrolled in 2019 were split into cardiorenal anaemia and non-syndrome groups. Cardiovascular outcomes were compared, testing whether the combined heart, kidney, and anaemia burden predicts events beyond valve severity alone. The findings help clinicians identify patients who need targeted therapy and tighter monitoring rather than routine follow-up.
pmc-13350009:
Shan Ren and co-authors compared radiation plan settings for brain metastases treated on MRI-guided machines in a 2026 planning study. Twenty patients with a single medium-sized brain tumour each received four test plans delivering 30 Gray in three sessions.

The plans varied the number of beams, nine or fifteen, and the smallest allowed dose chunk per segment. Each version was scored for dose quality, treatment speed, delivery accuracy, and how well doses held up in calculations. MRI-guided treatment adapts to daily anatomy, but planners lack agreed settings. Trading beam count and segment size against robustness shows where extra complexity actually pays off.
pmc-13350309:
Georgia Tzafa and co-authors charted in 2026 an acute pain reaction to transfusion in a patient with transfusion-dependent thalassaemia, a rare and little-known complication of unknown cause. Such reactions cause marked distress, at times needing symptom care and hospital admission, yet their biology remains obscure.

Patient and returned red cell unit samples from the event, plus prior and later transfusions, were weighed against matched reference groups for gene profile and storage time. Short- and long-term traits were tracked in depth. The detailed case hunt seeks clues to mechanism and prevention, helping transfusion services spot, probe, and handle a reaction that now lacks a clear account.
pmc-13351709:
Abouch V Krymchantowski discusses wider prevention choices for migraine in children and teens in 2026, centred on anti-CGRP antibody drugs. Migraine affects about 11 percent of young people worldwide and disrupts school, daily life, and social activity. Older preventive drugs often work weakly or are hard to tolerate in this age group.

Attention turns to a trial by Hershey and co-authors of fremanezumab in the New England Journal of Medicine. Krymchantowski presents it as the first strong prospective evidence for this drug class in youth migraine. Common older options such as topiramate and amitriptyline are reviewed, including a trial where they matched placebo. The piece argues the new option fills a real gap.
pmc-13352609:
Gerard Serrano-Gómez leads a 2026 gut microbe study of families at higher risk of inflammatory bowel disease. Close relatives of patients carry raised risk and can reveal changes before illness starts. Shotgun sequencing covered stool from 68 Crohn disease and 77 ulcerative colitis patients, their healthy relatives, and 497 unrelated healthy controls.

Relatives kept normal microbe diversity but sat midway between patients and controls in imbalance. Crohn relatives shared patient-like losses, including depleted Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and carried more adhesion and invasion genes. Yet their pathway profiles looked near-healthy, splitting taxonomic from functional change. Classifiers separated relatives from controls strongly using species and virulence gene patterns.
pmc-13352709:
Prakash Gangadaran and co-authors review membrane-coated liposomes for delivering mRNA in cancer care in 2026. mRNA drugs express proteins briefly and safely, but standard lipid particles suffer weak stability, poor cell entry, and stray immune activation. Hybrid shells fuse synthetic liposomes with natural membranes from red cells, platelets, immune cells, or cancer cells.

Natural proteins bring perks: CD47 helps dodge immune clearance, grip molecules extend circulation, and homing receptors steer particles to tissue. Cancer cell coats can even target their own tumour type. Once inside, fusogenic parts break the endosome and free the mRNA, beating standard particles in lab tests. Shells can also tune immune tone, widening their role beyond delivery.
pmc-13354409:
Hung Thanh Le and others tested a skin-flap method for rebuilding the glans in boys with posterior hypospadias and a small glans, ran the look-back study in 2026. Posterior hypospadias remains hard even for experienced child urologists, largely because a small glans and severe curvature complicate repair. The team tested two-stage urethroplasty with glans reconstruction using a skin flap.

Fifty-eight people with severe curvature and small glans were surveyed, and op results were tested after the reconstruction. The study reports whether the flap approach produced workable anatomy and acceptable problem rates. Surgeons gain useful evidence for a hard subgroup where standard repairs often fall short.
pmc-13354809:
P Ignacio A Bianco and others surveyed BCG beyond bladder cancer, in 2026. Germ Calmette-Guérin, first a TB vaccine, is standard immune care for non-muscle-deep bladder cancer, where start plus upkeep plans and patient choice decide success. Its trained defence effects have raised notice in other solid tumours.

The review splits rule-supported uses from investigational ones, covering intralesional and vaccine-adjuvant ways that show signals in selected melanomas and other cancers. It names contexts where BCG may remain in clinic key or ready for trials. Readers gain a disciplined map of a familiar immune care's growing, and still unclear, frontier.
pmc-13358809:
Rajagopal and colleagues explored in 2026 killing bacteria with ultrafast light pulses on gold nanorods. Biofilm infections and drug resistance demand alternatives to antibiotics. Gold rods turn light into heat and chemical activity at tiny scales. The team bound lipid-coated gold nanorods to Staphylococcus epidermidis, a common skin germ that forms biofilms. They then fired femtosecond laser pulses at the rods, tuned off the rods' peak response.

The pulses killed up to half of the bacteria at moderate energy doses. Analysis showed the killing was driven mainly by reactive oxygen species, with possible help from shockwaves that open up cells. Tuning the pulses off-peak balanced two goals: making enough reactive oxygen species while limiting damage to the nanorods themselves. They frame the work as a step toward treatments that bypass antibiotic resistance mechanisms.
pmc-13359009:
Peter Pongracz and Petra Dobos study how dogs learn from people in a 2026 paper. Dog breeds differ in how much they lean on human cues, but breed ancestry and job type give a coarse picture. The authors watched 187 adult purebred dogs try a detour task after seeing a person solve it first.

Two patterns of behavior stood out: how much a dog watched the person, and how much its own time improved. Sorting dogs by both patterns gave six types, from keen watchers who improved fast to dogs that barely watched yet still improved. The finer lens helps explain why breeds tackle human-taught tasks so differently.
pmc-13360609:
Nuri Can Tanrısever and co-authors present a 2026 study of upper jaw shape in teens with stuck canine teeth. A maxillary canine can get trapped on the cheek side or the palate side of the jaw. The team used CBCT scans and 3D digital models from 86 people with one stuck canine. Their average age was about 16 years.

Each canine was classed as cheek-side or palate-side based on the scans. The team then measured arch shape on the digital models and compared the two groups. Clear differences showed up between them on the measures taken. Knowing how arch shape links to the side of impaction can help orthodontists plan how to guide the tooth into place, and may flag which cases need earlier action.
pmc-13360909:
Małgorzata Grześkowiak and co-authors collected cases of the Lazarus phenomenon in older people in a 2026 review. This rare event is when the heart starts again on its own after resuscitation has failed or death has been declared. The team searched three databases for cases from 1982 through the end of 2025. Of 81 cases found, 48 involved people over 60 and entered the study.

The patients were split into two age bands, 60 to 79 and 80 plus. Heart-related and non-heart causes of the arrest each made up about half of the cases. Arrests in hospital and outside it occurred in equal shares. The authors also study what factors may trigger or mask this event. Their work can help doctors set waiting times and checks before death is confirmed.
pmc-13361509:
Ting Wang and co-authors surveyed Chinese health workers on prevention knowledge and mood in a 2026 study. China is merging medical care with prevention, and staff knowledge, attitude, and practice of that merge can be scored. The team asked whether those scores link to depressive symptoms. They also tested whether monthly income changes the link, and accounted for work stress.

Knowledge and attitude scores acted as protective factors: workers who scored higher reported fewer depressive symptoms. Practice scores, oddly, linked to more symptoms, perhaps because doing more prevention work adds load. The authors urge reform plans to weigh workload and pay differences. Fairer task sharing and stronger institutional support may protect the mental health of the workforce.
pmc-13362809:
Ali Abd El-Aty and co-authors present a 2026 modeling study on how a four-metal alloy, FeCoCrNi, flows when squeezed hot. Such high-entropy alloys mix several metals in near-equal shares and serve in tough, hot parts. To plan hot forming, engineers need math that predicts the metal's resistance across heat, speed, and stretch. The team built a new version of the Zerilli-Armstrong model with better terms for hardening and heat effects.

Tested against lab data, the new model tracked measured stress very closely, with an average error near four percent, beating the two older versions it was compared with. The authors offer it as a tool to tune hot forming, cut wasted material, and save energy when shaping parts from this alloy family.
pmc-13363409:
Weina Xu and colleagues present a 2026 winemaking study on skin contact for white wines, a step white production usually skips. They tried cold soaking before fermentation and fermenting on the skins for Chardonnay and Italian Riesling grapes grown near Yantai, China. The team then measured phenolic compounds, aroma chemicals, color, and trained tasters' scores against standard-made wines.

Both methods raised total phenolics sharply, with some compounds rising about ten-fold, and lifted aroma levels, above all fruity esters. Skin-fermented wines tasted fuller and more balanced, while cold-soaked wines seemed fresher. The two grapes shifted differently in color and scent profile. The authors give growers a menu for shaping each variety's character through maceration.
pmc-13363709:
Savannah Gluck and colleagues present a 2026 feasibility study on tracking baby sleep at home scale with a sensor-equipped smart bassinet. The bed logs motion and sound, and rocks and soothes on its own when fussing starts. From the device logs of 26,187 infants, the team derived standard sleep measures, such as longest sleep stretch and night sleep total. They added new measures of fussing and of how soothing changed the night.

The bassinet-based patterns lined up broadly with what earlier small studies report for the first six months of life. Some gaps remain, which the authors trace to method and to the bed's own soothing. The work shows that device data can map sleep growth curves for huge groups cheaply, opening studies of sleep and caregiver interplay.
pmc-13365409:
Andrea Farini and others authored a 2026 withdrawal note for their 2023 paper on gut bugs upset in dystrophin-lacking mice. The journal became aware of citation errors in the manuscript and, after internal testing and image screening of issued figures, found possible image reuse. The authors were contacted and provided corresponding first source data for the affected figures.

Withdrawal notes of this kind remove a paper from the standing papers while documenting the concerns that prompted the choice. Readers should not rely on the first paper's ends about gut microbes, defence, and muscle disease in dystrophin deficiency without independent verification. The note preserves transparency about why the work was withdrawn.
pmc-13369509:
Mikhail Tarasov and co-authors show that how sodium channels are set out, at the nanoscale in the cell membrane, changes how they act. Those channels are gated by voltage. Their 2026 study goes against what is forecast from single channels gauged on their own.

In made and native cell systems, forecasts from single channels put currents from clusters too high, by a share that counts. Modelling on a computer hinted that interactions between channels that sit next to each other make sense of the gap. The new model forecast how clusters act, and how the cell acts as a whole, in a true way. It also hinted that channels in clusters act in a unlike way to drugs whose effect rests on use. Tests then backed that hint. When clustering was changed, electrical dysfunction from flaws in channels was put right. Those flaws are linked to dangerous arrhythmias and seizures.
pmc-13369709:
Qiao-Yu Hsu and co-workers read in 2026 the load of cord stem cell shed bits as a set, cell free cure for dry eye ill. The bits come from a scale three D tank sys and a flow clean step. The team maps their protein and small RNA loads cross many make lots.

Loads stay near the same cross lots, rich in marks that hit dry eye paths. The bits speed eye skin wound close and calm fire cues in lab mods, dose by dose. One load mark ties in a straight line to fire calm force. Set make and a worth mark back clinic hopes.
pmc-13370209:
Laure Martinelli, Chao Sun, Nicolas Papon, and Vincent Courdavault comment on new work decoding how the fever tree builds its famed alkaloids. The bark of Cinchona trees gave the world quinine, the first strong malaria drug. Malaria still kills about six hundred thousand people a year. Knowing how the plant makes these compounds could aid supply and drug design.

Quinine was isolated in the early nineteenth century and ruled malaria care for decades. Resistance later pushed treatment toward other drugs. The alkaloids stayed prized for their chemistry and wide effects. The study under discussion maps the scaffold the plant builds first. Such maps show which enzymes do which step. That knowledge opens routes to making these compounds in labs or microbes. The commentary places the finding in a long arc from bark remedy to modern synthesis.
pmc-13370709:
Donald L Peden and colleagues test whether cutting off leg blood flow briefly after sprint training boosts muscle powerhouses in a 2026 study. Twenty active men followed a six-week sprint interval programme, with twelve getting post-exercise blood flow restriction and eight training without it. Muscle samples were taken before and after, alongside fitness and lactate tests.

The restricted group gained in a key enzyme marker of mitochondrial content and in breathing capacity through two mitochondrial complexes, while the control group showed no such gains. Overall fitness measures did not split the groups as clearly. The study suggests that a short, controlled blood-flow block after sprints can deepen the muscle response, though larger trials are needed before coaches adopt it widely.
pmc-13371609:
Leonardo Provetti Cunha and co-authors looked at swelling at the back of the eye after surgery in a 2026 study. They tracked 92 eyes that had a thin film peeled from the retina, a step used to fix blurred sight. Some eyes swelled in the weeks after the work.

Eight eyes, close to one in eleven, swelled and got a slow-release drug implant placed in the eye. Eye charts and scans were checked before and after care. Thickness at the eye center fell in both groups after surgery. The report adds real clinic counts that can help surgeons warn patients and plan follow-up visits.
pmc-13373709:
Jo, Byoun, Joo, Cho, and Yun present a study from twenty twenty-six on blood thinner timing before planned artery opening procedures. The drug clopidogrel needs hours to suppress platelets fully. Records cover over one thousand stable angina patients at one center. Patients split by whether the drug-to-procedure gap was six hours or less. Major bad heart events at thirty days are rare and equal across groups. Heart enzyme levels after the procedure run higher with shorter gaps. The gap matters most at one hour or less.

Higher enzyme bumps at low thresholds occur more with short gaps. Severe-level bumps do not differ between groups. The authors link late dosing to mild heart strain, not events. Weighting methods balance the groups for fair comparison.
pmc-13374209:
Shihan Fang and colleagues follow how families make sense of teen depression and self-injury over time in a 2026 study. Adolescent depression with non-suicidal self-injury is usually lived, talked about, and reshaped inside the family, yet most research tracks risk factors or caregiver burden alone. Ten adolescent-caregiver pairs were interviewed in hospital and again at one, three, and six months after discharge.

The analysis traces how meanings of illness, self-injury, and safety converge, diverge, and turn at key moments across the illness course. During hospitalisation, family interactions were reorganised around crisis and care. The study shows meaning as a joint, moving process, not a fixed label, and it points to family talks at turning points as places where safety can be rebuilt.
pmc-13374509:
Luigi Gamberini and co-authors mixed a plant plastic with a heal-able web in a 2026 study. The plant plastic breaks down in soil, a green plus, but can be stiff. The web can heal cuts when warmed, which may stretch a product's life.

Three mixes were made, from rich in plant plastic to half and half. Heat tests showed one blend point for the two light mixes, set twixt the parts' own points. The half mix held spare wet web that softened it. Scope views after the plant part was washed out showed the web's shape. The mix map guides green stuff that is both tough and repairable.
pmc-13377809:
Xuan Sha and colleagues link MEIOSIN gene variants to premature ovarian insufficiency in a 2026 study. Premature ovarian insufficiency drives female infertility, yet its genetic basis is incompletely known. MEIOSIN starts meiosis by activating key meiotic genes for the mitosis-to-meiosis switch in germ cells. Whole-exome sequencing in affected sisters, validated by Sanger sequencing, found two compound heterozygous variants.

The variants were c.980T>C and a novel deletion c.1068_1092del. Functional assays, including protein blots, immunostaining, structural modelling, and reporter assays, tested how the variants affect MEIOSIN activity and meiotic gene transcription. The work confirms MEIOSIN as a cause of premature ovarian insufficiency and gives families a genetic explanation for early ovarian failure.
pmc-13377909:
Bente Nyvad and Ole Fejerskov tell how the north lands cut tooth rot in a 2026 paper. Town water with added mineral is oft praised for that win. A new pool, though, finds its add-on gain is small where brush paste with the mineral is in all homes.

Big folk logs of the north for 50 years show low rot held for years by self brush with such paste alone. The paste heals first rot by halt of mineral loss at the tooth face. It shifts the whole rot curve, tail and all, so the worst-off gain too. The team backs brush drives as the core act.
pmc-13379509:
Inbar and colleagues interviewed Huntington's disease families in 2026 about genetic testing for themselves and for future children. The disease is inherited, so each child of an affected parent faces even odds of developing it, and embryo testing can screen for the faulty gene before pregnancy. Fifty-one people took part at a national clinic in Israel, where such services are fully funded: patients, at-risk relatives, and partners.

Three themes emerged. Many relatives had been unaware of their risk despite the clear inheritance pattern, a gap the authors tie to family silence and missed diagnoses. Views on personal testing split between wanting early knowledge and fearing the weight of knowing when no cure exists. The central pattern, the recommendation paradox, was that people who avoided or regretted their own testing still strongly backed embryo testing for their children. Counselors, the authors say, should address that split directly.
pmc-13380409:
Jayanjali Bodavula, Adam D Long, and Eric Delman report a 2026 case of a rapidly worsening deep abscess after surgery to remove a testicle through the groin. That operation, usually done for suspected cancer, rarely causes serious infection. Their patient was a man aged 32 whose type 2 diabetes was poorly controlled.

A week after surgery he developed mild groin swelling, first thought to be a harmless blood collection. Within days he had severe pain, redness, and blood signs of spreading infection. Scans found a large pocket of infection above the bladder tracking into the scrotum. Urgent surgery drained and cleaned the area, and cultures grew two bacteria, including a drug-resistant form of a common gut germ.
pmc-13380709:
Ehsan Zangene and co-authors introduce a 2026 online resource, called DORSSAA, for studying how drugs bind to proteins. New lab methods can show which proteins change their stability when a drug is added, revealing the drug's targets. Results, though, are scattered across many studies with no shared home.

The platform gathers such data into one searchable system with tools for comparison and display. It already holds more than a million records. They span 135 compounds, tens of thousands of protein targets, and 38 cell lines and organisms. Two worked examples show its use: profiling a known drug in lung cells, and tracing drug combinations in leukaemia cells. The resource is designed to keep growing.
pmc-13382709:
Jonathan B Wallach and colleagues argue in a 2026 article that radiation treatment for cancer spread to only a few sites should often be labelled curative, not palliative. The idea of an in-between state, called oligometastatic disease, dates to 1995. In it, cancer has spread in a limited way and cure or long control may still be possible.

Trial results presented in 2018 accelerated the shift toward high-dose targeted radiation for such patients, and larger trials followed. The authors draw on a survey by a veterans' health task force of cancer specialists in veterans' facilities. Most respondents agreed high-dose radiation benefits well-chosen patients. Redefining intent, they argue, changes planning, consent, and follow-up.
pmc-13383909:
Yan Sun and colleagues test whether electrical nerve stimulation eases knee osteoarthritis through gut microbes in rat studies in 2026 work. Rats with knee disease received one of three stimulation strengths, a standard joint drug, or no treatment. After three weeks, joint measures, gene signals, and gut microbe profiles were compared, followed by stool transfer tests.

Stimulated rats walked and loaded the joint better, with lower levels of three inflammatory messengers. Bone-building signals rose, bone density improved, and cartilage damage scores fell in the treated groups. Gut microbe mixes shifted with treatment, and transfers carried part of the effect, which supports a gut-joint link in the benefit.
pmc-13385809:
Kim, Oh, Moon, and Rho shrink a directional loudspeaker into a single compact device in this 2026 paper. Parametric speakers use ultrasound to beam sound into a narrow spot. Classic versions need arrays of tens to hundreds of emitters, which are costly and complex.

Their device pairs one piezoelectric driver with two kinds of metamaterial: an acoustic surface and elastic units, designed together. The metamaterials shape both the ultrasound and its conversion into audible sound. Experiments show directional audio across four octaves, from 500 hertz to 10 kilohertz. That bandwidth from one small unit is the advance. The authors pitch personal sound zones without the array price tag.
pmc-13386209:
Seiji Noda and Saeka Kondo report a fifty-six-year-old man whose hazy abdominal fat on a CT scan was the first clue to large vessel vasculitis. He arrived with two weeks of fever, headache, and upper abdominal pain, plus scalp tenderness and very high inflammation markers. The initial scan showed increased density in the mesenteric fat, a finding called misty mesentery.

Antibiotics for presumed infection failed and inflammation climbed further. A contrast scan then revealed thickening of the aortic wall, pointing to vasculitis of the large arteries. The authors present misty mesentery as an under-recognized early imaging sign that should prompt a search for large vessel inflammation.
pmc-13388509:
Raimundo Rafael Gamela leads a 2026 study of soybean tissue grown in the lab and exposed to copper nanoparticles. The team used transgenic soybean callus, a clump of plant cells, as a simple model for how crops respond to metal stress.

A combined instrument separated chemical species and measured both their molecular form and their copper content in a single run. Callus exposed to lower doses showed less chemical variety than callus at the highest dose, and the overall chemical pattern shifted step by step as the dose rose. Plant scientists and analysts will value the paired molecular and elemental view, which shows both what compounds are present and where the metal sits among them.
pmc-13389709:
Michael Salzle and co-authors report, in 2026, a 79-year-old woman with no symptoms who carried two separate tumours found by chance. Scans for painless blood in her urine showed a large left adrenal mass measuring more than nine centimetres across.

Blood and urine tests showed very high levels of metanephrine compounds, pointing to a pheochromocytoma, a tumour that releases stress hormones. A repeat scan before surgery then revealed a second, partly calcified mass in the belly lining, which proved after removal to be a spread midgut carcinoid tumour. Both masses were removed in one operation. Endocrine surgeons gain a reminder to keep scanning after the first answer, since a second rare tumour can hide behind the first.
pmc-13392009:
Gangbin Yan's team used tracer exchange to reveal non-Fickian ion spread in olivine lithium iron phosphate, a model one-axis carrier for cells. Standard models falter where trapping, jumble, lattice warp, and coupled ion-e motion complicate transport.

Lithium isotope exchange proved single-file spread, where ions cannot pass each other, and simulations plus current-time scans found e transport as rate-limiting in cell reactions. Lithium-sodium exchange instead showed apparent super-spread, attributed to sodium-boosted cross-channel hopping driving a switch from one-axis to quasi-2D transport. The work used tracer exchange in olivine lithium iron phosphate.
pmc-13392209:
Xiaoju Zheng and a large team report, in 2026, changes in neck blood flow and cognition after a microsurgical lymphatic operation in Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimer's has been linked more and more to poor drainage in the neck. Both vein flow and lymph flow play a part. Poor drainage may cut blood flow to the brain and slow the clearing of toxic waste.

Eighty-three patients had deep cervical lymphatic-venous anastomosis on both sides, an operation that reconnects lymph channels to veins to restore drainage. Ultrasound of neck veins and arteries and cognitive testing were done before and after surgery. Surgeons and brain doctors gain early data from just after surgery. The idea is still debated. Hard flow and thinking scores are what it needs next, and this work starts that task.
pmc-13392309:
Christine Ruffin's team weighed sleep-drug results in cats having rear urethra surgery in chest-down versus back-down lying pose, since posing effects were unknown and many such cats already carry acute kidney injury. pmc-13419009:

pmc-13419309:

pmc-13419409:

pmc-13419609:

pmc-13420109:

pmc-13420709:

pmc-13421109:

pmc-13421209:

pmc-13421609:

pmc-13421809:

pmc-13422009:

pmc-13422809:

pmc-13423309:

pmc-13424009:

pmc-13424309:

pmc-13424809:

pmc-13424909:

pmc-13426709:

pmc-13427109:

pmc-13427309:

pmc-13427609:

pmc-13427809:

pmc-13427909:

pmc-13428309:

pmc-13428409:

pmc-13429109:

pmc-13430809:

pmc-13431009:

pmc-13432909:

pmc-13434009:

pmc-13434109:

pmc-13434509:

pmc-13434709:

pmc-13435009:

pmc-13435409:

pmc-13437209:

pmc-13438809:

pmc-13439409:

pmc-13441809:

pmc-13442709:

pmc-13443109:

pmc-13445809:

pmc-13446209:

pmc-13446309:

pmc-13447109:

pmc-13447209:

pmc-13448009:

pmc-13448109:

pmc-13448809:

pmc-13449209:

pmc-13449409:

pmc-13449509:

pmc-13449809:

pmc-13449909:

pmc-13450409:

pmc-13450509:

pmc-13451209:

pmc-13451809:

pmc-13451909:

pmc-13452209:

pmc-13452409:

pmc-13452909:

pmc-13453009:

pmc-13453609:

pmc-13453809:

pmc-13454309:

pmc-13454609:

pmc-13454709:

pmc-13454809:

pmc-13455009:

pmc-13455309:

pmc-13455409:

pmc-13456709:

pmc-13457309:

pmc-13457609:

pmc-13457709:

pmc-13458609:

pmc-13459409:

pmc-13460209:

pmc-13460709:

pmc-13461309:

pmc-13461609:

pmc-13461709:

pmc-13462109:

Performance dipped when ambiguous cases were included, for both model and readers. Stroke teams gain a complementary diagnostic tool for acute settings where FLAIR imaging cannot be obtained.
pmc-13462209:
Jonathan Massie and colleagues examine, in a 2026 letter, the hidden advice work of blood specialists in the United Kingdom, called liaison haematology. Such work includes formal and informal guidance to other clinicians, plus help reading lab results, for patients not under the specialist's own care. The labor is skilled and in demand, yet rarely counted in planning. Other fields, such as microbiology and psychiatry, have tried to measure similar loads.

The team used a mixed approach, starting with stakeholder interviews to learn what data mattered most. Survey and workload elements drawn from those talks measured demand and barriers across the country. Their letter frames the problem: a large, valued service runs largely unseen, with little record of its time cost or worth. Naming and defining the work is a first step. The authors aim to ground future staffing decisions in real evidence about this advice burden.
pmc-13463009:
Mi-young An built and tested a health literacy scale in 2026 for food and supplement use by pregnant women and new mothers. Pregnancy raises needs for iron, folate, and other nutrients, yet no tool had gauged how well new mothers grasp food and supplement advice. The scale began with 60 draft items across word knowledge, familiarity, reading, and number skills.

Expert review cut the pool to 42 items, and testing with 315 women plus Rasch analysis left a final 23-item tool. Its internal consistency reached 0.87, and a cut score of 12.50 separated high from low literacy with fair accuracy. Clinics and community programs can use the short scale to spot mothers who need plainer, tailored food guidance.
pmc-13463709:
Yingxin Wang and eight co-authors validate a stool PCR test for Helicobacter pylori, a stomach germ tied to ulcers and cancer. The standard breath test needs special gear and carries small radiation concerns. A stool test would be easier to run if it proved just as exact.

Agreement with the breath test was near perfect, and accuracy in spiked control checks reached one hundred percent. Misses clustered where germ counts sat near the test floor.
pmc-13463809:
Khanate Sayasit and seven co-authors design one PCR test meant to catch a whole genus of mosquito-borne viruses. The Orthoflavivirus genus holds dengue, Zika, West Nile, yellow fever, and Japanese encephalitis viruses, whose gene codes differ sharply. The team skipped classic sequence alignment and mined short code chunks called k-mers instead.

Across 11,846 virus genomes the search found a conserved six-hundred-letter stretch in one gene, fit for primer design. The test sensed most target viruses at one to ten copies per microliter, though West Nile needed far more. On stored patient material the test reached high overall accuracy and matched dengue calls exactly. The method offers a template for broad tests against fast-changing virus groups.
pmc-13465509:
Jia Sun leads a team that knocks out the Adcy5 gene in Nile tilapia to probe pigment control. The gene makes cAMP, a cell messenger downstream of hormone signals, yet its pigment role was murky. Gene-edited fish lost their black vertical bars and paled across the body.

Inside black and red pigment cells, the granules clumped at the center and refused to spread, a transport failure. Melanin-making genes quieted and total melanin fell in several tissues. Flooding cells with cAMP partly restored spreading, while an upstream hormone push helped little, which places the gene mid-cascade. Red cell involvement widens its role past black pigment alone.
pmc-13466509:
Laura E. Hirshfield and colleagues asked in 2026 whether medical students who majored in social sciences or humanities choose different specialties than science majors. Past work tied such backgrounds to humanistic qualities, yet evidence on specialty choice was mixed and rarely national. The team analysed 49,214 United States graduates from 2018 to 2020, about 82% of allopathic graduates in those years.

Students who took patient-focused electives showed the same lean. Recruiting more humanities majors may thus help fill primary care gaps, though the study cannot prove major choice causes the preference.
pmc-13466809:
Carson Peters and colleagues evaluate Facebook advertising as a recruitment tool for clinical research, with attention to messages tailored for a key population, in a 2026 study. The design mixed numbers with voices: ad performance data on one side, and in-depth interviews with fifteen recruiters on the other. Targeted ads were compared against general ones on equal footing.

People who saw tailored ads joined at a higher rate than those who saw general ads, about a third versus about a quarter, and expressed interest more often too. Interview themes explained what recruiters believe makes targeting work. The combined display of both strands is meant to guide teams planning sign-up drives.
pmc-13466909:
Mıdık and a wide team of Turkish cancer doctors read in 2026 the charts of 32 patients with liver cancer that could not be cut out. All had a twin immune drug plan as first care. The plan, called STRIDE, pairs two drugs that free the immune system to hunt tumors. A world trial had shown a life gain, but proof from Türkiye was thin. The cases came from 18 hubs.

The mid point of time with no growth was just past seven months. Mid life span sat near eleven and a half months, with the top end not yet reached in the count. Half the group had liver harm not tied to a virus, and two in five had the B virus form. Grave side effects hit fewer than one in ten patients. The authors call the plan workable, and urge a bigger, head to head test.
pmc-13467309:
Simab Kanwal and colleagues describe in 2026 how they reworked a photosynthetic bacterium to make more of a key building block for natural pigments. The organism, Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803, can be pushed to produce geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, a starting material for carotenoids and other valuable compounds used in food and health products. The team blocked storage pathways so more carbon flowed toward pigment production.

Two engineered strains were compared with the normal strain under varied conditions, including added carbon and ultraviolet light. Cutting both glycogen and a bioplastic storage pathway gave the strongest gains in pigment buildup. The work points toward growing pigments and related compounds in sunlight-driven microbes instead of extracting them from plants or making them by chemistry.
pmc-13467709:
Sylvia Waschke and colleagues validate in 2026 a cheap handheld device for sorting recycled fishing net plastics at the point of collection. Good recycling needs correct polymer identification, but the precise laboratory method requires fixed equipment that coastal collection points do not have. Their device, called Melting Box 1.0, repurposes the controlled heater of a commercial vaporizer to watch small samples soften and melt.

Test plastics from Vietnamese fishing net recycling, including polyethylene, polypropylene, polyamide, and blends, were scored on a simple three-step visual scale. Agreement with the laboratory-grade Kofler hot bench was good, with an average offset of only 2.9 degrees on melting start across the comparisons. A field tool that sorts nets on the beach could raise the quality of recycled plastic before it ever reaches a factory.
pmc-13468209:
Ma and colleagues mapped the genes behind maize resistance to Fusarium ear rot in 2026, a fungal disease that cuts grain yield and quality worldwide. They crossed a resistant line with a susceptible one and followed 257 offspring lines over three years, scanning their genomes with over 6,800 markers.

Five resistance regions were found on five different chromosomes, each explaining a modest share of the variation in disease. The strongest region, on chromosome 5, explained about thirteen percent and held two candidate genes. Those genes behaved differently in the resistant and susceptible parents, supporting their role. No maize line is fully resistant, so the authors present these regions as breeding material for stacking partial protection into commercial varieties.
pmc-13468409:
Junpeng Wu, Yaoyang Zhang, Hancheng Zhang, Ning Bai, Yajin Ye and Kunrong He published this 2026 study of drought-response genes in pecan trees. The XTH gene family helps plants remodel their cell walls, which matters under water shortage, but its pecan members were unmapped. The team searched the pecan genome, catalogued the family, and then tested one standout gene by inserting it into a model plant.

They found 34 XTH genes in pecan, falling into four evolutionary groups. Several responded to drought, and one, CiXTH18, switched on strongly and stayed on. Arabidopsis plants carrying CiXTH18 grew longer roots under laboratory drought stress made with a water-binding chemical. Their detached leaves lost water more slowly, and their tissue held less hydrogen peroxide, a damage marker. The inserted gene also boosted two known drought-response genes after stress. The authors nominate CiXTH18 as a candidate for breeding hardier nut trees.
pmc-13469309:
Muhammad Ammar and colleagues profiled tick viruses in 2026 from livestock ticks in Punjab, Pakistan, beyond the known Crimean-Congo fever virus. Eighty-seven ticks from four genera were pooled into eleven groups for RNA sequencing, while blood surveys covered 319 livestock, 253 people, and 214 rats. The work aimed to set a first baseline for the country's tick virome.

Sequences matched 31 viruses across at least eleven families, with new strains of Jingmen, brown dog tick phlebovirus 2, and Liman tick viruses confirmed. Antibodies showed exposure in all three host groups, and neutralising antibodies in two livestock, one person, and one rat proved productive Jingmen infection. The hidden zoonotic risk argues for stronger tick surveillance and risk assessment in Pakistan.
pmc-13469409:
Jannatul Ferdous and colleagues build TL-RL-FusionNet in 2026, a ransomware detector that learns which training cases deserve the most attention. Modern ransomware behaves in mixed ways, some of them harmless looking, and it spreads fast through linked business systems. Older signature tools miss these shifting patterns.

The system turns sandbox behavior reports into color grids, then reads them with two pretrained image networks whose features are merged. A small learning agent adjusts the weight of each training case during learning, much like a gambler favoring better bets. Fresh scoring tables in each test round prevent information leakage. On the team dataset the detector scored above 99 percent accuracy. On a public benchmark it reached about 90 percent, showing a harder test.
pmc-13469609:
Hankare and colleagues in India told in 2026 of fifteen children with stiff one side cerebral palsy whose leg faults were fixed in one operation day. Such palsy warps the leg at three heights: the calf pulls the foot down, a thigh cord pulls the knee in, and toe cords curl the toes. Fix one height alone, and the rest still spoil the gait. Their single event plan cut all three in one go for each child.

The gains were broad. Ankle bend swung from a down pull to a sound up reach. Knee bend at walk fell to a quarter of its start mark, and toe curl cleared in each child. Gait grew more even, steps grew longer, and skill class rose for most. Snags were few: one over fix and one weak leg. The authors back the three cut plan as safe and strong for walk ready children.
pmc-13469909:
Xiaona Song and colleagues introduce BEV-Nexus in 2026, a fusion system that helps self driving cars detect objects in three dimensions from a bird eye view. Merging camera images with laser point clouds often stumbles on wrong depth guesses and poorly aligned features. Their design lets the point cloud guide the image branch as it predicts depth, using true depth data and projected points as anchors.

A second module weighs the two feature streams window by window, according to how well they agree, which reduces alignment errors. A third block widens the view of each feature while adding a light attention step. On the nuScenes benchmark the system beat its base model on both main detection scores, by close to two points on the validation set. Speed stayed nearly unchanged, which the authors count as a practical advantage.
pmc-13470009:
Mohammad Mahdi Kariminejad and colleagues analyze in 2026 how errors grow in a cheap motion sensor that sits perfectly still. A smartphone carrying a MEMS inertial unit was fixed at a surveyed point, giving a zero motion reference. Seventy five half minute recordings, taken ten times per second, fed a statistical workup of both raw readings and the positions computed from them.

The team checked whether the data looked normal, steady over time, and even in spread, then fitted time series models and examined the frequency content. A joint estimation method assigned error shares to each computed state at once. Acceleration and rotation readings on all three axes behaved like steady white noise. The study offers a baseline for judging how much drift such sensors add before any real movement begins.
pmc-13470409:
Yang and co-authors chart the womb-like shift in black rockfish, a fish that bears live young. The fish keeps sperm for near six months with no store pouch. While young grow, the egg bed swaps its job to feed them. That swap looks much like the womb bed shift in milk beasts. The team built a cell map of the egg bed in three states. States were no-egg, sound growth, and failed growth in the fish.

Cross-kind blends with human and mouse sets show shared shift plans. Each kind, though, runs the plan through its own cell types. A part clan named annexins ties to sperm store in the fish. Failed growth showed skewed drain cells and fat-hold marks. The work frames how fish and beasts met at like womb traits.
pmc-13470809:
Xiang Cheng and colleagues formulate in 2026 a modified cement grout for shoring up crushed sandstone deep in mines. Grouts must flow well into broken rock yet harden into strong support, a balance that water content controls. Their blend uses ultrafine cement with a waterborne polyurethane modifier plus additives for flow, expansion, and fast setting, tested across a range of water to cement ratios.

A small polyurethane dose shortened setting, cut shrinkage, and raised strength. As water rose, the slurry flowed better and set slower, while strength climbed then fell, peaking at a middle ratio. Grouted crushed sandstone at that ratio reached a peak strength about thirty nine percent above the plain control after twenty eight days. Microscopy and heat measurements tied the gain to how the polymer coats and bridges grains at each water level.
pmc-13471209:
Richard Daly and co-authors compile in 2026 the first national picture of venous thromboembolism rates in Ireland across eight years. More than fifty one thousand adult cases were recorded, giving a mean yearly incidence near one hundred seventy two per hundred thousand people. Primary clots averaged about ninety eight per hundred thousand. Hospital acquired clots ran near ten per thousand discharges. Pregnancy related clots came to about two and a half per thousand births. The authors offer the figures as a baseline for prevention policy and for judging the pandemic years.
pmc-13471409:
Huang and co-authors tested whether migraine weakens the ear's built-in protective reflexes, which are run from the brainstem. Having tinnitus on top of migraine added no further deficit, so the authors propose the reflex measure as an objective marker of migraine-related hearing pathway involvement.
pmc-13471509:
Le Moigne and co-authors grew twenty side-by-side lake-water bacterial groups under identical starting conditions to test whether chance alone shapes what a microbiome can do. Their 2026 metagenomics study focused on cellobiose, a plant sugar, and whether missing genes explained why some communities never used it.

The dispersal-limitation idea failed: several communities held every gene needed for cellobiose processing yet never touched the sugar. The team reconstructed 122 bacterial genomes with a median completeness of 94.67% across the microcosms, and found functional redundancy, many species able to do the same job, mirrored the random draw of genomes. That overlap was lower within groups than between them, a signature of similar species competing.
pmc-13471609:
In a 2026 study from Shanghai, Xindi Shen and three colleagues tested whether a short course built around patient stories could raise empathy in medical students. Eighty third-year students took part, with half taking an eight-week narrative medicine course and half following usual teaching. The course asked students to read closely, write notes beside the chart, and discuss reactions in groups.

Overall empathy and its thinking side rose more in the course group, while compassionate care scores did not differ. Interviews pointed to a move from disease to person, stronger story-based communication, and emotional reflection. As a single-centre pilot, the work shows short-term promise, and longer follow-up is still needed.
pmc-13471709:
Patrick Bedard and colleagues use brain and muscle recordings in 2026 to locate the source of rapid fatigability in myalgic encephalomyelitis, also called chronic fatigue syndrome. Force, forearm muscle electricity, and brain activity from scalp electrodes and scanners were recorded together, with fatigue onset set person by person.

Patients matched the healthy group on maximum force yet tired much sooner. Healthy volunteers ramped muscle and brain activity up until fatigue, then let it drift down. Patient muscles and brains, by contrast, barely fluctuated across the whole task. The flat central response points the authors toward the brain and its drive signals, rather than the muscle itself, as the seat of fatigability.
pmc-13473109:
Rabab Khaled and co-authors build a targeted drug carrier for cervical cancer in this 2026 paper. Cervical cancer is common worldwide and kills many women in poorer countries. pmc-13473309:
Kumar and colleagues modelled in 2026 how layered graphene materials respond when heat and load act together. Such graded materials shift their make-up gradually from one face to the other, mixing strength with low weight. The team studied two pairings, graphene with copper and titanium with zirconium, formed as a spherical shell. They applied two theories of thermoelasticity, the coupled physics of heat and strain.

Laplace transforms removed the time dependence from the equations, and finite element methods handled the spatial variation. The authors compared results across both theories and both pairings, presenting field values as graphs. The comparison showed where the graphene pairing behaved differently and where the numerical method mattered. The authors argue the finite element approach is needed for dependable design values in these coupled problems.
pmc-13474509:

Botanical extracts, hand removal of pests, planting-time shifts, and chili or tobacco sprays rounded out the list. Fall armyworm, maize stem borer, and African bollworm topped the pest list the practices target. The author reads the toolkit as generations-deep farming knowledge worth building into extension programs rather than replacing with purchased inputs these farmers largely lack.
pmc-13474609:
Tahvilian and co-authors pooled the randomized trial evidence on whether vegetarian diets calm C-reactive protein, the blood marker clinicians use to gauge body-wide inflammation. The answer was a near-perfect null. pmc-13474709:
Swain and co-authors investigated the July 2024 Chandipura virus outbreak in Gujarat, India, where a sandfly-borne virus caused explosive brain inflammation in children. pmc-13474909:

Every horse had at least one trigger point along the back, 85 percent showed a jump reaction when the spot was pressed, and 80 percent had restricted movement in the region. Behavior scores averaged 7.2 on the ridden checklist, and 40 percent of horses met the pain threshold of eight or more behaviors. Yet touch scores matched neither gait measures nor behavior tallies, so the authors keep palpation as the primary diagnostic tool.
pmc-13476209:

pmc-13477509:

Symptom measures appeared 205 times and thinking tests 146 times, while social functioning and quality of life appeared far less often. pmc-13479709:
Muneebah Vaid and coauthors present a 2026 review on skeletal muscle as an overlooked target of bisphenol A, the plastic chemical found in most human samples worldwide. pmc-13479809:

pmc-13479909:
Chaohui Wang and coauthors published a 2026 study of how sour jujube trees resist witches' broom disease, a germ sickness that twists growth and blocks fruit. pmc-13480809:

pmc-13482309:

pmc-13482609:
Wu and colleagues build a two-stage neural system in 2026 for direction-of-arrival estimation, the radar and sonar task of pinpointing where a signal comes from. pmc-13483709:

Among adults, a history of autoimmune disease appeared in 31.4 percent of positive patients versus 19.2 percent of controls. pmc-13483909:

The real-release group reported a significantly larger pain drop than the sham group across the sessions measured. Disability scores also improved more with real treatment, by an amount the authors judge clinically meaningful. Reach toward the floor trended better right after treatment but faded by the one-week check. Balance gains were mixed. Hejazi Yekta presents the brief therapy as a useful add-on needing longer trials.
pmc-13486309:

pmc-13486509:

pmc-13486709:
