pmc-13487709:
Ryan LaGrone reports a 2026 case of an infected aortic bulge that came back after repair, with two rare germ foes at once. Infected aortic bulges, called mycotic aneurysms, make up under five percent of all aortic bulges. Klebsiella germ cases fill just three past reports, with one repeat case. A threadworm, Strongyloides, joins the mix here for the first time in such a report.

The worm can ferry gut germs into the blood as it moves through the body. That path may have reseeded the aorta with Klebsiella. Care cut out infected chest and belly tissue in full. A bypass graft then ran from armpit to both groins, far from the tainted field. Open repair stays the top choice in such cases. How long drug care should last stays an open point.
pmc-13487909:
Jingmei Xiao and co-authors revisit trial data in a 2026 post-hoc analysis of people taking antipsychotic medicines for schizophrenia or bipolar disorder. Such drugs often cause weight gain and insulin problems. Volunteers had received a probiotic, dietary fiber, both together, or placebos for twelve weeks, with blood levels of short-chain fatty acids measured over time.

Higher levels of two gut-related acids, propionate and butyrate, were linked with lower weight, lower body mass index, and better insulin measures in the combined treatment context. The links were modest and come from a secondary analysis, so they suggest a mechanism rather than prove one. Still, the findings point to gut products as a possible route to ease metabolic harm.
pmc-13488209:
Melanie Arnreiter and co-authors test whether surgeon and patient sex pairing affects heart surgery outcomes in a 2026 nationwide Austrian study. Women patients fare worse after cardiac surgery on average, and some fields report benefits when doctor and patient sex match. The registry held 57,729 adults having one of four common first-time heart operations between 2012 and 2022, treated by 239 surgeons, of whom about a fifth were women.

Female patients had higher rates of the combined bad outcome, covering death, readmission, or complications within thirty days, regardless of surgeon sex in the reported figures. Surgeon sex alone showed no independent link with outcomes, and pairing mattered no more than chance. The authors direct improvement efforts toward clinical risk preparation instead.
pmc-13488609:
Karlsson and colleagues in Sweden fed in 2026 eight forms of nickel to human lung cells in dishes, to see which forms get in and which do harm. Nickel dust at work has long been tied to lung cancer, but its many forms, from salts to nano grains, act in unlike ways. The team sized and coated checked each form, then tracked cell uptake with fine scopes and metal gauges over two days.

One form, a nickel sulfur mix, did the most harm by far, and it also shed the most nickel ions into the broth. A plain nickel salt shed less and ranked next in harm, while one oxide form did no harm at all. All gritty forms showed up inside cells, tucked in sacs. Oddly, uptake rank and harm rank did not line up. The authors say harm springs from a tangle of uptake, ion shed, and form.
pmc-13490709:
Karakurt and two colleagues in Türkiye surveyed in 2026 how worn out health science students felt by online classes. They gave the Zoom Burnout and Fatigue Scale, a scored survey, to 570 nursing and dietetics students in their second, third, and fourth years. The group came from one university in the east of the country, and most had taken theory courses online in the prior school year.

The mean score sat near the mid point of the five point scale, so the group showed average levels of strain, not extreme ones. Scores ran higher for students who found distance study harder than face to face study. The same held for those who had trouble reaching course sources or using the tech. The authors urge active learning methods in online theory courses and easier access to class materials for all students.
pmc-13491709:
Lauren He and five co-authors ask in 2026 what women's health providers know about rheumatic diseases, which often strike during the childbearing years and complicate pregnancy choices. Guidelines exist, yet nobody had mapped what front-line clinicians know. A national online questionnaire tested 200 providers, mostly at universities, on new disease presentations, contraception, and drug management around pregnancy.

Scores were weakest for spotting new rheumatic disease around and after birth, where barely a quarter of answers were correct. Contraception counseling earned the best scores and the highest confidence, though gaps remained there too. Seven in ten respondents said the web was their main resource. Most wanted guidance as websites, printed guidelines, or phone apps. The authors call for shared resources built with rheumatology colleagues.
pmc-13491809:
Febe Hertveldt leads an eleven-author team listening in 2026 to families in crisis whose babies cannot settle, sleep, or feed normally long past the usual age. Persistent regulatory problems strain the bond between parent and infant, sometimes to breaking point. Six couples who had received specialist infant mental health treatment were interviewed in depth, and their accounts were analyzed thematically.

Parents described the experience as a rupture of everyday life rather than ordinary tiredness. Fathers often escaped into work while mothers stayed trapped in round-the-clock care, an imbalance that deepened exhaustion on both sides. Outside dismissal and inward shame cut families off from help, leaving them isolated on what felt like an island. Long after the worst phase, vulnerability and resilience coexisted in different mixes, and the authors press for recognition and accessible support.
pmc-13492009:
Negin Armide and others report a newborn with two rare from birth states together: neurocutaneous melanosis and Dandy-Walker malformation. In 2026, the case concerns a five-day-old girl born at term with many large pigmented skin moles over her body and no nerve symptoms at presentation. Brain imaging showed cystic expansion of the fourth ventricle, underdevelopment of the back brain vermis, and an enlarged posterior fossa.

Skin biopsy showed melanosis, and the merged finding has fewer than forty found cases. Both pigment cells and parts of the central nervous system arise from the neural crest, suggesting a shared developmental origin. Because hydrocephalus and central nervous system malignancy may follow, the authors call for multidisciplinary tracking despite the currently quiet presentation.
pmc-13492109:
Catriona M Steele leads a twenty-five-author team updating in 2026 a landmark review of how liquid thickness and food texture change swallowing. The question guides diets for people who struggle to swallow safely. The update covers studies from 2012 to 2024 that used the international IDDSI framework's standard consistency levels. From an initial pool of over sixty thousand records, 465 studies qualified.

Seventy studies with non-overlapping data anchored the synthesis, most using X-ray video of swallowing. Every study that measured safety found thicker liquids safer than thinner ones, since thin drinks slip toward the airway more easily. Smaller sips limited leftover residue when liquids were thickened, while solid textures rarely entered the airway but left more residue in patients. The reviewers stress tailoring texture changes to each person's measured swallowing.
pmc-13493809:
Oloruntola and colleagues fed Guinea hen weed leaf meal to rabbits raised in hot, humid tropical conditions, where heat stress normally slows growth and stirs inflammation. In the 2026 trial, 80 young rabbits received one of five diets, from a plain basal feed up to 20 grams of leaf meal per kilogram. The team tracked weight gain, feed efficiency, antioxidant enzymes in muscle, and inflammatory signals in blood and liver.

Rabbits on the highest dose finished far heavier than the control group, ending above 2,400 grams against roughly 2,085 grams for the unsupplemented animals. They also converted feed more efficiently, and their muscle antioxidant enzymes rose while a marker of fat damage fell. A key inflammatory messenger in the liver dropped steeply, from just under 289 to about 81 units, while a calming immune signal climbed. The authors recommend the two highest doses, while noting no cool-condition control group existed.
pmc-13493909:
Lee and colleagues watched how bacterial communities in water shift when arsenic or cadmium, two toxic metals from industry, leak in. Their 2026 microcosm study, a set of controlled indoor ecosystems, dosed water with each metal at two strengths and tracked the microbes by reading a standard bacterial identity gene. Some tanks included sediment, the mud layer at the bottom of real waterways, and others held water alone.

Communities in open water changed fastest, while sediment buffered the shift and kept communities steadier. Cadmium provoked bigger changes than arsenic at the same dose, marking it as the more disruptive contaminant here. The team also named fingerprint genera for each metal: two bacterial groups signalled arsenic exposure, and six different ones signalled cadmium. They propose such microbial fingerprints as early-warning tools, since bacteria react to pollution long before fish or visible damage appear, though field validation still lies ahead.
pmc-13495509:
Zixuan Yang, Ke Zhao, Yuanye Hu, Quan Zhang, and Qinhan Zhou rank, in a 2026 network meta-analysis, which exercise recipes best sharpen cognitive flexibility in children and teens. The skill means shifting thought and action as goals change, and it is tested with card sorting and switching tasks. The team gathered trials in five databases through late 2025.

Twenty-one studies with 3,099 young people qualified. Sessions of about half to most of an hour beat both shorter and much longer ones. Single aerobic exercise and exercise paired with thinking tasks each beat control conditions. Programs of five to eight weeks beat very long ones. Rankings pointed to a sweet spot: sessions near forty minutes, twice a week, over five to eight weeks, at low intensity. The authors offer the recipe as a guide for school and clinic programs.
pmc-13499709:
Ross, with Tatta and Bezner, argues that pain care for LGBTQIA+ people needs a new base. Rates of long-term pain run about twice as high in this group. Past care has stressed flaws and weak spots in the person. That view can hide bias, stress from stigma, and blocks to kind care. The authors call for care built on strength instead. It should back coping skills, free choice, and pride in who a person is. Ties to community count as part of care too.

Physical therapists sit in a strong place to lead this shift. They can build trust and safe sessions. They can plan movement around what each person values most.
pmc-13499909:
Marina Ruiz Piñero and colleagues test in 2026 whether minor hallucinations, faint false sightings such as sensing a presence nearby, can separate dementia with Lewy bodies from Alzheimer disease early on. Both dementias look similar at mild stages, with overlapping thinking profiles, yet correct naming increasingly guides treatment. Their prospective study enrolled 121 patients with probable disease at mild stages, all supported by disease-specific biomarkers, for clinical, thinking, and perception testing.

Memory loss ran deeper in Alzheimer disease across recall tests, while thinking scores otherwise overlapped heavily. Minor hallucinations appeared in over half the Lewy body group against a small minority in the other group in the reported shares. Seeing patterns in noise, called pareidolia, was also far more frequent, the strongest split among the perception tests. The authors argue that routinely asking about these experiences sharpens early diagnosis.
pmc-13500709:
Nuno José Lopes and co-authors examine in 2026 a familiar shopping habit, switching between options across repeated choices, when people choose together rather than alone. Variety-seeking is well documented for solo consumers, yet friends, couples, and colleagues pick restaurants, snacks, and trips jointly all the time, and the group dynamic might change the pattern. Two studies compared pairs choosing together against individuals choosing alone, probing fairness instincts, preference overlap, and worries about how each chooser appeared to the other.

Pairs sought more variety than solo choosers in the reported findings. Reciprocity drove the effect, with partners taking turns indulging each other's favourites across rounds, which naturally diversifies the basket. When both partners loved the same option, pair variety dropped, making preference alignment a brake on the process. Impression concerns mattered only through the gap between partners' scores, not their absolute levels, refining how marketers should think about group choice.
pmc-13500809:
Emi Ogasawara leads an eight-author team reporting a 2026 drug test in mice bred to model mitochondrial disease. The animals, called mito-mice, accumulate mitochondrial DNA carrying a large deletion, which damages cellular energy production and causes symptoms resembling human mitochondrial disorders. The team gave the mice mitochonic acid 5, an indole compound derived from a plant hormone, and tracked how the disease developed.

Treatment slowed the progression of symptoms such as low body weight and lactic acidosis, a buildup of lactic acid in the blood. In the kidneys, the compound protected breathing-like respiration inside mitochondria and prevented renal failure even when the deleted DNA exceeded 80 percent of the total. Heart tissue showed similar recovery of respiration. The authors suggest the drug could delay some mitochondrial diseases, especially those threatening the kidneys.
pmc-13501309:
Fang and colleagues presented SlotDeconv, a method for estimating which cell types occupy each spot in spatial transcriptomics data, in a 2026 paper. The technology measures gene activity at spots across a tissue slice. Unmixing fails when sister cell types look identical and when neighborhood information is ignored.

Fang split the problem in two: a reference module learns distinctive signature vectors for each cell type, trained with a diversity constraint that pushes similar types apart. A spatial module first estimates proportions spot by spot, then smooths them using neighborhood consistency. Removing the diversity constraint cut accuracy sharply, and using average profiles instead of learned signatures collapsed it entirely. Against four rivals on a twenty-seven-cell-type mouse brain dataset, SlotDeconv achieved the highest correlations, with the biggest gains exactly on the confused cortical neuron subtypes. It validated on human pancreatic cancer and mouse olfactory bulb tissues.
pmc-13501609:
Yusaku Yokotani leads an eleven-author team reporting a 2026 pilot study of early stomach cancer whose cells cannot repair DNA mismatches properly. Such dMMR tumours often respond to immune checkpoint drugs, but responses vary, so the team examined what distinguishes these cases. Twenty patients treated between November 2019 and July 2024 were included, and staining tests identified eight whose cancers were mismatch repair deficient. Those eight received extra staining for immune checkpoint molecules in the tumour surroundings.

The median age of the deficient group was 73 years. Among all twenty patients, female sex and severe stomach lining atrophy were associated with the deficient status in single-variable analysis, with a wide confidence interval reflecting the tiny sample. Checkpoint molecule patterns differed from case to case rather than following one signature. The authors present the work as hypothesis-generating groundwork for understanding why checkpoint blockade helps only some of these patients.
pmc-13501709:
Ruijun Xin leads a six-author team presenting a 2026 systematic review of cervical cancer screening policy and coverage across the world. The team searched three major databases to February 2025, plus websites and WHO sources, assembling official recommendations from 77 countries and regions. Only 62.3 percent of them even stated when their protocol was published or updated. Cytology, the Pap test approach, remained the primary method in 80.5 percent of countries, while visual inspection with acetic acid led in low-development settings and few countries had adopted HPV testing as the main screen.

Coverage tracked wealth starkly: 12.43 percent in low human development settings against 49.74 percent where development is very high, and 51.68 percent in high-income countries against 34.45 percent in low- and middle-income ones on those groupings. High-risk regions managed only 29.88 percent coverage. Screening peaked among women aged 30 to 39 and sagged at the youngest and oldest ages, far below the 70 percent global target.
pmc-13501809:
Huiwen Zhou leads an eight-author team reporting a 2026 analysis of the RZFP gene family in sugarcane. The family of E3 ubiquitin ligase genes tags proteins for disposal and tunes plant signalling. Tillering, the making of side shoots, decides sugarcane yield, yet its molecular control is murky. Working from the XTT22 genome, the team identified 47 family members and sorted them into three groups. Segmental duplication drove the growth, and most copies evolved under purifying selection.

Co-expression network analysis singled out six candidate genes tied to tillering, sitting in a module whose partner genes were enriched for photosynthesis. Predicted regulators included WRKY, AP2/ERF, TCP, and DBB transcription factors. Laboratory expression tests then showed all six candidates responding to the hormones that govern tillering, with the pattern suggesting they restrain shoot production. The authors offer the six as leads for breeding higher-yielding cane.
pmc-13502309:
Saurav Bathla leads a four-author team reporting a 2026 dental case series on horizontal root fractures, breaks that split a tooth root sideways through dentine, cementum, and pulp. Three teeth were each repaired by a different strategy, chosen for fracture position, looseness, and presentation. One root canal was sealed with a bioactive glass material in putty form. A second tooth took internal reinforcement from a fiberglass post. The third was steadied with orthodontic wire stabilization rather than a splint.

Fractures of this kind complicate between 0.5 and 7 percent of dental injuries and can end in pulp death, root resorption, or a lost tooth when handling is late or wrong. Middle and tip fractures sometimes heal quietly on their own, which makes blanket rules unwise. The authors argue the formula is early diagnosis plus a plan fitted to the individual break, balancing stability for healing against preserving the tooth's structure.
pmc-13503409:
Rotter and Seifert surveyed 895 doctors in Germany and Austria about medicine shortages. They asked which of twenty common drugs ran short between late 2022 and early 2024 and how much extra work each shortage created. Their 2026 study finds the burden uneven: the antibiotics penicillin V and amoxicillin hit doctors hardest overall, but which drug hurt most depended on country, workplace, and specialty. Doctors' experience often diverged from official shortage lists.

The hidden cost was time. Chasing substitutes, rewriting prescriptions, and counselling patients consumed the most added minutes per affected drug in haematology and oncology, at over three quarters of an hour. Psychiatry and kidney medicine ran close behind, and general practice was not far back. The authors argue official reporting should match what practices actually experience. They present the specialty and drug breakdowns as a map for where stockpiling and communication fixes would pay off fastest.
pmc-13505009:
Yumiko Saito-Nakano leads a team tracking how long an amoeba keeps the virulence that animal passage gave it, in a 2026 study. The parasite Entamoeba histolytica causes gut disease and liver abscesses. Lab strains lose their bite over time unless they pass through an animal host now and then.

The team cloned a strain fresh from hamster livers and tested three clones on hamsters over months of lab culture. All three began highly virulent, making abscesses over a third of the liver's weight. Each clone lost that power on its own schedule, gone by six, twelve, or eighteen months. Gene reads showed few letter changes, and gene activity shifts barely overlapped between clones. Virulence here looks like a fleeting state, not a fixed trait.
pmc-13506209:
Karipidis and Karipidis proposed a mechanism for post-exertional malaise, the crash after activity that defines some long COVID patients, in a 2026 hypothesis paper. These patients show symptoms a day or two after exertion with normal heart tests, which the authors argue are blind to microvessel dysfunction. Their model centers on an enzyme in vessel linings that makes nitric oxide, a vessel-relaxing gas.

Karipidis proposes the virus leaves the vessel lining inflamed and drains its supply of a helper molecule the enzyme needs. When exercise raises blood flow friction, the starved enzyme produces a damaging oxidant instead of nitric oxide, fueling an injury cycle. Their two-threshold model separates the exertion level that triggers malaise from a tolerance threshold for vessel stress. They specify blood markers and vessel tests, timed a day or two after a challenge, that could confirm or refute it.
pmc-13506509:
A Gheller and colleagues report a 2026 study from Brazil on how rectal tumors shrink after chemoradiation, and where stray tumor cells remain. They followed 40 people with lower rectal cancer treated first with short-course radiation and six cycles of CAPOX chemotherapy. The team then checked surgical specimens for spread patterns that matter for smaller, organ-saving surgery.

Nineteen patients reached the ypT0 to ypT2 range that could suit local excision. Most showed a solid shrink pattern, no spread beyond the visible tumor, and no lymph node disease. The widest hidden spread measured 8 mm. Such detail can help surgeons set safe margins and choose who can keep the rectum.
pmc-13507109: Francesco Morichetti tells of a silicon photonic chip that both makes and reads light polarisation. His short piece from twenty twenty-six lays out a circuit whose setup can be changed. Polarisation is a trait much used in photonics and data links. To steer that trait inside small circuits has stayed hard. The new chip joins making and reading in one device. That pairing opens paths to sharper sensing and new ways to work with light data. One base for both jobs makes future photonic work simpler.
pmc-13507309:
Joyce Evelyn Ansah, Daniel Apaak, and Thomas Hormenu run, in 2026 work, a prospective cohort study of gestational diabetes risk among pregnant women attending clinics in Ghana's Central Region. Gestational diabetes, high blood sugar first found in pregnancy, endangers mothers and babies and burdens health systems. The team followed 1577 women with questionnaires and records analysis.

About 7.2 percent developed the condition during follow-up. Prior gestational diabetes towered as the strongest predictor, with family diabetes history and age above forty also raising odds sharply. Higher income brackets predicted risk too, an unusual direction hinting at diet and lifestyle shifts. The authors urge Ghana's health service to fund earlier screening and pre-pregnancy education for high-risk women.
pmc-13508109:
Luca De Simone Carone leads a ten-author team describing two unusual sugar-based coatings found on a gut bacterium, in 2026 work. The bacterium, Bacteroides stercoris DSM 19555, lives in the human gut, where surface coatings shape talks between microbes and the immune system. Lab analysis showed one coating was a rough form of a common bacterial surface molecule with rare chemical tweaks. The second was a branched, positively charged capsule rich in amino sugars. Neither structure had been reported before.

Both coatings pushed immune cells toward calm rather than alarm. They raised levels of IL-10, a signal linked to quieting inflammation, while holding down classic alarm signals. The capsule had the stronger calming effect. In a lab model mixing gut lining and immune cells, both coatings kept responses low. The results recast gut bacterial coatings as active peacekeepers, not mere triggers.
pmc-13508309:
Jiayu Chen leads a thirteen-author team building an antibody drug aimed at stopping the spread of triple-negative breast cancer, in 2026 work. Spread causes most deaths in this hard-to-treat cancer type. A surface protein called PZR helps cancer cells move, invade, and travel. The team made antibodies against PZR and measured how they bind. Cell dish tests checked whether the lead antibody slowed movement and how the protein partners with a known adhesion molecule.

The lead antibody bound PZR and entered cancer cells that carry the protein. It cut migration and spread in dish tests and a mouse model of metastasis. PZR turned out to grip an adhesion partner that anchors cells to the protein mesh around them, switching on a growth signal. The humanized antibody kept its binding strength and anti-spread effect. The results support PZR as a fresh target in this cancer.
pmc-13508409:
Dorothy Hung and seven co-authors examine whether lean management helped American primary care practices weather the post-pandemic years, in 2026 work. Lean methods, borrowed from manufacturing, streamline work and cut waste in clinics. Data came from a national survey of 1,245 physician practices. They then compared lean and non-lean practices on crisis response, finances after the pandemic, and how workforce shortages hit patient care.

Lean practices tended to be larger, tied to health systems or community health centers, and heavier users of value-based payment deals. After accounting for those traits, lean practices were far more likely to run an incident command system during the pandemic. They were also more likely to act on clinician burnout. The authors argue that habits of structured problem solving double as crisis readiness. For small practices, the study frames lean adoption as resilience building, not mere efficiency chasing.
pmc-13508809:
Tripathy applied machine learning in 2026 to predict infant deaths in India, using data from the NFHS-5 national family health survey. Spotting the strongest risk signs could help target aid where infant deaths stay high. Newer computer methods may catch patterns that standard models miss.

Five models were trained and scored on how often they were right and how well they ranked risk. Random forest and decision tree models reached about 74 percent accuracy. That clearly beat the classic regression model at about 65 percent, and the tree models also scored higher on ranking skill. Six factors stood out as the strongest predictors: birth order, the mother's schooling, twin birth, household wealth, cooking fuel type, and the mother's age at her first birth. Tripathy argues such tools can guide focused programs for high-risk families.
pmc-13510209:
Yufeng Xie and eight co-authors test a plant compound called phellodendrine in a zebrafish model of inflammatory bowel disease, in 2026 work. The disease brings lasting gut inflammation, and current drugs often work weakly or carry heavy side effects. The team triggered bowel inflammation in zebrafish with a chemical irritant, then measured immune cell entry, gene activity, gut barrier strength, microbes, and oxidative stress with and without the compound.

Treated fish showed less immune cell invasion and a shift in immune cells toward a calmer state, with inflammatory genes turned down and protective ones turned up. The gut barrier held better, with more mucus protein, more mucus-making cells, and less leaking. Harmful microbes fell while helpful ones rose, and oxidative stress eased. Computer pathway work pointed to a few inflammatory routes and six candidate target genes for follow-up.
pmc-13511309:
María Casares-Jimenez and fourteen co-authors describe the clinical load of symptomatic hepatitis E virus genotype three infection in southern Spain, in 2026 work. This virus type is a leading cause of sudden liver inflammation in Europe. Ten hospitals sent suspected cases for central testing between 2022 and 2025, using a standard two-step check of antibodies and viral RNA, with viral typing for positive cases.

Of 1124 people tested, 267 infections were confirmed, and the positive share stayed high across the study years. About two fifths of patients needed hospital admission, a small share developed severe liver failure, and three died, each with major other illness. Major comorbidity on its own predicted both admission and severe disease. The authors say host health, more than viral differences, drove bad outcomes in routine care.
pmc-13511909:
Reeja Raj and eleven co-authors present an infant case of a life-threatening overreaction of the immune system, in 2026 work. The syndrome, called HLH, floods the body with inflammatory signals and can shut down organs. An eight-month-old girl with influenza A arrived with seizures, a swollen liver and spleen, and low blood cell counts. Her ferritin and two immune signals ran very high, all pointing toward the syndrome.

Treatment aimed at the syndrome and at the virus began, yet she died of heart and lung failure. Gene testing found single-copy changes in two genes tied to immune control, hinting at a built-in predisposition. The team stresses how hard it is to separate inherited forms from infection-triggered ones at the bedside. Early gene and signal profiling, they argue, could steer how hard to suppress immunity in each case.
pmc-13515109:
Ding Li and five colleagues compare gut microbes in grazing yaks and feedlot Holstein cattle living at high altitude, in a 2026 study from the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. Yaks evolved for thin air and sparse forage, while imported Holsteins often struggle there. Twenty animals of each type provided samples for gene surveys and deep DNA profiling, backed by lab fermentation tests, digestive enzyme tests, and blood measures.

Yak microbes were richer in enzyme families that attack plant carbohydrates, and lab cultures from yak dung digested dry matter more completely with stronger enzyme activity. Blood profiles diverged too, with yaks showing higher levels of several immune signals and Holsteins higher IgG antibody levels. Li's team links the contrasting microbes to the animals' different digestion and immune profiles, while cautioning that diet and management differed alongside species.
pmc-13516009:
Kanokwan Suwannarong and ten colleagues survey wildlife contact and eating habits in Thailand's border provinces in a 2026 One Health study. These rural, ethnically mixed communities live close to animals, and such contact is a known route for new infections. Between late 2020 and mid 2022 the team interviewed four hundred villagers face to face and tested blood for melioidosis, a soil-borne disease.

Wildlife eating was near universal over a lifetime, and almost two-thirds had eaten wildlife in the past six months. Wild boar led the menu, followed by rice-field rats. Most participants were women, many worked in farming, and understanding of zoonotic risk and immunity was thin. One subdistrict stood out, with about a fifth of its tested villagers carrying melioidosis antibodies. Suwannarong's team urges stronger health education for staff, village volunteers, and residents on the risks of wildlife contact and consumption.
pmc-13517209:
Zhen Liu and co-authors test in this 2026 study whether a coated feed additive helps young White King pigeons through weaning. Weaning is the stressful switch from parent-fed pigeon milk to eating on their own at about one month old. The additive is sodium butyrate, a gut-friendly acid salt, in a protective coating.

Birds receiving the supplement grew better and showed healthier intestines than unsupplemented birds at the same stage. Their gut lining developed more fully, and the mix of microbes in the intestine shifted in favorable ways, alongside improved immune measures. The coating also removes the additive's sharp smell and lets it blend evenly with the grit pigeons need. The authors recommend it as a tool for easing the weaning transition in meat pigeon production.
pmc-13518309:
Chunwei Li and Panfeng Zhao clone and measure a self-incompatibility gene across tomato species in a 2026 study. Many flowering plants reject their own pollen, a system steered by S-RNase genes in the style. The pair gathered partial copies of a relative gene, named ZS, from four tomato species. The lines mixed self-rejecters with self-accepters. They tracked where and how strongly each copy switched on.

The ZS genes spoke only in styles, never elsewhere. Volume differed sharply by species. One self-accepting clade, S habrochaites, ran its copies louder than the self-rejecting S chilense, an upset of the tidy expectation that expression level simply follows the mating system. Li and Zhao frame the atlas as groundwork: knowing which copies exist and how they behave is the step before anyone can explain, or breed around, tomato self-incompatibility at the molecular level.
pmc-13518809:
Yuxing Cai, Yuxuan Zhang, Hanyu Gao, and Yong Huang report a 2026 recipe for ring-shaped biaryl molecules, paired aromatic rings whose twist gives them handedness. Such ring-constrained structures interest drug designers, yet making them with adjustable ring sizes had few good methods. Medium rings are notoriously hard to close.

Their twist-expand-seal plan first opens a flat ring with a chiral carbene catalyst to set the twist. Alcohols of varying chain length then widen the ring, and a final bond-forming step seals it shut. Across 49 examples they reached yields up to 99 percent and near-perfect handedness control. Ring sizes ran from 9 to 14 members, widening the design space.
pmc-13518909:
Na Wei leads a seven-author study in 2026 asking whether circular economy practices cut production-based carbon emissions in six leading circular economies: Austria, Belgium, South Korea, Spain, Sweden, and the United States. The team used municipal waste generation and treatment as a stand-in measure for circularity, an angle earlier work had barely tested.

Data from 1991 to 2020 passed through several econometric methods, including pooled and country-level lag models plus causality checks. Circular economy activity linked to long-run emission reductions across the panel and in most individual countries. Spain was the exception. Wei and colleagues say the pattern supports circular strategies as climate policy, with room to learn why Spain diverged.
pmc-13519009:
Norbert Solymosi leads a nine-author team sequencing DNA from an ancient Egyptian corn mummy in 2026. Corn mummies are human-shaped ritual figures sprouted from grain, soil, and water for the Khoiak festival. The Budapest specimen dates to the later third century BC, and the team asked whether any ancient DNA survived inside it.

Metagenomic reads mixed obvious modern contaminants with material that could plausibly be ancient. Spore-forming Bacillus relatives dominated the bacterial traces. Wheat fragments matched ancient emmer wheat from Egypt and the southern Levant most closely, while moth traces resembled hawk moth genomes. Human fragments carried mitochondrial and Y-chromosome lineages common in Africa today, consistent with the object's origin.
pmc-13519409:
Ruchita Kishor Rathod and colleagues compared post materials used to rebuild teeth after root canal treatment, asking which spreads chewing stress most safely. Published in 2026, the review weighed fiber-reinforced composite posts against cast metal and stainless steel posts. A post anchors the rebuilt crown core inside the root, so its stiffness shapes where stress lands and whether the root cracks.

Fiber posts flex much like dentin, the tooth's own tissue, so they spread stress evenly and lower fracture risk. Metal posts, being far stiffer, pile stress at the root tip and neck, raising the chance of a vertical crack. The authors argue that dentists should weigh biomechanical fit alongside strength and grip when choosing a post. Readers gain a practical rule: the strongest post is not always the kindest to the tooth it must save.
pmc-13520409:
Belal Al-zu'bi and colleagues screen in 2026 bone tumours for a vitamin A processing enzyme called CYP26A1, which is raised in many cancers yet had not been mapped in bone tumours. Tissue staining covered 95 tumours spanning benign, intermediate and malignant types, plus normal bone.

Normal bone showed no staining, while about one third of tumours stained positive. Intermediate tumours stained most often, especially giant cell tumours, whereas bone-forming cancers such as osteosarcoma generally showed none. Rare chordoma and adamantinoma cases stained strongly despite tiny numbers. Protein network analysis adds context on what the enzyme may interact with in tumour tissue.
pmc-13520509:
Cevher İlhan Cevheri tests in 2026 whether mixing composted farmyard manure with mineral fertiliser lifts cotton yield and profit under semi-arid, irrigated conditions. Low soil organic matter and rising fertiliser prices squeeze growers of the Candia variety in chalky soils.

Nine feeding plans varied phosphate, urea and manure doses. Manure plus urea at the middle manure rate gave the highest seed cotton yield, about one third above the unfertilised control, with heavier bolls and better fibre output. Fibre quality traits stayed unchanged across plans. Tallest plants came from the highest phosphate plan. Economic results begin in the opening summary, supporting manure integration for profit.
pmc-13520609:
Christine Li, Julia Rogers, Haya Raef, and Laura Aspey present a case report, published in 2026. It describes one 54-year-old man with advanced cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. This is a skin-homing blood cancer. His severe itching had resisted many standard treatments. His mycosis fungoides covered most of his skin. He was receiving palliative chemotherapy. Dermatology was consulted during a hospital admission for infected skin wounds.

He was started on nemolizumab. This antibody drug blocks the receptor for interleukin-31, a key itch signal. Within seven days of a single loading dose, his itching resolved completely. The relief held at about six months. No side effects were reported. The authors offer this as support for this new use.
pmc-13522509:
Na Ju and colleagues report a battery study, published in 2026. It uses a single crystal as the electrode of a water-based proton battery. Most work on these safe, cheap batteries designs molecules. This team asked how molecular stacking changes proton storage. They studied a naphthoquinone compound. Diffraction, microscopy, and calculations were used.

Stacked molecular pairs formed a reinforced crystal face. It had the lowest energy cost for taking up protons. The electrode used nearly all of its theoretical capacity. A full cell built from the material performed accordingly. Crystal engineering matters as much as molecular design in these batteries, the study argues.
pmc-13523209:
Marwan Sheikh-Taha audits medication safety in older adults with heart failure in a 2026 retrospective study. Home medication lists for five hundred twenty-four patients aged sixty-five or older admitted to two hospitals were checked against the 2023 Beers Criteria. That list names medicines that can be risky in older adults. Medicines were sorted into categories such as generally inappropriate, risky interactions, and dose problems in kidney impairment.

Nine in ten patients were taking at least one flagged medicine, and about a quarter of all home medicines met the criteria. Stomach, heart, and brain medicines were the commonest flagged groups. Kidney disease, depression, prostate enlargement, and a higher total number of conditions each predicted a heavier flagged burden. The author recommends targeted medication review and careful deprescribing in such patients.
pmc-13523309:
Joshua Onyango and colleagues analyze risk factors for udder infection in Nigerian dairy cows in a 2026 multilevel study. A cross-sectional survey covered two hundred ninety-eight farms in Plateau State, collecting farm, animal, housing, milking hygiene, and treatment information. Infection was counted at herd level from farmer-reported cases in the current lactation, a definition the authors note could misclassify some herds without laboratory confirmation.

Nearly six in ten herds reported mastitis in the current year. Large herds had markedly higher odds, and the presence of working bulls also mattered. Post-milking teat dipping was strongly linked to lower odds, as were aspects of milking hygiene such as separate cleaning cloths. Treatment practices also entered the final models. The authors offer the layered analysis as a guide for targeted control on diverse farms.
pmc-13523509:
Marilyn Macdonald and others map, in a 2026 scoping review, models of publicly funded home care for older adults living in the community across six high-income countries. Home care supports aging in place, yet funding, governance, and delivery differ sharply between systems. Evidence about those models was scattered and hard to compare.

The review covered Canada, England, Denmark, Sweden, Australia, and New Zealand, searching three databases from 2005 onward plus grey literature. Nineteen sources were included. Five models emerged, ranging from provincially organized Canadian care and Australia's consumer-directed packages to municipal universal welfare in Denmark and Sweden, direct payments in England, and nationally framed services in New Zealand. Review evidence was uneven and mostly descriptive, with relational care and workforce conditions prominent in noted experience.
pmc-13524709:
Devika Nair and colleagues analyze, in a 2026 longitudinal study, symptom burden after starting dialysis and its link with hospitalization. Symptoms weigh heavily on people with kidney failure, yet which symptom patterns best predict hospital use was unclear. Latent transition analysis sorted patients into low, moderate, and high symptom burden groups. The high group combined severe symptoms with strong disease impact. Nearly every questionnaire scale, adjusted for patient characteristics, predicted higher hospitalization hazard. High overall burden raised the hazard by about one fifth. Worsening pain interference and fatigue each added measurable risk on their own. The authors propose symptom tracking as a practical prognostic tool at dialysis start.
pmc-13525109:
Julian Scherer replies to a letter about clinical guidance for tuberculosis of the spine. A cited case tells why: a teen treated for spinal TB in fact had a fungal infection and a hidden immune disorder.

Each recommendation must trace to a small set of chosen studies on set questions. Host immune strength never entered that frame. The reply thanks the critics while holding the method line. It shows how format rules can bound what guidance panels may say.
pmc-13527109:
Zhao and colleagues separate two miserable sensations in this 2026 mouse study of visceral pain, aching from the internal organs, and itch, asking how one brain region tells them apart. The authors argue the amygdala sorts these aversive signals by dedicated circuit and molecule, offering two precise drug targets for conditions that resist current treatments.
pmc-13527509:
Meng and colleagues reported a 2026 case of stubborn lower-leg ulcers linked to cabozantinib, in a man with kidney cancer that had spread widely. His cancer had first been treated with immunotherapy, stopped for a severe skin reaction, and he switched to cabozantinib in 2022 after radiation failed, with a good tumor response.

Meng describes how a small spontaneous ulcer appeared on his right leg about six months into cabozantinib treatment, on a background of untreated poor vein circulation. It worsened into a painful, treatment-resistant wound by mid-2024. The drug was paused on suspicion of toxicity, swabs found only normal skin bacteria. The authors discuss how vessel-blocking drugs impair wound healing and outline management lessons for similar patients.
pmc-13528109:
Syeda Humaida Hasan and six colleagues chart birth defects in a Bangladeshi newborn intensive care unit in a 2026 study. Defects were sorted with a standard disease code system.

Muscle and bone problems were the most common group, with sixty-seven cases. Cleft lip and palate came next, then heart and circulation faults. Sadly, about thirty-one percent of affected babies died. Their death risk ran about 1.6 times that of babies without defects. Mother's high blood pressure and diabetes each linked with far higher odds. Too much or too little fluid around the baby also linked strongly. The authors urge antenatal screening and routine newborn checks.
pmc-13530109:
Tian Niu, Qicong Li, and Ao Zhang search in 2026 for RNA-binding proteins that forecast survival in papillary kidney cancer. Such proteins control how gene messages get used inside cells, yet their role in this kidney cancer type was unclear. Data came from a large public cancer atlas.

From hundreds of altered proteins, seven stood out for their link to patient survival. A risk score built from those seven separated patients into groups with clearly different outcomes in both test sets. Lab checks on kidney cell lines confirmed changed levels for several proteins, supporting a scoring tool for treatment planning.
pmc-13530209:
Lu Weihua and co-authors devise a 2026 method for moving color schemes from paintings onto consumer products through felt emotion. Shoppers increasingly want goods that stir a feeling, yet product shapes leave little room for novelty. Color carries that emotional load across cultures without words.

Painting colors were grouped, product color plans were mapped by part and function, and volunteer ratings tied each group to emotion words. Matching emotion labels then bridged a painting group to a product plan. A coffee machine test using Chinese paintings showed richer color and stronger perceived design value.
pmc-13531809:
Xiaohai Luo and colleagues link belly-fat chemistry to poor bone healing in a 2026 hospital study of leg fractures. Records covered 485 adults whose thigh or shin shaft fractures were fixed with internal rods between 2022 and 2025. A visceral fat index combined waist size, body mass, and blood fat measures.

About 12 percent showed delayed union or nonunion at six months. The fat index ran clearly higher in that group, and each unit rise lifted the odds of poor healing by roughly 60 percent after full adjustment. The index beat plain body mass and waist measures at telling groups apart.
pmc-13531909:
Diederick BH Verheijen leads a 2026 tissue study of a risky heart anatomy where a coronary artery runs inside the aortic wall before exiting. That buried segment may act like a flap valve linked to sudden death. Fifteen surgical patients from several centers donated the removed wall segment for staining and review.

All segments showed a two-layered middle wall with no outer layer between artery and aorta. The aorta side carried dense fibrous tissue matching the nearby valve junction. The artery side showed widespread degeneration: elastic fiber damage, cell loss, and matrix buildup. Damage grew with age, informing risk judgment.
pmc-13536709:

Follow-up lasted up to three years after a first infection. Statistical models estimated how repeat risk grows over time and which age, job, and residence groups face the highest risk of catching flu again.

Repeat risk rose in yearly steps and reached a modest share by the third year. Most repeat infections clustered 9 to 12 months after the first illness. Children and teens faced notably higher repeat risk than middle-aged and older adults, and work and residence patterns also mattered. The authors suggest that vaccine and prevention plans focus more tightly on young people and heavily exposed jobs.
pmc-13536809:
Barik and colleagues map son preference across India's districts and show its drivers change with geography, a fact national averages flatten away. Reported son preference ranged from under a tenth of women in some districts to over two fifths in others, clustering strongly across the northern and central belts. The local models showed the leading factors, mothers' illiteracy and large households, biting hard in the north and centre while barely mattering in the south. Local explanatory power peaked in the northern districts.
pmc-13537909:

The carriers wore display molecules that present cargo to killer T cells. Two internal flu pieces, from mouse and human sets, held on best. In mice, loaded carriers raised flu-specific killer T cell responses. The human display version also loaded cleanly, hinting at use in people. pmc-13538709:

Mark counts were compared by timing, stroke circulation, and eye side, with risk factor adjustment.

Patients scanned before and after stroke both carried clearly more marks than controls. Counts did not differ between pre- and post-stroke groups, between circulation territories, or between the eye on the stroke side and its partner. Adjustment erased the post-stroke link. The authors read the marks as signs of long-standing vessel strain from risk factors rather than fresh stroke damage.
pmc-13539209:
Milton Anguyo and colleagues published a survey study in 2026. They studied cervical cancer screening in northern Uganda. Screening prevents deaths through early detection and treatment. Knowledge and uptake among university women were poorly known. Over three hundred students and staff answered questionnaires. Participants were aged twenty-five to forty-nine years. Sampling was random within staff and student strata. The team measured knowledge, attitudes, and actual uptake. Statistical models searched for factors linked to screening.

Access and personal factors shaped uptake more strongly. The gap between knowing and doing is the core finding. Campus health programs could close that gap directly. Targeted outreach to unscreened women matters most.
pmc-13542009:

CD74 was much higher in leukemia tissue than in healthy controls, especially in subtypes rich in monocytes and in patients whose white cell counts ran high. Patients with high CD74 survived less well overall. Its level also tracked with more memory B cells, monocytes, and a calming type of macrophage inside tumors, and with pathways for antigen display and immune response. The authors propose CD74 as both a prognostic marker and a possible target for immune-based treatment.
pmc-13543009:

It fits a national set of pathology teaching goals. Paget disease is a disorder where bone breaks down and rebuilds in a disordered way.

The patient is a seventy-six-year-old woman with three months of worsening arm pain. She reports no injury, and her hearing has faded over the past year. Students are led to weigh her history, medicines, and past joint surgery. The case asks them to explain the disease's phases under the microscope. It also covers the problems the disease can cause, from pain to hearing loss. Teachers can use it to test both knowledge and reasoning.
pmc-13543509:
Zhilong Wang's team ran a 2026 feeding study testing a blend of three probiotic bacteria in weaned yaks, whose immature rumens and unsettled microbes make weaning a risky, growth-stalling transition. Sixteen eight-month-old yaks were split into two groups of eight; one got the blend of Bacillus and Lactobacillus species at 0.2 percent of dietary dry matter, the other ate the basal diet alone. Growth, blood readings, and rumen microbes and their products were tracked.

Inside the rumen, ammonia nitrogen fell while microbial protein and useful fermentation acids rose, showing a more productive microbial community. The authors present combined probiotics as a handy lever for guiding rumen growth at weaning.
pmc-13543609:

The authors propose dual targeting as a biomarker-guided strategy for this subtype.
pmc-13545709:

Their analysis drew on the LANDMARK trial, which compared one valve family against two established rivals in patients with severe aortic narrowing. Complications counted were nonfatal events in the first 30 days, such as stroke, major bleeding, kidney injury, or a new pacemaker.

Of 742 patients alive at 30 days, about a quarter had suffered at least one such event. That group died at roughly twice the rate of the complication-free group over the rest of the year, while quality of life among survivors looked similar. The authors label the analysis exploratory and warn about bias from studying only survivors.
pmc-13546709:

The parasite causes diarrhea, dehydration, and losses on goat farms. About one goat in five carried the parasite, with the highest rate in Kohat district. Summer brought a clear peak, near 30 percent, and the youngest kids, under about two weeks old, were hit hardest at roughly a third infected. Rates barely differed between males and females. The authors recommend farmer training, timed deworming, early screening, and cleaner water and housing.
pmc-13547109:
Aisan Nouri, Lisa Jamieson, and Seyed Kian Haji Seyed Javadi made a policy case in 2026 for silver diamine fluoride, a liquid painted onto tooth cavities to stop them without drilling. Drawing on reviews, trials, cost studies, and guidelines, they weighed the treatment across clinical, workforce, economic, and fairness angles. The liquid is cheap, quick to apply, and workable in community settings for children, older adults, and people who struggle to reach a dentist.

Uptake still lags because of unclear rules, weak payment routes, training gaps, worries about the black stain it leaves, and patchy follow-up. pmc-13547209:

Two treatments pointed the other way: breathing support with continuous positive airway pressure and light therapy for jaundice were linked with lower mortality. The authors call for stronger intensive care, skilled birth attendance, and infection control.
pmc-13547309:

A voting protocol commits entries, and standard hashing and digital signatures prove records are untampered and traceable. Access follows job roles, and an index speeds up searches.

Tests with ten thousand health transactions across four to ten nodes processed a few hundred transactions per second, and indexed lookups answered in under 65 milliseconds even as the network grew. The authors note that real deployment still needs testing for energy use, storage growth, and recovery from node failures.
pmc-13547609:
Huseong Lee and colleagues measured methane-making microbes in the rumens of young crossbred calves in 2026, looking for early links between microbe load and how the animals eat, grow, and ferment feed. The high group's rumen favored the classic methane genus, while the low group carried more bacteria tied to propionate production. Starter intake across all calves rose with methanogen counts. The authors frame the patterns as early-life signatures worth following.
pmc-13547809:
Mihretu Sergindo, Begetayinoral Lahole, Abraham Dimore, and eleven colleagues measure a hidden cost of smoky kitchens in this two thousand twenty-six study. Using Global Burden of Disease twenty twenty-three data, the team estimated years of life lost to diabetes attributable to that pollution across Eastern Sub-Saharan Africa, by sex, age, and country.

For twenty twenty-three they estimated about two hundred seventy-six thousand years of life lost. The age-standardized rate was one hundred thirty-four per hundred thousand. Rates climbed with age, reaching about five hundred sixty-two per hundred thousand above age fifty-five, with no significant variation by sex or location. The rate showed no improvement between nineteen ninety and twenty twenty-three. The authors frame clean cooking as unfinished diabetes prevention.
pmc-13548709:

Average scores sat in the middle range for each scale. pmc-13549809:

One hundred seventeen residents at one hospital answered in late two thousand twenty-three. They rated current training as strong on clinical skills but wanted broader teaching across research and general competencies. Most were eager to join a new core programme, favouring online formats and lighter workloads as support. Wishes shifted with seniority: juniors wanted basics and stress care, seniors wanted research methods and writing. The authors back a year-aware design.
pmc-13550409:

The pipeline judges video input on the fly and flags posture errors as they happen, aiming to prevent the injuries that bad form can cause. The team also curated a dataset of chair yoga poses, which they describe as the first of its kind. pmc-13551709:

Women in interviews found instructions, wording, response options, and the recall period clear and relevant. The authors present the paired tools as a step toward person-centered, rights-based abortion care that services can actually measure.
pmc-13551909:
Yehualashet Belayneh, leading four colleagues, published a 2026 case-control study of precancerous cervical lesions among women screened at public facilities in Debre Markos town, Ethiopia. Rural residence, living alone, sexually transmitted infection history, early sexual debut, and age above forty also raised odds. The authors use the list to target screening and prevention in the town's facilities.
pmc-13552209:

pmc-13552609:

pmc-13554109:

pmc-13554609:

It also tracks whether the disease comes back, as seen by scope checks inside the bowel. The results may help teams spot high-risk patients early and feed them better before surgery.
pmc-13555709:

pmc-13557209:

Delayed first support contact after diagnosis raised the risk of work disability, defined as a disability pension or over 300 sick days, and late negotiations showed a similar pattern for mental-health patients. Support begun more than 30 days after diagnosis already carried higher risk. The authors urge occupational health services to start support as early as possible after a first diagnosis.
pmc-13558409:

pmc-13558609:

pmc-13558709:
