pmc-13559009:
Zohreh Akbari and colleagues report a young woman whose birth control pills likely set up a rare, dangerous clot in the veins around the brain's core. The case report is from twenty twenty-six. She was thirty-four and had taken oral contraceptives for a year for polycystic ovary syndrome. She arrived with severe headache, seizures, fading consciousness, and both eyelids swollen.

A plain CT scan showed extensive bleeding inside the brain, with signs pointing to cavernous sinus thrombosis, a clot in the venous caverns beside the pituitary. She was too unstable for the vein-specific imaging that would confirm it, so the diagnosis stayed presumptive. Treatment was heparin, pressure control inside the skull, and finally removal of part of the skull as she worsened. The authors urge emergency teams to suspect this clot early in patients with clot-promoting factors, and to image and anticoagulate fast.
pmc-13559109:
Shi and colleagues published a 2026 study on spotting infection risk in preterm babies. A germ called Ureaplasma can infect newborn airways without clear early signs. The team studied 430 preterm infants at one hospital in Jinjiang, China. They built a scoring chart from mother and baby facts available early.

Ninety-two babies tested positive for the germ in airway samples overall. A mother's own genital infection with the germ raised risk most sharply. Early water-breaking and womb inflammation also raised the odds strongly. The chart sorted babies with high accuracy in the study's checks. Early flagging could focus monitoring and spare antibiotics for low-risk babies. All five risk inputs come from routine records, not special tests.
pmc-13559809:
Aaron Machen, Muhammad Rizwan Sardar, and Gilbert Aidinian report the case of a 72-year-old man found to have a wire retained inside his left internal carotid artery. Their 2026 case report explains that the wire remained from an endovascular procedure performed more than a year earlier at another facility. The man came to attention with dizziness, and duplex imaging revealed the foreign body.

Angiography showed the wire's tip curled inside the carotid, with the wire trailing down toward the descending aorta. Because so much time had passed, the team feared the tip had embedded in the vessel wall, making snare retrieval through a catheter risky. They chose open surgery instead, removing the wire and repairing the artery with a patch angioplasty, without complications. The authors place the case against a thin literature on open retrieval, noting most retained objects come out percutaneously when caught early.
pmc-13561109:
Thamyris Santos-Silva, Lívea Dornela Godoy, Francisco Guimarães, and Felipe Gomes wrote this review paper, published in 2026. It explains why one class of brain cells, parvalbumin interneurons, is especially fragile under stress across the whole lifespan.

These fast-firing cells keep brain circuits in balance and pace the rhythms that thought and emotion need. They also sit at the center of how people withstand or break under stress. The review gathers rodent evidence on what goes wrong: derailed development, weak spots in energy and oxidation control, inflammation signals, and gene-regulating marks. Stress also reshapes the nets that wrap these cells and shield them. Effects differ by brain area and by sex. The authors close with treatments that might protect the cells, from mood drugs to ketamine-like agents.
pmc-13561209:
Subedi and co-authors reported a 2026 case report of macrophage activation syndrome in a thirteen-month-old boy with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, a rare inflammatory childhood disease. The syndrome is a life threatening overreaction of the immune system that often masquerades as severe sepsis. He arrived two months after steroids were stopped, with high fever, rash, and lethargy.

Blood counts fell across all lines while inflammation markers soared, so he was first treated empirically for sepsis with antibiotics. Fever persisted and clotting failed progressively, with ferritin climbing to a markedly elevated level that pointed away from infection. Subedi found blood cultures negative and bone marrow showed none of the cell eating pattern often expected in this syndrome. High dose intravenous steroids produced rapid clinical and laboratory improvement, and he stayed well at three months.
pmc-13561709:
Cheng Yang and colleagues describe their first two cases of robot-assisted single-port surgery to clear inguinal and pelvic lymph nodes in penile cancer. Their 2026 case report introduces a suprapubic antegrade approach through one concealed incision. Node dissection remains the cornerstone for controlling this rare cancer's spread, yet open surgery brings skin death, infection, and swelling at high rates.

The first patient, aged sixty-one, had node-positive squamous cancer and underwent the robotic dissection two weeks after radical penectomy. The second, aged fifty-three, had both operations in one sitting. Neither man suffered major complications, and neither showed recurrence at six and two months of follow-up respectively. Cosmetic results benefit from the single hidden cut. The authors call the technique feasible in this tiny preliminary series, while stressing that cancer outcomes need larger cohorts and longer follow-up.
pmc-13561809:
Biswabhusan Dash and a large team of co-authors review little-studied aromatic plants as a source of new cancer-fighting compounds. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-six. Cancer still kills and sickens many people, so safer and stronger treatments remain in demand.

Following standard review rules, the team gathered studies that isolated plant compounds, mapped their structures, and tested them on cancer models. The finds span many chemical families, from scented oils to bitter plant steroids. Several compounds were new to science and carry fresh names. The review records which plants they came from, how they were identified, and what targets they hit. The authors frame these neglected plants as a frontier for drug discovery.
pmc-13562109:
Valentina Bellini, Matteo Panizzi, and Elena Bignami take up a gap in how artificial intelligence reaches the operating room. Their 2026 commentary responds to a review of barriers between AI research and anesthesia practice, from messy data to alert fatigue. The missing piece, they say, is the effect of AI-assisted work on the anesthesia providers themselves.

They propose two parallel tracks: a strict one for bedside decision tools, which need large trials and regulatory clearance, and a lighter one for scheduling and paperwork tools, judged by provider wellbeing. A scheduling tool that granted every first-choice leave request for 27 residents shows the lighter path can work. Treating staff wellbeing as a real endpoint, they argue, could speed adoption where clinical arguments alone have stalled.
pmc-13562209:
Yutong Cheng and colleagues chart the global burden of inflammatory bowel disease from 1990 to 2021 through the Global Burden of Disease database, sorting patterns by development level and sex. Their 2026 analysis tracks incidence, prevalence, mortality, and disability rates, then breaks down what drives change in each stratum. Gene-based tests of candidate exposures ride along as an exploratory strand.

Global incidence crept upward year by year while prevalence, death, and disability rates eased downward across the period. Wealthy regions still carried the heaviest standardized burden in 2021, yet mid-level regions posted the fastest incidence and prevalence gains. Aging drove change in rich countries, population growth in poor ones. The disability gap between countries ran wider among women than men. Every genetic link vanished after correction for multiple testing. The authors press for locally fitted strategies against an unevenly shared burden.
pmc-13562609:
Yao Liang leads a large team on blood lipids and checkpoint inhibitor outcomes. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with cancer patients on such drugs. Baseline lipid profiles were the focus of the review.

Past records of solid tumor patients were analyzed. Kidney, bladder, and esophagus cancers formed the groups. Lipid levels were tied to survival and side effects. In kidney cancer, high bad cholesterol linked to shorter survival. Low good cholesterol also linked to worse outcomes there. In esophagus cancer, higher bad cholesterol linked to longer control. Effects thus split by cancer type.
pmc-13562709:
Thomas J. Wilschut and colleagues tested whether a short online memory check can measure forgetting in kidney transplant patients. Memory problems are common after transplant yet hard to measure at scale in large clinics. Their tool, the Seattle-Groningen Memory Assessment, estimates how fast a person forgets from a paired-word learning task lasting eight minutes. This 2026 cross-sectional study compared 556 transplant recipients with 408 kidney donors.

Recipients forgot faster than donors, and the eight-minute score proved reliable as a measure of long-term retention. Scores also tracked age, education, sleep quality, fatigue, and quality of life, and linked to blood measures including white cell counts and iron deficiency. The authors present the brief remote test as a low-burden way to follow memory in transplant care and research.
pmc-13562809:
Amin, Manna, Nahin, and Hawlader review the twenty twenty-three dengue surge in Bangladesh in twenty twenty-six. Dengue is a viral infection spread by mosquitoes. Cases and deaths rose sharply at national level that year. The team combined a narrative review with an ecological analysis of climate and case data.

Data covered twenty nineteen to twenty twenty-three, with a focus on Dhaka City. Cases in Dhaka surged from June to December despite slightly lower average temperatures. Across all five years, dengue cases correlated with minimum temperature but not maximum temperature. Reports from hospitals noted atypical features in children, including less of the classic rash. The authors stress the complex role of climate in transmission. They call for vaccine work and proactive mosquito control.
pmc-13563909:
Ömer Faruk Öz and five colleagues look for a fingerprint of overactive bladder in women's urine, focusing on two acids. Overactive bladder is diagnosed by symptoms alone, urgency and frequency without infection, and its biology stays fuzzy. Their 2026 study recruited 186 women, excluding anyone with heart or metabolic disease or related medication. An eight-question score split them into 81 with probable overactive bladder and 105 controls. Urine succinate and malate were measured by mass spectrometry and scaled to creatinine.

Both acids ran higher in the bladder group, who were older and more often postmenopausal. After adjusting for age, body mass, births, and menopause, the link held for succinate at a ratio of 1.69, and weakly for malate at 1.25. Succinate discriminated the groups, with an accuracy area of 0.678. The authors call the finding hypothesis-generating: a sign that the bladder's energy handling may differ, pending studies that track diet and urinary microbes.
pmc-13564409:
Teixeira and a large team reported a new natural compound, canalesolide A, in twenty twenty-six. It comes from a marine cyanobacterium, a water-dwelling microbe, of the genus Okeania. The compound belongs to a family of ring-shaped molecules rich in oxygen groups.

The team found it by screening microbe extracts against Trypanosoma brucei, the parasite behind sleeping sickness, guided by chemical fingerprinting. Detailed spectroscopy, model compound building, and controlled breakdown pinned down its unusual structure. Gene mining located the likely assembly instructions in the microbe. The compound killed parasites at very low doses within an hour in lab tests. It also harmed mammal cells somewhat, and mouse tests suggested a narrow safety margin. The authors say more work must widen that margin.
pmc-13566409:
Carsten A. Wagner, John A. Sayer, and Michael Straub review, in a 2026 article for a European endourology section, when genetic testing helps people with kidney stones. More than forty genes can cause single-gene forms of stone disease, often with early onset, frequent recurrence, kidney damage, and problems outside the kidneys.

Recent studies found a likely single-gene cause in up to about a third of affected children and in a smaller share of unselected adults. The authors recommend testing for patients under twenty-five and for those with high-risk metabolic profiles. A precise genetic answer can guide personal treatment, diet advice, and screening of relatives who may share the risk.
pmc-13571009: Filges, Kildemoes, and Møller lay out a protocol for a Campbell systematic review on asylum waiting times. Long waits for asylum decisions may harm mental health and daily social life. The planned review will gather studies on that question. It will pool results with standard meta-analytic methods. The protocol follows set procedures for systematic reviews. Its stated goal is to analyze how long processing times affect asylum seekers and refugees. The review will cover both mental health outcomes and social functioning.
pmc-13571809:
Kathryn Ross and seven co-authors pilot a new trial design for feedback messages in weight loss programs, in a study published in twenty twenty-six. Feedback on self-tracking helps people lose weight, but no one knew which message parts do the work. The design flips each part on or off week by week, at random, for each person.

Twenty-eight adults with obesity tracked food, activity, and weight daily with an app, a wrist monitor, and a smart scale. Each week for sixteen weeks, chance decided which of four feedback parts each person got by text. Most stayed to the end and tracked on most days. Nearly all messages were opened, and most rated ones were judged helpful. The pilot shows the design works.
pmc-13572409:
Marco Antonio Barroca, with eight colleagues, reports a 2026 study that runs chemistry calculations partly on a quantum computer. The test case is oxygen reduction at a battery electrode surface, a step that sets how well lithium batteries work. Exact math for such systems is out of reach, so the team picked a small active space of key orbitals.

A density-based screen chose the orbitals, and a quantum method called sample-based quantum diagonalization did the hard part. Circuits ran on up to 80 qubits of an IBM Heron R2 chip. For spaces up to 12 orbitals, results matched a trusted classic method. At 27 orbitals, the extended version beat the classic methods that could still run at that size. The work hints at quantum help for hard reaction problems.
pmc-13572509:
Alessia Manganaro, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 mouse study of two drugs given just before a sharp bout of social stress. One bout of social defeat does not cause lasting low mood on its own, yet it primes mice to react strongly to a mild stress a week later. The team asked whether a dose right before the first bout can block that priming.

Male mice got a single shot of propranolol, a heart drug that blocks adrenaline signals, or of corticosterone, a stress hormone, or of salt water. After defeat and a later mild stress, social tests gauged the outcome. Propranolol partly blocked the priming effect. The design isolates a narrow window: treatment at the first stress, not during the later one. Results may hint at ways to blunt stress effects early, before patterns set in.
pmc-13572609:
Quanyou Shang, Xiaoning Zheng, and Yujue Wang published a 2026 study of rural development, carbon emissions, and infectious disease across China’s 31 provinces. Rural revitalization policies have changed village economies and environments over the past decade. The team asked how those changes interact with pollution and the spread of infection, using data from 2013 to 2023.

Carbon emissions clearly raised disease transmission. Rural revitalization showed a U-shaped effect: it first lowered infection risk, then raised it as travel and trade links grew. Effects also spilled across borders, so one province’s risk depended on its neighbours. The authors argue for low-carbon rural planning that changes with each stage of development. They also urge provinces to govern these shared risks together.
pmc-13573309:
Junfeng Lu, with six colleagues, carried out a 2026 study of how protons move through protic ionic liquids, salts that are liquid and carry spare protons. Proton flow drives fuel cells and green chemistry, and its path in water is well mapped. In these thicker, water-free liquids, the path was murky.

The team joined machine-learned force fields, advanced motion simulations, and proton NMR measures on choline amino acid liquids. Protons crossed a range of fleeting setups, most often a shared pair form called Zundel-like, more than the single form common in water. Free energy checks showed that chain flex and bulk jointly set the hop barriers. Heat sped up exchange by reshuffling hydrogen bonds, and quantum effects lowered the barrier further. The map links liquid structure to proton speed for design work.
pmc-13574709:
Zhengjun Zhou and nine co-authors hunt key genes tied to the Wnt path and immune acts in liver hurt from blood stop-start. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Such hurt strikes past liver swaps and can spoil grafts. Three past gene sets were mined, and bulk and lone-cell gene reads were run with learn tools to sift path and immune genes.

Four key genes came up: two heat-shock genes, NFATC1, and THBS1. All ran high in post-swap parts and split hurt from well with strong marks. Cell maps tied them to macrophage and mast cell shares. Mouse checks at six hours past flow back showed all four high as hurt peaked.
pmc-13574909:
Thomas C. Kwee and colleagues surveyed Dutch public attitudes toward warning patients in advance that a scan might be wrong, publishing the study in 2026. Diagnostic errors affect a few percent of routine imaging, yet debate about pre-procedure disclosure has rarely asked the public what it wants. The team surveyed 1,524 adults with CT vignettes varying patient age and stated error risk.

Overall, 88 percent agreed patients should be told in advance, with support strongest for younger patients and higher-risk scenarios. Stating a very low risk actually lowered agreement versus leaving risk unspecified. The findings suggest clinicians should frame prospective disclosure around patient age and risk level rather than assuming reluctance.
pmc-13575209:
Anurag Srivastava and six colleagues study rust-like corrosion in 3D-printed nickel-titanium alloy in a 2026 paper. This shape memory alloy returns to its set form after bending, and laser melting can print complex parts from it. Print settings leave pores and surface flaws that may invite corrosion.

Samples printed at two power levels and two hatch spacings soaked for 72 hours in a salt solution that mimics body fluid. The low-power set, cut along the build direction, held the most pores at 5.4 percent and pitted deepest, up to 110 micrometres. Wider hatch spacing gave better resistance on the face tested. Surfaces with fewer defects formed thin, compact protective films. The authors stress build direction and surface finishing over bulk settings alone.
pmc-13575309:
Hu Xin and five co-authors trace how red light steers fiber growth in plant stems in a 2026 paper. Fiber cells give stems their strength and length, and the team had earlier found light shapes their wall building. Here they show a light sensing protein and its partner factor sit atop the control chain, acting through a family of growth genes.

Mutants missing the light sensor grew overlong fibers, while mutants missing the partner factor grew short ones. The module binds directly to one family member's control region. Plants missing three family genes had short fibers; overproducing one made them longer. That gene switches on wall loosening genes, letting cells stretch. The cascade suggests stem traits could be tuned through light signals.
pmc-13575809:
Will Wade, Sijung Hu, and James Fleming argue that assistive technology markets in poorer countries should be shaped by building shared digital foundations first. Assistive tools now run on phones, cloud services, dedicated devices, and built-in systems, but cost, weak connectivity, unreliable power, and thin language support decide what can survive at scale. Writing in twenty twenty-six, the authors propose a three-layer market stack. Its base holds governed data and language resources. Above that sit reusable core models and standard pipelines. Local small firms then handle sales and service on top.

The point is not to replace phones, the authors stress, but to keep many delivery routes open so buyers can choose what fits local conditions. They urge funders and policymakers to treat data sets, language resources, and basic tooling as public investments that widen the range of products people with disabilities can actually get.
pmc-13576009:
Katherine Staab, Noah Johnson, and Ana Chiddington report a pilot project that changed how continuing medical education gets planned, in a 2026 paper. At Southern California Permanente Medical Group, course planning had run in silos, with stakeholders joining late. The redesign brought key people together from the first consultation.

Eighteen faculty and planners who had worked under both the old and new models answered a survey. Support ran high under both systems. Views on how well people communicated, coordinated, and reached resources were more consistently positive under the shared model. Views on preparedness, efficiency, and teaching value were mixed. The authors read the results as early support for starting with collaboration, and call for larger studies with stronger measures.
pmc-13576109:
Tian Chao, Wang WenHui, and Zhao JinTao model land use and carbon flows for the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region in a 2026 study. Land serves production, living, and ecological roles, each with its own carbon emissions and uptake. The region faces heavy emission pressure from fast urban growth.

From 2000 to 2020 total emissions rose sharply, with a pattern of high values in the southeast and low in the northwest. Carbon uptake by land weakened overall, strongest in the northwest. The team then built a 2035 planning scenario using optimisation tools. Their plan beat the original land plan on economic benefit, reduction efficiency, compactness, and access, while cutting projected emissions by 19.04 percent. Prediction accuracy reached 82.24 percent. The authors offer the framework for regional carbon policy.
pmc-13576309:
Elif Seren Tanrıverdi and three colleagues hunt for hidden microbes in patients whose urine shows white cells yet grows nothing in culture, a pattern called sterile pyuria, in a 2026 study. Standard culture misses organisms that grow poorly in the lab. The team ran a DNA test for 14 candidate pathogens on samples from two university hospitals.

Urine came from 201 patients with the pattern and 180 controls without it. The DNA test found at least one candidate organism in 50.2 percent of patients against 10 percent of controls. Ureaplasma urealyticum led the list, ahead of Mycoplasma hominis and Gardnerella vaginalis, mostly in adult women. Higher white cell counts linked strongly to positive tests and to doctors starting treatment. The authors say these organisms deserve clinical attention, judged case by case.
pmc-13576509:
Agathe Chabassier and colleagues report a real-world study, published in 2026. It uses data from connected scales and blood pressure cuffs. It measures what changes after people start GLP-1 weight-loss drugs. Users were matched to similar non-users. Causal inference methods did the matching. Body composition was followed in about two thousand adults. Blood pressure was followed in a smaller group.

Starting a GLP-1 drug was associated with weight loss. The median loss was just under ten percent over the following year. Most of the loss was fat. Muscle loss was much smaller. Small drops in blood pressure were sustained. The starting ratio of muscle to fat best predicted the quality of weight loss. Lower-ratio users lost more fat while sparing muscle.
pmc-13577509:
Lucas Murrins Marques wrote this essay, published in 2026. It argues that the way societies measure resilience to climate change leaves out how people actually feel as their home environment changes around them.

Most resilience scores track roads, buildings, budgets, and institutions. Marques says they should also track shared emotional states that grow out of long contact with a changing place. Two states get the focus: solastalgia, the distress of watching a loved home degrade, and soliphilia, a caring drive to protect that place. The essay proposes using these states as gauges, as factors that shape outcomes, and as early warning signs inside current resilience frameworks. Feelings, the author argues, help decide whether adaptation efforts last.
pmc-13578209:
Yujiao Wang and co-authors report a 2026 field study on how height above sea level and nitrogen feed shape wheat yield and grain quality. Six winter wheat types, classed as strong, medium, or weak in gluten, grew for two seasons at three sites in China. The sites ranged from near sea level to Lhasa, high on the Tibetan plateau.

High ground cut mean yield sharply compared with Beijing, mainly through fewer spikes and lighter grains. Grain protein rose at Lhasa, yet bread-making quality did not improve, and strong gluten types lost dough strength there. Weak gluten wheat held up best. Nitrogen needs split by gluten type, so the authors advise matching both the seed choice and the feed rate to the site height.
pmc-13578309:
Berglund and co-authors map how gene activity in fruit fly clock neurons shifts across the day and with light. The adult fly brain holds 240 clock neurons in more than 25 subtypes. Past single-cell work hinted at a similar count of molecular types. Three new methods now test and extend those claims. One tags nuclei from several time points in a single run, cutting lab noise.

A nucleus method let the team sequence many cells from frozen heads. Sampling hit 12 time points under both day-night cycles and constant dark. The data show strong daily swings in gene activity by cell type. Light adds its own layer on top of the clock's rhythm.
pmc-13578509:
Christina K Cramer and colleagues ran a single-arm pilot trial testing ramipril, a blood-pressure drug, to protect thinking during chemoradiation for glioblastoma. Seventy-five patients took ramipril through chemoradiation and for four weeks afterward, with cognitive testing compared against the earlier NRG/RTOG 0825 trial. Retention at one month after radiotherapy reached only 48 percent under the trial's strict definition.

Cognitive scores at one month barely moved, with a median change of 0.01 against 0.10 in the historical group, a difference that was not statistically significant. The drug therefore missed its feasibility goal and showed no clear cognitive benefit here. The authors expect future protective trials to test other agents, especially in patients likely to stay on treatment longer.
pmc-13579909:
Brenda J Tittlemier and colleagues interview Canadians who do rehabilitation research side by side with the people who use its results, in a 2026 study. Partnered research brings clinicians, managers, and clients into study decisions, with hopes of making findings stick in practice. Talks were held with seven researchers alongside six knowledge users, most of them women, about how they judge such teamwork.

None had run a formal check on their partnership, citing time above all, though most saw value in one. Partners still named wide effects: studies shaped from the first question to the final share out, plus personal growth in skills and confidence. Many forces drove those effects, from trust to meeting habits. The authors warn that skipping evaluation leaves the field guessing about what partnering truly buys.
pmc-13581809:
Zhang studies how digital detox trips restore attention and well being in twenty twenty-six. Such trips ask travelers to log off and stay in nature rich places. Five hundred people took part in a two group design with three waves of surveys. Statistical weights evened out gaps from self selection into the detox group.

Detox time raised how restful the setting felt. That feeling lifted attention and life satisfaction, in part through a mindful state. Cheerfulness, though, depended almost wholly on mindfulness. How hard people logged off linked to restful ratings across all, but not within the detox group alone. The study splits the paths to calm thought and to good mood.
pmc-13582609:
Xining Li, Mingjie Bian, and Jing Li build a two drug nanoparticle against liver cancer in this 2026 paper. Doxorubicin kills tumor cells but poisons the body. Baicalin, a plant compound, attacks the same cancer yet dissolves poorly. Their carrier is a seaweed based polymer that answers to acid and to a common cell chemical.

The particles carry both drugs and release them inside tumor like conditions. Liver cancer cells took them up and died at higher rates. Death ran partly through ferroptosis, an iron driven cell death route. Marker tests tied that route to a known signaling axis. Mouse studies checked drug levels, tumor shrinkage, and safety together. Dual response targeting aims to raise dose where it helps and cut it where it harms.
pmc-13583209:
Fatima Alnaimat and colleagues offer the first portrait of systemic sclerosis in Jordan in this 2026 study. Systemic sclerosis is a rare autoimmune disease that hardens skin and can damage inner organs. Fifty-seven patients from a single clinic at Jordan University Hospital in Amman took part, answering questions on symptoms, mood, hand use, and daily quality of life.

Most patients were women, and just over half had the limited form of the disease. A color change in cold fingers, called Raynaud's phenomenon, appeared in 49 patients, and nearly half had finger ulcers. Lung scarring and high pressure in the lung arteries were each found in a large share. Scores for body and mind were equally lowered in both disease forms, which points to a heavy daily burden.
pmc-13583509:
Ramaswamy and co-authors set out a plan for a trial of drugs for badly fed children, in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. About 17 million children are far too thin for their health, most of them in South Asia. Field teams now hand out germ-killing drugs as a rule, on the guess of a hidden illness.

Yet checks find few such ills, and wide use breeds germs that no longer heed these drugs. The plan first counts how many children aged six to fifty-nine months have an illness, and which drugs still work. It also asks how parents and care staff seek and use these drugs. A trial then splits children by lot: seven days of amoxicillin, one dose of azithromycin, or no such drug. Weight gain and bounce back are the main things tracked. Results should shape how field teams treat these children.
pmc-13585809:
Diogo Santos and Anderson da Silva summarize a Cochrane review of amyloid-clearing antibodies in early Alzheimer disease, and then grade its meaning for clinicians, in this appraisal from twenty twenty-six. Seven antibodies have been trialled; only two won traditional approval. The review pooled all seven as one class across seventeen trials and twenty thousand participants.

The pooled effects were small: a whisper of cognitive benefit at eighteen months, against a tenfold rise in brain swelling side effects, about one hundred nineteen cases per thousand treated versus twelve. The authors' sharpest point is structural: four of the seven drugs cleared little or no plaque, so the class average cannot answer whether clearing plaque helps. The two approved drugs beat the average yet stayed below what counts as clinically important change. Counsel patients drug by drug, they advise, not by class.
pmc-13587509:
Shubham Pandey and colleagues explore the microbes of India's solar salterns, shallow ponds where seawater dries into salt. Such ponds are stable yet extreme, and their salt-loving microbes hold enzymes and compounds of industrial interest. Their 2026 study paired old-style culture growing with whole-community gene reading at four salterns spread across the country, tracking how salt, acidity, and conductivity sorted the life present.

At the saltiest sites, archaea, an ancient branch of microbes, took over, while milder sites held a more even mix with bacteria. The team also grew 42 hardy isolates in the lab. Gene reads brimmed with tools for ion pumping, sun-proofing, and DNA repair, plus clusters that could make new germ-killing compounds. Resistance genes stayed rare and patchy. The authors frame salt itself as the master filter shaping these communities.
pmc-13588209:
Sakoon Saggu and colleagues report a movement pattern never before tied to a slow measles brain disease. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, is a fatal brain inflammation that can surface years after measles, bringing mental decline and rhythmic jerks. Their case concerns a 14-year-old boy who had measles at age seven and came in with a year of falls and trouble standing.

On standing, his legs shook and his knees buckled without warning as the thigh muscles briefly lost their tone, a pattern classed as orthostatic hyperkinetic disorder with negative myoclonus. Sitting, lying, and walking freed him of the shaking, though the buckling could interrupt his steps and caused his falls. Scans showed frontal brain lesions, and his disease sat at an early-middle stage. The authors say this standing-linked pattern widens the known face of the disease.
pmc-13590709:
Su-Ting Chen and Fu-Ming Xu follow Chinese teens across four waves to untangle whether boredom proneness and problem social media use drive each other, in work from twenty twenty-six. Boredom proneness is a steady personal trait, while heavy use swings with circumstance. Between person and within person links needed separating.

Over two thousand students aged twelve to nineteen in Guangzhou answered from twenty twenty to twenty twenty-two. A panel model split stable traits from personal ups and downs. The stable parts of boredom and heavy use moved together. Inside a person, heavy use reliably preceded later boredom proneness at every step. Boredom predicted later use only once. The authors caution that pandemic era data needs a fresh replication.
pmc-13591809:
Zahra Bagheri-Hosseinabadi and four colleagues check, in 2026, how often metabolic syndrome appears in people with lupus, an autoimmune disease where the body attacks its own tissues. The syndrome bundles belly fat, high blood pressure, and poor sugar and fat control. Their clinic group held 200 lupus patients, classed by standard rules for both conditions.

Just over a quarter of the lupus patients also met the bar for metabolic syndrome. Their disease activity scores, though, were no worse than those of lupus patients without the syndrome. One inflammation marker ran higher in the combined group. Weight, waist size, blood sugar, and most blood fats all ran worse there too. The team says heart and metabolic screening deserves a firm place in lupus care.
pmc-13591909:
Rui Wang and three colleagues link, in 2026, a simple blood ratio to low muscle mass in people with type 2 diabetes. The ratio sets C-reactive protein, a sign of inflammation, against albumin, a sign of nutrition. Their study held 1,009 patients whose muscle was measured by X-ray scanning. Low muscle mass was classed by Asian working group rules.

One in five men and about one in seven women had low muscle mass. In men, a higher ratio paired with higher odds of low mass, and the link held after age, fats, blood pressure, and body size were weighed. In women no such link appeared. Wang and the team suggest the cheap ratio may flag men who need muscle checks.
pmc-13592209:
Joseph Carver and three colleagues teach a computer to design silver nanoparticle recipes backward from a wanted size. Particle size rules how silver specks perform in sensors, catalysts, and medicine, yet cooks still find recipes by trial and error. Their team pooled lab data from batch pots and flow reactors, then trained five prediction models. A Gaussian process model won, calling sizes with high accuracy.

Working backward, the system proposed recipes for target sizes from 20 to 70 nanometers, ranked by expected error, spread, and doubt. Fresh lab runs landed within a few percent of target in batch pots and close behind in flow rigs. Carver and the team call the validated loop a shortcut past blind recipe hunting.
pmc-13592409:
Min Su Kang and six colleagues tune, in 2026, a selector switch for dense phase change memory arrays. In crosspoint grids, stray current leaks through unchosen cells, so each cell needs a guard that opens only past a threshold voltage. Their guard uses a germanium tellurium sulfur glass mixed by sputtering, then dosed with nitrogen. The gas ties up weak bonds, trims traps, and evens the switching voltage.

The doped device endured around ten billion cycles, switched in under twenty nanoseconds, and leaked very little current while off. It also withstood heat far above working needs. Paired with a memory cell, it blocked current cleanly under voltage control. Kang and the team pitch the balance of speed, endurance, and low threshold for packed memory grids.
pmc-13594509:
Tingting Ni and colleagues extended a valve trial follow-up in 2026. The trial compared two anesthesia drugs during a heart valve procedure. The procedure threads a new aortic valve in through the leg. Patients under general anesthesia risk unstable blood pressure. An earlier trial found steadier pressure with the newer drug. Whether that steadiness improves later outcomes was unknown. The team rechecked patients at thirty days and one year. The main outcome mixed death, stroke, kidney injury, and heart events.

At one year, the combined outcome favored the newer drug numerically. The gap did not reach firm statistical proof. One part did differ clearly. New irregular heart rhythm arose less often with the newer drug. Earlier time points showed the same mild pattern. The authors label all these checks exploratory. Small numbers and many comparisons limit certainty. Findings apply only to general anesthesia cases, they stress.
pmc-13599709:

These groups may face barriers to services such as contraception advice and testing. Digital care is expanding as an alternative. Autistic females who did enter care used it as intensively as peers, suggesting the barrier is getting through the door. Gaps were smaller for digital care, hinting it may ease access.
pmc-13599809:
Kurniawan and co-authors report radiation used to stop life-threatening vaginal bleeding in trophoblastic disease. The patient was a 47-year-old woman after a partial mole removal. No hormone follow-up was done after that removal. She arrived weeks later with massive bleeding and shock. Her hemoglobin had fallen to 5.7 grams per deciliter.

Emergency surgery removed the uterus the same day. Tissue review showed an invasive mole in the muscle wall. Bleeding returned from a suspected vaginal spread lesion. Lung spread placed her at FIGO stage III. Radiation at 20 gray in five doses stopped the bleeding.
pmc-13603209:
Zhang leads a large team studying heat stress in cow ovarian cells, in work from twenty twenty-six. Heat stress is a critical factor that lowers reproductive performance in dairy cattle. Granulosa cells nourish the egg and make hormones, and they are especially vulnerable to heat.

Acute heat reshaped the inner structure of mitochondria, the cell power plants, in these cells. Gene activity landscapes shifted over time in tracked waves. Early molecular and subcellular events before overt damage were the focus. Knowing the earliest changes could guide cooling or breeding strategies that protect fertility as summers warm.
pmc-13603309:
Wanli Li and colleagues characterized two chicken enzymes in two thousand twenty-six that control how chickens break down tryptophan, an amino acid tied to immunity. Chickens are unusual: they lack the main enzyme other vertebrates use and rely on these two instead. Diet trials, gene profiling, and lab-made enzymes filled the knowledge gap.

Extra dietary tryptophan kept blood levels steady while switching on liver breakdown pathways and shifting fat and energy balance. Liver enzyme activity rose sharply with little change in gene or protein amounts, pointing to control after production. The enzymes worked best at chicken body conditions. Poultry scientists gain basics for feed design.
pmc-13604209:
Tariq Tayebi, Monique David, and Mourad Tayebi published a mini-review in two thousand twenty-six on machine learning for Alzheimer's biomarkers. Diagnosis research now blends molecules, scans, and body signals. Artificial intelligence is shifting the search from single markers to networks.

The review covers the current diagnostic frameworks and the newest antibody treatments. It then surveys studies applying learning methods to spinal fluid and blood proteins, light-based tissue readings, brain scans, gene activity, and gut microbe signatures. Combined platforms improved early detection and forecast marker paths in the cited work. The authors stress clear, interpretable models. They close with standing problems: outside validation, bias, and regulation.
pmc-13604509:
Sinem Nur Altun and Hurriyet Cetinok used a fast automated tool to measure brain parts in scans from seven hundred ninety-one people across the Alzheimer's disease range. The group held healthy adults, people with mild memory loss, and people with the disease. They measured memory-linked regions and the fluid spaces of the brain.

Memory regions were smaller and fluid spaces larger in the disease group, with the mild group in between. Memory test scores tracked these measures closely. Computer models sorted the three groups fairly well, but most of their power came from the memory test score itself. Without it, sorting dropped a lot. The authors weigh what scans alone can add.
pmc-13606009:
Philipp Heumann and five co-authors published a 2026 review of cutaneous T cell lymphoma, a group of cancers where rogue T cells home to the skin. Its two main forms behave very differently. Mycosis fungoides often grows slowly for years, while Sézary syndrome spreads through the blood and is far more aggressive.

The review argues that these cancer cells survive through a connected network rather than one weak point. The network includes constant inflammatory signalling, resistance to cell death, altered energy use, and changes in gene control. Each strand is a possible drug target, and combining targets may work better than single drugs. The authors urge matching treatment to both the disease stage and the tumour’s molecular profile.
pmc-13607009:
Iga Horodyska and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-six review asking whether liquid biopsy is the future of veterinary medicine. Liquid biopsy finds tumour DNA and cells in blood instead of cutting tissue. It can reveal cancer type, spread, and treatment response.

The review surveys methods from sensitive DNA tests to sequencing and vesicle analysis. Multi-cancer blood tests that screen for many cancers at once are also covered. Most evidence comes from human medicine, now moving toward animals. Veterinary readers get a map of tools that could make cancer checks in pets and livestock gentler and earlier.
pmc-13607909:
Nikmaram and Mostofi report a case series on a back pain operation in twenty twenty-six. The pain comes from worn facet joints in the lower spine. Standard nerve burning treatments often give only brief relief. Direct surgery on the joint surface itself has rarely been reported.

The series covers thirty-two patients treated from twenty twenty-two to twenty twenty-five. All had chronic axial back pain and a good response to a test injection. Surgery shaved the joint surface and removed bone spurs, without fusion. Pain scores fell from a high level at baseline to a moderate level by one month. Disability scores also improved and held through nine months. No complications occurred during or after surgery.
pmc-13608209:
Chulmin Kim and Seongjin Ahn build an AI moral advisor with many agents. Their work from twenty twenty-six rests on a model of thought and reflection. Full self run machine ethics is not real yet, they note.

Their design splits a long step chain among four agent roles. Help models search for rules, make counter points, and score each side. That makes deep thought steps clear and shared with the user. Tests compared one agent, many agents, and mixed forms. The aim is to aid human choice, not take its place.
pmc-13608609:
María García Forestier, José Nassar Badillo, and Armando Oliver overview eye care in Sjögren's disease in a 2026 paper. The disease dries the eye surface badly, and in the worst cases the cornea can ulcerate, melt, and perforate. New guidelines and treatments have changed care, and their narrative review gathers updates from a decade of literature across diagnosis and therapy.

Diagnosis is moving toward non-invasive tests on saliva, tears, and glands. Large contact lenses that hold fluid against the cornea help protect it. New drugs aim to restart tear production and calm the surface rather than just wetting it, and device treatments for the eyelid glands are joining the toolkit.
pmc-13608809:
Maria Rogalidou and Christina Kanaka-Gantenbein review metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease in children, now childhood's most common chronic liver disease. Its rise tracks global rises in child obesity and metabolic dysfunction. Once seen as benign, it is now seen as varied and progressive, from fat build-up to inflammation, fibrosis, and, rarely, cirrhosis, with lifelong effects.

The causes are many at once: insulin resistance, fat tissue dysfunction, and chronic low-grade inflammation. Most have no symptoms, so the call often comes from high liver enzymes or a scan for other reasons. Non-cut tools, from ultrasound and elastography to blood markers and new multi-omics, keep getting better at finding the disease and sorting risk, though biopsy stays the reference test in set cases. Changes in daily life stay the core of care.
pmc-13609509:
Wangxin Li and five colleagues build a generative system to fake microbial colony photos for training detection software. Deep learning can count colonies on Petri dishes, but it needs many labeled images, and real colony photos take time to produce. Their Double Deep Convolutional GAN creates synthetic colonies in two moves, overlapping small single colonies into composites and generating complete plates. It then tunes how many synthetic images to add using several quality metrics at once.

Starting from 236 real samples, the optimized recipe added 1,320 synthetic images. The realism score improved from 38.9 to 37.1, lower being better, and downstream detectors validated the approach: colony detection accuracy reached 0.975. The authors present the composite adversarial design as a practical answer to data scarcity in microbiology imaging. Labs could expand small photo collections into training sets for automated colony analysis, cutting manual counting in medical and food-safety testing.
pmc-13611809:
Manabu Mogitate links bumpy changes seen at the back of the nose to allergy sensitization, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The granular look under a scope is a hallmark of long-term inflammation there, but its meaning was unclear. He reviewed records of fifty-nine patients with the condition.

Patients with the granular changes carried higher antibody levels against mites and house dust than those without. Other markers told a different story: nose and blood allergy cell counts, total antibody levels, and an immune cell ratio showed no link to the changes. Scores also failed to track any marker directly. Mogitate reads the granular look as a sign of mite and dust sensitization rather than active allergy inflammation.
pmc-13611909:
Eniya and a large team show SARS-CoV-2 exposure elicits strong mucosal antibodies that may speed viral clearance, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The virus enters via mouth and airway mucosa, where secreted antibodies act first. Blood and oral fluid from one hundred seventy-three participants are sampled repeatedly. Spike antibodies and viral RNA are tracked over ninety days.

Viral RNA turns negative by day fourteen in most subjects. Oral and serum antibodies rise by day fourteen, then fall by day ninety. Higher oral antibodies correlate with faster decline in viral burden. Trends differ between major and minor COVID waves in India. Avidity of oral antibodies declines by day ninety as well.
pmc-13612609: Karel Allegaert and five colleagues issued this correction to their Pediatric Nephrology study of kidney function in cooled, birth-asphyxiated newborns. The notice is a correction only. Formulas in the original article were printed wrong in three places, the abstract, page 3, and the graphical abstract, missing a time term. The notice supplies fixed formulas so readers compute the estimated glomerular filtration rate across the first ten days of life. No data, results, or conclusions change.
pmc-13612809:
Boers and colleagues published a 2026 review on calcium given around childbirth to cut bleeding. Heavy bleeding after birth is a top cause of mother deaths worldwide. Calcium helps the womb muscle grip and keep contracting after delivery. The team pooled studies testing calcium given around the time of birth.

Pooled results linked calcium with less blood loss after delivery overall. Mothers given calcium also needed fewer extra womb-tightening drugs afterward. The womb's failure to contract drives most heavy bleeding cases after birth. Standard first drugs sometimes fail or cannot be used safely for all. Calcium may serve as a cheap helper beside them, they conclude. More trials must firm up dose and timing before routine use.
pmc-13613009:
Kokturk Dalcali and co-authors use metaphors to learn how intensive care nurses view death. ICU nurses meet death often in their work, and those encounters stir mixed feelings and thoughts. How nurses see death can shape care choices and the quality of end-of-life care they give.

Past studies covered nurses' experiences, but few used metaphor as the lens. The qualitative study asked nurses to express death through metaphors and sorted the replies for shared themes. Comparing images, such as journeys or battles, reveals hidden attitudes. The findings may guide support and training for ICU staff.
pmc-13615109:
Takuro Ariga and colleagues compare in 2026 the cost-effectiveness of chemoradiotherapy against surgery for stage I cancer of the oesophagus in Japan, the earliest stage of the disease. Their model combined survival figures from a Japanese trial with quality-of-life scores mapped from standard cancer questionnaires, counting only direct medical costs from the public health system's view. Future costs and life years were discounted at 2 percent per year.

The drug and radiation route cost about 26,313 United States dollars more than surgery, while adding 0.630 quality-adjusted life years, giving a ratio near 41,742 dollars per such year. Checks on the model's weak points showed which inputs moved the answer most. For a health system weighing two good treatments, the study prices the gentler, organ-keeping option in terms officials can judge.
pmc-13616909:
Rodney Alan Long and a large multi-institution team report a 2026 approach that uses large language models to speed up biomedical data standardization. Research groups describe their variables in incompatible ways, which blocks pooling of studies. Their system drafts common data elements, the shared definitions that let datasets line up, for clinical and research dictionaries.

The team processed thirty-one datasets through a GPT-4 based pipeline and had experts check the output. Most generated fields needed no revision, and accuracy was highest on well-structured sources. Tests on Alzheimer and Parkinson datasets mapped about a third of unseen variable names onto existing elements automatically. The authors argue that automating this tedious groundwork lowers barriers to collaboration across studies.
pmc-13617609:
Viquez-R and co-authors audit lab infection studies of bats and viruses for bias. Interest in bat-virus links is high, yet experiments use a narrow set of bat species and places. That narrowness limits what can be inferred about bat immunity and spillover risk to people.

The team searched the literature from 1900 to January 2025 and hand-checked peer-reviewed studies. Only work infecting live bats or bat-derived material in labs was kept. They mapped which bat species, viruses, and regions appear, and which are missing. The audit shows where future studies should widen their scope.
pmc-13618809:

Their patient, a woman with a permanent pacemaker, had persistent fever, pleuritic pain, and a productive cough and was being treated for right-sided pneumonia. Blood cultures stayed negative, but a markedly raised NT-proBNP, a heart strain marker drawn because of breathlessness and fluid on her chest film, pushed the team to scan her heart.

Ultrasound revealed a large, irregular, independently mobile mass clinging to the pacemaker lead inside the right atrium and flopping across the tricuspid valve with each cycle. A probe passed down the esophagus confirmed it. That picture, in context, meant infection of the device itself, and she was referred to a specialist center for complete extraction. The authors highlight culture-negative endocarditis as a diagnostic trap and echocardiography as the decisive tool.
pmc-13618909:
Sayida Al-Jamei and eight colleagues measure medication burden and quality of life in Yemeni cancer patients on chemotherapy. Their cross-sectional study ran at the National Oncology Centre in Sana'a from December 2025 to February 2026. Two hundred thirty-four adults were interviewed and their records reviewed. Polypharmacy meant five or more non-cancer medications, a common situation because chemotherapy demands many supportive drugs.

The burden was near-universal: about ninety-five percent met the polypharmacy threshold and over half took ten or more non-cancer medicines. Average global quality of life sat below fifty on a hundred-point scale, with financial difficulty the worst-scoring problem, ahead of fatigue and pain. Surprisingly, heavier medication burden did not independently predict worse quality of life. Being female did, predicting both lower quality of life and higher medication use, while older age and illiteracy showed borderline links to poorer scores.
pmc-13619909:
Jingyi Wu, Junfeng Huo, Xindan Wang, Juan Wei, and Gaiyan Du published a pharmacovigilance study in twenty twenty-six on whether hearing problems after vaccination were a real signal or a reporting mirage. The team mined the national adverse event system from twenty eighteen through twenty twenty-five, over one point three million reports, of which about twenty-eight thousand mentioned auditory events.

Interrupted time series showed reporting rates jumping right after the COVID vaccine authorization. Crucially, skin events served as a negative control for pure reporting enthusiasm, and comparisons across vaccine types tested specificity. Count models confirmed the level shift. pmc-13620009:

The team compiled registrations from national databases and drew market estimates from farmer surveys across two crop seasons, the later one covering more than sixteen thousand interviews.

By December 2025, Brazil had 297 Bacillus-based products built on 126 strains, led by four main species. Farmers apply them by seed treatment, soil drench, furrow, or leaf spray against fungal, bacterial, and nematode diseases. Treated area grew nearly fivefold between the two surveys, and sales value more than tripled, giving these products roughly half the national biocontrol market. The authors credit microbial science, regulation, and farmer trust for the climb.
pmc-13621409:

Testing showed clean straight-line responses across wide ranges for all three targets, with good selectivity against common interfering substances. Glucose readings in real human serum samples worked, proving the method outside pure lab water. To free the test from bench instruments, the team added smartphone photo analysis of the color and a small electronics board for data capture. Green chemistry scorecards rated the approach kindly. The authors present it as a template for bedside and field testing built on cheap, water-made materials.
pmc-13621609:

Both stories trace clinical harm back to ordinary office interactions rather than the dentistry itself.

The authors pair the cases with a literature review of barriers: higher substance use, postponed visits, scarce culturally competent providers, and bisexual adults facing especially poor outcomes. Simple practices made the difference in their telling: correct pronouns, chosen names, and communication that signals safety. They press for provider training, nondiscrimination policies, and clinic structures that earn trust before treatment starts. Affirming care, they argue, is not decoration; it changes whether patients return and whether treatment succeeds.
pmc-13623409:

The recurrence sat in the pyriform sinus, a groove beside the voice box, touching the rebuilt food passage. Surgeons removed the larynx and throat and rebuilt the missing circle of tissue with a flap of thigh tissue carrying its own blood vessels, sewn to the stomach conduit. Scarred, irradiated tissue and poor blood supply made failure likely. Even so, healing held and she returned to oral intake. The authors present the case as proof that careful salvage reconstruction can restore eating in medically complex patients, and she remained free of disease.
pmc-13623509:

Onset before age twenty counts as juvenile, and those patients carry far longer repeats.

These include gene expression errors and faulty message splicing in striatal neurons, disturbed building of synapses, the behaviour of protein clumps, and the failing of the cell's protein clean-up systems. Ongoing brain development is the thread tying the differences together, since the young brain is still wiring itself when the disease strikes. Symptoms differ too, with stiffness and slowness dominating in the young rather than the jerky movements of adults. The authors argue for diagnoses and treatments designed for juveniles specifically.
pmc-13624009:

Forty-nine camera sites logged more than four thousand sexed detections across three seasons: the rut, the period after it, and the birthing season. As a herd, the deer favoured twilight and night, above all in and after the rut. Splitting by sex changed the story. Females stayed strongly nocturnal, especially after the rut, while males added twilight and daytime activity in spring, driving the herd's daytime rise. Overlap between the sexes peaked during the rut, then shrank. The authors urge managers to read activity by sex and season.
pmc-13624709:

Swapping the inner, nonstructural parts back to the parent form restored parent-like plaques and strength, which marks that segment as a main weakening factor. Changing only shell parts also shifted behavior, so softness seems to come from mutation mixes rather than single changes. Such maps help vaccine makers tune live dengue vaccines with more care.
pmc-13625809:

In a crossover study, thirty-six healthy volunteers received rising doses while awake and again under general anesthesia, giving 417 paired blood readings.

More norepinephrine in the blood went with clearly higher melatonin, and levels ran higher while awake than under anesthesia. That state did not break the link between the two chemicals, and people who started with more melatonin responded the most. The finding matters for intensive care, where round-the-clock drips may quietly shift patients' body clocks.
pmc-13626309:

In a double-blind crossover trial, twenty-nine people endured a standard laboratory stress test. Then they either used the device or rested quietly, swapping on another visit. Stress, sleepiness, mood, heart rhythm, and brain waves were tracked throughout.

Subjective stress fell by nearly a third after the device session, sleepiness eased, and positive mood rose, all compared with plain rest. Body measures such as heart rate variability did not budge, and negative mood stayed put. The authors pitch the pairing for workplaces, while calling for tests that split the two parts and follow workers longer.
pmc-13628809:
Marco Moroldo and colleagues characterised two sunflower lines differing in a leaf-ageing gene region. Their study compared near-identical sunflower lines with contrasting LES10.179 variants under drought and cover-crop residues, profiling genes, chemistry, and physiology.

Drought broadly cut secondary metabolites and engaged minor antioxidant compounds. The gene region likely acts through a chlorophyll-breakdown gene cousin, NYC1, and its early-ageing variant cut seed protein while the other raised it. Cover crops barely mattered, with no drought-gene interaction. Moroldo and colleagues pitch the region as a breeding target for protein and nitrogen efficiency.
pmc-13630209:
Lorenzo D. Stafford and four colleagues ran a preliminary study of whether presenting food differently can restore some eating pleasure for people with smell and taste disorders. The ratings showed no clear effect of any presentation change, a null result the authors report plainly. Interviews told a richer story: since losing smell, participants most often reached for stronger textures and extra herbs and spices to make food interesting again. The mismatch between numbers and testimony leads the authors to call for more carefully designed studies rather than claiming the idea dead.
pmc-13630409:
Shuqi Wang and colleagues built a silicon battery anode coated and bound in one carbon-baking step, aiming to tame silicon's swelling problem. Silicon can hold far more charge than graphite, but micro-sized silicon swells by about 300 percent as it charges, cracking electrodes apart.

The process left a uniform carbon skin on the particles and through the whole electrode, with no added glue or conductive filler. First-cycle efficiency reached about 87 percent, a strong start for silicon anodes. After 400 cycles the electrode still held 84 percent of its capacity, and a graphite blend kept 91 percent after 500 cycles. A full pouch cell matched with a standard cathode also worked, supporting real-world use.
pmc-13630809:

Published in 2026, the account explains how Europe lagged North America and Australia in coordinated tracking infrastructure until the network formed as a grassroots effort in 2017.

It has since grown into a durable system with a central database, shared dashboards, and partners deploying receivers nationally while feeding one platform built on open data principles. The network supports cross-border studies of movement, habitat links, and behaviour, while wrestling with familiar strains: patchy funding, incompatible gear, false detections, and ownership questions. The authors position it within a coming global aquatic observatory.
pmc-13632009:
Sol Hooy Oh and five colleagues published this 2026 cohort study linking heart health scores to later emergencies in Korea. Earlier work tied the score to death rates, mostly in Western and Chinese groups. The Korean team asked whether it also predicts first major cardiovascular events in their own population.

They linked national health survey records from 2014 through 2018 with insurance claims that track hospital events over time. After removing people with prior heart attacks or strokes and those missing score parts, they kept just over twenty-one thousand adults for analysis. Korean eating patterns and body shapes differ from Western ones, so a local test matters. The study design lets readers judge how well a United States score travels to East Asia.
pmc-13633209:
Fan and coauthors review bile acid signals in health and illness. Bile acids were long seen as just soap-like aids for digestion. They are now known as broad signals across the body. They act through cell switches in the nucleus and cell skin.

Each switch starts its own chain of gene or cell effects. Gut germs reshape bile acids as they cycle through the bowel. That reshaping changes which switches each acid can trigger. The review maps acid forms, gut cycling, and switch paths. It also sums up roles in liver, gut, and metabolic illness.
pmc-13633309:
Whether teenagers who feel more vulnerable to disease actually keep their distance from classmates is tested by Fedurek and Danel. Most of it rests on short experiments rather than everyday contact. Sensor data counted classmates coming within two metres, giving a real-world picture of face-to-face contact. Higher perceived vulnerability did not predict fewer proximity contacts, which fails to support claims from earlier studies that disease wariness shrinks social interaction. pmc-13634409:

pmc-13635209:

Each taxon's label was rebuilt from scratch through a standard checking workflow that leaned on authoritative databases and the scientific literature. Every verification step and evidence source is recorded inside the dataset itself. That transparency lets later users reproduce why each species earned its label. The author offers the collection as a shared reference for calibrating screening tools and comparing how they perform across regions, strengthening the preventive side of biosecurity.
pmc-13635609:

The guide walks through each part of the setup: slide scanners, image management software, workstations, storage, and links to laboratory information systems. It stresses testing with a lab's real workload rather than vendor demos, checking that systems talk to each other, and planning for growth. The authors aim the advice at pathologists, IT teams, and managers matching a system to local needs.
pmc-13642909:
